Preface
Cranial artificial deformation has accompanied the human race for
thousands of years. The history of the surgical correction of congenital
or acquired cranial deformities is considerably shorter, extending for
little more than a century. Though commonly associated with the
Andean civilisation, the practice of artificial cranial deformation may be
encountered in the history of various populations in all continents. The
aim of such practice has been extensively discussed by historians and
anthropologists. For what concerns the Andean people, the common
belief is that the artificial alteration of the cranial shape was utilised to
distinguish ethnic differences among groups and in the same group to
individuate castes, social classes and professions. The main goal of the
surgical correction of craniosynostosis is just the opposite: to
‘normalise’ the altered cranial shape and prevent the affected subjects
from suffering from the social stigma brought about by the physical
deformity. We don’t know much about the possible cognitive defects
that the artificially restricted growth of the skull could have generated,
but we are aware of the possible cerebral damage following an
abnormally increased intracranial pressure, due to a decreased cranial
volume, or distorted vectors of cerebral growth. The correction of such
possible causes of cerebral damage is the main aim of the surgical
management besides the normalisation of the head shape and the
prevention of possible secondary morphologic and functional
anomalies and justifies the current attention to provide the appropriate
surgical correction carried out already in the first few months of life.
To operate a newborn requires several conditions to be met. First of
all, the knowledge of the disease on the part of the family physician and
the family itself. Then, the contribution of the paediatrician and the
radiologist for a timely recognition. The neurosurgeon has also a role in
the diagnosis, but they are called to have the necessary skills to operate
the infant or the young child, or to be able to provide the best cranial
reconstruction in case of delayed diagnosis.
Even though to a superficial analysis the surgical treatment of
craniosynostosis seems to have come back from complex
reconstruction with bone displacement and replacement which
characterised the operative procedures in the end of the last century to

the original linear craniectomies, a more thorough, deeper evaluation
shows the great advances made in the management of
craniosynostosis; advances made possible, as this book wants to
demonstrate, thanks to the newly introduced diagnostic tools,
refinements in anaesthesiological intraoperative care, extended and
appropriate postoperative follow-ups as well as the acquisition of
craniofacial surgical techniques.
Indeed, during recent years the knowledge of the pathophysiologic
mechanisms leading to the early fusion of cranial sutures has
substantially improved thanks to the genetic studies and the utilisation
of animal models.
While different surgical techniques have blossomed, the risks
associated with surgical and anaesthesiological manoeuvres have been
reduced. New surgical tools have been developed allowing less-invasive
procedures, especially in very young subjects. The long follow-up of a
large series of patients has allowed clinicians to better appreciate the
results and long-term outcomes and at the same time to recognize the
still existing limits of the surgical treatment in terms of late recurrences
or incomplete corrections leading to the necessity of redo-surgeries.
Also some functional difficulties in operating on patients which burden
the life of patients and their families have been identified and
addressed.
Nevertheless, in spite of these relevant progresses in the
understanding of craniosynostosis, most of the recent papers have been
focusing on aesthetical results of the surgical management rather than
the functional neurological issues. The neurosurgical aspects of the
conditions have been little by little put aside with the studies focusing
either on the length of the hospital stay and the costs of surgery or the
cosmetic outcomes.
Because managing a craniosynostosis is more than correcting a
cranial index, we wanted, with this book, to focus on the role of the
neurosurgeon, and in the same time to raise the interest of all the
specialists that form the team involved in the management of
craniosynostosis on neurosurgical issues with the ultimate goal of
enhancing its effectiveness for the best cure of our patients.
Federico Di Rocco
John Kestle

Lyon, France
Salt Lake City, UT, USA

1 1 Introduction
The beginning of the history of the surgical management of
craniosynostosis resembles a fairytale: Once upon a time a mother
noticed that her child’s head did not grow as expected and asked a doctor
to “unlock” its skull… This event happened in real life when the French
neurosurgeon accepted a mother’s request and performed the first
operation to release the skull of a child with sagittal craniosynostosis

by carrying out two linear strip craniectomies in the parietal bone
parallel to an early fused sagittal suture in 1890 [1] (Fig. 1.1).

Fig. 1.1 Prof Odilon Lannelongue, 1840–1911

The operation was successful and stimulated further surgical
attempts to manage craniosynostosis surgically. Two years later, in San
Francisco L C Lane responded again to a mother’s desire: Early in the
month of August, 1888, I received a letter from a lady residing in the
interior of California, stating that she desired to consult me concerning
her infant, then nearly 9 months of age, which presented signs of mental
imbecility. At the time appointed for the consultation, the lady presented
herself with her infant. The child, otherwise in good health and well
nourished, was decidedly microcephalic. The cranium was symmetrical,
and only deviated from normal type in the smallness of its volume. The
mother stated that at birth the anterior fontanelle was wholly closed, and
the posterior one nearly so. The mother was especially solicitous to learn
whether the child’s brain was otherwise healthy; and on being assured
that there was no evidence to the contrary, she asked if an operation were

not possible whereby the brain could enlarge [2]. Once more on a sagittal
craniosynostosis Lane performed an operation similar to that of
Lannelongue, that is strip parietal craniectomies, with, however, the
removal of the fused sagittal suture. Consequently, the surgical
management of craniosynostosis has been marked by technical
controversy since its beginning! It is worth noting how the title of
Lane’s report translated an unappropriated enthusiasm as his
operation was proposed “for relief of mental imbecility due to the
premature sutural closure and microcephalus”, thus likely contributing
to possible operations on microcephalic children. The wrong surgical
indication to treat microcephaly and the unsatisfactory surgical
outcomes, the lack of improvement in patients with true
craniosynostosis too old at the time of the operation with already
established neurological deficits, the high rate of morbidity and
mortality recorded in the pioneer operations arose deep doubts on the
surgical attempt of “unlocking” the brain utilizing linear craniectomies.

1 2 Non Nocere
Such doubts found their severe interpreter in the person of the founder
of modern American paediatrics Abraham Jacobi who blamed the
procedure at an American Academy of Pediatrics meeting held in Rome
in 1894 and in a paper entitled Non nocere [3] (Fig. 1.2).

Fig. 1.2 Abraham Jacobi, 1830–1919

On the grounds of the analysis of a series of 33 children who had
undergone linear craniectomies, 15 of them have died because of the
operation, he criticized these early attempts to release the skull with
vehement words: “The relative impunity of operative interference
accomplished by modern asepsis and antisepsis has developed an
undue tendency to, and rashness in, handling the knife. The hands take
too frequently the place of brains…Is it sufficient glory to don a white
apron and swing a carbonized knife, and is therein a sufficient
indication to let daylight into a deformed cranium and on top of the
hopelessly defective brain, and to proclaim a success because the victim
consented not to die of the assault? Such rash feats of indiscriminate
surgery…are stains on your hands and sins on your soul. No ocean of
soap and water will clean those hands, no power of corrosive sublimate
will disinfect the souls”. Even though an atlas describing the various

linear craniectomies was published in 1895 [4], the surgical treatment
of craniosynostosis was practically abandoned for nearly three decades
because of great Jacobi’s influence Also some eminent neurosurgeons,
like Cushing, contributed to the neurosurgeons’ disinterest of treating
craniosynostosis surgically at the beginning of the twntieth century,
though, however, he operated on craniosynostosis children later on [5].
The paper by Faber and Towne on five children who responded
favourably to the surgical “release” of the skull sutures when the
correction was done early in infancy re-established the due attention of
the effects of the premature fusion of the cranial sutures on the brain
development so contributing to the return of linear craniectomy in the
neurosurgical armamentarium [6].
The first surgical attempts to treat craniosynostosis by “releasing”
the skull were based on pathogenetic interpretations of the role of the
cranial sutures and the consequences of their early fusion on the
cranial growth already propounded at the beginning of the nineteenth
century when the German physician, anatomist, anthropologist and
inventor Samuel Thomas von Soemmering had published important
studies indicating the role of the cranial sutures in the active growth of
the skull and had pointed out the effect of their premature fusion on
skull growth and shape [7] (Fig. 1.3).

Fig. 1.3 Samuel Thomas Soemmering, 1755–1830

Another German scientist Rudolph Virchow is associated with the
surgical management of craniosynostosis because of the so-called law
or rule of Virchow which states that skull growth is arrested in the
direction perpendicular to a fused suture while expanding at the sites
of unaffected sutures, in a direction parallel to the fused suture leading
to characteristic skull deformations on which the various types of
craniosynostosis are still named (Fig. 1.4).

Fig. 1.4 Rudolph Virchow, 1821–1902

Craniosynostosis was considered by Virchow in a complex frame of
malformed skull shapes in a quite influential paper Über den
Cretinismus, namentlich in Franken, und über pathologische
Schädelformen [8]. It is quite interesting reading about the great debate
about the cause of mental retardation that took place in the second half
of the nineteenth century in the absence of a clear disease definition, as
described by Schlich in his paper Changing disease identities: cretinism,
politics and surgery (1844–1892) [9].
The reinstatement of linear craniectomies and suturectomies for
treating craniosynostosis and their diffusion in the 1930s and 1940s
were mainly based on the assumption that an early release of the
constricted skull, possibly carried out during the first 2 months of life,
could prevent secondary damage of the developing brain and also
decreasing the risk of re-ossification because of the expansive forces of

the growing brain. Indeed, re-ossification of the linear craniectomies
was observed to occur more frequently in older children. In the 50s,
several methods were suggested in the attempts to prevent this type of
failure from the mechanical obstacle created by enwrapping the cut
bone edges with tantalum foils [10] or polyethylene films [11] and to
the application of chemical agents, such as Zenker’s solution, on the
dura underlying the linear craniectomies to impair the osteoblastic
activity of the outer layer of the dura mater [12]. Failures to prevent reossification and infective complications related to the foreign material
led to the progressive abandonment of the attempts to block bone
formation at the borders of the craniectomies. Also, the use of Zenker’s
solution, a tissue fixative containing mercuric chloride, potassium
bichromate, sodium sulphate and glacial acetic acid, was suspended in
the late 1970s and early 1980s after clinical reports of postoperative
seizures in operated children and the experimental demonstration of
the immediate breakdown of the blood–brain barrier and inflammatory
response in the underlying brain with thickening of the arachnoid
membrane, associated with the procedure, likely being the cause of the
postoperative seizures [13–15].
In the second half of the twentieth century, linear craniectomies and
suturectomies were widely performed on the grounds of clinical
reports describing good results in large series of patients with low
morbidity and mortality rate such as, for example, that by Shillito and
Matson who recorded three deaths out of 519 operated on infants [16].
Linear craniectomies evolved in more complex surgical procedures
aimed at correcting some specific deformations of the head associated
with the craniosynostosis already at the time of the operation while
assuring a better prevention of the secondary re-ossification. Most of
the surgical variants concerned the management of sagittal synostosis
such as a major widening of suturectomy, the enlargement of the
restricted transverse diameters by out-fracturing the parietal bone
after having performed additional suturectomy along the coronal and
the lambdoid sutures, decreasing the resistance of the parietal bone
with additional bone vertical cuttings or bone morcellation,
maintaining the fractured parietal bones in the newly expanded
position by interposing bone fragments at the level of the sagittal
suturectomy, as well as addressing the frontal and occipital bossing

[17–27]. All the newly introduced surgical techniques corresponded to
the understanding that removing the fused suture was not sufficient
and that it was necessary to manage also the abnormal compensatory
calvarial growth that occurred at the level of the normal cranial sutures.
In other words, it became clear that surgical management should not be
limited to the “release” of the skull in the first months of life, necessary
to correct the increased intracranial pressure and its possible effect on
cognition, by profiting from the forces of the developing brain to
normalize the cranial shape but that the operation also should have
aimed at improving the child’s cosmetic aspect. The improvement of
the cosmetic aspects should have prevented the psychological
consequences eventually related to self-estimation and acceptance by
the social environment. The cosmetic indication was then accepted as a
further criterion for the surgical indication justifying the more
extended surgical corrections that had become possible for the
concomitant improvement in anaesthesiology intraoperative assistance
and in post-operative care.

1 3 The Functional Matrix
In the same years, a great debate was going on among orthodontists on
the reciprocal influences of developmental anomalies of the face, skull
base and cranial vault stimulated by the paper published in 1962 by
Melvin Moss [28], and his numerous publications in the subsequent
three decades [29–35] thatpropounded the so-called functional matrix
theory [28] (Fig. 1.5).

Fig. 1.5 Melvin Lionel Moss (1923–2006) (published under CC BY-SA 3.0)

The theory criticized the classic osteology the various bones of the
skull and facies classically distinguished as specific entities with a preestablished pattern of growth suggesting that they had to be considered
a series of segments related to a specific function and responding to
specific functional demands during their development. Grossly, the
theory could be simplified in the concept that bones do not grow but
are grown in response to the growth and function of soft tissue
matrices. The functional matrix, that is the soft tissue mass enclosed by
bones to form a functional unit, elicits secondary growth responses by
its corresponding skeletal unit. Functional matrices were individualized
into two main types: periosteal matrices serving as the functional
muscle/tendon attachments to skeletal units and capsular matrices

enclosing a mass or volume within a functional space. Anomalies of
functional matrices, according to the theory, were responsible for
abnormal bone growth, for example, the cranial alterations secondary
to defects in neural mass [34]. The actual role of cranial sutures as an
independent centre of bone formation, similar to the epiphyseal growth
plates, was challenged on the grounds of several experimental
observations, such as the possibility of halting their function by
extrinsic mechanical strains or the lack of bone formation in
subcutaneously transplanted sutures. Furthermore, clinical and
experimental evidence proved that the growth of the cranial and facial
bones could be determined by extrinsic factors as demonstrated by the
vertical growth of the facies and the skull in children with respiratory
problems or the unilateral hypo development of the maxillar and
mandibular bone induced by the homolateral muscle palsy obtained by
the unilateral sectioning of the facial nerve in perinatal rabbits [36–38].
To summarize: (1) The neurocranial capsular matrix, which is an
enclosure having contents that exert pressure, is the basic component
of cranial growth which in turn stimulates compensatory growth of its
skeletal unit. (2) Neuronal function and peripheral innervation appear
crucial for normal craniofacial development. (3) In ontogenesis,
genomic (intrinsic, prior) and epigenetic (extrinsic, proximate) factors
are each a necessary cause, but neither alone is sufficient as only the
interaction of both provides both the necessary and sufficient causes of
morphogenesis.
Though still debated, the concepts originated by Moss’s theory
influenced the neurosurgeon to develop new strategies beyond the
mere opening of the cranial sutures and eventually to elaborate pluristage surgical methodologies to face the more complex forms of
craniofacial stenosis, considered as inoperable for a long time. Multistage operations offered the possibility to offer the infant with complex
craniosynostosis an early protection of the developing brain with a
reasonable surgical risk, controlling the intracranial pressure and
assuring space for the growth of the brain prior to taking care of the
cosmetic problem at a later age.

1 4 The Modern Craniofacial Era

In the late 60s and 70s, Paul Tessier, and his colleague neurosurgeon
Gerard Guiot marked a significant step in the treatment of craniofacial
malformation introducing new surgical procedures for craniofacial
reconstruction that influenced the plastic and maxillofacial surgeons
and impacted on the neurosurgeons as well (Fig. 1.6).

Fig. 1.6 Paul Tessier (1917–2008)

Tessier’s innovative techniques led to the creation of a new
subspecialty, namely craniofacial surgery. Patients with complex faciocraniosynostoses, once considered inoperable, could finally be treated

with new surgical procedures with rewarding results [39]. Autologous
bone grafts and bone substitutes became increasingly utilized and new
instruments to bend and shape the bone grafts were progressively
introduced [40–42].
As an effect of Tessier’s contribution cranio-facial surgeons were
increasingly participating in surgical teams involved in the treatment of
the most severe forms of craniosynostosis though neurosurgeons
remained the essential components dealing with the calvarial
reconstruction, the safety of the underlying meninges and the
management of the neurological disturbances associated to
craniosynostosis, namely hydrocephalus and Chiari type 1 anomaly. On
the other hand, the neurosurgeon became acquainted with techniques
that utilize autologous calvarial bone grafts or bone substitutes and the
manipulation/dislocation/repositioning of the calvarial bones for both
increasing the intracranial volume and correcting the cranial
dysmorphia. In this direction, several techniques have been proposed
since the 70s, especially for the immediate reconstruction of the frontal
region and the orbit in simple craniosynostoses. The lateral canthal
advancement of the supraorbital margin in unilateral coronal
synostosis was introduced by Hoffman and Mohr with an explicit
reference to Tessier’s technique “The facility with which the
supraorbital margin could be mobilized in Tessier’s method of
craniofacial repair suggested to us that we could easily modify our
approach to coronal synostosis and advance the supraorbital margin,
creating an artificial suture at the base of the skull and allowing for
proper correction of this disorder” [43, 44] and widely utilized.
Technical modifications have been proposed in the subsequent years
such as, for example, the fronto-orbital advancement using an en bloc
frontal bone craniectomy [45] or the reconstruction of the frontal
region using reverse frontal bone graft without the use of an orbital bar
[46]. Fronto-orbital advancement has been also widely utilized to
correct the metopic synostosis associating the creation and correction
of a fronto-orbital bar, prepared according to Tessier’s and Marchac’s
principles [47] and repositioned in a more anterior position with
advancement, remodelling and rotation of the frontal bone, in one or
two pieces [48]. Also, for the correction of metopic craniosynostosis
several technical variants have been proposed [49–51]. At the end of

the twentieth century, the fronto-orbital and facial monobloc
advancement started to utilize the osteogenic property of the external
dura mater with temporary or internal distractors device which
allowed higher degrees of anterior dislocation of the cranial vault [52].
Posterior cranial vault expansion was introduced to increase the
skull volume available for cerebral growth, decrease intracranial
pressure, counteract the evolution towards turricephaly and prevent or
at least diminish the impact of secondary cerebellar tonsils descent in
syndromic and non-syndromic coronal or bi-lambdoid synostosis [53–
57]. Nowadays, the procedure is frequently adopted as the initial
treatment of syndromic complex craniosynostosis in order to postpone
the fronto-orbital advancement. Also, for the posterior cranial vault, the
introduction of osteogenic distraction resulted in more favourable and
long-lasting outcomes. The introduction of resorbable distractors
contributed to the current wide use of this type of procedure avoiding
the necessity of a second operation to remove the distraction devices
[58]. One of the major limits of the just described techniques was the
morbidity associated with the external manipulation of the distraction
devices, besides the child’s discomfort and the possibility of infective
complications.
All the above-described techniques are gratified by results that were
not possible in the previous years. However, they are weighted by the
major surgical risk of mortality and morbidity. It is not surprising that
the introduction of the device that did not need external manipulation
such as the internal springs devised by Claes Lauritzen [59] with the
goal of assuring a dynamic force acting on the margins of the
osteotomies is able to maintain the anatomical correction of the
malformed skull beyond the operation matching with the natural
growth of the child [60]. The obvious limit of the technique is again the
necessity of a second operation for the removal of the spring-mediated
distractors.
Cranial reconstruction with calvarial remodelling, fronto-orbital
advancement and prolonged osteogenic distraction has certainly met
the expectancy of families and patients for excellent functional and
cosmetic outcomes, nevertheless, they are relatively severe surgical
procedures with associated mortality and morbidity that seem to be
not justified in simple craniosynostosis. Hence, the return to linear

craniectomies currently carried out in very young infants with minimal
scalp incisions [61, 62], the aid of endoscopy and postoperative
moulding helmet mostly in sagittal synostosis but also anterior
plagiocephaly and trigonocephaly [63–68]. The effective advantages of
this minimal approach in terms of late outcome are currently under
evaluation [69–71].
To conclude, at first sight the surgical evolution of craniosynostosis
surgery from the early strip craniectomies to the complete calvarial
remodelling and now minimally invasive surgical interventions seems
to have come full circle. However, during such a journey a deep
understanding of the disease has been reached with the possibility to
select the most appropriate surgical procedure. The technical
instrumentation has been enriched considerably and the intraoperative
and postoperative care greatly improved. In this evolution, the
neurosurgeon has not been alone but accompanied by ever-enlarging
teams involving several surgical and medical specialists:
anaesthesiologists, maxilla-facial surgeons, plastic surgeons,
radiologists, ophthalmologists, otolaryngologists, paediatricians,
geneticists, neurologists, dentists, psychologists, speech therapists,
social workers…and families.

2 Embryology and Skull Growth: What
Is Important for the Neurosurgeon?
Yann Heuzé1
(1) Univ. Bordeaux, CNRS, Ministère de la Culture, Pessac, France

Yann Heu
Email: yann.heuze@u-bordeaux.fr
Keywords Development – Evolution – Neural crest – Mesoderm –
Dermatocranium – Chondrocranium – Animal models

2 1 Foreword
As a biological anthropologist, I was trained in Anatomy and Evolution.
During my postdoc in the Richtsmeier lab in the Department of
Anthropology at the Pennsylvania State University, I had the
opportunity to study developmental biology and birth defects such as
craniosynostosis which then became central to my research. The
purpose of this chapter is to present the embryology and growth of the
skull from an evolutionary and developmental perspective (evo-devo).
As such, the goal of this chapter is not to provide an up-to-date highly
detailed description of skull embryology and early skull growth in
humans. Those data have been previously published by other authors
and should be consulted for a thorough treatment of these important
topics. Many helpful reviews and original research exist in the current
literature. For my chapter, I have leaned heavily on “Larsen’s human
embryology” by Gary Schoenwolff et al. [1], “Craniofacial
embryogenetics and development” by Geoffrey H. Sperber and Steven
M. Sperber [2], and “Bones and cartilage” by Brian K. Hall [3].

2 2 From Fertili ation to Gastrula:
Fundamental Processes
Though the initial 2 days of human embryo formation are under the
control of factors expressed only by the oocyte, subsequent
differentiation of cells is governed by the genetic material inherited
from both parents. Three days after the fertilization of the ovum by the
spermatozoon that results in the formation of the totipotential zygote,
the first mitotic cycles have produced 16 smaller pluripotential cells
achieving the morula stage. In addition to the expression of genetic
material within the cell, interactions between cells and their
environment are essential for differentiation. These interactions
between newly differentiated cells happen by induction. Induction can
occur by direct cellular contact, diffused agents, or agents embedded in
vesicles targeting mechanisms such as gene activation or inactivation,
protein translation, modification of cell membrane selectivities,
intercellular adhesion or repulsion, and cell migration. Timing is an
additional dimension that is crucial to normal development. Alteration
or disruption of this complex symphony referred to as morphogenesis
can lead to abnormal development.
At the end of the first week after fertilization (preimplantation
period), the embryonic period starts with the implantation of the
blastocyst (around 100 cells at the time) into the decidual layer of the
uterine wall. The embryonic period comprises 7 weeks of
embryogenesis. The polarized blastocyst consists of an outer layer
(trophoblast) and an inner cell mass adherent to the trophoblast, filling
only one part of the newly formed blastocyst cavity. Eventually, the
inner cell blast will give rise to the definitive structures of the fetus,
while the trophoblast will form the extra-embryonic tissues.
At day 10, newly formed structures called fetal membranes are
visible: the chorion deriving from the trophoblast and delimiting the
embryo; the amnion, a membrane delimiting the future amniotic sac
filled with amniotic fluid; the yolk sac, providing nutrition and gas
exchange before the forming placenta becomes functional; and the
allantois, a transient sac allowing gas exchange and liquid waste
handling. With the establishment of the two layers, the dorsoventral

axis is defined. The two-layer germ disk is connected dorsally to the
amnion through the epiblast and ventrally to the yolk sac through the
hypoblast. The germ disk, amnion, and yolk sac derive from the inner
cell blast.
Between days 14 and 17, a process called gastrulation initiates and
will reorganize the two-layer blastocyst into a three-layer embryo
(gastrula) consisting of ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. Signaling
pathways such as Hedgehog (HH), fibroblast growth factor (FGF),
wingless (Wnt), bone morphogenetic protein (BMP), and Notch are
active and regulate the activity of Nodal (a transforming growth factor
beta, TGF- ) that is essential to the formation of mesoderm and the
establishment of left–right asymmetry of visceral organs. At the caudal
end of the two-layer germ disk, nodal signaling causes epiblast cells to
proliferate, differentiate, and migrate toward the midline of the germ
disk. This accumulation of cells produces a bulge and ultimately forms a
linear band of cells called the primitive streak. The primitive streak
elongates cranially in the midline and the progression stops when the
streak is about halfway across the embryonic disk. While the
lengthening stops, epiblast cells are still migrating toward the rostral
end of the primitive streak creating the primitive node and thereby
establishing the cranial-caudal axis. The primitive node is a major
signaling center and will subsequently induce the formation of the
neural plate and notochord rostrally (see below). Epiblast cells
continue to migrate toward the primitive streak and primitive node and
eventually pass through the primitive groove and primitive pit,
respectively, via a process known as ingression. Ingression is made
possible by the epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT, see for a
review [4]) in which epiblast cells lose their polarity and adhesive
properties and migrate ventrally to form a layer between the epiblast
and hypoblast. Through EMT, these cells proliferate and form the
intraembryonic mesoderm. As the ingression process continues, the
hypoblast and epiblast form the endoderm and ectoderm, respectively.
The embryonic disk is now trilaminar and the three primary germ
layers, ectoderm, endoderm, and mesoderm, will give rise to all
structures and organs of the body.
The role of the primitive node is essential during gastrulation. At
day 16, epiblast cells migrating through the primitive node differentiate

to form the notochord which develops cranially and stops caudally to
the prechordal plate. The notochord, surrounded ventrally by the
endoderm, dorsally by the ectoderm, and laterally by the mesoderm
(now called paraxial mesoderm), is achieved around day 20.

2 3 Neurulation: A Focus on Cranial Neural
Crest Cells
One of the main evolutionary innovations of vertebrates is the
appearance of an embryonic stem-cell population from the
neuroectoderm called the neural crest. With the “new head hypothesis,”
Gans and Northcutt [5] proposed that many elements of the vertebrate
head represent an addition rather than a modified portion of the
protochordates’ trunk. More precisely, anterior structures such as
sensory, integrative, and motor systems, as well as the associated
supportive skeletal structures derive from the neural crest and
epidermal placodes [5]. These structures are pivotal in functions such
as the detection and capture of prey as well as the exchange and
distribution of respiratory gases [5].
The specification of neural tissues creates the neural plate which is
an ectodermal structure that forms cranially to the primitive node and
dorsally to the forming notochord (i.e., notochordal process). The
neural plate results from a process called neural induction when
signaling (downregulation of BMP by FGF) causes the apicobasal
thickening of epiblast cells. The neural plate then elongates cranially
along the midline. The neural plate is composed of neural ectoderm and
is separated from the nonneural ectoderm by the neural plate border
that will give rise to a population of stem cells called the neural crest
and to placodes during the process of neurulation. Neurulation, the
transformation of the neural plate into a neural tube, is induced and
regulated by TGF-beta signaling molecules such as Chordin and Noggin
that downregulate BMP signaling [6], as well as FGFs [7], Wnt signals
[8] and a Dlx gradient [9]. At day 19, a neural groove appears in the
neural ectoderm. The neural groove is bordered laterally by the neural
folds formed through the ingression of the neural plate. The folding
process and the fusion of the neural folds allow the formation and

closure (dorsally) of the neural tube at day 21. The neural crest cells
also undergo ingression through EMT and pass momentarily between
the ectoderm (dorsally) and the neural tube (ventrally) [10] as they
begin their migration process. The closure of the cranial and caudal
openings of the neural tube (neuropores) takes place on days 24 and
26–28, respectively.
The neural crest cells are multi-potent stem cells unique to
vertebrates that arise on the dorsal aspect of the embryo and stretch
from the cranial to the caudal tip. Neural crest cells migrate, proliferate,
and differentiate into various tissues (connective, muscle, nervous, and
endocrine) and pigment cells (melanocytes). Martik’s et al. [11] work
on lamprey (jawless fish; agnatha) led them to propose that the neural
crest of early vertebrates formed a single and uniform cell population
similar to neural crest cells of the amniote trunk, and that during early
vertebrate evolution, a new subpopulation of neural crest cells
appeared; the cranial neural crest. These authors propose that Hox
genes and other regulatory modifications are sufficient to account for
the small transcriptional differences observed between the cranial and
trunk neural crest subpopulations. Co-option of distinct genes into a
cranial neural crest-specific module likely allowed the cranial neural
crest gene regulatory network to progressively give rise to
morphological novelties such as the lower jaw [11]. After induction,
cranial neural crest cells migrate to the frontonasal process and the
first four pharyngeal arches [12–14]. Throughout interactions with
neighboring structures such as surface ectoderm, neuroectoderm, and
endoderm, neural crest cells contribute to the development of many
cranial structures and are critical to normal development of the
craniofacial region [15]. The cranial neural crest gives rise to the frontal
bone, most bones of the facial skeleton, and most facial connective
tissues.
The dorsal closure of the neural tube (day 21) ends the presomite
period and initiates the somite period marked by the appearance of 42–
44 bilaterally paired blocks of paraxial mesoderm along the rostrocaudal axis of the embryo that are characteristic of segmented animals:
the somites. Intermediate and lateral plate mesoderm are situated
lateral to the paraxial mesoderm. Somitogenesis starts rostrally with
paraxial mesoderm condensations forming incompletely segmented

structures called somitomeres. Cranial somitomeric mesoderm
migrates ventrally to contribute to the future pharyngeal arches. Caudal
to the somitomeres, a craniocaudal sequence characterizes the
formation of the somites establishing the segmented nature of the body
with 4 occipital, 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 8–10
coccygeal somites. The segmentation of the somites is driven by a
number of “clock” genes. Periodical activation of these clock “genes”
generates a signaling wave propagating in the rostral direction
involving Notch, Wnt, and FGF. Boundaries between somites are formed
through EMT. The somites subsequently differentiate into three parts:
the sclerotome (ventromedial aspect), dermatome (lateral aspect), and
myotome (intermediate portion). The sclerotome contributes to the
vertebral column except in the occipital region where it fuses to form
the occipital bone. The dermatome gives rise to the dermis of the skin.
The myotome differentiates into muscles. By the end of the somite
period, the cardiovascular, digestive, respiratory, nervous, urinary, and
reproductive systems are established. The optic and otic placodes,
which will give rise to the eyes and internal ears, respectively, are
formed. It is also the time when the embryo folds ventrally. At day 31,
the head of the embryo is composed of a prominent brain ventrally
associated with the pharyngeal arches prefiguring the face and neck,
altogether flexed over the developing heart due to this folding. At this
time the nasal placode and limb buds are also visible. The postsomite
period initiates at day 32. Head development occurs at the center of the
postsomite period when eyes, ears, and nose acquire a human
characteristic morphology. At the end of the postsomite period (day 56,
end of the eighth week), the embryo is termed a fetus.

2 4 Role of Neural Crest Cells in Head
Development: The Example of the Frontonasal
Ectodermal one (FE )
At the end of the fourth week (day 28), while the neural tube is closed,
the cranial section of the embryo experiences major expansion,
bending, folding, and constriction. The neural tube then forms three
primitive brain regions: the prosencephalon or forebrain, the

mesencephalon or midbrain, and the rhombencephalon or hindbrain.
The segmentation process goes on and at the end of the seventh week
(day 49), the secondary brain regions are visible. The prosencephalon
gives rise to the telencephalon and diencephalon, and the
rhombencephalon to the metencephalon and myelencephalon. Later,
the telencephalon will differentiate into the cerebral cortex,
hippocampus, basal ganglia, basal forebrain nuclei, and olfactory bulbs.
The diencephalon will differentiate into the thalamus, hypothalamus,
and neural portion of the eye. The metencephalon will differentiate into
the cerebellum and pons, and the myelencephalon into the medulla (for
a review on brain patterning and associated signaling pathways, see
[16]).
During the fourth week of development (at the time the neural tube
is closing), seven prominences prefiguring the face and organized
around the stomodeum (future mouth) are visible: the midline
frontonasal prominence and three paired lateral structures, the lateral
nasal (sometimes considered part of the frontonasal prominence),
maxillary, and mandibular prominences. The maxillary and mandibular
prominences derive from the first pharyngeal arch. Craniofacial
development results from interactions between neural crest cells and
the surrounding epithelia such as the neural ectoderm of the forebrain,
the facial ectoderm of the frontonasal prominence, and pharyngeal
arches, as well as the endoderm of the inner surface of the pharyngeal
arches. Pioneering experiments on chick and quail by Le Douarin and
lab members showed that the fate of neural crest cells is restricted by
Hox genes such as Hoxa2 (reviewed in [17]). However, the neural crest
is not pivotal in the formation and patterning of the pharyngeal arches.
The pharyngeal endoderm is involved in the patterning of the
pharyngeal arch skeleton [18].
Many transcription factors contribute to craniofacial development.
Brugman et al. (2008), for example, provide a review that highlights the
role of FGF8 in normal craniofacial development. Fgf8 signaling from
the neuroectoderm promotes the development of the jaws in birds,
while the expression of Fgf8 in the first branchial arch ectoderm is
dependent on signaling from the neural crest [19]. This illustrates how
interactions between epithelia and mesenchyme are pivotal to
craniofacial morphogenesis. Another key signaling pathway in

craniofacial development is associated to sonic hedgehog (Shh) from the
Hedgehog family. Shh expression takes place in the prosencephalon,
and then in the ventral part of the telencephalon [20]. Shh signaling is
pivotal for the proper morphogenesis of the frontonasal prominence.
Fgf and Shh signaling emanating from the forebrain neuroectoderm are
essential for the patterning and differentiation of the frontonasal neural
crest [21]. Of particular importance to facial development is the
frontonasal ectodermal zone (FEZ). The FEZ was defined by Hu et al.
[22] as a key signaling center for the morphogenesis of the face located
in the surface cephalic ectoderm in mammals and avians. The FEZ is
formed by the boundary between Shh and Fgf8 expressing cells located
within the frontonasal prominence ectoderm [22]. While the FEZ is a
single site of expression, in mice the FEZ is divided into paired regions
associated with the median nasal prominence [23]. Shh expression in
the FEZ starts with the arrival of NC cells into the frontonasal
prominence and is probably induced and maintained by Bmps [24].
Several ectopic transplantation experiments demonstrated that the FEZ
induces skeletogenesis and determines the dorsoventral polarity of the
upper jaw as well as its morphogenesis through patterning of the
underlying mesenchymal cells [22, 23]. However, when the FEZ was
transplanted into regions expressing homeobox genes such as the
second pharyngeal arch, no effects on the mesenchymal cells were
observed [23]. FEZ positively regulates Bmp expression in NC
mesenchyme of the upper jaw in birds [23] and as such participates in
craniofacial phenotypic variation. For example, Young et al. [25]
showed that downregulation of Shh in the brain caused a continuous
narrowing of the frontonasal prominence, hypotelorism, and medial
maxillary rotation, while upregulation of Shh causes the opposite
phenotype. Besides physical interactions between the developing brain
and face (see [26] on the role of brain growth on the positioning of the
facial prominences and eyes), FEZ is an example of a molecular
signaling center active in craniofacial morphogenesis.

2 5 Different Units of the Skull in Evolutionary
and Developmental Biology

The skull is a complex skeletal system whose primary function is to
protect the brain and the major sense organs (olfactory, optic, and
auditory) as they carry out their functions. Multiple and sometimes
conflicting definitions of the different elements of the skull exist
depending on the authors’ area of study; e.g., human anatomy,
comparative anatomy, embryology, evolution, or developmental biology.
The skull is often compartmentalized into divisions on the basis of
varying criteria and/or based on certain developmental derivatives.
Examples of these divisions include regions or modules labeled as facial
skeleton, braincase, cranial base, cranial vault, chondrocranium,
splanchnocranium, dermatocranium, pharyngeal skeleton, and
viscerocranium. Most researchers and clinicians have a fairly clear idea
of what each division comprises, though these definitions are rarely
made explicit. To more clearly define aspects of the craniofacial
skeleton, Kawasaki and Richtsmeier [27] proposed to follow the
nomenclature used in evolutionary and developmental biology that
defines the skull into the cranial endoskeleton (composed of the
chondrocranium and pharyngeal skeleton) and the cranial dermal
skeleton (dermatocranium). The pharyngeal skeleton, composed
primarily of cartilage, arose as simple gill supports in stem jawless
vertebrates and became specialized into the more complex lower jaw
that includes the ear ossicles. The chondrocranium, composed of
cartilage and cartilage bone arose to support the brain. The
dermatocranium composed primarily of dermal bone, enamel, and
enameloid was the last to evolve [28]. Bone forming from the
endoskeletal precursors (cartilage bone) and from the dermal or
exoskeleton (dermal bone and membrane bone) is distinct
ontogenetically and/or phylogenetically [3, 29]. The dermal bone of the
exoskeleton forms in contact with the epithelial ectoderm through
intramembranous ossification, whereas the endoskeleton forms mainly
through endochondral ossification but not in contact with the epithelial
ectoderm.
The two principal skeletal tissues are bone and cartilage (the other
two being enamel and dentin). Cranial cartilage and bone that form
endochondrally and intramembranously can derive from either the
mesoderm or neural crest. Endochondral ossification is a process in
which cartilaginous models are replaced by bone. Intramembranous

ossification occurs when aggregated mesenchymal cells directly
differentiate into osteoblasts and form bone. In both types of
ossification, bone consists of cells distributed on a collagen matrix that
is mineralized into a vascularized skeletal tissue. Ossification per se
starts with the condensation of mesenchymal cells and upregulation of
tissue-specific genes. Condensation consists of successive stages;
initiation, formation of boundaries, cell adhesion, proliferation, growth,
and end of growth [3].
Osteoblasts manufacture the extracellular matrix called osteoid and
also mineralize that matrix trapping them within the mineralized tissue
where they differentiate into osteocytes and function in bone
homeostasis. The bone grows by apposition and mineralization of new
osteoid perichondrially (outer surface of cartilage), periosteally (outer
surface of bone), or endosteally (inner surface of bone).
Cartilage consists of cells and extracellular matrix that may or may
not mineralize and is avascular. Cartilage is formed by chondroblasts
and chondrocytes and resorbed by chondroclasts. The extracellular
matrix is rich in water, glycosaminoglycans, and type II collagen.
Cartilage grows by apposition, but unlike the bone, it can also grow
interstitially and is therefore capable of changing its shape rather
quickly during development.
Though the two modes of ossification are active in craniofacial
development, the relationship between the chondrocranium and
dermatocranium during intrauterine development remains elusive.
This is in part related to the transient nature of the chondrocranium.
However, a recent study by Motch et al. [30] provides experimental data
on a mouse model for Crouzon syndrome (Fgfr2cC342Y/ ) supporting
the existence of a developmental relationship between cartilaginous
elements of the chondrocranium and bones of the dermatocranium.
Together with the data published earlier by Kawasaki and Richtsmeier
[27] and Pitirri et al. [28], these studies lead the members of this group
to hypothesize that the chondrocranium is pivotal in establishing the
initial formation and spatial distribution of the dermal bones during
embryogenesis. These authors propose that the chondrocranial
elements serve as a scaffold guiding and influencing the location and
morphology of developing dermal bones. If these results were to be
confirmed in future studies, they would advocate for a reassessment of

the classic definition of intramembranous ossification which is not
supposed to involve cartilage elements.

2 6 Neural Crest Vs Mesoderm-Derived
Tissues and Premature Suture Fusion
Bones forming the craniofacial skeleton are either derived from the
cranial neural crest or paraxial mesoderm. The facial skeleton, anterior
parts of the braincase floor, the squamous temporal, and frontal bones
are derived from the cranial neural crest. The mesoderm gives rise to
the occipital bones, parietal bones, and the nonsquamous part of the
temporal bone [31–33]. Many of these bones articulate at cranial
sutures (and synchondroses) which form major bone growth sites as
long as the mesenchyme forming the suture remains undifferentiated
[34]. As a consequence, the coronal suture forms a boundary between
the neural crest and mesoderm-derived bones of the skull.
When a craniosynostosis-associated mutation is present in a human
patient, that mutation is present in all cells of the body—including all
bone cells whether derived from neural crest or from mesoderm.
Laboratory animals and recent developments in Cre-mediated DNA
recombination provide an established method for the conditional
control of gene expression in animal models. There exist Cre-LoxP
systems that allow spatial and/or temporal control over the
recombination of the target gene. For example, it is possible to create an
Apert mouse model bearing a Cre-inducible mutation on fibroblast
growth factor receptor 2 (Fgfr2S252W). When using mesoderm-specific
Cre driver (i.e., Mesp1Cre) and neural crest-specific Cre driver (i.e.,
Wnt1Cre) and such Cre-inducible Apert mouse model, it then becomes
possible to express the Apert mutation only in mesoderm- or neural
crest-derived tissues [35].
Premature fusion of the coronal suture (i.e., coronal
craniosynostosis) can be caused by the expression of the Fgfr2S252W
Apert syndrome mutation in the mesoderm-derived mesenchyme of
the coronal suture in mouse. In the conditional expression mouse
model for Apert syndrome, the expression of this mutation is
responsible for abnormal osteogenesis though it does not alter the

lineage border integrity between mesoderm and neural crest [35]. A
subsequent study on the same mouse models showed that the
conditional expression of the Fgfr2S252W mutation in the suture
mesenchyme of other craniofacial sutures was not sufficient to induce
its premature fusion and that suture-specific variation in the timing of
fusion might also play a significant role [36]. Though mice expressing
the Fgfr2S252W mutation only in the neural crest-derived tissues
possess a patent coronal suture at birth, these mice displayed a more
severe phenotype than the mice expressing this same mutation only in
the mesoderm-derived tissues (and possessing a fused coronal suture)
[36]. This can be explained by the fact that the majority of the
craniofacial bones are neural crest-derived and that mice expressing
the Fgfr2S252W mutation only in the neural crest-derived tissues
displayed a premature fusion of several facial sutures such as the
premaxillary–maxillary, maxillary–palatine, and maxillary–zygomatic
sutures.
Paralleling the dual nature of brain influence on craniofacial
development (physical and molecular) besides the primary effect on
craniofacial phenotype of the expression of a specific mutation,
secondary effects related to physical interactions between the neuralcrest derived and mesoderm-derived tissues exist as well. Indeed, both
mouse models conditionally expressing the FGFR2 S252W mutation
either in the neural crest- or mesoderm-derived tissues also displayed
dysmorphologies in bones not expressing the mutation. The authors
proposed that these secondary changes could be caused by four
potential sources: (1) disrupted morphogenesis of the bone not
expressing the mutation caused by a neighboring prematurely fused
suture; (2) displacement of the bone not expressing the mutation
caused by neighboring dysmorphic mutant bones; (3) abnormal
physical constraints of soft tissues expressing the mutation; and (4)
abnormal signaling or soluble factors produced by mutant cells that
alter the development of the neighboring nonmutant cells [36].

2 7 Conclusion: What Is Important for the
Neurosurgeon?

This chapter is an attempt to deliver a solid, not-too-detailed summary
of the early development of the whole embryo and then of the bones of
the head which, I hope, will be of interest to neurosurgeons.
Throughout this chapter, the complex developmental stages and
associated mechanisms were described from an evolutionary and
developmental perspective. After the first 3 weeks of development and
the establishment of the three primary germ layers, I focused on the
activities of cranial neural crest cells during neurulation with some
insights on their evolutionary origin. A focus was then provided with
the interesting example of the frontonasal ectodermal zone illustrating
the pivotal role of interactions between epithelia and mesenchyme in
craniofacial morphogenesis. The FEZ also allowed illustrating the
integrative nature of craniofacial development with the complex
interactions between the growing brain and skull either through
physical interactions or molecular signaling centers. Subsequently,
osteogenesis of the skull was described providing an evolutionary and
developmental perspective on the cranial endoskeleton formed by the
chondrocranium and pharyngeal skeleton, and the cranial dermal
skeleton or dermatocranium. The work from the Richtsmeier group
was used to illustrate how the chondrocranial elements might serve as
a scaffold guiding and influencing the location and morphology of
developing dermal bones. Finally, through the example of the
conditional expression of the Fgfr2S252W Apert syndrome mutation in
mouse models, the role of sutures in craniofacial morphogenesis was
described as well as the nature of the interactions between the
mesoderm- and neural crest-derived craniofacial bones.
Surgical techniques to operate on patients with craniosynostosis,
either syndromic or nonsyndromic, sometimes focus on the
rearrangement of bones that make up the facial skeleton and cranial
vault. However, we need to remember that these causative mutations
(for a review, see [37]) affect all cells and all tissues (soft and hard) and
that understanding how different tissues impact the growth pattern of
others is critical to the proper correction of craniofacial anomalies.

3 Genetics of Craniosynostoses: What Is
Important for the Neurosurgeon?
Federica Tiberio1 and Wanda Lattanzi1, 2
(1) Department of Life Science and Public Health, Universit Cattolica
del Sacro Cuore, Rome, Italy
(2) Fondazione Policlinico Universitario A. Gemelli IRCCS, Rome, Italy

Federica Tiberio

Keywords Craniosynostosis – Cranial suture – Gene mutations –
Chromosomal abnormalities – Clinical management

3 1 Introduction
Craniosynostosis (CS) represents a highly clinically and genetically
heterogeneous group of congenital craniofacial malformations due to
the premature ossification of cranial sutures. Cranial sutures are
fibrous joints interposed between skull flat bones that play a key role
during craniofacial development, enabling the physiological
synchronous growth of the skull and the brain [1, 2]. The premature
suture fusion occurring in CS leads to a skull growth constraint
perpendicularly to the closed suture, with a compensatory growth in
the direction of lower resistance (perpendicularly to the patent
sutures) according to “Virchow’s law” [3].

CS occurs overall in 1 of 2000–2500 live births, being the second
most prevalent craniofacial defect [4, 5]. Indeed, the number of children
diagnosed with CS worldwide has been recently estimated to be nearly
85,000 in a year [6].
CS treatment is predominantly surgical, representing a major
indication of decompressive craniectomy and cranioplasty procedures
in newborns and infants (see dedicated chapters in this volume).
Therefore, not only CS contributes significantly to infant morbidity and
disability, but represents a major economic burden, with millions of
dollars spent annually, considering the costs for genetic diagnosis,
imaging, neurodevelopmental, and standard surgical treatments, which
may vary in types and number of procedures and for associated care.
Despite CS being ethologically heterogeneous as in most cases it
results from a combination of environmental and genetic factors,
genetic testing is an essential part of the diagnostic workup of patients.
This chapter aims to provide a detailed and comprehensive update
on the genetic causes and risk factors for CS, integrating the
consolidated knowledge of genetic pathophysiology with recent
scientific findings achieved during the last decades. With a dedicated
focus on the relevance of genetic knowledge for neurosurgical planning,
and on the implications for prognosis, it may serve as a useful guide for
pediatric neurosurgeons in the management and treatment of these
conditions.

3 2 CS Types and Classification
CS is classified according to different alternative criteria. Firstly, based
on the number of fused sutures, simple CS refers to single-suture
ossification, whereas complex CS is used to describe a multi-suture
ossification pattern [7].
Based on the underlying pathophysiological mechanism, CS is
defined as primary when the skull developmental abnormality is
caused directly by a genetic mutation, acting alone or in combination
with environmental factors, and secondary when it results from other
conditions that indirectly affect cranial suture biology during the
perinatal stage (e.g., maternal hyperthyroidism, hypercalcemia, or

rickets, and/or neurodevelopmental abnormalities of the fetus, such as
microcephaly) [5, 8, 9].
More commonly, CS is classified based on the clinical manifestation
as nonsyndromic craniosynostosis (NCS), when it occurs as an isolated
phenotypic trait, or syndromic (SCS) when it represents a feature of a
complex syndrome with associated extracranial defects [5].
NCS represents around 70% of all CS cases and usually occurs as a
primary simple CS [10, 11]. They are classified according to the affected
suture site (sagittal, metopic, uni- or bi-coronal, and uni- or bilambdoid CS) and to the resulting skull dysmorphism (scaphocephaly
or dolichocephaly, trigonocephaly, and anterior or posterior
plagiocephaly/brachycephaly) [10].
NCS etiology is yet to be entirely clarified. They can be due to
genetic background (more commonly single gene mutations and/or
polymorphisms) with the concurrence of environmental factors (e.g.,
intrauterine fetal head constraint due to multiple pregnancies,
primiparity, abnormal fetal position, oligohydramnios, and prenatal
exposures to teratogens) that delineate a multifactorial etiology [11,
12]. Large cohort studies revealed that a genetic cause is detectable
more frequently in NCS cases affecting coronal and/or multiple sutures
[13], despite novel causative and/or risk-associated genes being very
recently identified also in CS affecting midline sutures [14–16].
In syndromic forms, which comprise 25–30% of all CS cases, the
premature fusion of sutures is associated with additional variable
inborn defects, and/or developmental delay, defining the phenotypes of
more than 150 Mendelian disorders annotated in the OMIM database
(www.​omim.​org) [17]. Currently, a genetic etiology—single gene
mutations or chromosomal structural abnormalities—can be confirmed
in about 80% of syndromic cases [5]. In the last two decades, significant
progress has been made in understanding the genetic basis of CS as a
whole, with diverse large cohort studies that enabled identifying
causative gene mutations and/or risk-associated polymorphisms also
in NCS [5, 13, 18, 19]. These studies have strongly contributed to
defining the influence of specific gene mutations on the surgical
outcome and on the overall clinical prognosis for most CS patients [5,
13, 19, 20].

3 3 Molecular Genetics of Craniosynostosis
The etiology of CS is extremely heterogeneous and an identifiable
genetic basis is estimated to be found in up to 45% of CS cases
nowadays [5, 13, 19]. Among all genetic diagnoses, 86% of cases
represent single-gene mutations, while the remainder are
chromosomal structural aberrations [4]. As a rule, syndromic CS is
most frequently associated with a genetic defect (75–80% of cases);
instead, nonsyndromic CS results from multifactorial etiopathogenesis
involving strong genetic and epigenetic influences usually combined
with environmental factors, which contribute to the onset to this
congenital defect [4, 19].
During the last decades, genetic studies focused on the molecular
mechanisms of craniosynostosis have greatly improved enabling the
discovery of new disease genes and disease-causing mutations in
previously identified genes associated with the syndromic phenotype
[5, 13, 18, 19]. In addition, recent genomic discoveries have extensively
elucidated the genetic basis for nonsyndromic cases, implicating the
newly identified genes in signaling pathways previously found in
syndromic cases [21, 22]. In this regard, both CS forms will be
considered altogether in this paragraph as parts of a unique nosological
continuum.
Currently, the OMIM (online Mendelian inheritance in Men database
(www.​omim.​org, accessed on January 5, 2022) reports 150 conditions
that feature CS either as a hallmark (CS syndrome properly said) or as a
frequent clinical feature (other syndromes) (Table 3.1). Currently, these
conditions can be associated with mutations in 125 different genes,
corroborating the wide genetic and allelic heterogeneity of CS.
