Interestingly, the best characterized CS-associated genes
(highlighted in Table 3.1) are part of functionally interconnected
signaling cascades mainly involved in skeletal and craniofacial
development [5, 12, 23]. In approximately 75–80% of all syndromic
cases, the phenotype is caused by monogenic mutations in either of a
short list of 7 genes encoding for developmental and bone-related

signaling molecules, namely, Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor 1–3
(FGFR- 1, -2, and -3), TWIST family bHLH transcription factor 1
(TWIST1 , Muscle Segment Homeobox 2 (MS 2), Ephrin B1 ( FNB1),
and Transcription Factor 12 (TCF12) [4, 5, 19].
The most frequently diagnosed CS syndromes include Muenke
syndrome (1/10,000–1/30,000, 4% of all CS), Saethre-Chotzen
syndrome (1/25,000–1/50,000), Crouzon syndrome (1/25,000–
1/61,000, 4.8% of all CS), Apert syndrome (1/65,000–1/100,000, 3%
of all CS), Pfeiffer syndrome (1/100,000, 1–2% of all CS), and
craniofrontonasal syndrome (1/120,000, 0.8% of all cases) [5, 24].
These tend to share an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance, due
to either gain-of-function (e.g., FGFR2 3 and MS 2 mutations), loss-offunction, or dominant negative mutations (e.g., TWIST1, FNB1, and
TCF12 mutations). Indeed, the genetic pathophysiology of CS mostly
results from gain-of-function and haploinsufficiency, whereas rarely
consists in a complete loss-of-function as these genes play key roles
during embryonic development and thus, their complete loss is lethal in
utero [12, 23]. Nonetheless, other alternative patterns of inheritance
are described for additional rare syndromes encompassing the CS
spectrum (e.g., Carpenter syndrome, autosomal recessive;
Craniofrontonasal dysplasia, and X-linked dominant, among others; see
Table 3.1).
The best-characterized disease-associated genes along with
recently identified pathogenic and risk-related gene variants are
systematically described.

3 3 1 Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptors (FGFRs)
FGFRs are single-pass transmembrane proteins that serve as highaffinity tyrosine kinase receptors for fibroblast growth factors (FGFs).
FGFs binding to the extracellular IgII-IgIII domains of FGFR induces
receptor activation triggering the intracellular downstream signaling
that culminates in the phosphorylation of target proteins [25–27].
FGFRs are expressed in a spatial-dependent manner by controlling
the proliferation and differentiation of mesenchymal and
neuroectodermal cells during skeletal development [27]. Specifically, in
cranial sutures, FGFR2 is predominantly expressed in osteoprogenitor
cells, FGFR1 is located in more differentiated osteoblasts, whereas

FGFR3 has lower expression in the periosteum and in sutural
osteogenic fronts at the late stage of suture niche development [28].
Gain-of-function missense mutations affecting hot spot domains in
FGFR -1, -2, and -3 have been extensively associated with syndromic CS
[5, 29, 30]. The clinical spectrum of these conditions varies from
complex multi-suture CS syndromes (including Apert syndrome, BeareStevenson cutis gyrata syndrome, Bent bone dysplasia, Crouzon
syndrome, Crouzon syndrome with acanthosis nigricans, Jackson-Weiss
syndrome, Muenke syndrome, and Pfeiffer syndrome) to isolated
monosutural CS [30].
Specifically, the majority of FGFR-related CS syndromes have been
associated with autosomal-dominant mutations located within exons 8
and 10 of the FGFR2 gene (encoding IgIIIa and IgIIIc domains,
respectively) or in the intron sequence flanking exon 10 (IIIa/exon 8
and IIIc/exon 10) [29, 31]. Additional mutations have been described in
the IgI–IgII domains and in the tyrosine-kinase domains of this
receptor [31–33].
Interestingly, identical FGFR2 mutations (i.e., C278F, G298P, and
C342T) have been found in patients with Crouzon, Pfeiffer, and JacksonWeiss syndromes, suggesting that unknown genetic modifiers could
contribute to the wide phenotypic heterogeneity observed in patients
carrying the same FGFR2 mutation [34].
Furthermore, mutations in FGFR2 (c.1576A G; p.Lys526Glu, and
c.1032G A; p. Ala344Ala) have been found in familial cases of sagittal
synostosis [20, 35].
A mutation affecting the FGFR1 gene (p.Pro252Arg) has been found
in 5% of individuals with Pfeiffer syndrome 1 (the less severe
phenotype) and in a patient with Jackson-Weiss syndrome [36, 37].
FGFR1 variants have also been associated with NCS cases. In particular,
a heterozygous missense mutation (c.899T C, p.Ile300Thr) and a
frameshift mutation (due to a c.730_731insG insertion) in FGFR1 were
found in two nonsyndromic cases presenting metopic and sagittal
synostosis, respectively [11, 38].
Furthermore, heterozygous mutations in FGFR3 have been
specifically associated with Crouzon syndrome with acanthosis
nigricans (p. Ala391Glu) and with Muenke syndrome (p.Pro250Arg) as
well as with nonsyndromic cases [39–42]. Specifically, the latter is one

of the most common alterations in the human genome with a mutation
rate of 8 10 6 [43].
FGFR-related syndromes usually display an overall decreased
reproductive fitness, with probands carrying, in most cases, de novo
mutations [5, 29, 30]. Nonetheless, due to the extremely variable
phenotypic expression, familial forms, with wide intrafamilial
heterogeneity, have been described. The widely variable expression and
penetrance of FGFR missense mutations also explain the rare
occurrence of milder phenotypes that may be sometimes disguised.
Mutations in FGFR genes represent a significant surgical prognostic
factor, being associated with a worse clinical course, including the
frequent need for re-intervention to treat relapses (i.e., re-synostosis;
[44]). In this regard, it has been suggested that patients operated on
below 6 months of age have a three-fold greater risk of developing resynostosis compared with children treated between 6 months and
2 years old [45]. However, it is not clear whether the high risk of
developing postoperative reossification results from the progressive
nature of these conditions, the age at the time of surgery, or the
presence of germline mutations in these patients [44, 46, 47].
Overall, it is reasonable to consider FGFR -1, -2, and -3 genetic
testing in complex nonsyndromic and syndromic cases, especially in the
presence of additional clinical features and developmental delay (Fig.
3.1) [4, 48].

Fig. 3.1 Tentative flowchart for genetic diagnosis. The path toward a complete and correct
diagnosis of a CS case starts with the clinical evaluation, which should be based on the shared
effort of a multidisciplinary team of specialized medical and surgical professionals. To achieve
the correct categorization of the specific CS subtype, the neurosurgeon must first establish the
site and number of affected suture(s). Experienced clinical geneticists/dysmorphologists
should physically examine the patient to assess the presence of additional malformations and
anomalies throughout the body and analyze the pedigree for intrafamilial recurrence. Pediatric
neuropsychologists/psychiatrists will assess the psychomotor performance of patients. Genetic
counseling will then serve to complete the differential diagnosis and plan the correct testing,
which largely varies based on CS type. If genetic testing is mandatory for syndromic and/or
unclear complex CS forms, a more temporizing strategy, with careful follow-up may be
exploited in the management of nonsyndromic CS, which may disguise genetic forms, especially
in the case of coronal involvement, of familial recurrence, or in the presence of subtle and often
neglected associated cognitive or somatic anomalies. See the chapter text for additional details

3 3 2 TWIST Family bHLH Transcription Factor 1
(TWIST1) and Related Genes
The basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor (bHLH) TWIST1 is a key
regulator of skeletal development. Specifically, during calvarial

development, TWIST1 controls the specification and the differentiation
of cells within the cranial suture mesenchyme and osteogenic fronts by
first homo- or heterodimerizing with other bHLH molecules and then
binding to conserved motifs on DNA [49]. In this context, it has been
shown that TWIST1 transiently inhibits the expression of RUNX family
transcription factor 2 (RUN 2 , encoding the master bone transcription
factor, and negatively regulates the transcription of FGFR genes [50–
52]. TWIST1 is believed to regulate osteogenesis particularly in the
coronal suture domain [53].
Saethre-Chotzen syndrome (OMIM 101400) is an autosomal
dominant disorder belonging to CS syndromes and characterized by
uni/bi-coronal synostosis with additional facial and limb abnormalities
[54]. The disorder is due to loss-of-function mutations in the TWIST1
gene including SNPs, deletions, insertions, duplications, and complex
rearrangements [13].
Also for TWIST1 mutations, a wide clinical heterogeneity can be
described. Indeed, point mutations were found in patients with an
apparent nonsyndromic phenotype, affecting sagittal, metopic, and
coronal sutures [5, 38]. For these reasons, TWIST1 mutational
screening is widely recommended in complex CS with negative FGFR
mutation results, and in coronal NCS, even in the absence of clear
syndromic traits (Fig. 3.1) [4, 48].
Also, TWIST1 mutations are associated with a worse surgical course
due to increased risk of developing intracranial hypertension, thus
requiring more invasive surgery and/or multiple procedures [44, 54].
The transcription factor 12 gene (TCF12) encodes another member
of the bHLH transcription factor family, which is involved in the
maintenance of coronal suture patency by forming heterodimers with
TWIST1 and thus inhibiting osteogenic differentiation acting on RUNX2
and FGFR signaling pathways [55]. TCF12-related CS (OMIM 615314)
caused by heterozygous mutations in TCF12 was identified in
syndromic multi-suture CS associated with additional abnormalities
closely resembling the Saethre-Chotzen phenotype. Also, TCF12
mutations have been found in apparently nonsyndromic patients with
unilateral/bilateral coronal synostosis, though in most cases a mild to
moderate cognitive impairment was observed in patients [5, 55, 56].
TCF12 variants include small frameshift, nonsense, splicing, and

missense changes, along with large intragenic rearrangements leading
to haploinsufficiency [55, 57].
Epidemiological studies of mutation-positive cases suggested a
benign clinical course showing that these patients usually require only
a single surgical procedure without complications [57, 58].
TCF12 molecular testing is currently included in first level tests in
patients with unilateral and bilateral coronal CS (with or without
syndactyly) and is recommended in all FGFR3-, TWIST1-negative
patients, and aCGH-negative multi-suture forms (Fig. 3.1) [23, 58].

3 3 3 Eph-Ephrin Pathway Genes
Eph-ephrin is another important family of tyrosine kinase receptors
and ligands that control skull development [5]. Specifically,
EphB/EphrinB1 interaction controls skeletal patterning and
craniofacial morphogenesis, whereas Ephrin A4 is a downstream
effector of Twist regulating coronal suture formation and patency [12,
59, 60]. In this regard, loss-of-function mutations in FNA and FNB1
encoding Ephrin A4 and Ephrin B1 ligands have been found in
nonsyndromic coronal CS and in X-linked craniofrontonasal syndrome
(featuring coronal CS), respectively [5]. Mutations in FNB1 are also
described in unclear syndromic phenotypes, including both coronal and
multi-suture CS, and should be considered for second-level genetic
testing in these cases (Fig. 3.1) [23, 44].

3 3 4 ETS2 Repressor Factor (ERF)
The ETS2 repressor factor gene ( RF) encodes a repressor
transcription factor expressed by neural crest cells that antagonizes
RUNX2-induced osteogenic signaling [61, 62]. RF loss-of-function
mutations have been found in 2% of syndromic CS cases and in 0.7% of
clinically nonsyndromic patients. ERF haploinsufficiency causes the
loss of RUNX2 inhibition enhancing osteoprogenitors’ differentiation
within the cranial sutures niche [62]. RF mutations are typically
associated with sagittal and uni-/bi-lateral lambdoid synostoses or less
frequently a multi-suture involvement up to pansynostosis [13, 61, 62].
Regarding the clinical management of ERF-related craniosynostosis,
it is extremely important to consider that these patients develop a
progressive ossification of sutures, presenting an asymptomatic course

until the appearance of multi-suture synostoses and raised ICP during
early infancy [61]. For these reasons, RF mutation screening could be
considered in suspect nonsyndromic CS and in complex CS cases
involving at least sagittal or lambdoid suture (Fig. 3.1) [61].

3 3 5 Msh Homeobox 2 (MS 2) and Homeotic
Transcription Factors
The Msh homeobox 2 (MS 2) encodes a homeodomain transcription
factor mainly expressed by the neural crest cells and strongly
contributes to craniofacial development [5].
MS 2 gain-of-function was the first genetic abnormality described
in a CS phenotype, later named Boston-type CS [63]. This is a rare
condition, with full penetrance and variable expressivity, involving
either sagittal, coronal, or multi-suture CS [5]. MS 2 copy number
variations have also been associated with CS, confirming that correct
cranial suture development requires an appropriate MSX2 dosage [64].
Similarly, gain-of-function mutations in the homeobox gene named
aristaless-like homeobox 4 (A
) have been associated with both
syndromic multi-suture CS involving at least sagittal suture (i.e.,
frontonasal dysplasia) and nonsyndromic sagittal, coronal, or metopic
phenotype [65, 66]. Similar to MSX2, a high dosage of ALX4 causes CS,
while loss-of-function mutations lead to defective ossification of the
skull (i.e., parietal foramina 2) [5, 66].
Whole exome and genome sequencing (WES/WGS) in unsolved CS
cases allowed the identification of heterozygous variants in the SIX
homeobox 1 (SI 1) gene, which encodes a homeodomain-containing
transcription factor of the sine oculis class [15]. The patients presented
sagittal and/or bi-lambdoid sutures’ fusion associated with additional
features that are typically found in SIX1-related syndromes (branchiootic syndrome, MIM 608389; nonsyndromic, MIM 605192; and
branchio-oto-renal syndrome) [15].
Finally, the SIX homeobox 2 (SI 2), another member of the
aristaless family, was found mutated in patients with syndromic
complex CS or single-sagittal suture synostosis, resembling frontonasal
phenotype [67]. SI 2 encodes a transcription factor that controls neural
crest cells’ proliferation and migration during early skull development
[67].

Given the low prevalence and the poor reproducibility of associated
phenotypes, mutation analyses of homeotic genes are not currently
suggested as a first-line test, although MS 2 testing is advised in the
presence of Boston-type CS (Fig. 3.1) [68]. Based on the available pieces
of evidence, it should be also considered in nonsyndromic sagittal
and/or unicoronal synostosis with familial recurrence and/or history
of syndactyly (Fig. 3.1) [68].

3 3 6 Ciliary Genes
Primary cilium (CP) is a nonmotile cellular organelle that protrudes
from the apical surface of almost all human cells, receiving and
transducing physical and biochemical extracellular stimuli into
intracellular cascades (i.e., Hedgehog (HH) and Wnt family member
(WNT)) to regulate tissue development and homeostasis [69].
Ciliopathies are a group of Mendelian conditions due to mutations in
primary cilium-related genes and are characterized by several
anomalies (i.e., retinal degeneration, renal disease, and cerebral
anomalies) including skeletal defects [70]. Among these,
craniosynostosis has been recurrently reported in ciliopathies caused
by mutations in over 18 CP-related genes, becoming a clinically relevant
phenotype [69].
Specifically, genes encoding the intraflagellar transport (IFT)
components involved in protein traffickings along CP such as IFT122,
IFT 3, and IFT1 0 have been implicated in the etiopathogenesis of
cranio-ectodermal dysplasia 1 and 3 (CED, also named Sensenbrenner
syndrome) and of short-rib thoracic dysplasia 9 (SRTD 9), respectively
[69, 71]. These conditions are characterized by limb and facial
abnormalities and sagittal or metopic CS [69].
Furthermore, biallelic mutations in the Centrosomal protein 120
(C P120) and in NIMA-related kinase 1 (N 1) genes, both involved in
centrosome organization, centriole biogenesis, and cell cycle
progression control, have been associated with different forms of STRD
characterized by uni- and bicoronal synostosis, respectively [69].
In addition, the dysregulation of the HH pathway, one of the most
important cilia-related signaling, has been found in ciliopathies
characterized by complex clinical defects including sagittal synostosis.
Of these, Joubert syndrome 2 is caused by a homozygous mutation in

the transmembrane protein 216 (TM M21 ) gene, encoding for a
ciliary base protein that regulates the HH pathway and ciliary
membrane composition [69]. In addition, microduplications of the IHH
(Indian hedgehog signaling molecule) gene have been found in the
Syndactyly type 1 featuring syndactyly and sagittal CS [72].
A recurrent somatic mosaic mutation in the gene encoding the
ciliary membrane receptor Smoothened, frizzled class receptor (SM )
causes Curry–Jones syndrome, a multisystem disorder characterized by
patchy skin lesions, polysyndactyly, cerebral malformations, and
unicoronal craniosynostosis [73].
Besides, HH signaling is mediated by the GLI family zinc finger
proteins, including GLI3 which is involved in the intramembranous
ossification process of skull bones [74]. Heterozygous loss-of-function
mutations in the G I3 gene are indeed associated with Greig
cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome, characterized by craniofacial
anomalies, including sagittal and metopic CS, along with hand/foot
abnormalities, and cognitive impairment [75].
Finally, loss-of-function mutations in the RAB23, member RAS
oncogene family (RAB23) gene, acting as a negative regulator of HH and
ERK1/2 signaling, cause Carpenter Syndrome 1, a rare pleiotropic
disorder featuring either single (sagittal) or multi-suture (sagittal and
metopic; cloverleaf skull) synostosis as a hallmark [76]. These patients
also present multisystem developmental impairment, with variable
severities, affecting the brain, genitourinary system, heart, and
appendicular skeleton [69].
Genome-wide association study (GWAS) identified susceptibility
loci for sagittal nonsyndromic craniosynostosis near Bone
Morphogenetic Protein 2 (BMP2) and within the Bardet-Biedl
syndrome gene 9 (BBS ) gene, which encodes a protein of the
multimeric complex “BBSome” required for ciliogenesis [77]. In this
regard, Barba et al. [78] observed specific upregulated splice variants of
BBS9 in nonsyndromic patients with sagittal or metopic synostosis.
Recently, a WGS study detected a novel variant of the CP-related
fuzzy planar cell polarity protein gene (FU ) (c.851 G C, p.
(Arg284Pro)) in monozygotic twins exhibiting metopic
craniosynostosis [79]. In this study, the authors highlighted that the
FUZ protein is a planar cell polarity (PCP) effector, which is essential for

normal ciliogenesis, although it also acts as a negative regulator of
osteogenesis [79].
In this context, to date, it has become important to consider genetic
screening of CP-related genes in patients featuring single- or multisuture synostosis and core phenotypic manifestations of ciliopathy (Fig.
3.1).

3 3 7 Recently Identified Genes
Next-generation sequencing has greatly enhanced the discovery of new
disease-associated genes expanding the genetic spectrum of CS
disorders at an unprecedented pace [5, 13, 19].
Homozygous missense and nonsense mutations along with a
duplication in the gene encoding the IL11 receptor alpha ( 11 A)
have been reported in patients showing a Crouzon-like phenotype with
multi-suture synostosis and dental anomalies [80–84]. I 11RA testing
is hence recommended in familial pansynostosis CS, specifically in
complex form associated with teeth anomalies [4] (Fig. 3.1).
The ZIC family member 1 ( C1) gene encodes another regulator of
embryo development that drives the membranous ossification by
regulating FGF signaling and Sonic hedgehog signaling molecule (SHH)
within calvarial suture mesenchyme [85]. Heterozygous gain-offunction mutations in IC1 have been found in patients with severe
bicoronal and complex CS phenotypes, including learning disability
[85]. The diagnosis of a IC1 mutation has significant implications for
prognosis; hence, ZIC1 testing is advisable for FGFRs/TWIST1/TCF12negative coronal synostosis and complex CS forms [85] (Fig. 3.1).
A unique homozygous mutation in the beta-1,3glucuronyltransferase 3 (B3GAT3) gene, known to be involved in
linkeropathy syndrome, was found in 6 patients exhibiting a severe
clinical spectrum consisting in craniosynostosis, midface hypoplasia,
skeletal defects involving limbs and extremities, bone fragility, and
cardiovascular abnormalities [86].
De novo variants of CD96, a member of the immunoglobulin
superfamily, were identified in two cases with C syndrome/Opitz
trigonocephaly (OMIM 211750) exhibiting trigonocephaly, facial
deformities, wide alveolar ridges, multiple buccal frenula, limb defects,
visceral anomalies, redundant skin, psychomotor retardation, and

hypotonia resembling Bohring-Opitz syndrome (caused by mutations in
AS 1) [87, 88]. It has been supposed that mutations in CD affect cell
adhesion and cell growth [88].
Homozygous mutations in the diphthamide biosynthesis 1 (DP 1)
gene have also been associated with a phenotype characterized by
unusual skull shape due to sagittal/coronal synostosis, developmental
delay, central nervous system malformations, cardiac defect, short
stature, and early lethality [13, 89, 90].
Heterozygous missense mutations in FGF9 were identified in 2
families with multiple synostoses syndromes, 3 exhibiting multiple
synostoses including the premature fusion of sagittal suture [91, 92]. It
has been suggested that these mutations led to dysregulation of FGFR3
signaling by impairing the homodimerization of FGF9 and its binding to
the receptor FGFR3 [92].
Craniosynostosis involving metopic suture has been reported in few
patients with severe polymalformative syndrome associated with
homozygous missense mutations in the FTO alpha-ketoglutarate
dependent dioxygenase (FT ) gene [13, 93]. FTO belongs to the AlkBrelated dioxygenase family, playing a role in genome integrity only
partially known [94].
Skeletal abnormalities, including sagittal synostosis, have been
associated also with heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein K
( N NPK) haploinsufficiency resulting in Au-Kline syndrome (OMIM
616580) [13, 95]. Affected individuals also showed intellectual
disability, unique craniofacial phenotype, and brain and connective
tissue anomalies [95].
Two male patients with sagittal suture synostosis and a clinical
spectrum extending from Lin-Gettig syndrome to genitopatellar (GPS)
and Say Barber Biesecker Young Simpson (SBBYS) syndromes have
been associated with de novo frame-shift mutations in the lysine
acetyltransferase 6B (KAT6B) gene [96]. The affected individuals also
showed hypoplastic male genitalia, agenesis of the corpus callosum,
thyroid abnormalities, and dysmorphic features such as short palpebral
fissures and retrognathia [96].
Mutations in genes encoding proteins of the lectin complement
pathway such as MBL-associated serine protease 1 (MASP1) and
collectin subfamily member 11 (C EC11) have been reported in 3MC

syndromes (Carnevale, Mingarelli, Malpuech, and Michels syndromes)
associated with a clinical spectrum comprising craniosynostosis [13,
97, 98].
A heterozygous missense mutation and a deletion in the prolyl 4hydroxylase subunit beta (P4 B) gene have been associated with ColeCarpenter syndrome (OMIM 112240), which consists of frequent
fractures, coronal and metopic synostosis, ocular proptosis,
hydrocephalus, and distinctive facial features [99, 100].
Compound heterozygous mutations in the sodium voltage-gated
channel alpha subunit 4 (SCN4A) gene have been reported in two
siblings featuring lower facial weakness, highly arched palate,
synostosis of the sagittal and metopic sutures, axial hypotonia,
proximal muscle weakness, and mild scoliosis [101]. Nevertheless,
Gonorazky et al. [101] revealed that these mutations caused full and
partial loss of function of the Nav1.4 channel leading to a reduction of
muscle contraction. These data did not correlate with the premature
fusion of cranial sutures suggesting that craniosynostosis could be an
incidental finding in these two patients [101].
De novo missense mutations in the SLC25A24 pseudogene 2
(S C25A24) gene, which encodes for the calcium-binding
mitochondrial carrier protein (SCaMC-1, also known as SLC25A24)
have been described in complex syndromes including Gorlin-ChaudhryMoss syndrome (GCMS; OMIM 233500) and Fontaine syndrome cases
both including coronal craniosynostosis, among their clinical spectrum
[102, 103]. In addition, a potential influence between TWIST signaling
and SLC25A24 function has emerged due to the overlapping clinical
features between disorders caused by TWIST2 (i.e., Barber-Say
syndrome and Ablepharon-Macrostomia syndrome) and GCMS [102].
Moreover, recent data reported craniosynostosis as a novel
phenotype of RASopathies that are caused by gene mutations in the
RAS-MAPK (mitogen-activated protein kinase) signal cascade [104].
Specifically, alterations in the KRAS proto-oncogene, GTPase (K AS),
protein tyrosine phosphatase nonreceptor type 11 (PTPN11), SHOC2
leucine-rich repeat scaffold protein (S C2), B-Raf proto-oncogene,
and serine/threonine kinase (B AF) genes have been described in
patients with sagittal and/or lambdoid synostosis and additional
features like-Noonan syndrome or like-cardio-facio-cutaneous

syndrome (CFC) syndrome [104–107]. In this context, it has been
postulated that the insurgence of craniosynostosis in these patients
could be due to downstream signaling interaction between FGFR and
the RAS/MAPK pathways [105, 107].
Whole-exome sequencing studies of a large nonsyndromic
craniosynostosis cohort (sagittal and/or metopic; sagittal and coronal)
revealed that SMAD family member 6 (SMAD6) damaging variants
comprise about 5% of all midline NCS (including 8% of all metopic,
2% of all sagittal, and 30% of cases with both sagittal and metopic) [14,
42]. Specifically, these variants were mostly transmitted by apparently
unaffected parents and resulted in the loss of SMAD6 inhibitory effects,
thus promoting BMP signaling and the premature fusion of cranial
sutures [42, 108]. Concerning this, it is still debated if the presence of
BMP2 polymorphism, detected in some SMAD6-positive patients, can
predict their phenotype [14, 42].
In addition, these patients presented worse clinical outcomes due to
an increased risk of developing raised ICP after surgical procedures,
highlighting that SMAD genetic testing is recommended in unsolved CS
patients [14] (Fig. 3.1). Moreover, echocardiographic screening is
suggested in asymptomatic SMAD6-positive cases since it has been
reported that patients with cardiovascular disorders ((i.e., bicuspid
aortic valve (BAV) and ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA)) were
enriched for SMAD variants [14].
In addition, damaging de novo mutations in other inhibitors of WNT,
BMP, and RAS/ERK signaling pathways have been documented in a
wide cohort of patients with nonsyndromic midline craniosynostosis
[20, 42, 109]. These included mutations in negative regulators of WNT
signaling as axin 1 (A N1), mesoderm posterior bHLH transcription
factor 1 (MESP1), nephrocystin 4 (NP P4), proteasome 26S subunit,
ATPase -2 and -5 (PSMC2 and PSMC5), and Dishevelled segment
polarity protein 3 (D 3) as well as inhibitors of Ras/ERK signaling
including sprouty RTK signaling antagonist 1 and 4 (SP 1 and
SP 4), RAS protein activator like 2 ( ASA 2), and ArfGAP with
RhoGAP domain, ankyrin repeat, and PH domain 3 (A AP3) [42].
Miller et al. [109] described a boy showing sagittal synostosis, blue
sclerae, micrognathia, ligamentous laxity, bilateral recurrent inguinal
herniae, tall stature, and mildly abnormal aortic contour on

echocardiography caused by two rare heterozygous variants in the
fibrillin 1 (FBN1) gene.
In addition, a heterozygous mutation in the SH2 domain encoded by
the signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3), which
was previously reported in a case of hyper-IgE/Jobs syndrome, was also
found in a patient with midfacial hypoplasia, progressive airway
distress, and pansynostosis [109].
Heterozygous nonsense mutation in the neurotrophic receptor
tyrosine kinase 2 (NT K2) gene has been associated with a female
proband exhibiting an asymmetric face, left coronal synostosis, and
later developmen [109].
Loss-of-function variants in the zinc finger protein 462 ( NF462)
have been described in nine individuals with multiple congenital
syndromes including metopic ridging/craniosynostosis [40, 110].
Biallelic variants in cell division cycle 45 (CDC45), which encode a
member of the pre-initiation complex in DNA replication, have been
reported in Meier-Gorlin syndrome (MGS) associated with
craniosynostosis [111, 112]. Clinical presentation of these patients
varied from uni- and bicoronal synostosis and mild short stature, to a
severe phenotype of MGS associated with multi-suture synostosis [111,
112].
Furthermore, a novel homozygous missense variant in the GINS
complex subunit 2 (G NS2) gene was identified in a patient with MGS
associated with bilateral coronal synostosis, phenotypically
overlapping with the CDC45-related MGS [113]. The authors supposed
that missense change disrupted the effective interaction between the
GINS complex and CDC45, which is necessary for the correct function of
the CMG helicase complex (Cdc45/MCM2–7/GINS) [113].
Pathogenic variants in the BCL11 transcription factor B (BC 11B),
which play a key role in the maintenance of cranial suture patency, have
been associated with about 20 cases featuring immunodeficiency,
neurological disorders, dermal defects, congenital diaphragmatic
hernia, and craniosynostosis [13, 114]. In this context, Zhao et al. [114]
have recently described a novel frameshift variant in the BC 11B gene
in a 25-month-old Chinese boy with severe multi-suture
craniosynostosis and global developmental delay.

Furthermore, recent studies described craniosynostosis as an
unseen clinical feature in chromatinopathies, which are genetically and
clinically heterogeneous Mendelian disorders caused by genetic
alterations of various components of the epigenetic machinery [115–
117]. These conditions are characterized by a distinctive phenotype
comprising intellectual disabilities, limb malformations, immune
dysfunction, growth impairment, and skeletal anomalies [117]. In this
regard, the craniosynostosis phenotype observed in a few cases could
reflect the alteration of molecular pathways acting downstream of the
mutated genes [116, 117].
Indeed, CS has been rarely associated with KANS 1 (KAT8
regulatory NSL complex subunit 1) haploinsufficiency in Koolen-de
Vries and Mowat-Wilson syndromes, with KAT6B (lysine
acetyltransferase 6B)-related disorders and with pathogenic variants of
KMT2D (lysine-specific methyltransferase 2D) in Kabuki syndrome
[117].
In addition, Bukowska-Olech et al. [118] described six patients
carrying pathogenic alterations in epigenetic regulators such as
ARID1A (AT-rich interaction domain 1A), KMT2A (lysine
methyltransferase 2A), and NSD1 (nuclear receptor binding SET
domain protein 1) resulting in Coffin-Siris syndrome type 2,
Wiedemann-Steiner syndrome, and Sotos syndrome type 1,
respectively. They were all characterized by intellectual disability,
immune deficiencies, or skeletal anomalies including CS as a rare
observation [118].
Metopic CS (trigonocephaly) has been recurrently described in
Bohring-Opitz syndrome resulting from mutations of the chromatin
modifier ASXL transcriptional regulator 1 (AS 1) gene [117].
Based on such evidence, cranial sutures’ evaluation and genetic
testing should be considered in intellectual disabilities, to allow an
accurate diagnosis and to improve the clinical outcomes of the patients
(Fig. 3.1).

3 3 8 Chromosomal Structural Rearrangements
Despite CS being frequently regarded as a monogenic disorder,
structural chromosomal aberrations can be identified in up to 15% of
cases, mostly syndromic [5, 44]. These alterations are usually assessed

by integrating standard karyotyping with array comparative genomic
hybridization (aCGH) [5].
Chromosomal alterations are poorly reproducible across patients,
as the involved loci are extremely heterogeneous; nevertheless, some
recurrent mutation hotspots can be identified and may allow
identifying additional putative candidate genes [5, 11].
In this regard, Gajecka et al. [119] proposed a list of candidate genes
regulating cranial suture closure based on the analysis of subjects with
duplication/triplication or the deletion of 1p chromosome presenting
or not anomalies in suture ossification. Indeed, chromosome 1p36
duplication and triplication have been reported in complex
conditions including metopic or coronal craniosynostosis [119–121].
Conversely, monosomy 1p36, the most commonly observed terminal
deletion, has been associated with late-closing anterior fontanelle,
mental retardation along with other signs [119].
Among genes identified, the authors supposed that the matrix
metalloproteinase-23A and -23B genes (MMP23A and MMP23B), which
map to 1p36 and are responsible for extracellular matrix remodeling
also during osteogenesis, could be involved in the suture phenotype in
these patients [119].
In addition, two different intragenic microdelections in the NFIA
gene (Chromosome 1p31 1 deletion) have been reported in four
patients with developmental delay, macrocephaly, hypoplastic corpus
callosum, metopic/sagittal or lambdoid synostosis, and hematuria [122,
123]. Subsequently, Serra et al. [124] described a female with
1p31 3p22 2 deletion exhibiting craniosynostosis, facial
dysmorphisms, and a severe global developmental and growth delay.
The deleted region of the proband contains about 90 genes including
interleukin 23 receptor (I 23R), RP 5 (retinoid isomerohydrolase
RPE65), RRC (leucine rich re-peat containing 7), SRSF11 (serine and
arginine rich splicing factor 11), AN RD13C (ankyrin repeat domain
13C), CTH (cystathionine gamma-lyase), N GR1 (neuronal growth
regulator 1), TNNI3 (TNNI3 interacting kinase), H 8 (LIM homeobox
8), ACADM (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase medium chain), PIG
(phosphatidylinositol glycan anchor biosynthesis class K),
3 (zinc
finger ZZ-type containing 3), USP33 (ubiquitin specific peptidase 33),
N N (nexilin F-actin binding protein), FUBP1 (far upstream element

binding protein 1), ADGR 2 (adhesion G protein-coupled receptor L2),
PAR3 (lysophosphatidic acid receptor 3), BC 10 (BCL10 immune
signaling adaptor), CCN1 (cellular communication network factor 1),
C CA3P (chloride channel accessory 3, pseudogene), and SH3G B1
(SH3 domain containing GRB2 like, endophilin B1) [124]. Of these,
I 23R may have a potential association with craniosynostosis since it
was already described in a patient with atypical CS [125].
Sowi ska-Seidler et al. [126] identified a previously unreported de
novo 1.26 Mb duplication at chromosome 1q22 q23 1 in a male
proband affected by complex CS, including metopic and lambdoid
synostosis, muscular hypotonia, psychomotor retardation, and facial
dysmorphism. The chromosome region described encompasses two
genes involved in osteoblast differentiation: bone gammacarboxyglutamate protein (BG AP), encoding osteocalcin protein, and
lamin A/C (LMNA), encoding lamin A/C [126].
In addition, a duplication of the N 2 locus on 6p21 1 was
associated with metopic CS as well as partial trisomy 6p12 3 p21 1
and N 2 locus quadruplication was found in patients with more
complex syndromic phenotypes, including combined coronal and
sagittal synostosis or pan-craniosynostosis, respectively [127, 128].
These data suggest a dosage effect of RUNX2 alterations, with midline
(metopic and sagittal) sutures appearing to be the primary target sites
of the dysmorphic insult [127–129]. RUN 2 encodes a transcription
factor critical for skull development, considered as the bone master
gene as its function is key to initiate skeletal formation during early
prenatal stages [130]. Interestingly, a recent study in a sagittal NCS
cohort reported the presence of gain-of-function nonsynonymous
variants in the RUN 2 locus [129].
Interstitial deletions of chromosome 7p have been found in
patients with complex Saethre-Chotzen-like phenotypes [5, 131]. The
TWIST1 gene along with H A (homeobox A cluster) genes, mapping to
this locus, could be involved in the pathogenesis of these patients [5,
131].
Karyotyping by both G-bind staining and array-based DNA
hybridization allowed the identification of novel microduplications on
chromosomes 8p11 22 q12 1 and 16q11 2 q21 in a 2-year-old boy
with dolichocephaly craniosynostosis [132]. The authors hypothesized

that being 8p11.22 q12.1 merely 1 Mb downstream of FGFR1,
duplication of this region might regulate the expression of FGFR1,
thereby causing the development of craniosynostosis [132]. In addition,
BBS2 (Bardet-Biedl syndrome 2, Ch-Band: 16q21), SA 1 (spalt-like
transcription factor 1, Ch-Band: 16q12.1), and CDH8 (cadherin 8, ChBand: 16q22.1) genes are plausible candidates of patients’ phenotype
[132].
The 9p deletion syndrome (MIM 158170) is a multiple congenital
disorder characterized by dysmorphic facial features, trigonocephaly,
multiple congenital anomalies, and mental delay [133]. In the majority
of cases, the 9p22.3 deletion position is a specific hotspot for metopic
CS, causing over 15% of syndromic trigonocephaly [134, 135]. The
FRAS1-related extracellular matrix 1 (FR M1) gene, mapping to this
locus, is considered a putative candidate for the CS phenotype since it
usually acts as an inhibitor of FGF signaling within the suture
mesenchyme [136]. Further studies have identified additional genes
that could be responsible for the 9p deletion syndrome phenotype,
such as Cerberus 1 DAN family BMP antagonist (C R1), tyrosinaserelated protein 1 (T RP1), and protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor
type D (PTPRD) [133, 137].
Duplications at chromosome 11q locus (11q11-q13 3
duplications), including FGF3 and FGF genes, have been also rarely
found in patients with complex syndromic CS involving coronal/multi
suture synostosis, congenital heart defect, and developmental delay
[138, 139].
Microdeletion at 9p22 p24 and 11q23 q24 has also been
associated with syndromic metopic craniosynostosis [134].
In addition, a de novo balanced translocation t(9 11)(q33 p15)
was observed in a patient, who exhibited synostoses of both the
lambdoid and the distal part of the sagittal sutures with a gaping
anterior fontanelle and midfacial dysmorphisms [140]. The breakpoint
disrupts the SRY-box transcription factor 6 (S
) gene locus on
chromosome 11p15, known to be involved in skeletal growth and
differentiation processes and a region on chromosome 9 with a large
number of highly conserved nongenic sequences [140]. In addition,
heterozygous missense mutations in the S
gene and a partial gene
deletion encompassing exons 5–7 have been found in four patients with

mild/moderate sagittal, coronal, and/or sutures synostosis and
additional clinical features [140, 141].
Metopic synostosis has been reported also in a few cases of partial
and complete trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome) as well as in less severe
trisomy 13 mosaicism characterized by a triad of the cleft lip and
palate, postaxial polydactyly, and microcephaly [142, 143].
Cases of partial distal trisomy (or tetrasomy) of chromosome
15q25qter, housing the insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF1R)
gene, have been reported in patients featuring craniosynostosis [144–
150]. In addition, Cunningham et al. [151] identified five variants in
IGF1R in patients with isolated sagittal or coronal suture synostosis,
corroborating the idea that these genes could be associated with
premature fusion suture. IGF1R is a tyrosine kinase growth factor
receptor expressed in the developing cranial sutures, where it regulates
osteoblasts’ differentiation in response to tensile force [151].
1-bp duplication in the ring finger and the SPRY domain
containing 1 ( SP 1) on chromosome 16q13 leading to a frameshift
and premature truncation of this protein have been found in a Saudi
family presenting premature ossification of the right coronal suture and
progressive skeletal dysplasia phenotype [152].
Variable degrees of CS, ranging from simple metopic or bicoronal
synostosis to severe multi-suture CS, have been also observed in a rare
22q11 deletion syndrome, although the molecular basis of this defect
is still unknown [153–155].

3 4 From Genetics to Clinical Management of
Craniosynostosis
3 4 1 Relevance of Genetics in CS Diagnosis
The clinical management of patients with craniosynostosis is complex
and requires a multidisciplinary team of specialists including
neurosurgeons, clinical geneticists, pediatricians, maxillofacial, and
plastic surgeons, depending on the case complexity [24, 156–158].
Craniosynostosis is usually diagnosed at birth or shortly after,
through clinical evaluation, physical assessment, and genetic testing
[157–159]. As far as genetic diagnosis is concerned, the improved

knowledge of the genetic causes along with the rapid progress of
genome sequencing technologies and data analysis pipelines have been
recently showing an even wider etiological heterogeneity and
complexity than originally thought. This scenario offers unprecedented
opportunities for patient-tailored management of each single CS case,
improving genetic counseling and testing, risk assessment,
reproductive advice, prognostic guidance, treatment planning, and, last
but not least, favoring the study of disease mechanisms and the
development of advanced therapies.
Nonetheless, the management of a correct molecular genetic
diagnosis of CS and its clinical interpretation is extremely challenging
and debated due to the complex and heterogeneous genetic
background previously described.
Tentative diagnostic flowcharts [4, 48] have been proposed based
on more recent discoveries to drive tailored patients’ management but
need to be constantly updated. Figure 3.1 displays a tentative and
extremely simplified flowchart for CS genetic diagnosis, which does not
take into account a number of country- and institution-specific issues
that may cause significant variation in the overall management of
patients.
The updated guidelines for the care and treatment of
craniosynostosis recommend genetic counseling and testing for
patients with proven disease (following clinical and physical
evaluations) [156, 157]. Indeed, a genetic cause, represented by either a
mutation in a single gene or a structural chromosomal aberration, is
increasingly detected in CS cases and can dramatically affect the
surgical outcome and the overall clinical prognosis [4, 5, 156, 157].
Specifically, the direct sequencing of one or a few specific target
genes is advised for children with proven and clearly recognizable
Mendelian syndromes with reduced genetic heterogeneity and a
defined set of disease-associated genes, in order to have faster results
with fewer costs (Fig. 3.1) [156, 157].
Since NGS allows scalable high-throughput analysis of large
portions of the genome, wide panels of multiple target genes can be
sequenced altogether, after a clinical-driven hypothesis. The cost for
NGS technologies is slowly but progressively decreasing, enabling their
implementation in the diagnostic routine of many developed countries.

Indeed, extended diagnostic CS gene panels tested through Next
Generation Sequencing (NGS), along with karyotyping plus aCGH, are
currently often proposed for patients presenting craniosynostosis and
additional birth defects and/or developmental disorders, which overall
refer to Mendelian disorders or complex syndromic phenotypes with
inherent genetic heterogeneity, or for patients with proven
craniosynostosis without a recognizable phenotype, as they grant the
highest chance of identifying rare genetic causes [156, 157].
Targeted sequencing of selected genes can be not suitable whenever
the scarcity of genetic data or the poor definition of the phenotype
impedes the correct selection and completion of the target gene list. In
this case, whole exome sequencing (WES) could be exploited to detect
new mutations in unpredicted sites of the coding portion of the DNA.
Furthermore, whole genome sequencing (WGS) could be finally
considered to also analyze noncoding (putatively regulatory) regions of
the DNA.
It is worth noting that NGS technologies cannot be considered yet a
manageable tool without the correct interpretation of the wide data
sets that they yield. While increasing the chance to find new variants,
WES and WGS also increase dramatically the volume of yielded data
and the complexity of their interpretation, hence the possibility of
translating NGS data into a relevant diagnostic outcome. The vast
majority of sequencing results, especially when obtained through WGS,
are represented by “variants of unknown significance” (VUS). These
remain in the limbo of experimental data, requiring a long and detailed
path of research to validate and confirm their clinical significance,
before translating them into a diagnostic outcome to be transferred to
patient families.

3 4 2 Relevance of Genetics in CS Prognosis
Patients with proven single gene mutations require more frequent
multiple surgical procedures and develop peri- and post-operative
complications [44]. These include hyperthermia, severe blood loss
(transfusion-related adverse events), wound infection, meningitis,
subgaleal and subcutaneous hematoma, rupture of the dura mater,
cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage, intracranial empyema, venous air
embolism, and seizures [160–162]. In addition, up to 40% of complex

syndromic cases develop delayed complications such as basal
encephalocele and re-synostosis [46, 162, 163].
Conversely, chromosomal abnormalities seem not to significantly
affect the surgical course in these patients [44]. Current guidelines
recommend standard karyotyping and aCGH in complex patterns of
suture fusion CS or isolated metopic synostosis cases mostly associated
with developmental delay and cannot be clearly classified as a known
monogenic disorder (see the previous section).
The updated guideline recommends skull remodeling within the
first year of life in nonsyndromic craniosynostosis [157]. Specifically,
surgery is indicated for sagittal, unilateral coronal, unilateral lambdoid,
and moderate metopic synostosis since no spontaneous improvement
of the abnormal skull shape is expected [157].
In addition, the indications suggest performing minimally invasive
surgery on NCS patients from the ages of 3–6 months to prevent periand post-operative risks and to avoid an increased ossified skull area
[157]. Conversely, open cranial vault remodeling is counseled in NCS
cases older than 6 months to reduce the risk of growth limitation of the
skull [157].
Literature data reported that surgical treatment is indicated as soon
as there are signs of increased ICP in syndromic CS and multi-suture
cases [157]. In this context, occipital cranial expansion with distraction
performed within the first year, especially between the age of 6 and
9 months, results in greater clinical outcomes in patients with Apert
and Crouzon syndrome or with multi-suture synostosis involving at
least both lambdoid sutures [157]. Skull remodeling through frontosupraorbital expansion is strongly encouraged for Saethre-Chotzen and
Muenke syndrome [157].
Finally, surgical procedures should be chosen based on cranial
deformity for other types of syndromic craniosynostosis [157].

4 Craniofacial Anomalies and
Neurocognitive Aspects in FgfrsCraniosynostoses Mouse Models

Keywords Neurocognitive aspects – Craniosynostosis – FGFR – Mouse
model

4 1 Introduction
Craniosynostoses—reported in 1:2000 to 1:3000 live births,
comprising at least 20% of syndromic cases [1]—are defined by the
premature fusion of one or more cranial and facial sutures, leading to
various craniofacial anomalies, among which: skull vault deformation,
potentially causing increased intracranial pressure, shallow orbits
leading to exorbitism and midfacial retrusion that can be associated
with obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome [2–4].
To better understand the physiopathology of these anomalies
several mouse models have been generated in the past decades, based
on the underlying mutations found in syndromic craniosynostoses.
Indeed, various mutations have been reported in patients with
syndromic craniosynostoses, and several key signalling pathways
involved in craniofacial development are affected by these variants.
Mutations in FGFR (fibroblast growth factor receptor) genes are
reported in almost 75% of syndromic craniosynostoses [5]. Such FGFRrelated conditions are caused by specific heterozygous activating
mutations in FGFR1 (Pfeiffer syndrome type 1) [1], FGFR2 (Apert,
Crouzon, Pfeiffer type 2 and 3 syndromes, Antley-Bixler, BeareStevenson cutis gyrata syndromes, Bent Bone Dysplasia and SaethreChotzen like syndrome) [5–9] and FGFR3 (Muenke syndrome and
Crouzonodermoskeletal syndrome). Muenke syndrome is the most
frequent FGFR-related syndromic craniosynostosis [10].
Crouzonodermoskeletal syndrome is an exceedingly rare syndrome
sharing similarities with Crouzon syndrome and including skin lesions
(acanthosis nigricans) [11]. Most of these FGFR variants are gain of
function mutations, inducing high receptor activity in the presence or in
the absence of its FGF ligands, which disrupts bone formation. Today,
the impact of FGFRs activating mutations on skull formation is well
understood, however neurocognitive development remains to be
elucidated.
Here, we describe mouse models carrying Fgfrs-activating
mutations generated in the past decades allowing a better
understanding of the impact of these mutations during craniofacial and
suture formation. In addition, we describe the impact of an Fgfr variant
on the brain and in particular on behaviour.

4 2 Fgfrs-Craniosynostosis Mice Models
Several mice models carrying Fgfr1, Fgfr2 and Fgfr3 activating
mutations known to be involved in human FGFRs-related
craniosynostoses have been reported.

4 2 1 Mouse Model Mimicking Pfeiffer Syndrome
(Fgfr1P250
)
The Fgfr1P250R mouse model has been generated by Zhou et al., by
inserting the P250R mutation in the Fgfr1 gene by homologous
recombination [12], corresponding to the human Pro252Arg mutation,
leading to the mild form of Pfeiffer syndrome. Heterozygous mice
(Fgfr1P250R ) developed an abnormal craniofacial phenotype from
postnatal day 3 with premature fusion of coronal, frontal and sagittal
sutures, without skull base anomalies. Although heterozygous mice
showed decreased body size, analyses of the growth plates did not
reveal any anomalies, highlighting that Fgfr1P250R mutation
preferentially impacts membranous ossification but not endochondral
ones [12, 13].

4 2 2 Mice Models Mimicking Apert Syndrome
(Fgfr2S252
, Fgfr2P253
)
The first mouse model for Apert syndrome to be reported is the
Fgfr2S252W mouse model, generated by the ubiquitous expression of
the Ser252Trp mutation in the Fgfr2 gene, corresponding to the most
frequent mutation observed in human pathology. Mutant mice showed
early premature fusion of coronal sutures, from embryonic stage E18.5,
with thinner calvaria bones, and reduced presphenoid bone length,
leading to significant craniofacial anomalies (dome-shaped skull,
midface hypoplasia, wide-spaced eyes and malocclusion). Mutant mice
presented reduced naso-anal length, without significant anomalies of
the growth plates [14].
The second mouse model for Apert syndrome to be described is the
Fgfr2P253R mouse model, generated by the insertion of the Pro253Arg
mutation in the Fgfr2 gene, reported to be of concern in one-third of

Apert patients. Mutant mice presented brachycephaly, with domeshaped skull, wide-spaced eyes, midface hypoplasia and malocclusion,
and a shortened skull base. Syndactyly was also observed. As for the
Fgfr2S252W mouse model, Fgfr2P253R mice presented reduced size,
but contrary to the first mouse model, growth plate anomalies were
observed, highlighting the impact of the Fgfr2P253R mutation in the
process of endochondral ossification [15].

4 2 3 Mice Models Mimicking Crou on Syndrome
(Fgfr2C342
, Fgfr2 290
)
The first mouse model mimicking Crouzon syndrome has been
generated by Eswarakumar et al. [16]. This model has been established
by the insertion of the Cys342Tyr mutation, frequently associated with
Crouzon/Pfeiffer syndromes, into the Fgfr2 gene by a Cre recombinase
under the control of the PKG promoter. The Cys342Tyr mutation affects
exon 9 of the gene and only affects the Fgfr2IIIc isoform. Fgfr2C3 2
mutant mice present a dome-shaped skull, shortened face,
exophthalmia, shortened skull base and malocclusion. Frontal and
parietal bones overlapped from embryonic stage E16.5, and premature
closure of coronal and lambdoid sutures occurred postnatally [16].
The second Crouzon model reported is the Fgfr2W2 0R mouse
model, generated by the N-ethyl-N-nitrosourea (ENU) mutagenesis
screen. The mutation affects both the b (epithelial) and c
(mesenchymal) isoforms of the Fgfr2 gene. Fgfr2W2 0R mutant mice
presented premature fusion of coronal and lambdoid sutures, with a
dome-shaped skull, short snout and malocclusion of the incisors. The
presence of skull base anomalies, thickened nasal septum cartilage and
abnormal sternum cartilage highlight the impact of this mutation on
endochondral ossification processes [17].

4 2 4 Mouse Model Mimicking Beare-Stevenson Syndrome
(Fgfr2 394C )
This mouse model has been generated by the ubiquitous insertion of
the Tyr394Cys mutation into the Fgfr2 gene. Heterozygous mice
presented reduced growth and premature death at 2 weeks of age.

Premature fusion of coronal, zygomatic and squamosal sutures
occurred with subsequent brachycephalic skull and midface hypoplasia.
In addition to the skeletal anomalies, mutant mice present cutaneous
anomalies, including cutis gyrata, epidermal acanthosis and
papillomatosis [18].

4 2 5 Mouse Model Mimicking Muenke Syndrome
(Fgfr3P244
)
To generate this mouse model, the Fgfr3P2 R mutation located in
exon 7 of the Fgfr3 gene was inserted using a Cre-LoxP system. The
craniofacial phenotype was mostly mild and variable, and premature
fusion of coronal sutures did not frequently affect mutant animals.
Fusion of zygomatic bone and synostosis of the premaxillary suture
were observed. Premature closure of the intersphenoidal and sphenooccipital synchondroses frequently affected mutant mice, highlighting
the impact of the mutation during endochondral ossification. In
addition, delayed development of the mandibular condylar head was
observed with condylar cartilage anomalies, harvesting arthritic
features. Sensorineural hearing loss was also detected in mutants, in
accordance with otologic impairments observed in patients with
Muenke syndrome [19, 20].

4 2 6 Mouse Model Mimicking Crou on Syndrome with
Acanthosis Nigricans (CAN) (Fgfr3A385E )
This mouse model has been generated by inserting the A385E
mutation, located in exon 9 of the Fgfr3 gene, using a Cre-LoxP system,
under the control of a Prm1 promoter [21]. No significant craniofacial
morphological changes have been observed in mutant mice, without
abnormal premature fusion of cranial sutures. Abnormal transient
morphological changes of the mandible have been reported, as
observed in human pathology [21, 22]. No obvious cutaneous
anomalies were observed in mutant mice, unlike in patients.
The absence of significant craniofacial phenotype in the CAN
Fgfr3A385 mouse model, Fgfr3P2 R Muenke mouse model and
Fgfr3 knock-out mice [23–25] emphasises that the Fgfr3 receptor is

less involved during craniofacial formation and intramembranous
suture formation in mice than in human or in zebrafish [13, 26].

4 3 Neurocognitive Aspects in Human FGFRRelated Craniosynostoses and New Insights
Using Fgfr3A385E Crou on with Acanthosis
nigricans Mouse Model
Cognitive impairment, including mental retardation, learning
disabilities and behaviour/psychopathology, has been reported in up to
24% of the patients with single-suture craniosynostosis [27]. In
syndromic multiple-suture craniosynostoses, the exact incidence of
cognitive impairments is difficult to determine, depending on the
clinical assessment performed, with the lack of standardised protocols.
In addition, the highly heterogeneous cerebral conditions of these
patients, depending on the intrinsic brain anomalies and those linked
to intracranial pressure, increase the lack of objective data concerning
cognitive impairments in syndromic craniosynostosis.
Among FGFR-craniosynostoses, Pfeiffer syndromes type II and type
III, linked to activating FGFR2 mutations, are generally associated with
severe neurological impairments and severe developmental delay [28–
30]. In Crouzon syndrome, craniofacial phenotype and the impact of
neurocognitive functions are highly heterogeneous, linked to the
numerous distinct mutations described in this spectrum [31–33]. In
Apert syndrome, although normal cognitive development has been
reported, mild to severe mental retardation is often described [34, 35].
In other rare FGFR2-related craniosynostosis syndromes, including
Jackson-Weiss syndrome and Beare Stevenson syndrome, there is a lack
of reported data on cognitive impairment, especially in Beare
Stevenson syndrome leading to frequent premature death [36, 37].
In FGFR3-related craniosynostoses, severe neurocognitive disorders
have been reported, including anxiety, learning impairments, as well as
memory, attention and emotional control disturbances [13, 38–40].
Cognitive impairment in syndromic patients is multifactorial,
resulting from a combination of the raised intracranial pressure due to

the synostosis, alterations in cerebrospinal fluid dynamics and
anomalies in venous outflow. The possibility of a direct impact of the
underlying mutation on the brain function has also been hypothesised
[41].
To study the potential direct impact of the FGFR3 mutation,
Fgfr3A385 knock-in mice without a craniofacial phenotype are
particularly interesting [21].
Indeed, neuro behavioural experiments performed in the mouse
model for Crouzon with acanthosis nigricans (CAN) Fgfr3A385 for the
first time give new insights into the impact of FGFR3 activating
mutations on neurocognitive functions. Fgfr3A385 mutant mice
presented severe memory and learning impairments, a structurally
abnormal hippocampus, low activity-dependent synaptic plasticity and
overactivation of MAPK/ERK and Akt signalling pathways in the
hippocampus. Pharmacological inhibition by infigratinib (BGJ398), a
tyrosine kinase inhibitor, rescued memory impairments in Fgfr3A385
mutant mice [13], Fig. 4.1. These results demonstrate for the first time
the impact of activating Fgfr3 mutation on brain development and
neurocognitive functions, independently of craniofacial anomalies and
premature closure of cranial sutures and skull base synchondroses.
Overall, this study provides a better understanding of the role of Fgfr3
on brain development and neurocognitive functions and gives new
therapeutic perspectives in neurocognitive disorders with the potential
use of tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

Fig. 4.1 MicroCT of Crouzon with acanthosis nigricans (CAN) Fgfr3A385
and controls mice
showing a normal craniofacial phenotype without skull vault and base anomalies in CAN
mutant mice. Behavioural studies showing memory impairments in CAN mutant mice when
compared with controls, 7 days of subcutaneous injections of a tyrosine kinase inhibitor
(BGJ398) in 4-month-old mice rescued memory impairment [13]

4 4 Therapeutic Approaches in FGFR-Related
Growth Anomalies
Current therapeutic approaches are many and varied and include
targeting the FGFR3 receptor, inhibiting the tyrosine kinase activity of
FGFR3 and antagonisation of FGFR3 downstream signalling pathways.
Several preclinical studies have demonstrated the positive effects of
FGFR3 antagonists on bone growth in mouse models of achondroplasia
carrying an Fgfr3-activating mutation, including tyrosine kinase
inhibitor (Infigratinib) [42–44], CNP analogs (vosoritide) [45, 46] and
more recently ( )-Epicatechin [47] (Fig. 4.2). The treatments rescued
the bone phenotype of an Fgfr3-related mouse model of achondroplasia
bearing a Fgfr3 3 C gain-of-function mutation [42, 45, 47].

Fig. 4.2 Pharmacological approaches using FGFR3 antagonists to rescue the defective
endochondral ossification process in mouse models of achondroplasia (adapted from [48])

Interestingly, taking advantage of the Fgfr3-related Crouzon mouse
model which has no craniosynostosis, Cornille et al. confirmed that
memory impairments in FGFR3-related Crouzon mice were due to the
increased activation of the Fgfr3 in the central nervous system. This
concept is also in line with a hypothesis raised several years ago, in
which certain cognitive impairments found in patients with FGFRrelated synostosis are caused by abnormal FGFR expression in the
brain—rather than through an effect of the skull size or the associated
hydrocephalus [41]. Daily intraperitoneal and intracerebroventricular
administration of the Fgfr3 inhibitor BGJ398 (Infigratinib) to adult mice
rescued the learning and memory impairments observed in the FGFR3related Crouzon mice suggesting that the modulation of FGFR3
signalling might be of value for treating the neurological disorders
associated with craniosynostosis (Fig. 4.1) [21].
These findings suggest that in the future patients might benefit from
a combination of medical and surgical treatments aiming to correct the
different aspects of craniosynostosis-related impairments. The different
surgical approaches that have been developed in the last years allow
the correction of the suture synostosis and more in general of the
associated skull deformation but also to reduce effectively a raised
intracranial pressure (ICP) or decompress a too small foramen magnum
and thus indirectly improve the functional outcome of the patients.
Pharmacological treatments seem to directly improve the functional
outcome. But these treatments because they improve bone growth
metabolism will probably also reduce the risk of developing a raised
ICP or a significant descent of cerebellar tonsils (Table 4.1).

In conclusion, thanks to the promising results observed in mouse
models we can expect pharmacological approaches to play a role in the
management of patients with craniosynostosis in the near future.

Keywords Craniosynostosis – Skull growth – Suture – Infant –
Cephalometrics – Stereophotogrammetry – Maxillofacial surgery –
Neurosurgery
Within the broad array of neurosurgical procedures, craniosynostosis
surgery is somewhat of an outsider, as the final result can only be
evaluated many years later. Even when all short-term surgical goals are
reached, it could be that in time mid-term and long-term results are not
reached at all, due to the continuing growth of the brain and skull.
Therefore, taking into account the physiological growth of the cranial
vault and the underlying brain is of paramount importance during the
consideration of all viable surgical options and the corresponding
timing of the surgery as part of the optimal treatment plan.

5 1 Underlying Principles and Mechanisms
Understanding the physiological growth of the cranial vault is
fundamental to understanding the pathophysiology involved in
craniosynostosis. It is clear that a detailed description of the complex

processes giving rise to the development and growth of the craniofacial
skeleton is far beyond the scope of this chapter and the interested
reader is referred to textbooks focussing only on this subject [1]. But
still, it is good to have a notion of the main processes at play.
The physiological growth and development of the neurocranium
start with osteogenesis, both as intramembranous ossification and
enchondral ossification. Intramembranous ossification begins with the
differentiation of mesenchymal cells into groups of osteoblasts in
ossification centres. In these centres, the connective membrane is
turned into bone, with the remainder of this membrane giving rise to
the endosteum, periosteum and sutures. In this way, most of the cranial
vault is formed from the intramembranous bone of paraxial
mesodermal origin: the frontal and parietal bones and parts of the
occipital and temporal bones. Endochondral ossification occurs on a
segment of hyaline cartilage. The chondrocytes grow, the cartilaginous
matrix mineralizes and decreases, and the chondrocytes are replaced
by capillaries and adjacent connective tissue cells, which differentiate
into osteoblasts. The cranial base is formed in this way from the
endochondral bone of neural crest origin [1].
These mechanisms of osteogenesis are well studied and agreed
upon in histology literature. However, on a larger scale, the subsequent
processes regulating the (mainly postnatal) further growth and
development of the neurocranium are far more complex and less
understood. Historically, the role of the sutures and growth centres in
bone formation and the regulation of the mechanisms at play have been
extensively debated. Basically, two main theories have been postulated.
The genetic theory in which the phenotypic expression is determined
by genetic transcription: the growth and development of the
neurocranium are to a high degree independent from environmental
influences and interaction with surrounding tissues. This is opposed by
the theory stating that growth and development are a major result of
complex interaction with environmental factors and surrounding
tissues and are only basically defined by the genetic constitution. Both
theories have been used to try to offer an understanding of mechanisms
involved in pathology, such as craniosynostosis [2].
We will shortly discuss some historical milestones, but the
interested reader is referred to the recent publications giving a concise

overview of the history of craniofacial studies and evolving theories [2,
3].
The first reports on craniofacial growth date back to 1791, when
S mmering described cranial deformity resulting from cranial suture
pathology. Otto described microcephaly or premature sutural closure
resulting in craniosynostosis 40 years later. In 1851, Virchow put forth
the hypothesis that cranial growth perpendicular to the fused suture
was limited and growth in the plane parallel to the fused suture was
enhanced [4].
In the early twentieth century, with the advent of X-ray,
cephalometric studies were undertaken. At first, these were merely
descriptive and focussed on the description of the craniofacial growth
pattern with little interest in the relation between growth and function
of parts of the craniofacial skeleton. Growth of the craniofacial skeleton
was considered to be intrinsic and following growth of the rest of the
body, more or less equal in all mankind, not influenced by interaction
with surrounding tissues nor a resultant of function. It was believed
that growth and development were genetically determined. However, in
time, it became apparent that craniofacial growth showed more
variation than what could be explained by genetic patterns only. Now,
more and more studies have shifted towards the relationship between
function and anatomy and it became clear that, to some extent, growth
and variation could be considered an adaptation to changing functional
demands.
In the 1960s, Moss and co-workers put forward the functional
matrix hypothesis. In this hypothesis (which did apply to the whole
body and not only to the head), they stated that the head served
different functions, and every function was carried out by a functional
cranial component’. Each cranial component consisted of a functional
matrix’ carrying out the function and a skeletal unit’ designed to
protect and support its functional matrix. They hypothesized that any
change in size, shape, spatial position and maintenance in all skeletal
units were always secondary to primary changes in their specific
functional matrices. On a larger level, all the functional cranial
components were organized in the form of cranial capsules’, mainly the
neurocranial capsule and the orofacial capsule. A capsule’ was defined
as an envelope that contains a series of functional cranial components

which are sandwiched in between two covering layers. For the
neurocranial capsule, this was the skin and the dura mater. Each
capsule surrounds and protects a capsular’ functional matrix. For the
neurocranial capsule, this is the neural mass’, consisting of the brain,
leptomeninges and cerebrospinal fluid. Capsular matrices, as the neural
mass, are defined and act as a volume. With this neurocranial functional
matrix hypothesis, Moss and co-workers posed that the cranium is in
large formed due to secondary passive growth at the sutures, in
response to the active growth of the cerebral mass, where the sutural
location, morphology and patency give direction to this growth [5]. This
hypothesis shifted the presumed role of the sutures from being active
growth centres creating the cranial vault in the genetically
predetermined form and dimensions towards passive, compensatory
growth centres that only reacted to the changes of the neural mass. In
this hypothesis, the structural growth and shape of the cranial vault
bones are not genetically predetermined, but reactive in nature to the
functional matrix-neural mass. Although the functional matrix
hypothesis has been criticized (mainly on the notion of the intrinsic
growth propensities of the cephalic cartilage at the skull base), the
concept of skull growth being the result of driving intracranial forces
being limited by diminishing growth potential of sutures and growth
centres has been widely observed and accepted. So what about the
undeniable role of genes in regulating the growth of the neurocranium
and what about their role in the occurrence of craniosynostosis?
Richtsmeier and Flaherty built an argument that the brain and skull
phenotypes take shape resulting from communication between cells
and tissues by regulating gene expression affecting morphogenesis [6].
Twigg and Wilkie described clearly the way bone formation processes
at the sutures are influenced/regulated by genetic transcription in
response to internal/external stimuli, see also Fig. 5.1 [7]. Disruption of
this equilibrium could then result in early, pathological, closure and the
occurrence of craniosynostosis [7].

Fig. 5.1 Overview of clinical causes and classification of craniosynostosis. (a) Cross-section of
coronal suture showing the developing parietal bone (p) overlying the frontal bone (f).
Internally, the dura mater (d) separates the calvaria from the brain; skin (s) is external. Left,
normal growth of the skull vault is regulated by a delicate balance of proliferation and
differentiation occurring within the suture (green shading) co-ordinated with the enlargement
of the underlying brain (black arrows). Right, in craniosynostosis this balance has been
disturbed by excessive external force on the skull, usually during pregnancy (unfilled arrows),
inefficient transduction of stretch from the growing brain (grey arrows), or intrinsic
abnormality of signalling within the suture itself (red shading). (b) Approaches to clinical
classification. Left: view of the skull from above (front at top). Normal skull with major vault
sutures identified is central. To either side, the examples show skull shapes resulting from
sagittal synostosis (left) and bilateral coronal synostosis (right). Note the metopic suture closes
physiologically at the age of 3–9 months. Centre: the clinical history can reveal possible
environmental predispositions such as teratogen exposure (most commonly maternal
treatment with the anticonvulsant sodium valproate) or twinning (intrauterine constraint);
affected relatives with craniosynostosis (filled symbols in pedigree) suggest a likely genetic
cause, which can be confirmed by diagnostic genetic testing. Right: clinical examination can
reveal facial dysmorphic features such as hypertelorism (wide spaced eyes) and grooved nasal
tip, suggesting craniofrontonasal syndrome (left), or other physical features such as syndactyly
characteristic of Apert syndrome (right). (Clinical photographs reproduced, with permission,
from Johnson and Wilkie and Twigg et al. Reproduced with permission from Elsevier [7])

To summarize, the current understanding is that the origin of
neurocranial growth is genetically predefined up to the point that the
calvarial growth at the sutures is becoming the resultant of intracranial
driving forces, regulated by a complex interplay of different genes that

control the proliferation-differentiation balance of a population of
undifferentiated stem cells in the mid-sutural mesenchyme.

5 2 Neurocranial Growth Patterns
How does this give rise to normal growth patterns? And how do these
differ from what is seen in craniosynostosis? Although many
cephalometric studies have been done in the twentieth century [8], the
timing and amplitude of regional growth of different calvarial skull
bones and resultant skull shape are not totally elucidated yet. The same
holds true for the regional growth patterns of the developing brain.
Research investigating the growth of the cranial vault and the cerebrum
in the first stages after birth has always been difficult because of
limitations with regard to data collection. Computed tomography (CT)
has been used only in the case of suspected abnormalities, due to its
use of ionizing x-rays. Magnetic resonance (MR) imaging may not use
harmful radiation, but MR images are often degraded due to the
neonates’ motion [9]. Additionally, unmyelinated white matter can be
difficult to differentiate from grey matter [10] and myelination of white
matter may cause changes in contrast and brightness inhomogeneities
on MR imaging [11]. Recent advances in using non-ionizing 3Dstereophotogrammetry have provided the first limited data sets on
normal growth patterns of the head. However, this technique only
covers the outer surface of the head and cannot distinguish the skull
from the intracranial mass [12].

5 2 1 Brain Growth Patterns
The increase in the cerebral volume results from progressive
phenomena, such as cell proliferation, arborization and myelination
[13]. The traditional quantification of neonate cranial growth is based
on the head circumference, where the head circumference shows a
natural logarithmic growth pattern, as displayed in Fig. 5.2 [12].
Although the direct measurement of the head circumference is still
widely used as a parameter, this metric has shown low reliability and
high inter-and intra-observer variability [14]. Pfefferbaum and
colleagues were the first to publish the overall brain, white and grey
matter volume of infants, children and adolescents based on MR

imaging, though the number of infants in the subject group was very
limited [13]. Matsuzawa showed that MR image analyses showed that
volumetric growth of the cerebrum followed a natural logarithmic
curve, similar to the curve of the head circumference [15].

Fig. 5.2 Boxplots of circumference measured on 3D photographs for boys (left) and girls
(right). Circumference reference values based on the Dutch cross-sectional growth study are
plotted in the background. (Reproduced with permission from Elsevier [12])

The total brain volume increase is the largest in the first year of life
(from 36% of adult volume at 4 weeks of age to 72% of adult volume
at 1 year), and then starts to slow down (with total brain volume
reaching 83% of adult volume at 2 years of age) and reaching an
approximation of its final volume at around 5 years of age [11, 15].
Knickmeyer found that the cerebellum showed disproportionate
enlargement when compared to the cerebral hemispheres in the first
2 years of life. Within the cerebral hemispheres, volume enlargement
was larger in grey matter than white matter, with a doubling of the
cortical grey matter volume during the first year of life. However, they
did not report on volumetric changes of the separate lobes or regions of
the brain, with an exception for the cerebellum, see Table 5.1 [11].
