The early fast growth rate of the cerebellum was confirmed by
Holland et al., who defined regional growth rates and left-right
asymmetries in the first 3 months of infant brain development. They

found a volume increase of the cerebellum of 108% at 90 days
postnatally, in contrast to a total brain volume increase of only 64%.
They did not study the grey and white matter and did not look at the
volume increase of separate lobes or regions of the brain [9].
Matsuzawa and colleagues were the first to compartmentalize the
cerebrum partly based on anatomical boundaries and analysed
(relative) volumetric data on the compartments. However, the
volumetric evolution of these cerebral compartments over time was not
publicized [15].
With the development of new MRI techniques, brain development in
neonates and infants is gaining more attention and regional differences
are being studied and slowly clarified. Lyall et al. looked at the
development of the regional cortical thickness and cortical surface area.
They found that cortical thickness and cortical surface area have
distinct and regionally heterogeneous growth patterns. In the first
2 years of life, primary and secondary sensory cortices displayed a
slower increase in thickness when compared to cortices of regions
involved with speech and language as well as the insula and cingulate
cortex. In general, cortical thickness approaches 97% of adult values in
the first 2 years of life. However, the cortical thickness did not show a
clear relationship to the total cortical volume, whereas the cortical
surface area had a strong and direct relationship to the total cortical
volume [16].
During the first 2 years of life, the cortical surface area showed an
average increase of 115%, three-quarters of which occurred during the
first year. Almost all regions of the brain show a large increase in
surface area in the first year of life, but the most expanding regions
include lateral frontal lobes, lateral parietal lobes and occipital lobes, as
well as left Heschl’s and left inferior temporal gyri, as is displayed in
Fig. 5.3 [16]. This includes typical sensory-specific association cortices,
such as superior occipital gyrus (visual association), superior and
middle temporal gyrus (auditory association) and superior parietal
gyrus (sensory/tactile association and spatial correspondence). The
rapid increase in the surface area of these cortices could be related to
the rapid expansion of the topographic maps that each of these area’s
harbour early in childhood. These maps are highly plastic and refined
with increased experience. However, they noted that many of these

regions did not show a large amount of cortical thickness growth,
suggesting that topographic map plasticity could be regulated primarily
by surface area expansion [16, 17].

Fig. 5.3 Early cortical surface measures development from birth to 2 years. Regional percent
change for CT. (a–c) and SA (d–f) from birth to 1 year (a, d), 1–2 years (b, e), and birth to
2 years (c, f). Warmer colours indicate larger per cent changes than cooler colours.
(Reproduced with permission of Oxford University Press [16])

Although Lyall has given us insight into the development of cortical
thickness and cortical surface area in the first 2 years of life in relation
to possible functional developmental stages, their data did not provide
data on the regional differences in volume gain on the level of separate
lobes or regions of the brain, including white matter [16].
With regard to the timeframe in which most craniosynostosis
treatments are performed, we can summarize the growth as follows: it
is shown that the total volume of the brain, the volume of the cerebral
hemispheres and the volume of the cerebellum increase dramatically
during the first year of life, with an increase of 101%, 88% and an
extraordinary 240%, respectively. The volume increase of the cerebral
hemispheres is mainly the result of the volume increase of the grey
matter. In turn, the volume increase of the cortical grey matter has a
strong relationship with the cortical surface area and less with the
cortical thickness. The increase of the cortical surface area is large for
almost all regions of the brain in the first year of life, but the most
expanding regions include lateral frontal lobes, lateral parietal lobes

and occipital lobes, as well as left Heschl’s and left inferior temporal
gyri.
Currently, there are no data available on the specific timing of the
volume increase of separate regions of the hemispheres during the first
year of life, it is nonetheless becoming increasingly clear that the brain
development in early childhood is very complex and regionally and
temporally diverse. This has not been properly clarified in the literature
to date, one can assume that this heterogenous development would
result in non-uniform volume gain of the brain during the first year of
life. If so, bearing in mind the functional matrix hypothesis, this would
mean that skull growth is not uniform either in the first year of life.

5 2 2 Skull Growth Patterns
Despite the long history of two-dimensional cephalometric studies, the
interest in the 3D skull growth patterns in infants has gained new
interest in only recent years. Even though some studies still report
using radiation techniques [18, 19] the renewed interest is mainly due
to the development of radiation-free evaluation methods, such as
stereophotogrammetry, allowing for a prospective and longitudinal
study on the skull growth patterns in infants [12, 20, 21]. We strongly
believe that this knowledge is crucial to understanding deviations of
what is considered normal growth’ and to evaluating both pathology
and treatment results of growth deviations, such as craniosynostosis.
The use of radiation-free stereophotogrammetry allows for repetitive,
longitudinal and prospective measurements in large groups of
individuals without the concerns of radiation on the developing brain.
This is a huge benefit over traditional radiation-based techniques, still,
a critical note needs to be addressed: this technique only captures the
surface and is therefore prone to measurement errors induced by
increasingly larger amounts of hair. This means that this study method
is feasible and reliable on a group level up to the age of 18–24 months
and can allow for individual follow-up and comparison in selected
individuals up to the age of 4–5 years [12]. Another important feature
to remember is that stereophotogrammetry techniques always include
soft tissue and the measurements and growth patterns derived from it
are strongly correlated with the measurements and growth patterns of
the skull, but are not the same. In general, stereophotogrammetry-

based measurements tend to be larger, depending on the age of the
subject and type of measurement.
Using prospectively collected stereophotogrammetry data,
comparing them to retrospectively collected CT data, Meulstee et al.
documented the very fast growth of the cranium in the first 2 years in
infants, showing the fastest expansion during the first 6 months and
generally slower rate of growth after 12 months. They looked at more
regionally detailed growth patterns and found that, between age
3 months and 6 months, the largest growth occurred in the frontal and
parietal regions and, between age 6 months and 12 months, most
growth was anteriorly located, resulting in an elongation of the head
shape. In the following period of 12 18 months, the posterior part of
the skull developed more rapidly. Because of the overall slowing of the
growth after 12 months, they looked at a larger time interval of up to
24 months. This showed that most growth was located at the frontal
and posterior parts of the skull. This focus on posterior growth from 12
to 24 months corresponds to the time when toddlers start developing
walking skills, increasing balance and muscle coordination, and
suggests a relationship with the continuing volume increase of the
cerebellum at that time. See also Fig. 5.4 [12].

Fig. 5.4 Growth maps of 3D photographs, illustrating the focus of growth between the different
time intervals. (Reproduced with permission from Elsevier [12])

Meyer-Marcotty et al. looked at the growth patterns of infants’
heads with stereophotogrammetry techniques from age 4 until
10 months. Unfortunately, they did not produce growth maps but
presented 2D measurements such as length, width, cephalic index and
vertex height. Even so, they confirmed the fast growth in the first year
of life, showing that the fastest growth was seen between age 4 and
6 months, with a total head volume increase of 13%. In the time span of
6–8 months, this dropped to 8.6% increase and was only 5.6% between
8 and 10 months. Of importance, they found that the initial relative
increase in head length and head width was equal from 4 to 6 months,
but thereafter the increase in head width was less than head length,
showing a decrease in the cephalic index after 6 months of age. This
was even more pronounced in the timespan of 8 10 months, with a
relative increase of head width of 1% and head length of 2.4% [21]. In
an earlier study of the same group, they looked at the time interval of
6–12 months and found a relative decrease of CI of 2.5% [22].
This finding was also documented by Kuwahara et al. who recently
produced skull growth patterns of Japanese infants based on CT scan
data. They created 6 average’ skull models of infants ranging from age
1 to 17 months producing 2D measurements and detailed 3D growth
patterns, see Figs. 5.5 and 5.6 [19].

Fig. 5.5 The average cranial models of six different age groups, viewed in six directions.
(Reproduced with permission of author [19])

Fig. 5.6 Heat map showing the shortest interplanar distance in the perpendicular direction
between two average models of adjacent age groups. The larger the increase related to growth,
the more reddish the colour will be. (Reproduced with permission of author [19])

In their study, they found the same fast growth up to the age of
5 months as described by Meyer-Marcotty et al. and Meulstee et al. [12,
19, 21] The detailed growth patterns showed a more homogeneous
growth during the early phases (up to the age of 5 months), with the
exception of the occipital region. In the time span from 4–5 to 6–
8 months, they found frontal and occipital growth, leading to a higher
increase in length and elongation of the head with a cephalic index
decrease of 5%. The following period from 6–8 to 9–11 months showed
a higher relative increase of width, with most growth occurring at the
posterior temporal and lower parietal sites. After this short period of
increase in the cephalic index (2.2%), they found for the last period
from 9–11 to 12–17 months again a decrease of the cephalic index of
2%, with growth now focusing on the occipital region [19].

It would be interesting to compare the growth patterns found by
Meulstee et al. and Kuwahara et al. Unfortunately, this is rather difficult
because of the different grouping according to age in both studies.
Being the result of a mathematical difference in the position of vertices
of created average skull/head models for a certain age group, the
presented heat maps of both studies are highly influenced by the
grouping of the original CT scans/stereophotogrammetry data.
However, it looks like the general trend reported by Meulstee et al. is
also reported by Kuwhara et al.: at first a more evenly distributed
growth, followed by a clear growth of frontal and then posterior parts.
Interestingly, when comparing the 2D data of Meulstee et al., MeyerMarcotty et al. and Kuwahara et al., the same trend of increase in length
of the head/skull is seen after 6 months, even when considering that
the study population of Kuwahara et al. displayed a more
brachycephalic head shape overall [12, 19, 22].
To summarize, we can state that skull growth shows a very fast
expansion in the first year of life, with a peculiar fast rate during the
first 6 months of life accommodating the exceptional volumetric
increase of the developing brain. Although studies on skull/head
growth patterns differ in timing and methodology, in general, we can
state that skull growth is more evenly distributed in the first 5–
6 months of life. Thereafter, an elongation of the head occurs, with first
a period of frontal growth up to the age of 8–12 months, followed by a
period of increased posterior and occipital growth up to the age of 17–
18 months (or longer), which is then again followed by frontally located
growth. We hope that more studies with uniform methods regarding
age grouping and larger study groups will elucidate these growth
patterns further in the future.

5 3 Implications for Craniosynostosis
Treatment
Notwithstanding the fast-increasing knowledge about the different
genes that control the proliferation-differentiation balance of the midsutural mesenchyme, there are no medical/genetic therapies yet that
can prevent or cure the premature fusion of sutures in

craniosynostosis. As soon as a suture closes too early, the normal
growth pattern of the skull is disrupted. Because of the lack of growth
potential at the fused suture, the intracranial driving forces (i.e. the
fast-expanding brain) will induce increased growth at the remaining
non-fused sutures and will continue to do so as long as the fused suture
is not treated. Both lack of growth and compensatory growth will in
turn give rise to the well-known deviant head shapes.
It is clear that the uniform growth of the cranial vault is the fastest
during the first 6 months of life. Already half of the total volumetric
growth of the neurocranium has been completed at 6 months after
birth [1]. The cranial vault reaches approximately 86% of its adult size
by 1 year of age and 94% of adult size by 5 years of age [8].
By extension, the influence of a prematurely closed suture on
normal growth and shape development, including the occurrence of
possible compensatory growth, is the greatest in the first 6 months of
life but will continue and slowly diminish after 1 year.
Bearing in mind the functional matrix hypothesis, in which the
expanding intracranial mass is designated the motor for the calvarial
growth by stimulating and inducing growth at the sutures, we strongly
advocate an early re-opening of a prematurely closed suture in order to
restore as fast as possible the normal growth potential of the skull and
limit both the duration of growth restriction and the increasing amount
of compensatory growth.
This argument for very early surgical treatment of craniosynostosis
should, of course, be balanced by the risks and morbidity of the
proposed type of surgery.
The surgical treatment of craniosynostosis can generally be divided
into two main modalities: open cranial vault reconstruction surgery
(OCVRS) and minimally invasive surgery, such as endoscopically
assisted craniosynostosis surgery (EACS) [23]. A detailed description
and comparison of both open and minimally invasive techniques would
exceed the scope of this chapter.
To be brief, OCVRS has been considered the golden standard’ in the
treatment of craniosynostosis for a long time. As it entails large
craniectomies and thorough remodelling of the skull, it is considered a
major surgery and is typically performed at the age of 10–12 months in
order to allow some general body growth to balance the surgical risks.

This means that growth restriction and subsequent compensatory
growth continue upto 10–12 months, possibly leading to disturbing
secondary changes that are not routinely dealt with during primary
surgery (e.g. biparietal widening in trigonocephaly that is not corrected
with a fronto-orbital advancement).
More and more treatment centres, however, are shifting towards the
use of minimally invasive techniques such as EACS. Because of the
much better safety profile, these techniques can be performed in very
young infants and are typically performed around the age of 3–
5 months [24].
In endoscopically assisted suturectomy followed by helmet therapy,
the goal is to shorten the time between sutural closure and re-opening,
reducing the development of progressive cranial deformity. The helmet
moulding therapy then guides the multidirectional driving force of the
expanding cranial mass, without being constrictive, towards the region
that was previously restricted in order to compensate for the inability
to surgically reconstruct the already existing deformity at the time of
surgery.
When comparing our postoperative stereophotogrammetry data of
trigonocephaly patients treated with endoscopically assisted
suturectomy followed by helmet therapy to the normative data of
Meulstee et al., we see a remarkable shift towards a normal growth
pattern, as depicted in Fig. 5.7 [12, 25].

Fig. 5.7 Mean head shapes with heatmaps of the absolute head growth in mm for the
trigonocephaly group (please note the different colour scales). Top-left: Pre-surgery to
6 months post-surgery. Top-right: 6–12 months post-surgery. Middle-left: 12–18 months postsurgery. Middle-right: 18–24 months post-surgery. Bottom-left: 24 months post-surgery to 36–
48 moths post-surgery. Bottom-right: Pre-surgery to 36–48 months post-surgery. (Reproduced
with permission of Elsevier [25])

Directly after surgery, the growth pattern between 0 and 6 months
is quite distinct from the early growth pattern in normal infants (3–
6 months), but the growth pattern at 6–12 months post-surgery is very
similar to the normal growth pattern of infants age 6–9 months! [25].
To summarize, the fast-expanding brain is the motor of the fastgrowing skull, especially in the first 6 months of life. If this normal
growth is limited by the premature closure of a suture, we believe it is
paramount to lift this growth restriction as soon as possible to restore
the normal growth potential and avoid progressive deformation of the
skull. Treatment before the age of 6 months should be the goal and is
only possible if there are no diagnostic delays. Therefore, it is crucial
that every patient in which the diagnosis of craniosynostosis is
suspected is instantly referred to a craniofacial unit for further
diagnosis and treatment.

6 Clinical Diagnosis of
Craniosynostosis: What Is Important
for the Surgeon

6 1 Introduction
When the neurosurgeon is faced with a cranial deformity, a reliable
diagnosis on the ground of the clinical features is possible in the great

majority of cases based on the specific morphological features the skull
develops in case of premature fusion of one or more sutures. However,
the clinician should keep in mind that there are some limitations in the
clinical diagnosis as different nosographic entities can share similar
abnormal features in early life which then can evolve successively with
specific features that characterise distinct syndromes. This is the case
for example in Crouzon syndrome due to the asynchronous closure of
the sutures starting with the fusion of the sagittal suture that may lead
to an early clinical scaphocephaly and progressing later on with the
fusion of the remaining sutures resulting in oxycephaly and specific
facial phenotype. The diagnosis can also be unclear in some newborns
presenting with cranial moulding secondary to a prolonged abnormal
position of the foetus in the intrauterine life, or after a difficult delivery
where the skull deformation can be induced by instrumental
manoeuvres. Patent sutures are mobile at birth and during the first
weeks of life, giving the possibility to mobilise calvarial bones manually
for differential diagnosis. However, in most cases, this type of
mechanical skull deformation tends to resolve spontaneously in the
first weeks of life (Fig. 6.1). Finally, the clinical diagnosis can remain
doubtful in case of partial fusion of a suture as the resulting
deformation might be mild or atypical so requiring further radiological
or echographic exploration.

Fig. 6.1 Cranial molding with the head at birth (a), when the child was referred for suspicion of
scaphocephaly, rapidly dismissed on account of a mobile sagittal suture and the lack of parietal
narrowing, frontal bossing, occipital bullet and temporal narrowing. The deformation corrected
spontaneously in less than a month (b)

6 2 Diagnostic Features
6 2 1 Clinical Diagnosis of the Synostosis
In most of the cases of craniosynostosis, the diagnosis is made at first
glance by evaluating the phenotypic appearance of the head and
possible associated malformations, for example, finger and toes or
external ear. The early fused suture is often seen to bulge under the
scalp or the frontal skin.
Firstly, anamnestic information should be collected, namely the
family history and family tree (familial cases, pregnancy, delivery
modalities, mother’s drugs and father’s age). In some cases, one of the
parents may have a mild form of the same craniosynostosis as their
child, and be unaware of it. The neurosurgeon should inquire about the
growth pattern of the child’s head (rate of increase of its perimeter)
and then evaluate its proportions (horizontal, transverse and vertical
diameters, symmetry and head circumference) as well as the shape and
position of the forehead (bulging, high and flat, retroverted, etc.), the
occiput (bossing, flattening and abnormal increased vertical diameter)
and the temporal regions (protruding and flattened). Also, the
preferred craniocervical posture can provide important information.
The face should also be assessed (symmetry, exorbitism, midface
retrusion, mandible mal-occlusion, etc.).
The different suture-related skull deformities associated with the
most common forms of craniosynostosis have been described
extensively and are well known to the paediatrician, the neurosurgeon
and the craniofacial surgeons. We will review here briefly the key
features of the various types of craniosynostosis that are described in
dedicated chapters of this book extensively.

6.2.1.1 Scaphocephaly
The premature fusion of the sagittal suture results in an elongation of
the skull and its reduction in width. The skull has a boat-shaped
deformation with an increase in the antero-posterior diameter and a

reduced bi-parietal diameter. The ratio between these two dimensions,
the cranial index (CI), is decreased, whereas the head circumference is
compensatory increased. The forehead and the posterior aspect of the
skull may be very prominent. The parietal prominences are often
absent. The vertex of the skull is lowered. A median ridge
corresponding to the fused suture can be apparent in the typical
scaphocephaly. The anterior and posterior fontanels are reduced in size
or even absent. However, the anterior fontanel may remain open in
some subjects, or be even larger than normal and tense in cases of an
associated intracranial hypertension. This finding as well as incipient
ocular bulging are hints of a possible Crouzon’s syndrome.
The degree of head deformation is extremely variable and
sometimes limited to the parieto-occipital aspect of the skull sparing
the forehead. The orbital region is usually within normal limits as are
the maxilla and mandible. However, subtle changes might be present
when some measurements are taken [1]. The cranial index can
sometimes be deceptively normal because of compensatory bulging of
the temporal squama, making the CI a poorly accurate criterion in the
clinical diagnosis of scaphocephaly (Fig. 6.2).

Fig. 6.2 Cranial index (CI) in non-synostotic dolichocephaly (a, b) and in authentic sagittal
synostosis (c, d); the CI is an highly imperfect criterion for the diagnosis

Incomplete fusion of the sagittal suture may result in limited
morphological modifications of the calvaria, which can escape the

correct recognition or delay the clinical diagnosis until restricted
cranial volume becomes apparent at adolescence, on account of
tonsillar herniation or “pseudo-pseudotumour”.

6.2.1.2 Trigonocephaly
The presence of a crest of bone along the metopic suture should be
differentiated from true metopic craniosynostosis as it does not
interfere with the volume of the skull, does not induce malformations of
the neighbouring structures and tends to resolve in time spontaneously.
The hallmark of true trigonocephaly is the keel-like prominence of the
forehead associated with flattened and retruded supraorbital ridges
often resulting in exorbitism. Viewed from above, the forehead is small
and triangular in shape, whereas in the frontal view hypotelorism is a
typical feature. In some infants, the latter is masked by the frequently
associated epicanthal fold, which may give a false aspect of
hypertelorism. A compensatory widening of the temporal regions may
be present too.

6.2.1.3 Frontal Plagiocephaly
Unilateral premature fusion of the coronal suture results in a marked
asymmetry of the skull vault and base because of the reduced
development of the hemicranium on the side of the fused hemicoronal
suture. There is a depression in the supraorbital region on the affected
side that may be associated with an actual or only relative protrusion of
the contralateral side, which is especially apparent when the metopic
suture remains patent. Because of the associated homolateral deviation
of the vomer bone, the cranium appears scoliotic when seen from
above. The homolateral deviation of the vomer bone shows different
degrees of severity from patient to patient from mild to severe and
determines the severity of the cranial base asymmetry together with
the changes of the sphenoidal wings and the anterior displacement of
the nasal bones. Clinically, the changes of the sphenoid account for the
increased vertical diameter and flattening of the orbit, which may result
in the characteristic “harlequin’s eye”, with a recessed orbital rim and a
relatively bulging globe. The anterior displacement of the pyramidal
bone as compared to the contralateral side translates into an anterior
displacement of the ear on the side of the affected suture. While the

bridge of the nose may be attracted towards the affected suture, the
nasal tip is deviated with a variable degree of severity contralaterally.
The mandibular bone is also asymmetrical, its branch being shorter on
the affected side, while the chin is usually deviated contralaterally,
although a significant functional mandibular malocclusion is rare.
Most of the infants and toddlers present with torticollis and a
particular type of squint, due to the higher position of the caruncola.
This torticollis is typically corrected by occlusion of one eye. Older
children often develop an obvious cervico-facial scoliosis and torticollis
on account of the abnormal posture secondary caused by orbital
dystopia and the crossed asymmetry of the cranio-vertebral junction,
the occipital condyle being smaller and the lateral mass of the first
cranial vertebra larger on the affected side.
The rare fronto-shenoidal variant of synostotic anterior
plagiocephaly shows typical features, with a lowered orbit on the
synostotic side, while the chin is deviated towards the synostotic side,
contrary to the classical anterior plagiocephaly caused by unicoronal
synostosis (Fig. 6.3).

Fig. 6.3 Plagiocephaly: facial features and CT-scanner in typical anterior plagiocephaly caused
by unicoronal synostosis (a, b), and the rare variant fronto-sphenoidal synostosis (c, d); note
the inverted facial features, the orbit being displaced upward (a) versus downward (c), and the
chin deviated toward the non-synostotic side (a) versus the synostotic side (c)

6.2.1.4

ambdoid

Similar to hemicoronal synostosis, uni lambdoid synostosis causes an
asymmetry of the hemicranium which is hypoplasic on the affected

side, especially because of the restricted growth of the posterior cranial
vault. The ear on the affected side is drawn backward and downward
compared to the contralateral side. Viewed from above the skull has a
trapezoid shape, different from the parallelogram resulting from the
posterior positional deformation with patent sutures.
In some cases, the deformation of the skull and face can be
influenced by the additional closure of other sutures.

6.2.1.5 Brachycephaly
In children with coronal synostosis, the antero-posterior diameter of
the head is reduced while the transverse diameter is increased. The
forehead is wide, high and flattened in its lower segment with a
retrusion of the supraorbital bar, and bulging in its superior aspect with
upper frontal bossing. Hypertelorism can also be present. In some
cases, the posterior aspect of the skull might be also flattened resulting
in a turricephaly (Fig. 6.4).

Fig. 6.4 Typical turricephalic appearance of bicoronal synostosis (a), with correlated CT
scanner showing closed coronal sutures, and persistent metopic suture accounting for the
widened and flattened forehead (b)

6.2.1.6 Bilambdoid and Sagittal ( Mercedes type)
In the case of fusion of the sagittal and both lambdoid sutures, the skull
is usually short and narrow posteriorly resulting in the so-called “coup
de serpe” (“sickle cut”). The skull can be flattened or even introverted
in the central occipital region at the confluence of the fused lambdoid
and sagittal sutures (Figs. 6.5 and 6.6). The frontal region is usually
enlarged and the coronal sutures are displaced posteriorly. It is
important to note that in some cases the skull might be dolichocephalic
[2].

Fig. 6.5 Synostosis of the right coronal and lambdoid sutures cause by FGFR3 P250 familial
mutation. (a) View from above, note the marked trapezoidal shape, markedly different from
positional deformations

Fig. 6.6 Mercedes type synostosis (lambda region synostosis)

6.2.1.7

xycephaly

In multiple synostoses diagnosed later in infancy and in childhood, the
deformation is characterised by a high and steep forehead with a
depression above the supraorbital bar. A protrusion of the bregmatic
region is often present and gives the head a typical pointed shape. The
antero-posterior diameter is reduced. The nasofrontal angle is often
extremely obtuse. In some cases, the morphology remains harmonious
because all sutures are fused, but the intracranial volume is reduced,
and these missed cases can be diagnosed at the time of visual loss
caused by optic atrophy.

6.2.1.8 Clo erleaf Skull
Also named Kleeblattschaedel or cr ne en tr fle, it describes a very
early manifestation of multiple-suture synostosis resulting in severe
intracranial hypertension. Because all the main sutures are fused, brain
growth causes bulging of the bregmatic and pterional fontanels,
resulting in the typical three-lobed craniofacial aspect. It is associated
with dilated scalp veins, hypotelorism and exorbitism, and a reduced
head circumference.
Having made the positive diagnosis of synostosis, the surgeon needs
to carefully evaluate the clinical status of the child to search for

symptoms and signs related to the restricted skull growth.
The presence of symptoms and signs of raised intracranial pressure
(ICP) needs to be taken into account with great attention due to the risk
of neurological deterioration. Although clinical signs of significantly
increased intracranial pressure may be observed in multiple-suture
synostosis already at a very early stage, in most cases they develop later
on during the first year of age or even later. Stagnating calvarial growth
may precede the clinical evidence of a rise in ICP in multiple-suture
synostosis. Parents and children if old enough should be interrogated
for chronic headaches. The frequency and time of the episodes of
headache should also be noted.
Fundus oculi examination may disclose papilledema and mandate a
complete ophthalmological examination.
In the same way, symptoms and signs compatible with a descent of
cerebellar tonsils in syndromic synostosis, and more rarely, in sagittal
synostosis, as well as breathing difficulties or hearing issues should
prompt a specific ENT examination.

6 2 2 Importance of Evaluating the Anomalies of the
Middle and Lower Face
After examining the skull, it is essential to examine the face in search of
signs of faciostenosis. Indeed, the prognosis will be drastically different
in the case of a faciocraniostenosis compared to a non-syndromic
single-suture synostosis.
All the different types of craniosynostosis can be associated with a
syndrome, where the face might be also affected. Thus, is it essential to
examine the face in all types of synostosis. However, the face can also be
totally normal in syndromic patients. This is especially the case in
bicoronal synostosis, which is rarely non-syndromic.
The essential role of the face shape in establishing the diagnosis is
highlighted by the antenatal diagnosis of the synostoses. Ultrasound
examination allows the analysis of the forehead, orbits and face
permitting a proper diagnosis of faciocranio-synostosis.
The orbits should be carefully examined. Indeed, a proptosis might
be present as well as a hypertelorbitism both suggestive of a syndromic
craniosynostosis. In case of severe proptosis, the complete ocular
occlusion can be impaired, consequently, the integrity of the cornea

should be verified. In most severe cases an early tarsorraphy might be
needed. Ptosis of the eyelids, in most cases unilateral, more rarely
bilateral, is evocative of a TWIST1 or TCF12-related synostosis, and
may require specific treatment when the eyelid impinges on the pupil.
Similarly, anomalies of the ear’s shape, namely the presence of a
crux cymbae, may suggest the just mentioned mutations. In particular, a
hammered and thickened aspect of the upper part of the helix is
suggestive of TCF12 mutation [3, 4] (Fig. 6.7). Muenke’s syndrome,
related to the P250 mutation of FGFR3, which affected specifically the
coronal sutures, also causes sensorineural and/or conductive hearing
loss so that the hearing function should be grossly stimulated during
the evaluation.

Fig. 6.7 Malformations of the conch; (a) typical crux cymbae, characteristic of Twist mutation;
(b) battered and thickened upper of the upper part of the helix, characteristic of TCF12
mutation

The aspect of the nose should be assessed. An enlarged bifid nose
tip can be seen in craniofrontonasal dysplasias. A beaked nose is
associated with syndromic faciosynostosis, such as Crouzon’s
syndrome. However, in infants, the nose may be apparently normal
even in overt syndromic forms. Restricted upper airways can manifest
with mouth breathing. The family should be questioned about the
nocturnal sleep of their infant, with regard in particular to the
occurrence of obstructive sleep apnoeas, poor feeding and recurrent
otitis media caused by the constriction of the Eustachian tube.
A maxillary retrusion with an arched palate and an associated
malocclusion are highly suggestive of a syndromic form. A palatal cleft
can be present and may help compensate for nasal breathing in case of
nasopharyngeal constriction. Hypomaxillia can be present at birth, and
even be evident on prenatal imaging, but it can also develop later in life,
on account of its different growth rate with the calvaria and mandibula.
The mouth shape, the palatal arch and the philtrum length should
be checked (a thin mouth and shallow philtrum being features of foetal
Valproate syndrome associated with metopic synostosis). The
mandible, palate and teeth eruption should also be verified. Delayed
dental eruption and dental anomalies, in general, might be an early sign
of a bone metabolic anomaly [5]. Buccal hygiene should be checked and
encouraged in faciosynostoses because orthodontic treatments, which
will be the first step before orthognathic surgery, cannot proceed with
poorly maintained teeth.

6 2 3 Importance of Extracranial Features
The examination of the child should not be limited to the head. Indeed,
some anomalies in the extremities might be present in children with
synostosis and might be an indication of the presence of an underlying
syndrome.
Hands and feet should be examined for syndactyly, in the form of
paddle-shaped extremities, or a subtle membranous syndactyly. The
shape of the fingers and toes should be also carefully assessed for
brachydactyly, clinodactyly or abnormal thumbs or big toes. The
presence of a palmar crease should also be taken into account as an
indicator of possible underlying syndromes.

In case of deformation of the hands and feet in Apert syndrome, the
family should be instructed on the necessity of early specific
management. Similarly, in some genetic syndromes involving midline
craniosynostosis, especially trigonocephaly (smad6-related
trigonocephaly for instance), the opportunity of a cardiac evaluation
should be suggested because of the possible associated cardiac
malformations.

6 3 Limits of the Clinical Diagnosis
The clinical diagnosis of the synostosis is usually based on the
phenotypic appearance. However, the improvement of neuroimaging
investigations and the availability of echoencephalography as well
molecular analyses may overcome the limits of mere clinical
observation contributing to the correct diagnosis, especially in doubtful
cases. In fact, especially in the neonatal period some syndromes cannot
be diagnosed with certainty as their typical phenotypic appearance will
develop only later, such as in Crouzon syndrome in which some sutures
fuse and the facial anomalies become obvious only in a late phase of the
clinical course. Also, the closure of the sagittal synostosis, which
characterises some metabolic forms of craniosynostosis [6, 7], occurs in
a late phase without affecting significantly the shape of the head. In all
these cases, and more broadly whenever the diagnosis remains
doubtful, the clinical evaluation should be coupled with laboratory
investigations, namely genetic and metabolic tests and neuroimaging
studies when necessary.
Ultrasound examination may confirm or rule out the closure of the
sagittal suture in the case of a newborn with a dolichocephalic skull
without the necessity of irradiating the child. The exam could also
detect an associated ventricular enlargement. Ultrasounds, computed
tomography scanners (TDM) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is
widely used in order to assess abnormally enlarged or compressed
cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) spaces, the presence of bony spiculae or
craniolacuniae, cerebral abnormalities, namely cerebellar tonsillar
herniation, that can be associated in particular with syndromic
synostosis but might also be present in single suture synostosis, and
also study the cerebral circulation, in particular the venous drainage.

6 4 Importance of Follow-Up
6 4 1 Evolution in Time
The evaluation of a child with craniosynostosis and to a certain extent
the diagnosis-making process are somehow a dynamic process as the
disease and its clinical features evolve over time. This concept is
established for specific syndromes but is not yet fully understood for all
forms of craniosynostosis. Typically, the synostosis is progressive in
Crouzon syndrome, where the sutures fuse also in a late phase of
development, as well as in TWIST1-related synostosis that can also
progress and has the potential risk of developing a pansynostosis,
affecting sutures that were patent at birth. Metabolic synostoses also
have a chronic evolution and develop in children despite a previously
normal skull. Consequently, prolonged follow-up is necessary, even in
subjects who have been operated on. Such control should not be limited
to the evolution of the cranial sutures but should involve other organs
of the body and cognitive development.
Delayed teeth eruption might for instance suggest a metabolic
disorder that might become overt only after the surgery. Some other
features related to bone metabolism need also to be checked during the
follow-up of children with craniosynostosis, in particular the possibility
of late long bone anomalies. Leg bowing in toddlers are potential sign of
abnormal phosphocalcic metabolism as in vitamin-resistant rickets that
can be associated with metabolic craniosynostosis and treated prior to
the associated bone alterations leading to the correct but delayed
recognition of the syndrome.
Melanodermia, a hallmark of FGFR3-related Crouzon syndrome, will
become evident with time (Fig. 6.8). The parents and the child should
be informed of such an evolution.

Fig. 6.8 Melanodermia caused by acanthosis nigricans, associated with FGFR3-related Crouzon
syndrome

Indeed, missing an underlying syndrome bears the potential risk of
inappropriate management as well as incomplete understanding by the
parents of its consequences [5].

Also, some anomalies of the brain may develop in a late phase of the
disease; the most known of these is the progressive descent of the
cerebellar tonsils, absent at birth in Crouzon’s syndrome or in some
metabolic craniosynostoses. The phenomenon is progressive and may
remain ignored until causing neurological dysfunction or
syringomyelia. Thus, closer follow-up controls, coupling clinical
examination and MRI investigations until the end of statural growth are
mandatory in most syndromic cases. The early genetic confirmation of
an underlying mutation might also allow anticipating the potential
evolution: for instance, the risk of future closure of other sutures (high
in some syndromic FGFR2-related syndromes) or the risk of
postoperative recurrence of the synostosis (high in Twist1 mutation).
Cognitive development might also be hindered either by the
synostosis itself or by an associated underlying condition. The
incidence of cognitive delay is relatively known for some syndromic
synostosis, e.g. Apert’s syndrome but it is still unclear for many types of
craniosynostoses, the single suture craniosynostoses being included.
Cognitive impairment and learning difficulties are often diagnosed
when the child enters school. Consequently, specific management
(ergotherapy, speech therapy, etc.) and school adaptations are adopted
in several cases relatively late, especially if the early post-operative
controls do not address cognition appropriately, starting already in the
first years of life.
The recognition of neurodevelopmental impairment in an
apparently isolated single suture synostosis should prompt a thorough
genetic evaluation for an underlying genetic condition. Indeed, some
gene mutations are nowadays known to be associated with cognitive
impairment and synostosis (e.g. SMAD6).

6 4 2 Interest of Clinical Classification Coupled with
Genetic Analysis
As mentioned earlier, the proper diagnosis and classification of the
synostosis are of paramount importance for the individual patient, in
order to assess and tailor his individual management, and also to
analyse clinical series and long-term results. The lack of specific
investigations in most of the past series makes them relatively useless

for understanding the role of surgical treatment in avoiding the
secondary effects of the disease.
Even today different nomenclatures and classifications of
craniosynostosis are still based essentially on the type of fused suture
and the type of deformation, consequently limiting the meaning of
clinical reports in terms of neurological and cognitive development.
Indeed, underlying genetic mutations that may participate significantly
in the functional outcome independently from the synostotic aspects
and their surgical management are investigated in only a minority of
cases [8, 9].
The ideal classification should merge the clinical and anatomical
description, which is necessary for management purposes, to the
potential underlying genetic mutation that may impact the patient’s
development. Outcome studies of genetically defined cohorts are
necessary to help foresee the outcome of operation on children with
craniosynostosis and predict their future cognitive development.
Unfortunately, currently, the genetic workup frequently identifies
new gene variants of unknown significance or incomplete penetrance
[10].
In its present state, this new knowledge does not allow us to
establish any reliable prognosis. In the future, a better definition of the
associated phenotypes could help to validate the clinical significance of
these new variants.

7 Sagittal Suture Synostosis: Key Points
for Surgeons and Management
Principles (Diagnosis, Surgical
Considerations and Timing)
Michael M. McDowell1 , Ian F. Pollack1 , Michael R. Bykowski2 and
Jesse A. Goldstein2
(1) Departments of Neurological Surgery, UPMC Children’s Hospital of
Pittsburgh, University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, Pittsburgh,
PA, USA
(2) Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, UPMC Children’s Hospital of
Pittsburgh, University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, Pittsburgh,
PA, USA

Michael M McDowell
Email: mcdowellmm2@upmc.edu
Ian F Pollack (Corresponding author)
Email: ian.pollack@chp.edu
Michael R Bykowski
Email: michael.bykowski@chp.edu

Keywords Sagittal suture – Synostosis – Scaphocephaly – Nonsyndromic

7 1 Introduction
Sagittal synostosis (SS) represents 40–60% of all surgically treated
craniosynostosis diagnoses and has a prevalence of approximately 1 in
4000–5000 live births [1–5]. Non-syndromic SS affects male patients in
approximately 75–80% of cases [6–9]. Sagittal synostosis is widely
recognized by the scaphocephalic or synostotic dolichocephalic, cranial
morphology, in which the premature closure of the sagittal suture
results in the relative elongation of the cranium in the anteriorposterior direction. An underlying genetic syndrome is identified in less
than 3% of cases [8]. The causal factor of sporadic cases is frequently
unclear but may reflect a combination of genetic predisposition and
metabolic and environmental factors.

7 1 1 Embryology and Natural History
Craniosynostosis is a dysfunction specific to the membranous type of
bone formation, a mechanism most associated with skull and other flat
bone development [10]. The common mechanism purported for
craniosynostosis is based on an imbalance of osteoblast and osteoclast
function, in which excessive osteoblast function is not proportionately
compensated for by osteoclastic activity. This results ultimately in
premature fusion of one or more sutures. Under normal conditions, the
sutures function as the growth centers of each bony plate of the
neurocranium which is driven by underlying brain volume and
pulsation [6, 11, 12]. Rarely, overdrainage in a neonate with a
ventricular shunt may result in premature suture fusion due to a
reduction in pressure exerted on the skull from the brain [13, 14]. This
phenomenon, in addition to craniosynostosis from other reductions in
brain volume or pressure such as peri-natal stroke, is known as
secondary craniosynostosis [6]. Sagittal synostosis restricts skull
growth along the midline between the fontanelles, resulting in relative
overgrowth at other sutures, producing cranial deformity due to excess
elongation of the skull relative to its width. Some authors have
hypothesized an association between SS and dysfunction of language,
speech, memory, and executive function due to a negative effect on the
dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, but data to support this are sparse and
typically not specific to SS [3, 15–17]. A direct correlation between

intracranial pressure or the timing of surgery and neurocognitive
outcomes remains controversial [18–20].

7 2 Diagnosis
The diagnosis of SS is typically made clinically based on the presence of
scaphocephaly and often a palpably closed sagittal suture, ridging, or
subtle depression between the fontanelles known as a saddle deformity
or clinocephaly. During the first year of life, the deformity produced in
severe cases is particularly noticeable in part due to the potential for
low hair volume combined with the disproportionate size of the head
relative to the infant’s body [6]. It is our preference to obtain a low-dose
volumetric CT scan with 3D post-processing imaging for surgical
planning and long-term post-operative comparisons, although some
sites will rely on clinical diagnosis alone [21, 22]. CT imaging helps to
ensure the appropriate diagnosis of other suture fusions and rule out
nonsynostotic scaphocephaly, and is typically of high enough resolution
to identify major parenchymal abnormalities such as Chiari
malformation which may be associated with craniosynostosis [18, 23].
Other commonly seen associated conditions with SS include extra-axial
fluid collections (25%) and copper-beaten skull morphology (3%) [8].
Surgically relevant anatomic characteristics such as sagittal sinus or
large emissary vein exposure through atypical bony defects may also be
detected.
Despite the classic appearance of single suture synostoses, studies
have shown that the presence of additional undiagnosed suture fusions
can occur in 2–7% of cases overall [8]. In a study including 235 patients
with a clinical diagnosis of SS and a pre-operative CT, Ravinda et al.
found that patients with SS were the most likely to have additional
suture involvement of all presumed single suture clinical diagnoses,
with 8% of patients having one or more additional suture fusion. In
addition, six patients with clinical diagnoses of SS were ultimately
found to have a syndromic condition [8]. Magnetic resonance imaging is
not routinely obtained in the absence of other clinical findings of
concern.

7 3 Operative Decision-Making and Timing
Sagittal synostosis is broadly divided into “early presentation” and “late
presentation” categories, with the former consisting of children with
characteristic scaphocephalic head shapes at or shortly following birth
and the latter consisting of children who initially have relatively normal
head shapes that either become somewhat scaphocephalic with time or
remain relatively normocephalic but are noted on imaging for
headaches or after head injuries to have sagittal synostosis. For
children who present with obvious scaphocephaly in infancy, the
management focuses on deformity correction and in untreated cases,
on the detection and treatment of increased intracranial pressure,
whereas in those older children with sagittal synostosis in the setting of
a relatively normal head shape, intervention centers on identifying and,
if needed, treating elevated intracranial pressure.
For children with obvious deformities, early detection and referral
of SS are critical to ensure the most versatile opportunity for
individualized decision-making in order to take advantage of the
doubling of brain volume in the first 6 months of life and again by
2 years of age. There are two main indications for surgical correction of
SS: to improve appearance and to prevent or treat intracranial
hypertension. Studies have shown a negative cosmetic perception of
untreated synostosis from both clinicians and lay-persons [24].
Uncorrected SS may result in significant impairment in self-esteem and
socialization. However, a subset of parents elect expectant
management, based on their belief that the esthetic issue may stabilize
later in life after the completion of head growth, thickening of the scalp,
hair growth, and the reduction in head size relative to body size [6]. In
such patients, the development of intracranial hypertension provides a
more pressing indication for intervention at later time points. At a
mean age of 1 year, one cohort of untreated patients with SS who
underwent intracranial pressure monitoring were found to have
developed intracranial hypertension (15 mmHg or greater) in 13.4% of
cases overall; this phenomenon was observed in approximately 25% of
patients older than 1 year [25]. Whether 15 mmHg is an appropriate
threshold is a matter of some debate, but it is clear that a substantial
portion of children do suffer significant intracranial pressure elevations

well beyond the normal range that can have adverse visual and
cognitive sequelae, making surgical intervention more than simply a
cosmetic consideration.
For those children with obvious scaphocephaly, the management
options vary depending on the age of the patient and the nature of the
deformity. It is imperative that parents are disabused of the notion that
one approach is the “right” treatment, since over the years many
approaches have been found to yield excellent outcomes with
acceptable morbidity. Rather, parents should be counseled that both
less-invasive (endoscopic) approaches and open remodeling techniques
are valid approaches with different strengths and weaknesses that
must be considered in the context of the patient and family in question.
For example, if the child has a physical or behavioral issue that might
complicate the consistent usage of a molding helmet, open correction at
an older age or the use of a spring-mediated cranioplasty may be more
optimal.
Although the senior neurosurgeon has done a variety of open
approaches over the years in infants younger than 6 months, including
open sagittal strip craniectomy with mid-parietal and posterior parietal
wedge osteotomies or barrel stave osteotomies [26], and pi and reverse
pi techniques [27], and such approaches are well described in the
literature, it has been our preference in recent years to perform
minimally invasive/endoscopic strip craniectomy with either postoperative helmeting or spring placement in patients between 3–
6 months of age. The strategy behind this is well described by previous
authors [28–31], and our main innovations (described and illustrated
in the spring-mediated cranioplasty chapter), are (1) to accomplish the
procedure through a small, well-placed vertex incision, rather than two
separate anterior and posterior incisions, to minimize later cosmetic
sequelae in patients who may have receding hair lines later in life and
(2) to use a diamond burr to achieve bone-thinning and hemostasis
over the thick posterior sagittal ridge, simplifying the craniectomy. The
general concepts and illustrations in that chapter apply also to
craniectomy with helmeting, rather than springs. The preferred timing
follows recovery from the transient anemia of infancy that can mark the
transition from fetal to adult hemoglobin [32, 33]. One multi-center
study found the addition of 33 min of total surgical time for the second-

stage spring removal [9], which counterbalances the time commitment
and need for compliance with helmet usage that factor into family and
surgical decision-making for a given child.
Conceptually, all of the above approaches are considered “early”
surgeries and take advantage of the intrinsic growth potential of the
brain and pliability of the infant skull to achieve a desirable outcome.
The exact consequences of earlier, shorter anesthesia versus later,
longer anesthesia in children under the age of 1 year remain under
investigation, but the current literature suggests a favorable risk profile
in terms of the development of neurocognitive dysfunction and lower
IQ due to general anesthesia, provided it is limited in duration.
Specifically, good outcomes have been reported in one prospective
multicenter study by McCann et al. focused on children in early infancy
exposed to approximately an hour of anesthesia and followed until age
five [6, 34–37]. Patient families should be counseled that early
endoscopic techniques with molding helmets or springs have
advantages that include shorter average anesthesia and hospitalization
times, lower blood loss, and smaller scars [3, 38, 39]. However, these
approaches result in anesthesia exposure at an earlier age compared to
open techniques [33, 40]. Families should be counseled on the potential
minor dermatological complications such as alopecia from nearly fulltime helmet use, and the need for a second short surgery if a springmediated approach is used. Additional factors that may inhibit
endoscopic intervention with postoperative helmeting in some regions
are the availability of insurance to cover the cost of helmeting and easy
accessibility to orthotists for helmet adjustments. Because the minor
second procedure is required for spring removal if that option is
pursued, some families may simply opt for an open strip resection or a
deformity-targeted approach with more intraoperative recontouring in
slightly older infants, and it is important that the surgeon is
comfortable with all the various options, and their pros and cons. From
a financial standpoint, however, multiple studies have suggested that
the overall cost, including indirect costs such as missed work and
travel, tends to strongly favor endoscopic cases, with the cost of the
endoscopic surgery alone averaging over 11,000 less than open cases
in one study [3, 39, 41, 42].

In contrast to early surgeries, later procedures are typically open
operations. Although some surgeons will perform less-extensive
surgeries, such as pi or other extended strip approaches in children
slightly older than 6 months, the diminishing growth potential with age
generally necessitates more extensive surgeries as time goes on,
particularly after 9–12 months. In patients who present closer to 1 year
of age or develop symptoms of intracranial pressure later in childhood,
it is our recommendation to pursue an open cranial remodeling
procedure due to the reduced growth potential to drive remodeling
from less-invasive operations. These more extensive surgeries typically
result in greater blood loss and thus are generally performed at age
6 months or older, although the lower age cutoff varies between centers
[3]. The anesthesia time and hospital stay are greater and the scalp
incision more extensive. Open approaches typically result in a more
immediate cranial expansion, but the clinical and cosmetic
consequences of this versus earlier less-invasive interventions are
unclear.
A number of studies have suggested that cranial index scores in
particular seem to be comparable despite the differences in the
operative technique and timing of surgery [24, 39, 40]. However, others
have questioned the utility of craniometric metrics in SS beyond a
general confirmation of morphological impact. In particular, the outer
head circumference may overestimate the inner volume in SS, resulting
in overcorrection [43]. More complex metrics such as the Rotterdam
scaphocephaly morphology score (RSMS) have been proposed that use
a graded rating of specific features such as frontal bossing, temporal
pinching, and vertex height, but these are cumbersome and ultimately
subjective despite their effectiveness at correlating to correction [43].
One study by Lepard et al. suggested a slight, statistically significant
increase in aesthetic outcomes at a median of 20 months postoperatively, perceived both by professionals and laypeople, in favor of
endoscopic repair, but the interrater and intrarater reliabilities were
low, the mean outcomes for each group favorable, the choice of open
procedure varied, and the confounding factor of scar prominence may
have affected the perception of cranial deformity [24]. A contrasting
study by Millesi et al. reported that at 12 months post-operatively, the
cosmetic outcome was rated as good or excellent by 89% of caregivers

and 97% of surgeons for open procedures, with 73% of caretakers
feeling the head shape was completely normal. Multiple studies have
suggested similar cosmetic outcomes and surgical complications,
though some have reported a lower rate of revision surgery in
endoscopic cases [3, 33, 40, 44]. However, this may reflect substantial
differences in patient selection, particularly when factoring in the
reduced capacity for further head growth to drive expansion in many
open cases.
Also complicating comparison between procedures is that many
children who undergo early surgery have unmistakably severe
deformity at birth, whereas those undergoing later surgery may have
more subtle findings that are initially missed or may present with
relatively normal craniometric parameters, but signs of increased
intracranial pressure.

7 4 Operative Technique
7 4 1 Endoscopic Surgery
The patient is placed prone with the head secured in a horseshoe and
generous local anesthetic with epinephrine injected into the scalp after
being scrubbed with a chlorhexidine brush. The head of the bed is
rotated 180° away from the anesthesia team. The scalp is the
generously sterilized with betadine solution after the incision is
marked out. It is our preference to make a 2–3 cm incision just anterior
to the midpoint between fontanelles to allow for most of the
endoscopic work to be done in a single direction (Figures and caveats
for this are provided in the Spring-Mediated Cranioplasty
chapter). The scalp is incised down to galea sharply and both edges are
then elevated with skin hooks. Spot hemostasis is performed as needed
and the pericranium is separated bluntly from the galea along the
intended craniectomy pathway. Two lines are made off the midline
bilaterally with needle electrocautery, marking out the 1 cm bony strip
to be removed. A burr hole is drilled at the posterior edge of the
incision and off the midline to avoid directly drilling on the sagittal
sinus. The dura is dissected off of the adjacent bone with a modified
Penfield 4. A Kerrison ronguer is used to extend the burr hole along the
demarcated bone anteriorly. It is our preference to always perform the

craniectomy first in the dependent direction to prevent additional
pooling of blood in the operative field from bony edges in the caudal
aspect of the craniectomy. Skin hooks can be used to shift the scalp
forward to allow for a greater length of removal with sequential dural
dissection. We find that dependent suturectomy is best extended to the
fontanelle predominantly with rongeurs via scalp retraction with skin
hooks or a lighted retractor. The use of endoscopy in the reverse
direction can be disorienting, and in severe cases that require extensive
anterior and posterior visualization, we use endoscope monitors at
both the head and foot of the patient to allow normal viewing
orientation in both directions. However, in most cases, an endoscope
monitor is only required at the foot of the patient for the posterior
craniectomy.
The lighted endoscope is then inserted by a co-surgeon and
additional bites with a small eye rongeur are taken after extending the
dural dissection. It is our experience that the utilization of sinus
instrumentation greatly reduces the time and difficulty of distal
suturectomy. Once the comfortable reach of the rongeur has been
exceeded, a straight Blakesley Thru-Cut forcep (Karl Storz, Germany) is
utilized to take additional midline bites. Curved Blakesley Ethmoid
forceps (Karl Storz, Germany) can be used to add additional lateral
width to the suturectomy distally if the Thru-Cut is obstructed. The
dura is sequentially dissected as the suturectomy is further extended. It
is critical to withdraw the endoscope intermittently to better visualize
the course being taken. It is our experience that surgeons typically veer
off over time away from the side of their dominant hand without
intermittent correction. The sagittal sinus can serve as a good guide to
the midline as well, but can become increasingly difficult to visualize
during the distal portions of endoscopic work due to the increasingly
parallel view of the endoscope relative to the dura. In some cases, the
bone thickness may be difficult to address with sinus instruments. By
using the endoscope to retract the scalp and a suction tip to retract the
dura, this bone can be drilled down to the inner cortex safely under
irrigation with a 4 mm coarse diamond round drill bit. A short, angled
drill handle (Stryker, Kalamazoo, MI) is more ergonomic and allows for
more distal access. This is also helpful in addressing bone bleeding, as
the coarse diamond bit provides a cauterizing effect. Depending on the

angle, the drill or Thru-Cut can be used to complete the inner cortex
craniectomy efficiently until the fontanelle is reached. The parietal
bones are palpated through the scalp while being visualized with the
endoscope to confirm appropriate mobility. In some cases, the parietal
bones are insufficiently mobilized despite extending the suturectomy
from fontanelle to fontanelle. In this case, the proximal lambdoid
sutures may be dissected off of the dura, and additional suturectomy
performed until the mobility is satisfactory. Depending on the operative
plan, distractor springs may be inserted at this point of the procedure.
It is important if springs are to be applied that the thickness of the bone
along the suturectomy be examined. Particularly in young patients the
bone may be insufficiently resistant to allow for spring insertion
without subsequent erosion and the operative plan may require
revision to a helmet-assisted approach, where a slightly wider (2 cm
versus 1 cm) craniectomy may be preferable. The dura should also be
inspected to ensure a sufficiently wide dissection off of the bone to
prevent inadvertent dural injury with the insertion of the spring
footplates. The scalp is then closed in a standard fashion with
absorbable sutures.

7 4 2 Open Surgery
Since its initial description by Lane in the 1890s, open treatment of
craniosynostosis has had numerous variations of fluctuating popularity
that can be generally characterized as cranial vault expansion with or
without recontouring [45]. Major factors in the determination of
operative planning of an open procedure are the timing of surgery, the
nature of the deformity, and the presence of increased intracranial
pressure. While open surgery is more effective than endoscopic surgery
in older patients, some open procedures still make use of remaining
skull growth potential, whereas others are better suited to SS that was
missed until later in childhood or in cases of late onset SS.
It is our preference to make a zig-zag incision bilaterally starting
just anterior and superior to the pinna, ensuring partial exposure of the
temporalis muscles, adjusting the curve to best reflect the cranial
target. For patients presenting earlier than 9 months in which an open
approach is taken, we prefer to perform a modified pi procedure. Burr
holes are made lateral to a 3 cm strut of bone covering the sagittal sinus

and a linear cut is made parallel to the strut, spanning the distance
between each fontanelle. Barrel stave osteotomies are performed every
2–3 cm extending laterally to the extent allowed by the soft tissue
exposure or the limits of the cranial vault. Each bony strip is then bent
outward using a heavy needle driver or Tessier bone bender.
For patients greater than 9 months of age but still within the skull
growth period, a deformity-focused approach is taken. This includes
extended frontal-orbital advancement and expansion; posterior vault
recontouring with the approach noted in the prior paragraph combined
with an occipitotemporal craniotomy and bone remodeling to provide
sagittal shortening and coronal widening; biparietal “clam-shell” and
barrel-stave expansions; and a frontoparietal/occipitotemporal
“switch” cranioplasty approach. These techniques and related
variations are discussed in more detail in later chapters. In selected
cases with significant deformity of both the frontal and occipital
regions, a total calvarial reconstruction [46] or a staged approach may
be undertaken. In many cases, families are most concerned about a
particular aspect, such as the frontal bossing and biparietal narrowing
which can be addressed with an anteriorly or posteriorly focused
reconstructive strategy, avoiding the potentially increased morbidity of
a total calvarial reconstructive approach.
A special situation relates to those children who present with a
relatively normal head shape and size, with increased intracranial
pressure associated with presumed late-onset sagittal synostosis. Such
children typically present with headaches and have evidence of
papilledema or findings of significantly increased intracranial pressure
on invasive monitoring. For patients presenting with little or no
deformity after the majority of skull growth has been achieved, we
focus on achieving a significant expansion without dramatically altering
their appearance. In such cases, we have generally proceeded with a
“mid-vault” bilateral parietal craniotomy with barrel staves directed
toward the frontal, temporal, and parieto-occipital regions for
circumferential expansion (Fig. 7.1). Bi-parietal craniotomies are
elevated, leaving a midline 3 cm strut of bone covering the sagittal
sinus. Barrel stave osteotomies are performed every 2–3 cm
circumferentially, except toward the midline, to the extent allowed by
the soft tissue exposure or the limits of the cranial vault. Each bony

strip is then partially out fractured or bent depending on the rigidity
using a large needle driver or Tessier bone bender. The bone flaps are
then secured using resorbable plates and screws to the midline strut
and sutures are used laterally to secure the bone flaps to the barrel
staves. In some instances where late-onset increased pressure occurs in
the context of a metabolic disorder with bone thickening associated
with sagittal synostosis, endocranial thinning is used to further expand
the intracranial volume [47].

Fig. 7.1 Operative photo of middle vault expansion with bilateral parietal craniotomies and
barrel staves (left). Simplified depiction of the cuts made (middle). Post-reconstruction photo
(right)

7 5 Complication Avoidance
Synostosis surgeries are by their nature high-risk surgeries, with the
potential for life-threatening blood loss as the most serious
complication. Avoidance necessitates vigilance in intraoperative
monitoring, having adequate intravenous lines for blood infusion,
immediate availability of blood in the operating room, and care during
the dissection of dura from the bone. Adherence of the sinus to the
bone or extension through the bone requires particular attention to
dissection. Likewise, a subset of children will have sizeable bridging
veins between the dura and bone, which must be identified, coagulated,
and divided, regardless of whether the exposure is being done in an
open or endoscopic fashion. Venous blood loss can often be controlled
with judicious head elevation, but that must be balanced with the risk

of air embolism, another potentially life-threatening complication,
particularly in the setting of hypovolemia. Treatment requires lowering
the head, filling the field with saline, and waxing of the bone edges.
Other complications that can occur include brain injury and dural
tears. For the former, it is essential to exercise care in separating the
dura from the bone and minimize excessive retraction. This in part
applies to the latter as well; particular caution is required when
stripping dura that is adherent to a nonclosed suture during extended
calvarial expansion techniques. Our preference is to close any visible
defect primarily, to avoid the risks of a growing leptomeningeal cyst or
late cerebrospinal fluid leakage from the wound. Infection is
uncommon with these procedures, but by no means rare, even with the
use of careful aseptic technique and perioperative antibiotics. Helpful
tactics to avoid this complication are to minimize areas of bone, plate,
screw, or spring prominence adjacent to the incision to limit stress on
the incision line and the potential for erosion of the skin at nearby
pressure points.
Late events that should also be considered are the presence of
associated hydrocephalus and the need for further surgical
intervention. In children with underlying syndromic or metabolic
etiologies for their sagittal synostosis who present primarily with
increased intracranial pressure, it is essential to follow them closely for
the resolution of papilledema. In some instances, patients with
syndromic or metabolic etiologies will also have impaired CSF
absorption or cranial venous outflow obstruction, and will have
persistent papilledema, with a pseudotumor-like pattern of little or no
ventriculomegaly. In such children, secondary shunt insertion may be
required. Although postoperative reclosure of the sagittal suture line or
other cranial openings is not uncommon after correction, a minority of
patients require additional surgery [26, 29, 33]. They nonetheless
require ongoing follow-up until approximately 8 years of age, when
most cranial growth has been completed. A small percentage of
children, ranging from 3 to 5% in most large series, will require a
secondary cranial expansion surgery, either for recurrent cosmetic
deformity or late onset of increased intracranial pressure or a
symptomatic Chiari malformation. A subset of these children will have
a mild form of an underlying craniofacial syndrome that only becomes

apparent in retrospect, but others will have no discernible genetic
etiology. Although this is not a complication that can necessarily be
avoided, it is one that can be anticipated and managed expeditiously,
before the onset of visual loss or other sequelae. This highlights the
importance of conscientious craniofacial follow-up, even for the most
straightforward cases of sagittal synostosis.

7 6 Conclusions
The management of sagittal synostosis is aided by multiple operative
approaches that allow for satisfactory cosmesis and, where needed, the
alleviation of intracranial hypertension. An individualized approach
should be taken based on patient’s age, deformity, presence or absence
of increased intracranial pressure, and family factors and preferences,
recognizing that there is no single “right” approach to patient
management. The most critical step in management is to ensure early
diagnosis and work-up to allow for the greatest flexibility in operative
management. In some cases, with late-onset synostosis, this can be
challenging, and dependent upon the availability of high-resolution
imaging, reliable ophthalmology assessments, and in some cases
intracranial pressure monitoring. Pre-operative CT imaging and genetic
testing are commonly performed at our site in order to screen for
concomitant synostoses and syndromic conditions, which may
influence surgical planning.
