Keywords Metopic craniosynostosis – Trigonocephaly – Fronto-orbital
advancement – Endoscopic suturectomy – Craniofacial

Metopic craniosynostosis, premature fusion of the metopic suture,
causes the abnormal head shape described as trigonocephaly. It
accounts for approximately 5–10% of all single-suture synostoses, with
a prevalence of approximately 1 in 15,000 children. Metopic
craniosynostosis is sporadic in approximately 75% of cases, though up
to 5% of patients have a positive family history, without a known
underlying genetic defect; the other 25% are syndromic, associated
with Jacobsen/11q23 deletion, chromosome 9p deletion, Opitz C
syndromes, and other aneuploidies. Metopic craniosynostosis has also
been associated with other congenital malformations, including
neuromuscular dysfunction and developmental delay, but without a
specific syndromic diagnosis. The metopic suture physiologically closes
by 9 months of age, though normal closure can occur as early as
3 months.

8 1 Diagnosis
8 1 1 Clinical Exam
Initial diagnosis of metopic suture synostosis, as with any
craniosynostosis, is based on clinical exam findings. From the vertex
view, the head is noted to be triangular in shape, with a keel deformity
of the forehead, resulting in pseudohypotelorism, anterior
displacement of the coronal sutures, posterior displacement of the
superolateral orbital rims, temporal narrowing, flattening of the frontal
bones, and compensatory bulging of the parieto-occipital region (Fig.
8.1). The anterior fontanelle is also triangular in shape, with a flat edge
anteriorly. Because metopic synostosis is a symmetric deformity, more
subtle cases may go undiagnosed. It is important to differentiate
metopic craniosynostosis from metopic ridging associated with the
physiological closure of the suture which occurs in about one-third of
people. The former is treated with surgical cranial vault expansion
while the latter does not require surgery.

Fig. 8.1 Vertex view of the head. Note the triangular in shape, keel deformity of the forehead,
anterior displacement of the coronal sutures, posterior displacement of the superolateral
orbital rims, temporal narrowing, flattening of the frontal bones, and compensatory bulging of
the parieto-occipital region

8 1 2 Imaging
The imaging modality of choice for workup of any craniosynostosis is a
three-dimensional computed tomography (CT) scan. This radiological
study is not only diagnostic but can also be used to help guide surgical
management and planning. The 3D CT scan provides a detailed look at
the fused suture, overall head shape, and facial and skull base
deformities (Fig. 8.2).

Fig. 8.2 Three3-dimensional computed tomography (CT) scan. The 3D CT scan provides a
detailed look at the fused suture, overall head shape, and facial and skull base deformities

8 2 Decision Making
Previous studies have shown that 8–13% of patients with single suture
synostosis develop elevated ICP ( 15 mmHg); however, to date, there is
no way of predicting which patients will fall into this category.
Therefore, early surgical intervention is advocated for children with
metopic, as well as other forms of craniosynostoses, in order to make
adequate room for normal brain growth and development. The surgical
intervention also provides the patient with the best esthetic outcome to
alleviate the psychosocial impact a skull deformity may cause.

8 3 Surgical Technique
Most craniofacial centers of excellence offer both open cranial vault
remodeling (fronto-orbital advancement) and endoscopic techniques.
The pros and cons of each are discussed in more detail in the following
sections. Often the decision is based on the age of the patient at the
time of diagnosis. In cases where the family has the option to proceed
with endoscopic treatment or wait until the child is old enough to
undergo a fronto-orbital advancement, the decision comes down to the
severity of the deformity, surgeon preference, and family preference.

8 3 1 Fronto-Orbital Advancement (FOA)
While a detailed discussion of the operative procedure itself is beyond
the scope of this chapter, there are important surgical principles to
keep in mind. Fronto-orbital advancement is a major operative
procedure, with anticipated blood loss, and as such, involves the
collaboration of a skilled and experienced pediatric anesthesiology
team. The procedure should be done under general anesthesia, with at
least two good IVs, an arterial line, a Foley, and precordial Doppler
monitoring. All patients should have cross-matched blood available
prior to the start of the surgery.
The patient is positioned supine, with the head on a padded
horseshoe headrest. Per the preference of the family, either the entire
head, or a wide strip is shaved, and a zigzag bicoronal incision is
marked out. The zigzag incision results in better cosmesis of scalp
alopecia, with the bicoronal approach allowing for access all the way to
the nasion. The scalp flaps are elevated in the subperiosteal plane along
with the temporalis muscle, anteriorly to the superior orbital rims and
laterally to the temporal fossa. If the supraorbital neurovascular
bundles are within a true foramen as opposed to a notch, this must be
opened with an osteotome in order to release the bundle and protect
the nerves bilaterally.
The planned craniotomy cuts can be drawn out with a bone pencil
(Fig. 8.3a). A bifrontal craniotomy is performed, with special care taken
when dissecting in the epidural plane along the midline. The epidural
space is then dissected underneath the parietal bones, and multiple
barrel stave osteotomies are made (Fig. 8.3b). Out-fracturing of this
bone expands the intracranial volume. Next, the epidural dissection is
carried out on the floor of the anterior and middle fossa, with cotton
paddies placed along the interface. Temporal extensions are cut
beneath the sphenoid wing on either side, and orbital osteotomies are
carried out via cuts along the orbital roof bilaterally and a cut across
the nasal glabella medially. The orbital bandeau can then be removed as
a single piece. Once the bone is removed, one should carefully inspect
the dura to ensure there are no dural tears. If there are any tears in the
dura, these can be primarily repaired using 4–0 Nurolon sutures and
Tisseal.

Fig. 8.3 (a) Once the exposure is completed, the bifrontal craniotomy is marked using a sterile
pencil. Bur holes are drilled and a complete epidural dissection is completed. The craniotomy is
completed and the bone flap removed. (b) Barrel stave osteotomies are marked out with a
sterile pencil. The epidural space is then dissected underneath the parietal bones, and multiple
barrel stave osteotomies are made. Out-fracturing of this bone expands the intracranial volume

The orbital bandeau is split in the middle, with an interpositional
bone graft used to both widen and advance the fronto-orbital region.
Closing osteotomies are made at the lateral orbit to advance the lateral
bandeau. The recontoured bandeau and frontal bones are secured in
place with a mix of PDS suture, resorbable plates and screws, and 26gauge wires. Bone graft is harvested from the inner table of the frontal
bone flap. The split calvarial bone graft and bone particulate graft are
used to fill in the defects created by the vault expansion. Meticulous
hemostasis is achieved, and a 7 Jackson-Pratt drain is left in the

subgaleal space. The scalp is reapproximated with absorbable sutures,
with antibiotic ointment applied liberally to the incision line.

8 3 2 Endoscopic Suturectomy
Endoscopic suturectomy involves shorter operative time and less blood
loss compared to an open cranial vault expansion. However, unlike with
a fronto-orbital advancement, the cranial vault is not reshaped at the
time of surgery. By cutting out the abnormally fused suture, and then
keeping the child in a series of helmets to direct bone growth,
endoscopic techniques take advantage of the growing brain and still
malleable skull.
The patient is positioned supine, with the head on a padded
horseshoe headrest. A small, approximately 1–2 in., zig-zag incision is
made just behind the hairline (Fig. 8.4). After the incision is opened,
two burr holes are made, one on either side of the fused suture and
underlying sagittal sinus. Bone is then removed with a Kerrison
rongeur posteriorly to the anterior fontanelle. The epidural space is
dissected anteriorly, with the aid of endoscopic visualization. Bone
scissors are used to cut out the fused suture as far anteriorly as
possible, down to the nasion. After about 4 months of age, the bone
becomes too thick to cut in this fashion. Hemostatic agents are used,
and the incision is closed with absorbable sutures.

Fig. 8.4 Skin markings for proposed endoscopic suturectomy. A small zig-zag incision is made
just behind the hairline. The epidural space is dissected anteriorly, with the aid of endoscopic
visualization. Bone scissors are used to cut out the fused suture as far anteriorly as possible,
down to the nasion

8 4 Timing of Intervention
It is our practice to offer endoscopic intervention through 4 months of
age. As the endoscopic technique relies on the rapidly growing brain to
reshape the skull, once the rate of head growth slows, the cosmetic
results are arguably not as good. Furthermore, as the child ages and the
skull becomes thicker, it becomes technically more challenging to cut
through the bone without the use of a drill.
Fronto-orbital advancement is generally performed between 9 and
12 months of age. Though most children will present before this time,
the reasons for waiting are twofold: (1) the bone strength increases
with age. This allows for a more stable reconstruction and less chance
of relapse. Higher revision rates are often seen when an open cranial
vault procedure is performed prior to 6 months of age (2). The older
child is better able to tolerate the associated blood loss and prolonged
anesthetic time associated with the open procedure.
For children who present prior to 4 months of age, families are
generally given the option to proceed with endoscopic treatment or
wait until the child is old enough to undergo an open fronto-orbital
advancement.

8 5 Post-Op Care and Follow-Up
Patients who undergo open fronto-orbital advancement typically spend
the first post-operative night in the intensive care unit. Post-operative
blood counts and electrolytes are checked, and children are transfused
as necessary. All patients are started on standing acetaminophen, as
well as IV narcotics as needed. Patients are given a total of 24-h of perioperative antibiotics. Most children transfer to the surgical floor on
post-operative day one. Parents should be prepared for the fact that
periorbital edema usually peaks on post-operative day two or three,
often to the extent that the child cannot open their eyes. Once patients
are tolerating a PO diet, pain medications can be transitioned from IV to

oral. The Jackson-Pratt drain remains in place until the output
decreases. Discharge criteria, once the drain is removed, include pain
well controlled with oral pain medications, tolerating a diet, voiding
appropriately, and having bowel movements. This usually coincides
with at least one of the eyes starting to open. On average, patients are
discharged home on post-operative days 3–4. The wound is managed
with twice daily application of antibiotic ointment for 7 days.
Patients who undergo endoscopic metopic suturectomy often go
directly to the surgical ward post-operatively. Given the shorter
anesthesia time, less blood loss, and significantly less post-operative
swelling associated with this procedure, many children are able to be
discharged home as early as post-operative day 1. They are fitted for
their helmet 7–10 days post-operatively once the swelling has subsided
and the helmet is delivered 2–3 days later. The helmet is worn 23 h per
day, generally until the patient’s first birthday. Visits with the orthotist
are every 2 weeks for adjustment.
It is our institutional practice for patients to come for a wound
check at 2–4 weeks. Then at 1 year and 2 year post op with surface
imaging at the 2-year visit. Further visits occur as the patient begins
school at age 5 or 6 and finally before graduation at age 16–18.

8 6 Complications and Management
The overall morbidity and mortality rates for craniosynostosis surgery
are low, and the surgeries are generally very well tolerated. However, it
is important to remember that due to the young age and small size of
the patient, their circulating blood volume is relatively small. Given the
highly vascular nature of both the scalp and the bone, blood loss,
especially during an open cranial vault procedure, can be significant. It
is important to maintain euvolemia and transfuse crystalloid, colloid,
and blood as necessary. In fact, it is our team’s practice not to begin an
open cranial vault expansion without cross-matched blood in the room.
During epidural dissection or during bone removal, there can be
injury to the venous sinuses. It is of utmost importance to recognize
this and treat it expeditiously, to avoid possibly catastrophic
complications. Venous sinus injury should be occluded with gelfoam
and cotton patties to apply direct pressure, followed by repair with a

muscle plug. It is also important to carefully inspect the dura and
directly repair any dural tears in order to avoid post-operative CSF
leaks and potential infection.
Given the degree of bone work and the head position, which is
usually higher than the child’s heart, there is a risk of air embolism. It is
our practice to pre-operatively place a precordial Doppler on all
patients in order to help monitor for air embolism. Significant air
embolisms can lead to hemodynamic instability. As soon as there is a
concern for an air embolism, the field should be flooded with saline
irrigation, the entry site occluded, and the head of the bed lowered
below the level of the heart to prevent further air entrapment.
Other complications, though rare, that the family should be
counseled preoperatively about injury to the underlying brain
parenchyma, transfusion reactions, seizures, and wound infections.
Additionally, patients may present years later with post-reconstruction
calvarial defects that may require additional surgery to fill the defects.

8 7 Evidence and Outcomes
Generally, outcomes following either open cranial vault expansion or
endoscopic strip craniectomy for metopic craniosynostosis are
excellent [1–14], both in terms of cosmetic results and long-term
neurocognitive development. Short-term, endoscopic strip craniectomy
is associated with shorter OR time, less blood loss, lower rates of blood
transfusion, and shorter hospital stays. However, long-term,
standardized studies are still lacking in comparing the two techniques.
It is important to recognize that children even with single-suture
craniosynostosis require multidisciplinary care provided by pediatric
neurosurgeons, craniofacial plastic surgeons, pediatric
anesthesiologists, pediatricians, ophthalmologists, geneticists, and
pediatric nurses. Due to the complexity of their care, we recommend
treatment at craniofacial centers of excellence that can tailor the
approach to each individual child.

9 Unilateral Coronal Craniosynostosis:
Clinical Presentation and Management
Principles
Yosef Dastagirzada1, Hammad Khan1, Sean Neifert1, Henri Kolb1 and

Richard C E Anderson

Keywords Coronal – Craniosynostosis – Unilateral – Anterior
plagiocephaly

9 1 Introduction
Unilateral coronal craniosynostosis (UCS, or anterior plagiocephaly) is
the second most common type of craniosynostosis, occurring in
approximately 1/10,000 births [1]. It accounts for between 20 and 35%
of nonsyndromic cases, with a female predominance of 3:2 [2, 3].
Although a number of syndromes, including Apert, Crouzon, and
Pfeiffer Syndrome, are associated with coronal craniosynostosis, these
account for only 8% of cases overall and are most commonly bilateral
[4, 5]. By contrast, sporadic cases account for the vast majority of
coronal craniosynostosis and are typically unilateral. Interestingly,
authors have identified unilateral craniosynostosis in images of
Abraham Lincoln and eight other individuals from his family lineage [6]
(Fig. 9.1). This is likely consistent with familial nonsyndromic cases

which are shown to have an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance
[7].

Fig. 9.1 Photo of President Abraham Lincoln demonstrating features of coronal
craniosynostosis (elevation and anterior location of left ear, smaller left orbit with elevated
ipsilateral eyebrow)

Advances in the realm of genomics, specifically next-generation
sequencing and molecular classification, have traced the pathology to
embryonic gene dysregulation and neural crest migration/proliferation,
which are discussed in more detail in Chap. 3 [8, 9]. Although numerous
advancements have been made across many disciplines related to
craniosynostosis over the last several decades, the clinical management
begins with an accurate diagnosis. In this chapter, we will discuss the
pathophysiology, clinical presentation (history and physical exam),
imaging, and clinical management of unilateral coronal
craniosynostosis, including indications and timing of surgery and a
brief discussion of surgical techniques.

9 2 Pathophysiology

The cranial vault initially serves as a capsular membrane overlying the
developing brain. The process of intramembranous ossification occurs
in accordance with the direction of brain growth and leads to the
development of the frontal, parietal, occipital, and temporal bones that
form the calvarium [10, 11]. Dural attachments strongly adhere to the
cranial sutures at the sites of approximation between cranial bones.
The dura mater secretes various growth factors that regulate
mesenchymal stem cells and largely dictate the growth of the cranial
vault. Disruptions in these signaling pathways may lead to premature
fusion of the sutures and have been implicated in the pathophysiology
of syndromic and nonsyndromic craniosynostosis [12, 13]. These
include mutations in three of four fibroblast growth factor receptors
(FGFR-1, FGFR-2, and FGFR-3), transforming growth factor-beta (TGFB), insulin-like growth factors (IGFs), as well as the transcription
factors MSX2 and TWIST1 [14–20]. Premature fusion of a suture
restricts the growth of the cranial vault perpendicular to the line of the
suture, with compensatory growth occurring along nonfused sutures.
This phenomenon, known as Virchow’s Law, leads to the stereotypical
abnormal skull growth and head shape that characterize
craniosynostosis, restricting the development of the growing brain [21]
(Fig. 9.2).

Fig. 9.2 Virchows’ law explains the restriction of growth perpendicular to the line of the
abnormal suture and compensatory growth along nonfused sutures

9 3 Management
9 3 1 Diagnosis
Craniosynostosis typically occurs in utero and is visible at birth. It often
becomes more evident to family and providers at one year of age, when
the brain and skull growth is most rapid and the architecture of the
skull is extremely malleable. In nonsyndromic/unilateral cases, the
child is most often neurologically and developmentally normal.

9.3.1.1 Physical Exam Findings
The physical exam is the most important tool in the diagnosis of
craniosynostosis, with up to 98% accuracy in cases of nonsyndromic
craniosynostosis [22]. Unilateral coronal craniosynostosis presents
with anterior plagiocephaly, ridging along the fused suture, retrusion of
the lateral superior orbital rim, harlequin eye deformity, nasal root
deviation, and other findings. The diagnosis can occasionally be difficult
in mild cases, but careful attention to the shape of the craniofacial

skeleton (forehead, ear location, orbital shape, and nose) allows for the
correct diagnosis in the vast majority of cases. The primary
phenotypical findings can be found in (Table 9.1) and a classic
appearance of unilateral craniosynostosis from the vertex view is
demonstrated in Fig. 9.3.
Table 9.1 Phenotypical findings of unilateral coronal craniosynostosis
Flattening/retrusion of the ipsilateral forehead and compensatory contralateral forehead
protrusion or bossing
Ridging along the ipsilateral coronal suture
Retrusion of the ipsilateral supraorbital rim
Superolateral elevation of the ipsilateral sphenoid wing/superior orbital margin (also known
as a harlequin eye deformity, a pathognomonic finding)
Elevation of the eye on the ipsilateral side (vertical dystopia)
Widening of the ipsilateral palpebral fissure
Nasal root deviation to the ipsilateral side and nasal tip deviation to the contralateral side
Forward displacement of the ipsilateral ear
Deviation of the chin to the contralateral side

Fig. 9.3 Vertex view of a child with unilateral craniosynostosis demonstrates the classic
flattening/retrusion of the ipsilateral forehead (R) with contralateral forehead protrusion (L)

Because of the proximity of the coronal suture to the skull base and
its sequelae on the development of the sphenoid wing, ophthalmologic
findings including strabismus and amblyopia are also common. It has
been postulated that the deformed orbital shape changes the insertion
of the orbital muscles and can lead to superior oblique muscle palsy
and trochlea displacement [23, 24]. Many patients require
ophthalmologic corrective procedures after their primary craniofacial
surgery. Papilledema has been noted to be present in up to 10–15% of
craniosynostosis cases (more common in syndromic cases) but rare
among unilateral craniosynostosis cases [25]. In a study of 84 patients
with nonsyndromic unicoronal craniosynostosis, no papilledema was
detected in any case preoperatively [26].

9.3.1.2 maging

Plain radiographs are not commonly obtained in children with
craniosynostosis because the sensitivity and specificity are low. Historic
data have reported sensitivities with a range of 57–80% and
specificities of 54–100% [27]. However, of all types of nonsyndromic
craniosynostosis, plain radiographs are probably the most useful in UCS
due to the pathognomonic finding of a harlequin eye deformity (Fig.
9.4).

Fig. 9.4 AP radiograph demonstrates the classic Harlequin eye due to the superolateral
elevation of the ipsilateral sphenoid wing/superior orbital margin

Computed tomography (CT) scan with three-dimensional
reconstructions is the gold standard imaging study to diagnose
craniosynostosis. However, when the diagnosis of UCS can be made
unequivocally from the history and physical exam, CT scans are often
bypassed to minimize radiation exposure in young children. There is
still equipoise regarding the utility of CT scans, as some studies support

its use and others do not. For instance, Ulma et al. reported that
preoperative CT for patients with UCS led to changes in management
for up to 48% of patients and helped with the avoidance of inadvertent
complications (e.g., damage to deviated anterior superior sagittal sinus
and anomalous venous drainage) [28]. However, other studies have
questioned the need for CT given the high reliability of the physical
exam and the low likelihood of altering the surgical plan [22].
There have been some attempts to utilize ultrasound and MRI as
radiation-reducing imaging modalities with some promising results,
although CT imaging remains the most widely used technique [7].

9 4 Treatment
9 4 1 Indications for Surgery
Surgical techniques have transformed since the first major studies
addressing UCS in the 1970s. Historically, orbitofrontal advancement
(OFA) has been the primary method of surgical treatment, and it is
typically performed between 6 and 12 months of age. The main goals
are to immediately expand the intracranial space to preclude
intracranial hypertension and restore more symmetric contour to the
skull, specifically the frontal/fronto-orbital bar regions [29, 30].
Secondary goals include the potential for preventing psychosocial
disadvantages and improving neurological development, although
these have not been demonstrated scientifically.
Over the last 20 years, endoscopic-assisted strip craniectomy
followed by helmet therapy has become increasingly popular for
younger patients. This technique is typically performed between 2 and
6 months of age. In contrast to an OFA, where the skull and orbital bar
are removed, recontoured, and replaced, in an endoscopic craniectomy
only the fused/abnormal suture is removed, thereby recreating the
normal physiology of an open suture. A postoperative orthotic designed
to restrict the growth of the contralateral frontal region and facilitate
the expansion of the ipsilateral region is then commonly used for 9–
12 months postoperatively to facilitate gradual improvement in head
shape.
The optimal timing and treatment strategy for UCS remain
controversial. Although rare, sequelae that can accompany untreated

craniosynostosis include developmental delay, neurologic dysfunction,
facial and eye abnormalities, and/or respiratory compromise. The
surgical techniques for both approaches will be described in detail in
the following chapters and are only briefly reviewed here.

9 4 2 Surgical Principles of Unilateral Craniosynostosis
9.4.2.1 rbitofrontal Ad ancement Techni ue
Patients are typically positioned supine with the head on a Mayfield
horseshoe headrest or gel donut. The scalp and upper face are prepped
and draped in a fashion that facilitates the exposure of the brows,
eyelids, and proximal aspects of the nose. Perioperative antibiotics,
decadron, and mannitol are given intravenously. Recent data also
support the use of tranexamic acid (TXA) in the perioperative period,
with a statistically significant reduction in intraoperative blood loss and
transfusion requirements, without adverse outcomes [31, 32].
A bicoronal curvilinear or zig-zag incision behind the hairline is
made at the level of the mid-vertex with careful lateral extension to the
frontozygomatic sutures. During the incision, the superficial temporal
artery and soft tissue at the frontozygomatic suture should be
preserved. The anterior flap is reflected to the level of the orbital rims,
with care to preserve the supraorbital neurovascular bundle during flap
dissection when possible. Exposure typically includes the nasion,
supraorbital rims, anterior fontanelle, coronal sutures, and
frontozygomatic sutures. Once exposure is complete, the affected and
unaffected coronal sutures must be identified. The objective is to
fashion and contour the bifrontal bone graft in a manner that achieves
bifrontal symmetry; careful measurements of the orbital rim on the
unaffected side are taken and used to contour the affected side.
Depending on the magnitude of the deformity, a bifrontal craniotomy
that extends posteriorly to around the normal coronal suture on the
unaffected side and a similar distance on the fused side (typically 1.5–2
cm posterior to the fused suture) is subsequently performed. The
orbital rim is transected around 1 cm from the supraorbital ridge to
prevent fracture of the bone when the orbital bar is advanced. Several
peripheral burr holes or slots are then created, including one across the
midline near the anterior fontanelle and one just superior to the orbital
rim, to facilitate dissection of the dura from the cranium. The dura is

stripped off the bone and the bifrontal bone flap is removed in a single
piece.
Removal of the orbital bar is then performed. Cottonoids are placed
along the dura to gently retract the frontal lobes as the dura is dissected
from the floor of the anterior fossa. The periorbita is dissected from the
roof of the orbit. A high-speed drill, ultrasonic bone scalpel, or
osteotome is then used to make cuts along the roof of the orbit,
medially through the nasion, and laterally through the sphenoid wing to
release the orbital bar in a single piece.
At this point, the remodeling and reconstruction are performed,
typically together with the plastic surgery team. The orbital bar is
contoured and advanced differentially to achieve orbital symmetry and
increase the intracranial space, and then it is secured to the nasion and
bilateral temporal bones with an absorbable plating system and
sutures. The bifrontal bone flap is then divided, trimmed, contoured,
replaced, and secured to the orbital bar and surrounding parietal bone.
Remaining bone fragments are used to fill in any gaps and the wound is
closed in layers after copious irrigation and hemostasis.

9.4.2.2 Endoscopic-Assisted Craniectomy Techni ue
Patients are typically positioned similarly, supine with the head on a
Mayfield horseshoe headrest or gel donut. The abnormal suture is then
palpated and an 8–10 mm wide craniectomy extending from the
anterior fontanelle to the base of the coronal suture is mapped out and
marked on the skin. As the bone thickens inferiorly into the sphenoid
bone, the craniectomy is taken posteriorly behind the sphenoid down
to the temporal-squamosal suture [33]. A small one-inch incision is
marked longitudinally about midway along the fused suture and behind
the hairline. The scalp is prepped and draped and perioperative
antibiotics and decadron are given intravenously. An incision is made,
and an avascular plane is developed between the galea and pericranium
from the anterior fontanelle to the temporal squamosal suture using a
0° endoscope and a scalp retractor. A burr hole is then created using a
small burr at the level of the incision, and the endoscope is used to
dissect and strip the underlying dura from the bone. A strip
craniectomy removing the fused suture as described above is then
performed using the Kerrison rongeur, Jansen Middleton nasal

rongeurs, and other long-handled bone rongeurs. The wound is
copiously irrigated, hemostasis is achieved, and the wound is closed
with absorbable sutures in the galea and skin.
Approximately 1 week postoperatively, patients are fitted for cranial
molding helmets, which are generally worn for 23 hours a day and
tolerated very well. Children typically require 2–3 helmets for a total
duration of 9–12 months [33].

9.4.2.3 pen ersus Endoscopic Techni ues: ationale and
Timing
As previously mentioned, while the optimal timing for surgical
correction has not yet been clearly defined, orbitofrontal advancements
for coronal craniosynostosis are generally performed between 6 and
12 months of age. This is partially because children have more
favorable bone pliability until approximately 1 year of age, and fusion of
the nonpathologic sutures occurs around 2 years. Endoscopic-assisted
craniectomy, on the other hand, is typically performed only up to
6 months of age [34].
Early data with endoscopic techniques for coronal synostosis
demonstrated benefits over open surgery with respect to ophthalmic
outcomes (need for strabismus surgery) and correction of variables like
vertical dystopia, nasal deviation, and sagittal imbalance [35, 36].
Postoperative cosmetic results also were comparable [37].
Furthermore, reductions in operative time, blood loss, blood
transfusions, length of stay, and cost have all been demonstrated with
the endoscopic approach compared to orbitofrontal advancement [37,
38]. There is sparse literature surrounding the recurrence rates among
cases of unicoronal craniosynostosis treated with endoscopic or open
techniques.
Complication rates for both procedures are relatively low, including
dural tears, CSF leaks/pseudomeningoceles, and wound infection. Data
have demonstrated no significant differences in complication rates
among minimally invasive/endoscopic versus open approaches,
although a trend towards decreased complication rates in endoscopic
treatments has been delineated [39, 40]. The complication rate has
been well described to increase in cases with multiple sutures involved
[40].

Key Points for the Neurosurgeon
Unilateral coronal craniosynostosis is the second most common form
of craniosynostosis.
Unilateral cases are almost always sporadic, while bilateral cases are
frequently associated with syndromic presentations.
Stereotypical physical examination findings include ipsilateral
plagiocephaly, contralateral frontal bossing, nasal root deviation,
ridging along the suture, and a harlequin eye deformity.
Radiographic confirmation with plain radiographs or CT scans is
generally performed when a definitive diagnosis cannot be made
based on the physical exam.
OFA is generally performed between 6 and 12 months of age, while
endoscopic-assisted craniectomy is performed up to 5–6 months of
age.
Unlike OFA, endoscopic-assisted surgery typically requires the use of
a contoured helmet for 9–12 months after surgery.
The most common complication of surgical intervention for coronal
synostosis is blood loss requiring transfusion. The overall
complication rate for these surgical interventions is relatively low.

10 Lambdoid Sutures Synostosis: Key
Points for the Neurosurgeons,
Management Principles (Diagnosis,
Surgical Principles and Their Rationale,
Timing)
Matthieu Vinchon1
(1) Service de Neurochirurgie Pédiatrique, H pital Femme-MèreEnfant, Bron, France

Matthieu Vinchon
Email: matthieu.vinchon@chu-lyon.fr
Keywords Clinical presentation – Associated malformations – Surgical

10 1 Introduction
Long held as an exceptional occurrence, lambdoid synostosis (LSy) is
increasingly recognized as being not so exceptional, and often a key
element of a complex problem. The true prevalence of LSy has long
been occulted by a large number of positional head deformations
(PHD), a haystack in which just a few needles are to be found. Unlike
other craniosynostoses which have a tell-tale morphology or are part of
a typical syndromic association, LSy is often inconspicuous, involving
the rear of the head and masked by hair, and has a protean
presentation.

LSy can be either isolated, uni- or bilateral; associated with other
synostoses, most notably of the sagittal suture (the aptly named
“Mercedes-Benz” syndrome) [1]; or be part of an ever-increasing
nebula of very rare syndromes [2].
Little is known of the pathogenesis and pathophysiology of LSy, and
the diagnosis may be challenging, with some cases masquerading as
tonsillar herniation, or idiopathic intracranial hypertension [2].
Because it is now acknowledged that LSy has a potential for serious
complications, it has become increasingly a surgical concern. Several
surgical solutions can be proposed, including craniectomy, cranioplasty,
osteogenic distraction, and foramen magnum decompression. However,
the indications for surgery, the choice of these different techniques, and
their results are unclear. In this chapter, we shall focus on isolated LSy,
uni- or bilateral, and study their pathogenesis, pathophysiology,
diagnosis, and surgical management.

10 2 Anatomy and Physiology
10 2 1 Embryology
The lambdoid suture (LSu), extending from the lambdoid to the
asterion fontanelles, is the remnant of the mesodermal soft tissue after
the appearance and spread of the parietal and interparietal ossification
centers medially (membranous ossification), and the exo-occipital and
petrous-temporal bones inferiorly (enchondral ossification) [3]. The
LSu is also tightly intricated with the underlying dura mater; it thus sits
at the junction between the membranous cranium and the
chondrocranium, between derivatives of the mesoderm and the cranial
neural crest [4].

10 2 2 Functions of the Lambdoid Suture
The most obvious function of the LSu is calvarial growth, although to
which extent it contributes to the overall development, and at which
period of life it is at play are unclear. The rarity of incidental findings of
LSy suggests that this function is of crucial importance for the
harmonious calvarial growth, and the onset of clinical manifestations
during childhood and until adolescence suggests that its functions
continue to be necessary late during development.

Owing to its peculiar geometry, the LSu provides calvarial growth in
the three dimensions; superposition of 3D-CT scanners in LSy with an
age-matched normal skull helps understand a contrario the function of
the LSu, which enlarges the posterior calvaria following a posteroinferior vector, following a pattern similar to the growth of conch shells
(Fig. 10.1).

Fig. 10.1 (a, b) Vestibule-oriented CT scanner 3D CT scanners of a 5-month female, FGRF2
muted, with closure of both lambdoid and the left coronal sutures, superposed with agematched male control (head injury), showing the pattern of deformity and compensation in
bilambdoid synostosis; shaded green: growth deficit; shaded red: compensation growth. The
posterior green area shows a contrario of the role of the lambdoid suture in the posterior
extension of the calvaria following a postero-inferior vector. Courtesy of pr Philippe Pellerin

Another, poorly documented function of the LSu is the transmission
of strains from muscular contraction; studies in reptiles have shown
that the sutures play a role in the repartition of strains during biting
[5]. In this perspective, it may be interesting to note that the LSus are
placed at the crossroads between the most powerful of craniocervical
muscular systems: the sternocleidomastoid (rotation), the nuchal
(craniocervical extension and head support in the erect position), and

the temporal muscles (biting). These powerful strains may account for
the many variations in shape and number of the epactal bones
developing from the lambdoid suture (Fig. 10.2a).

Fig. 10.2 Female infant with Crouzon syndrome caused by FGFR2 mutation. (a) CT scanner at
9 months showing bilambdoid synostosis, all other sutures being patent; note the epactal bone,
attesting overstimulation of the lambdoid suture, and split sagittal suture, attesting raised
intracranial pressure. (b) MRI at 9 months shows tonsillar herniation, causing severe central
sleep apneas (23/h). She underwent posterior fossa decompression, aged 24 months with good
results on sleep apneas

10 3 Pathology and Pathophysiology
10 3 1 Closure of the Lambdoid Suture
Synostosis of the LSu is a developmental condition, the timing being
either pre- or postnatal. LSy can develop as an isolated
craniosynostosis, or as part of a multisutural disease, or as a sporadic
as well as a syndromic condition [2]. When LSy is unilateral, Shahinian
and other authors have reported a right-sided predominance [2, 6],
which mirrors the right-sided predominance of unicoronal synostosis.
These asymmetries can be put in relation with the asymmetry of the
physiological closure of the coronal and lambdoid sutures with age [7].
In multisuture synostosis, the different sutures often do not close
synchronously, meaning that with time, an initially isolated LSy can
become a complex, multisutural synostosis (Fig. 10.3). It is estimated

that, in syndromic synostoses, in due course, LSy will develop almost
constantly [8].

Fig. 10.3 (a, b) Newborn female, CT performed because of dystocic birth: bilambdoid
synostosis with patent coronal and sagittal sutures. (c) CT aged 15 months: secondary closure
of the sagittal sutures. (d) MRI, aged 4 years, showing acquired prolapse of the cerebellar
tonsils. Genetic evaluation was negative

10 3 2 Determinants of the Closure
The etiologies of LSy are diverse, some being inborn genetic diseases,
others possibly environmental [2]. Some authors considered that
antenatal mechanical compression or traumatic birth can cause LSy [6],
an attempt to bridge the conceptual gap between synostotic and

positional posterior plagiocephaly [9]. However, with increasing
prenatal diagnosis, it is now well known that birth difficulties are more
likely the result of craniosynostosis than its cause [2]. The prenatal
compression hypothesis has also lost momentum since we now know
that a genetic disease is found in three-quarters of patients with LSy,
although this mostly applies to LSy associated with multisuture
synostosis. LSy is also often present in multisuture synostoses
developing in shunted patients; however, we consider that overall,
cases of acquired, nongenetic LSy are marginal.
Genetic causes of LSy are very diverse, being associated with a
variety of mutations or chromosomal imbalances with gene disruption
[10]. Some molecular determinants of the closure are now documented,
like in a rodent model of Gli3-deficient mice, in which LSy was
explained by a downregulation of Twist1, resulting in an expansion of
the population of osteogenic precursors of the suture, with osteoblastic
differentiation leading to a bony bridge; interestingly, this molecular
disturbance could be rescued by FGF2 [11].

10 3 3 Impact on Calvarial Growth
In unilambdoid synostosis (ULSy), the local flattening on the synostotic
side is compounded with compensatory bulging taking place in the
contralateral LSu, the ipsilateral upper parietal squama, and the
mastoid region (Fig. 10.4). The lambdoid bulge is responsible for the
downward displacement of the ear lobe, while the posterior tether
displaces it backward. When severe, ULSy can even impact facial
morphology on account of frontal retrusion [12], with mandibular
malalignment [13]. This is unlike the PHD, where the ear lobe is
displaced upward and anteriorly, and some frontal advancement is
often perceptible (Fig. 10.5). In addition, in ULSy, the nonsynostotic LSu
is overstimulated and commonly develops several epactal bones (Fig.
10.4a). ULSy is mostly a morphological concern, and often has little or
no impact on health, as attested by the long survival of a premodern
human with ULSy [14].

Fig. 10.4 Twelve-months male with right-sided unilambdoid synostosis, without syndromic
context. (a) bird’s eye view, (b) posterior inferior view, (c) line diagram of b unilambdoid

In bilambdoid synostosis (BLSy), the occiput is symmetrically
flattened, the compensation growth being spread over the sagittal and
coronal sutures, resulting in an overall harmonious face and forehead,
with a brachycephalic tendency. Superposition of a synostotic skull with
a normal age-matched control in vestibular orientation (Fig. 10.1)
illustrates the pattern of malformation and compensation in BLSy [8].
Impaired calvarial growth results in intracranial hypertension,
mostly in BLSy, but also in ULSy, with local bone imprinting, or

holocranial intracranial hypertension.

10 3 4 Associated Lesions
Tonsillar herniation is commonly associated with all types of synostosis
[15], but appears especially prevalent in LSy, in particular BLSy when it
is associated with sagittal synostosis [1]. It is also prevalent in pure LSy,
mostly bilateral (Figs. 10.3, 10.6, and 10.7), but also unilateral; we
present an observation of ULSy with symptomatic tonsillar herniation
and syringomyelia (Fig. 10.8). Tonsillar descent appears to result from
intracranial hypertension due to restricted calvarial growth rather than
from closure of the skullbase synchondroses [16]. Impaired venous
drainage can also play a role; however, hydrocephalus is a rare feature
in isolated LSy [2].

markedly improved neurologically. Midfacial distraction-osteogenesis is to be scheduled later

In a previous study [2], we also found that a majority of ULSy were
associated with hypoplasia or agenesis of the ipsilateral transverse
sinus. We also observed a patient with atretic cephalocele, who
developed ULSy (Fig. 10.8). The association of anomalies of the bone,

meninges end venous sinuses suggests that LSy is a regional disorder of
the pericerebral tissues, rather than just a bone disorder. By contrast,
the brain is generally intact and development appears normal [17],
unless the LSy is part of a systemic, genetic, or chromosomal disorder.

10 4 Clinical Diagnosis
10 4 1 Positive and Differential Diagnosis of Unilambdoid
Synostosis
The diagnosis of ULSy is generally straightforward, made on gross
asymmetrical deformation of the posterior aspect of the calvaria (Fig.
10.9) with, on the synostotic side, the ear lobe attracted backward and
downward, the parietal bone elevated and no frontal swelling [18].
Facial asymmetry can be present, on account of fontal retrusion [13,
19]. Head circumference is generally normal in isolated LSy, while the
cephalic index tends to be above normal values [2]. The prevalence of
torticollis in this population appears to be high and may require
specific management [19]. Rarely, ULSy can cause brain compression
resulting in symptomatic tonsillar herniation (Fig. 10.8).

Fig. 10.9 Four months male, with marked occipital deformation; however, clinical examination
could not exclude positional flattening with certainty, because of apparent flattening and ear
lobe advancement on the nonsynostotic side (a), although the lateral view shows loss of
posterior volume of the calvaria (b). Plain X-rays (c) brought an unequivocal diagnosis of
unilambdoid synostosis with marked imprinting of the calvaria

The main differential diagnosis of ULSy is with PHD, because of the
profusion of PHD while LSy are so few, all the more since both entities
have at times been considered as extremes of a continuum [9]. The
confusion is often made and may have introduced some uncertainty in
the medical literature: “The current evidence is difficult to navigate
because of deformational plagiocephaly being misdiagnosed as
unilateral lambdoid synostosis” [17]. In theory, the diagnosis of PHD is
generally easy when watching from above (Fig. 10.5a) and from behind
(Fig. 10.5b). However, in some cases of ULSy, compensatory excessive
growth of the patent contralateral lambdoid suture can mimic PHD (Fig.
10.4); combined with the lower-set ear on the synostotic side (Fig.
10.9a), this can create confusion with PHD.

10 4 2 Positive and Differential Diagnosis of Bilambdoid
Synostosis
BLSy can be more difficult to spot because of the absence of asymmetry,
especially when hair is abundant. The inspection of the lateral aspect
usually discloses the telltale flat occiput (Fig. 10.6a), but overall, the
deformation may go unnoticed, the child does not suffer bullying at
school, and his parents are often not in great demand for morphological
correction. Synostotic brachycephaly is unmistakable because of its
typical turricephalic appearance, with a wide, tall, and flat forehead
with a major morphological impact, very much unlike BLSy. Positional
nonsynostotic brachycephaly, by contrast, is associated with normal
facial features and is remarkable only for the shortness of the head
viewed from the lateral aspect, showing a regular parieto-occipital
flattening, compensated by parietal widening [20], while in BLSy the
depression sits much lower, and the parietal region is not widened
(Figs. 10.3b and 10.6a).
Being a bi-sutural craniosynostosis, BLSy can cause focal or
holocranial compression, and these patients are diagnosed because of
signs and symptoms of tonsillar herniation or intracranial
hypertension. In these cases, masquerading as Chiari malformation or
pseudotumor [2], it is important to search systematically for bone
anomalies, and, whenever in doubt, to complete the MRI with a CT
scanner.

10 4 3 Other Clinical Findings
Other anomalies should be looked for, especially indicating a
faciostenosis, as well as stigma of FGFR (Fig. 10.6), or Twist, or Twistrelated mutations, in the child and his family, since many cases of LSy
are syndromic. Finally, some cases of LSy, more often bilateral, are
asymptomatic and diagnosed during a screening for syndromic
diseases.

10 5 Explorations
In most cases, the diagnosis is made on clinical examination; in some
cases, however, plain X-rays or ultrasound may be necessary to confirm
the diagnosis, and differentiate ULSy from PHD (Fig. 10.9c).
Preoperative evaluation requires a high-quality CT scanner, in order to
analyze all the sutures, the cranio-cervical junction, locate bone
lacunae, emissary veins, and encased venous sinuses, and also get
preliminary information on the presence or not of hydrocephalus and
tonsillar herniation. It is important to take into account the persistent
sutures and epactal bones, which are points of intense adherence to the
dura mater and can make surgery tricky (Cf. infra).
MRI is also necessary, in order to evaluate brain compression,
hydrocephalus, tonsillar descent, and associated brain anomalies.
Careful analysis of the venogram is very important, on account of
venous sinus compression, encasement, and large emissary veins;
moreover, hypoplasia or agenesis of a transverse sinus, which is found
in a majority of ULSy, warrants special care during surgery for ULSy.
Neuro-ophthalmological examination with fundoscopy, and,
whenever possible, evoked potentials and optical coherence
tomography, are necessary. ICP monitoring can be discussed, especially
in older children, for example, if they complain of symptoms while the
fundoscopy remains normal while head circumference appears to
progress along normal values. Genetic evaluation should also be
proposed systematically in these patients.

10 6 Surgical Management

10 6 1 Rationale
The rationale of surgery for LSy is mostly morphological correction and
cerebral decompression; functions are little if ever impacted by LSy,
even when asymmetrical. Shape correction is a valid justification for
surgery especially in ULS; however, morphology is often mildly
impacted by this posterior deformity, especially in BLSy. Regarding
morphology, the parents’ opinion is thus determinant in the surgical
decision.
The most imperative indication for surgery is thus decompression,
which can be urgent, but is more generally slowly evolving. BLSy, like
most multisutural synostoses, is likely to cause intracranial
hypertension in the long run, causing visual and developmental
problems, and it is generally accepted that early surgery is indicated
[17], especially if imaging shows tonsillar herniation. In ULSy, as
reported above, brain compression can already be present in an
asymptomatic child, both local (Fig. 10.10c) and holocranial, resulting
in tonsillar herniation (Fig. 10.8). However, data on visual and
developmental outcomes in isolated ULSy are scant and insufficient to
mandate preventive decompressive surgery. On the other hand, the
evidence is a little clearer in other monosutural synostoses. As a last
resort, it is a matter of clinical judgment, and most pediatric
neurosurgeons will deem reasonable to perform decompressive
surgery for ULS, especially in a young infant [13].

Fig. 10.10 Same patient as Fig. 10.9, operated aged 13 months, in the prone position. (a, b)
Preoperative CT scanner. (c) Bilateral occipital bone flap; the inner aspect shows marked
imprinting. (d) Bilateral occipital bone flap exposing the transverse sinuses, repositioned
turned 180° and fixated with slow-resorption sutures (note the inverted situation of the
persistent lambdoid). (e) The parietal bulge on the synostotic side is remodeled with barrel
staves, shaped using Tessier bone-bender. (f h) Postoperative CT scanner showing good cranial
expansion with correction of the deformity

In the case of clinically eloquent or radiologically severe posterior
fossa crowding, a decision has to be made regarding surgery and the
choice of the approach. Both calvarial expansion and occipital foramen
decompression can be indicated, depending on clinical presentation,
severity of posterior fossa crowding, presence of syringomyelia,
syndromic context, age of the patient, and expertise of the surgeon.
In the case of abstention, there is no consensus on the modalities of
follow-up of nonoperated patients, however, the possibility of longterm decompensation and nonsynchronous closure of other sutures
certainly warrants prolonged clinical and ophthalmological follow-up.

10 6 2 Surgical Techniques
10.6.2.1 inear Craniectomy
Craniectomy is the simplest technique, and the only one practicable in
very young infants, when they require emergency decompression [21].
However, this indication applies mostly to multisutural synostoses, and

almost never pure LSy [22]. The aim is to free the occipital and parietal
squammae by restoring sutural lines. The dissection is subgaleal in
order to minimize bleeding and to avoid dural tear through bone
lacunae. The fused sutures are removed piece-meal, taking great care to
elevate the bone from the dura before biting in order to avoid dural
tears, progressing by “tango steps” (two steps forward, one step
backward). Several variants of this technique have been proposed, like
direct incision along the fused LSu with a “meander-shaped”
craniotomy, spread and maintained with plates [23]; or minimally
invasive technique, with the use of the endoscope followed by helmet
molding [24], or open technique through narrow portals, followed by
helmet molding [25]. Whatever the technique, linear craniectomy is
mostly indicated in young infants [13, 22], where it can be a salvage
surgery; however its long-term effect may be inferior to other
techniques [17].

10.6.2.2 Posterior Cal arial emodeling
This technique, also named posterior pole reshaping, can be indicated
both in ULSy and BLSy [26, 27]. In ULSy, like in unicoronal synostosis,
there is no normal side, only a synostotic (flat) and a nonsynostotic
(bulging) side. The simplest technique consists of a roughly
quadrangular bone flap, turned 180° in order to expand the synostotic
side and flatten the bulging side (Fig. 10.10). The parietal region can be
reshaped with barrel-staves, using Tessier’s bone-bender, in order to
avoid a parieto-occipital gap, and also to redirect the thrust of the brain
posteriorly in order to optimize posterior expansion (Fig. 10.10e). The
risk of dural tear should not be underestimated in ULSy, because of the
tight dural adhesion of the LSu on the nonsynostotic side, which is also,
incidentally, the side of the hypertrophic persistent transverse sinus
(Fig. 10.11).

Fig. 10.11 (a) Multiple burr holes may be necessary in order to elevate the bone from the tight
dural adhesions. Additional burr holes [4, 5] may be necessary; even so, elevation of the dura
may be perilous because of additional sutures and epactal bones in the region of the lambdoid
and asterion fontanelle. (b) Split dura due to tight adherence of the dura to the persistent
suture on the left, nonsynostotic side; note the size of the left transverse sinus, in relation to
agenesis on the right, synostotic side. A more complete dural tear would have created in a dire
situation. (c) MR angiogram showing agenesis of the right transverse sinus in the same patient

In BLSy, we trace a tongue-and-groove craniotomy line (Fig. 10.6e)
which allows to swivel the flap back along a curvilinear vector
(mimicking the growth of the lambdoid, Cf. Fig. 10.1). The inferior limit
of the craniotomy usually runs along or below the transverse sinus (Fig.
10.7c). A variant of this technique includes fan-shaped parietal flaps,
which are used (mostly in young children) to buttress the occipital
bone flap and contribute to expanding the posterior calvaria (Fig. 10.7d,
e). Other authors have described a “bucket-handle” bandeau parallel to
the coronal suture, inverted in order to correct unilateral flattening, and
swiveled 90° in order to cover the occipital region [28]. When tonsillar
herniation is present, extending the approach down the nape gives
access to the occipital foramen, which can be enlarged during the same
session [29]. Reliable bone flap fixation can be achieved using slowresorption sutures and stabilizing it with sutures (Fig. 10.7d); we think
the use of foreign material is unnecessary and should be minimal
because it can lead to extrusion [30], which is all the more menacing in
this region of the calvaria on which the child’s head rests.
The main drawback of this technique is that expansion of the
posterior pole is limited to 1.5–2 cm, because excessive scalp tension
during closure can cause necrosis and skin breakdown [31]. Scalp
expansion using subgaleal inflatable balloons in the weeks before
craniotomy is an option, in order to achieve greater cranial expansion.

10.6.2.3 Distraction
Distraction osteogenesis has gained wide acceptance in the
management of all types of craniosynostoses, and in particular in LSy
[32]. Although the distraction period of several weeks and the need for
reoperation in order to remove the hardware are a drawback, cranial
expansion with distraction is especially appealing, because osteotomy
is performed after subgaleal dissection, limiting blood loss, and
progressive distraction can achieve considerable calvarial expansion
[31], with anteroposterior diameter increase of up to 3 cm. Extending
the craniotomy down to the foramen magnum allows the distraction to
act directly on the posterior fossa crowding, rather than indirectly by
reducing intracranial hypertension. The direction of the vector of
distraction, descendant, or ascendant, is debated [31, 32].
Complications of distraction are a concern, mostly related to
“interaction of the device with the dura, device extrusion, and infection”
[33].

10.6.2.4 Foramen Magnum Decompression
When tonsillar herniation is present and causes craniocervical
compression, in particular syringomyelia, occipital foramen
decompression can be discussed (Fig. 10.8). We think it is indicated in
older children when the LSy has otherwise a mild impact on
morphology and intracranial pressure. These indications have to be
balanced with the results obtained with distraction techniques. The
advantages and disadvantages of posterior calvarial remodeling,
craniectomy, distraction, and posterior fossa decompression are
discussed in Table 10.1.

Technique: Tricks, Traps, and Pearls
Scalp incision should be versatile, in case an anterior approach might
be needed later; a bitragal incision allows both a posterior access,
which can be extended to the foramen magnum, and an anterior
approach down to the floor of the orbits.
Sub-periosteal dissection incurs the risk of dural effraction on
account of cranial lacunae, which require meticulous dissection.
Subgaleal dissection is less hemorrhagic, a key factor in very young
infants, and an argument in favor of distraction in older children.
Dural adherence to persistent sutures and epactal bones in the
region of the lambda and asterion fontanels incurs the risk of dural
tear and lesion of an enlarged transverse sinus (Fig. 10.11).
When elevating the midline bone flap, caution should be taken with
the sagittal sinus which can be embedded.
Emissary veins, especially posterior parietal and of the torcular, can
be large and bleed a lot when the bone is stripped of its periosteum;
hemostasis is obtained with wax, then, when the bone is elevated, the
venous stumps can be easily coagulated.

10 7 Postoperative Follow-Up
After surgery, prolonged follow-up is necessary, because of the risk of
recurrence, and also of asynchronous multisuture synostosis. Overall,
the reoperation rate is evaluated between 5% and 8% [17, 27].
Functional impairment with persistent refractory torticollis can also be
a concern in ULSy, with a prevalence estimated at 37% [19]. By
contrast, it is estimated that LSy have no cognitive impact [17],
although this has to be confirmed in long-term studies. Genetic

reevaluation may become necessary by the time the child becomes
adult, on account of rapid advances in this domain.

10 8 Conclusions
LSy is a complex condition which is difficult to apprehend, on account
of its rare occurrence, its being easily confused with PHD, and because
of its association with synostosis of other sutures, at the time of
diagnosis of later in time, as well as with a dazzling variety of very rare
conditions. The different techniques developed to treat the different
aspects of this rare condition allow satisfactory decompression and
morphological correction; however, a long follow-up is required.

11 1 Introduction
Bilambdoid and sagittal (cranio-) synostosis (BLSS) is a trisutural
craniosynostosis, described iconically as Mercedes-Benz syndrome or
Mercedes-Benz synostosis due to the characteristic occipital bony
ridges that resemble the Mercedes-Benz logo. Its incidence is reported
in the range of 0.3–0.7% of all craniosynostoses [1, 2] (Fig. 11.1).

Fig. 11.1 Lateral photographs and mid-sagittal MR of a baby with BLSS. Typical head shape
before surgery (left) at the age of 19 months (middle) and 1.5 years (right) postoperatively (W.
Wagner)

BLSS occurs as isolated type as well as a rare fusion pattern in the
course of a syndromic multisutural disease—in this case with a
reported incidence of 3% of the complex multisutural craniosynostoses
[1]. These facts underline the need for a genetic testing in every type of
craniosynostosis that includes one or both lambdoid sutures. As
syndromal pansynostoses are described elsewhere, this chapter focuses
on the isolated form and its specific management.
This chapter conveys the general information but also reasonable
diagnostic steps as well as management strategies be it surgical or
important follow-ups.

11 2 Key Points for the Neurosurgeon
Historically Moore et al. employed the descriptive term “Mercedes-Benz
syndrome” in 1998 [3]. However, this specific fusion pattern was
already described earlier and named “craniofacial dyssynostosis” by
Neuhäuser et al. in 1976.
Isolated BLSS is a rare entity of a trisutural craniosynostosis that
mainly affects males (4:1). If the lambdoid suture is part of the
craniosynostotic pattern, a syndromic context should always be
excluded. Even if intracranial abnormalities are rare in isolated BLSS
the shortage of space in the posterior fossa might cause a Chiari
malformation. Reports on minor mental delays exist, although most of
the patients develop within normal limits.

11 3 Diagnosis
Moore et al. described morphology with a narrow posterior cranial
vault, a frontal bossing and posteriorly angulated, patent coronal
sutures [3]. The head shape in BLSS is described as anterior
turricephaly with mild brachycephaly [4]. In a series of 31 isolated
cases of BLSS, Chivoret et al. describe a flat occiput in more than 70%.
Nevertheless, the authors distinguish between over 70% with a sotermed “short BLSS,” with narrow occiput and almost 30% of a “long
BLSS” with dolichocephaly and occipital bossing [5]. A sudden
angulation of the occipital skull might resemble a scythe’s cut and is
therefore described as “coup de serpe” [4]. As both lambdoid sutures
are involved the ears appear symmetric but low set.
For diagnosis, the abnormal head shape is suspicious for further
investigation. Palpable bony ridges are often a clear hint for synostosis,
while involuted sutures usually appear in positional skull deformations.
Within the first year of life an ultrasound examination helps to
differentiate between patent and fused sutures [6]. If the situation
remains unclear, plain skull radiographs with lacking patency or
reduced serration of the fused sutures will help to set up a proper
diagnosis [7]. These radiographs will also help to depict digital
impressions, suggestive of elevated intracranial pressure. However,
some experience is needed to differentiate these digital impressions
from signs of bone immaturity. A CT scan will clearly demonstrate fused
sutures unfortunately; however, it is associated with radiation exposure
and possible malignancies, especially in the very young [8–10]
Although some authors strongly recommend a preoperative CT scan in
order to detect possible bony defects from previous operations or
caused by emissary veins, we are persuaded that any indication for CT
diagnostics should be very strict. The argument of a possible
intracranial or vascular abnormality justifies an MRI with
MRangiography [11]. By combining plain skull radiographs and an MRI
with MRangiography, our group gets the same information with far less
radiation exposure. Advances in MRI techniques (ultra-fast sequence
MR, black bone MRI) with better illustration or depiction of bony
structures will help to optimize these strategies.

The premature fusion of both lambdoid sutures restricts the space
in the posterior fossa, possibly causing a tonsillar herniation with its
sequelae. This fact as well as the association with brain anomalies is not
yet diagnosed complex craniosynostoses justify an MRI. As the altered
posterior fossa might also cause a pathologic venous drainage pattern,
this MRI should include an MRangiography, depicting not only the
arterial supply but also the venous drainage above the jugular foramen.
A second MRI at the age of 4–6 years serves to rule out a secondary
tonsillar herniation (which might develop during the first years of life)
or its evolution as well as to judge hydrocephalus, possible syrinx
development or any other specific brain abnormalities and should
therefore be part of the strategy (Fig. 11.2).

Fig. 11.2 MR before surgery at the age of 3.5 months and 2 years after surgery (W. Wagner)

Tonsillar herniation is reported in almost two-thirds of the patients.
However, symptomatic cases are rare [4, 5]. The cerebellar tonsillar
herniation and its impairment of the CSF outflow might lead to dilated
ventricles/hydrocephalus and entail a discussion on subsequent
foramen magnum decompression.
Major advances in genetic diagnostics have and will continuously
close our knowledge-gap and enable us to characterize more and more
mutations and associated phenotypes of craniosynostoses [12].

11 4 Surgical Principles and General
Considerations
It is not useful to present a timetable including the different surgical
therapies, as the distinctive options should not follow a general
algorithm but should be based upon individual decisions considering
the individual combination of problems. Especially the premature
fusion of the lambdoid sutures, frequently associated with restricted
space in the posterior fossa hosting the brain stem, medulla and
cerebellum calls for individual and thorough strategies of care. This
includes consideration of the possible problems arising from the
structures in the posterior fossa or from impaired CSF-circulation but
also esthetic topics. Although not automatically required in every case
of BLSS, surgery might become an issue. Goals of a surgical intervention
therefore consist of increasing intracranial volume and consecutive
lowering of elevated ICP, improving a possible tonsillar herniation and
its sequelae and/or correcting a striking deformity. Different principles
have to be taken into account.
The positioning of the child depends on the strategy and goals.
While most procedures addressing the lambdoid suture and the
direction toward the foramen magnum are performed in prone
position, some strategies allow either prone or supine positioning,
which is mentioned in the specific paragraph.
Pre- as well as intraoperatively marking of the sagittal and both
transverse sinuses both at skin and at the surface of the skull by using a
neuronavigation device will help to prevent life-threatening sinus
injuries.
The dural matrix is the decisive matrix for bone formation.
Therefore, the surgeon should meticulously take great care of the dural
layer, which should always be kept moist. The use of bipolars on the
dura should be restricted to short and punctual usage if ever.
Noteworthy the reossification will also restore the pre-existing fusion
status of the sutures of a BLSS—a fact that should be remembered in
every treatment strategy.
The reduced intracranial volume and an existing deformation as
well as the explicit surgeon’s experience will strongly influence the

choice of the technique. Another aspect is the needed extent of
intracranial volume gain. Nowinski et al. analyzed different expansion
techniques in respect to achievable volume gain with the distraction
osteogenesis (see below) being superior to the rest [13].

11 4 1 Different Surgical Strategies Exist
11.4.1.1 Posterior Decompression
Due to the very potent osteoplasticity of the dural layer in the first 7–
8 months of life, a pure parieto-occipital decompression is a possible
first strategy.
A curved incision posterior to the coronal suture, periosteal
dissection and bone removal after meticulous dissection between
internal lamina and dural layer through burr holes is performed. The
sagittal synostosis might be addressed by an enlarged median
craniectomy in the same intervention—surgery in this case might also
be performed in supine position.
In case of dilated ventricles or even hydrocephalus, it can be
discussed to address this circumstance after the primary
decompression: the dilated ventricles might serve as a biological
expander in order to enlarge the skull size in between the relatively
“short” time span of 8–10 weeks until reossification takes place. If still
needed, the correction of disturbed CSF flow can be addressed another
3 months later after renewed diagnostics.
A free-floating parieto-occipital cranial vault release uses a
craniotomy in front of both lambdoid sutures leading either to the
lambdoid suture or even downwards under the torcula to the foramen
magnum. Intrinsic brain growth then is the driving force for gradual
occipital displacement of the free-floating bone flap [13].
In case of an associated Chiari malformation, one might even
perform an enlargement of the decompression downwards to the
direction of the foramen magnum. Due to the large sinus as well as the
general hemorrhagic situation in those young infants, a foramen
magnum decompression is not a suitable strategy. As the key issue of
surgery consists of posterior or even occipital cranial vault release, a
patient is usually placed in prone or semi-sitting position.

11.4.1.2

ccipito-Parietal emodeling

An active repositioning is an option in children older than 12 months.
Positioning may be either prone or supine, depending on the surgical
planning. Bicoronal curved skin incision, periosteal dissection, burr
holes and dissection between dural and internal bony lamina are
performed. The surgeon must be aware of tight dural adhesions
especially at the site of the fused sutures. Especially in syndromic
children deeply embedded bony spiculae on the inner surface need
attention and meticulous preparation. Our center usually uses the fixed
posterior cranial vault expansion as described by Di Rocco and
colleagues [14]. A parietal coronal bone strip with a width of 1.5–5 cm
is mobilized, tilted and newly fixated at the occipital bone rim. This
bony bandeau, enabling stable overcorrection and harmonization of
existing asymmetries, serves as basis in order to fix and rebuild the
occipital bone segments. Depending on the operative strategy, defined
parietal and occipital osteotomies are drawn and a whole posterior
calvarial bone flap is removed. This bone flap might reach up to or even
beyond the transverse sinus. The occipital bone flap may be rotated
and/or provided with additional barrel-stave incisions for further
remodeling [14]. For fixation of bone segments resorbable plates,
titanium plates or resorbable sutures may be deployed [15]. Titanium
plates have to be removed in a further surgery to prevent trans-osseus
migration. The authors held resorbable sutures for a very good option,
as they enable stable fixation at very low costs without another surgery.
Wagner and colleagues describe a very suitable technique for
posterior calvarial augmentation by creating intersecting calvarial
tongues through a meander-shaped craniotomy followed by
subsequent distraction. Fixating resorbable sutures (Vicryl 2.0)
substitute plates and screws Fig. 11.3 [16].

Fig. 11.3 Schematic drawings of the intersecting tongues for calvarial augmentation [16, 17]

Modifications of this technique describe intersecting tongues
perpendicular to the sagittal sinus with the basis of these intersecting
tongues shifted to the side, where more expansion is needed. This
approach enables asymmetric elevation of the calvarium in order to
address an asymmetrical occipital skull shape [17].

11 4 2 Posterior Skull Distraction
A parieto-occipital remodeling enables a significant enlargement
mainly in the sagittal plane. For craniotomy a supratorcular, an
infratorcular as well as a combined supra- and infratorcular craniotomy
may be applied. Special care has to be taken above the sagittal and both
transverse sinuses—these regions being separated last—if necessary
even using a piezoelectric drill. Distraction osteogenesis is supported
by external or internal distractors or is spring assisted. All these
distractors need a second surgery for removal of the implanted devices.
As the distraction period bears possible risks of infection, regular and
close controls of the entry points of the distractors are recommended.
Our group usually uses one distractor on each side and another close to
the vertex in order to be able to correct asymmetries by modulating
and adjusting distraction “speed” on each side individually. After active
distraction of 0.5–1 mm per day for 2–4 (6) weeks, distractors are

removed after another 6-week period without any further active
distraction. A possible decompressive effect on a Chiari malformation is
reported by McMillan et al., who described improvements of a Chiari
situation after posterior calvarial distraction in several cases [18].
Preoperative printing of individual 3D-skull-prototypes for planning
of the osteotomy lines, the optimal trajectories and suitable distraction
devices can be helpful. Distractors itself should have the right size to
pass the osteotomy line, set at the right position for the planned
trajectory with its activation arms as close as possible to the skull.

11.4.2.1 Endoscopic Suturectomy
An endoscopically assisted suturectomy may be performed, especially if
the dolichocephalic aspect is not too prominent. Surgery is performed
at 3–4 months of age. Patient is placed in prone position. Burr holes are
placed at the former small fontanelle and at each side in the course of
both lambdoid sutures. Although this approach is reported to have
decreased time of surgery and less blood transfusion rates, the result is
more often suboptimal. Due to the early time of surgery reclosure and
relapse of the abnormal head shape appears frequently no matter,
whether an additional external orthosis was employed or not [19].

11 4 3 Foramen Magnum Decompression
A decompression of the foramen magnum is advisable in the presence
of a progressive hydrocephalus or syrinx in the cervical spine. We plan
decompression of the cranio-cervical junction in three steps:
First: Bony decompression by enlargement of the foramen magnum
and laminectomy of C1.
Second: Dural expansion (with a patch graft).
Third: Resection of the cerebellar tonsils.
The decision to proceed to the next step is made intraoperatively by
ultrasound examination. Even if a plastic dural expansion surgery is
performed a recurrence of the bony compression can occur, especially if
surgery was performed very early. Therefore, an additional MRI should
be planned [20].

11.4.3.1 Complications of Surgery

Dural acerations
In contrast to syndromic synostosis, where the surgeon might
encounter dysplastic areas as signs of bone immaturity with bony
spiculae extending deep into the sulci, the isolated types usually only
demonstrate areas of digital impressions if associated with reduced
intracranial volume. Careful preparation is indeed mandatory, as dural
lacerations may occur anyway. In these cases, the surgeon should try to
achieve a watertight dural closure, in order to repair the CSF space and
preserve the dural layer as supplying matrix for the bone and sutures.
nfection
For surgery, we generally recommend an antibiotic prophylaxis,
according to the hospitals’ strategy. Commonly used precautions for
general wound care are self-understood, especially in those cases
where distractors are used.
We experienced one case of relevant superficial infection at an
external distractor entry point at the skull after a posterior skull
distraction. Meticulous wound care and regular blood samples
prevented an abortion and removal of the devices before planned
schedule. We recommend regular follow-up, while the distractors are in
situ.

11.4.3.2

enous Sinus n ury

Venous anomalies are frequently described in syndromic
craniosynostosis. In case of suspicion, an MRI with MRangiography
including imaging of the venous drainage should be performed before
surgery in order to identify large emissary veins in the galea.
Preparation or dissection over the sagittal or transverse sinus
should always be the last step, after the other craniotomy lines have
been set, in order to be able to compress the sinus directly and take
care for the bleeding. Knowledge of pathologic venous drainage and
emissary veins through the galea are obvious requirements before
starting any surgery.

11 5 General Strategy

As BLSS is a multisutural condition that might lead to elevated
intracranial pressure, a strategic follow-up is mandatory. Although
problems usually arise only after some time, it is crucial to realize a
possible development early enough to define a specific (surgical)
strategy. The follow-up should assess the changing dynamics of brain
growth, therefore an ophthalmologic surveillance every 6 months
seems reasonable as well as annual clinical follow-ups in the first
6 years of life, then every 2 years until the age of 12, when brain tissue
stops to grow.
In case of clinical suspicion of a BLSS, ultrasound clarifies suture
status and excludes striking intracranial abnormalities. Additional plain
skull radiographs confirm the suture status as well as depict digital
impressions as possible signs of elevated intracranial pressure. An MRI
will depict a cerebellar tonsillar herniation and possible CSF-circulation
problems due to an outflow restriction inside the posterior fossa. In
order to detect an altered venous drainage and pathologic emissary
veins, an additional MRangiography (including imaging of the venous
drainage above jugular foramen level) in the first 6 months of life is
highly recommended. In contrast to existing recommendations, a CT
scan is avoidable in many cases [21].
Independent of performed surgical therapies ophthalmoscopic
surveillance every 6 months to rule out papillary edema should be
routinely planned in the first 12 years. Regular follow-ups every year
for the first 4 years and every 2–3 years until 12 years of life seem
reasonable.
At these outpatient clinic appointments, plain skull radiographs in
lateral projection should be performed to rule out possible signs of
elevated intracranial pressure. Routine imaging surveillance must
include a second MRI during the first 4 years of life.
A cranio-facial center and expertise should include an experienced
pediatric neurosurgeon, a cranio-maxillo-facial surgeon, a (neuro-)
pediatrician, an ophthalmologist (at the center as well as at home), a
sensible and reliable radiological work-up and experienced specialists
(such as pediatric anesthesiology and ICU teams) in case of surgery.
