12 1 Introduction and Definitions
Isolated oxycephaly (from Greek ὀξύς, “sharp, pointed”) is a lateappearing form of non-syndromic craniosynostosis characterized by
premature fusion of both the coronal and sagittal sutures, and, in some
cases, of one or both lambdoid sutures [1–4].
Its prevalence and etiology are unknown, and it is not usually
congenital as isolated oxycephaly is never diagnosed at birth [2].
Compensating growth in the anterior fontanel region results in the
formation of a pointed or cone-shaped skull. In oxycephaly, the sagittal
suture is typically fused, and lambdoid sutures may or may not be
involved. The continuation of the coronal suture into the cranial base
(i.e., the sphenofrontal suture) may be also prematurely fused, while
the synchondroses of the cranial base appear to be normal. Sutures of

the orbit and the maxillary complex are typically not involved or fused
[3].
Isolated oxycephaly is often unrecognized because of its late onset,
but it is responsible for insidious intracranial hypertension (ICH), with
loss of visual acuity that can lead to blindness, headaches, and cognitive
delay if not treated on time.
Described since antiquity and often confused with brachycephaly or
other multisuture craniosynostoses, the term oxycephaly was initially
coined by Graig [3, 5], although Galen had already used the term
oxycephalus for a head in the shape of a tower [6, 7]. According to
Shimoji, Graig would have considered acrocephaly a misnomer and
tower-skull, harsh and inelegant [3, 5]. The terms acrocephaly and
oxycephaly have been used interchangeably although inconsistently in
the past. For some authors, oxycephaly refers to the premature fusions
of all the sutures; for others, these terms are used to mean stenosis of
the coronal plus one other suture [8–11]. A relative consensus has been
reached to accept the term oxycephaly for a premature synostosis of
both coronal and sagittal sutures [3, 4, 10, 12, 13] and isolated
oxycephaly, when this condition occurs without a concurrent
craniofacial syndrome, such as Crouzon or Pfeiffer. In literature, related
synonyms such as hypsi- or hypsocephaly (gr. ὕψος height, top),
pyrgocephaly (gr. Πύργος, tower), or turricephaly may be found.
In this chapter, we will address isolated oxycephaly as a nonsyndromic form of late craniosynostosis characterized by the
premature fusion of coronal and sagittal sutures.

12 2 Oxycephaly in History and Arts
Craniosynostoses have been known since ancient times. In the past,
identification of two pre-Columbian skulls with scaphocephaly (dated
between 6000 and 250 BC) due to early synostosis of the sagittal suture
[14], confirm that craniosynostoses have accompanied human beings
since the beginning of time. The Egyptian pharaoh Tutankhamun and
his father Amenophis IV were depicted with a dolichocephalic skull,
and it is believed that the pharaoh Akhenaten may have suffered from
craniosynostosis [15, 16]. The ancient gods of good fortune and long
life in traditional Eastern culture, Fukurokuju and Shou Lao were

depicted with domed heads with high and wide foreheads [5, 17] as a
sign of intelligence and superiority.
Perhaps the first literary reference to a craniosynostosis in the form
of an oxycephaly is that of Thersites, in the Iliad, whose behavior—he
opposed the right of the Achaean nobles to receive all the spoils of war
—was criticized by Homer (Iliad, book II, CCXV) [18]. The poet mocks
the “erroneous” (ignoble) attitude of Thersites –which could be
explained by a cognitive delay in the context of a craniofacial syndrome
—with a bitter description of his physical defects: “the most
horrendous man–aiskistos—that the walls saw from Troy... he was
cross-eyed and lame in one foot; his hunched shoulders sank against
his chest, and his head was pointed and covered in sparse hair. Achilles
and Odysseus hated him alike....”
Vulgar, obscene, and somewhat dull witted, Thersites disrupts the
rallying of the Greek army:
He got up in the assembly and attacked Agamemnon in the words
of Achilles calling him greedy and a coward
dysseus then
stood up, delivered a sharp rebuke to Thersites, which he coupled
with a threat to strip him naked, and then beat him on the back
and shoulders with Agamemnon s scepter; Thersites doubled over,
a warm tear fell from his eye, and a bloody welt formed on his
back; he sat down in fear, and in pain gazed helplessly as he wiped
away his tear; but the rest of the assembly was distressed and
laughed There must be a figuration of wickedness as selfevident as Thersites the ugliest man who came to Troy who
says what everyone else is thinking [19].
He is not mentioned elsewhere in the Iliad, but it seems that in the
lost Aethiopis, Achilles eventually killed him “for having torn out the
eyes of the Amazon Penthesilea that the hero had just killed in combat”
[20] (Fig. 12.1). He was represented by Polygnotus at the Porch (λέσχη)
of the Cnidians (located at Delphi) playing dice with Palamedes [21,
22].

Fig. 12.1 Relief from the sarcophagus of Aurelia Botania Demetria, preserved in the
Archaeological Museum of Antalya (Turkey): Achilles beating Thersites (second century AD)

12 3 Description and Clinical Patterns
The name oxycephaly meaning “pointed head” refers to the “clown’s
hat” found at the site of the ossified bulging bregmatic fontanel.
Compensating growth in the anterior fontanel region results in the
formation of a pointed or cone-shaped skull [3, 4] (Fig. 12.2).

Fig. 12.2 Bicoronal and metopic or sagittal synostosis, together with a compensating growth in
the anterior fontanel region, results in the formation of a pointed or skull-shaped cone
(“clown’s hat”) at the site of the ossified bulging bregmatic fontanel

Secondary to premature synostosis of the coronal and sagittal
sutures, oxycephaly is defined by a receding forehead especially tilted
back in continuity with the nasal bridge (Fig. 12.3).

Fig. 12.3 Oxycephaly is defined by a receding forehead, tilted back in continuity with the nasal
bridge

The calvaria is characterized by a high, steep forehead often with a
depression of the supraorbital region. The sagittal diameter is short,
and the head may appear pointed in the bregmatic region. The cephalic
index is usually increased (brachycephaly) and the head circumference
decreased, with microcephaly being common. The anterior cranial base
is short: the greater wing of the sphenoid is protruded, and the lesser
wing exhibits a steep upward and lateral slope with a frontalization of
the orbital roof [3, 23]. The vertical development of the face is
characterized by increased anterior and decreased posterior face
height, typically narrow and surmounted by a median projection
located at the level of the bregmatic fontanel. The facial bone is normal

in this type of craniosynostosis. The altered jaw relations, which can be
related to the marked flattening of the cranial base, may lead to a
malocclusion with frontal open bite, extreme maxillary overjet, and
distal molar occlusion. Because of the marked flattening of the cranial
base, the head is carried in an extended position in relation to the
cervical column [23]. Longitudinal radiographic and roentgen
cephalometric studies have shown that the growth of the calvaria is
markedly eccentric, with diminished forward growth of the frontal
bone and concomitant increased vertical development [24].
Pronounced frontal bossing may be seen in infancy but becomes
reduced by virtue of continued increments of the growth in the glabella
area combined with decreased growth of the supraglabellar region
[23]. In fact, isolated oxycephaly very often goes unnoticed in childhood
due to the harmony of the cranial morphology by the end of youth and
tends to be diagnosed lately when the child presents with visual loss or
signs of intracranial hypertension [3, 25]. A reason for this could be the
late fusion of bicoronal and sagittal sutures that may cause symptoms
later than in other conditions.

12 3 1 Clinical Forms
Often in the past [1, 2, 5, 13, 26], the term oxycephaly became a
synonym of multisutural craniostenosis characterized by a
brachycephaly [27, 28] or severe forms of craniostenosis affecting
multiple sutures, mostly in the newborn [2, 29]. All these forms should
be differentiated from the isolated oxycephaly.
Mantaut and Striker described three types of oxycephaly [30, 31]:
type I acrocephaly or turricephaly with a verticalized and receding
forehead; type II, true oxycephaly, with a receding forehead plus a
bregmatic protrusion responsible for a pointed skull; and the type III,
an oxycephaly without deformity but with a small skull reduced in all
its diameters. This classification has been subjected to criticism. Type I
(Fig. 12.4a) corresponds in fact to a brachycephaly in which the age of
onset and management are completely different [2]. This distinction is
significant, as functional risks and treatment options in oxycephaly are
completely different from those in brachycephaly [32]. Type II is the
true oxycephaly ( xus = pointed) with a pointed skull tilted back in
continuity with the nasal bridge and a bregmatic bump (Fig. 12.4b).

The frontonasal angle is wide open giving an impression of exorbitism.
Type III has a harmonious shape of the skull, which appears rounded
and has no visible dysmorphism, despite multiple sutures being closed
(Fig. 12.4c).

Fig. 12.4 Clinical patterns of oxycephaly. (a) Type I acrocephaly or turricephaly corresponds to
a bicoronal synostosis (brachycephaly) and should be excluded from this term; (b) Type II
oxycephaly is the typical case with a pointed skull tilted back in continuity with the nasal bridge
and ending in a bregmatic bump; (c) Type III is a harmonious form with closure of multiple
sutures and without any visible dysmorphism. This girl had an ophthalmological debut at the
age of 4 years

Some cases of isolated oxycephaly present at birth or even
prenatally with gross dysmorphism and severe brachycephaly; others
present later in life with harmonious restriction of intracranial volume
and are at risk for neurodevelopment and vision. At the same time,
some forms evolve from initially unisutural synostoses [3].

12 4 Epidemiology
Oxycephaly is often diagnosed lately due to harmonious morphology of
the skull and, perhaps, postnatal suture closure [2, 3]. Prevalence is
unknown, but it has been shown to be under 1/1,000,000 live
newborns.
The largest evaluation of the frequency of nonsyndromic
craniosynostosis from Paris [2] reported that the incidence of
oxycephaly had been decreasing during their 20 years analysis period.
From 1975 to 1995, 1483 patients with craniosynostosis were
hospitalized in the neurosurgery department of the Hospital des
Enfants-Malades in Paris. Among these, 129 patients (8.7%) had
nonsyndromic oxycephaly, including 86 boys (66.7%) and 43 girls
(33.3%) with ages between 1 and 22 years old (average: 6 years old,
average: 4 years 9 months). An anomaly of the calcium phosphate
metabolism was found in 22 observations: two cases of
hypophosphatasia (in two brothers) and 20 antecedents of rickets
(15.5%) [2]. A recent series from the same group reported 1.2% of all
the patients with oxycephaly in 2007, compared with 8.8% in 1988.
This reduction might be due to better care that is provided to these
patients in their countries or to a reduction in the prevalence of this
subtype of craniosynostosis [33]. The improvement of the standard of
living and the socioeconomic and nutritional conditions can also play a
role in this sense.
Although isolated oxycephaly is common in North Africa [2, 25], it is
a rare craniosynostosis among Caucasian–European patients.
Oxycephaly would be more frequent on the periphery Mediterranean,
where it could represent up to 40% of craniostenosis [2, 8, 31], while it
would represent only 6–13% in the northern American series [34].

12 5 Physiopathology
Oxycephaly is a common manifestation of different diseases involving
premature fusion of coronal and sagittal sutures. Typically, isolated
oxycephaly is of late onset, and it is never diagnosed before the age of
three [2], which differentiates it from other non-syndromic
craniosynostosis evident at birth. There are reports of children that
presented with a typical oxycephaly at the age of 4 years and have been
studied in the past with a normal x-R at the age of one [2, 35]. Certain
elements are specific to this particular type of craniosynostosis. The
average age is much later than in other nonsyndromic craniosynostosis,
and no cases are usually observed during the first year of life [2, 3].
Oxycephaly, as discussed before, may be also a feature of certain
syndromes like Crouzon or Pfeiffer syndrome. The syndromic and
nonsyndromic forms can be distinguished by the absence of limb
and/or facial anomalies in nonsyndromic forms.

12 5 1 Chiari Malformation in Oxycephaly
The association between Chiari malformation (CM) and premature
craniofacial synostosis was first noted by Saldino et al. [36] in 1972 in
one patient with Pfeiffer syndrome. Since then, numerous authors have
reported the incidence of chronic tonsillar herniation in multiple suture
craniosynostosis [37–43], and it is a frequent finding in syndromic and
multisuture craniosynostosis, characterized by early fusion of lambdoid
sutures and cranial base synchondroses. The incidence of CM has been
reported as high as 70% in Crouzon syndrome [2, 42, 43], 75% in
nonsyndromic oxycephaly [2], 50% in Pfeiffer syndrome, and 100% in
kleeblattschädel deformity [44]. In the series from Renier [2], of the 16
children in whom an MRI was performed, Chiari type I malformation
was present in 12 (75%), one of them associated to hydrocephalus. CM
has been found in other types of syndromic craniosynostosis, in some
cases of nonsyndromic complex craniosynostosis involving the
lambdoid suture, and in some rare cases of scaphocephaly [42, 45].
The frequency of Chiari malformation in the oxycephaly is elevated,
and it approaches that observed in Crouzon’s syndrome [2, 44] (Fig.
12.5). In this syndrome, Cinalli et al. have shown that chronic
involvement of the cerebellar tonsils is probably an acquired anomaly

and not an associated congenital malformation, and that this anomaly
was probably related to a decrease in volume of the posterior cerebral
fossa due to a premature synostosis of lambdoid sutures [39] or a
decreased intracranial volume motivated by the closure several sutures
in the anterior region [46].

Fig. 12.5 Chiari malformation is a frequent finding in multisutural craniosynostoses. The
incidence has been reported as high as 75% in oxycephaly. (a) Phenotipic appearance in an 18month-old boy; (b) Chiari malformation is present at first diagnosis

Downward herniation of neural tissue through the foramen
magnum is usually an acquired malformation in craniosynostosis and

may be secondary to a disproportion between the posterior fossa and
the growing hindbrain structures [39, 47]. In most cases of
craniosynostosis, hindbrain herniation is not present at birth; rather, it
develops in response to the changes in the skull base and posterior
fossa secondary to premature closure of the lambdoid and cranial base
sutures, supporting the pathogenetic hypothesis of overcrowding of the
posterior fossa secondary to premature suture fusion [43, 44, 48]. The
rest of the sutures (lambdoid, sagittal, coronal, and metopic) also play a
role in the development of CM. In the setting of a postnatal (or in utero)
closure of sagittal and coronal sutures, a cephalocranial disproportion
in the supratentorial compartment occurs early, forcing the neural
growth to be directed posteriorly and inferiorly and pushing down the
tentorium. This can induce a lower attachment of the tentorium (near
the foramen magnum), reducing the size of the posterior fossa and
increasing the risk of CM, especially if premature lambdoid synostosis
is also involved. More than one-third of patients with hindbrain
herniation become symptomatic for CM or develop syringomyelic
cavities. Usually, the onset of symptoms occurs late in life, but they may
be dramatic, especially in very young children [39]. Careful radiologic
and clinical follow-up is needed in patients with syndromic or complex
craniosynostosis to assess the presence and evolution of CM. MRI with
venous angiography is the gold standard for the evaluation of these
patients [49].

12 6 Etiology
The cause of oxycephaly is unclear, but it has been demonstrated a clear
relationship between rickets and the development of craniostenosis [2,
50–52]. In the past, a frequent history of rickets, including involvement
in oxycephaly, has been reported by different groups [2, 25, 31, 52].
Reilly et al. [52] have shown that about one-third of children with
rickets were susceptible to develop cranlostenosis and that this was
related to the severity of rickets. The observation of cases of oxycephaly
complicating hypophosphatasia also favors a metabolic cause, and
points to a postnatal physiopathological mechanism of this
craniostenosis.

The advances of genetics also lead to the discovery of new genetic
entities. Unlike synostoses involving the sagittal system (sagittal and
metopic sutures), which are most likely idiopathic or secondary to
environmental causes, synostoses involving the coronal system are
often genetic and warrant systematic genetic evaluation [12, 53].
In some patients, the evolution toward craniofaciostenosis and the
diagnosis of other syndromic features or other familial cases are often
delayed [4, 54, 55]. The diagnosis is often provisional since closure of
the coronal suture is often the first element of a craniofaciostenosis [4,
12]. On the other hand, some patients diagnosed initially with a sagittal
or unicoronal synostosis will evolve into an oxycephaly or
brachycephaly. The diagnosis of isolated oxycephaly is thus often
provisional or retrospective.

12 6 1 Genetic Syndromes Associating Oxycephaly
Isolated oxycephaly is usually sporadic, but familial cases have been
reported.
Craniosynostosis-6 (CRS6) is a bicoronal form associated with bony
defects in the sagittal, metopic, or lambdoid sutures [56]. Twigg et al.
identified a third-generation family in which two affected individuals
had bicoronal synostosis and two had a calvarial abnormality
(brachycephaly or plagiocephaly). All affected individuals had some
degree of impaired intellectual development; one lived in a supervised
environment at age 19, two had mildly delayed development, and one
had a full-scale IQ of 89 on formal psychological testing. One affected
individual had a Dandy-Walker malformation as well as spina bifida
occulta, sensorineural hearing loss, and LHRH deficiency; several
others had more subtle abnormalities in the conformation of the
posterior fossa. The transmission pattern of CRS6 was consistent with
autosomal dominant inheritance. The underlying molecular genetics
likely correspond to a heterozygous missense mutation in the ZIC1
gene. Human ZIC1 (zinc finger protein of cerebellum 1), one of five
homologs of the Drosophila pair-rule gene odd-paired, encodes a
transcription factor previously implicated in vertebrate brain
development. Recent studies have shown that pathogenic variants in
ZIC1 have deleterious effect in developing human central nerves system
and skull bone. ZIC1 related clinical conditions are reported and

include cerebellum malformation, Dandy-Walker malformation, spinal
dysraphism, microcephaly, and craniosynostosis with associated
intellectual disability [57, 58]. The diagnosis of a ZIC1 mutation has
significant implications for prognosis, and genetic testing for this
condition has been recommended, when common causes of coronal
synostosis have been excluded.
Oxycephaly is also a common finding in different diseases involving
premature fusion of the cranial sutures as a secondary event such as
TOLCAS or craniorhiny [12, 59–64].
Mindikoglu et al. (1991) published the first cases of
craniosynostosis combined with unusual nasal abnormalities. The skull
shape was oxycephalic with recessed forehead and lack of nasofrontal
angle. The nasal changes consisted of wide nose, anteverted nostrils,
and nasal hirsutism. Bilaterally symmetrical spherical cyst-like
formations with fistulas were present just below the nose. This
condition was termed craniorhiny [65].

12 6 2 TOLCAS Syndrome
Tolchin-Le Caignec syndrome (TOLCAS) is caused by heterozygous
mutation in the SOX6 gene on chromosome 11p15. TOLCAS is a
developmental disorder characterized by mildly to moderately
impaired intellectual development and behavioral problems, such as
autism, attention deficit (ADHD), labile mood, and aggressive episodes.
Many patients have bony abnormalities, including osteochondroma,
craniosynostosis, dysmorphic facies, arachnodactyly, and large head
circumference. Rarely, additional congenital anomalies may also be
observed [66]. Clinical depiction of these patients revealed dysmorphic
features, including prominent occiput, high forehead, micrognathia,
hypertelorism, bitemporal narrowing, broad nasal bridge, large or lowset ears, and full eyebrows.
The heterozygous mutations in the SOX6 gene that were identified
in most patients with TOLCAS occurred de novo. However, 2 families
showed autosomal dominant transmission of the disorder. Tolchin et al.
(2020) noted that SOX6 plays a role in neurogenesis and
chondrogenesis, which could explain the phenotypic features [66].

12 7 Management and Surgical Treatment
Isolated oxycephaly is a non-syndromic form of late onset
craniostenosis, responsible for insidious intracranial hypertension that
can lead, if not treated early, to unnoticed progressive blindness or
other related severe complications. Unlike sagittal or metopic
synostoses, which do not cause intracranial hypertension and for which
the aim of surgery is above all the restoration of normal shape,
intracranial hypertension is the rule in oxycephaly [2, 4]. For this
reason, decompressive surgery is needed even in newborns when signs
of increased intracranial pressure are found. During childhood, it
should be performed as soon as the clinical diagnosis has been
established. The high prevalence of visual loss caused by optic nerve
atrophy and the number of children with oxycephaly and
developmental delay confirm that for many of these patients, surgery is
not optional [25].
Cranial expansion surgery is essential for relieving intracranial
pressure and stabilizing intellectual deficit which, in the absence of
treatment, becomes significantly more profound. Following surgery, the
intracranial pressure returns to normal, papilledema usually resolves,
and the intellectual deficit seems to stabilize. However, secondary
surgery is more commonly required in oxycephaly than in patients with
a single suture craniosynostosis.
The timing of surgery and the surgical technique used for correction
will depend primarily on the patient’s age at presentation. The aim of
the surgery is mainly to expand intracranial volume trying to achieve a
proper ratio between skull and brain, providing adequate aesthetic
correction at the same time.
In infants and older children, fronto-orbital advancement with
frontoparietal remodeling is the technique of choice, providing good
cranial decompression and satisfactory morphological results.
However, decompressive surgery may be needed soon after birth. In
the newborn with soft bones, no cranioplasty is possible. For this
reason, different techniques including endoscopic assisted
suturectomies or open perifrontal craniectomy have been described
and will be later discussed.

12 7 1 Early Surgery Newborns
12.7.1.1 Perifrontal Craniectomy (Peri-Fronto-Orbital
Craniectomy)
The French group in Lille introduced Peri-Fronto-Orbital Craniectomy
(PFOC) for early treatment of nonsyndromic oxycephaly and
brachycephaly [4, 67]. This technique has been used in newborns
requiring emergency decompression, and it would be indicated for
children below the age of 4 months.
A conventional bicoronal incision is performed and a frontal scalp
elevated in a subgaleal fashion. A 2-cm wide strip of the periosteum is
removed along the coronal sutures and the orbital rim on both sides.
The craniectomy (Fig. 12.6) removes the coronal suture down to the
temporal fossa on each side, taking out the pterional bone, which is
usually very thick in this type of pathology [67] and reaches the frontomalar suture The resection is carried on to the lateral orbital wall and
along the orbital roof, removing almost all of it. Osteotomies continue
medially to the roof of the orbit behind the orbital rim and extend to
the fronto-nasal suture. These craniotomies join on the nasion, which is
resected as well. The released frontal bone, only maintained by a thin
sagittal bridge, is then able to respond to the brain’s growth stimulation
[3, 4]. In addition, coagulation is applied to the dura mater along the
site of the coronal suture to prevent early ossification and to initiate the
formation of a neosuture, as published earlier [68].

Fig. 12.6 Perifronto-orbital craniectomy, a technique used in newborns requiring emergency
decompression. The craniectomy removes the coronal suture down to the fronto-malar suture,
the roof of the orbit behind the supraorbital rim, and extends to the fronto-nasal suture. The
frontal bone is, in this way, set free and allows the growing brain to remodel the skull. (Taken
from Vinchon et al. [4] with permission)

Great care must be exerted to avoid tearing the dura mater,
especially near the midline (because of the risk of venous bleeding) and
in the temporal region because the temporal squama is swiveled into
the frontal plane, and the dural folds are intricated with the sphenoid
ridge [4]. PFOC technique has the advantage that the bone flap is left
undissected from the dura: this preserves its vascular supply and
avoids unnecessary bleeding [67].
There are important issues regarding the surgical technique for a
satisfactory outcome:
1. The child must be younger than 4 months.

2. The craniectomy should take away not only the periosteum and the
frontoparietal fused suture but also the sphenoid wing and a bony
strip all around the frontal bone flap along the orbital roofs and the
nasion, opening the superior orbital fissure. This is a point to bear
in mind when discussing endoscopic approaches.
3. The dissection of the dura must be exclusively limited to the site of
the craniectomy to preserve the frontal bone flap vascular supply,
and
4. The dura should be gently coagulated along the coronal suture to
avoid bony reossification [67].

12.7.1.2 Endoscopic-Assisted Suturectomies
Minimally invasive surgery, involving endoscopic suturectomy
combined with cranial molding with helmets, has been advocated for
multiple suture craniosynostoses. While craniectomy in a newborn is a
large surgery, which requires expertise from both surgeon and
anesthetist, other “less invasive” techniques have been reported for the
treatment of oxycephaly in infants, below the age of 3–4 months [69,
70].
Given the satisfactory long-term results reported with endoscopy
for young infants with single-suture synostosis [69], some groups have
started treating infants with nonsyndromic multiple-suture calvarial
synostosis using the same principles of minimally invasive endoscopy:
assisted craniectomies followed by postoperative cranial orthotic
treatment. For most authors, endoscopic technique must be followed by
the use of cranial orthesis [69, 71]. The goal of the helmet is to redirect
cranial growth and achieve normal head shape and size after releasing
osteotomies.
In a series from Jimenez [69], every patient presenting with
nonsyndromic multiple-suture synostosis and who were under
6 months of age were selected for endoscopic treatment achieving
excellent results. In all patients, the cephalic indices decreased an
average of 26% after surgery. Antimongoloid orbital slant was
corrected to produce a normal orbital alignment as well as the
bitemporal widening seen with brachycephaly. Helmet therapy

following release of the stenosed coronal sutures led to internal
distraction and forward movement of the nasoorbital complex. None of
their cases needed a secondary bifrontal orbital advancement due to
proptosis or corneal compromise. Furthermore, longitudinal analysis of
their entire cohort demonstrated that all the patients’ measurements
followed standard population isocurves appropriate for each patient
and therefore, there were no cases in which head or brain growth was
restricted. The mean preoperative cephalic index was 98 (range 82–
111), and the median was 97. Late postoperative cephalic index
(≥1 year) was 83 (range 79–92), and the median was 82. Overall, there
was a 15% decrease from preoperative baseline [69].

12.7.1.3 Endoscopic Assisted Suturectomies in Oxycephaly
Technique
Access to a stenosed coronal suture is reached with a 2- to 3-cm
incision located over the coronal suture at the level of the stephanion
[69]. Subgaleal dissection is performed between the anterior fontanel
and the squamosal suture behind the pterion. If needed, the metopic
suture is reached using a new 2- to 3-cm incision located over the
metopic suture in front of the anterior fontanel with subgaleal
dissection between the nasofrontal suture and the anterior fontanel.
Finally, the sagittal suture is reached via two incisions. The first is made
over the anterior fontanel, and the second immediately in front of the
lambda. The dissection plane proceeds between the galea and
pericranium, using monopolar electrocautery. Thus, the loose areolar
tissue is separated in a completely bloodless fashion.
Then, a pediatric 7-mm craniotome is used to create a bur hole at
each incision. The bur hole is enlarged longitudinally along the suture
axis when the coronal, metopic, or lambdoid sutures are involved. In
the case of sagittal involvement, the bur hole is placed at the lateral
edge of the incision and an osteotomy is carried across the midline to
the other side, to a symmetrical distance from the suture. A 4-mm rigid
0° or 30° angled endoscope is inserted into the epidural space for
visualization and dissection of the space. The dura mater is fully
dissected from the overlying bone from the anterior fontanel to the
nasofrontal suture (metopic), squamosal suture behind the pterion
(coronal), or lambda (sagittal). In the case of lambdoid involvement,

epidural dissection is undertaken between the lambda and asterion.
Removal of bone is done with a combination of angled Kerrison
rongeurs, bone (pituitary type) rongeurs, and Mayo scissors. The
craniectomy size for the metopic, coronal, and lambdoid sutures
averages 7 mm (range 5–10 mm) and 50 mm (range 40–60 mm) for
sagittal involvement. Osseous hemostasis is obtained using a suctionmonopolar unit. The bone is cauterized under direct visualization until
all oozing and bleeding stops. The incisions are closed with 4–0
Monocryl (Ethicon, Inc.), and the dermis sealed with Ethibond (Ethicon,
Inc.). A custom-made helmet is fitted on the sixth postoperative day and
kept for 12–18 months postoperatively.

12.7.1.4 Controversies
The concept of surgery at a very early age may look appealing in severe
cases of uni- or bicoronal synostosis diagnosed at birth. Based on the
success of strip craniectomies as a simple and efficient method
routinely used for treatment of sagittal synostosis, some authors have
extended this indication to multisutural (nonsyndromic)
craniosynostosis. The very invasive nature of the conventional calvarial
remodeling techniques used in most craniofacial centers requires that
these patients are treated at later stages (at 6–12 months of age).
Invariably, such delay in treatment leads to changes in skull base, nasal,
and orbital morphology and alignment that cannot be easily corrected
with the use of subsequent surgical procedures. The end result tends to
be suboptimal, particularly when more than two sutures are involved.
The goal in approaching these patients with minimally invasive
endoscopic techniques at a very early age intends to halt, and even
significantly reverse, the progression of associated craniofacial
deformities [69]. By releasing the stenosed sutures early, adequate
brain growth takes place, which in turn leads to cephalic normalization.
Extensive surgeries (mostly fronto-orbital advancement) could then not
be needed and could save the children all the risks associated with
open procedures.
However, for many authors [4, 17, 45, 67, 71], the deformation of
the skull base in multisutural synostosis affecting the anterior fossa
requires a more invasive approach in order to obtain a definitive
correction.

Oxycephaly has a more complicated pathology compared with
bilateral coronal suture synostosis. Linear craniectomies in the region
of the coronal suture early in infancy have been shown to have a very
limited effect on the growth pattern of the calvaria in most of the
patients with oxycephaly [24, 72]. Coronal craniectomy per se does
little to alter the pattern of growth in the frontal region over the long
term [24, 73]. Simple suturectomy was abandoned in coronal
synostosis in the past due to early bony reclosure and failure to achieve
satisfactory cranial shape [4, 67]. This could be explained because the
coronal suture, in association with the frontosphenoidal and
sphenoethmoidal sutures, makes up the largest cranial suture complex
[28]. Anderson et al. had described that synostosis of this complex
cannot be compensated for by the other sutures [8]. For this reason,
Seeger and Gabrielsen had recommended that the coronal strip
craniectomies should be extended downward and inward, to include
the heavily overgrowth sphenoid ridge [71]. This is one of the main
concerns about endoscopic coronal suturectomy: a single incision over
the lateral portion of the suture does not allow osteotomies on the
orbital roof and resection of the lesser wing of the sphenoid.
Probably more data are needed on the results obtained with
minimally invasive surgery, especially on long-term follow-up. In any
case, whatever the technique selected for the correction of this
malformation is, a close follow-up of these patients is mandatory in a
short and long term to recognize early signs of recurrence and
increased intracranial pressure.

12 7 2 Late 6 12 Months Early Childhood
Since Tessier’s innovative work in 1967, the principles of craniofacial
surgery established fronto-orbital advancement as an acceptable
treatment for craniosynostosis, and it remains the standard for anterior
unilateral or multisutural synostoses [72]. This surgery, usually
performed within the first year of life to correct the bony deformity and
improve cosmetic appearance, involves excision of the fused suture and
remodeling/repositioning of the frontal bone and orbits.
Fronto-orbital advancement with frontoparietal remodeling is the
technique of choice and provides good cranial decompression and
morphological results in oxycephaly. Tessier’s tongue-in-groove

advancement of the orbital bandeau (supraorbital rim together with
roof of the orbits) followed by remodeling and osteosynthesis of the
reconstructed forehead bone remains one of the most commonly
reported techniques [3].
There are multiple variations of this procedure, but all techniques
typically include the resection of the affected sutures and the expansion
of the anterior fossa by means of projecting a fronto-orbital bandeau.
Based on the observation by Seeger and Gabrielsen [71] that the
sphenofrontal suture (together with the coronal) is also prematurely
fused in brachycephaly, the concept of the surgery led to release the
sutures of the anterior cranial base, with advance of the supraorbital
rim [74–76], and the creation of free-floating flaps in the frontal region
[35, 77]. These techniques have been shown to lead to marked
improvement in calvarial growth [78].
Hoffman and Mohr used Tessier’s method combined with their own
technique for advancing the lateral canthal segments of the
supraorbital region for the treatment of metopic synostosis [74]. Soon
after, Marchac and Renier published the “floating forehead” technique,
later combined with a fronto-orbital bandeau remodeling. Marchac
advised the use of the floating forehead technique for children under
6 months of age, while for children older than 6 months, he used a
horizontal tongue-in-groove advancement [1, 2, 13, 32, 35, 79–81]. In
the floating forehead technique, they removed the orbital bar and
advanced it by 2 cm after remodeling. This bar was fixed only to the
frontal process of the zygoma. The frontal bone was wired to the
supraorbital bar leaving a wide craniectomy behind. This allowed the
brain to push freely on the forehead [13]. To provide support, a small
bone graft was placed between the root of the nose and the advanced
supraorbital bar [80]. Although theoretically feasible, their floating
forehead technique resulted in temporal hollowing and craniolacuniae
and, for this reason, different techniques have been reported since then
[4, 68, 81–83].
Since oxycephaly is due to both coronal sutures and an additional
sagittal suture synostosis, the forehead is recessed and tilted backward
in continuity with the nasal dorsum (frontonasal angle). The
supraorbital rim is recessed, producing an impression of exophthalmos.
Therefore, Renier et al. modified their surgical technique for the

treatment of brachycephaly [13]. They lifted and repositioned the
superior orbital bar with an anterior rotation and transposed the upper
forehead and lower forehead to obtain better aesthetic results (Fig.
12.7).

Fig. 12.7 Modification of the Renier fronto-orbital advancement technique for brachycephaly.
Their technique advances the superior orbital bar with an anterior rotation and transposes the
upper and lower forehead to improve the aesthetic results

The tongue-in-groove procedure is not easily adapted to
repositioning the supraorbital bar when rotation in the coronal plane
(sagittal axis) is required. Whitaker et al. published their own
technique on the correction of craniofacial dysostosis in which threefourths of the abnormal orbit is osteotomized and advanced to become
level with the normal orbit [84]. They used a lateral bone graft between
the advanced orbit and the temporal bone to maintain the newly
advanced position. Some years later, they published a modified
technique in which the orbit advancement was completed with a bony
Z-plasty at the lateral orbit or by a tongue-in-groove procedure to
reassure the bone firmly positioned (Whitaker 1980) (Fig. 12.8).

Fig. 12.8 (a) Preoperative CT; (b) Fronto-orbital remodeling. (c) Intraoperative image
obtained with the image guided therapy platform Azurion (Philips): observe the distance
between the lateral wall of the orbit and the fronto-malar suture corresponding to an
advancement of 1.4 mm (white arrows)

Persing et al. stated that the most difficult cranial dimension to
correct is excessive skull height [85]. He described a one-staged
procedure for turricephaly, made possible largely by using modified
prone position. This position allows simultaneous access to both the
anterior and posterior cranium. In summary, bifrontal and
biparietooccipital “quadrant” craniotomies are performed. A bone plate
remains at the vertex of the skull and over the superior sagittal sinus to
avoid its injury. The lowering of the vertex and thus, shortening in
heights is accomplished by bone resection from the caudal ends of the
anterior and the lateral bony struts. Parallel vertical cuts are made into
the bone of the basal cranium and occipital osteotomies are carried out
down to the foramen magnum. After the reshaping of the bone flaps by
the “quadrant” craniotomies, they are replaced and the scalp flap are
returned to their normal position. Although this method seems to be
very aggressive, the barrel stave osteotomies would act to decrease the
resistance of the vertical compression of the skull and increase the
capacity of the cranium [3].
Vinchon et al. [4] reported a modification of the bandeau with a
two-tongue bone cut: a temporofrontal anterior tongue, a part of the
bandeau which is translated and kyphosed; and a posterior tongue,
which prolongs the temporoparietal region, on which the anterior
tongue is rigidly fixed. This technique is able to withstand the pressure,
when the scalp is reapproximated and allows significant frontal
advancement providing great stability [4]. However, it may be
inapplicable for older children with a thick and rigid bone. In these
cases, remodeling of the frontoparietal region will require cutting and
remodeling frontal and parietal bone flaps. Repositioning of the parietal
flaps laterally and anteriorly provides advancement and widening of
the calvaria; in addition, “fan-like” anterior rotation provides a reliable
buttress to secure the advancement of the fronto-orbital construct.
Another important technical detail is the correction of the bulging
temporal squama to narrow excessively wide interparietal diameter.
This usually requires resection in the temporal squama, remodeling
with barrel staves, or inversion of a temporal bone flap [53].

Shen et al. had described their surgical method in a case report. This
consisted in a multiple bone flap rotation-reposition technique to
reconstruct the calvaria with the osteotomy bone flaps rotated,
repositioned, and fixed in a design to reduce the cranial height [86].

12 7 3 Other Treatments
More radical procedures of subtotal calvariectomy for oxycephalic
patients with multiple synostosis have been used in the past [87, 88].
Hanson et al. proposed a wide excision of the bony calvarium from the
supraorbital ridge to near the foramen magnum including the entire
area of the coronal sutures. They saw a regeneration of the calvarium
occurring from 2 to 12 weeks by the presence of the “neosutures” in
their usual location. This radical procedure had allowed for normal
brain growth without reoperation up to 2 years old. Also, neurologic
and intellectual performance was satisfactory, and the cosmetic results
appeared to be preferable to those obtained by more limited surgery.
These techniques have been mostly abandoned and left for the most
severe forms of cloverleaf skulls (kleeblattschädel) or complex
craniosynostosis, which need emergent decompression in the first
weeks of life [89].
Distracting procedures have been advocated to increase cranial
volume and used in the treatment of brachycephaly [90]. The
advantages of osteogenic cranial distraction would be the lack of a dead
space just after surgery because the distraction is applied gradually and
equally to the dura, skin, and soft tissues with simultaneous expansion
of bone and soft tissues. It is also very unlikely a bone resorption
because blood supply is not hindered during surgery. The amount of
blood loss and the duration of surgery also decreases because the
release of the membrane from the bone is minimal. The main
disadvantage for these techniques would be the limitation of the
vectors of the distraction (impossibility for three dimensional vectors)
and the necessity for an additional second surgery to remove the
device.
Uemura et al. described three-dimensional cranial expansion using
distraction osteogenesis to treat oxycephaly [91]. In his technique, a
bifrontal craniotomy is extended laterally downward on both sides,
including supraorbital rim and orbital roofs. A biparietal bone flap is

designed to apply the lateral expanding devices. The frontal expansion
device is attached to the bilateral lower area of the frontal bone,
including the orbital roof. The bilateral expansion device is attached
further backward from the parietal area of the bone flap, supported by
the bilateral lower temporal area (Fig. 12.9). Osteogenic distraction is
initiated after 5 days after surgery, and the distraction devices activated
simultaneously 1 mm per day. The devices were removed after a
consolidation period of 3–5 months.

Fig. 12.9 The debut of this patient consisted of a profound alteration of vision at the age of 5.
Funduscopy revealed severe papilledema. His father became blind at the age of 16 in his
country of origin, without a clear diagnosis. On his arrival at our institution, an oxycephalia was
clear and treatment (ICP monitoring and CT/MR studies) was offered, but he refused due to
lack of symptoms, other than his long-standing bilateral amaurosis. Treatment in her son’s case
began with a posterior parieto-occipital distraction, followed by a fronto-orbital advancement,

which proved to be very effective in controlling his symptoms and from a cosmetic point of
view. His papilledema resolved, and he has been free of symptoms since the first surgery. (a) CT
and phenotypic appearance at initial diagnosis. (b) Posterior (parieto-occipital) advancement.
(c) “Monobloc” fronto-orbital distraction. Hirabayashi technique [98]. (d) Final appearance of
the boy, 1 year after the completion of both procedures

12 8 Outcome of Oxycephaly
Isolated oxycephaly is a form of multisutural non-syndromic
craniosynostosis characterized by premature fusion of both the coronal
and sagittal sutures. Elevated intracranial pressure is a common clinical
feature (affecting more than 60% of the patients) leading to frequent
ophthalmologic complications (papilledema) and moderate to severe
intellectual deficit, although individuals may have a completely normal
cognitive outcome [92]. When left untreated, it is responsible for
insidious intracranial hypertension that can lead to severe related
complications.
Intracranial hypertension (ICH) is the rule in oxycephaly, and it will
definitely appear at some point in life [4, 93, 94]. For this reason,
decompressive surgery is needed even in newborns when signs of
increased intracranial pressure are found or as soon as a clinical
diagnosis has been established. Cranial expansion is essential for
relieving intracranial pressure and stabilizing intellectual deficit.
Usually, intracranial pressure returns to normal after proper surgery,
and papilledema resolves. However, secondary surgeries are more
commonly required in oxycephaly compared with patients with a single
suture craniosynostosis.
There are several publications describing outcomes in simple
brachycephaly. In the Lille group report [67], patients who underwent
peri-fronto-orbital craniectomy before the age of 4 months reached
school age and attended normal school programs [4]. None of them
presented signs of developmental delay, and no visual deterioration
was encountered. From a morphological point of view, peri-frontoorbital craniectomy allowed a satisfactory improvement in most of
their cases (83%). For this reason, their report insisted on the
importance of an early surgery.
In a series of 99 children with isolated nonsyndromic bicoronal
synostosis followed prospectively to study mental outcome, Arnaud et

al. reported also a statistically significant difference between the group
that underwent surgery before 1 year of age and those who underwent
surgery after 1 year of age. Before surgery, mental status was also
statistically lower in the group of older than 1 year [3, 95].
However, there are not many reports describing the outcome of
oxycephaly. Due to a late diagnosis in this insidious form of harmonic
multisutural craniosynostosis [2, 25], there is a higher risk of increased
intracranial pressure and mental retardation compared with
brachycephaly. Raised intracranial pressure is characteristic of this
pathology and leads frequently to ophthalmological complications
(even blindness) and moderate or severe intellectual disability [96]. In
a series of 646 patients, the proportion of normal mental development
in non-syndromic craniosynostosis ranged from 67% to 86%, except
for oxycephaly, where it was 42% [1]. The main factor for this ICH is the
reduction in cranial volume that can be harmonious, without visible
dysmorphism.
The severity of oxycephaly is related to ICH, which is present in
61.6% of cases, with papilledema in only 10% of cases (!) but with a
13% of an optic atrophy at diagnosis [2, 28]. It is necessary to insist on
the frequent dissociation that exists between intracranial pressure and
the funduscopy, which remain normal in almost two-thirds of children
who have ICH, despite its chronic nature [2]. According to Renier et al.
[2], in their review of 129 cases, papilledema disappeared and the
intracranial pressure returned to normal in all cases with preoperative
increased intracranial pressure. The mental level seemed to stabilize;
the mean postoperative IQ being strongly correlated with the
preoperative level. In non-operated patients, the mental level worsened
significantly [2, 3].
In the series of Vinchon et al., although it is a combined series of
brachycephaly and oxycephaly, 28 patients out of 61 patients (including
30 patients suffering from brachycephaly and 31 from oxycephaly) had
shown signs and symptoms of increased intracranial pressure. Thirteen
patients had shown ophthalmological abnormalities. There were four
cases of oxycephaly that had developmental delay at the time of
diagnosis. Thirteen oxycephalic patients had cognitive and/or
behavioral problems. The mean age at surgery was 50.6 months in
oxycephalic patient compared with 20.4 months in brachycephalic

patients [4]. The higher age in oxycephalic cases can show that this is a
late appearing craniosynostosis, which Renier had also posted [2].
From a cosmetic point of view, most of the surgical procedures
reported an acceptable aesthetic result, as described previously [1, 2,
13, 35, 68, 75–81, 84, 87, 88, 97].

12 9 Conclusion
Oxycephaly is a late-appearing form of non-syndromic craniosynostosis
characterized by the premature fusion of both the coronal and sagittal
sutures. It is a rare and serious condition that can pass unnoticed
exposing these patients throughout their lives to risks of chronic and
insidious ICH. This may result in severe optic atrophy and blindness or
cognitive delay if not treated on time. Sudden decompensation can also
occur following an intercurrent disease, including a head trauma. A
high index of suspicion must be bear in mind since, due to the harmonic
microcephaly often associated, its diagnosis that can go unnoticed.
For this reason, decompressive surgery is needed when signs of
increased intracranial pressure are found or as soon as a clinical
diagnosis has been established. Different techniques for cranial
expansion have been described, and all of them have been proved to
relieve intracranial pressure and stabilize cognitive decline. Intracranial
pressure usually returns to normal after surgery and papilledema
resolves. Good results can be obtained also from a cosmetic point of
view. However, secondary surgeries are more commonly required in
oxycephaly compared with patients with a single suture
craniosynostosis to achieve a definitive control of the disease.
The timing of surgery and the most appropriate technique,
including the benefits and results of minimally invasive procedures, are
still a matter of debate.
