13 Multiple Sutures Synostosis: Key
Points for the Neurosurgeons and
Management Principles
Dale Swift1
(1) Department of Neurosurgery, University of Texas Southwestern
Medical Center, Dallas, TX, USA

Dale Swift
Email: dale.swift@utsouthwestern.edu

13 1 Introduction
The involvement of multiple cranial sutures renders care of the patient
with craniosynostosis significantly more complicated. In addition to a
more complex deformity of the skull, these patients are more likely to
develop brain dysfunction related to progressive structural
abnormalities. Persons with multiple cranial suture synostosis are
more likely to have raised intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus,
cerebellar tonsil herniation, and syringomyelia (Fig. 13.1). It is not only
incumbent upon the neurosurgeon to be able to perform appropriate
surgical interventions but also to anticipate the development of these
conditions in order to minimize their ultimate impact.

Fig. 13.1 Effect of ventricular shunting on the posterior fossa. (a) Sagittal MRI before VPS. (b)
Sagittal MRI after VPS. (c) Sagittal MRI after shunt ligation. This now adult patient had a VPS
placed at 8 months of age for progressive ventriculomegaly. Her clinical diagnosis at that time
was Crouzon syndrome. Post-operatively she developed CTH. After cranial vault remodeling the
shunt was removed. With the availability of genetic testing her diagnosis was changed to
Muenke syndrome. This historical case is presented for instructive purposes to illustrate the
potential effect of ventricular shunting in complex craniosynostosis

As part of a dedicated craniofacial team, the neurosurgeon must be
able to identify those patients most at risk for the development of
specific neurologic complications (e.g., intracranial hypertension).
Thus, the neurosurgeon should have a working knowledge of the
expected course for each type of multisuture craniosynostosis and can
be able to choose the appropriate technique executed at the
appropriate time in order to maximize efficacy and minimize surgical
complications and long-term sequelae.
Many forms of multisuture craniosynostosis are described by
various eponymous craniofacial syndromes. Syndromic forms of
craniosynostosis include Apert, Crouzon, Pfeiffer, Muenke, SaethreChotzen as well as others. There are reportedly over 180 different
syndromes associated with scraniosynostosis [1]. These syndromes are
usually associated with some variant of FGFR mutation [1]. Individual
craniosynostosis syndromes may also be associated with noncranial
somatic malformations such as syndactyly in Apert syndrome and
sensorineural hearing loss in Muenke syndrome. Comprehensive care
of these patients in a multidisciplinary setting will allow timely
attention to these associated conditions. For example, the prevalence of
intestinal malrotation is significantly elevated in patients with FGFRassociated craniosynostosis and may be diagnosed and treated before
intestinal complications occur [2].

Sporadic, nonsyndromic forms of multisuture craniosynostosis may
fall into recognized patterns such as the trisutural “Mercedes Benz”
craniosynostosis [3, 4] or may consist of an apparently random
association of suture involvement. It must be suspected that these
conditions will ultimately be found to have genetic alterations as well.
Ultimately, abnormalities of skull growth and subsequent effects upon
the brain depend on the pattern of suture involvement, including
sutures of the skull base as well as the calvarium. Although patterns of
suture closure tend to follow the syndrome, there is variability within
groups [5]. Perhaps, genetic or epigenetic markers may help to
distinguish further subgroups of patients in the future.
Due to the relative infrequent prevalence of these conditions, many
publications group multiple craniofacial syndromes together. As
experience is gained and genetic identification advances, we look
forward to more syndrome and morphology-specific investigations. To
that end, many groups are now utilizing genetic markers instead of
eponyms [6] and recategorizing syndromes based on genetics [7]. For
example, Crouzon and Pfeiffer syndromes, both of which usually have
FGFR2 mutations, are increasingly considered part of a spectrum [7].
For this chapter, syndromic and multisuture craniosynostosis will
be referred to as “complex craniosynostosis” and abbreviated “CCS.”
The terms “Type 1 Chiari malformation,” “hindbrain herniation,”
“cerebellar tonsil ectopia,” “tonsillar prolapse,” “chronic tonsillar
herniation,” and “cerebellar tonsil herniation” will all be considered the
same entity and referred to as “cerebellar tonsil herniation” with the
abbreviation “CTH.”

13 2 Intracranial Hypertension
Although relatively rare in single-suture synostosis, elevated
intracranial pressure (ICP) is common in syndromic and multisuture
craniosynostosis [8–11]. Despite variations in methodology and patient
selection, published incidences of intracranial hypertension (ICH) are
consistently higher in syndromic patients and increase with the
number of involved sutures [9–11]. The incidence of ICH appears to
increase with age in untreated patients [10], although some claim that
newly elevated ICP occurs rarely after the age of 8 years [12].

Particularly, informative are the reports of ICP measurements in
patients managed expectantly. In these unoperated patients, ICH was
reported in 61% of patients with Crouzon syndrome [13] and 83% of
patients with Apert syndrome [14]. A recent scoping review of ICH in
syndromic synostosis identified 18 studies using invasive ICP
monitoring as part of routine prospective screening in patients without
signs or symptoms of ICH and reported ICH in 41% [15].
The diagnosis of ICH in patients with CCS may be made definitively
with invasive ICP monitoring or inferred by noninvasive methods. The
“gold standard” for determining intracranial pressure is invasive
intraparenchymal pressure monitoring. Although there are no accepted
standards for normal ICP in children of different ages, the values
proposed by Renier in 1982 [8](normal 10 mmHg; abnormal
15 mmHg) are generally accepted today [15]. We aim to obtain 48–
36 h of continuous tracing to ensure that there are no effects of
anesthesia and that normal sleep and variations in daily activities are
recorded. As experience is gained with noninvasive means of ICH
detection in this patient population, invasive monitoring is used less
frequently [13].
In some patients, the diagnosis of elevated ICP is visually obvious.
Patients with a Kleeblattschädel phenotype often demonstrate marked
bony construction in some areas with tense dural bulging through
cranial defects in other areas. These patients usually exhibit a beaten
copper appearance on skull X-rays which is also commonly considered
an indicator of elevated ICP [15].
Papilledema is a highly specific indicator of raised intracranial
pressure, but is not necessarily sensitive [15]. Sensitivity is significantly
higher in patients 8 years or older [16]. Other ophthalmologic
measures, such as optical coherence tomography, optic nerve sheath
diameter, and visual evoked potentials, have received less widespread
use [15].
Simple head growth measurements may be difficult to interpret in
CCS patients. Interpretation must consider the patient’s surgical
history. Fronto-occipital circumference (FOC) has been highly
correlated to intracranial volume, and an arrest in FOC growth has been
associated with ICH only in patients who have undergone prior cranial
expansion [17, 18]

13 2 1 Etiology of Intracranial Hypertension
Four separate physiologic conditions are considered to contribute to
elevated ICP in patients with CCS: cranial growth restriction,
intracranial venous hypertension, hydrocephalus, and hypoventilation
secondary to upper airway obstruction. The contributions of each of
these conditions will vary with each syndrome and each patient and
must be ascertained individually in each case. A brief description of
each of these contributory conditions follows. Hydrocephalus will be
described in a later section. Doerga et al. provide a comprehensive
review and concise summary of the pertinent literature [15].

13 2 2 Growth Restriction
It seems intuitive that premature closure of multiple cranial sutures
would result in restricted growth of the cranium. Normal rapid brain
growth in infancy in the setting of restricted cranial growth may
therefore be envisioned to be the cause of elevated intracranial
pressure. Interestingly, however, measurements of intracranial volume
in CCS have demonstrated normal values in most syndromes and
increased ICV in Apert syndrome [15, 19–21]. Similarly, brain volume in
patients with CCS is reported to be normal [22]. Thus other
explanations apart from a simple mechanistic theory of restricted
cranial growth are required.
Simple single-suture craniosynostosis has long been known to
redistribute the convexity CSF in predictable patterns [23]. Thus,
synostosis could reduce skull compliance while maintaining normal
volume. This could result in altered pulse pressures leading to elevated
pressure. Although this concept has not been explicitly addressed,
increased intracranial pulse pressures with normal ICV and elevated
ICP have been reported in CCS [21]. Thus, the empiric observation that
ICP decreases after cranial vault expansion may be explained by an
increase in skull compliance and not necessarily an increase in
intracranial volume. Indeed, the description of craniosynostosis as
“premature” suture fusion may be a simplistic understanding of a more
complex pathology.

13 2 3 Intracranial Venous Hypertension

Intracranial venous hypertension in patients with CCS was first noted
only in patients with hydrocephalus and was localized angiographically
to the narrowing of the jugular foramen [24]. Subsequently, stenosis or
occlusion of the jugular foramina has been found to be a consistent
finding in CCS, especially Apert, Crouzon–Pfeiffer, and Saethre-Chotzen
syndromes [25–28]. Jugular foramen stenosis has been found to be
more severe in CCS patients with ICH even in the absence of
hydrocephalus [25, 26, 28]. The etiology of jugular foramen stenosis in
CCS is presumed secondary to premature closure of the skull base
synchondroses [29].
In addition to bony stenosis of the jugular foramen, varying degrees
of collateral vein development surrounding the foramen are
consistently observed [25, 30]. Demonstration by MR angiography has
replaced conventional catheter angiography in more recent studies [25,
30]. It is theorized that as venous collaterals develop in response to
jugular foramen stenosis, intracranial venous hypertension is relieved.
The degree of collateral formation does not, however, consistently
correlate with the development of ICH [27]. Nonetheless, venous
collateral formation may at least partially account for the observation
that primary ICH in CCS rarely develops after 6–8 years of age [12, 25].
If intracranial venous hypertension due to jugular foramen stenosis
is a major contributor to the ICH observed in CCS, it would seem
desirable to address this pathology directly. Attempts at venous bypass
initially reported in 1984 have not been subsequently repeated [24].
Indeed, venous bypass graft patency may be difficult to maintain,
especially in very young children. In another condition notable for
jugular foramen stenosis and achondroplasia, surgical decompression
of the jugular foramen has been reported once without follow-up [31].
Certainly, one must be concerned that a surgical approach to this region
may disrupt potentially beneficial collateral venous drainage. As yet
there are no endovascular options and angioplasty or stenting seems
impractical if bony stenosis of the foramen magnum is indeed the
primary cause of intracranial venous hypertension.
Thus, cranial expansion remains the procedure of choice for ICH in
CCS even when intracranial venous hypertension is a major contributor
despite the fact that it does not directly address the problem.
Knowledge of abnormal venous anatomy is important during any

cranial procedures in these patients as the sinuses may be occluded,
deeply embedded in the cranial bone, or even extracranial. Accessory
venous drainage must be anticipated as interruption of these collaterals
may result in severe cerebral edema [32]. The fact that cranial
expansion does not address the venous issue may explain the rapid
recurrence of ICH which can be seen in these patients [33].

13 2 4 Upper Airway Obstruction
Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is common in patients with syndromic
CS [15, 34, 35]. OSA is caused by midface hypoplasia and therefore
occurs mostly in the relevant syndromes. Thus, OSA occurs most often
in Apert syndrome (80%), Crouzon–Pfeiffer’s syndromes (68%), and to
a lesser degree in Saethre-Chotzen and Muenke syndromes [35, 36].
The severity of OSA in these syndromes is maximal during the first
3 years of life [34].
OSA has been found to correlate with ICH [37] and indeed to be a
predictor of ICH [18]. In addition, marked differences in ICH between
quiet sleep and active sleep have been observed with active sleep
resulting in increased ICP [37, 38]. These active sleep periods are
associated with OSA on polysomnograms and result in significant ICH
plateau waves and reductions in cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP)
[38]. Although CO2 levels were not measured in this study, marked
hypoxemia was documented [38].
Airway surgery, usually consisting of tonsillectomy and
adenoidectomy, improves sleep architecture but has not been
documented to obviate the need for cranial vault expansion [34, 36].
Often, the result is incomplete, and nocturnal oxygen with or without
continuous positive airway pressure is required to maintain safe
arterial oxygen levels during sleep. In the most severely affected
children, especially those with Pfeiffer syndrome, tracheostomy may be
lifesaving and should be considered early [39]. Ultimately, however,
midface advancement may be beneficial for both esthetic, dental, and
respiratory concerns. Craniofacial surgeons differ regarding the optimal
age and technique for midface distraction, but when successful,
patients should be able to be decannulated from any prior
tracheostomy [39, 40].

13 2 5 Consequences of Intracranial Hypertension
The consequences of chronic intracranial hypertension in patients with
complex craniosynostosis include vision loss and cognitive impairment.
Vision loss may occur in the absence of other signs or symptoms [41].
Khan reported that 40% of 141 children with a syndromic form of
craniosynostosis had visual impairment sufficient to preclude them
from obtaining a driver’s license in the UK [42]. Often vision loss is
associated with delayed presentation to medical attention. Visual acuity
with papilledema may improve with effective ICP treatment but does
not when optic atrophy is present [43]. It is essential that CCS therefore
receives regular ophthalmologic assessment.
The causative influence of intracranial hypertension on cognition is
less as well substantiated. A few studies suggest that elevated ICP is
associated with cognitive impairment and that earlier treatment results
in improved cognitive outcomes (Renier,1982) [44]. As there are many
confounding variables, the causation of this association remains to be
proven [45]. Supporting evidence is provided by the observation that
decreased cerebral cortical thickness is correlated with papilledema
and hydrocephalus independently in patients with CSS [46]. In the end,
this author agrees with the concept put forth by Hayward in 2015; the
neurosurgeon s default position must always be to assume that raised ICP
left untreated can indeed impair developmental outcome [12].

13 2 6 Treatment
13.2.6.1 Timing
The decisions of if, when, and how to surgically intervene are highly
intertwined. It is well established that early (less than 6 months)
surgical calvarial expansion and reconstruction will inevitably require
further procedures. However, later (over 1 year of age) procedures may
expose the patient to prolonged deleterious effects of elevated ICP. In an
effort to minimize surgical procedures and maximize functional and
esthetic outcomes, each patient must be considered individually,
anticipating growth tendencies based on the patient’s genotype. At this
point in time, “There is no clear consensus on the ideal operative
window for syndromic craniosynostosis” [47].

13.2.6.2 Techni ue

Cranial procedures designed to relieve ICH can be divided into two
broad groups, “passive” and “active.” [48] Passive procedures consist of
bone removal and decompression of the dura and brain. Active
procedures include cranial vault expansion and remodeling as well as
cranial distraction osteogenesis techniques which aim to reshape the
skull to increase intracranial volume. Both types of procedures are
carefully planned together by craniofacial and neurosurgeons to
consider esthetic as well as neurosurgical concerns.
During “passive” procedures, variable amounts of cranial bone are
removed without reconstruction. These procedures are usually
performed at less than 3 months of age, in patients with documented or
suspected ICH. These decompressive craniectomies have traditionally
involved a bicoronal scalp incision and removal of large portions of the
calvarium which at this age can reliably be expected to re-ossify. In fact,
calvarial regrowth usually reconstitutes the previous pattern of suture
pathology. These “passive” procedures are not definitive and nearly
always require additional surgery at a later date [48].
Although conceptually simple, these procedures pose considerable
surgical risk in this population. Apart from airway and general
anesthetic concerns, excessive blood loss is always a concern in
neonates. Continuous diligent protection of the dura and underlying
brain during the procedure is mandatory. The bone is markedly thin in
places and often completely deficit. In other areas, especially at the
involved sutures, the bone may be thickened and embedded in the dura.
Often spicules of bone deeply embedded in the dura are surrounded by
outpouchings of the dura and brain. Even with careful dissection of the
bone, often the underlying dura is attenuated and the incidental
durotomy is frequent. At times, complete bone removal may not be
possible due to severe ingrowth of bone around a dural venous sinus. In
that case, the bone may be liberated from all surrounding bones,
resulting in a “floating island” of bone, which then assumes a new
decompressed position. The author rarely uses a craniotome in this
situation for fear of dural injury. At all times, care must be taken to
protect the soft infant brain. Often encephalomalacia is apparent on
postoperative neuroimaging in areas of most severe compression and
may be related to surgical technique. At the completion of the
decompression, some of the pieces of bone may be laid on the dura

without fixation, or the bone may be omitted. Postoperatively, patients
should be carefully positioned to protect the incision, pressure points
on the scalp, and the underlying unprotected brain.
The Kleeblattschädel skull deformity represents the most severe
manifestation of cranial growth restriction. It consists of synostosis of
the coronal, squamosa, and lambdoid sutures and is generally
associated with Pfeiffer, Crouzon’s, or Apert syndrome. The
Kleeblattschädel phenotype is one instance in which early
decompressive craniectomy is indicated.
With the development of minimally invasive treatment of singlesuture synostosis, endoscopic suturectomy in CCS has also been
described [49, 50]. These early reports have few patients, are not
syndrome-specific, and report limited follow-up. However, with a 50%
durotomy incidence and high recurrence, the practicality of this
technique appears limited [50]. Apart from a shorter scalp incision with
potentially less blood loss, there is no expectation in multisuture CCS
that further surgery would not be required.
Cranial ault Procedures
In older patients ( 1 year) with structurally sufficient cranial bone,
open cranial vault expansion and remodeling have been the mainstay of
treatment of intracranial hypertension in complex craniosynostosis.
Both anterior and posterior cranial vault expansions and remodelings
have been used with the dual goals of decreasing ICP and improving
cosmetic appearance. The choice has often been surgeon-dependent
depending upon the individual cranial and orbital morphology [40].
Due to the pioneering work of Paul Tessier in the 1970s [51], for many
years attention was predominantly concentrated on anterior cranial
expansion. This approach, which includes forehead advancement,
allowed a reduction in ICP with an improvement in apparent proptosis
when present [40]. The benefits of anterior cranial vault
reconstruction, however, appear to be short-lived in CCS as elevated ICP
often recurs [18, 52]. Recurrence may be rapid and evidenced only by
persistent or recurrent papilledema [33].
From an esthetic standpoint, multiple operations involving the
anterior cranial may lead toward irregular growth and an unacceptable
appearance of the orbits and forehead. Accordingly, many craniofacial

surgeons began using posterior vault expansion as the first
intervention, reserving anterior reconstruction until skeletal maturity
and a more durable anterior contour could be anticipated [53, 54].
Posterior expansion was also found to provide a greater increase in
head circumference and a diminished tendency toward papilledema
and progressive CTH and anterior procedures [54].
Despite this apparent improvement in surgical technique,
intracranial hypertension recurs in a substantial proportion of cases
[27]. Despite what appears to be rigid reconstruction in an expanded
position, maintenance of this expansion may be inhibited by a lack of
scalp elasticity exacerbated by patient positioning.
Distraction osteotomy was initially developed as a limb-lengthening
technique in the 1950s. Application to the facial skeleton was
developed in the 1990s first to the mandible and midface. In 1998,
Sugawara reported applying the distraction technique to the anterior
cranium [55]. In 2009, White published the first cases of posterior
cranial vault distraction osteogenesis (PCVDO) reporting resolution of
intracranial hypertension and improved head shape [56]. Since that
time, the techniques have been refined and the procedure has become
widely accepted with numerous published results [57–63] (Fig. 13.2).

Fig. 13.2 Male patient with sagittal and lambdoid synostosis (Mercedes Benz pattern) who
underwent PCVDO with foramen magnum decompression. (a) CT at 10 days of age. (b) Skull Xray at beginning of distraction. (c) Skull X-ray at completion of distraction

Multiple theoretical advantages of PCVDO have been proposed.
Since the cranial bone is not removed from the dura, vascularity to the
bone is maintained and an epidural dead space is avoided. This should
promote growth and minimize infection. In addition, gradual expansion

with bone formation in the osteotomy gap should allow a more durable
expansion. In practice, PCVDO has been shown to provide a greater
increase in intracranial volume than traditional cranial expansion [64–
66]. Patients operated at less than 1 year of age experience an even
greater proportional increase [67, 68]. Interestingly, PCVDO in patients
with turricephaly also appears to improve the anterior bossing
deformity [56].
The complication rate of PCVDO is relatively high but appears to be
diminishing consistently as multiple craniofacial centers adopt and
perfect the technique. Meta-analysis of complications reports aggregate
rates of 25–30% with most being device failures and CSF leaks [69, 70].
Device failure is decreasing as the hardware design improves and is
standardized. Infection rates were 4.9–6.9% mostly consisting of local
infections at the device exit site [69, 70]. Presumably due to the
presence of a transcutaneous device, shunt infections are more
frequent after PCVDO than traditional posterior vault remodeling [71].
Although the emergence of PCVDO has been primarily driven by the
craniofacial community, the role of the neurosurgeon remains integral
to safe surgery with minimal complications. Craniotomy cuts must be
carefully planned and executed to avoid dural or venous sinus
lacerations. Often a high-speed cutting burr should be used instead of a
craniotome to cut a trough along the craniotomy path. This should
minimize the risk of dural or venous sinus injury and create a furrow
wide enough to prevent premature bone fusion during the distraction
phase. The neurosurgeons should carefully monitor device placement
for potential dural perforations. All dural lacerations should be repaired
as CSF leakage is to be expected in these patients with elevated ICP.
Even partial thickness dural tears should be addressed as the rent may
extend as distraction proceeds [69]. In patients with ventricular shunts,
the subgaleal path of the shunt should be assessed and rerouting is
considered if the shunt will be subjected to bacterial contamination
from the distraction device [72]. PCVDO has also been found to improve
the radiographic appearance of CTH as will be discussed later. Thus, the
neurosurgeon will continue to be crucial to success as indications for
cranial distraction expand.

13 3 Hydrocephalus
13 3 1 Incidence
Whereas the occurrence of hydrocephalus in children with singlesuture craniosynostosis is not increased over the general population,
hydrocephalus is commonly seen in multisuture and syndromic
craniosynostosis [73–75]. The incidence of hydrocephalus in complex
craniosynostosis varies with each particular syndrome and with the
patterns of suture involvement. Hydrocephalus appears to occur more
often when the lambdoid sutures are involved and when CTH is present
[73, 76] (Fig. 13.3).

Fig. 13.3 Mid sagittal MRIs of patient in Fig. 13.2. (a) MRI at 10 days of demonstrated a small
posterior fossa without CTH. (b) MRI at 7 months demonstrates the acquisition of significant
CTH. (c) MRI at 17 months of age, 6 months after removal of distractors demonstrates
significant improvement in head shape and CTH

The published incidences of hydrocephalus in CCS vary widely and
must be considered only approximations due to differences in patient
referrals and variable definitions of hydrocephalus and
ventriculomegaly. The overall rate, however, may be considered to be
around 15% [77]. By syndrome, hydrocephalus necessitating
intervention has been reported in 47% of patients with Pfeiffer
syndrome, 20% of patients with Crouzon syndrome, 8% of patients
with Apert syndrome [74], and essentially 100% of patients with a
Kleeblattschädel skull deformity [73, 76, 78, 79].
Although hydrocephalus has been reported to be present “at onset,“
[7] in the author’s experience hydrocephalus is not present if

neuroimaging is obtained around the time of birth. Thereafter, serial
neuroimaging generally reveals progressive ventricular dilatation
during the first few months of life which may stabilize (and thus be
considered “ventriculomegaly”) or progress. Patients with Apert
syndrome are more likely to demonstrate stable ventriculomegaly than
patients with Crouzon/Pfeiffer syndrome [73]. In patients followed
closely during the first years of life, it may be difficult to determine at
what point ventricular enlargement becomes sufficiently severe to
warrant surgical intervention. Hydrocephalus necessitating treatment,
however, is generally apparent within the first 2–3 years of life.
Occasionally, especially in patients with the Kleeblattschädel
phenotype, hydrocephalus becomes apparent only after cranial vault
decompression and may progress rapidly [80]. Early postoperative
neuroimaging is thus recommended in infants after cranial
decompressive and expansion procedures. Patients with Apert
syndrome may demonstrate increased extra-axial CSF after cranial
expansion which usually resolves spontaneously [73].

13 3 2 Etiology
The etiology of hydrocephalus in complex craniosynostosis is likely
multifactorial. The two main pathophysiologic mechanisms which have
been considered are (1) dural venous hypertension, resulting in a
communicating type of hydrocephalus, and (2) fourth ventricle CSF
outflow obstruction (from posterior fossa crowding and cerebellar
tonsil herniation) resulting in an obstructive hydrocephalus. The
relative contribution of each of these pathologies may vary with each
syndrome and may change with age. Indeed, the consequences of dural
venous hypertension and cerebellar tonsil herniation may influence
each other [24, 81].
Understanding of hydrocephalus associated with CCS has evolved
with advances in neuroimaging. Early investigations were performed
using pneumoencephalography, angiography, or first-generation
computed tomography [24, 82, 83]. Angiographic findings revealed
jugular foramen stenosis (as discussed in the previous section on
Intracranial Venous Hypertension), and the resulting increased dural
venous pressure was thought to impair CSF absorption [24]. In 1984,
Sainte-Rose et al. simultaneously measured pressures in the lateral

ventricles, superior sagittal sinuses, and jugular veins of children with
various forms of hydrocephalus, including many with craniosynostosis
[24]. In patients with craniosynostosis and presumed stenosis of the
jugular foramen, elevated pressure in the dural venous sinuses
persisted after the removal of CSF from the ventricle. By contrast, in
patients without presumed dural sinus obstruction, the venous sinus
pressure decreased with CSF removal. It was therefore concluded that
hydrocephalus in CSS was the result of impaired CSF absorption due to
dural venous hypertension. This communicating type of hydrocephalus
would not ostensibly be amenable to endoscopic third ventriculostomy
[24] [74]. Some investigators consider this vascular pathophysiology to
be similar than that seen in achondroplasia [24]. In achondroplasia, it is
currently believed that intracranial-to-extracranial venous collaterals
develop in response to jugular foremen stenosis and stabilize
intracranial pressure, albeit perhaps slightly above normal.
With the development of MR imaging, it was found that many
patients have a “crowded” appearing posterior fossa with herniation of
the cerebellar tonsils. In these patients, although there is an open
aqueduct of Sylvius, there appears to be resistance to CSF outflow from
the fourth ventricle. The fourth ventricle is often small, the aqueduct is
flared, and the floor of the third ventricle is bowed outward. This
appearance has led to an obstructive theory of hydrocephalus in
complex craniosynostosis.
The correlation of hydrocephalus with cerebellar tonsil herniation
in complex craniosynostosis is quite high. In Crouzon/Pfeiffer
syndrome, it appears that nearly all patients with hydrocephalus also
have cerebellar tonsil herniation [7, 84]. In contrast, only 53% of
patients with cerebellar tonsil herniation were found to have
hydrocephalus [84]. Thus, it appears that in patterns of
craniosynostosis that involve premature closure of the lambdoid
sutures (most commonly Crouzon/Pfeiffer syndrome), cerebellar tonsil
herniation may add an obstructive component to extant communicating
hydrocephalus due to venous hypertension.

13 3 3 Treatment
The decision to treat hydrocephalus in the setting of complex
craniosynostosis must not be made without careful consideration.

Seemingly minor complications such as CSF leaks often result in
prolonged hospitalizations, multiple surgeries, cerebrospinal fluid
infections, and consequent central nervous system sequelae. There are
no universally accepted indications for hydrocephalus intervention in
this complicated patient population. Because the ventricles are normal
size at birth, ventricular enlargement must be due to some increased
CSF resistance—unless due to cerebral atrophy. Although many
publications differentiate between ventriculomegaly and “active”
hydrocephalus, there are no accepted measurements which distinguish
these two entities, and enlarged ventricles which stabilize may still be
under abnormally high pressure, especially in patients with impaired
cranial growth. Ventricular dilatation probably represents a spectrum
of abnormal CSF resistance. Intuitive surgical indications include
obviously large ventricles with periventricular edema and tense
bulging cranial defects/fontanelles in patients with large ventricles.
Other clinical indications such as poor feeding or decreased activity
levels are less obvious in this population.
Especially in infancy, the timing of CSF diversion in relation to
cranial vault decompression is variable [85]. In the author’s experience,
cranial vault remodeling generally precedes CSF diversion, however, as
previously mentioned, rapid ventricular expansion can appear after
cranial decompression. Cranial vault surgery does not generally
improve hydrocephalus [59, 76, 80]. This fact should be considered
when planning the sequence of surgical procedures. Posterior cranial
vault distraction, however, has the potential to improve cerebellar
tonsil herniation [59, 60, 62] and with further experience may
potentially prove to influence hydrocephalus. In cases in which the
optimal sequence of procedures is not clear, we have occasionally
performed ETV concomitantly with cranial vault remodeling or
distraction. It is not, however, advised to perform shunting procedures
simultaneously with cranial expansion procedures as there may be an
increased risk of shunt infection and/or migration in the presence of
large postoperative subgaleal fluid collections.
Currently, treatment options for hydrocephalus in these patients
consist of CSF diversion either via ventricular shunting (usually
peritoneal) or endoscopic third ventriculostomy. Lumboperitoneal
shunts were in use in the 1960s but were found to have a high

incidence of cerebellar tonsil herniation [86–88]. Indeed, in this
population, diversion of CSF from the spinal intrathecal space carries a
high risk of inducing or worsening hindbrain herniation and may
increase mortality from brainstem compression [89] (Fig. 13.4).

Fig. 13.4 Severe hindbrain herniation with brainstem compression in a 14 year-old male with
Crouzon syndrome and a ventricular shunt

13 3 4 Ventricular Shunting
For many years, the only treatment available was VPS. The limitations
and frustrations of ventricular shunts are well known to all
neurosurgeons. However, shunts in patients with complex
craniosynostosis manifest an additional complement of concerns.
Ventricular shunting is known to induce premature cranial suture
fusion, cranial deformity, and impair cranial growth even in patients
without craniosynostosis [90]. Thus, in patients with complex
craniosynostosis, the lack of normal outward dural pressure may result
in a more irregular cranial shape and impaired cranial growth following

cranial reconstruction surgery. Although this is a common observation
amongst craniofacial surgeons, this interface of neurosurgery and
esthetics has received little academic attention. One study, however, has
claimed improved esthetic outcomes in patients with programmable
shunt valves compared to fixed pressure valves [85]. Another concern
of craniofacial surgeons is the potential for epidural and cranial bone
infection from a large epidural dead space in shunted patients.
Although not documented in cranial reconstruction for complex
craniosynostosis, an increased infection rate in patients with
ventricular shunts has been observed in cranioplasty following
decompressive craniectomy [91].
One interesting complication that may occur in patients with
complex craniosynostosis after extrathecal CSF shunting is the
development or worsening of cerebellar tonsil herniation [92].
Although not subject to systematic analysis, the degree of cerebellar
tonsil herniation has been observed to be worse in patients with
ventricular shunts [92, 93]. This may seem counterintuitive since CSF
shunting should decrease ICP and potential downward pressure on the
cerebellar tonsils. However, in the presence of increased venous
pressure, diversion of CSF may result in relative venous congestion of
the brain which encourages hindbrain herniation in an anatomically
small posterior fossa [92]. A similar pathophysiologic mechanism has
been described in patients with achondroplasia in whom ventricular
shunting is notoriously complicated [94].
Thus, we see that ventricular shunting should be carefully
considered in patients with complex craniosynostosis. As an
alternative, endoscopic third ventriculostomy (vide infra) should be
highly considered. Nonetheless, there are situations where a
ventricular shunt is the only option and must be provided to control
hypertensive hydrocephalus. In these situations, we alter our usual
surgical technique in order to minimize expected complications.
Although in other types of hydrocephalus, we generally place frontal
shunts, in complex craniosynostosis we insert the ventricular catheter
from an occipital approach in order to avoid hardware exposure during
repeated craniofacial surgeries. The hole-bearing segment of the
ventricular catheter is positioned in the frontal horn either
endoscopically or with stereotactic guidance. We utilize a burr hole

style valve in order to avoid positioning any bulky hardware below the
superior nuchal line where muscular action may result in
disconnection. We also attempt to plan the subgaleal shunt path under
the most robust scalp possible and avoid areas where the overlying
scalp might be at risk for breakdown.
The use of programmable or high-resistance valves in this setting is
advisable for a few reasons. Although in infancy the valve pressure may
need to be relatively low, ultimately shunt valve resistance should be as
high as tolerated to avoid many of the complications mentioned
previously. We have often observed changes in the level of the
cerebellar tonsils with adjustments in shunt valve resistance. In
addition, some patients with complex CS and hydrocephalus become
shunt-independent with age. Occasionally, ventricular shunting is used
to control CSF fistulae [95]. In these situations, programmable valves
can provide low pressure initially to close the CSF leak. Later, the valve
resistance can be increased with potential shunt removal.

13 3 5 Endoscopic Third Ventriculostomy
The observation that hydrocephalus associated with complex
craniosynostosis is triventricular appears to invite the consideration of
ETV. Given the well-described vascular theory, ETV has been slow to be
accepted as a viable option [74]. Di Rocco reported 11 children in
whom ETV was performed with a success rate of 60% [77]. The
children were operated on at a mean of 20 months with some as young
as 3 months of age [77]. The group was selected based on anatomical
features which suggested CSF obstruction in the posterior fossa. Most
had Crouzon or Pfeiffer syndrome. Anatomic features such as tonsillar
ectopia and outward distention of the floor of the fourth ventricle did
not reliably predict success. Importantly, success was achieved in twothirds of patients with jugular stenosis [77]. Since this initial report,
some have suggested ETV as an alternative to VPS [96, 97], while others
reject ETV in favor of extrathecal CSF diversion [85].
The author’s experience with ETV has a similar success rate of 65%
[98]. Our selection criteria include crowding of the posterior fossa and
outward bowing of the third ventricle. Initial failures were
predominantly due to CSF leakage and as such we now perform
watertight dural closure after ETV. It is presumed that ETV can only

improve one of the multiple causes of elevated intracranial pressure
seen in complex craniosynostosis. Thus, even after successful ETV,
some degree of intracranial hypertension may persist. Care must be
taken in the postoperative period to anticipate residual elevated ICP
and minimize risks of CSF leak and subgaleal fluid collections. In severe
cases, a ventricular reservoir may be placed at the time of ETV followed
by serial aspirations to minimize the risk of CSF leak as success of the
ETV is established.
The treatment of hydrocephalus in patients with complex
craniosynostosis must be considered in the totality of care. Simply
placing a shunt may not be the best course of action in the long term.
The observed success of ETV argues against a purely vascular etiology
of hydrocephalus in patients with favorable posterior fossa anatomy.
Apart from failure requiring shunt placement, ETV in these patients has
not been associated with significant adverse effects. Thus, it is
recommended that ETV can be considered primarily when treating
hydrocephalus associated with complex craniosynostosis. In the event
that ventricular shunting is required, specific modifications to standard
techniques should be considered to minimize complications.

13 4 Cerebellar Tonsil Herniation
Cerebellar tonsil herniation in association with craniofacial syndrome
was first noted in 1972 [99] and postulated to be an acquired condition
in 1988 [100]. With advances in neuroimaging, the prevalence of CTH
in the various craniofacial syndromes has been defined. Along with
airway obstruction, CTH with brainstem compression represents one of
the leading causes of morbidity in complex craniosynostosis. As with
CTH in general, syringomyelia and its attendant complications and
disabilities may also result. The CTH seen in CSS may be anticipated
and its effects minimized with appropriate surgical care. Given the
observation that CTH is usually acquired, the condition is best referred
to as a postnatal “deformity” than a malformation [93].

13 4 1 Incidence
In the absence of involvement of the lambdoid suture, single-suture
synostosis is rarely associated with cerebellar tonsil herniation [101,

102]. CTH is, however, common in multisuture craniosynostosis [101,
103]. The incidence varies with the syndrome and pattern of suture
involvement. It is highly correlated with premature lambdoid suture
closure [84]. About 75% of patients with Crouzon/Pfeiffer’s develop
hindbrain herniation, whereas it occurs in less than 5% of patients with
Apert syndrome [39, 84]. CTH is rare in bicoronal synostosis, and
Muenke and Saethre-Chotzen syndromes in which early lambdoid
suture closure is not usually a feature [93, 104]. In apparently random
associations of multiple suture fusion, CTH depends upon the
involvement of the lambdoid sutures and tonsil herniation may involve
only the affected side. The so-called “Mercedes Benz” pattern of
bilateral lambdoid and posterior sagittal synostosis appropriately has a
high incidence of CTH of at least 60% [10, 53]. With respect to cranial
phenotype, essentially all patients with a Kleeblattschädel skull shape
develop hindbrain herniation [103] and about 60% with oxycephaly
[106].
Similar to hydrocephalus, in patients with complex
craniosynostosis, CTH is an acquired condition; thus, estimations of
incidence will depend upon the age at which neuroimaging is obtained.
Neuroimaging obtained in the neonatal period usually reveals a
relatively normal-appearing cerebellum. The time course over which
CTH develops has not been fully elucidated but appears to be during
the first few months of life and precedes the development of
hydrocephalus.
As in patients with other forms of CTH (Chiari I Malformation),
syringomyelia is observed frequently in the setting of CCS. The true
incidence is not known but in Crouzon patients with CTH has been
observed to be about 20% [84]. The pathophysiology of syringomyelia
resulting from CTH has been extensively investigated in patients
without craniosynostosis [107]. Although presumed to be similar,
syringomyelia observed in complex craniosynostosis may also have
genetic influences [108].

13 4 2 Etiology
As seen with the development of intracranial hypertension and
hydrocephalus, herniation of the cerebellar tonsils in CCS appears to be
the result of multiple predisposing forces. These primarily include

growth restriction and dural venous hypertension but can be modified
by CSF forces.
Hindbrain herniation occurs most commonly in syndromes which
exhibit prematurely lambdoid suture closure [103]. Thus, it appears as
though growth restriction is a major driver of cerebellar tonsillar
herniation. Indeed, in unilateral lambdoid synostosis, there is often
asymptomatic herniation of the cerebellar tonsil on the affected side.
Volumetric studies of the posterior fossa reveal mixed results with
some showing decreased volumes [109] and others showing more
normal posterior fossa volumes [110, 111]. Interestingly, one of the
studies of unoperated Crouzon patients reported normal posterior
fossa volumes despite documenting premature closure of the lambdoid
suture and skull base synchondroses [110]. Another study of children
with CCS measured posterior fossa and cerebellar volumes and found
both to be normal [111]. The ratio of cerebellar volume to posterior
fossa volume was, however, found to be increased in patients with CTH
[111]. Thus, as discussed in the section on intracranial hypertension,
simple growth restriction fails to adequately explain the observed
hindbrain herniation.
The role of venous hypertension must again be emphasized as a
potential factor in CTH. Venous engorgement of the cerebellum due to
elevated dural venous sinus pressure from jugular foramen stenosis
may result in engorgement of the cerebellum resulting in cerebellar
tonsil herniation. An interesting study of infants with a vein of Galen
malformations (without craniosynostosis) revealed CTH which
correlated with dural venous hypertension and congestion within the
cerebellar veins [81]. CTH reduced after embolization resulted in
improved cerebellar venous outflow [81]. The authors also noted that
CTH was not the result of raised intraventricular pressure [81]. Others
have reported CTH with syringomyelia in adult patients with high-flow
AVMs which have reduced after embolization [112, 113]
Thus, there may be some interplay between the effect of premature
suture closure and increased venous resistance that predisposes
toward CTH. The fact that CTH nearly always develops early in life may
be attributable to the exuberant growth demonstrated by the
cerebellum in the neonatal period. It is well known that brain growth is
rapid during the first year of life. Growth, however, is disproportionate

with cerebral hemisphere volume increasing by 90% and cerebellar
volume by 240% [114].
Although some consider CTH to be a CSF disorder [6], it is unlikely
that hydrocephalus is the main cause of CTH seen in CCS [93]. As
mentioned in the section on hydrocephalus, CTH seems to be a
prerequisite for hydrocephalus, but hydrocephalus does not necessarily
result in CTH. Nonetheless, hydrocephalus may exacerbate brainstemrelated symptoms resulting from hindbrain herniation as is commonly
observed in patients with Chiari II malformations and myelodysplasia.
Thus, control of intracranial and intraventricular hypertension should
be achieved in conjunction with craniovertebral decompression.
Unintuitively, however, the treatment of hydrocephalus with extrathecal
CSF diversion in these patients may worsen or incite cerebellar
herniation [92, 93]. As mentioned in the section on hydrocephalus, all
efforts should be made to minimize the adverse effects of CSF
overdrainage in these patients by either performing ETV or utilizing
programmable or high-resistance shunt valves.

13 4 3 Treatment
In patients with CCS, clinical symptoms of CTH may be more difficult to
detect than in patients without craniosynostosis. Perhaps, due to the
presence of chronic illness, these patients often do not admit to classic
tussive occipital or cervical pain. Chronic respiratory obstruction may
mask central or obstructive sleep apnea from brainstem compression.
We routinely obtain sleep studies in patients with significant CTH on
MRI to assess for central sleep apnea even if a tracheostomy is in place.
It is estimated that surgery is indicated for 30% of CSS patients with
CTH by virtue of either clinical symptoms or the discovery of
syringomyelia [103]. Since syringomyelia is present in 20% of patients
and may be asymptomatic, routine MRI of the spine is recommended in
patients with known CTH [103]. Despite the high prevalence of CTH in
CSS, most patients with radiographic CTH do not require surgical
attention. The symptoms are notoriously insidious, and all members of
the care team as well as the patients’ families should be aware of this
potential.
Surgical approaches to CTH in this population may be divided into
two groups: traditional direct neurosurgical procedures and more

craniofacially oriented combined procedures. Direct approaches are the
same as performed in patients without craniosynostosis while
combined approaches typically include remodeling of the posterior
cranial vault with or without suboccipital decompression. The recent
technique of distraction osteogenesis which is rapidly displacing
traditional cranial vault remodeling is also providing another option for
CTH treatment.
The options for surgical treatment of patients with typical type 1
Chiari malformations without craniosynostosis are controversial and
continue to be debated [115]. The mainstay of surgery is suboccipital
decompression with or without duroplasty and potential intradural
reduction of the cerebellar tonsils [115]. This standard approach is
associated with a higher failure rate in patients with craniosynostosis
[116]. Accordingly, the author often performs subpial resection of
herniated cerebellar tonsils in order to more effectively reduce
brainstem compression and reestablish the patency of the cisterna
magna. Obviously, extreme care must be taken when manipulating the
intradural structures so as not to damage the brainstem and to
minimize intradural scarring postoperatively. This technique has
proven effective and safe in patients without CSS [115].
In patients with CCS, direct decompressive surgery is often much
more challenging. Although large studies in CCS are lacking, bony
decompression and duraplasty are often insufficient to provide durable
improvement. Bone usually regrows over intact dura at the level of the
foramen magnum; hence, we nearly always attempt duraplasty. In the
presence of dural venous hypertension, opening the dura, especially in
infants may be accompanied by significant blood loss. Dilated and
aberrant venous collaterals, while an irritant in the subcutaneous
tissues, may be life-threatening in the bone and dura [32]. Careful
planning with a review of dural venous sinus imaging is advised.
Routine surgical approaches may need to be modified when large dural
venous collaterals are encountered. For example, a typical dural
opening crossing the craniovertebral junction may be complicated by
the presence of large marginal and occipital sinuses. In this situation,
we have had success by opening the spinal dura in the midline to the
level of the foramen magnum and then subpially resecting the
cerebellar tonsils from this approach.

Given the observation that hindbrain herniation is worsened by
ventricular shunting, we attempt to minimize the effects of CSF
diversion when planning surgical intervention in these patients. This
usually entails changing an existing shunt valve to a programmable
version and then increasing the resistance as high as tolerated. The
absolute need for the shunt is seriously investigated toward a goal of
shunt removal if possible. ETV may be required. With this aggressive
minimization of CSF diversion accompanied by careful microscopic
cerebellar tonsil resection, we have had success in alleviating
syringomyelia in patients who have previously had multiple
unsuccessful surgeries.
Surgery for CTH associated with complex craniosynostosis,
although potentially more difficult, has more options than direct
decompression with its variants. Multiple craniofacial combined
approaches have been assessed. Even anterior cranial vault expansion
alone has been observed to improve Chiari symptoms and radiographic
appearance [100, 117]. As noted in the section on intracranial
hypertension, anterior and posterior cranial expansion/remodeling
procedures have been utilized for years with success in ameliorating
ICH and often improving CTH [101]. The durability of this result,
however, has proven insufficient. Progression of CTH, especially in the
first 2–3 years of life, in Crouzon/Pfeiffer patients occurs despite
posterior cranial vault expansion procedures [7, 80].
Posterior cranial vault expansion has also been performed with
concomitant suboccipital decompressive craniectomy and even upper
cervical laminectomy from a bicoronal scalp incision with patients in a
prone position [118, 119]. Long-term results are not reported, but the
procedure appears safe and could be added to standard posterior
cranial vault procedures to potentially minimize the progression of CTH
even in asymptomatic patients.
Posterior calvarial vault distraction osteogenesis (PCVDO) in CCS
was first reported in 2009 [56]. Although not specifically intending to
treat CTH, they reported an improvement in the degree of tonsillar
herniation observed on MRI in one patient [56]. Further series have
consistently reported radiographic improvement in CTH following
PCVDO [59, 60, 62, 120]. Interestingly, improvement appears to result
even when the distracted calvarium is supratentorial. In fact, using

routine anterior-posterior vectors, a distraction which incorporates
calvarium below the torcula appears less efficient than a distraction
above the tentorium—perhaps indicating a constricting effect of the
tentorium on potential dural expansion [61]. This may explain the
authors’ observations that PCVDO generally decompresses the superior
aspect of the posterior fossa, but often the cerebellar tonsils remain
herniated.
Many technical details remain to be perfected in distraction
osteogenesis of the calvarium, and modifications can be made to
specifically address the posterior fossa and CTH [121]. Park, in 2021,
described “complete” PCVDO in which a foramen magnum
decompression is performed and the osteotomy extends to the foramen
magnum [62]. Four distractors are used instead of the usual two in
order to provide an additional vector of distraction to the infratentorial
skull [62]. In this study, all patients demonstrated ascent of the
cerebellar tonsils postdistraction with nearly 50% achieving complete
reduction [62]. Improvement in syringomyelia after PCVDO has also
been reported [60, 122, 123].
Ostensibly, the mechanism by which PCVDO improves CTH is simply
by increasing intracranial volume. Cinalli, however, has recently
observed that dural sinus volume increased after PCVDO, and
measurements of dural venous obstruction improved [123]. Since the
jugular foramen was not manipulated, the authors concluded that much
of the venous hypertension observed in CSS may be due to compression
of the dural sinuses between the skull and the compressed underlying
brain—especially in the posterior fossa [123]. This concept may have
important consequences and the role of the jugular foramen may have
to be revisited with more modern imaging techniques.
Since CTH is known to be acquired in the early postnatal period, it
should be anticipated. Appropriate identification and surveillance of
these at-risk patients should be the mandate of the craniofacial team.
Although more experience is needed, early PCVDO may potentially
prove to be of benefit in actually preventing the development of CTH in
patients at risk [54, 59].

14 1 Genetic Basis of Neurologic Dysfunction

In recent years, advancements in genomic sequencing have permitted
research on the genes and pathways that contribute to
craniosynostosis. Indeed, uncommon Mendelian mutations in
syndromic craniosynostosis (mostly in FGFR and TWIST1 genes) have
been identified as causal in these forms of craniosynostosis [1, 2].
These mutations commonly cause increased signaling of Wnt, BMP,
Ras/ERK, ephrin, hedgehog, STAT, or retinoic acid pathways, which
converge on shared nuclear targets that promote bone formation [3, 4].
Nonsyndromic craniosynostoses (NSC), on the other hand, are more
genetically heterogenous. Patients show variable neurodevelopmental
outcome; however, nearly half of the patients are ultimately diagnosed
with some form of neurocognitive dysfunction despite timely and
comprehensive surgical intervention [5, 6]. Given that the sutures,
meninges, and parenchyma of the forebrain and midbrain have shared
neural crest cell origin, this raises a potential role for a genetic injury
affecting these early cell lines to affect the sutures and intrinsic brain
function concurrently.
FGFR3 has been known to occur with high frequency in
nonsyndromic coronal craniosynostosis [7]. The more recent advent of
genomic sequencing has allowed identification of several other
mutations. Sharma et al. [2] performed exome sequencing on patients
with different types of craniosynostosis, and found TCF12 mutations in
32% of bilateral coronal and 10% of unilateral coronal craniosynostosis
cases. No TCF12 mutations were seen in sagittal, metopic, or lambdoid
craniosynostosis. TCF12 encodes a partner protein of TWIST1 which
has been found to be critical for coronal suture development, and
combined TCF12 and TWIST1 mutations result in more severe cases of
coronal synostosis [2]. Similarly, Justice et al.’s genome wide association
study in nonsyndromic metopic synostosis patients found mutations in
SPRY3, BMP7, PCDH11X, and upstream from TGIF2LX [8].
Timberlake et al. performed exome sequencing of genes within the
highest quartile of expression in the developing brain in 404 trios with
sporadic sagittal, metopic, lambdoid, and combined sagittal and
metopic NSC [9]. The authors sequenced the genes that were identified
to have a high probability of intolerance to loss of function and found
that a striking 34% of their cohort had damaging de novo mutations in
these intolerant genes. All NSC patients in this cohort underwent

surgical correction, but those who had the high-risk genotypes had a
two-fold greater incidence of neurodevelopmental delay, 20-fold
greater incidence of intellectual disability, and 3.6-fold higher incidence
of persistent delays after 5 years of age compared to NSC patients who
did not harbor these mutations. These comparisons were based on
patient-reported incidence of diagnosed developmental delays
including intellectual disability, and motor, speech, or language delay.
Though the findings of this study are likely to be strengthened by in
depth standardized neurologic testing, it provides initial compelling
evidence of a genetic contribution to neurologic outcome in NSC that
may not be completely corrected with surgery. Table 14.1 provides a
summary of known genetic mutations in NSC.

Genes implicated

Further evidence for the role of genetics in neurocognitive
dysfunction in NSC is the identification of loss of function (LOF)
mutations in negative regulators of Wnt, BMP, and Ras/ERK signaling in
NCS patients [8, 11–13]. Precise regulation of these pathways is crucial

for bone formation as well as normal brain development. The most
common of these studied mutations is in SMAD6, which accounts for
5% of all midline NSC cases (13% of individuals with metopic NSC and
3% of those with sagittal NSC) [11]. SMAD6 is a negative regulator of
SMAD signaling via the BMP pathway, and loss of SMAD6 leads to
uninhibited transcription of genes that promote osteoblast
differentiation. This cascade plays a role in the development of the bony
cranial vault and leads to closure of cranial sutures. Interestingly,
genomic analyses on intellectual disability identified SMAD6 as a locus
involved in poor intellectual ability; however, the presence or absence
of craniosynostosis was not noted in this study [14]. Wu et al.
subsequently demonstrated that NSC patients with SMAD6 mutations
performed significantly worse on intellectual tasks including numerical
operations, performance IQ, full scale IQ, visuomotor integration, and
motor coordination compared to their matched controls with NSC
without SMAD6 mutation [15].
Taken together, knowledge of high-risk genotypes can be useful for
identifying children who are most likely to benefit from surgery.
However, NSC can also be influenced by complex polygenic and
epigenetic factors. For example, the SMAD6 mutation demonstrates
strikingly variable penetrance, and is dramatically influenced by a
common risk allele near BMP2 [10, 11]. An LOF mutation in SMAD6
plus the common BMP2 risk allele conferred 100% risk of NSC,
whereas SMAD6 mutation without the BMP2 risk allele only resulted in
a 19% risk. BMP2 is an inducer of osteogenesis via SMAD signaling, and
it is therefore postulated that this risk allele might increase the
penetrance of SMAD6 mutations by increasing BMP2, leading to
accelerated and uninhibited SMAD signaling. This two-locus
inheritance pattern demonstrates the complexity of epigenetic
interplay, and suggests that identification (or lack) of any specific
mutation alone should not dictate whether a child with NSC receives
surgical intervention.

14 2 Bony Constriction and Neurologic
Consequences

Virchow’s law states that skull growth is restricted perpendicular to the
fused suture and enhanced parallel to it, and it is postulated that
constricted growth poses a risk to the developing brain. The detection
of elevated intracranial pressure is a frequent indication for surgical
intervention; however, the degree to which intracranial hypertension
(ICH) affects neurological development outcome remains unclear.
Indeed, 61–83% of patients with syndromic craniosynostoses have
clinically significant ICH [17–19], yet there is no direct correlation
between ICH and IQ.
Cerebral cortical thickness has emerged as a promising indicator of
cognitive ability [20–22]. While cortical thickness is an indicator of
neuronal density, dendritic arborization, and glial support [23], cortical
thinning has been correlated with decreased IQ [20–24]. A recent study
used FreeSurfer MRI analysis of cortical thickness evaluated common
manifestations of ICH as risk factor for cortical thinning [25]. The
authors found that only papilledema and hydrocephalus are associated
with thinning of the neural cortex. Other clinical markers of ICH such as
tonsillar herniation, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), and occipitofrontal
circumference were not associated with abnormal reduction in cortical
depth. The study did not find gender differences; however, it did note a
higher rate of neurologic deficit in Apert syndrome compared to other
syndromes. Overall, this study suggests that the frequency of neurologic
deficit may be more limited, and advocates for timely intervention in
the setting of papilledema and prolonged hydrocephalus.
Interestingly, MRI studies of syndromic patients with FGFR
mutations after vault expansion procedures in fact demonstrated
greater intracranial volume (ICV) in patients compared to normal
controls [26]. But despite having seemingly adequate volume, the
cerebral cortex in FGFR-mediated craniosynostosis shows abnormal
development, as evidenced by reduced cortical surface area, due to
decreased cortical folding that is normally driven by grey matter
expansion and white matter tension. This reduced surface area was
most notable in the parietal and occipital regions, even though the
synostosis was along the coronal suture [26]. The parietal cortex plays
a role in several measures of intelligence, including working memory,
processing speed, and perceptual organization, while the occipital
cortex is involved in visual processing ability. When impaired, these

could manifest as reading disability and reduced scholastic potential.
Furthermore, structural MRI studies demonstrated that syndromic
craniosynostosis patients show apparent morphologic deformities at
near and distant areas of the brain, including the corpus callosum,
septum pellucidum, hippocampus, cortex, cerebellum, and ventricular
system [27–31]. Taken together, these findings link brain
maldevelopment to the observed neurocognitive dysfunction in
syndromic craniosynostosis. However, the pathology remains to be
elucidated, and contributions from genetic and compressive forces are
expected.
Patients with NSC, on the other hand, rarely present with increased
ICP, with reported rates ranging between 6 and 20% [17, 32, 33].
Despite the lack of overt signs of intracranial hypertension, infants with
single suture NSC were found to have significantly higher cerebral
perfusion and increased cerebral glucose metabolism after surgical
release, detected by pre- and post-operative single positron computed
tomography (SPECT) [34] and positron emission tomography (PET)
scans [35]. Glucose metabolism increases were most consistent in the
occipital region, the area of visual development and visuospatial
coordination [35].
Structural brain data in NSC patients have also been found to have
fundamentally different patterns of morphologic malformation
compared to syndromic patients. Untreated NSC patients demonstrate
abnormal distances between brain structures that strongly correlate
with the phenotype of the particular suture fusion [36–39]. Diffusion
tensor imaging (DTI) studies in rabbit models show abnormal changes
in white matter tracts that showed signs of subsequent normalization
after early suturectomy [40].
Functional MRI (fMRI) has become a very important tool for
revealing different aspects of micro- and macrostructures as well as
white matter tracts. Cabrejo et al. recently published fMRI study
followed patients with isolated sagittal craniosynostosis from infancy
to adolescence using fMRI to document aberrancies compared to age
and gender matched controls [41]. The test subjects in this cohort
underwent whole vault cranioplasty by a single surgeon before
12 months of age. While the pre-operative fMRI demonstrated different
connections in most of the defined cerebral networks compared to their

matched controls, much of the abnormal network connections corrects
by adolescence. Specifically, these positive changes in the brain
microstructure were demonstrated as increased connectivity in the
insula, putamen, and inferior frontal gyrus, increased anisotropy and
connectivity in the putamen and insula. These findings correlate
surgery with normalization of brain microstructure and connectivity,
which may improve neural function [41, 42]. Table 14.2 provides a
summary of structural brain changes in NSC.
