14 3 Timing of Surgery
14 3 1 Sagittal Craniosynostosis
Sagittal NSC is the most common form of NSC and is the most studied.
Although there remains conflicting opinion in the literature regarding
the optimal treatment period in a young patient’s life [43, 44], recent
systematic reviews have highlighted the neurocognitive advantages of
early surgical intervention (before 7 months of age) for sagittal
craniosynostosis [45]. Patients undergoing early surgery have been
documented to have 10–20-point IQ increases than their later/nosurgery counterparts.
From an anatomical perspective, the decision to operate early
dramatically increases the selection of procedures, as many might
require major modification in older patients (greater than 12 months of
age) due to mineralization of the calvaria. Decreased pliability of the
skull at later stages of development creates the necessity for weakening
kerfs or channels, in the bone to allow more extensive remodeling, and
stabilization of the skull bone(s). Additionally, defects left in the bone
structure, such as burr holes, will often heal without intervention in
younger patients but can require a form of bone replacement in older
patients with decreased regenerative capabilities.
For these reasons, it is often recommended that surgical
intervention take place in the first few months of life, with variation in
timing, given the type of surgical procedure to be done (e.g., linear
craniectomy 3 months versus whole vault cranioplasty 6 months,
with or without spring aided expansion) and appropriate indications
and acceptable risk for blood loss and operative time.

14 3 2 Metopic and Unicoronal Craniosynostosis
Unlike in sagittal craniosynostosis, no study to date has compared the
neurologic outcomes for early versus late surgery. Most surgeons favor
surgery between 3 and 9 months of age [46–48]. In the absence of
pressing issues like increased ICP, some surgeons advocate waiting
until 4–6 months of age, when the bone is easier to work with and rigid
enough to maintain a stable reconstruction. Ophthalmologic data
suggest that binocular vision is fully developed by approximately

6 months of age, and it has also been advocated that surgery for
nonsyndromic metopic and unicoronal craniosynostosis patients after
6 months of age may increase the risk for abnormal visual function
such as astigmatism and strabismus [49].
In the case of metopic craniosynostosis, timely diagnosis and
referral to a craniofacial center may be delayed given that the metopic
suture can be physiologically fused 30% at 3 months of age, 60% at
6 months of age, and 90% at 9 months of age [46]. While phenotypic
presentation remains a common indication of pathologic versus
physiologic fusion, objective measurements to quantify the severity,
such as that of the endocranial bifrontal angle, have garnered attention
[50–52]. Objective measurements, including these, can greatly support
a surgeon’s decision regarding the need for intervention.

14 3 3 When Is It Too Late?
Treatment of delayed presentation of craniosynostosis is different
because the bulk of brain growth has been completed. Nearly 90% of
peak adult brain mass develops by the age of 3 [53]; therefore, benefits
to the developing brain, including allowing space for normal growth
and geometric spatial arrangement, IQ, and behavioral or emotional
regulation, is lessened. A child with no concomitant problems related to
this pathology could be counseled that the indication to treat is
primarily aesthetic, although this is not known for sure. To date, no
substantive testing has been done to clarify whether there is benefit to
this type of late surgery in asymptomatic patients. However, other
sequelae may drive these later presentations: Headaches, increased ICP,
or Chiari malformations. These presentations may require treatment
just as they would for those presenting at an earlier age.
In the US, unrepaired craniosynostosis after 1 year of age is rare.
Several small case series of mixed types of NSC reported that untreated
patients over the age of 1 year have high rates of headaches,
developmental delay, Chiari malformation, elevated ICP, and abnormal
head shape [54, 55]. The authors note that this high rate may reflect the
ultimate result of restricted suture growth, or it may be due to selection
bias for symptomatic patients, and currently it is not known what the
incidence is of asymptomatic individuals with similar skull deformities.

In contrast, an extensive series from the University of Pittsburg
consisting of 52 patients with untreated isolated sagittal synostosis
over 1 year of age at presentation reported that only a minority of
patients (17%) required surgery [56]. Indications for surgery in this
group were severe scaphocephaly and abnormal ophthalmologic exam.
Non-operative patients were managed by maintaining serial follow-up
and ophthalmologic evaluation with fundoscopic exam and visual
evoked potentials, which were recommended to continue until growth
maturity (at least 18 years old for males, 16 years old for females).
Authors reported that these patients were late-presenting due to mild,
missed, or late-developing synostosis.
While larger children may allow for a lesser risk anesthetic, and the
well-developed diploic space allows for split calvarial bone grafting, the
osteogenic potential of the dura is largely lost after the age of 1 year,
implying a lesser ability to heal bony defects spontaneously. However,
the periosteum is still influential in some bone regeneration in early to
mid-infancy. In addition, there is reduced potential for smoothing of
contour irregularities or residual shape deformity with further brain
and skull growth. Older patients, therefore, often require more
extensive cranial remodeling procedures. Despite these concerns, it has
been demonstrated that children presenting at an older age can be
safely treated with cranioplasty, albeit they may not derive the same
functional benefits. There was no significant difference in postoperative
transfusion and hospital stay length in older patients undergoing
craniosynostosis repair versus those who underwent repair under
12 months [54–56]. Furthermore, they do not appear to have an
unacceptably high rate of bony defects or contour problems. Long term
outcome data regarding cosmesis, bony defects, and the need for
revisions are scant. Neurocognitive testing to assess for changes in
mental functioning is yet to be undertaken, but would be essential to
determine whether this approach should be adopted.

14 4 Type of Surgery
14 4 1 Sagittal Craniosynostosis
Historically, the decision to operate on patients presenting with sagittal
craniosynostosis has been contingent upon the degree to which head

shape is affected from a psychosocial perspective. Another factor to
consider is the extent of the synostosis itself, affecting the suture along
its total length or a specific portion of it. There are several surgical
techniques, and the unique benefits and drawbacks of different surgical
treatments must be balanced when deciding to operate.

14 4 2 Strip Craniectomy with Helmet Therapy
When treating single suture sagittal craniosynostosis in patients less
than 3 months of age, strip craniectomy with subsequent helmet
therapy may be the chosen technique due to limited incision size and
reduced blood loss [57, 58]. These benefits are further enhanced when
endoscopic techniques are utilized. Helmet therapy is necessary,
however, often for prolonged periods to enable the skull to heal
optimally. More recent analysis indicates that variability of outcome
may be more contingent on helmet design than previously thought.
Compared with more invasive procedures, patients undergoing strip
craniectomy also have shorter hospital length of stay, less ICU stay, and
lower hospital costs. A drawback associated with strip craniectomy,
however, is its limited scope of effectiveness for patients more than
3 months of age, after which cranial stiffness has begun to limit
effectiveness of helmet therapy. A second drawback is that suturectomy
only achieves regional release at the time of surgery, and an additional
8–14 months of post-operative helmet therapy may be required on
average to gradually achieve adequate correction of skull shape [59].
This additional course of active cranial molding coincides with crucial
periods of postnatal brain development. Between birth and 24 months
postnatally, the brain undergoes significant cortical maturation
processes such as synaptogenesis, synaptic pruning, dendritic
arborization, and myelinization of intracortical white matter, which are
all essential for achieving normal brain connectivity [60, 61]. Thus,
incomplete correction during this time may yield inexact neural
connections, ultimately leading to dysfunction of the brain circuitry.

14 4 3 Cranial Vault Reconstruction
Unlike strip craniectomy, cranial vault reconstruction (CVR) can be
used at any age regardless of calvarial mineralization, assuming low
risk for major blood loss, lung maturation, and the ability to monitor

and treat appropriately for volume changes intra and post operatively.
For patients 3 months or more, CVR is considered first-line definitive
therapy to restore skull morphology to normality. CVR has also been
associated with significant IQ and visuomotor integration increases
compared to strip craniectomy or spring-assisted cranioplasty [62, 63].
Despite advancements, CVR is a more invasive procedure, with
higher risk of blood loss and subsequent need for blood transfusions.
Efforts to raise the patients’ baseline hematocrit or lessen
intraoperative blood loss are commonly employed [64].

14 4 4 Spring-Assisted Cranioplasty
Spring-assisted cranioplasty can also allow for the dynamic and gradual
reshaping of the cranium compared to other techniques, such as CVR,
which generate more complete and timely changes. However, certain
variables, such as spring strength, are difficult to predict without
significant experience and are contingent upon age, bone thickness, and
synostosis location. Springs are often custom-made and can require
close monitoring using imaging to ensure appropriate distraction.
However, downsides include univector expansion, migration of the foot
plates through younger bone, erosion through bone, and
unpredictability of final lengthening [65]. It should be noted that
expansion plateaus at around 50 days after spring placement, and
begins to restrict growth after approximately 60 days in an animal
experimental model. A final downside to this procedure is that a second
operation is required to remove the springs and complete closure of the
calvarium.

14 4 5 Metopic Craniosynostosis
Trigonocephaly is characterized by a triangular or wedge-shape
forehead resulting from suture fusion and supraorbital retrusion, with
a wide range of severity. Patients often also demonstrate deficient
lateral orbital rims, bitemporal indentations, and hypocanthus.
Teardrop shaped orbits and ethmoidal hypoplasia are additional
radiological findings, and 55% of cases have prematurely closed
anterior fontanels [66].
In addition to phenotypic abnormalities, there is increasing
evidence across multiple modalities revealing long-term neurocognitive

deficits. Neurodevelopmental dysfunction in patients with metopic
craniosynostosis range from 15 to 61%, with reported deficits in
speech/language, attention, and behavior, as well as high incidence of
attention deficit hyperactivity disorder [66, 67]. The metopic suture
overlies the frontal lobe, which is intricately connected with the
cingulate gyrus and the limbic system—structures that are responsible
for executive function, impulse inhibition, and personality.
Notably, infant event-related potential (ERP) measurements of
neurodevelopment and neurocognitive testing in childhood and
adolescence have all been demonstrated to correlate with radiographic
severity as measured by the pre-operative endocranial bifrontal angle
[51, 52].
Historically, the first reports of surgical treatment for
trigonocephaly described simple strip craniectomies. In present day,
limited suturectomy is considered by most to be insufficient to correct
the three-dimensional sequelae of metopic craniosynostosis [66, 68,
69]. Marchac published his landmark technique using the “floating
forehead technique” combined with remodeling of the supra-orbital
bandeau in 1978. Modifications of this technique have evolved to
address post operative temporal hollowing, but the general concept still
continues to be the standard.
For correction of hypocanthus, a sagittal osteotomy with or without
bone grafting are options. Distraction osteogenesis with conventional
screws or with springs has also been proposed, and has gained some
popularity. However, there is controversy regarding whether
hypotelorism really needs to be directly corrected. Fearon noted
improvement in intercanthal distance in his cohort without any
deliberate attempt at surgical correction [70]. Careful measurements
revealed that patients who underwent surgery earlier (before 6 months
of age) had greater improvement than those treated after 6 months of
age, and those with more severe initial hypotelorism showed
significantly more improvement than their milder counterparts within
a mean of 21 months of follow up. Opponents of direct surgical
correction of hypocanthus argue that doing so would only widen the
nasal bones without increasing the interorbital distance.

14 4 6 Unicoronal Craniosynostosis

Unicoronal craniosynostosis (UCS) results in a complex set of
craniofacial dysmorphologies affecting the fronto-orbital region, skull
base, and facial symmetry. In addition to the cognitive and aesthetic
concerns shared with other forms of NSC, as many as 89% of UCS
patients have exotropia or vertical deviation of the ipsilateral globe. A
series of studies by Ricci et al. found that patients experience high
incidences of ocular abnormalities in both eyes—including strabismus,
atypical eye movements, astigmatism, and visual field deficits [71].
Formal visual testing is a critical element in evaluating UCS patients,
and ocular anomalies are an essential indication for surgical correction.
Open cranial vault remodeling with fronto-orbital advancement is
the conventional technique for correcting unicoronal synostosis and
remains the most common approach. Alternative techniques such as
endoscopic strip craniectomy, distraction osteogenesis, and springassisted cranioplasty offer shorter operating time and shorter hospital
stays. Another proposed benefit is improved craniofacial growth due to
maintenance of blood supply to the cranial bones and limited scarring
of the soft tissue [72, 73].

14 4 7 Fronto-Orbital Advancement
Despite being the most commonly used method, long term results of
fronto-orbital advancement (FOA) for UCS are mixed. Many studies’
outcomes report significant asymmetry at long term follow up even
with some initial overcorrection [72]. Poor long term outcome scores
are often due to temporal hollowing and supraorbital retrusion with
the appearance of “relapse.” This has led some to propose
hypercorrection as a variation in traditional FOA. The group led by Dr.
Buchman at University of Michigan reported on a cohort of 40 patients
followed for an average of 4.75 years after hypercorrection [74]. They
noted that the hypercorrection appearance persisted for 6–8 months
and gradually normalized. However, it is unclear whether in the short
term the hypercorrection is more or less displeasing to the child and
parents.

14 4 8 Distraction Osteogenesis
The first described use of distraction osteogenesis for forehead
distraction in UCS was in 1999 by Kobayashi [75]. Since then, this

technique has been known for achieving good improvements in cranial
volume and cephalic index, with minimal bleeding and bony defect,
short operative time, and no dural tears. Distraction of the cranial base
was also successful in improving the angulation of the anterior and
posterior cranial fossa.
Compared to FOA, distraction osteogenesis was shown to have
advantages of shorter hospital stay and lower incidence of
postoperative strabismus [72, 76].

14 4 9 Endoscopic Strip Craniectomy
Though the endoscopic strip technique is characterized by short
operative time, low transfusion rates, and low perioperative morbidity
[77], the downside of this option is that it does not directly address the
concern about cranial base and brain distortion caused by bony
constriction as rapidly or completely in the critical time periods for
brain growth. Another concern is the limited ability to address the
degree of asymmetry of the orbit and temporal region.

14 4 10 Spring-Assisted Cranioplasty
Yet another surgical option that can be used is the spring-assisted
coronal strip craniectomy. Shortfalls of this technique for UCS are
similar to those for sagittal patients—namely, the unpredictability of
final correction, unidirectional vector, and the need for a secondary
procedure to remove the springs.

14 4 11 Bicoronal Craniosynostosis
Bilateral coronal craniosynostosis results in turribrachycephaly, which
is characterized by a tower-shaped calvarium that is shortened in the
anteroposterior dimension and tall in the vertical dimension.
Turribrachycephaly is more frequently seen as a feature of syndromic
multisuture craniosynostosis such as in Crouzon’s and Apert’s
syndromes, but may be present without a syndrome [78]. The most
challenging aspect in the treatment of turribrachycephaly is correction
of the excess skull height. Due to its difficulty, the excess height was
initially not addressed, and patients underwent staged procedures to
address the anterior and posterior cranial vault. In 1987, Persing et al.
popularized using barrel stave osteotomies to vertically reduce the

skull while increasing the capacity of the cranium [79]. The authors
described a modified prone position that allowed access to the anterior
and posterior cranial vault in a single procedure.

14 4 12 Posterior Vault Distraction Osteogenesis
First described for treatment of multisuture craniosynostosis in 2009
[80], posterior vault distraction osteogenesis (PVDO) has become
widely used as a first step in treatment of turribrachycephaly, especially
for syndromic craniosynostosis cases. Though multiple procedures are
required, it has been suggested that PVDO provides a larger volumetric
increase compared to anterior vault remodeling procedures, and may
delay the need for frontal surgery [81].

14 5 Perioperative Safety
14 5 1 Limiting Blood Loss
Cranial surgery is an invasive procedure, with attendant blood loss and
subsequent need for blood transfusions, even with minimally invasive
techniques. Efforts to raise the patients’ baseline hematocrit or lessen
intraoperative blood loss have been studied.
Among these approaches, iron supplementation, EPO,
intraoperative cell saver devices, acute normovolemic hemodilution
(ANH), preoperative autologous blood donation, and tranexamic acid
(TXA) have been studied [82, 83]. Pre-operative EPO and
administration protocols have been found to increase the preoperative
Hct and reduce the rate of transfusion from 100% to 64%. Studies on
cell saver and ANH as sole means to avoid transfusion have shown
mixed efficacy; however, when these methods are combined with EPO,
Velardi et al. demonstrated only a 15% rate of transfusion [84]. Use of
the antifibrinolytic agent and TXA agent has been studied extensively in
craniosynostosis and facial trauma patients. Multiple studies have
found that perioperative TXA reduces amount of blood loss and the
need for blood transfusions in craniosynostosis patients [83–87].
Furthermore, the effects of TXA and EPO appear to be additive [85].
Dadure et al. performed a randomized control trial and found that
patients receiving both agents had a 37% rate of perioperative
transfusion, compared to 70% in the EPO only group [85].

There is currently no consensus regarding the optimal dosage for
using TXA for CVR for craniosynostosis surgery. A recent study by
Goobie et al. showed no difference in blood loss and blood transfusion
rates between a “high” loading dose of 50 mg/kg compared to a “low”
loading dose of 10 mg/kg, both followed by 5 mg/kg/h [83]. No
differences in adverse effects related to TXA were observed. Another
study investigated the length of time the TXA was continued, and found
no difference in blood loss, hemoglobin levels, need for transfusion, and
length of ICU stay between a 4 h continuous drip of TXA versus a 24 h
continuous drip [86]. No differences in untoward events related to TXA
were noted. The lower dosages of TXA were, however, associated with
significantly lower cost.
Risks associated with EPO include thrombosis, thrombocytosis,
hypertension, and death, and are usually associated with long term use
in adults or chronically ill patients. The risk profile of TXA is also
related to thrombosis, and again usually seen in adults. To date,
thrombotic events have not been found to be associated with use in the
craniosynostosis population. It is felt that this may be due to the lower
baseline risk for thrombosis in the pediatric population.

14 5 2 Post Operative Monitoring
At many centers, cranial vault surgery is generally managed
postoperatively in the intensive care unit (ICU). However,
overutilization of the ICU can result in lower volume of patient care due
to lack of space in the ICU. A recent report from McGill University
demonstrated a safe 8-year experience with routine postoperative
management of healthy NSC patients on the regular surgical floor [88].
Only 2% of patients in their cohort required transfer to the ICU due to
adverse intraoperative events. Subsequent studies have identified
factors that increase the risk for post operative events that require ICU
admission, including 10 kg body weight, ASA status 3 or 4,
intraoperative transfusion 60 cc/kg, and significant intraoperative
complication [89]. Taken together, these studies may promote use of
risk stratification pathways to determine the optimal usage of hospital
resources.

15 Ventricular and Pericerebral
Cerebrospinal Fluid Accumulation in
Craniosynostosis
Federico Di Rocco1, 2

Keywords Cerebrospinal fluid – Ventricular dilation – CSF dynamics –
Subarachnoid spaces

15 1 Introduction
Alterations of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dynamics leading to
hydrocephalus and increased intracranial pressure are common
features of complex craniosynostoses while they are uncommon in
simple craniosynostoses. Indeed, the incidence of hydrocephalus in
simple craniosynostoses does not apparently differ from that of the
general pediatric population although the studies concerning this
specific point are rare [1–3]. In 1998 Cinalli et al. reported a 0.28% rate
of hydrocephalus though the series they evaluated included a few
children with oxycephaly and brachycephaly that nowadays the modern
genetic analysis would probably identify as complex forms [4].
Increased intracranial pressure may be detected in about 15–20% of

subjects with simple craniosynostoses often associated with moderate
ventriculomegaly and enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces. In many
cases the phenomenon may remain clinically silent and escape even to
the fundus oculi examination, to be recognized only by means of
prolonged intracranial pressure recordings [5]. The presence of
papilledema, which is commonly thought to be a reliable indicator of
chronically increased intracranial pressure, does not seem to have a
good sensitivity in children with craniosynostosis [6]. Two main
explanations have been provided, the first of them takes into account
the great compliance of unfused normal sutures of the immature
cranium that can protect the optic nerve from the raised intracranial
pressure, thereby reducing the incidence of papilledema in infant. The
second explanation postulates a reduced communication of the
subarachnoid spaces with the optic nerve sheath in the very young [6].
However, several studies have demonstrated that the incidence of
abnormally high intracranial pressure in craniosynostosis can be
underestimated especially in infants when only the clinical and
radiographic findings are utilized. In a series of 45 children with
craniosynostosis, whose intracranial pressure was recorded
preoperatively, abnormally high values ( 15 mmHg) were recorded in
24 subjects (53%). However, only 4 (8.9%) of them had papilledema on
preoperative funduscopic examination [7].

15 2 Abnormal Dilatation of the Subarachnoid
Spaces
An abnormal dilatation of the subarachnoid spaces is often detected in
cases of early fusion of the metopic and sagittal sutures as well as in
unicoronal synostosis [8] (Figs. 15.1, 15.2, and 15.3).

Fig. 15.1 Axial CT scan in two infants with sagittal synostosis. Note the ventriculomegaly
associated with an abnormal dilation of the frontal subarachnoid space (left)

The pathogenesis and the possible role in the evolution and
morphological appearance of the skull possibly exerted by the focal
enlargements of the subarachnoid spaces are not completely
understood yet. An impaired CSF absorption related to the possible
compression, focal stenoses, and limited elasticity to expand of the
superior sagittal sinus in an abnormally narrow bone groove, created
by the premature fusion of the overlying suture, has been proposed to
explain the genesis of these fluid accumulations and the enlargement of
the subarachnoid spaces [4]. Such an interpretation is supported by the
results of the lumbar subarachnoid constant-infusion manometric test
which demonstrates an impaired fluid absorption at the low
intracranial pressures, that could account for the intracranial abnormal
fluid accumulations, and an enhanced ability for fluid absorption at
high intracranial pressures, which could have an important role in
preventing the occurrence of a frank intracranial hypertension [9, 10].
The absence of warning signs of increased intracranial pressure such as
headache and vomiting in the presence of a full or tense anterior

fontanel in sagittal synostosis could be explained on these grounds. As
a consequence, the occurrence of chronically high intracranial pressure
may be underestimated in infants with simple craniosynostosis [11]. A
direct damage of the arachnoid granulations induced by the bony
changes secondary to the early fusion of the sagittal suture has also
been suggested to be the cause of impaired fluid absorption in
scaphocephaly and elevated intracranial pressures [12]. However, no
definitive correlation has been established between such increases in
intracranial pressure and neurocognitive development yet [13]. In
general, the degree of abnormally high intracranial pressure in simple
craniosynostosis is related to the number of precociously fused suture.
Intracranial hypertension is more frequently observed in syndromic
patients than in simple craniosynostoses with a prevalence of 30–40%
[5]. Several factors are known to contribute to a pathological increase
in intracranial pressure (ICP) in these patients besides the number of
fused suture. Though the cephalo-cranial disproportion induced by the
early fusion of multiple sutures is regarded as one of the main
pathogenic mechanisms, since the early 1990s, several studies have
highlighted the lack of a predictable correlation between intracranial
volume and ICP [14, 15]. Such lack of correlation between intracranial
volume and intracranial pressure in some subjects with complex
craniosynostosis has been confirmed by recent studies [16] and
explains the failure to reduce intracranial hypertension in these
patients by the mere cranial expansive surgical cranial vault
reconstruction [17]. Intracranial hypertension in complex
craniosynostoses has a multifactorial genesis that may vary in various
syndromes, in different subjects, and also in relation to the age. The
main factors, besides the reduced skull volume, should be identified in
venous anomalies leading to defective CSF absorption, abnormal
hypoplasic, and malformed foramen magnum resulting in impaired CSF
movements, respiratory abnormalities, related to the possible
associated facial malformation, responsible for elevated levels of CO2,
the presence of hydrocephalus and hindbrain malformations, preexisting to the cranial vault expansive remodeling or developing after
the surgical operation. The correct recognition of these pathogenetic
factors and the specific role exerted in the single subject is crucial for
the successful management of the condition.

15 3 Hydrocephalus in Complex
Craniosynostoses
It is well established that hydrocephalus in complex craniosynostoses
frequently requires CSF diversion procedures, and in most of the cases
already in the first months after birth. In a great proportion of cases,
hydrocephalus associated with complex craniosynostosis is
multifactorial and progressive. Hydrocephalus is commonly
encountered in Pfeiffer and Crouzon syndromes, where it is detected in
almost half of the affected subjects usually requiring a prompt surgical
treatment. However, nonprogressive ventriculomegaly can also be
noted in a minority of children with Crouzon syndrome. On the other
hand, nonprogressive hydrocephalus, which rarely needs CSF shunting
procedures, is an almost constant characteristic of Apert’s syndrome. It
represents a maldevelopmental process rather than an active process in
the majority of the affected children.

15 3 1 Apert Syndrome (OMIM 101200)
Among the multiple anomalies harbored by subjects with Apert
syndrome, ventriculomegaly is a common feature. The larger expansion
of the cerebral ventricles occurs at the side of cranial expansive
compensatory growth and can be accompanied by enlarged
subarachnoid spaces. However, the brain volume itself is normal and
the ventriculomegaly tends to remain stable over time (Fig. 15.4).
At the end of the last century, CSF shunting procedures were
considered to be necessary for managing this ventricular enlargement
in subjects with Apert syndrome. For example, in 1993 at the Sick
Children Hospital in Toronto Hendricks and co-workers operated on 10
out of 44 children with Apert syndrome, whose computed tomography
(CT) scans or pneumoencephalograms had revealed a
ventriculomegaly. The authors performed a spino-lumbar CSF shunt in
seven cases and a ventriculo-peritoneal CSF shunt in the remaining
three subjects. In six patients, the CSF shunts were carried out
immediately after a decompressive cranial procedure because of postoperative CSF leakage (five cases) or subgaleal fluid collection (one
Case). On this ground they propounded an underlying CSF absorption

deficit [18]. It is worth to note that the same authors did not find a
relation between the volume of the ventricular enlargement and the
mental development. Pre- and post-operative (after decompressive
cranial procedures) subarachnoid fluid collections were also observed
by other authors who proposed an alternative explanation of the
phenomenon that they interpreted on the grounds of a defective and
slow brain enlargement after the operation rather than an impaired
CSF absorption [4].
In 1993, Hanieh and David reporting on 33 cases of the syndrome
treated in the Australian Craniofacial Unit at the Adelaide Children’s
Hospital emphasized that mild ventricular dilation was common among
their patients but without associated intracranial hypertension. The
ventricular dilation was severe only in one child. A further support to
the stability of the ventricular dilation was given by the observation
that after cranial decompression the obtained new intracranial volume
was occupied by the expansion of the cerebral parenchyma without any
further dilation of the cerebral ventricular cavities [19].
Cinalli et al. (1995) performed a CSF shunting procedure because of
progressive hydrocephalus only in 4 patients out of a series of 65
patients with Apert syndrome. They pointed out that only 1.9% of their
cases had chronic herniation of the cerebellar tonsils in contrast with
the 72.7% of patients with Crouzon syndrome [20]. Cranial
neuroimaging studies performed by Quintero-Rivera et al. (2006) in 30
patients with Apert syndrome showed ventriculomegaly in 76% of
patients but showed an active hydrocephalus only in 13% of the cases.
The authors also reported on associated cerebral malformations,
Namely, complete absence of the septum pellucidum (17%), partially
absent septum pellucidum (23%), and defects of the corpus callosum
(23%) that could account for mental retardation independent of the
ventricular dilation. The same authors focused on other abnormalities
that could also impact on CSF dynamics such as jugular foraminal
stenosis (28 cases), Chiari I malformation (5 cases), or low-lying
cerebellar tonsils (5 cases) [21].
A higher rate of active hydrocephalus requiring CSF diversion
procedures was recently reported by Munarriz et al. (2020) who placed
an extra-thecal CSF shunt device in a quarter (24.3%) of their subjects
with Apert syndrome. A further 8.1% of patients required

decompressive surgery for Chiari malformation. In this series, 18
patients (48.7%) presented a normal ventricular size, with an Evans’
index from 0.15 to 0.28. Ten patients (27%) harbored nonprogressive
ventriculomegaly, with an Evan’s index ranging from 0.31 to 0.44 [22].
The prenatal ultrasonographic diagnosis of non-evolutive
ventriculomegaly in Apert syndrome supports the malformative nature
of the phenomenon in majority of the cases. When its progression after
birth occurs, it is related to the impact of factors that may impair CSF
dynamics such as the craniostenosis itself, the jugular foramen stenosis,
and the possible insufficient cranial blood venous discharge [23–25].
On the other hand, patients who do not develop an active form of
hydrocephalus are characterized by normal size of both jugular
foramina, normal course of both jugular veins, absence of
compensatory emissary veins, and patent cranial lambdoid sutures.
The observation of patients with Apert syndrome harboring
ventriculomegaly without a concomitant craniosynostosis further
support the possible primary nature of the hydrocephalus in this
syndrome [26].

15 3 2 Pfeiffer Syndrome
Pfeiffer syndrome (PS, OMIM 101600) is an inherited craniofacial
disorder that is associated with primary craniosynostosis, midface
hypoplasia, broad thumbs and great toes, and soft tissue syndactyly of
hands (usually second and third digits) and feet of varying severity. It is
also defined as Type V acrocephalosyndactity, the other types being
Apert syndrome (Type I), Vogt/Crouzon syndrome (Type II), Saethre–
Chotzen syndrome (Type III), and Waardenburg syndrome (Type IV).
The premature closure of the coronal and lambdoid sutures
accounts for the cloverleaf appearance of the skull which characterizes
the type II Pfeiffer syndrome, usually associated with hydrocephalus.
Pfeiffer syndrome type III share the cranial and extracranial
malformations of type II except for the cloverleaf modification of the
skull and is associated with mental retardation as type II. On the
contrary, type I is associated with normal intelligence.
Increased intracranial pressure is a common finding of all types of
the syndrome mainly due to the reduced intracranial volume resulting

from the hypoplastic skull base and the premature fusion of the cranial
sutures (Fig. 15.5).
Actually, hydrocephalus in cloverleaf skull deformity is invariably
associated with bilateral lambdoid stenosis while it is absent in
unilateral or absent lambdoid stenosis [27].
Further contributing factors to CSF dynamics anomalies is the
abnormal development of the air pathways which results in respiratory
problems and secondary increase in cerebral vascular CO2 content in
several affected children and the tracheal cartilaginous sleeve, that
accounts for respiratory complications in some cases of Apert and
Crouzon syndromes.
The frequently associated hydrocephalus is often related to a
concomitant aqueduct stenosis [28, 29]. However, the pathogenesis of
the phenomenon should be considered multi-factorial resulting from
the restricted volume of the basal and cerebral convexities
subarachnoid spaces, posterior fossa hypoplasia, anatomical and
functional anomalies of the cranial venous outflow, as well as the
development of a caudal herniation of the cerebellar vermis and tonsils
(Fig. 15.6).

15 3 3 Crou on Syndrome
Crouzon syndrome (OMIM 123500) is characterized by
craniosynostosis resulting in secondary anomalies of the facial bones
and facial structure. The syndrome includes ventriculomegaly and
hydrocephalus among the other common features, namely,
hypertelorism, exophthalmos and external strabismus, parrot-beaked
nose, short upper lip, hypoplastic maxilla, and a relative mandibular
prognathism. Approximately 30%–40% of individuals with Crouzon
syndrome develop hydrocephalus and increased intracranial pressure
early in life. Besides hydrocephalus, intracranial hypertension depends
on a variety of pathogenic factors, namely, the reduced intracranial
volume, secondary to the early fusion of cranial sutures, the
constriction of pericerebral subarachnoid spaces, the posterior fossa
hypoplasia, the impaired venous circulation, the effect of upper airways
obstructions, and the caudal herniation of cerebellar vermis and tonsils
that can lead to a syringomyelia (Fig. 15.7). Indeed, in Pfeiffer and
Crouzon syndromes with cerebellar tonsils descent, an MRI of the spine

should be performed in order to rule out the development of an
associated syringomyelia.
More than a quarter of the 68 individuals with Crouzon syndrome
described by Cinalli et al. (1995) required a CSF shunting procedures
because of progressive hydrocephalus. In most of these subjects,
hypertensive hydrocephalus was associated with cerebellar tonsils
herniation. Four patients presented syringomyelia confirming the
complex pathogenesis of the CSF dynamic alterations that occur in the
syndrome [20].
Hydrocephalus is even more frequent in Crouzon subjects with
acanthosis nigricans involving approximately 40% of the cases. In early
life, these patients show ventriculomegaly, ocular proptosis, midface
hypoplasia, and choanal atresia whereas the cutaneous anomalies
become clinically evident only during childhood. The association of
hydrocephalus and choanal atresia in a subject with Crouzon syndrome
should arise the suspicion of Crouzon with acanthosis nigricans even
prior to the appearance of the typical cutaneous stigmata [30–33].
The early fusion of the lambdoid suture within the first 2 years of
age has been proposed to account for the major incidence of
hydrocephalus in Crouzon than in Apert syndrome [20, 34]. The
precocious closure of this suture together with other basal
synchondroses would be responsible for the hypoplastic posterior
cranial fossa and the possible stenosis of the jugular vein foramina,
commonly observed in patients with Crouzon syndrome [34, 35]. Both
phenomena concur in subjects with Crouzon syndrome to cause a
Chiari type I anomaly, that in turn would add its obstructive effects on
CSF dynamics.
Also, the size and the shape of the foramen magnum, that in the
Crouzon syndrome differ as compared to controls, may have a role in
the occurrence of the Chiari type I anomaly and in determining its
clinical severity. Indeed, among all groups, FGFR related syndromes,
especially Crouzon syndrome, show reduced anteroposterior diameter
as compared to controls (p = 0.005) [36, 37].
As previously mentioned, cerebellar tonsils’ descent may further
alter the CSF dynamics resulting in the development of a syringomyelia.
On the one side, these observations highlight the importance of a
routine clinical and radiological examination, in order to search for

signs and symptoms related to the tonsil’s descent or to the syrinx. On
the other side, they also underline the complex physiopathology of CSF
disorder in these patients associating with the craniocerebral
disproportion, focal alterations in CSF dynamics at the craniovertebral
junction level, and increased venous pressure through dural sinuses
and jugular veins.

15 4 Surgical Management of Intracranial
Hypertension, Focal CSF Collections,
Hydrocephalus in Craniosynostosis
A strict collaboration of a large team of specialists that comprise
neurosurgeons, cranio-facial surgeons, plastic surgeons, pediatric care
intensivists, pediatricians, ENT surgeons, ophthalmologists,
orthodontics, and specialized nurses is necessary for the appropriate
management of children with complex craniosynostoses. However, the
decision on when and how to correct intracranial hypertension and
associated CSF dynamics alterations should to be taken by the pediatric
neurosurgeon. Consequently, the appropriate treatment requires that
the neurosurgeon is familiar with the specific pathophysiological
mechanisms that have caused the intracranial hypertension in the
single individual.

15 4 1 The Correction of Focal Enlargement of the
Subarachnoid Spaces and Intracranial Hypertension in
Simple Craniosynostoses
Focal CSF collections are frequently found in sagittal, metopic, and
unicoronal synostoses developing in specific anatomical sites related to
the precociously fused sutures (Figs. 15.1, 15.2, and 15.3).

Fig. 15.2 Axial CT scan in two infants with metopic synostosis. Note the abnormally enlarged
frontal and sylvian subarachnoid space (left)

Fig. 15.3 CT scan in two infants with unicoronal synostosis. Note the asymmetrical enlarged
subarachnoid space in the non-affected hemicranium (left)

Fig. 15.4 Axial brain MR image of an infant with Apert syndrome. To note the co-existence of a
dilated ventricles and enlarged peripheral subarachnoid space

Fig. 15.5 CT scan of a 3-month-old infant with a Pfeiffer syndrome. To note the restricted skull
base, the enlarged transverse diameter and the acrocephaply. The ventricular system is dilated
while the peripheral subarachnoid space is effaced

Fig. 15.6 Sagittal brain MR image of a 5-month-old infant with Pfeiffer syndrome showing an
obvious triventricular dilation of the ventricular system associated with aqueductal stenosis,
hypoplasic posterior cranial fossa with the disappearnce of the cisterna magna, and to an initial
caudal displacement of the inferior cerebellar vermis. The volume of the subarachnoid spaces
of the cerebral convexities is altered alternating area of focal dilations and compression from
the overlying bone structures. The CSF subarachnoid circulation is impaired by the presence of
skull bone spicule indentating the membrane coverings

Fig. 15.7 Sagittal MR in an infant with Crouzon syndrome. To note the elongated sagittal
diameter, the macrocrania and frontal bossing related to the anomalies in CSF dynamics
involving both the ventricular system and the peripheral subarachnoid spaces. The inferior
cerebellar vermis is caudally dislocated causing a local obstacle on CSF circulation at the craniocervical junction leading to syringomyelia

Fig. 15.8 Axial and 3D reconstruction in a 1-month-old infant with scaphocephaly
demonstrating the effect of the frontal subarachnoid fluid accumulation on the shape and
spatial positioning of the anterior skull

Fig. 15.9 Pattern of bone ridge commonly associated with pericerebral CSF collection. Adapted
from Ref. [62]

In nearly all the cases, these focal enlargements of the subarachnoid
spaces appear to be well tolerated and do not require specific surgical
corrective measures even though they appear to play a certain role, at
least in scaphocephaly, in defining the resulting morphology of the
skull. For example, in scaphocephaly, the pericerebral fluid collection in
the frontal region contributes to enlarge the bulging forehead and
modifies the frontonasal angle (Figs. 15.1 and 15.8) [62].
A correlation with the shape of the fused suture overlying the
superior sagittal sinus and the presence of CSF collections has also
been found: the abnormal CSF collections are found more commonly in
children with an “omega” type configuration of the fused sagittal
synostosis [61] (Fig. 15.9).
These findings may suggest that the CSF collection results from a
focal venous resorption impairment, but such hypothesis needs to be
confirmed. However, the presence of focal frontal collection in
unicoronal synostosis seems to suggest that venous sinus compression

is not the sole mechanism for such subarachnoid space enlargement
(Fig. 15.3). The expansive remodeling of the skull vault is usually
followed by the volumetric reduction of pericerebral fluid collections
and finally by their complete or nearly complete disappearance.
The preoperative presence of the enlarged CSF spaces (ventricular
or periventricular) seems to play a role in the early post-operative
course, at least in cases of endoscopic sagittal suturectomies where the
immediate post-operative parietal expansion is greater in case of
enlarged CSF spaces. However, the potential impact of such CSF
collection on functional results remains unknown.
Bilateral expanding craniotomies induces total relief from the
symptoms and signs of raised intracranial pressure even in older
children with mild forms of craniosynostosis that were not treated in
infancy [38]. Actually, chronically increased intracranial pressure and
ocular fundi anomalies are a frequent finding in older children with
untreated mild craniosynostosis which are investigated because of
neurocognitive delay. Late cranial vault expansive cranioplasty proved
to be effective in these patients [39]. The risk of under-evaluating
intracranial hypertension in subjects with sagittal synostosis was
pointed out by Wall et al., in 2014 [11]. The authors recorded the
intraparenchymal pressure in 39 children (mean age: 58 months)
whose surgical treatment had been considered to be not indicated on
the grounds of the minimal cranial deformity and the absence of clinical
manifestations of increased intracranial pressure or refused by the
parents. When re-examined at an older age, 16 out of the 39 (41%)
individuals presented with marked dolichocephaly, 11 (28%) with mild
scaphocephaly and 12 (31%) with a near normal skull shape. Raised
intracranial pressure was recorded in 14 (44%) out of the 39 children
without any significant difference in incidence among the three groups
and in the absence of clinical symptoms and signs and
ophthalmological or radiological anomalies that could have suggested
intracranial hypertension. The same team of scientists, in 2015 [40],
challenged the efficacy of the modified strip craniectomy versus the
calvarial remodeling in normalizing the intracranial pressure in sagittal
synostosis suggesting the need for a long-term observation, especially
for those that had undergone linear craniectomies. They recorded the
intracranial pressure in 217 children that had undergone one or two

surgical procedures, either a modified strip craniectomy or a calvarial
remodeling. Abnormally high-pressure values were found in 6.9% of
the cases (mean post-operative period: 51 months), more commonly in
subjects treated with modified strip craniectomy (13 out of 89 patients,
14.6%) than with cranial remodeling (2 out of 128 subjects, 1.6%).
Most of the children operated on by strip craniectomy were less than
1 year of age at the time of the operation. These data should not be
overlooked when considering the recent shift toward strip craniectomy
as the result of the introduction of the endoscopic techniques.
A retrospective study on 284 patients with isolated non-syndromic
sagittal craniosynostosis operated by cranial vault reconstruction
provided a figure of 7.07% of children requiring a second surgical
procedure because of the recurrence of abnormally high intracranial
pressure, with a double incidence in subjects operated on before
6 months of age compared with those treated later on [41].
Unfortunately, no information on the CSF spaces was provided.

15 4 2 The Management of CSF Disorders Associated with
Complex Craniosynostosis
The management of hydrocephalus, and in particular, the timing of a
CSF shunting procedure, in children with syndromic craniosynostoses
has been and still is a subject of discussion. The early occurrence and
rapid progression of ventricular dilation in subjects with Pfeiffer
syndrome and, less frequently, Crouzon syndrome may challenge the
most common attitude to perform CSF draining procedures only after
cranial decompression [42, 43]. Indeed, the insertion of a CSF shunting
device to treat immediately the intracranial hypertension may allow to
postpone the cranial reconstruction so decreasing the risks of
postoperative complications (excessive bleeding, wound infection,
meningitis, seizure, pneumonia) that can weigh the very early cranial
remodeling of the trilobar skull in case of Pfeiffer and Crouzon
syndromes. Actually, after controlling the hypertensive hydrocephalus
by means of a ventriculo-peritoneal CSF shunt in the neonatal period,
the calvarial remodeling (fronto-orbital advancement or posterior vault
enlargement) can be made at 3–6 months and further remodeling at
1 year of age with major safety [35].

In subjects, who appear to tolerate the hydrocephalus relatively
well, most of the authors are reluctant to proceed with an immediate
insertion of a CSF extrathecal shunt device. Such a cautious attitude is
based on three main considerations. First of all, the observation that
the expansive calvarial reconstruction may be sufficient to control the
hydrocephalus in some cases. Then, the concern that the action of the
inserted CSF draining device may reduce the expansive force of the
intracranial content necessary to allow the adequate post-operative
skull growth. Finally, the high incidence of CSF shunting complications
in the pediatric population with craniosynostosis. An incidence of 59%
complications rate associated with the extrathecal CSF shunting leading
to further surgical procedures has been reported in a recent study [44].
The reluctance to insert a CSF draining device in infants with
Crouzon disease and hydrocephalus is further justified by the
observation of ventriculomegaly, even quite significant in size, that
tends to remain stable in some patients without any CSF shunt
diversion procedure [42]. This is the case for the frequent non evolutive
ventriculomegaly associated with Apert syndrome for which an
intrinsic abnormality in the embryological development of the brain
has been postulated [45].
The rate of hydrocephalus regression following the mere expansive
remodeling of the cranial vault, that is, the correction of the
“constrictive” forces impairing CSF circulation and absorption, cannot
be evaluated by the analysis of the literature. Indeed, such an evenience
depends on the variable equilibrium of many variables that can play a
specific role in the single individual such as an impaired CSF absorption
related to the restricted volume of the subarachnoid spaces, venous
anomalies, and aqueduct stenosis. Actually, some of the just mentioned
pathogenic factors can continue to exert a role even after cranial vault
remodeling accounting for the progression of hydrocephalus that can
be observed in some infants even after the surgical expansion of the
skull.
The still persisting debate on the most appropriate managing of the
hydrocephalus associated with complex craniosynostosis continues the
discussion about its physiopathogenesis, that can be recognized already
in the first proposal of the “constrictive” hypothesis by Rieping, more
than a century ago that indicated the mechanical compression exerted

by the hypoplasic posterior fossa as the mechanism leading to the
impairment in CSF absorption [46]. The hypothesis of an impaired
venous discharge resulting in a defective CSF absorption was first
propounded by Günther in 1936 [47] and subsequently accepted by a
wide number of scientists that pointed on the obstacles in venous
circulation exerted by the bony anomalies of the posterior cranial fossa,
in particular at the level of the jugular foramina [48, 49]. Sainte-Rose
and co-workers individuated in the structural obstruction of the
sigmoid sinus as the pathogenic anomaly responsible for the
hydrocephalus on the grounds of the pressure variations that they
recorded in the sagittal superior sinus, jugular vein, and lateral cerebral
ventricles simultaneously following CSF withdrawal and re-injection
tests. Based on these tests and the results of sonography, the authors
carried on a venous bypass between the lateral sinus and a jugular vein
in three patients, a procedure that did not become popular [50].
Cerebellar tonsils caudal herniation is commonly associated with
the premature fusion of the lambdoid suture in subjects with Crouzon
disease. It can be not obvious in the neonatal period becoming obvious
during the first year of life. Such a low position of the cerebellar tonsils
is often referred to as “Chiari type I malformation.” Indeed, rather than
a “malformation,” the caudal herniation of the hindbrain structures
should be regarded in subjects with Crouzon syndrome as an acquired
alteration depending on the cranio-cerebral disproportion brought
about by the reduced volume of the posterior cranial fossa secondary to
the premature fusion of the lambdoid sutures. Indeed, it is often
associated with an upward migration of the upper cerebellar vermis
into the pre-vermian cistern that indicates the hypoplasic posterior
cranial fossa as the cause of both phenomena, having become the
structure unable to accommodate for the growing cerebellum. The
possible cerebellar turgor induced by a concomitant local venous
hypertension should be considered a further factor accounting for such
dynamic events [51].
The caudal herniation of the cerebella tonsils and its clinical
manifestations can be precipitated by the pressure “from above”
exerted by the further dilatation of the supratentorial ventricular
system that can occur because of a functional stenosis of the aqueduct
and the block in the CSF circulation at the level of the cranio-vertebral

junction. Such a block interferes not only with the CSF upward
movements toward the major sites for its absorption into the superior
sagittal sinus but also precludes its downward circulation so limiting its
absorption by the meninges of the spinal cord and the ependyma of the
central spinal canal. In other words, the caudal herniation of the
cerebellar structures may result in a functional dissociation between
the cranial and spinal compartments so creating a pressure gradient
that constitutes a further pathogenic factor for the progression of the
hydrocephalus.
The morphology of the foramen magnum also appears to play an
important role in both the genesis and the clinical presentation of the
acquired caudal descent of the cerebellar tonsils [36]. The foramen
magnum area is reduced in size in subjects with Crouzon syndrome and
hydrocephalus, with diminished sagittal diameter (p = 0.023), sagittal
posterior diameter (p = 0.0173), and transversal diameter
(p = 0.03985) as compared to the normal population [52, 53]. The
reduced area of the foramen magnum does not only differentiate
individuals with Crouzon and Pfeiffer syndrome from the normal
population but also from subjects with Apert, Saethre-Chotzen, or
isolated bicoronal synostosis (p = 0.37, p = 0.71, p = 0.40, respectively)
[37, 54].
In recent years, endoscopic third-cisternostomy (ETV) has been in
subjects with craniofacial synostosis, caudal herniation of the
cerebellar structures, and hypertensive hydrocephalus proposed in the
attempt to avoid the insertion of an extrathecal CSF drainage. Out of 11
patients (Crouzon syndrome 5, Pfeiffer syndrome 3, and unclassifiable
syndrome 3) the hydrocephalus was controlled in 7 cases, whereas the
remaining 4 patients required a ventriculo-peritoneal CSF shunt at a
variable temporal distance ranging from 1 week to 6 months,
consequently, demonstrating the necessity of a strict prolonged
monitoring of the operated-on patients [55]. The posterior cranial fossa
bone decompression seems effective in decreasing the incidence of late
failure of the ETV [44]. The effectiveness of ETV in treating the
hydrocephalus associated with the caudal herniation of the cerebellar
tonsils in a good percentage of cases has been demonstrated by several
studies and proposed as a measure to post-pone the skull
reconstruction for a few months in order to decrease the surgical risk

and select the most appropriate age for the operation [56–59]. The
same approach has been suggested for the rare cases of isolated cranial
synostosis, namely, sagittal synostosis, presenting with hydrocephalus
and hindbrain structures descent [60].
In conclusion, the accurate evaluation of the morphology of the CSF
spaces and the CSF dynamics aimed at identifying the pathogenic
mechanisms of the hydrocephalus associated with craniosynostosis is
mandatory to decide for a timely surgical correction and to select the
appropriate surgical procedure, as well as, to recognize those subjects
whose ventricular dilation is likely to not progress or being controlled
by the mere cranial remodeling.
