16 Craniocerebral Disproportion,
Cerebral Perfusion, and Raised
Intracranial Pressure in
Craniosynostosis
Jeffrey Nadel1 and John R. W. Kestle1
(1) Department of Neurosurgery, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT,
USA

John R W Kestle
Email: neuropub@hsc.utah.edu
Keywords Intracranial pressure – Craniosynostosis – Cerebral
perfusion – Developmental delay
The timing of intervention in a child with premature fusion of the
cranial sutures has long been debated. In part, this debate centers
around how craniosynostosis affects brain development and,
specifically, whether increased intracranial pressure (ICP) from
premature bony fusion is causally related to worse cognitive outcomes.
This chapter will discuss the data surrounding craniocerebral
disproportion, its effect on cerebral perfusion and ICP, and clinical and
cognitive outcomes in children with single-suture, multisuture, and
syndromic craniosynostosis.
Not surprisingly, the relationship between premature fusion of the
cranial sutures and ICP has long been of concern to neurosurgeons.
Indeed, historically, one of the primary drivers of intervention in
craniosynostosis has been to avoid secondary brain injury from chronic

elevations in ICP. Before reviewing the data on raised ICP in
craniosynostosis, it is worth discussing the definition of raised ICP in
childhood.

16 1 Establishing Normative Values
There is a paucity of normative data on ICP in childhood. Because of
significant physiologic variation, age-related changes, changes in
pressure due to sedation at the time of measurement, and the effects of
body mass index and position on ICP, the definition of a normal ICP in
childhood has been elusive [1]. Directly measuring ICP in pediatric
patients without an intracranial pathology necessitating its
measurement (e.g., traumatic brain injury) is challenging. Therefore,
medical professionals have largely relied on using lumbar puncture
opening pressure in the lateral decubitus position as a surrogate for
ICP. In 2010, Avery et al. [2] reported the results of a large, single-center
prospective study of children receiving a lumbar puncture as part of
their routine clinical care. The purpose of the study was to develop a
reference range for normalcy of lumbar puncture opening pressure in
children. Abnormally elevated or reduced values were defined a priori
as those in the 90th percentile or higher or 10th percentile or lower,
respectively. Abnormally elevated opening pressures were determined
to be those 28 cm H2O and abnormally reduced opening pressures
were those 11.5 cm H2O. Statistically significant factors impacting the
value of the opening pressure were sedation administered for the
procedure and body mass index. Opening pressure was not found to
significantly vary across age.
In recent years, several studies have called into question the validity
of lumbar puncture opening pressure as a true representation of ICP
because of the aforementioned factors [1, 3]. In fact, one study that
measured ICP via a bolted intracranial ICP monitor and compared it
with lumbar puncture opening pressure performed during the same
hospital admission found that lumbar puncture opening pressure
significantly overestimated the true ICP value [3]. One historical report
argued that normal ICP was approximately 2 mmHg in neonates,
5 mmHg in infants, 6–13 mmHg in children up to 7 years, and less than
20 mmHg in older children and adults [4]. Indeed, understanding how

ICP changes across childhood remains a topic of ongoing debate, and
true normative data have not been clearly established. Below, we
discuss the literature on ICP measurement in patients with
craniosynostosis and how the commonly accepted ICP thresholds in
children with craniosynostosis were determined.

16 2 Historical Investigations of Raised ICP in
Craniosynostosis
The first comprehensive evaluation of ICP in patients with
craniosynostosis was performed by Renier et al. [5] in 1982. In a
seminal study, they examined 92 cases of craniosynostosis—both
single-suture and multisuture—with preoperative and postoperative
epidural ICP monitoring. They defined ICP 15 mmHg as elevated, 10–
15 mmHg as borderline, and ICP 10 mmHg as normal. On the basis of
these criteria, they concluded that preoperative ICP was elevated in
approximately one-third of patients, borderline in one-third, and
normal in the final third. ICP spikes were frequently observed during
REM sleep, and there was a direct, positive relationship between the
number of sutures involved and elevation in preoperative ICP. In those
patients with preoperative elevated and borderline ICP, ICP
progressively returned to normal within weeks after surgery. Notably,
in a post hoc analysis, an examination of ICP as a function of age
demonstrated that ICP peaked at age 6 years in this population and
decreased with increasing age. This work served as the foundation for
evaluating ICP in children with craniosynostosis. It is worth noting,
however, that not all craniofacial groups adopted this threshold of
abnormal ICP values. Instead, it became common to consider elevated
ICP as 20 mmHg, borderline ICP as 15–20 mmHg, and normal ICP as
15 mmHg based on values adopted from the traumatic brain injury
literature.
Over the next decade, the focus of further research efforts was
understanding how craniosynostosis of different etiologies and among
distinct patient groups affected ICP. Using subdural ICP monitoring, it
was determined that raised ICP was more common in those with
syndromic and multisuture craniosynostosis than in those with

nonsyndromic and single-suture craniosynostosis [6, 7]. This finding
makes intuitive sense. Those with multiple fused sutures have less
ability to accommodate brain tissue expansion throughout childhood
development. Furthermore, patients with syndromic craniosynostosis
generally have multiple fused sutures, worse clinical deformity, and
additional pathologies that may predispose them to have increased ICP.
Interestingly, regarding the effect of age on ICP in craniosynostosis,
additional studies confirmed the positive relationship between age and
ICP that Renier et al. [5] originally described. When fused sutures were
discovered later in childhood—even in the setting of single-suture
synostosis—it was common for patients to have preoperative elevated
ICPs when measured using a ventriculostomy catheter [8]. One reason
that patients may come to surgical attention later in childhood is mild
or minimal clinical deformity from their synostosis. Nearly 44% of
patients older than 12 months with sagittal synostosis but mild or no
clinical scaphocephaly had elevated ICPs in the preoperative setting [9].
As such, one cannot assume that a patient with only mild clinical
deformity will not have elevated ICP.
From a radiographic perspective, chronically elevated ICP can lead
to the appearance of a “copper beaten skull” [10–13]. This is often seen
in the setting of long-standing congenital hydrocephalus but is clearly
pertinent in patients with untreated craniosynostosis as well.
Specifically, a copper beaten skull is one in which the calvaria has a
scalloped appearance on skull X-ray or computed tomography scan,
with multiple convolutions and involutions (Fig. 16.1a). It is
hypothesized that chronically increased intracranial tension can induce
bony remodeling of the calvaria (Fig. 16.1b). The discovery of a copper
beaten skull on imaging warrants further investigation into possible
causative factors for elevated ICP.

Fig. 16.1 (a) Plain radiograph demonstrating the “copper beaten skull” appearance of
chronically elevated intracranial pressure. (b) Intraoperative photograph demonstrating the
anatomic correlation to a radiographic “copper beaten skull,” with chronic bony remodeling of
the calvaria in response to elevated intracranial pressure

In summary, most pediatric craniofacial surgeons and
neurosurgeons today consider an abnormally elevated ICP to be greater
than 15–20 mmHg. It is widely accepted that untreated
craniosynostosis is associated with elevated ICP, and this relationship
strengthens with increasing age. Syndromic and multisuture
craniosynostosis are risk factors for elevated preoperative ICP, although
even patients with single-suture synostosis and mild or no clinical
deformity may have elevated preoperative ICP.

16 3 Etiology of Raised ICP in
Craniosynostosis
The cause of elevated ICP in craniosynostosis is complex and
multifactorial. As discussed above, restricted skull volume with
resulting craniocerebral disproportion is one element that leads to
raised ICP, although it is clearly not the only responsible cause [5, 7, 14–
16]. Additional factors discussed below include hindbrain herniation

through the foramen magnum [17–19], intracranial venous congestion
causing venous hypertension or other venous anomalies [14, 17, 20–
27], hydrocephalus [28–34], and airway obstruction [26, 35–46]. Each
of these factors likely influences the others and, in combination, leads
to issues with raised ICP. Further, the majority of these factors are
present in syndromic and multisuture craniosynostosis and are
therefore part of the reason that these conditions have a higher
incidence of raised ICP when compared with nonsyndromic and singlesuture synostosis.
Posterior fossa hypoplasia is a common finding in patients with
complex craniosynostosis because of skull base developmental
abnormalities. The small posterior fossa volume in these patients can
lead to higher rates of tonsillar herniation through the foramen
magnum and other hindbrain compression syndromes. The literature
on Chiari malformation has shown that crowding at the craniocervical
junction alters cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow dynamics, decreases CSF
drainage, and reduces venous outflow from the cranial vault [47–52].
The consequence of this type of mechanical obstruction is elevated ICP.
Additionally, because of direct compression onto the adjacent
brainstem, tonsillar herniation may lead to central respiratory
insufficiency with hypoventilation and CO2 retention, thereby also
leading to an elevation in ICP [17–19].
Intracranial venous congestion leading to venous hypertension is
another leading cause of elevated ICP in the setting of complex
craniosynostosis. Physiologically, in accordance with the Monro-Kellie
doctrine, impaired venous drainage from the cranial vault results in a
backup of blood that cannot escape the calvaria. Unless a concomitant
decrease in CSF volume or brain tissue is achieved, ICP will rise. In
patients with craniosynostosis, the most common reasons that patients
might have reduced cerebral venous outflow are congenitally
anomalous venous drainage pathways and inborn stenosis of
anatomically normal venous outflow channels that worsen with
premature fusion of the cranial sutures. Interestingly, several studies
have suggested that anomalous venous vasculature in complex
craniosynostosis is common. Especially in syndromic craniosynostosis,
there are disproportionately elevated rates of patients with
angiographically demonstrated venous sinus malformations, stenotic

transverse-sigmoid or sigmoid-jugular junctions, large intraosseous
draining veins, and intracranial–extracranial venous drainage
anomalies such as sinus pericranii (Fig. 16.2) [14, 17, 20–27]. Without
normal channels for venous drainage, venous hypertension is common
and develops quickly in these patients. This has consequences both for
preoperative ICP management as well as for intraoperative planning so
as not to inadvertently occlude a primary venous outflow tract causing
rapid-onset venous hypertension and ICP crisis [27].

Fig. 16.2 CT venogram in a child with Crouzon syndrome and multisuture synostosis
demonstrating (a) prominent extracranial venous drainage and (b) protruding torcula

The development of hydrocephalus in craniosynostosis, as in
hydrocephalus from other causes, may be due to problems in CSF
outflow or CSF malabsorption. As discussed previously, patients with
craniosynostosis have craniocerebral disproportion. With brain tissue
in excess of what the hypoplastic posterior fossa can accommodate,
mechanical obstruction of CSF outflow can result in obstructive
hydrocephalus. This is primarily due to osseous constriction. In
contrast to CSF outflow obstruction, patients may also develop
hydrocephalus from CSF malabsorption. We have previously discussed
that venous hypertension is common in patients with craniosynostosis.
Venous hypertension creates increased intravascular resistance to the
absorption of CSF at arachnoid granulations and can thus impair CSF
reabsorption into the systemic venous circulation [28–34]. This may
also lead to the development of hydrocephalus. Importantly, some
patients with complex craniosynostosis may not have progressive

hydrocephalus but instead demonstrate nonprogressive
ventriculomegaly from abnormal brain development or the involution
of normal brain parenchyma during disordered development [32].
Progressive hydrocephalus requires treatment with either ventricular
shunting or endoscopic third ventriculostomy [30], whereas
nonprogressive ventriculomegaly may not require CSF diversion.
Hydrocephalus in either form, however, can drive elevated ICP in these
patients.
Finally, upper airway obstruction is a common finding in patients
with complex craniosynostosis. Especially in syndromic children,
midface hypoplasia and other congenital anomalies in the formation of
caudal face and neck structures can lead to issues with mechanical
airway obstruction. Whether while the patient is awake or asleep—
such as in the setting of obstructive sleep apnea, airway obstruction
leads to an elevation in ICP from mechanical hypoventilation [26, 35–
46]. On a physiologic level, with poor respiratory ventilation, the body
retains carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide is a vasodilatory substance, thus
increasing the volume of blood in the intracranial compartment. With
increased intracranial blood volume, the body must reflexively decrease
intracranial CSF or brain parenchyma to maintain a normal ICP. As
reviewed, most patients with craniosynostosis already have a
decreased ability to dynamically control CSF flow. Therefore, because of
this decreased reserve, obstructive hypoventilation often leads to
increased ICP in patients with craniosynostosis. It is worth noting that
in sleep studies of patients with craniosynostosis, ICP often peaked
during periods of active sleep [53]. Active sleep, compared with passive
sleep, is associated with periods of respiratory compromise due to
paralysis of the tongue and pharyngeal musculature. Thus, in patients
predisposed to have obstructive apnea, active sleep can lead to
worsening of their apnea with concomitant increases in measured ICP.

16 4 Clinical Impact of Craniocerebral
Disproportion
From the perspective of a practicing clinician, craniocerebral
disproportion may significantly impact child development and impede

normal central nervous system (CNS) maturation. In normal childhood
development, a delayed fusion of the cranial sutures allows for
progressive CNS maturation and brain growth without osseous
constraint. Premature fusion may disrupt brain perfusion and neuronal
plasticity via mechanical compressive forces, thereby impeding normal
brain growth, hindering the formation of appropriate neural networks,
and negatively affecting a child’s special senses (Fig. 16.3).

Fig. 16.3 Constrained brain growth due to calvarial restriction from premature fusion of
sutures

It is widely accepted that craniosynostosis can negatively affect
ophthalmic outcomes and, in some cases, result in devastating loss of
vision [54]. The visual system is arguably the part of the CNS most
affected in craniosynostosis, whether as a direct result of the premature
fusion itself or as a secondary effect of it. As discussed, elevated ICP is
common in single-suture and multisuture synostosis. Both acute and
chronic elevations in ICP are known to lead to optic disc edema (Fig.
16.4). If persistent, this can eventually result in atrophy of the optic
apparatus and worsening visual dysfunction over time. Further,
extraocular ophthalmic issues may arise in craniosynostosis. These
include extraocular muscle entrapment by abnormal bony maturation,
strabismus, ptosis, proptosis, and resultant corneal exposure issues
[54–56]. Initial consultation with ophthalmology and, in many cases,
long-term surveillance are essential to prevent permanent loss of vision
and enable early intervention for treatable visual sequelae.

Fig. 16.4 Retinal photograph demonstrating papilledema and optic nerve edema in response
to chronically elevated intracranial pressure

As previously mentioned, airway obstruction is a common finding in
craniosynostosis. This may lead to significant sleep disturbance and
disrupted sleep architecture due to obstructive sleep apneas or central
hypoventilation [38, 46]. The chronic effects of poor sleep and sleep
deprivation are out of the scope of this review; however, it has been
demonstrated that respiratory compromise during active sleep in
children with craniosynostosis can result in transiently decreased
cerebral perfusion [53]. Over time, the cumulative effects of such
decreased perfusion may contribute to the ophthalmic and
psychomotor disability seen in this disease.
A discussion of clinically relevant aspects of craniosynostosis would
be incomplete without considering how craniosynostosis impacts
cerebral perfusion. Premature skull vault maturation can not only lead
to elevated ICP but also affects brain perfusion. Indeed, this hypothesis
led investigators in the mid-1990s to study local and global cerebral
perfusion in patients with craniosynostosis as a means to fully
understand the physiologic impact of the disease. At the time, these
studies were performed using positron emission tomography and
single-photon emission computed tomography and aimed to examine
cerebral perfusion and cerebral metabolism. Unsurprisingly, it was
determined that brain perfusion under a fused suture is hypoperfused
relative to adjacent brain tissue because of mechanical compressive
forces [9, 23, 53, 57–61]. Importantly, this perfusion deficit is seen
along the spectrum of disease severity. Specifically, local hypoperfusion
is seen in both nonsyndromic, single-suture craniosynostosis and
syndromic, multisuture synostosis. Thus, mild cases of single-suture
synostosis cannot be presumed to be completely benign. Surgical
intervention for craniosynostosis was also successful in relieving this
perfusion deficit in many cases.
The long-term effects of a chronic cerebral perfusion deficit in
children are unclear. Adequate cerebral perfusion is essential for
proper brain development, early neural plasticity, and formation of
neural networks [62–66]. Research on adult traumatic brain injury has
shown that a persistent perfusion deficit, even in the absence of frank
ischemia, can lead to poor cerebral reserve, compromised neurologic
recovery, and worse neurologic and neuropsychologic outcomes [67,
68]. It would not be surprising that failure to relieve a perfusion deficit

may have negative effects on overall neurologic development and
outcome. Thus, in addition to relief of elevated ICP, improvement in
local cerebral perfusion is another compelling argument for early
surgical intervention.

16 5 Impact of Craniocerebral Disproportion
on Cognitive Development
The relationship between craniocerebral disproportion and cognitive
development is complex and contentious. In 1982, Renier et al. [5] first
suggested that elevated preoperative ICP from craniocerebral
disproportion might be related to low intellectual quotient (IQ),
because they found a significant statistical relationship between the
two in their seminal work. They qualified this assertion by stating that
increased ICP and low IQ might be two consequences of a third
variable. Since that time, there has been significant debate regarding
how craniocerebral disproportion itself—i.e., the constrained skull
alone—impacts neuropsychological and cognitive outcomes in patients
with craniosynostosis and raised ICP.
By way of background, across the spectrum of disease, patients with
craniosynostosis are at increased risk for developmental delays, lower
intellectual attainment, poorer cognitive performance, and
psychological and linguistic problems. The type and severity of
craniosynostosis likely have a significant impact on cognitive and
developmental outcomes. In many series, more than 50% of patients
with syndromic, multisuture craniosynostosis score lower on metrics of
infant developmental outcome preoperatively and have persistent
developmental delays in childhood and poorer eventual neurocognitive
outcomes when compared with their age-matched counterparts [26,
41, 69–73]. The landscape of cognitive outcomes in patients with
nonsyndromic, single-suture craniosynostosis is somewhat less clear
[9, 74–90]. Numerous studies have demonstrated that patients with
idiopathic single-suture synostosis, even with intervention early in
infancy, remain at risk for developmental delays and cognitive and
learning disability during childhood and have higher rates of these
issues than age-matched counterparts; however, many of the early

studies were plagued by small sample sizes and nonstandardized
methodologies, making it difficult to generalize the results. Recent
systematic reviews and meta-analyses do suggest that children with
idiopathic, single-suture synostosis warrant increased surveillance and
screening for developmental delay and neuropsychological
impairments because of their disproportionate likelihood of having
these problems [79, 80, 86]. There is also inconclusive evidence to
suggest that earlier surgery may be beneficial in preventing negative
developmental outcomes in the setting of single-suture synostosis [88,
89].
The cause of cognitive and neuropsychological impairments in
craniosynostosis is widely debated. It should be stated that there is no
controversy about whether patients with craniosynostosis have
craniocerebral disproportion with frequently elevated ICP, locally
compromised cerebral perfusion, and concomitant poor cognitive and
neuropsychological outcomes. Rather, the debate centers on whether
there is a causal relationship between restricted skull volume and
neurocognitive impairment. In a controversial 2014 editorial, Hayward
and colleagues argued that the data directly linking restricted skull
volume/high ICP with neurocognitive impairments are sparse [91].
Historically, the rationale for surgically expanding the cranial vault
centered on relieving elevated ICP and thereby preventing the
secondary brain injury that causes neurocognitive impairments.
Although this is a rational assumption, Hayward et al. asserted that the
data only partly support this claim and that what data exist are poor in
quality. As they noted, this mattered because if there is no clear
evidence linking elevated ICP and neurocognitive development, then
infants may be subjected to operations that are unnecessary and carry
significant risk.
Although restricted skull volume and craniocerebral disproportion
are factors, other variables may also affect neurocognitive development
in patients with craniosynostosis. Whether these variables mediate or
simply contribute to the relationship among craniocerebral
disproportion, elevated ICP, and cognitive impairment remains unclear.
In syndromic craniosynostosis, one such factor is the genetic cause of
the disease. In addition to the dysmorphic craniofacial anatomy, genetic
alterations in the disease process may directly affect neuronal

development, capacity for neuronal plasticity, development of neural
networks, and the function of neurons on a cellular level [26, 69–71, 84,
91]. As such, it is feasible that neurocognitive impairments in
syndromic patients may be inborn and at least in part a result of
abnormal cellular brain development. Additional variables, some of
which have been discussed previously at length, include coexistent
hydrocephalus; chronic respiratory obstruction and insufficient
oxygenation during sleep and wakefulness; feeding difficulties from
midface hypoplasia leading to failure to thrive; a lack of stimulation
from impaired vision or hearing that results in delayed cognitive
development; the ill-effects of surgical intervention in infancy including
exposure to prolonged anesthesia; and low familial and societal
expectations due to the craniofacial deformity that lead to fewer
enriching opportunities in early childhood [29–34, 37, 38, 43, 45, 46,
53, 91–102].
In reality, it is likely that the cause of cognitive impairment in
children with craniosynostosis is multifactorial and quite
individualized. For the practicing craniofacial surgeon, it is important to
understand that this topic is nuanced and that appropriate
preoperative counseling with parents should include a discussion about
the downstream development of potential neurocognitive
abnormalities, even in the setting of early surgical intervention.

16 6 Conclusion
In summary, many children with craniosynostosis will present with
elevated preoperative ICP by any definition of ICP thresholds.
Craniocerebral disproportion with restricted skull volume is a driving
force for elevated ICP, although other factors that may lead to high ICP
in this group of patients include posterior fossa hypoplasia and
hindbrain herniation through the foramen magnum; anomalous
intracranial venous drainage, venous congestion, and venous
hypertension; hydrocephalus; and chronic airway obstruction.
Clinically, craniocerebral disproportion can manifest in ophthalmic
compromise, local hypoperfusion of the brain beneath the affected
suture(s), and neurocognitive impairment. There is no clear, causative
link between neurocognitive impairment in these patients and

restricted skull volume. Rather, neurocognitive impairment in
craniosynostosis is multifactorial and may be related to craniocerebral
disproportion/elevated ICP, abnormal cellular brain development due
to genetic or chromosomal anomalies, hydrocephalus, chronic
respiratory insufficiency, failure to thrive, poor cognitive stimulation in
development due to impairment of the CNS special senses, exposure to
surgical intervention in early infancy, and low societal expectations
leading to a paucity of enriching opportunities during development.
Further research is warranted to better understand these relationships,
as they may influence the timing and extent of surgery.

17 Non-invasive Assessment of ICP and
Perfusion in Craniosynostosis
Llewellyn Padayachy1, 2
(1) Department of Neurosurgery, University of Pretoria, Pretoria,
South Africa
(2) Steve Biko Academic Hospital, Pretoria, South Africa

Llewellyn Padayachy
Email: LC.Padayachy@up.ac.za
Keywords Intracranial pressure – Non-invasive monitoring –
Perfusion – Craniosynostosis

17 1 Introduction
Raised ICP is a common finding in children with craniosynostosis. The
frequency in single-suture synostosis is between 15% and 20% [1–3]
and is higher in complex craniosynostosis with a described prevalence
of 30–40% [4, 5]. The clinical signs and symptoms associated with
raised ICP in craniosynostosis can be quite subtle with a slow,
progressive clinical course and therefore may be of limited diagnostic
value. Radiological features consistent with raised ICP are also
observer-dependent and have a variable diagnostic accuracy [6]. The
rates of post-operative raised ICP, especially in syndromic
craniosynostosis, even in aesthetically successful corrective procedures,
also appear to be unclear due to the lack of reliable indicators of raised
ICP [7].
The value of a reliable non-invasive diagnostic technique to detect
raised ICP in children with craniosynostosis is also underscored by the

current limitations related to invasive ICP monitoring [8]. Continuous
advancements in technology have also made.

17 2 Methods for Detecting Raised ICP
17 2 1 Clinical Assessment
Neurological evaluation and accurate history-taking remain the
mainstay of diagnosis and monitoring. Careful history-taking is of
paramount importance when making a diagnosis of raised ICP.
Symptoms suggestive of raised ICP include headache, nausea and
vomiting, visual impairment, altered level of consciousness and
developmental delay.
The clinical presentation due to raised ICP differs in neonates and
older children. In neonates, where the anterior fontanelle is still patent,
an increasing head circumference, bulging of the anterior fontanelle, an
upward gaze palsy, distended scalp veins, a thin, shiny scalp and,
depending on the type of craniosynostosis, splaying of the sutures,
remain the most prominent clinical findings. In older children and
adults, the findings related to raised ICP can be more difficult to elicit.
On fundoscopic examination, papilledema, loss of spontaneous venous
pulsation or optic atrophy (depending on the duration of the raised
ICP) are helpful findings. Palsies of the third and sixth cranial nerves
and abnormalities of gaze (specifically Parinaud’s syndrome) are
consistent with severely raised ICP. Cushing’s response of hypertension,
bradycardia and abnormal respiration usually signal impending
herniation, requiring urgent treatment. In diagnosing raised ICP, good
history and proper examination cannot be highlighted enough.

17 2 2 Neuro-Ophthalmologic Findings in
Craniosynostosis
Visual complications related to craniosynostosis are common and
include optic neuropathy, especially papilledema or optic atrophy due
to raised ICP, strabismus, refractive errors, exposure keratopathy due to
exorbitism and amblyopia. These ophthalmological conditions have
been described more frequently in syndromic craniosynostosis [9].
Visual field deficits are also common, highlighting the value of

ophthalmological assessment and monitoring of visual function in the
diagnosis of raised ICP in craniosynostosis patients [10].

17 2 3 Radiological Markers
Imaging in children with raised ICP forms a cornerstone of decisionmaking. The spectrum of imaging modalities available ranges from Xrays to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
-rays: Skull X-rays have limited value in the modern imaging
armamentarium. The appreciation of the copper-beating’ of the skull
and erosion of the clinoid process are still valuable in detecting
chronically raised ICP [11].
Ultrasound: The usefulness of bedside imaging and the benefit of
being radiation-free, portable and easy-to-use, have made ultrasound
an attractive tool for confirming the diagnosis of craniosynostosis
and positional plagiocephaly, especially in the outpatient department
[12]. In addition, ultrasound can be used as a prenatal diagnostic
technique to detect cranial malformation during the third trimester
[13]. For experienced operators, ultrasound has even been suggested
as the first-line imaging tool where craniosynostosis is suspected,
especially for infants aged 8–12 months [14]. Transorbital imaging of
the ONSD and transcranial Doppler (TCD) have also made use of
ultrasound as a screening modality for raised ICP in craniosynostosis,
but these will be discussed in more detail later in the chapter.
CT scan: This imaging modality remains the most widely used for
diagnosing craniosynostosis and suspected cases of raised ICP. The
features on the CT scan which are suggestive of raised ICP include—
midline shift, enlarged ventricles, transependymal fluid shift,
presence of a space-occupying lesion/haematoma, effacement of the
basal cisterns, loss of grey/white differentiation, CSF volume in the
subarachnoid space (can be either enlarged or decreased, depending
on the condition) [15–17]. 3D-CT imaging and reconstruction have
emerged as valuable diagnostic and surgical planning tools [18, 19].
Despite the widespread use of CT scans in children with
craniosynostosis and raised ICP, the exposure of the developing brain
to repeated, high doses of radiation has been criticised and the
indications should be carefully considered [20]. CT angiography and
perfusion studies are valuable.

MRI: The role of MRI in brain imaging has become almost
indispensable. The exquisite structural and functional detail that it
provides, has become fundamental to our decision-making. The
features on standard T1- and T2-weighted images related to raised
ICP are somewhat similar to those assessed on CT scan. Vascular
imaging using MR angiography and venography (MRA and MRV) are
widely used for, but their value in the context of ICP assessment is
unclear.
The change in apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) in the frontal
white matter measured on diffusion MRI before and after surgery for
craniosynostosis indicates that it may reflect change in ICP and could
therefore provide a useful non-invasive technique for assessing ICP
[21].
Arterial spin labelling sequences provide an attractive non-invasive
imaging method for assessing cerebral blood flow (CBF). This noninvasive MR perfusion technique utilises arterial blood water as a
diffusible endogenous tracer to quantitatively assess absolute CBF.
While still considered a research tool, several advances and
descriptions of its utility in clinical conditions such as hypoxicischaemic encephalopathy, paediatric cerebrovascular disease, e.g.
moyamoya disease, paediatric brain tumours, infection, traumatic brain
injury and hydrocephalus [22]. The applicability of this technique in
certain craniosynostosis procedures to establish and perhaps quantify
perfusion pre- and post-surgery, certainly provides an interesting value
proposition.
A strong relationship between ICP and brain elastance has been
described using the MRI-derived elastance index. This is a technique
using cine phase-contrast pulse sequences to estimate blood and CSF
flow in the brain by calculating changes in intracranial volume based on
arterial inflow, venous outflow and CSF flow between the brain and
spine [23]. This technique demonstrated a good correlation with shunt
valve opening pressures in children with hydrocephalus [24].

17 3 Non-invasive Techniques for Assessing
ICP

Estimating ICP and especially detecting and diagnosing raised ICP
remains a challenge for the paediatric neurosurgeon. Invasive
techniques for measuring ICP and other haemodynamic and perfusion
parameters have role to play in traumatic brain injury patients,
especially in the neurocritical care unit. While an overall benefit of
invasive ICP monitoring has been described in a population of children
with craniosynostosis [25], several publications describe higher
complication rates in adults and children [26, 27], especially in TBI.
The appeal of reliable non-invasive methods of assessing ICP, which
are portable, easy-to-use, reproducible, cost-effective and radiationfree, is therefore quite clear.
The most relevant of these non-invasive methods in
craniosynostosis patients will be discussed here.

17 3 1 Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter (ONSD) Measurement
The relationship between CSF pressure in the intracranial space and
CSF pressure in the optic nerve sheath, as well as the association with
oedema of the optic disc, was described by Hayreh in the 1960s [28].
Since then several publications have supported the association of an
increase in the optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) and raised ICP, and
the measurement of the (ONSD) has been widely described as a useful
non-invasive technique for assessing ICP in a wide variety of conditions
[29]. The applicability of this technique in adults and children as well as
its relative reproducibility have made it an attractive option for noninvasive assessment [30]. Transorbital ultrasound measurement of the
ONSD is the most widely reported imaging technique in children, as it
provides a radiation-free, portable, cost-effective, easy-to-use and
reproducible alternative [31]. The issue of an optimal cut-off value for
detecting raised ICP remains contentious, though. Studies comparing
ONSD measurement to directly measure ICP in children suggest that
where the anterior fontanelle is closed, a measurement of above 5.5 cm
is consistent with an ICP above 15 mmHg, and an ONSD above 5.8 cm
suggests ICP above 20 mmHg [32, 33]. Other studies reporting on this
technique describe normative age-related values, 4.5 mm in patients
over 1 year of age and 4.0 mm in children less than 1 year old [34].
Limitations of this technique include inter-rater variability, hyperechoic
artefacts and variation in described ONSD cut-off values for detecting

raised ICP [35]. Despite these limitations, this technique demonstrates
promise as a non-invasive marker of raised ICP.

17 3 2 Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)
OCT is a non-invasive imaging technique using infrared light, that
provides high-resolution images of the retina and optic nerve in
seconds. It can be used to measure and segment the retinal nerve fibre
layers as well as the optic nerve head [36]. The use of OCT to measure
total retinal thickness has demonstrated favourable diagnostic accuracy
for the detection of papilledema in raised ICP when compared to
conventional fundoscopy, especially in lower-grade abnormalities [37].
A described limitation of this technique, especially in young children,
has been the table-mounted nature of the equipment, which required
that patients be taken to the ophthalmology department where the
equipment was located. A recent publication describing the use of OCT
in children with craniosynostosis undergoing surgery found the
technique to be a potentially sensitive marker of raised ICP [38]. As a
screening tool for children with craniosynostosis, the use of OCT may
not yet have enough evidence to support its role [39].
The feasibility of a portable OCT system for assessing raised ICP in
children with craniosynostosis was recently described and appears
promising [40, 41].

17 3 3 Pupillometry
Quantitative measurement of changes in pupil size in response to light
stimulus using infrared pupillometry. The pupil size decreases by
around 34% in response to a standard light stimulus. In patients with
ICP 20 mmHg, this response is reduced to 10% [42, 43]. The appeal of
this portable technique is its ease of use in children; however, the
clinical applicability and repeatability of this technique still requires
further investigation.

17 3 4 Intraocular Pressure (IOP)
The use of handheld tonometers require very little in the way formal
training and can easily be performed by junior members of the team.
This makes the technique appealing as a rapid screening tool for
detecting raised ICP. The described relationship between IOP and

increased ICP was demonstrated at quite high values of around
46.8 mmHg [44]. While the relationship between an increase in IOP and
raised ICP appears useful, the pooled diagnostic accuracy is not enough
to predict individual patient ICP [45].

17 3 5 Visual Evoked Potentials (VEP)
Disturbances of the visual pathways can be recorded from electrodes
placed over the occipital scalp [46]. Use of the N2 latency during flashevoked VEPs has demonstrated a good correlation with ICP in children
with hydrocephalus [47]. The inter-subject variability however, is a
limitation of this technique [48]. Pattern reversal VEPs are useful in
monitoring visual pathway function, as a proxy for raised ICP in
children with craniosynostosis [49]. Combining pattern reversal VEP
and fundoscopy to assess for papilledema appears to improve the
diagnostic accuracy for detecting raised ICP in children with
craniosynostosis [50].

17 3 6 Transcranial Doppler (TCD) Sonography
The use of TCD to assess blood flow through major intracranial vessels
is based on the Doppler effect’, which determines the difference
between incident and reflected waves to estimate the speed of blood
flow [51]. The technique has been described extensively to measure
intracranial CBF velocity. The most commonly described parameters
include the pulsatility index (PI), the resistance index (RI) and the peak
systolic and diastolic velocity. The PI, in particular, has demonstrated a
good correlation with ICP in adults [52]. In children however, this
relationship appears less consistent when compared to absolute ICP
values [53], but may serve as a good screening tool to identify patients
requiring invasive ICP monitoring [54]. For craniosynostosis, TCD may
be used to assess patients with decreased intracranial compliance due
to raised ICP and to monitor the effects of surgery [55].

17 3 7 Near Infrared Spectroscopy (NIRS)
This technique is useful for assessing regional cerebral blood volume
(CBV) and cerebral blood oxygen saturation (rSO2). Variation in the
absorption of infrared light allows the detection of changes in
oxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin concentration as a marker of

rSO2, which demonstrated a significant difference in TBI patients with
raised and normal ICP [56]. Limitations of this technique are that is
presently does not provide an estimation of absolute ICP, or changes in
ICP [57]. Detecting regional compromise of cortical metabolism and
CBF in craniosynostosis patients provides very useful information preand post-operatively [58].
There are several other techniques which have been described in
the quest for developing a reliable non-invasive method for assessing
ICP. These include tympanic membrane displacement, otoacoustic
emissions, venous ophthalmodynamometry and spectral analysis
electroencephalography (EEG). Combinations of techniques have also
been used to improve diagnostic accuracy [59].
Several of the techniques described in this chapter show promise in
terms of demonstrating a relationship with increasing ICP. Currently
however, there is no standalone non-invasive technique the provides
sufficient diagnostic accuracy to guide the diagnosis and treatment
regimen for raised ICP, especially in children with craniosynostosis. The
most attractive solutions appear to be methods aimed at combining
certain static and dynamic parameters to refine the overall userfriendliness and diagnostic accuracy [60].

18 Venous Anomalies in
Craniosynostosis
Tatiana Protzenko1 , Ant nio Bellas1 and José Francisco M. Salom o1
(1) Division of Pediatric Neurosurgery, Department of Pediatric
Surgery, National Institute of Health for Women, Children and
Adolescents Fernandes Figueira, Oswaldo Cruz Foundation (IFFFiocruz), Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

Keywords Venous anomalies – Hypoplastic posterior fossa –
Syndromic craniosynostosis – Venous outflow

18 1 Introduction
In the world of craniofacial surgery, patients with syndromic
craniosynostosis represent some of the most complex and challenging
conditions to manage. They are usually submitted to multiple surgical
procedures, including skull vault posterior expansion, fronto-orbital
advancement, monobloc advancement, decompression of the posterior
fossa, and/or treatment of hydrocephalus. Anomalous intracranial
venous anatomy is a well-described phenomenon in these patients and
interruption of important collateral drainage routes during surgery can
lead to massive hemorrhage and intractable intracranial hypertension,
and the study of the venous outflow is nowadays recognized as
essential in the preoperative planning [1–3]. However, there is still
controversy about the origin of collateral venous circulation and its
relation to the skull base morphology. The authors discuss here the
pathophysiology and the study findings in different syndromes.

18 2 Pathophysiology
Abnormal intracranial venous anatomy is described in patients with
syndromic craniosynostosis and is of significant importance in terms of
surgical morbidity [1, 4, 5]. Literature reports suggest that dural venous
sinus stenosis occurs due to changes in the skull base (jugular foramen
stenosis), which would lead to the development of compensatory
collateral circulation or persistence of fetal venous sinuses [6].
The jugular foramen is a gap between the occipital and the temporal
bone that contains the sigmoid sinus and the jugular bulb, the inferior
petrosal sinus, meningeal branches of a pharyngeal and an occipital
artery, the glossopharyngeal nerve, the vagus nerve and the accessory
nerve, the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (Jacobson’s
nerve), the auricular branch of the vagus nerve (Arnold’s nerve), and
finally the cochlear aqueduct [7]. Thus, it would not be difficult to
imagine that the stenosis of this foramen could lead to stenosis of the
drainage pathways. Asymmetries between the two jugular foramina
were observed in postmortem studies, with the right jugular foramen
being larger than the left in 68% of cases, the same size in 12% of cases,
and smaller in 20% of cases [8].
However, in patients with syndromic craniosynostosis, jugular
foramen stenosis is a reality and is related to the hypoplastic skull base.
In the 1970s, Hoffmann was the first to describe the posterior fossa as
small in patients with syndromic craniosynostosis, and Saldino in 1972
associated Chiari I malformation with Pfeiffer syndrome [9, 10]. Cinalli
et al. also demonstrated that the posterior fossa is small in FGFR2related craniosynostosis, and these authors associated this hypoplastic
posterior fossa with the early closure of lambdoid sutures and
synchondrosis of the skull base [11]. Martinez-Perez et al. proposed
through a case report of a patient with Crouzon syndrome and
acanthosis nigricans that bilateral atresia of the jugular foramen was
the cause of intracranial hypertension, venous hypertension, and
dilatation of the scalp veins [12]. Other authors [1, 13] have associated
venous alterations with the state of intracranial hypertension, thus
being considered a compensatory mechanism.
On the other hand, other authors described that evidence of venous
outflow obstruction may not be indicative of significant intracranial

venous hypertension, even in intriguing cases presenting venous
obstruction, hydrocephalus, and tonsillar herniation [14, 15]. This lack
of relationship between venous obstruction and intracranial
hypertension was also proposed by Cinalli et al. [16]. In an
angiographic study of patients with syndromic craniosynostosis, only
1/3 of them had unilateral or bilateral stenosis of the jugular foramen
and intracranial hypertension.
The results presented by Florisson et al. [2] agree with those found
by Cinalli. Although they found small jugular foramina in all patients
with syndromic craniosynostosis, the number of collaterals were not
different between groups with and without papilledema and are
therefore not considered related to intracranial hypertension.
Although most literature publications agree that the jugular
foramen is restricted in syndromic craniosynostosis, Coll et al. reported
that, in their population, the only patients with a truly narrow jugular
foramen were the Apert syndrome group [17]. Then, if collateral
circulation is associated with jugular foramen stenosis, it would be
obvious to admit that these patients would have the greatest number of
collaterals. However, a prospective series showed that, in Apert
syndrome, the venous anomalies are generally less exuberant than in
Pfeiffer and Crouzon patients [1]. This makes us wonder if the stenosis
of the jugular foramen is directly related to the venous anomalies or if
an intrinsic trouble could be associated.
A possible intrinsic theory is based on a primary vascular
abnormality resulting from a similar dysplastic process that occurs in
the bones of the skull. FGFR gene expression products have been
detected in cranial vascular endothelium—as well as present in
synostotic sutures—in patients with syndromic craniosynostosis by
immunohistochemical examination [18, 19]. Premature endothelial
proliferation may cause stenosis of these vessels. Tischfield et al. also
support this theory and describe that cerebral venous malformations
can result from loss of expression of the Twist 1 gene [20]. The
presence of collaterals in inborn patients found in a retrospective series
also imply that collateral development could be an intrinsic disorder
[2]. Therefore, the true origin of collateral venous circulation, whether
it is related to stenosis of the jugular foramen or whether intrinsic
mechanisms exist and when it plays a role in intracranial hypertension,

remains a mystery in the literature. Probably intracranial hypertension
has a multifactorial origin, and prospective studies based on molecular
analysis may clarify the true role of genetic mutations in these patients.
Regardless of the mechanism of abnormal venous outflow, studies
are increasingly focused on its study in preoperative planning, since the
rupture of this circulation can have fatal consequences.

18 3 How to Study: How Do I Do It
The study of venous outflow in patients with complex craniosynostosis
has been previously documented using cerebral arteriography,
venography, computed tomography (CT)-venography, and magnetic
resonance (MR)-venography [1–3, 13, 14, 21, 22]. Although cerebral
arteriography is considered “gold standard,” it is a very invasive exam,
being reserved for special cases. MR venography has the advantage of
being a noninvasive method but with problems with saturation effects,
especially in newborns and young children [14]. CT venography, despite
the inconvenience of exposure to irradiation, is able to show cerebral
veins or smaller venous sinuses with low flow and its relationship to
the skull bones and skull base foramina and, for this reason, it has been
used by many authors [1–3].
From our ongoing prospective study, we agree with the use of CT
venography to study the venous outflow in patients with syndromic
craniosynostosis. CT venography allows us to visualize the true
relationship between collateral veins and bone foramina, allowing safer
surgical planning. Figure 18.1 shows the outstanding difference
between MR venography and CT venography in the same patient.

Fig. 18.1 Difference between MR venography (left) and CT venography (right) in the same
patient. The occipital transosseous veinous drainage (red arrow) is not explicit in MR
venography

The available studies consider the following collateral veins, as
proposed by Jeevan et al. [3]: parietal emissary vein from the superior
sagittal sinus, occipital emissary vein from the transverse sinus or
torcula, mastoid emissary veins from the transverse or sigmoid sinus,
condylar emissary vein from sigmoid sinus or jugular sinus to the deep
cervical vein, occipital sinus from the margin of the falx cerebelli, the
marginal sinus at the rim of the foramen magnum, and venous

collaterals from the ophthalmic vein. The intracranial sinuses are also
studied: sagittal, transverse, sigmoid, jugular bulb complex, and straight
sinus. In addition, the inferior sagittal sinus, pericallosal vein, and
pterygoid sinus plexus were studied by Florisson et al. [2]. Figure 18.2
shows the different collateral circulation that can be found.

Fig. 18.2 Example case of abnormal venous outflow. CT venography reconstruction with
enlarged condylar emissary vein (yellow arrow), occipital transosseous emissary vein (red
arrow), and parietal transosseous emissary vein (blue arrow)

18 4 Presentation in Different Syndromes
Few papers compare collateral circulation among the different
syndromes presented. Rollins et al. describe that functional stenosis of
the jugular foramen occurs in 100% of patients with Pfeiffer syndrome,
62% in Crouzon syndrome, 50% in Apert syndrome, and 83% in
complex craniosynostosis [14]. Today, these data make us wonder if
these patients with complex craniosynostosis really did not have any
associated syndrome, since molecular studies modified the
identification of mutations not previously found. This interpretation
may also extend to other case reports on complex nonsyndromic
craniosynostosis [15, 22]. Florisson et al. reported that collateral
venous outflow is more frequent in Apert syndrome, followed by

Crouzon-Pfeiffer syndrome and Saerthre-Chotzen syndrome, and the
most important route of drainage was the condylar emissary vein [2].
On the other hand, Copeland et al. described that emissaries were
found in 100% of patients with Pfeiffer syndrome, 74% in Crouzon,
36% in Apert, 33% in Saerthre-Chotzen, and 0% in Muenke. Occipital
and mastoid emissaries were most common [1].
In our experience, patients with Crouzon and Pfeiffer syndromes
have the highest number of collaterals, followed by Apert syndrome
(Fig. 18.3). Patients with Muenke and Saerthre-Chotzen syndromes
have a more benign course. Interestingly, many patients have a large
jugular foramen and still important collateral circulation, making us
agree with the relationship between venous anomalies and intrinsic
problems of the syndrome.

Fig. 18.3 Differences in CT-venogram reconstruction between Crouzon, Pfeiffer, Apert
syndromes and nonsyndromic brachycephaly

18 5 Venous Outflow in Clinical Practice
The importance of the venous study in children with syndromic
craniosynostosis was described in a remarkable case in the literature,
in which a transosseous circulation was, in fact, the main route of
cranial venous outflow [5]. Other authors described that the venous

analysis allowed the modification of the surgical approach or even the
decision of conservative treatment to avoid disastrous consequences [1,
3, 21, 23]. In reality, it is not only the presence of anomalous circulation
that seems to prevent surgery but whether this circulation is the main
route of venous outflow to determine a surgical decision.
The literature is clear about the use of posterior vault expansion to
control intracranial hypertension and correction of Chiari 1
malformation, as a first approach to the syndromic patient. In Fig. 18.4,
the authors present a case of a patient with Pfeiffer syndrome and
Chiari 1 malformation, whose approach performed consisted of
posterior vault expansion using springs. The presence of collateral
circulation was previously studied in order to avoid large drainage
veins, which could lead to massive hemorrhage, and a craniotomy was
defined in the supratorcular region, avoiding collateral circulation in
the mastoid and suboccipital region. Note the important increase in the
volume of the posterior fossa, resolution of the Chiari 1, without the
need to approach the infratentorial skull, being a simpler surgery, with
little blood loss and, undoubtedly, safer.

Fig. 18.4 Venous analysis of Pfeiffer syndrome patient and surgical approach. Important
collateral circulation is shown on a 3D CT venogram (mastoid emissary vein, condylar vein, and
occipital circulation). A posterior vault expansion was performed with 8N springs. Pre- and
post-op CT scans show tonsillar herniation improvement with the increase in posterior fossa
volume

18 6 Should We Study All Complex Types of
Craniosynostosis?
Whether genetic mutation plays a role or not in the formation of
collateral circulation has already been discussed in the scope of this
chapter. According to the literature, important studies show that the
jugular foramen is reduced in complex and syndromic craniosynostosis,
and thus, both can develop collateral circulation [1, 2, 6, 14, 15]. Some
cases reported in the literature of unclassified complex
craniosynostosis demonstrate an exuberant collateral circulation [22,
23]. In such cases, it is possible that a mutation not previously
identified is associated. Regardless, all multisutural craniosynostosis
has the risk of presenting changes in the skull base and, consequently,
changes in venous outflow. Copeland et al. claim that, in small sample
groups of syndromes, it is not possible to determine the risk of venous
anomalies, like in Saerthre-Chotzen and Muenke syndrome [1]. Thus,
the study of all syndromic patients is still recommended. We can extend
this statement to all patients with suspected syndromes. Further
molecular investigation will probably help us to solve this question and
to improve our current protocols.
