19 Cerebellar Tonsils Herniation and
Syringomyelia in Craniosynostoses
Luca Massimi1, 2
(1) Pediatric Neurosurgery, Fondazione Policlinico Universitario A.
Gemelli IRCCS, Rome, Italy
(2) Universit Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Rome, Italy

Luca Massimi
Email: luca.massimi@policlinicogemelli.it
Keywords Cerebellar tonsils – Chiari I malformation –
Craniosynostosis – Posterior cranial fossa – Syringomyelia –
Hydrocephalus

19 1 Introduction
The hypoplasia of the posterior cranial fossa (PCF) is an issue often
addressed by embryologists and physicians when dealing with children
with craniosynostosis. Actually, the physiopathological changes
occurring in this subset of patients, especially in case of syndromic
synostoses, are investigated with the goal to explain and prevent not
only the signs/symptoms related to the craniosynostosis but also the
possible consequences of these changes, as the secondary chronic
tonsillar descent and the syringomyelia. Moreover, the continuously
increasing number of tonsillar caudal ectopia and/or syringomyelia
diagnoses among the pediatric population gives reason for the great
attention payed by the Scientific Community to these entities and to
their proper management. Therefore, to rule out the presence of a
craniosynostosis has become a mandatory step for the correct

management of a child with hindbrain herniation and syringomyelia as
well as the occurrence of the latter conditions is constantly taken into
account for the appropriate treatment of craniosynostosis.
This chapter is focused on the pathophysiological and clinical
relationship between craniosynostoses and chronic tonsils
herniation/syringomyelia and on their management.

19 2 Pathophysiology
19 2 1 Cerebellar Tonsils Herniation (CTH)
Phylogenetically, human PCF would have been originated from an
increase of the supratentorial brain volume combined with the
acquisition of the bipedal stance that has led to a progressive weight
redistribution. The prominence of the human tentorium would have
played a crucial role in this redistribution, bearing the cerebral weight
and distributing the resulting load to the skull. Therefore, the
downward rotation of the fetal tentorium would be the intracranial
response to a disproportion between the human cerebrum and
cerebellum [1]. On the other hand, the bony response would be
represented by the two phases of PCF growth. The first step occurs
during the early childhood, when PCF grows in length mainly alongside
the intra-occipital, petro-occipital, and spheno-occipital synchondrosis,
while the second step takes place during the puberty, when PCF
enlarges mainly following the spheno-occipital growth [2]. These two
different patterns of growth are favored by the initial absence of
ossification of the petro-occipital, the occipitomastoid, and the sphenooccipital synchondroses. The time for PCF to grow is shorter and faster
in girls compared with boys [3]. In spite of that, boys show a bigger PCF
at the end of the development because of the smaller PCF at birth in
girls [4].
Some hypotheses have been formulated so far to explain the genesis
of CTH in craniosynostosis, starting from the evidence of the increased
rate of CTH in children with an early fusion of the posterior sutures.
The most accepted theory is based on the cephalo-cranial
disproportion (between a normal or enlarged neural tissue and a
narrowed PCF) induced by the progressing, premature fusion of the
lambdoid arch sutures [5]. It is an acquired disorder, which is not

present at birth and which develops in the first months of life (namely,
between the third and the sixth month), as soon as the lambdoid
sutures start closing. The venous engorgement, resulting from the
occlusion of the jugular foramina, and the associated hydrocephalus,
which are common in syndromic craniosynostoses, can further increase
such a cranio-cerebral disproportion because of the subsequent brain
turgor. Moreover, in this subset of patients, the brain turgor is
exacerbated by the chronic CO2 retention due to the upper airway’s
obstruction [6]. The cranio-cerebral disproportion has been proposed
by Cinalli and coworkers as the main causal factor for the tonsillar
descent [2]. This hypothesis is supported by the progressive
appearance of CTH/syringomyelia in craniosynostosis depending on
the time of suture closure: the earlier the premature suture fusion, the
higher the risk of CTH. As known, children affected by early closure of
the lambdoid arch (e.g., Crouzon patients) are more prone to develop
(early) CTH than those where these sutures close later (e.g. Apert
patients) (Figs. 19.1 and 19.2). The disappearance of hindbrain
herniation following cranial vault expansion is another robust
argument in favor of this theory [7].

Fig. 19.1 Seven-month-old girl with Crouzon syndrome: (a, b) CT scan showing the early and
severe pansynostosis with fingerprintings and sellar deformation of the cranial vault; (c, d) The
MRI shows the severe hypoplasia of PCF with early CTH (c) and ventriculomegaly (d). The
anteroposterior diameter of the foramen magnum is minimally reduced (c, asterisk), while the
latero-lateral is reduced (d, asterisk)

Fig. 19.2 Eight-month-old boy with Apert syndrome: (a, b) 3D CT scan showing acrocephaly
and brachicephaly with partial fusion of the coronal and lambdoid sutures, fingerprintings and
compensatory bilaterale mastoid bossing. (c–e) The MRI shows severe PCF hypoplasia,
brachicephaly, mild ventriculomegaly but absence of CTH. The missing hindbrain herniation,
compared with the Crouzon syndrome in Fig. 19.1, could depend on the incomplete closure of
lambdoid sutures, the compensatory mastoid bossing and the large cisterna magna

Coll and colleagues enlarged the spectrum of etiologic factors by
considering also the CSF in the occurrence of disproportion. The
authors postulated that the presence of a small PCF would result in a
mechanical increase in resistance to the CSF flow, which is complicated
by the venous hypertension determined by the jugular foramina
stenosis and by the foramen magnum stenosis with subsequent
subarachnoid CSF blockage [3, 8]. This theory would explain also the
occurrence of hydrocephalus in children with craniosynostosis and
CTH. Accordingly, the following timeline should be considered: (a)
progressive fusion of the lambdoid suture with secondary skull base
alteration (the age below 2 years is critical because of the
physiologically enlarged cerebellum compared with the forebrain); (b)
stenosis of the jugular foramina; (c) growth of hypoplasic PCF; (d)
cerebellar herniation; (e) venous hypertension; (f) crowding of the
posterior fossa; and (g) CSF hydrodynamics alteration. Some basic and
clinical genetic observations allow us to better understand the
differences that can be found among syndromic children. For example,
FGFR2 mutations involving exons 3a and 3c are more frequently
encountered in craniosynostotic patients developing CIM [2, 4, 9].
Moreover, in spite of the shared FGFR2 involvement, Apert patients
tend to have an enlarged basiocciput, while the Crouzon ones tend to
show a narrowed one (and expanded supero-inferiorly rather than
antero-posteriorly) with subsequent normal volume PCF in Apert
syndrome and hypoplasic PCF in Crouzon syndrome [2, 10].

19 2 2 Radiological Findings

To further understand the PCF changes leading to CTH and their clinical
implications, several bidimensional parameters have been investigated
and their relationships have been studied. The main measures are
represented by (1) PCF cephalic index: ratio between skull width
(measured between the orifices of the right and left internal auditory
canals) and skull length (measured from the posterior edge of the
clivus to the inner table of the occiput); (2) tentorial angle: angle
between the tentorium and a line running from the internal occipital
protuberance to the tuberculum sellae; (3) occipital angle: angle
between the tentorium and a line running from internal occipital
protuberance to opisthion. According to some studies, CTH is more like
to occur in syndromic and bicoronal synostoses than in single suture
synostoses because of the brachycephalic skull and the vertical
tentorium (high PCF cephalic index and large tentorial and occipital
angle) [2, 11, 12]. In spite of the small PCF, in sagittal synostosis, the
risk of CTH is inferior compared with the previous conditions because
of the flat tentorium. Overall, craniosynostostic children with CTH have
been found to show a significantly shorter anteroposterior PCF length
than those without CTH (33.4 mm versus 36.7 mm) [13]. The PCF
cross-sectional area too is significantly reduced in CTH children (654.1
versus 764.9 mm2). As a result, the foramen magnum cross-sectional
area in CTH children is about 88% of no-CTH children.
Additional information comes from the volumetric analysis of PCF.
The study of Calandrelli et al. on children (both syndromic and nonsyndromic) with lambdoid arch synostosis, showed an involvement of
the lambdoid sutures alone (major sutures) in 40% of cases, of the
minor sutures alone (occipito-mastoid and occipito-petrosal sutures) in
another 40% of cases, and of both major and minor sutures in the
remaining 20% of cases [14]. The comparison with healthy agematched controls revealed normal measurements (included PCF
volume, PCF brain volume, PCF volume/PCF brain volume ratio,
cerebellum and CSF volume) except for the exocciput lengths and the
anteroposterior diameter of the foramen magnum (significantly
reduced) and the tentorial angle (significantly increased) in case of
major sutures involvement. On the other hand, in case of minor sutures
involvement, a significant increase of the tentorial angle and a
significant decrease of meatus-opisthion lengths, diameters of the

foramen magnum (both anteroposterior and latero-lateral) and jugular
foramina area were found (once again, the volumetry as normal). These
findings suggest that as follows: (1) In case of major sutures synostosis
of the lambdoid arch, the PCF hypoplasia depends on a reduced
exocciput length; therefore, the cerebellum is forced to growth both
rostrally and caudally and, due to a normal anteroposterior diameter of
the foramen magnum, early CTH occurs (80% of children with this
condition harbored CTH) (Fig. 19.1). These data would explain also the
higher incidence of CTH in isolated major suture involvement (e.g.
asymmetrical, ipsilateral tonsillar herniation in lambdoid synostosis)
than in minor one, even though both conditions are characterized by
PCF hypoplasia; (2) In case of closure of minor lambdoid arch sutures,
PCF is hypoplasic because of the reduced length of the two hemi-fossae;
therefore, the cerebellum is allowed to growth mainly rostrally. Such a
rostral growth of the cerebellum together with a complete reduction of
the area of the foramen magnum gives reason for the absence of CTH in
this subset of patients (CTH may occur later on, when the tentorium
reaches its maximum slope). The combination between skull base
anomalies and size of the foramen magnum has been recently
confirmed to be crucial for the final position of the cerebellar tonsils in
syndromic subjects, especially in Crouzon syndrome (largest foramen
magnum) [15].
A mismatch between the reduced compliance of the skull base and
the compensatory increase of the supratentorial cranial volume has
been identified as the possible cause of CTH in children with severe
sagittal synostosis [16]. Accordingly, anterior, middle and posterior
cranial fossae are symmetric as well as the anterior and middle length
of the skull base are increased in all scaphocephalic children. Similarly,
the lengths of the posterior fossae are comparable in all children,
independently form the severity of their sagittal synostosis (assessed
by cephalic index). Nevertheless, the compensatory enlargement of the
anterior fossae is relevant only in case of mild or moderate sagittal
synostosis. On these grounds, it has been postulated that a spontaneous
calvarial remodeling drives the anterior and middle skull base
enlargement probably because the central section of the sagittal suture
is the first to fuse. Subsequently, in case of the severe scaphocephaly,
the minor elongation of the skull base would result from an earlier

fusion of the sagittal suture. Under a volumetric point of view, this
corresponds to a major compensatory intracranial volume in mild
scaphocephalic forms compared with the severe ones. Actually, in spite
of the normal overall PCF volume found in all scaphocephalic children,
patients with moderate and severe groups showed a significant
reduction of PCF volume/PCF brain volume ration and infratentorial
CSF volume, thus revealing a “brain constriction” that leads to the
hindbrain herniation in the more severe cases of sagittal synostosis.
The volumetric analysis also explains some apparently paradoxical
findings, as the more frequently occurrence of CTH in some bicoronal
synostosis than some bi-lambdoid ones. In the study provided by Rijken
and coworkers, for example, children with Muenke syndrome showed
both a bigger cerebellar (CV) and PCF volume (PFV) than those with
Apert syndrome (in whom only PCF volume was larger than normal)
[17]. For these reasons (together with the higher frequency of mega
cisterna magna in Apert syndrome), Apert children show a significantly
lower CV/PFV ratio and, therefore, a lower risk of CTH. The author
proposed the CV/PFV ratio as a reliable indicator of PCF crowding
because, even in case of significant PCF hypoplasia, CTH does not occur
if also the cerebellum is hypoplasic.
It is worth noting that the volumetric analyses usually point out a
normal volume of PCF in children with craniosynostosis and CTH.
Therefore, CTH would result from the PCF overcrowding rather than
PCF hypoplasia. A support to this theory comes from a study on the
whole exome sequencing of 232 CIM families (668 patients), where
CHD3 and CHD8 genes (chromodomain genes) were hypothesized to
contribute to CTH genesis [18]. These genes are demonstrated to cause
macrocephaly in zebrafishes and macrocephaly was predominant in the
families enrolled for this study. Thus, one could conclude that CTH is
the result of an excessive brain growth rather than a too small PCF.
Moreover, also the presence of venous obstruction can help in justifying
the occurrence of CTH and the differences among the various
craniosynostoses and syndromes. Actually, the stenosis of the jugular
foramina is an additional factor causing the increased risk of CTH in
syndromic subjects (compared with non-syndromic ones) as well as the
increased risk of CTH in Crouzon and Pfeiffer patients (higher incidence

of jugular stenosis and more extensive venous collaterals) compared
with Apert and Saethre-Chotzen ones [19, 20].

19 2 3 Altered CSF Dynamics
The aforementioned observations provide the basis to better
understand the changes in the CSF dynamics possibly leading to
hydrocephalus and syringomyelia, two diseases often associated with
craniosynostosis-related CTH. The physiopathology of these two
conditions is complex and not completely understood yet. The current
theories, in particular, cannot explain why, starting from a similar
anatomical picture, only some subjects develop hydrocephalus and/or
syringomyelia.
Hydrocephalus is found in about 12–15% of syndromic
craniosynostosis and up to 90% of hydrocephalic children with
syndromic synostosis are affected by CTH too (Fig. 19.3) [21]. The
impaired CSF circulation causing hydrocephalus in syndromic
synostoses results from a vitious circle including all factors involved in
the genesis of CTH: PCF hypoplasia, basilar invagination, foramen
magnum overcrowding, compression of the IV ventricle, jugular
foramina stenosis [2, 22]. Such a multifactorial etiology origins from the
impairment of CSF circulation at level of the fourth ventricle (direct
compression due to PCF overcrowding because of the cephalo-cranial
disproportion and subsequent obstruction of the fourth ventricle
outlets) and at level of the foramen magnum (limited CSF flow due to
the overcrowding of the foramen magnum because of CTH). The raised
ICP resulting from the impaired CSF circulation starts the vitious circle
by worsening the foramen magnum overcrowding. At the same time,
the stenosis of the jugular foramina enhances the vitious circle through
the venous engorgement, which produces cerebellar edema (thus
worsening the PCF overcrowding), raised intracranial pressure (by
increasing the upward venous hypertension) and decreased CSF readsorption. When these mechanisms are activated, hydrocephalus
occurs. The stenosis of the jugular foramina alone can induce
hydrocephalus, even in case of normal PCF.

Fig. 19.3 MRI showing the typical features of supratentorial hydrocephalus in Crouzon
syndrome (1 year-old boy). Note the enlargement of the third (a) and lateral ventricles (b) and
the PCF hypoplasia with CTH (c). The posterior recess of the third ventricle is enlarged, the
aqueduct is patent, and the CSF spaces of PCF are completely effaced (d): these findings suggest
a CSF obstruction at level of IV ventricle/foramen magnum

The prevented CSF outflow from the cranial compartment at level of
an overcrowded foramen magnum would be responsible for the
occurrence of syringomyelia. More in details, the foramen magnum
overcrowding would generate an intra-extracranial CSF pressure
gradient pulsating with the cardiac cycle. The resulting abnormal
pressure waves would force the CSF to penetrate into the perivascular
spaces of the spinal cord generating the syringomyelia [23],
independently from the severity of the overcrowding and the tonsillar
ectopia [24, 25]. In this context, the platybasia could play a role in
favoring the syringomyelia and in differentiating CTH subjects with and
without syringomyelia. Yan and coworkers hypothesized that the CSF
turbulences and flow alterations occurring in the anterior aspect of the
foramen magnum would be responsible for the syringomyelia
formation [26]. Indeed, patients with more pronounced platybasia
show a reduced pre-pontine and pre-bulbar cisternal space with
consequent local turbulences in the anterior PCF compartment. The
authors did not find differences in their 67 CTH patients as far as the
PCF parameters were concerned (clival length, posterior fossa length
and height, supraocciput length) apart from the clival gradient defining
the platybasia (anterior angle between the clivus and McRae’s line).
Interestingly, the clival gradient of CTH patients without syringomyelia
was similar to normal controls. The indirect CSF flow measurement by
MRI cine sequences confirmed that the most relevant alterations of CSF
flow occur in the anterior portion of the foramen magnum of CTH
patients, in particular, some unilateral or bilateral small regions of the
anterior quadrants [23]. The faster the CSF velocity flow in these

regions, the higher the risk of syringomyelia. The decrease of CSF
velocity flow in these regions after surgery accounts for the
syringomyelia reduction or disappearance.

19 3 Peculiar Clinical Aspects
19 3 1 Non-syndromic Craniosynostosis
The aforementioned pathophysiological studies are useful to explain
the occurrence of CTH in some types of not syndromic synostosis. As
expected, the highest incidence is found in multi-sutural synostosis like
Mercedes syndrome (60%) (Fig. 19.4) and oxycephaly (80–100%) [27,
28]. Among single suture synostosis, lambdoid craniosynostosis is the
most involved one (60% of the affected children present CTH) followed
by sagittal craniosynostosis (3–5%) [29–31]. Unicoronal
craniosynostosis shows a higher incidence of CTH than sagittal
synostosis in some series (6%) [31]. This is because of the secondary
anterior attraction and shortening of one posterior hemi-fossa in this
apparently less predisposing synostosis. However, a reason for the
relatively low incidence of CTH in sagittal synostosis could be
represented by the missed diagnosis of this craniosynostosis among
CTH patients (Fig. 19.5). For example, Valentini et al. reported on 48
scaphocephalic children who received the diagnosis of CTH (mean age:
9 years) before the diagnosis of their previously unrecognized
synostosis (mean age: 10.5 years) [32]. Interestingly, 21 children were
completely asymptomatic (43%; mean tonsillar descent: 5–6 mm) and
did not receive any treatment, while only 3 out of the remaining 27
subjects showed symptoms related to the craniosynostosis and were
managed by cranial vault remodeling (24 children received surgery for
CTH/syringomyelia; mean tonsillar descent: 12 mm). A further,
possible cause of low incidence of CTH in non-syndromic
craniosynostosis at diagnosis is the still incomplete expression of the
clinical picture. Indeed, according to the largest series available in the
literature about this topic (377 scaphocephalic children), the incidence
of CTH was 1% among children with early diagnosis (2/161) versus
9.2% among those with delayed diagnosis (20/216) [33]. As expected,
the incidence was statistically significantly higher also in operated on
patients (7%) compared with not operated on children (4.5%). Another

typical example of delayed expression is the late appearance of CTH due
to the delayed occurrence of a pansynostosis in children initially
treated for a single suture synostosis and without genetic alterations
[34]. The occurrence of CTH and syringomyelia in patients with delayed
diagnosis of craniosynostosis has been reported even in adults [35].

Fig. 19.4 Eight-month-old girl with Mercedes syndrome: (a, b) 3D CT scan showing the early
sagittal and bi-lambdoid fusion with PCF indentation. The MRI demonstrates the bilateral CTH
(c) with PCF hypoplasia (d) and dorsal syringomyelia (e)

Fig. 19.5 Radiological picture of a 7-year-old boy with delayed diagnosis of sagittal synostosis.
3D CT scan shows the closure of the sagittal synostosis and a spontaneous bi-parietal

expansion (a). MRI demonstrates a mild ventriculomegaly (b), moderate PCF hypoplasia with
CTH (c) and a focal hydromyelic spot in the upper cervical spinal cord (d). The child, who
presents symptoms of Chiari I without signs of raised ICP, is candidate to PCF decompression
alone

CTH in non-syndromic subjects meanly varies from 5 to 12 mm [30]
(Valentini et al. 2019). As far as the laterality of the tonsillar herniation
is concerned, an asymmetry between the two sides is usually observed
in the clinical practice, with a predominance to the synostotic suture
side in asymmetric synostoses [28].
With regards to the primary clinical picture, it is hard to
demonstrate symptoms of CTH/syringomyelia in children with single
suture synostosis. Actually, if treated for the craniosynostosis within
the standard rage of time (3–8 months), most of the patients tend to be
asymptomatic both at the diagnosis (short clinical history) and at
follow-up (CTH/syringomyelia are likely to have disappeared or
improved). Moreover, if treated at the time of a delayed diagnosis of
craniosynostosis, some symptoms can be confused with those caused
by the synostosis (namely, headaches). Finally, most case of single
suture synostosis are likely to present just a tonsils descent rather than
a symptomatic Chiari I malformation. In the aforementioned series
provided by Davies and coworkers, 27% of children with CTH in
sagittal synostosis (6 out of 22) required treatment for their Chiari
malformation [33]. In the series provided by Chivoret et al. on bilambdoid-sagittal synostosis, only 2 out of 19 subjects presented a
symptomatic CTH [27]. Anyway, based on the clinical experiences
reported in the literature, the most common signs or symptoms
attributable to CTH/syringomyelia are headache, scoliosis, neck pain,
gait disorders, dizziness, hydrocephalus, sleep apneas, and dysesthesias
in the hands and feet [36–38] (Valentini et al. 2019).

19 3 2 Syndromic Craniosynostosis
The rate of CTH in syndromic subjects is as high as 2–10% in Apert
syndrome, 50% in Pfeiffer syndrome, 70–75% in Crouzon syndrome
and 100% in cloverleaf skull, Saethre-Chotzen syndrome being the less
affected one ( 2%) thanks to the enlarged cisterna magna [39, 40] (Fig.
19.6). Overall, the incidence of CTH in syndromic synostosis is around
14% (versus 1% in the general population) [41]. The reasons for such
an incidence and such differences have been discussed in Sect. 19.2.

Here, it is important to remind that CTH and the possibly associated
syringomyelia are intrinsic part of the complex clinical picture of these
patients and have to be considered for their appropriate management.
Indeed, CTH is one of the predominant clinical signs, together with
facial dysmorphism, speech and language delay, learning difficulties,
and behavioral problems even in recently detected syndromes, like the
ERF-related craniosynostosis [42]. This entity arises from mutations in
the ERF gene, which codes for ETS2 repressor factor. It is characterized
by a sagittal and bi-lambdoid sutural pattern with late expression
(mean age: 42 months), a Crouzon-like facial dysmorphology and
frequent speech delay. CTH is the rule when the complete multisutural
pattern is expressed. Another typical association between
craniosynostosis and CTH can be found in patients with X-linked
hypophosphatemic rickets. Accordingly, about 60% of these patients
show a complete or partial sagittal synostosis and one-fourth of them
present CTH [43].

Fig. 19.6 Six-month-old boy with Saethre-Chotzen syndrome. 3D CT scan shows the premature
bicoronal fusion with compensatory enlargement of anterior fontanel and sagittal suture (a, b).
In spite of the subsequent brachicephaly, visible on MRI (c), CTH does not occur thanks to the
large cisterna magna (d), which is a distinctive characteristic of this syndrome

As far as the clinical symptoms are concerned, the occurrence of
neurological deficits seems to correlate with the presence of the
synostosis rather with CTH/syringomyelia. This is mainly because of
two reasons: (1) the diagnosis of the synostosis is generally obtained
before the occurrence or the diagnosis of CTH, thus preventing the
appearance of CTH symptoms thanks to the management of the
synostosis in many cases (of course, CTH can persist even after the
surgical treatment of the synostosis and can become symptomatic later
on). The diagnosis of CTH before the syndromic synostosis has been

exceptionally reported [44]; (2) The facio-cranial dysmorphism is
basically more symptomatic at diagnosis than CTH (ocular proptosis,
obstructive apnea syndrome, psychomotor delay, and so on). In the
historical series by the Necker Hospital in Paris, indeed, only 6 out of 44
Crouzon patients and none out of 51 Apert patients showed CTHrelated neurological symptoms [45]. In a recent study on 63 children
with syndromic synostosis specifically addressing this topic, Doerga et
al. did not find any difference between patients with and those without
CTH/syringomyelia as far as the neurological symptoms were
concerned [46]. Twenty out of 63 patients showed CTH and/or
syringomyelia (32%), with a typical distribution: 16/34 with Crouzon
syndrome, 2/11 with Muenke syndrome, 2/12 with Apert syndrome,
and no cases out of 7 with Saethre-Chotzen syndrome. The neurological
deficits (cerebellum: motor delay and coordination deficits; cranial
nerve: nystagmus, pharyngeal asymmetry, and dysphagia; sensorymotor pathways: pyramidal syndrome, sensory dysfunction, and motor
dysfunction) were present in 73% of cases, but there was no
relationship between neurological picture and CTH/syringomyelia in
any combinations matching the types of symptoms and CTH and/or
syringomyelia. Only 3 out of 23 children undergoing surgery (all with
Crouzon syndrome and presenting severe pyramidal syndrome and gait
problems) harbored CTH and/or syringomyelia.
Also in syndromic subjects, CTH/syringomyelia typically cause
headache, neck pain, ataxia, muscle weakness, altered sensation
(paresthesia and dysesthesia), dysphagia, hydrocephalus, scoliosis, and
obstructive apneas. The problem of central sleep apneas could be
underestimated because of the predominant occurrence of obstructive
sleep apneas. In their recent study on 89 syndromic children
undergoing polysomnography and MRI, den Ottelander et al. did not
find a significant rate of cervical cord compression by the odontoid
process (compared with controls), but they detected an increased rate
of compression at level of the foramen magnum in Crouzon children
[47]. Such compressions as well as the age of the patients did not
correlate with the obstructive apneas, while the age correlated with the
central apneas. The authors concluded that the prevalence of central
sleep apneas is low in this subset of patients (compared with
obstructive apneas), and it is not associated with cervical spinal cord

compression, but polysomnography is indicated in any case as
important part of the clinical work-up. Central apneas usually improve
significantly after foramen magnum decompression [48].

19 4 Preoperative Radiological Screening
The rationale for a radiological assessment in syndromic synostosis is
quite obvious. Neuroimaging is actually required to define timing and
modality of surgery and to define the optimal follow-up. Moreover, it is
necessary to detect possible anomalies characterizing the clinical
phenotype, such as extracranial (midface retrusion, high-arched palate
or cleft lip and palate, widely spaced eyes, ptosis, proptosis ) or body
anomalies (vertebral fusion, ankylosis, syndactyly, polydactyly, and
heart malformation). However, a crucial reason to perform 3D CT scan
of the skull, angio-MRI of the brain and MRI of the spinal cord in these
subjects is to rule out associated diseases such as hydrocephalus (40–
70% of cases), venous anomalies, callosum hypoplasia, syringomyelia,
and CTH, the latter being the most common one (70–75%) [49].
The matter is more complicated in non-syndromic children with
single suture craniosynostosis. Actually, some authors question the
need for a neuroimaging screening in this subset of patients. Engel et al.
emphasized that only one asymptomatic child with lambdoid
synostosis out of 89 of their patients with isolated synostosis harbored
CTH (1.1%), thus suggesting the avoidance of routine brain MRI in
these patients unless symptomatic [50]. In spite of the limitation of this
study (only 89 out of 215 children composing the entire series were
investigated by MRI), this position could be acceptable when dealing
with low-risk patients, as those with metopic or sagittal synostosis.
However, in spite of the same low rate of CTH (1.2%) in their 80
patients with non-syndromic craniosynostosis, Magge and coworkers
found other incidental findings (prominent extra-axial cerebrospinal
fluid, ventriculomegaly, choroid fissure cyst, cavum septum pellucidum)
in more than 50% of cases, 6.25% of them requiring an additional
management just because of these findings [51]. The authors
recommended the use of preoperative radiological screening. In their
series of 121 non-syndromic children (most of them were
scaphocephalic), all investigated by MRI, Hukki et al. found brain

anomalies in 18% of cases [52]. The rate of CTH was 9%. These figures
suggest, once again, that a preoperative imaging is useful also in single
suture synostoses. On these grounds, the main problem would not
concern the utility of preoperative neuroimaging but rather the use of
preoperative MRI, which is burdened by the risk of anesthesia in young
children. In the author’s center, all non-syndromic children are
screened by low-dose CT scan (according to pediatric protocols) and, if
possible, by cerebral ultrasounds and doppler: only those with brain
anomalies undergo preoperative (angio) MRI.
Instead, in case of lambdoid synostosis, the use of MRI has been
demonstrated to be mandatory because of the high incidence of CTH
(45–60% in single suture synostosis, 71% in complex synostosis) and
PCF venous anomalies (36%), the possible occurrence of syringomyelia
(4.5%), and the need to plan an appropriate management (e.g.,
simultaneous cranial vault remodeling and posterior fossa
decompression) [29, 53]. Moreover, some synostoses require a
radiological assessment by definition. This is the case, for example, of
the craniosynostosis of the coronal arch, where CT scan is used to rule
out the involvement of minor sutures (spheno-squamous and sphenopetrosal sutures) or to confirm the differential diagnosis (e.g., coronal
suture synostosis versus fronto-sphenoidal synostosis), to correctly
plan the surgical operation and to formulate a reliable prognosis based
on the deformation of the skull base [54–56]. In these instances, CT
scan can be utilized also to detect CIM (which, as mentioned, is not
infrequent in coronal synostosis), thus driving the following use of MRI.
Furthermore, it is worth mentioning that, in several centers, a
radiological assessment may be required not only for planning surgery
but also for legal purposes. Of course, in these cases, the diagnosis can
be first obtained by skull X-rays or ultrasounds, the use of CT scan or
MRI being limited to doubtful cases [57]. However, “black bone” MRI, a
peculiar sequence of fast MRI developed to investigate sutures, has
been proposed to avoid CT scan-related radiation in these patients [58,
59]. Its modification could represent another useful tool to rule out
CTH in this subset of patients without radiation (and sedation). In any
case, once CTH is diagnosed, the presence of syringomyelia must be
evaluated by MRI of the whole spinal cord.

19 5 Surgical Management
The management of CTH/syringomyelia still misses guidelines, also
when associated with craniosynostosis. However, according to the
recently published results of the International Consensus Conference
on Chiari malformation and Syringomyelia held in 2019, most of the
issues on the management of these conditions in children reached a
significant agreement among the 34 international experts who were
called to address this topic [60]. Those of interest for this chapter can
be summarized as follows: (1) In CTH children with non-syndromic
craniosynostosis, the craniosynostosis should be treated before CTH
(agreement: 100%); (2) In infants with syndromic craniosynostosis and
CTH, surgery should first aim at increasing the cranial volume, with a
proper cranial vault remodeling for each syndrome (agreement:
90.9%); (3) In case of persistent CTH in children already treated for
their syndromic craniosynostosis, the surgical management depends on
syndrome, cranial volume obtained by previous operations, posterior
fossa volume, and CTH symptoms/associated syringomyelia
(agreement: 100%); (4) In symptomatic children with CTH and
hydrocephalus, hydrocephalus should be treated first to relieve raised
intracranial pressure and to avoid post-operatory complications. CTH
can be treated afterwards if symptoms do not disappear (agreement:
90.9%).

19 5 1 The Craniosynostosis Should Be Treated First by
Increasing the Cranial Volume
The indication to surgery in children with craniosynostosis and
CTH/syringomyelia is provided according to the clinical picture
(presence of symptomatic synostosis and/or CTH/syringomyelia
and/or progressing syringomyelia) and the need to prevent of the PCF
narrowing [2, 17]. To treat CTH/syringomyelia, independently from the
synostosis, could be a valid option in subjects with symptomatic
CTH/syringomyelia and stabilized synostosis [61, 62]. As for the rest,
there is a wide agreement on to address the treatment of the
craniosynostosis as first step because of the secondary character of
CTH, which results from the synostosis and its consequences (PCF
hypoplasia, venous engorgement and so on). The rationale of the initial

treatment, therefore, is to perform a cranial decompression aiming at
protecting the brain structures (especially the vital ones of the PCF),
decompressing the venous outflows, and preventing at the same time
the occurrence or the worsening of hydrocephalus and/or
CTH/syringomyelia.
In case of exclusive involvement of lambdoid arch sutures, the gold
standard management is represented by the posterior cranial vault
expansion. This can be realized through a fixed bi-occipital expansion
or by a posterior distraction advancement [63]. The description of the
techniques goes beyond the goals of this paragraph, since they are
reported in other chapters. Here, it is important to remind that the
technique should be tailored on each patient’s characteristics. The
posterior distraction, for example, has the advantage of shorter
operative times and lower rate of blood transfusion (because of the
reduced manipulation of bones and dural sinuses) compared with fixed
occipital expansion but, at the same time, it is burdened by the risk of
skull fractures due to the implants, breaking or dislocations of the
distractors, and by the need of a second operation to remove the
implants themselves [5]. Although some of these limits can be
overcome by resorbable distractors, the posterior distraction should be
used in children not too small and with an enough thick bone. On the
other hand, the fixed posterior expansion is not limited by the use of
mechanical tools but by the need to detach the bone from the dura that,
often, takes long operation times and a risk of significant blood losses.
Therefore, this option is considered mainly in small infants, where the
distractor devices cannot be utilized. To reduce the morbidity resulting
from the blood losses, a posterior expansion obtained by free bone
flaps is successfully used in many centers in infants with honeycomb
bones to achieve a good decompression and to gain time for the
anterior vault advancement [64].
In case of involvement of other sutures or pansinostosis already at
the diagnosis, as not infrequently happens in Crouzon subjects, a total
calvarial remodeling is advised to manage CTH/syringomyelia [27, 31,
40]. The discussion, in this instance, concerns the use of the total
cranial vault expansion versus the use of the posterior distraction
alone, the concurrent performance of a suboccipital decompression
and, in case of suboccipital decompression, the need to open the dura

and to perform a cervical decompression. The total vault reconstruction
is of course the most “radical” approach, which ensures good results
not only on the synostosis but also on CTH [65]. It is usually indicated
in children with the most severe picture of synostosis, where an (early)
fronto-orbital advancement is needed. The total vault remodeling can
be realized by a single procedure, using the prone position with
hyperextension of the head to manage both the occipital expansion and
the front-orbital advancement [66]. However, in children with CTH, it
seems more reasonable to avoid such a prolonged hyperextension of
the neck and to realize the operation in two steps, by alternating the
prone (occipital expansion) and the supine position (fronto-orbital
advancement). The two steps approach offers also the advantage to
include the treatment of hydrocephalus, if required [37].
Currently, however, the posterior calvarial distraction alone is more
and more proposed, even in children with syndromic pansynostosis, to
manage CTH and syringomyelia. This approach is actually indicated
mainly in patients, where CTH/syringomyelia (and the hypoplasic PCF)
represent the main clinical problem. Nevertheless, the posterior
distraction has been proved to increase not only the PCF volume but
also the supratentorial volume, thus providing an advantage also on the
overall management of the synostosis. Actually, Lo et al. observed that
only 2 out of their 16 cases managed by posterior distraction needed a
fronto-orbital advancement later (one of them only for cosmetic
purposes), as result of the increased supratentorial volume [67]. The
series was composed of 14 children with pansynostosis (8 of them
were syndromic subjects) and 2 cases of bi-lambdoid synostosis. CTH
meanly improved from 9.3 to 6.0 mm, while syringomyelia was reduced
from 7.9 to 3.1 mm in thickness and from 203 to 136 mm in length (all
these results were statistically significant). Hydrocephalus needed a
separate treatment in two cases. In their series of 72 children with
craniosynostosis (64.3% with syndromes), Lin and coworkers found a
major protection against the new appearance of CTH in children
undergoing posterior cranial distraction (1 out of 49 cases) compared
with those receiving total vault reconstruction (4 out of 23 cases) [68].
No significant differences were detected between the two techniques
about the occurrence of hydrocephalus.

A further point of discussion concerns the “direct” increase of PCF
volume by the use of PCF suboccipital decompression in addition to
total cranial vault remodeling or posterior cranial distraction. The
rationale of a focused PCF decompression in the context of a wide
decompression of the skull is to give the PCF an immediate relief from
their constriction, namely in children with clear CTH/syringomyelia
symptoms or, if asymptomatic, with significant hindbrain
herniation/constriction and/or large and progressing syringomyelia.
However, in several centers, such an indication is extended to every
craniosynostotic patient with CTH/syringomyelia because of the
possibility to reduce the occurrence or progression of CTH with a onestep operation carried out for the synostosis [29, 69]. Scott et al., for
example, combined the posterior vault remodeling with the
suboccipital decompression in 34 children (80% were syndromic) just
because of the coexistence of synostosis and CTH [70]. The procedure
was effective (only two patients require a further treatment of CTH, 19
and 36 months after the first surgery) and the authors did not detect
intraoperative problems or relevant complications. Other authors,
instead, question the usefulness of this approach due to the
effectiveness of the posterior remodeling/distraction alone in
improving CTH [71]. To avoid the suboccipital decompression allows
also to reduce the operation times and morbidity. In the author of this
chapter’s experience, the suboccipital decompression is combined to
the posterior expansion whenever possible, but it is not carried out at
any cost. More in details, in case of posterior expansion, the skin flap is
designed to expose and decompress also the foramen magnum so that
the procedure is realized with a single surgical field. When the
anatomical conditions or the kind of operation are not favorable to
realize a single wound incision, a second, suboccipital skin incision is
performed but only if the PCF decompression is clinically necessary and
the need to perform a C1 laminectomy is expected. In case of profuse
dural bleeding during the posterior expansion, the suboccipital
decompression is not performed or, if necessary, it is postponed,
waiting for the improvement of the intracranial hypertension and the
venous engorgement.
Generally, the dural opening and the duraplasty are not routinely
required (unless the clinical and/or radiological picture is severe: e.g.,

significant brainstem compression); they are even contraindicated in
several patients because of the copious bleeding from the dural sinuses
[31, 40].

19 5 2 Persistent CTH
As mentioned above, old children with stabilized synostosis and
previously asymptomatic CTH are managed following as for Chiari
malformation and syringomyelia, if they have become symptomatic
(Fig. 19.5). Accordingly, a suboccipital PCF decompression alone versus
a dural opening with or without shrinkage of the cerebellar tonsils are
considered according to the clinical and radiological picture. On the
other hand, if an adequate cranial volume has not been achieved after
the previous cranial vault expansion and/or signs and symptoms of
raised intracranial pressure are still present, CTH/syringomyelia are
better managed by performing a new skull expansion [31, 36]. Once
again, the surgical technique (posterior expansion or distraction versus
total cranial vault remodeling) should be tailored on the patient’s
characteristics.

19 5 3 Hydrocephalus Should Be Treated First
Significant venous anomalies and ventriculomegaly/hydrocephalus are
found in 35% and 52% of children with craniosynostosis and CTH,
respectively [31]. Although the venous anomalies are crucial in the
pathogenesis (namely, the stenosis of the jugular foramina), their
management is limited to the diagnostic work-up, an operative
approach being usually unnecessary or even contraindicated [72].
Actually, if the attempt at decreasing the venous engorgement by
cranial vault expansion is the rule, the direct bony decompression of
venous outflows is risky and often insufficient.
On the other hand, hydrocephalus represents a common operative
issue. The indication to treat the hydrocephalus first originates from
the association between this condition and Chiari I malformation. In
CTH subjects, indeed, hydrocephalus is likely to result from the
impaired CSF circulation due to the compression of the fourth ventricle.
Such hydrocephalus is “obstructive” and, therefore, it can be
successfully treated by endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) in the
great majority of cases [73] (Fig. 19.3). It is treated first because usually

more symptomatic than CTH and also to prevent a cerebellar ptosis in
case of suboccipital decompression (and persistent hydrocephalus). In
children with synostosis and CTH-related hydrocephalus, however, the
matter is a little different. First of all, it has to be considered that
hydrocephalus complicated very rarely the clinical course of single
suture synostoses; therefore, the management of these subjects is
tailored according to etiology and the clinical picture of each patient.
Once again, it is advisable to treat the hydrocephalus before the surgical
correction of the synostosis to normalize the intracranial pressure
before opening the cranial sutures and to reduce CSF-related
complications [74]. ETV or ventriculo-peritoneal shunt (VPS) are
proposed according to the type of hydrocephalus. Second, in
multisutural synostoses of syndromic children, where hydrocephalus is
common, the symptomatic hydrocephalus should be differentiated by
the non-tense ventriculomegaly. The latter condition, usually found in
Apert subjects, can be managed by clinical and radiological monitoring.
The active hydrocephalus, present in 12–15% of cases (up to more than
80% in some syndromes, like Pfeiffer II), on the other side, may require
an operative approach [75]. In these instances, if the hydrocephalus is
not clinically predominant, it is advisable to start the surgical treatment
by cranial vault expansion with the twin goal to relieve from
intracranial pressure and to avoid a worsening of the cranio-cerebral
disproportion (that could lead to an increase of CTH/syringomyelia).
Moreover, the cranial vault expansion (namely, the increased volume of
PCF) has been proved to stabilize the hydrocephalus itself, thanks to
the re-opening of the fourth ventricle outlets, at least in the early
follow-up [5]. On the contrary, if hydrocephalus is clinically prominent,
it has to treated first because of the aforementioned reasons. A
successful treatment of hydrocephalus is expected to improve also the
associated alterations of CSF dynamics, like syringomyelia. Once again,
ETV, if feasible, is the first option for the treatment of this kind of
hydrocephalus because it offers a good rate of success (about 65%) and
allows to avoid the worsening of the cranio-cerebral disproportion [76].
If ETV is not feasible or has failed, extrathecal CSF shunting remains the
last resource. VPS does not represent the first option, indeed, because it
favors the cranial shrinkage (working in contrast to the cranial vault
expansion) and because of its well-known complications. The use of

self-regulating valves and antisyphon devices can help in reducing the
risk of slit ventricles syndrome/increased cranio-cerebral
disproportion. Third, it is worth noting that hydrocephalus may
progress from ventriculomegaly, often after cranial vault
expansion/PCF decompression [40, 75]. In these instances, it is
mandatory to carry on a clinical and radiological monitoring and, in
doubtful cases, to perform a measurement of the intracranial pressure
to identify the candidate to ETV or VP shunt.

20 1 Introduction
During normal human embryogenesis, skull development starts with the formation of bone centers
within the membranous anlage and enlarges by ongoing ossification at the edges [1, 2]. Skull sutures
start to develop at the sites where the bones come in close proximity and consist of the main site of skull
growth [1, 2]. The premature closure of one or multiple sutures defining craniosynostosis is known to
start during the early second trimester of pregnancy, starting 15 weeks of gestation (WG) for
trigonocephaly and 18 WG for scaphocephaly [2, 3]. Skull sutures may be visualized as echo-free linear
structures as early as 15 weeks of gestation [2] (Fig. 20.1). The classification of skull deformation in
craniosynostosis is based on the suture involved (Fig. 20.2). Premature closure of the sagittal, coronal,
and metopic sutures is associated with scaphocephaly (Fig. 20.3) or dolichocephaly, brachycephaly, and
trigonocephaly (Fig. 20.4), respectively. Plagiocephaly develops when only one coronal or lambdoid
suture is closed. Craniosynostosis constitutes a group of heterogeneous conditions with often distinct
clinical, genetic, and molecular characteristics. They are classified into syndromic craniosynostosis when
associated with other abnormalities (15%) and nonsyndromic when they are isolated (85%). Prenatal
diagnosis of craniosynostosis remains rare and challenging, its detection in the prenatal period is
difficult, in nonsyndromic forms or in the absence of family history. Its diagnosis is made late during the
third trimester of pregnancy [3–8] and in a large majority of these cases, the positive diagnosis of
craniosynostosis is made postnatally, during the first year of life [1, 2]. The commonest isolated forms
are scaphocephaly and trigonocephaly. In this chapter, we will discuss how we assess prenatal diagnosis

of craniosynostosis. We will describe prenatal imaging findings and the different imaging modalities,
additional anomalies that should be sought in case of syndromic craniosynostosis and finally, we will
focus on prenatal counseling in case of prenatal diagnosis of craniosynostosis.

20 2 Prenatal 2D-Ultrasound Findings in Craniosynostosis
Ultrasound (US) imaging using the 2D mode is the reference tool in many countries for fetal exploration
since it is an easy, nonradiating, and commonly available imaging modality. While prenatal detection is
straightforward when distinguishing cranial shape abnormalities, such as cloverleaf skull, there are
conditions that cause minimum cranial shape deformity making prenatal diagnosis of craniosynostosis
challenging, especially in single-suture fusion which are detected only sporadically during pregnancy
and, if so, almost invariably during the third trimester [5–7]. Therefore, prenatal diagnosis of isolated
cases of craniosynostosis is relatively rare and the majority of the described cases are syndromic as
shown by Harada et al. in their cohort of 41 newborns with a prenatal diagnosis of craniosynostosis, in
which the detection rate was of 61%; however, 73% (30 cases) were syndromic craniosynostosis, 7% (3
cases) were secondary craniosynostosis of chromosomal deletion syndromes, and only 20% (8 cases)
were isolated [4]. Several authors have reported characteristic US findings for the prenatal diagnosis of
craniosynostosis in 2D-US to increase the detection rate of this condition. These signs are divided into
direct (loss of hypoechogenicity of the skull suture, a bony ridge “inverted V” sign) and indirect signs
(wide concurrent open sutures, abnormal skull shape, brain shadowing sign, abnormal fetal face, and
ventriculomegaly).
During routine mid-trimester fetal US scan, sonographers examine the fetal head in order to realize
the cephalic measurements (biparietal diameter (BPD) and head circumference (HC)) and check the
head anatomy by evaluating its size, shape, integrity, and density. The coronal and lambdoid sutures can
be visualized clearly in this cephalic view as well as the normally oval shape of the skull (Fig. 20.1). In
routine US examination, prenatal diagnosis of craniosynostosis relies mainly on the abnormal shape of
the fetal skull [9] not always straightforward to detect [5, 7]. Skull deformity results from a combination
of lack of growth perpendicularly to the fused suture and compensatory overgrowth at the open sutures

[3, 4, 10]. Skull shape is partly and objectively appreciated by the cephalic index which is the ratio
between the biparietal and the occipitofrontal diameters, which is automatically calculated by most US
devices. Normal range of the cephalic index is defined between 0.75 and 0.85 [4]. An increased cephalic
index was thought to be a reliable marker of brachycephaly secondary to bilateral coronal synostosis
with a sensitivity of 95%, which is helpful during the third trimester [3, 4, 6, 11, 12]. A reduction in the
biparietal diameter curve with a subsequent decrease of the cephalic index is found in fetuses with
scaphocephaly, starting at 20 WG and being an ongoing process for which a repeated measurement could
be informative [6, 13]. Bilateral bulging of the temporal, occipital, and frontal lobes, and a high cranial
vault (acrocephaly) are seen in a cloverleaf skull ( leeblattsch del) secondary to coronal and lambdoid
synostosis, and often result in an increased cephalic index [11, 12]. In sagittal synostosis, growth of the
lambdoid sutures leads to an elongated skull with decreased biparietal diameter and cephalic index, and
an occipital bulging [12, 14]. Sagittal synostosis is of variable onset and can occur from the late first
trimester to the early postnatal period [15]. It can affect only a segment or the whole length of the suture
and may be either isolated or in association with premature fusion of other sutures [16]. However, these
objective measurements have several limits. The standard prenatal biometric parameters are not reliable
to diagnose prenatal craniosynostosis in all cases, as for example, in cases of trigonocephaly, cephalic
measurements do not differ significantly from control cases as well as in cases of partial sagittal
synostosis. In such cases, the diagnosis is mainly based on the subjective assessment of the abnormal
skull shape during the US examination [3, 6]. The metopic synostosis leads to a narrowed and pointed
forehead with bitemporal narrowing (trigonocephaly) [8]. Premature fusion of a single coronal
(frontoparietal or frontosphenoid) suture results in an ipsilateral cranial flattening or plagiocephaly with
elevation and posterior displacement of the ipsilateral orbit and anterior displacement of the ipsilateral
ear canal [11]. Premature fusion of a single lambdoid suture is less common and leads to parietooccipital plagiocephaly [16] (Fig. 20.2).
Despite these tools, the rate of prenatal diagnosis of craniosynostosis is low, it is mainly a secondary
finding when associated anomalies are identified. Thus, when facing abnormal cephalic biometry, the
patient should be referred for a more detailed US examination. Notably, direct observation of a fused
cranial suture with loss of hypoechogenicity of the synostotic suture is possible after 4–16 weeks of the
skull deformity [4, 5, 17]. Other US findings of great value in the assessment of the cranial sutures are the
presence of an “inverted V” ridge, corresponding to a bony ridge and wide orthogonal open sutures [3].
Sutures have to be examined along their entire length because only a short segment of the suture needs
to be fused for the entire suture to be functionally closed [5, 18]. In 2D-US, the acoustic beam is directed
tangentially to the skull surface, then moved along the long axis of the suture back and forward from the
metopic to the sagittal suture, and finally turned into 90° to explore the coronal and lambdoid sutures
[5]. Direct 2D-US examination of the sutures shows an excellent negative predictive value contrary to
isolated skull shape abnormalities [5]. However, such direct exploration of the sutures is not a routine
practice and requires expert skills in ultrasound fetal exploration. The “brain shadowing sign” was
described in craniosynostosis due to the sutures obliteration [3] that leads to the absence of penetration
of US beam through the fetal cranial vault, creating an acoustic shadow on the underlying brain tissue
that may be either complete or partial according to the degree of synostosis [3]. The brain shadowing
sign corresponds to the difficulty in obtaining a proper transthalamic axial view in 2D-US due to acoustic
shadow which persists despite repeated tilting movements of the probe [7]. One should note that an
incorrect position of the transducer over the fetal head to scan the brain may cause misinterpretation of
this finding because insonation through calcified skull bones always provides acoustic shadows that
should not be mistaken for the brain shadowing sign [3]. So, the identification of this sign depends on the
sonographer’s expertise in fetal neurosonography and in fetal position [3]. Dall Hasta et al., have
reported this sign starting at 24 WG in the absence of obvious abnormality of the skull shape. Its
detection should lead to a direct examination of the fetal suture to exclude overlapping sutures and head
molding (false-positive diagnosis of craniosynostosis) [3]. Although sensitive, this sign does not allow
the detection of all cases of craniosynostosis, especially if sutures other than the coronal and the
lambdoid are concerned [7]. Ventriculomegaly was also described as an indirect sign of craniosynostosis,
it is the third most common 2D-US sign found in syndromic craniosynostosis as noted by Harada et al. in
41% of their series in association with skull deformation [4, 19]. Ventriculomegaly may be helpful in
detecting craniosynostosis when skull deformation is minimal [4]. However, if isolated, this is not a

reliable specific sign [4]. Dysmorphism was also described as an indirect sign of craniosynostosis [5, 7],
thus in the case of turricephaly, the midsagittal view of the fetal profile is abnormal [7]. Proptosis and
frontal bossing have been reported in fetuses with bilateral coronal suture synostosis [3, 4]. Interestingly,
Harada et al. have reported three cases of craniosynostosis who presented with proptosis and
ventriculomegaly without abnormal skull shape or abnormal cephalic index or biometry [4].
Hypertelorism (defined as an interorbital diameter exceeding the diameter of one globe) or
hypotelorism was also observed in cases of brachycephaly and trigonocephaly, respectively [15, 16].

20 3 What Is the Additional Value of the Other Imaging Modalities?
In a selected high-risk population of craniosynostosis, there is a high-positive predictive value of the
direct examination of the sutures using a 2D-US, however, the specificity of such an exploration is low in
low-risk populations [12, 20]. In such cases, 3D-US, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), or computed
tomography (CT) may be of a good help to investigate prenatal diagnosis of craniosynostosis (Table 20.1)
[5, 21–23].

Abbreviations: 2D-US two-dimensional ultrasonography, 3D-US three-dimensional ultrasonography, MRI
magnetic resonance imaging, CT scan computed tomography scan
Although 3D-US requires some skills and devices for high-definition rendering, this imaging modality
can be useful to visualize the skull sutures as early as 13–15 WG, showing closure, irregularly thickened
inner sutural margin with a high-negative predictive value for the diagnosis of craniosynostosis (Fig.
20.5) [3, 5, 16, 21, 24, 25]. It represents also a potential complementary tool for the measurement of the
bony gaps of the uninvolved sutures with the multiplanar mode, contributing to the differential diagnosis
between craniosynostosis and overriding sutures in severe fetal head molding [3, 7, 21, 26, 27]. Krakow
et al. have demonstrated the superiority of 3D-US over 2D-US in a case of fetal molding which was
initially thought to be an isolated craniosynostosis, by showing the open suture [28]. Some authors have
also reported better visualization of fetal facial dysmorphism using this technique [21, 24, 29]. However,
in their series of 60 craniofacial malformations, while admitting that 3D-US helped parental
understanding and medical communication, Ghi et al. have noted no objective diagnostic benefit
compared to 2D-US [30]. In conclusion, 3D-US can be a useful additional tool associated with 2D-US
during parental counseling that may help parental–fetal bonding [24, 31, 32].

Fig. 20.5 3D-US of the cranial sutures. Major sutures involved in craniosynostosis. Coronal suture(arrow in a, b), lambdoid suture (dotted
arrow in a, c), the anterior fontanelle (asterisk in d, e), the sagittal suture (head of the arrow of d, f), and the metopic suture (arrow on d, g)

Reports on prenatal MR examination of craniosynostosis are rare in the literature. The fetal skull
sutures are not directly visualized by MRI but this modality facilitates the evaluation of brain
abnormalities or small changes in hands and feet [4]. Fj rtoft et al. presented the first evaluation of fetal
MRI in a series of patients with suspicion of craniosynostosis [33]. They noted that the MRI showed
abnormal skull shape, bone thickening, and slight skull indentations at the level of the closed sutures
with a high-negative predictive value in their series [16, 33, 34]. For example, temporal indentations,
which were also visible in the US, were correlated with coronal synostosis [33], the “lampshade” sign
reflecting the bulging of the temporal regions, the undeveloped frontal lobes, and the turricephaly were
more easily assessed on coronal MRI sequences than on 2D-US [35]. Boog et al. showed that MRI
contributes to additional findings during the imaging assessment of craniosynostosis, such as
verticalization of the clivus and the flattened angle of the skull base during the second trimester [23].
However, the great advantage of MRI concerns the better assessment of brain abnormalities that might
be associated with craniosynostosis such as ventriculomegaly and agenesis of the corpus callosum,
especially because US exploration is limited by suture synostosis [33, 35, 36]. MRI could be of good help
in the assessment of facial fetal abnormalities such as proptosis which is defined as a protrusion of more
than 50% of the ocular globe beyond the orbital rim [35]. Thus, the contribution of fetal MRI to the
diagnosis of isolated craniosynostosis seems minimal. Therefore, US and MRI should be considered
complementary imaging modalities [16].
Prenatal 3D-CT seems to be very useful, as it allows direct visualization of the cranial vault sutures,
the skull shape, and all the skeletal abnormalities in syndromic craniosynostosis, which is not possible
with MRI [3, 4, 22, 33]. Moreover, it allows the exploration of the entire length of the suture in the three
dimensions, which is useful during the assessment of craniosynostosis since even though a tiny segment
of the suture is fused, the entire suture could be functionally closed [5].

20 4 Syndromic Craniosynostosis: What Should the Sonographer
Look for?

Despite the imaging tools at our disposal, prenatal diagnosis of craniosynostosis relies mainly on the
skull deformity and the associated anomalies [4, 5, 37]. Distinguishing between isolated and syndromic
craniosynostosis during the prenatal period is crucial for appropriate counseling since syndromic cases
present generally a higher rate of developmental delay (56% vs. 25% in a series of 41 cases by Harada et
al.) [4, 35]. The median gestational age at diagnosis in the context of syndromic craniosynostosis [6, 8,
38] is 25 WG versus 31 WG in cases of isolated ones [3]. An extensive list of syndromes with
craniosynostosis includes Antley–Bixler, Apert, Baller-Gerold, Beare–Stevenson, Carpenter, Crouzon,
Jackson–Weiss, Meckel–Gruber, Muenke, Pfeiffer, Ruvalcaba, Saethre–Chotzen, Williams, 9p deletions,
chondrodysplasia punctata, hypophosphatasia, thanatophoric dysplasia, and cranioectodermal dysplasia
or Sensenbrenner syndrome. Distinguishing between these different syndromes of craniosynostosis is
difficult during the prenatal period considering the great heterogeneity of the diseases and the overlap of
phenotypic features among fetuses with different genetic variants and syndromes [8]. Molecular analysis
of fetal DNA can be used in Apert (Fig. 20.6), Crouzon (Fig. 20.7), Pfeiffer and Jackson-Weiss syndromes
when the family history is informative. The imaging findings of 15 syndromes with craniosynostosis are
described in Table 20.2 [4, 5, 8, 12, 16, 35, 39–51]. Brachycephaly due to bilateral coronal synostosis is
typical of, though not specific for, Pfeiffer and Apert syndromes. Coronal synostosis associated with
lambdoid synostosis leads to a cloverleaf shape of the skull with bitemporal and bifrontal bulging that is
more frequently observed in thanatophoric dwarfism, Pfeiffer, Apert, and Crouzon syndromes [5, 11, 15,
16, 52–55]. Crouzon syndrome is the most frequent syndrome with craniosynostosis but is more
challenging to diagnose during the prenatal period than Pfeiffer syndrome because of mild skull
deformities without any specifically associated anomalies during gestation [4]. Indeed, the fetuses with
Pfeiffer syndrome present with more evident and severe skull shape abnormalities that developed
earlier during the gestational period than other syndromes [4]. The location of the synostosis varies
even within the same syndrome [4, 56], thus, Pfeiffer syndrome is divided into three different subtypes
with overlapping features and different skull shapes: mild cases (type 1 with midface hypoplasia and
limbs malformations), severe cases (type 2 with cloverleaf skull, limbs malformations, and elbow
ankylosis), and intermediate cases (type 3 similar to type 2 but without cloverleaf skull) [8, 35].
Moreover, depending on the degree of suture synostosis, the skull shape abnormalities may be absent or
subtle until the third trimester [2], which leads in some cases to the suspicion of the underlying
syndrome in the absence of skull shape abnormality [6]. Exploration of the central nervous system
during the assessment of suspected craniosynostosis is mandatory using US and MRI if required. In
Apert syndrome, temporal lobe dysgyria has been reported in association with agenesis of the corpus
callosum and may precede the detection of craniosynostosis [57]. Ventriculomegaly is common in
craniosynostosis and can be associated with subtle scalloping of the inner skull table due to the high
intracranial pressure [8, 35]. Additional imaging findings of dysmorphism were associated with
syndromic craniosynostosis including hyper- or hypotelorism, proptosis, cleft palate, and midface
hypoplasia [8, 16]. Proptosis is generally more pronounced in Crouzon syndrome, in association with
mild hypertelorism, starting the second trimester [39, 58]. The association of microphthalmia and
craniosynostosis is a very rare condition and was reported in Curry-Jones, Gorlin-Chaudhry-Moss, and
oculo-facio-cardio-dental syndromes [46]. Inner ear anomalies are classic in Apert syndrome [59]. Other
sonographic features such as limb abnormalities and hand anomalies are encountered in syndromic
craniosynostosis. US observation of fetal “mitten hands” (complete symmetrical syndactyly of the hands
and feet seen as smooth oval shapes) is highly characteristic of Apert syndrome that in association with
molecular diagnosis allows the prenatal detection of sporadic Apert syndromes during the second
trimester [22, 35, 60, 61]. In Baller-Gerold syndrome, radial aplasia or hypoplasia is considered a very
evocative finding [62]. Radio-humeral synostosis and joint contractures as well as fractures or bowing of
the long bones [63] are suggestive of Antley-Bixler syndrome. Additional malformations can be
associated with syndromic craniosynostosis such as diaphragmatic hernias, abdominal wall defects,
heart malformations, echogenic kidneys, and abnormal airways with echogenic and hyperexpanded
lungs with effusions [3, 35, 64]. MRI is useful for the detailed evaluation of fetal airways and lung
changes [35]. In addition to midface hypoplasia that leads to a decrease in nasopharynx and oropharynx
diameters, a tracheal cartilaginous sleeve is common in Crouzon, Apert, and Pfeiffer syndromes, and is
thought to contribute to premature death in the affected newborns [65, 66].

20 5 Implications of Prenatal Diagnosis of Craniosynostosis in
Prenatal Counseling
Once prenatal diagnosis of fetal craniosynostosis is confirmed and considered as isolated or associated
with other malformations, fetal genetic assessment including fetal chromosomal microarray on amniotic
fluid cells as well as molecular confirmation, when possible, should be recommended and is crucial for
prenatal counseling regarding the prognosis [3, 11, 15, 62, 63]. Thus, the risk for cognitive disabilities in
the affected infant depends on the underlying syndrome [11]. In cases of isolated brachycephaly and
dolichocephaly, Delahaye et al. have found a normal outcome in 80% of these cases and therefore they
confirmed that these isolated features are rarely associated with fetal abnormalities. However, some of
the nonsyndromic craniosynostosis may have an underlying genetic etiology but less commonly
identified antenatally [8]. Regarding high-risk fetuses with a family history of craniosynostosis, future
parents are often requested to know if the newborn will be affected or not, irrespective of their
willingness to terminate or not the pregnancy [5]. Interestingly, in cases of nonsyndromic
craniosynostosis, siblings of an affected child have approximately double the estimated risk of
craniosynostosis than the general population [9].

Since most cases of craniosynostosis are compatible with survival, prenatal diagnosis of
craniosynostosis allows the careful planning of delivery modality and perinatal care since delivery
complications seem to be associated with craniosynostosis [58]. Indeed, an important function of the
sutures is to enable molding of the skull when passing through the birth canal and craniosynostosis may
avoid this adaptation [59]. Thus, a higher rate of vaginal breech deliveries and secondary cesarean
sections have been reported in newborns with craniosynostosis compared to the general population as
well as a lower Apgar score and a lower pH value [58]. In addition, a high mortality rate is observed
during the neonatal period in some conditions, since infants with craniosynostosis are at increased risk
of concomitant abnormalities of the upper airways due to midfacial hypoplasia and may require
ventilatory support and delivery in an adequate structure [7, 8, 15, 60]. Moreover, craniosynostosis may
be complicated by various types of neurological anomalies including elevated intracranial pressure, and
hydrocephaly that may require prompt surgical treatment after birth for which time for referral is critical
[6, 15]. Prenatal diagnosis of such conditions requires a multidisciplinary approach to provide optimal
care and allow timely decision-making for the newborn [34].
Prenatal diagnosis of fetal craniosynostosis enables psychological support for future parents. They
will be aware of the main treatments that their child may require during the postnatal period and this
may decrease the stress caused by the diagnosis of craniosynostosis [61].

20 6 Conclusion
Prenatal diagnosis of craniosynostosis remains challenging in particular in isolated single-suture forms.
Abnormal skull shape, abnormal cephalic index, the brain shadowing sign, and ventriculomegaly are the
main key features for detecting fetal craniosynostosis in 2D-US. Once craniosynostosis is suspected,
patients should be referred to a fetal medicine unit in order to perform a second-level scan by an expert
in fetal neurosonography to confirm the diagnosis and to assess the associated malformations. A 3D-US
may be an optional additional tool to improve the exploration of the skull sutures and to help future
parents visualize the malformation. MRI, as a complementary imaging modality, allows detection and
better assessment of central nervous system malformations which may be associated with
craniosynostosis. Distinguishing between isolated and syndromic craniosynostosis is crucial during the
prenatal period for appropriate counseling, and scrutinizing for fetal limbs and facial anomalies is useful.
Once the diagnosis of craniosynostosis is made, fetal chromosomal microarray and molecular analysis
should be recommended.

21 Neuroimaging in the
