21 1 Introduction
The craniosynostoses (CS) are usually suspected, diagnosed, and often
assessed, by clinical examination only. Confirmation with imaging may
be needed to confirm the stenoses and to evaluate the associated skull
base, calvarial, brain, and vascular structures, particularly in cases with
complex and syndromic craniosynostosis.
Skull shape in the craniosynostoses reflects compensatory growth
at patent sutures and lack of growth perpendicular to the fused suture.
Brain abnormalities commonly associated with both the simple and
complex craniosynostoses (CS) may result from brain deformation
reflecting that focal or diffuse constriction of the bony vault. They may
also be mediated by the CSF when the venous drainage is impeded by

the bony abnormality, as occurs when the craniosynostosis involves the
skull base foramina, or they may be developmental, part of the
syndromic constellation. While brain deformations related to bone
deformities are the most apparent, modern imaging has also revealed
cerebral developmental changes that are part of the disease. These
associated changes seem logical in syndromic craniosynostoses, but
modern imaging demonstrates that it may also occur in seemingly
“isolated” single-suture craniosynostoses, suggesting that the
developmental disorder that affects the bone may also interfere with
brain development. Additional abnormalities such as dentofacial
problems (Apert, Crouzon mostly), inner ear (Apert), exoptosis (FGFR
mutations), limb anomalies (Apert, Pfeiffer, Saethre-Chotzen, AntleyBixtler, Muenke, and Baller-Gerold RECQL4 syndromes), and upper
airway obstruction (highest in Apert, Crouzon, and Pfeiffer) are imaging
clues to aid in phenotype-genotype assessment.

21 2 The Imaging Tools
The choice of imaging modalities required is based on the need to
evaluate the calvarium, brain, and CSF for a given clinical presentation.
In clinically complex cases, that may also include the assessment of the
minor sutures, the skull base and synchondroses, the craniocervical
junction, and the upper cervical spine. Assessment of arterial and
venous structures is also required in cases where surgical access may
be compromised. Imaging tools include Photogrammatic analysis, fetal
and postnatal ultrasonography, plain film radiography, CT with 3D
surface reconstructions, MRI, and vascular studies on either CT or MRI
[1–4].
Photogrammatic analysis, with an overlay of pre-and postoperative
scans, has been used to objectify calvarial changes in the single-suture
synostoses by assessment of cranial length and width, diagonal
measurements, quadrant volumes, anterior and posterior asymmetry
ratios, and cranial index, but is not able to provide information
regarding intracranial contents [5, 6].
Ultrasonography (U/S) is considered an efficient tool to evaluate
single-suture stenosis in infants under 8 months of age. It can be used
to provide a first postnatal sutural evaluation, as it is relatively cheap,

easily available, without radiation, easy to repeat, and can be
performed without sedation at the infant’s bedside. It also allows a first
assessment of the brain and peri-cerebral spaces. Hyperechogenic
osseous thickening with external periosteum is seen with bony
bridging, while a hypoechogenic gap reflects the unfused suture.
Sagittal sutures are shown to have an end-to-end appearance, while the
coronal and lambdoid sutures typically have a beveled junction. The
metopic suture shows a beaked appearance, whether fused early or at
the age-appropriate time [7–13]. Normative values of suture width are
available for both US and CT. The measurements should be obtained
well away from the fontanels. The average width of the proximal
sagittal suture at birth on ultrasound is 0.9–1.4 mm, but 5.0 0.2 mm
on CT, decreasing by approximately half at 1 month of age. The
difference between modalities may reflect the inclusion of a fibrous
portion of the suture. It should be noted that while postnatal U/S
readily evaluates the entirety of the sagittal, metopic, and lambdoid
sutures, it cannot evaluate the skull base synchondroses in the coronal
synostosis, which involve the coronal hemi-ring and skull base, or in
complex craniosynostoses. It is strongly operator-dependent, needs to
be performed by an experienced professional, and acoustic
transmission may be hindered by thick hair [14] (Fig. 21.1).

Fig. 21.1 Coronal US (a) in a GA 37 week old newborn demonstrates a patent sagittal suture.
The arrows demarcate the bony border of the suture. Coronal US (b) in a 17 day old neonate
with Apert syndrome shows markedly widened sagittal suture width (arrows) at location well
behind the anterior fontanel. Coronal US (c) in a 13 day old neonate with Muenke syndrome
and unicoronal synostosis reveals the elevated orbital roof (arrow) ipsilateral to the unilateral
coronal synostosis. Coronal US (d) reveals sagittal synostosis (arrow) in a 5 month old infant
with microcephaly

Calvarial bones appear hyperechoic on prenatal ultrasound at or
after 9 weeks GA, while cranial sutures are identifiable by focal
through-transmission at 15–16 weeks gestation and when the imaging
plane is perpendicular to the synostosed suture. Loss of the suture
visualization precedes thickening of bone and subsequent indentations
or “divets” at the site of the fused suture or minor fontanel. The coronal

and lambdoid sutures are more readily accessible on fetal ultrasound
than metopic or sagittal sutures, although metopic synostosis is
identifiable if trigonocephaly is pronounced. A triangular appearance of
the skull is present on axial images in metopic synostosis, while a
triangular calvarial appearance may be seen on coronal images of
sagittal synostosis. Syndromic cases are usually easier to identify due to
the severity as in cases of the cloverleaf skull, abnormal brain imaging,
and associated features like limb anomalies. Evidence of calvarial
deformity due to constraint by uterine malformations, fibroids, or
multiple gestations is easily assessed. Identification of calvarial
deformity is furthered by the use of 3D surface reconstructions on both
CT and MRI [15–18]. Milder cases of single-suture synostosis may be
missed. Additional useful features include an abnormal cephalic index,
normally between 75% and 85%, for example in sagittal synostosis, the
head circumference remains stable, while the BPD drops centiles. In
scaphocephaly, the CI is below 75%, and in brachycephaly above 86%.
Syndromic synostosis may be noted at the first anatomy ultrasound
scan around 20 weeks of gestation [16, 18, 19]. Additionally, the
presence of the “Brain Shadow Sign” with acoustic shadowing due to
the failure of sound waves to penetrate a closed suture increases the
diagnostic rate [20] (Fig. 21.2).

Fig. 21.2 Fetal US. Axial fetal US (a) performed at GA 27 6 weeks in a pregnancy with
maternal FGFR1 Kallmann mutation reveals trigonocephaly (arrow). Follow-up postnatal
oblique 3D CT at 7 weeks of age (b) confirms beaking and fusion (arrow) of the metopic suture.
Axial fetal US (c) performed at GA 26 0 weeks in confirmed Apert syndrome demonstrates the
brain shadow sign, with the shadow (arrow) from the fused coronal sutures obscuring the
frontal lobes. Postnatal oblique 3D CT at 6 weeks of age (d) confirms bicoronal synostosis
(arrow). Note early midface and glabellar retrusion

Plain film radiography was formerly the method of choice to
confirm a clinical diagnosis of CS, but not anymore with the advent of
more sophisticated techniques. In our institution, infants seen for skull
asymmetry are referred instead for an ultrasound if single-suture
synostosis is suspected or for ultra-low-radiation dose CT if synostosis

appears complicated, syndromic, or the infant is preoperative. While no
longer having an important role in the preop evaluation of the
craniosynostoses, plain films remain useful in the serial postoperative
assessment of surgical apparatus, for example, posterior cranial vault
distraction hardware, or to assess the extracranial component of
ventricular catheters in the presence of shunt. Plain film radiography
may, however, be obtained as part of a skeletal survey for genetic
assessment. Low calvarial density in the neonate, blurring of the
sutures, inability to assess the minor sutures and basal synchondroses,
and the presence of partial fusion render suture assessment on
radiography difficult. Absence or straightening of the sutures, bridging
or breaking, and sclerotic bands reflecting the fused sutures and
pressure-related inner table scalloping or lacunae are classically
described. Serrations of the closed coronal, squamosal, sagittal, and
lambdoid sutures may remain visible into the fourth decade or later.
The metopic suture fuses between 3 and 9 months of age and is the
only suture that fuses completely without visible serrations of
hydrocephalus (Fig. 21.3).

Fig. 21.3 Radiographs. Lateral skull radiograph (a) obtained as part of genetic skeletal survey
at 5 days of age demonstrates microcephaly and coronal synostosis (arrow). Lacunae are
present (open arrow). Ultralow-dose axial 3D CT reconstruction (b) performed in the same
infant at 30 days shows both sagittal (open arrow) and coronal (white arrow) synostosis and
confirms multiple bony lacunae around the fused sutures. 22q11DS mutation was confirmed.
Lateral radiograph (c) demonstrates posterior distraction apparatus (white arrow) and
separation of the operative margins in a nearly 9-year-old child with Alagille syndrome (JAG1
mutation). Preoperative lateral CT 3D reconstruction (d) in the same child revealed
brachycephaly, pansynostosis, and maxillary retrusion (arrow)

Computed tomography (CT) allows for a fast, ultra-low-radiation
dose examination of the skull with 3D-volumic reformatting. Images in
this manuscript were performed with 20–30 mAs (DLP of 29.7 with an
effective dose of 0.09 mSv). While radiographs can demonstrate many

of the salient features of craniosynostoses, such as skull and orbit shape
and involvement of the major vault sutures of the cranial vault arches,
specific advantages of CT and 3D calvarial and skin surface
reconstructions include an exquisite demonstration of the skull base,
minor sutures, and synchondroses [21] (Fig. 21.4). The width of the
major and minor sutures and synchondroses are easily measured and
correlated with published controls of both measurements and the
expected timing of suture closure, confirming the presence or absence
of synostosis as the cause of skull and orbit deformity [14]. A common
cause of nonsynostotic causes of skull deformity is positional
plagiocephaly (Fig. 21.5). An additional cause of plagiocephaly is
growth at accessory sutures (Fig. 21.6). Finally, focal calvarial
thickening due to bone dysplasia, intraosseous vascular malformations,
or neoplasms may simulate synostotic causes of skull deformity (Fig.
21.7). Data obtained from postnatal ultra-low-radiation dose CT can be
used for virtual surgical planning (VSP) 3D printed templates,
computer-aided design/computer-aided manufacturing (CAD/CAM),
and in simulators for surgical training [22–24].

posterior intraoccipital synchondroses (arrow). A normal Kerkring ossicle has been
incorporated into the posterior arc of foramen magnum. Axial 3D reconstruction (b) in a
different 4-week-old infant with multiple congenital anomalies shows patent anterior
intraoccipital synchondroses (open arrow), but unilateral fused posterior intraoccipital
synchondrosis (black arrow). Axial 3D reconstruction (c) of the child seen in (b), now nearly 5
years of age, shows hypertrophied margin of foramen magnum (open arrow) and fused

crest (black arrow). Coronal T1 (d) of the same child shows acquired displacement of the
cerebellar hemisphere by the hypertrophied bony protuberance (arrow)

demonstrate frontal lobe hypoplasia (asterisk) and calvarial thickening (arrow)

Low and ultra-low dose in vivo fetal CT and 3D CT, performed after
20 weeks gestation and using doses as low as 0.5–2 mSv and modelbased iterative reconstruction (MBIR), are used in some centers in the
evaluation of fetal skeletal dysplasias and anomalies [17, 25–27].
Autopsy-based CT with 3D reconstructions can be very helpful in the
evaluation of calvarial sutures and skull base synchondroses.

Microfocus-CT (micro-CT) takes considerably less time than UHF-MRI
and can be used to evaluate bone and soft tissue structures in fetuses
20 weeks’ GA. Evaluation of soft tissues with micro-CT, however, does
require iodine-based staining prior to imaging [28–31].
Pre- and postoperative Vascular Imaging provides an illustration of
the intracranial venous and arterial systems in selected cases utilizing
CT venography (CTV) or CT angiography (CTA), both of which require
contrast injection and specific postinjection timing and/or MR
venography (MRV) and MR angiography (MRA), which require neither.
Arterial abnormalities are less common but do occur. Venous
abnormalities are common in the syndromic or complex
craniosynostoses, and include persistent fetal sinuses, dural sinus
stenosis or obstruction, aberrant venous drainage, sinus pericranii,
collaterals, and dilated emissaries [32–35] (Fig. 21.8). In one study of
41 patients with FGFR mutation-related craniosynostosis, venous
abnormalities occurred in 76%. They were universal in Pfeiffer patients
and present in 84% of Crouzon patients and 64% of Apert patients
[35]. During development, the skull base foramina surround nerve and
vascular structures, mesenchyme clearing, condensing, and then
ossifying around them. While the shape and size of the skull base
foramina during development is dictated by traversing nerves and
blood vessels, abnormal skull base ossification, and
sutural/synchondrosis fusion in FGFR mutations, for example, can in
turn lead to progressive foraminal stenosis with resultant compression
and deformity of those traversing structures over time [36–39]. Jugular
foraminal stenosis in FGFR mutations leads to dural sinus stenosis at
the junction of the sigmoid sinus and internal jugular vein resulting in
venous outflow resistance [38, 40–43]. Similarly, MRV studies are
suggested in TWIST1-related craniosynostoses due to the progressive
nature of foraminal stenosis [44]. Even compression on the flattened
side in patients with posterior positional plagiocephaly is associated
with a higher incidence of venous abnormalities on that side [45].
Sinovenous sinus volume has been shown to increase following
posterior cranial vault distraction plus foramen magnum
decompression due to the “dural traction effect” in a small cohort of
children with syndromic synostosis and chronic tonsillar herniation
[43]. Imaging features can be used to differentiate between physiologic

IJV slenderness and pathologic IJV stenosis or narrowing. Important
features of clinically significant IJV stenosis include local stenosis,
abnormal venous collaterals, local white matter hyperintense signal,
and mismatch between the transverse diameter of IJV and the caliber of
the jugular foramina or bony transverse sinus groove on the inner table
of the calvarium [46]. While intracranial hypertension in complex or
systemic craniosynostosis may reflect venous outflow obstruction,
craniocerebral disproportion, Chiari 1 malformation, and obstructive
sleep apnea are also implicated [47–49].

Fig. 21.8 Venous obstruction and collaterals. MRV (a) in a 17-month-old toddler with Crouzon
syndrome shows bilateral jugular vein stenosis (arrows). CT venogram (b) in an 8-month-old
infant, also Crouzon syndrome, with jugular vein obstruction reveals extensive suboccipital

venous flow in a thrombosed straight sinus (arrow) after shunt placement, but prior to cranial

(arrow)

Sinus pericranii associated with occipital and cervical venous plexi
can be seen with obstruction of the usual outflow foramina and
redirected flow. These have been reported in the FGFR2, FGFR3, and
TWIST-related syndromes, including Apert, Crouzon, Pfeiffer, JacksonWeiss, Achondroplasia, and Saethre-Chotzen syndromes, and can also
be seen in cases of mutation-unconfirmed complex craniosynostoses.
Communication between internal and external compartments can be
suggested by a bony defect on CT and must be evaluated with vascular
imaging for preoperative planning, as they may significantly
compromise access during cranial vault reconstruction. Additionally, as
most are the dominant venous drainage, surgical planning needs to
include preservation rather than occlusion of the abnormal venous
connection to avoid stroke or fatal outcome [50–56] (Fig. 21.9).

Fig. 21.9 Sinus pericranii. Sagittal CT image (a) in a 12-year-old with Crouzon syndrome
demonstrates focal skull defect (arrow) and typical scalloped clivus (open arrow). T1 sagittal
image (b) in same preteen shows multiple flow voids (arrows) from associated sinus pericranii
and extracranial collaterals. Note also the Chiari 1 malformation (open arrow). 3D CT venogram
(c) in a 4-year-old child with pansynostosis reveals a prominent suboccipital venous plexus
(arrow). Axial MRV (d) in the same child demonstrates the sinus pericranii (open arrow)
supplying the extracranial suboccipital venous plexus

Specific arterial features in the craniosynostoses include those
related to the skull base, such as progressive stenosis of the carotid
canal following fusion of the contiguous petro-occipital fissure or due
to pseudomigration of the juxtasellar carotid arteries following

arrested skull base growth due to early fusion of the central skull base
synchondroses in the syndromic craniosynostoses with FGFR
mutations. Other craniosynostosis syndromes may also exhibit vascular
abnormalities. Vasculopathies, both venous and arterial, are present in
30–40% of patients with Alagille syndrome (JAG1 or NOTCH2). Specific
arterial abnormalities in Alagille syndrome, such as stenoses,
aneurysms, dolichoectasia, and moyamoya are felt to reflect defects in
angiogenic vascular remodeling [57–59]. Displaced vessels may
interfere with a surgical approach. Intrasphenoid- or intrasellar kissing
or contiguous carotid arteries have been reported in association with
empty sella syndrome, with dolichoectasia and with acromegaly, but as
previously discussed, may be present in the FGFR mutations due to
early fusion of the intersphenoidal and spheno-occipital synchondroses
[37, 60–64] (Fig. 21.10). Additionally, medially displaced and kissing
retropharyngeal carotid arteries and abnormal high or low position of
the cervical carotid bifurcations may be seen, for example with 22q11.2
deletions, both in velocardiofacial and DiGeorge patients [65]. Arterial
spin labeling (ASL) fused with MRI images may be used to study
regional cerebral blood flow in craniosynostosis patients. Frontal lobe
CBF in trigonocephaly patients under 18 months of age is normal, while
patients under 1 year of age with syndromic craniosynostosis have
demonstrated lower panlobar, cortical, and white matter CBF than
controls. CBF has been shown to be greater in treated than untreated
syndromic craniosynostosis patients, falling into the range of the
control subjects although the expected CBF childhood peak occurred
somewhat later than in controls [66, 67].

Fig. 21.10 Arterial abnormalities. Axial CTA (a) in an 8-year-old with Alagille syndrome and
multisuture synostosis reveals absent left carotid canal (arrow). MRA (b) confirms absent ICA
and origin of the left MCA from the PCA (open arrow). Axial CT (c) in a 14-year-old with

carotids”

Concomitant brain imaging utilizing routine brain CT doses or
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is required when evaluating for
syndromic involvement or for perioperative complications, as ultralow-dose CT does not provide a detailed evaluation of brain anatomy.
The presence of microcephaly or marked asymmetry also alerts us to

the need for further brain imaging. MRI avoids ionizing radiation but
may require sedation or general anesthesia. MR imaging aids in the
evaluation of clinical features associated with craniosynostosis such as
increased intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus, and vascular anatomy,
and may clarify the etiology of headache, epilepsy, and abnormal
cognitive development (Fig. 21.11). Routine 3D T1 MRI and particularly
3D T1 spoiled gradient echo-based (T1SGRE) sequences have shown
some facility visualizing vault suture and 3D reconstructions are
reported with the latter, but visibility is currently inferior to that of CT
[68, 69]. With the currently available technology, “black bone” 2D MR
prenatally and postnatally, and “CT-like MR-derived” source images
postnatally demonstrate the skull and the sutures well, both and fast
imaging allows a good appreciation of the fluid-filled spaces [70–73].
The use of “black bone” technology to plan 3D printing CAD/CAM and
assisted cranial vault reconstruction has been reported [74, 75].
However, while postprocessed 3D reconstructions of the skin surface
and skull shape are possible with MR imaging, 3D demonstration of the
minor sutures and actual visualization of the skull base synchondroses
is not yet robust (Fig. 21.12).

21 2 1 Specific Features of the Craniosynostoses
Restricted growth perpendicular to early fused suture or sutures in
association with persistent growth and enlargement of the adjacent

uninvolved sutures leads to characteristic head and orbital shapes.
Patterns of fusion reflect the involvement of the vault arches. The
sagittal arch includes the metopic and sagittal sutures, but also the
ethmoidofrontal suture. The lambdoid arch includes the lambdoid
sutures, but also the occipitopetrosal, occipitomastoid sutures, and
spheno-occipital synchondrosis. The parietosquamosal arch consists of
the parietosquamous and parietomastoid sutures. The coronal arch
consists of the coronal sutures, the anterior branch of which includes
the frontosphenoidal and ethmoidosphenoidal synchondroses, while
the posterior branch is composed of the sphenosquamous,
sphenoparietal, and sphenopetrosal synchondroses [76, 77]. Partial or
asymmetric involvement or variation in the timing of fusion of arch
components may lead to atypical plagiocephaly and orbital shapes and
to skull base scoliosis or endocranial base deflection due to asymmetric
shortening of the cranial base [60, 61, 78–81].
Metopic synostosis can present as an isolated single-suture
synostosis, or may be involved in syndromic, complex, or
pansynostosis. Partial fusion originates at the nasion around 3 months
of age, with fusion extending toward the anterior fontanelle. The
window of complete closure ranges from 8 to 14 months. Early fusion
leads to trigonocephaly with forehead breaking, a narrowed anterior
cranial fossa, and hypotelorism are present in metopic synostosis. Ageappropriate physiologic metopic fusion occurs without forming the
serrated fusion lines seen after fusion of the sagittal, coronal, and
lambdoid fusion and may exhibit some midline ridging. Assessment of
the fusion site may help confirm early synostosis. A midline endocranial
ridge or spur, the “M” sign, is present at the site of physiologic fusion,
and an endocranial notch, the “omega sign,” is present in synostotic
patients, although there is crossover. In addition to the superomedial
displacement of the orbits, also known as “quizzical” orbits, there is the
medial displacement of the supraorbital foramina. While no single
feature was pathognomonic of metopic synostosis, these signs were
especially helpful if multiple were present [82–85] (Fig. 21.13).

Fig. 21.13 Metopic synostosis. 3D CT (a) in a non-syndromic 4-week-old infant shows beaking
of the fused metopic suture (short arrow) and medial uptilted (“quizzical”) orbits (arrow). Axial
T2 (b) reveals trigonocephaly (arrow), mild lateral flattening of the frontal lobes, and
prominent frontal peri-cerebral fluid (asterisk) in the same infant. SSFSE-T2 fetal MRI (c) at GA
19 weeks demonstrates a lobar holoprosencephaly and trigonocephaly. T1 axial image (d) in an
8-day-old with microcephaly and trisomy 13 reveals trigonocephaly (arrow) and undersulcated frontal lobes (asterisk)

Scaphocephaly due to sagittal synostosis is the result of elongation
of the skull in the anterior-posterior direction. Patterns of calvarial
deformity are dependent upon the site of sagittal fusion (anterior,
central, or posterior), as well as the presence or absence of additional

suture and synchondrosis involvement [86]. Early onset of fusion of the
sagittal suture occurring in the first year of life tends to occur in the
posterior third of the suture with small remnants of open suture more
pronounced anteriorly than posteriorly. When the metopic suture
remains patent, the shape is called sphenocephalic with the typical
relative enlargement of the anterior fontanel and frontal bossing [1, 87,
88]. Additional specific features of calvarial shape and facial features in
sagittal synostosis are biparietal narrowing or narrowing of the vertex
on AP view, occipital bulleting, and a longitudinal “beak and groove”
containing the superior sagittal sinus. Less commonly, fusion of the
metopic suture concomitant with sagittal synostosis results in a
leptocephalic (narrow forehead) shape [89]. Localized fusion
originating in the anterior or middle third of the sagittal suture may
lead to a retrocoronal vault depression and a saddle-shape deformity
known as clinocephaly. Children presenting with clinocephaly tend to
be slightly older. Early or atypical sagittal fusion or the presence of
additional suture involvement requires CT assessment of the minor
sutures and skull base synchondroses [90, 91]. The skull base
synchondroses are typically spared in isolated sagittal synostosis,
however, the foramen magnum often has a smaller volume than
normocephalic controls and the transverse and anterior sagittal
diameters reflect this [92]. Bathrocephaly, a steplike deformity of the
occiput due to overgrowth at lambdoid or accessory occipital
ossification centers or at mendosal sutures remaining patent past
6 months of age is more common in sagittal synostosis than in controls.
Mendosal suture fusion extends centrally to laterally to the asterion,
begins in utero, and usually completes by 8 months of age, although a
delay to 18 months may occur and the presence of lateral mendosal
remnants in normal adult skulls has been reported [93–97]. Unless
syndromic, intracranial abnormalities other than Chiari 1 are
uncommon in isolated sagittal synostosis, however, Chiari 1
malformation is more common with familial cases of sagittal synostosis
and with involvement of multiple sutures or skull base synchondroses
(Fig. 21.14).

Fig. 21.14 Sagittal synostosis. Sagittal-oblique 3D CT reconstruction (a) in a 3-month-old expremature multiple birth infant with scaphocephaly demonstrates typical sagittal synostosis
with bridging (arrow) of the mid to posterior sagittal suture, bullet-shaped occiput, and frontal
bossing. Sagittal T1 (b) in the same child at 19 months old reveals normal AP dimension
following strip craniectomy, but Chiari 1 protrusion (arrow) of the cerebellar tonsils through
foramen magnum. Clinocephaly, saddle-shape depression (arrows) of the retrocoronal vault
due to fusion of the anterior or middle third of the sagittal suture is shown on sagittal (c) and
axial (d) 3D CT reconstructions in a 5-month-old with elongated AP calvarium

Lambdoid synostosis is relatively uncommon, although imaging may
be obtained to differentiate it from posterior positional plagiocephaly.
In unilateral lambdoid synostosis cases, ipsilateral mastoid prominence
occurs due to growth related to the patent posterolateral fontanel and

occipitomastoid synchondrosis and is best shown on frontal or
occipitomental (Waters’ view). Downward shift of the ipsilateral ear
and petrous bone occurs. There may be posterior fontanel deviation
and skull base tilting. While ipsilateral forehead flattening occurs in
unilateral lambdoid synostosis, contralateral forehead flattening occurs
in posterior positional plagiocephaly, leading to a trapezoid
configuration in unilateral lambdoid synostosis and a parallelogram
configuration on axial CT in posterior positional plagiocephaly (Fig.
21.5). Bilateral lambdoid synostosis is often syndromic, seen in cases of
FGFR-related bicoronal synostosis, where Chiari 1 malformations and
increased intracranial pressure are common. Syndromic lambdoid
synostosis may progress to involve contiguous sutures and
synchondroses. Associated mendosal suture synostosis is often present
in both unilateral and bilateral lambdoid synostosis. Lambdoid
synostosis, brachycephaly, and posterior skull flattening have also been
reported in rhombencephalosynapsis [98–100] (Fig. 21.15).

Fig. 21.15 Lambdoid synostosis. Posterior 3D CT (a) obtained in a 3-month-old infant without
a defined genetic mutation shows an indented skull base (asterisk), bilateral lambdoid
synostosis (arrow), closed mendosal sutures, and lacunae. Sagittal T2 MRI (b) in same infant
confirms parieto-occipital shelf (arrow), but no Chiari 1 malformation at this time. Posterior 3D
CT (c) in a 30-day-old infant shows unilateral fused lambdoid suture (black arrow) and typical
prominent mastoid protrusion (white arrow). Frontal radiograph (d) in a different 11-week-old
infant demonstrates right forehead depression (asterisk) associated with right lambdoid
synostosis and ipsilateral mastoid protrusion (white arrow)

Trisutural fusion of the posterior sagittal suture and both lambdoid
sutures with fusion across the posterior fontanel has been called
Mercedes-Benz synostosis or bilamdoid and sagittal synostosis (BLSS).
This complex craniosynostosis blunts the occipital bullet shape and

may present with brachycephaly and indentation of the suboccipital
bone adjacent to the posterior arc of foramen magnum. Extension to
involve the mendosal sutures and posterior intraoccipital
synchondroses leads to fusion of the inferior internal occipital crest and
to decreased posterior fossa volume. It is associated with Chiari 1
deformation in greater than 50% of involved patients. It also may be an
early presentation of pansynostosis [98, 101–103] (Fig. 21.16).

Fig. 21.16 BLSS (Mercedes-Benz) synostosis. Posterior (a) and lateral 3D CT reconstructions
(b) in a 6-month-old infant with frontal bossing and large anterior fontanel show BLSS-type

fusion of the lambdoid sutures, lambda point (open arrows), and posterior sagittal suture.
Lacunae related to the asymmetric lambdoid fusion are present (black arrows). T2-weighted
axial image (c) in the same infant reveals prominent frontal pericerebral fluid (arrow)
associated with frontal bossing. Sagittal T2 image (d) demonstrates Chiari 1 malformation
(open arrow)

Unlike metopic, sagittal, and lambdoid synostosis, the coronal
suture rarely fuses in isolation. The coronal synostoses are more
complex due to the involvement of the coronal ring/hemi-ring. In
unilateral coronal synostosis, an angle forms between the unfused
sagittal and metopic sutures, with a fulcrum at the bregma. There is a
shallow anterior cranial fossa with flattening of the ipsilateral forehead.
Due to the involvement of the facial sutures, the frontomaxillary,
nasofrontal, and nasomaxillary sutures, there is facial twisting, and the
nasal root points toward the side of the synostosis [104]. Severity of
craniofacial change is related to the differential timing of closure [76].
There may be associated skull base scoliosis or endocranial base
deflection ipsilateral to the side of the involved coronal suture due to
shortening of the ipsilateral zygomatic, sphenoid, and temporal bones
along the sphenozygomatic, sphenoparietal, and sphenotemporal
suture fronts [77, 78, 105] (Fig. 21.17).

Fig. 21.17 Unicoronal synostosis, brain and CSF deformation. Axial 3D CT (a) in a 6-month-old
infant with trisomy 9 demonstrates right unilateral coronal synostosis (arrow) resulting in
tilted sagittal-metopic angle. Axial FLAIR (b) at 9 months of age shows bone buttressing at the
site of fusion (arrow) and deformation of the frontal lobes. Coronal T2 (c) in the same infant
shows prominent fat within “Harlequin” orbit (arrow). Coronal T2-weighted MRI (d) in a
different 1-month-old infant with 22Q11DS and unilateral coronal synostosis shows frontal
lobe dysplasia (asterisk). Lack of anterior falx results in frontal lobe interdigitation. Similar
“Harlequin” orbit is present (arrow)

Bilateral coronal synostoses result in brachycephaly or
brachyturricephaly and narrow bitemporal measurement [1, 87, 88].
Additionally, closure of the posterior branch (sphenoparietal,
sphenosquamous sutures, and the sphenopetrosal synchondrosis) of

the coronal ring in bilateral craniosynostosis leads to nasal stenosis,
and insufficient facial growth. Posterior branch fusion and sphenooccipital synchondroses contribute to maxillary retrusion [106]. Orbital
exophthalmos is present in bilateral syndromic synostosis. Involvement
of the anterior branch of the coronal ring leads to differences in orbital
shape in the coronal synostoses. Coronal suture synostosis begins in
the middle of the suture and progresses outward. “Isolated” coronal
synostosis is diagnosed at a younger age and there is usual progressive
involvement to the lateral frontosphenoidal suture. In a small
percentage, variations of this occur, dependent upon the order of
involvement of the sutures and synchondroses. Vertex (coronal) to
cranial base (frontosphenoidal) vector of fusion involvement is typical,
base to vertex less common. With earlier involvement of the
frontosphenoidal suture, there is a limitation of the vertical deviation of
the greater wing of the sphenoid that gives rise to the taller or
“Harlequin” orbit, while the involvement of the frontosphenoidal suture
leads to a shorter, more oval orbit [77, 78, 107, 108] (Fig. 21.18).

Pansynsostosis or universal synostosis can be acquired or genetic.
Pansynostosis may be seen following severe perinatal insult, such as
hypoxia with brain atrophy. It may also reflect genetic causes, such as
FGFR mutation-related kleeblatschädel, microcephaly, aneuploidy, or

hereditary osteodystrophies (Fig. 21.19). For example, premature
suture fusion has been seen in up to 20% of children with sickle cell
anemia [109]. Progressive postnatal pansynostosis, with normal head
shape, a slowly falling head circumference, and increased intracranial
pressure, may be idiopathic or may be present as a mild syndromic
phenotype [110]. Genetically associated pansynostoses may lead to
typical or atypical skull configurations with or without lacunae. While
symmetrical progression to cloverleaf or kleeblatschädel with orbital
shapes occurs typically with Apert or Crouzon syndromes, asymmetric
multisuture involvement has been reported in Muenke syndrome, all of
which harbor FGFR mutations (Fig. 21.20).

As previously noted, ultra-low-dose CT excels in the evaluation of
the major and minor sutures and synchondroses of the vault arches and
skull base. Early fusion of the skull base synchondroses is a clue to
potential complex or progressive craniosynostosis and for
complications related to the foramen magnum and craniocervical
junction. Ventrally, the basioccipital bone joins the basisphenoid at the
spheno-occipital synchondrosis, a component of the lambdoid arch. The
spheno-occipital synchondrosis is considered a pivot point for
craniofacial growth. A dense focal nodule of midline ossification
bridging the spheno-occipital synchondrosis is usually visible on axial
and sagittal reformats at around 8 years of age. Symmetric ossification
centers lateral to this center may be seen within the synchondrosis
before fusion and a dense continuous line, or fusion scar, can be seen
upon fusion. While fusion is essentially complete in most by 17 years of
age, the age range of complete fusion is variable, ranging between 6 and
27 years. Remnants may persist until later. Once fused, the sphenoid
sinus reaches the clivus in nearly half [60–62, 79]. The spheno-occipital
and intersphenoid synchondroses fuse considerably earlier in patients
with FGFR mutations, including Apert, Crouzon, Pfeiffer syndromes,
and achondroplasia, correlating with severity of midface hypoplasia
and retrusion, and giving rise to a narrow skull base with potential
intrasphenoid or intrasellar “kissing” carotid arteries [37, 63, 64, 79,
111] (Fig. 21.10c, d). Surrounding the foramen magnum are the
basioccipital, exoccipital, and supraoccipital bones. The basioccipital
and exoccipital bones are joined by the anterior intraoccipital
synchondroses on each side. The posterior intraoccipital (innominate)
synchondroses join the exoccipital and supraoccipital bones bilaterally
and fuse. Neither the posterior nor anterior intraoccipital
synchondroses belong to the sutural arches. The anterior intraoccipital
synchondroses show partial fusion at 3.5 years and complete fusion
around 7 to 10 years of age. The posterior intraoccipital synchondroses
show partial fusion between 12 and 17 months of age and complete
fusion by 4 years of age. Anterior and posterior intraoccipital
synchondroses should be compared with age-matched controls, as
early fusion may predate progressive cranial synostosis. Foramen
magnum restriction can be marked and progressive in the FGFR
mutation-related syndromes, including achondroplasia, Crouzon,

Pfeiffer, Apert, and Muenke syndromes. Decrease in size of the
synchondroses and early closure or ossification in the youngest infants
and newborns is associated with foramen magnum coarctation and
progression to pansynostosis and kleeblatschädel (Fig. 21.21). Foramen
magnum restriction may already be restricted at birth, prior to the
development of demonstrable calvarial suture fusion. There are some
differences amongst the various syndromic synchondroses. Evaluation
of the cranial base in achondroplasia and thanatophoric dysplasia
demonstrates earlier bridging of the anterior intraoccipital
synchondrosis [112]. The foramen magnum in achondroplasia narrows
rapidly in the first year of life, particularly in the transverse dimension.
In Crouzon, the spheno-occipital, petrooccipital, and intraoccipital
synchondroses fuse earlier than controls and may completely fuse in
the first year of life [113, 114]. Foramen magnum surface area is
smaller in Crouzon and Pfeiffer syndromes than Apert, while the
transverse diameter of the foramen magnum is smaller in
achondroplasia, Crouzon, Pfeiffer, and Apert syndromes. Of the FGFRrelated syndromes, Crouzon shows a reduced AP dimension, while
Pfeiffer and Apert show elongation. Saethre-Chotzen, related to TWIST1 mutation, only shows a mild decrease in the foramen magnum area,
reflecting a decrease in the AP measurement of the anterior foramen
magnum from basion to the posterior margin of the anterior
intraoccipital synchondrosis. Not all Muenke cases show early
intraoccipital synchondrosis fusion. A similar decrease in the anterior
foramen magnum AP dimension is reported in scaphocephalic patients,
resulting in a decrease in area, but to a lesser degree than in the
brachycephalic patients. The foramen magnum is typically spared in
isolated bicoronal synostosis [42, 92, 115–119]. There is also a small
Kerckring supraoccipital synchondrosis between the inferior margin of
the supraoccipital bone and Kerckring’s ossicle, the latter forming the
opisthion, or midpoint of the posterior arc of the foramen magnum.
Kerckring’s ossicle or center may appear ossified in the late third
trimester. This ossicle is variably visible in term births, with fusion in
the first 3–4 months of postnatal life. Early or delayed incorporation of
Kerckring’s ossicle leads to stenosis in the former and a keyhole-shaped
foramen magnum in the latter [21, 79, 113, 120].

21 3 CNS Abnormalities in the
Craniosynchondroses

The first mechanism suggested to explain the clinical manifestations of
CS sounded obvious: brain growth restriction, based on the thendominant idea that the skull expanded as an effect of the cerebral
growth during the first months of life. Premature fusion of the sutures
would thus prevent adaptation to cerebral growth. Modern CT and MR
morphometry studies, however, show that the volume of the brain and
of the intracranial spaces is normal or even increased in patients with a
craniosynostosis of any type, except in the rare cases of pansynostosis.
Increased ventricular volume is largest in the syndromic bicoronal
synostoses, Apert Syndrome in particular [121–125]. Also, modern data
has made it clear that it is not the brain parenchymal volume, but CSF
pressure, that drives the expansion of the vault. Neuroimaging
demonstrates that the peri-cerebral space can be prominent in the fetus
and maintained after birth, and for life, over the supra-Sylvian convexity
in normal individuals. Therefore, while the cranial expansion may be
prevented locally by an early sutural fusion, the force exerted by the
CSF may induce a compensatory enlargement of the skull away from it
[126–129], resulting in typical cranial deformities, which in turn allow
the commonly observed “deformation” of the brain, as it adapts to the
shape of the cranial cavity (Fig. 21.22).

Fig. 21.22 Brain deformation. Axial 3D CT (a) reconstruction in a 28-day-old infant with
congenital plagiocephaly and skull base deflection demonstrates buttressed right sphenoid
greater wing (black arrow) associated with unicoronal synostosis. There is right mendosal and
lambdoid synostosis (open arrow). The ipsilateral posterior intraoccipital suture is closed.
Axial T2 (b) shows right cerebellar compression (open arrow) and enlargement of the left
middle cranial fossa CSF (white arrow) contralateral to the synostosed coronal suture. Coronal

reveals associated distortion (arrow) of the left frontal lobe

21 3 1 The CSF in Craniosynostoses

Increased intracranial pressure (ICP) has been suggested as a possible
cause for delays in neurodevelopment, by affecting the cerebral (mostly
cortical) blood flow, or even by preventing a normal development of the
cortex. It may also affect vision and is made worse by the occurrence of
obstructive sleep apnea in patients with facial deformities. A high ICP
can be identified by clinical evidence, such as increased cranial
volume/head circumference, or even papilledema, and can be
confirmed and monitored instrumentally. It is quite common in complex
forms of craniosynostosis: Apert (up to 83%), Crouzon (up to 64%),
Saethre-Chotzen (up to 43%), multisuture (up to 67%), and bicoronal
(up to 31%) synostosis. It is also observed in a significant number of
single-suture craniostenosis cases: sagittal (up to 14%) coronal (up to
16%), or metopic (up to 8%) [4, 124, 129, 130]. It may be present
without enlarging the head. It may also present as an accumulation of
CSF, either due to a deficit of absorption, or with an obstruction the CSF
pathways; both absorptive and obstructive (loss of compliance)
processes are usually associated. Useful imaging features include inner
table scalloping, crowding of the posterior fossa, and distortion or
disruption of the venous system.
In infants, a defect of CSF absorption typically results in the pattern
of an external hydrocephalus (or benign arachnoid CSF collection),
intracranial accumulation of CSF with macrocephaly. This can appear
and develop whenever the arteriovenous compliance is reduced by an
increased venous outflow resistance while the CSF absorption is
decreased, occurring when the venous outlets are restricted. A study
evaluating the utility of MR venograms has shown that the pattern of
the dural sinuses is commonly incomplete in young children with
external hydrocephalus [45], in a way that is actually often referred to
as a “normal anatomic variant,” possibly erroneously. Such a process of
restriction of the venous outlets is evident in cases of sagittal
synostosis when the abnormal growth of the sutural tissue surrounds
the superior sagittal sinus. The ridges of the resultant furrow may form
an -like overgrowth on either side of the superior sagittal sinus [130,
131], which may impact the CSF absorption by reducing the caliber of
the sinus itself, or by partially obstructing the outlets of the cortical
veins when they connect with the sinus, either directly or through the
parasagittal dura. The alleged involvement of the arachnoid

granulations seems unlikely in infants, as the practice of cranial
venography at this age has revealed that they have not really developed
yet. In any case, the high venous pressure associated with CSF retention
may produce a CSF collection as long as the calvarium is capable of
expansion. A similar process of bony overgrowth with venous
compromise has been convincingly demonstrated in a series of cases of
metopic craniosynostosis, with, in addition, the early development of
emissary veins along the anterior sagittal midline correlating with both
an -shaped bony ridge and subarachnoid prominence of the CSF
spaces [132]. Consequentially, whenever the development of an
external hydrocephalus is suspected, neuroimaging must include
coronal images in addition to the traditional axial images, to better
appreciate the bony changes and the peri-cerebral spaces of the vertex.
It should also include imaging of the dural venous sinuses, as low down
as the upper cervical region to evaluate the patency of the cranial
venous drainage.
By contrast, an obstructive hydrocephalus is characterized
morphologically by a dilatation of the ventricles with an effacement of
the peri-cerebral spaces, clinically by the evidence of intracranial
hypertension, clinically by a slowly enlarging head, and on serial (if
needed) imaging, by a progressive enlargement of the ventricle. It is
important to stress that the ventricular dilatation is not, in itself, a
proof of obstructive hydrocephalus. It is present, although usually mild,
in nonobstructive hydrocephalus. More importantly, a nonprogressive
ventriculomegaly is common in complex craniosynostoses, reported in
30–70% of Crouzon/Pfeiffer patients, and in 40–90% of Apert patients
[133], and can be explained by a developmental defect of the white
matter. Hydrocephalus is considered as probably incidental, when
observed in a simple craniosynostosis. In syndromic craniosynostoses,
on the contrary, real progressive obstructive hydrocephalus does occur,
affecting up to 15% in the whole group of patients, but up to 88% in the
group of Pfeiffer type 2 [134]. It is generally closely associated with the
presence of a Chiari 1 deformity, which is particularly common in
Crouzon, Pfeiffer/Cloverleaf skull, and multisuture synostoses involving
the lambdoid suture. Yet, its pathogenesis in complex craniosynostosis
is unclear, and it probably results from the occurrence of several
separate but convergent actors. Of course, the effacement of the

posterior fossa cisterns and the small size of the foramen magnum may
play a role, but cannot be the whole story, as in other contexts, a Chiari
1 deformity is typically not associated with hydrocephalus, and a
surgical correction of the Chiari 1 in complex craniosynostosis does not
necessarily cure the hydrocephalus. The association of the venous
factors to the posterior fossa abnormalities is therefore felt to be
determinant. This restriction of the venous outflow can convincingly be
explained by the severe bony narrowing of the jugular and possibly
also, by an abnormal dural proliferation [47, 48]. The effects of this
narrowing may be made more severe in the context of the anatomical
and physiological changes of the cranial drainage that take place when
the standing position is being acquired. Subsequently, with progressive
bony restriction of the jugular foramen and jugular vein attenuation,
collateral drainage develops via the emissary veins of the posterior
fossa [36, 47, 48]. In the meantime, however, three factors are
significant: (1) the anatomical restriction of the venous outflow
decreases the compliance of the system to the force exerted by the
systolic wave, as most of the systolic blood volume goes directly into
the veins (continuous systolo-diastolic arterio-venous flow); (2) the
high venous pressure opposes the parenchymal and trans-dural
absorption of the CSF; (3) the turgor of the venous channels adds its
own mass effect the intracranial content. The CSF compliance being at
the same time reduced by the effacement of the cisternal spaces and
fourth ventricle in the posterior fossa, the addition of those factors may
well explain the development of a progressive hydrocephalus. Of note,
however, it has been mentioned that hyperactivation of FGFR2 could
also be involved in a hydrocephalic process [135].

21 3 2 Brain Abnormalities in Craniosynostosis
The most striking deformity of the neural axis that results from the
bony abnormalities is Chronic Tonsillar Herniation, also known as a
Chiari 1 deformity. In syndromic craniosynostosis, hydrocephalus is

associated with a Chiari 1 deformity in most of the cases, but only 47%
of cases of Chiari 1 deformity are associated with hydrocephalus [99]. It
is now admitted that in general, Chiari 1 is not a cerebellar
malformation per se (except in very rare instances), but a cerebellar
deformation that appears when the cerebellum expands normally into
too small a posterior fossa; it is a primarily bony, not neural problem
[136]. It is a common finding in the context of some, but not all,
syndromic craniosynostosis: 72.7% of Crouzon; 50% of Pfeiffer; 100%
of Cloverleaf; but only 1.9% of Apert syndrome. The difference reflects
the variation in fusion of the intraoccipital synchondroses [99]. In
Crouzon and Pfeiffer syndromes, all spheno-occipital, posterior
intraoccipital, and anterior intraoccipital sutures close early as
compared with normal individuals; in Apert syndrome, only the
spheno-occipital and posterior intraoccipital sutures do so, while the
anterior intraoccipital sutures close at a more normal time [118]. This
results in the posterior fossa being reduced in all diameters in the two
former ones, while remaining transversally preserved in the later. In
addition, it was demonstrated [99] that it is the early fusion of the
lambdoid suture that precipitates the process of chronic tonsillar
herniation through the foramen magnum: this happens much earlier in
Crouzon or Pfeiffer syndromes than in Apert syndrome. The anterior
fontanel remains enlarged in Apert syndrome well beyond the time of
closure in the other bicoronal craniosynostoses [122].
Although the presence of a Chiari 1 is occasionally seen in the
presence of an otherwise isolated sagittal suture stenosis, the presence
of it should alert to the possibility of either an undiagnosed syndrome
or a familial case. In particular, the bony components of the fourth
occipital sclerotome should be evaluated. Also, while a Chiari 1
deformity is not usually seen in association with a single-suture
metopic, or coronal craniosynostosis, it is found in 25–50% of cases of
nonsyndromic bilateral lambdoid synostosis, and in 70% of the cases of
nonsyndromic multiple-suture craniosynostosis when the lambdoid
suture is involved, against 7% if it is not [4]. On MR imaging, the
diagnosis of a Chiari 1 deformity in this context is not different from
what it is in other contexts: complete effacement of the cisterna magna,
descent of the cerebellar tonsils across the foramen magnum, and
depending on the severity, effacement the prepontine cistern and

fourth ventricle, within, often, an abnormally shaped bony posterior
fossa with a concave clivus and an abnormally oriented tentorium.
Other cerebral deformities are observed in craniosynostoses, but
with no, or less significant clinical consequences. As a general rule,
cerebral deformation follows the deformity of the skull. A posterior
displacement of the parietal lobules was described in dolichocephaly,
and a shortening of the anterior frontal lobes in trigonocephaly; the
anterior temporal lobes in the cloverleaf phenotype bulge laterally, and
the temporal horns may be enlarged as well, following the bulge of the
temporal squama. It has been suggested by some authors that these
deformations might explain some of the neurodevelopmental defects
that are observed in growing children. However, such changes develop
progressively, which allows the axons to grow and collaterals to adjust
and probably to maintain normal connections with the cortex.
Many children with single-suture craniosynostosis develop
intellectually in the low range of normality, and more severe intellectual
defects or epilepsy are common in syndromic craniosynostosis, even in
the absence of complications like hydrocephalus. If an early corrective
surgery improves the situation, there is now ample evidence,
pathologically and radiologically, that in most subtypes of
craniosynostosis, the bony changes are associated with abnormal brain
development. In syndromic craniosynostosis, this is consistent with the
fact that Fibroblast Growth Factors FGFs (and their receptors FGFRs)
are ubiquitous in the body and are, beyond the development of bone,
involved, among others, in the development of the central nervous
system (cell proliferation, neuronal differentiation, migration and
apoptosis, presynaptic differentiation). Besides FGFR1, 2, and 3,
TWIST1 (Saethre-Chotzen) modulates the response of FGFRs to FGF
ligands; MSX2 (Boston-type craniosynostosis) modulates the
downstream FGF activity; RAB-23 (Carpenter) regulates negatively the
Hedgehog signaling in the ventral neural tube [137]. The frontal bone,
the coronal suture in part, and the sagittal suture derive from the
anterior Neural Crest Cells [138], which also participate in the
development of the interhemispheric fissure and of the early
commissural plate via Fgf8; FGFR1 and 2 mediate the action of Fgf8,
which acts as an early organizer of the dorsal telencephalon (and of the
brainstem); FGRF1 is essential for the early development of the corpus

callosum, and acts as a receptor for L1CAM in the process of axonal
fasciculation in the brain [139]. The gross malformations that can be
observed in syndromic craniosynostoses concern the midline and the
mesial temporal structures mostly; radiologically, they are more
apparent at the level of the white matter (nonprogressive
ventriculomegaly, callosal hypoplasia).
Apert syndrome (FGFR2; s252w; p253r) is the most common of the
syndromic craniosynostoses, characterized by an early bilateral
coronal, spheno-occipital, and posterior intraoccipital synostosis. Most
children present with a significant developmental delay. They may
present with seizures. The main brain abnormalities are a
nonprogressive ventriculomegaly, rather than hydrocephalus, a
significant callosal hypoplasia, an absence or attenuation of the septum
pellucidum, and an “ammonic hypoplasia,” abnormalities of the
“rhinencephalon” or “olfactory complex”: absence or midline fusion of
the olfactory bulbs, tracts and tubercles; hypoplastic cornu ammonis,
with triangular section of the temporal horn; prominent temporal lobes
with anterior temporal over-convolution (Fig. 21.23) (but the cortex is
histologically normal), yet poorly developed white matter;
characteristically, there is a prominent abnormal inferior-medial
transverse sulcus; All this is already present before the sutural closure
in the fetus [140]; Additionally, the pyramidal tracts are incomplete in
the brainstem [139–145]. Interestingly similar temporal abnormalities
are found in the Pfeiffer syndrome (FGFR2) [140], and in different
syndromes related to FGFR3 mutations (thanatophoric dwarfism,
achondroplasia, and hypochondroplasia) [146–148]. This combined
involvement of the mesial temporal and midline structures suggests the
possibility of hyperactivity of the telencephalic hem, which corresponds
to the lips of the dorsal fusion line of the telencephalon, that is, the
embryonic anterior neural ridge [140]. The hem, which persists in
adulthood as a medial hemispheric medullary velum that contains the
fornix and the septocingulate perforating pathway (septum
pellucidum), is in the 4–5-week-old embryo the inducer laterally, of the
early telencephalic cortical plate (primordial hippocampus) and
medially, of the telencephalic tela choroidea [149].
Crouzon syndrome (FGFR2, multiple mutations) is characterized by
the early closure of the coronal, then lambdoid, spheno-occipital, and

intraoccipital sutures, resulting in a brachycephaly with a small
posterior fossa, in addition to the facial anomalies. Patients usually
present with a Chiari 1 deformity and hydrocephalus is common, with a
venous turgor. Even before hydrocephalus develops, a ventriculomegaly
is observed; defects of the corpus callosum and septum pellucidum may
be present [139, 145]. Abnormalities of the cortex have been described,
as thicker in the frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes and thinner in the
temporal, insular, and cingulate regions [150].
Pfeiffer syndrome type I (FGFR1,2) is characterized by brachycephaly
(coronal synostosis), flat face, and hypertelorism, with a small posterior
fossa with a concave clivus. Neurodevelopmentally the patients may be
normal, or present a mental deficiency; a passive ventriculomegaly or a
Chiari 1 deformity may be observed [139, 151].
Pfeiffer syndrome type 2 (FGFR2) is the most spectacular of all
syndromic craniosynostoses as it presents with a cloverleaf skull: major
brachycephaly and acrocephaly, exophthalmos, a very small posterior
fossa with concave clivus, a diffusely dysplastic calvarium, and a
massive bulging of the temporal squamae. Clinically, mental deficiency,
seizures, and features of severe intracranial hypertension are observed.
Morphologically there is a huge hydrocephalus associated with a severe
form of Chiari 1 deformity. The septum pellucidum is absent, likely due
to hydrocephalus, although a developmental defect cannot be ruled out.
Venography would show a venous turgor with stenosis of the jugular
foramina. There is a major deformation of the brain structures that
results from the abnormal morphology of the calvarium: bulging
temporal lobes with ballooning temporal horns, kinking of the brain
that may be made apparent by the kinking of the corpus callosum, the
occipital lobe being displaced below the third ventricle [139, 151, 152].
Such deformities of course preclude the identification of gross
malformations of the mesial temporal lobes in vivo. The typical
temporal lobe overfolding may become more apparent following
shunting. A pathological study of four fetuses has demonstrated an
outgrowth of the temporal lobes with malformation of the
hippocampus and amygdala, suggesting that the hyperactivity of FGFR2
could, like in the Apert syndrome, result in hyperactivity of the
hemispheric hem with a mesiotemporal dysplasia [135].

Pfeiffer syndrome type 3 (FGFR2) doesn’t present with a cloverleaf
skull, but there is a short anterior cranial fossa and a very small
posterior fossa with a concave clivus. The patients present with
epilepsy, severe neurodevelopmental deficiencies, high intracranial
pressure, and hydrocephalus that can be explained by a Chiari 1
deformity and a stenosis of the venous jugular outlets [136, 151].
Saethre-Chotzen syndrome (TWIST1) is uncommon, and there is only
scarce literature that describes the brain abnormalities [139, 153]. It is
characterized by an acrocephaly/brachycephaly with proptosis and
upper lid ptosis and is due to an early closure of the coronal, lambdoid,
and metopic sutures, which may be associated with late-closing
fontanels however, and parietal foramina. Clinically, affected children
are said to be mentally normal, but some degree of mental retardation
is often observed. Hypotonia is common, and they may present a
pyramidal syndrome (lower limbs). Also, the occurrence of seizures is
not exceptional, and slow waves and spikes are reported [153]. Brain
imaging may be normal, or show enlarged subarachnoid spaces only,
but ventriculomegaly is not mentioned. An abnormal gyration with
pachygyria is described in some cases. No mention is made of the
corpus callosum either, but in one case at least, it appears short and
thickened [139], and “upright” in another report quoted by [153]. A
most striking finding, although subtle, is the abnormal signal of the
white matter, which may indicate a gliosis or a myelination defect.
TWIST1 is an upstream regulator of the FGFR pathways.
Muenke syndrome (FGFR3, p250r mutation) is characterized by a
premature uni-or bilateral coronal synostosis with a variable
phenotype, sensory-neural hearing loss, some intellectual disability,
epilepsy, and a special risk of obstructive sleep apnea [154].
Neuroradiological studies in different patients mention a persistent
cavum septi pellucidi (finding of uncertain significance), agenesis of the
corpus callosum, periventricular hyperintensities (of unclear origin),
and hemimegalencephaly [154]. In one report, illustrations of an MR
study show ventriculomegaly and a striking bilateral dysplasia of the
mesial temporal lobes with a thick, abnormally convoluted cortex, a
poorly defined hippocampus and white matter, and a dilated
ventricular horns, strikingly similar to what is shown in a fellow case in
the same article of a patient with hypochondroplasia, also due to an

FGFR3 mutation [155]; the images presented however do not allow a
complete comparison with the abnormalities described in other
imaging studies of the Apert syndrome [139], thanatophoric dysplasia
[146], and hypochondroplasia [147].
Finally, descriptions of the brain abnormalities in the Carpenter
syndrome (RAB-23 mutation) are few as it is a rare syndrome. The
affected sutures are the uni- or bilateral coronal, sagittal, and lambdoid
sutures. The patients present typically with acrocephaly, but other bony
morphotypes, such as a cloverleaf skull, may be encountered. Patients
present with an (often) profound developmental delay. A poor, bilateral
but asymmetric hemispheric development, an agenesis of the anterior
part of the corpus callosum, and an abnormal gyral pattern have been
described [156].
There are many additional syndromes associated with
craniosynostosis that are worth noting. These include Loeys-Dietz
Syndrome, Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome, velocardiofacial syndrome
(22q11DS), and various aneuploidies including Trisomy 13, amongst
others.
In nonsyndromic craniosynostoses, neural development may be
altered, even if only mildly, typically within the lower range of normal
[124–129, 157, 158]. The cranial deformity, factors like a high ICP, or
even a prolonged hospital environment, may play a role. But even if no
specific genetic disorder is usually identified, it is generally considered
that the same developmental alteration that resulted in the bony
pathology may also have resulted in a cerebral organization disorder.
This is confirmed by multiple studies using MRI tractography, and
functional MRI. The changes in brain organization seem to depend on
the suture involved. In sagittal synostosis, there appears to be a
decreased connectivity in the parietal lobes, involved in visuospatial
cognition, visuomotor integration, and attention; right coronal
synostosis seems to be associated with a decreased connectivity of the
prefrontal cortex, involved in executive functions, language fluency, and
visual attention [159]. Another study suggested that the changes were
not unlike, in their mechanism, those of ADHD, but affected different
cortical areas, with decreased connectivity of the primary visual cortex,
visual association cortex, and visuospatial integration cortex, with loss
of the ability to generate mental images [160]. These troubles may be,

at least in part, corrected by an early release of the sutural synostosis
[157].

22 ENT and Craniosynostosis
Romain Luscan1 and Vincent Couloigner1
(1) Pediatric ENT Department, H pital Necker—Enfants Malades,
Assistance Publique—H pitaux de Paris, Université Paris Cité,
Centre de Référence Malformations Rares en ORL (MALO), Paris,
France

Romain Luscan
Email: romain.luscan@aphp.fr
Vincent Couloigner (Corresponding author)
Email: vincent.couloigner@aphp.fr
Keywords Craniosynostosis – ENT surgeon – OSA – Cartilaginous
sleeve trachea – Hearing loss
ENT specialists are primarily involved in two areas of the follow-up and
treatment of patients with craniosynostosis (CS): obstructive sleep
apnea (OSA) and hearing impairment.
OSA is related to reduced airway patency during sleep. In the case of
CS, it is mainly due to hypoplasia of the middle third of the face, with
subsequent stenosis of the nasal cavities and narrow rhinopharynx
(Fig. 22.1). However, it can also be present in CS forms which do not
encompass midface hypoplasia, such as Muenke or Saethre-Chotzen
syndromes [1].

Fig. 22.1 Cranial CT scan in a 2-month-old child with Crouzon syndrome. (a) Axial section.
Stenosis of the nasal cavities. (b) Sagittal section. Narrowing of the nasopharyngeal airway

Considering the management of nasal obstruction, both medical
(nasal washing with saline, topical steroids, antihistamines in case of
mucosal inflammation) and surgical treatments can be used. The
surgical treatment consists of a bilateral turbinoplasty or turbinectomy
(Fig. 22.2). Enlargement of piriform aperture stenosis is sometimes
necessary. Nasopharyngeal narrowing can be addressed by an
adenoidectomy and a resection of the posterior part of the vomer in
order to artificially increase the depth of the nasopharynx.

Fig. 22.2 Perioperative endoscopic view of a laser turbinectomy (removal of the inferior
turbinates) in a 3-month-old child with Apert syndrome

Tonsillar hypertrophy is also frequently involved in CS-related OSA.
Tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy decrease the apnea—hypopnea
index (AHI) and desaturation index by 5/h and 8.5/h, respectively [2].
It improved OSAS in 60% of cases, but AHI normalization is rare [2].
Drug-induced sleep endoscopy is a very useful procedure to
accurately guide the optimal treatment strategy in children with CS and
severe OSA [3]. It can be proposed before any treatment or after of
adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy.
For patients with very severe OSA and impossibility or failure of
surgical treatment, noninvasive ventilation (NIV) can be proposed.
When NIV is not insufficiently effective or is not tolerated, a
tracheostomy is required.
Tracheal cartilaginous sleeve is another airway disorder that can be
observed in patients with CS [4, 5]. This malformation seems to be

associated with an increased risk of tracheostomy and an increased risk
of morbidity and mortality related to tracheostomy.
Hearing impairment is frequent in CS [6]. The main cause is otitis
media with effusion (OME), which is related to the constitutional
narrowing of the Eustachian tube linked in these patients. Insertion of
ventilation tubes is sometimes necessary to restore normal hearing.
Much more rarely, external ear or ossicular malformations can be
present [6]. Sensorineural hearing loss is mostly observed in Muenke
syndrome [7].

22 1 Conclusions
Given the frequency and the potential severity of respiratory and
auditory disorders in children with CS, yearly ENT visits with wake
upper airway endoscopy and hearing tests are recommended. Early
ENT assessment may be required in case of neonatal respiratory
distress. Additional consultations are sometimes necessary if additional
ENT symptoms appear.
