23 1 Introduction
The life of a child affected by craniosynostosis is impacted in many and
highly variable ways, on account of both of his condition and of the
surgery it leads to. Craniosynostoses are serious malformations, with
often dire consequences, even more so when associated with
faciostenosis. On the other hand, despite constant effort to optimize
results and decrease morbidity, surgery is always an important
undertaking and is associated with a number of unwanted
consequences, during operation, in the immediate postoperative
course, or later in life. For these reasons, it is important to know the
complications of synostoses and of their treatment, in order to inform
the decision to the operated, taken conjointly by the surgeon and the
child’s parents, as well as anticipate surgical difficulties. In the present

chapter, we shall review chronologically the different complications of
craniosynostoses before, during, and after surgery, and their
management and prevention. We shall conclude on the issues of
surgical decision and informed consent and the need for consensual
quantitative scales to evaluate the morphological results as well as
surgical complications.

23 2 Preoperative Complications
23 2 1 Birth Difficulties
The calvarial sutures play an important role in the biomechanics of
birth, and their fusion can have dire consequences [1]. In an earlier,
unpublished study conducted in Lille during the years 2016–2021,
among 233 new cases of craniosynostoses, we found that the overall
prevalence of dystocia (difficult or instrumented birth) was 45.5%;
among these, 30.5% were delivered by C-section (compared with 20%
in the general population in France during that period), 24.4% of them
because of fetal distress. The prevalence of C-section was highest
among boys, and patients with metopic or multisutural synostosis (Fig.
23.1). Dystocia was the cause of birth trauma in four identified cases:
one with sagittal synostosis who developed a large subperiosteal
hematoma (Fig. 23.2a, b); one with metopic synostosis who had
petrous bone fracture and subdural bleeding associated with forceps
delivery (Fig. 23.2c, d); one with unilambdoid synostosis who
developed a subdural hemorrhage; and one with complex multi-suture
synostosis who developed intracerebral hemorrhage (Fig. 23.2e).
Although the mechanical trauma was predominantly mild and had no
or few consequences, dystocia could also cause fetal distress during and
after birth, with potential impact on the patient’s later development.
Birth difficulties could thus be a confounding factor when studying the
developmental impact of brain compression by the synostosis.
Although the majority of children with craniosynostosis are delivered
by natural vaginal delivery, a prenatal diagnosis should reinforce the
vigilance regarding possible dystocia and lower the threshold for
cesarean section.

Fig. 23.1 Conditions of birth in 233 cases of craniosynostoses followed during the period
2016–2019 in Lille. Close to half of these children had delivery difficulties, 30.3% born by Csection, 24.4% by C-section for fetal distress. These birth difficulties can be anticipated in case
of prenatal diagnosis, and may be a confusion factor regarding the developmental outcome

Fig. 23.2 Birth trauma in children with craniosynostosis; (a and b) Sagittal synostosis, with the
characteristic bilateral cephalhematoma, because no periosteal midline adherence limits its
spread; (c and d) Metopic synostosis, with difficult forceps delivery, scalp laceration, fracture of
the petrous bone and subdural bleeding; and (e) A newborn with complex multi-suture
synostosis who developed intracerebral hemorrhage

23 2 2 Brain Compression
Brain decompression by calvarial expansion is the cornerstone of
surgery for craniosynostoses. However, the relation between reduced
intracranial volume and intracerebral pressure is complex, certainly
underpinned by poorly understood hydrodynamic mechanisms [2].

Multiple suture synostoses, mostly syndromic, are associated with
raised intracranial pressure (ICP), which increases with the number of
fused sutures [3]. Calvarial growth restriction is often the main
presenting symptom of multisuture craniosynostoses, sometimes
present at birth in case of cloverleaf malformation, or later during
progression toward oxycephaly, with progressive closure of the
different sutures [4].
By contrast, in unisutural synostoses, the initial presentation in
early childhood is mostly related to morphological concerns, and the
brain is generally not compressed initially. Typically, the closure of the
sagittal suture is compensated by the coronal and metopic sutures,
giving the child his typical dolichocephalic appearance with a bulging
forehead and an above-normal head circumference. However, in older
children, sagittal synostosis can mimic pseudotumor cerebri [5], and is
a not an uncommon finding in clinically eloquent tonsillar herniation
[6]. Similarly, ICP can rise late after correction of unisutural synostosis,
because of non-synchronous multisuture synostosis [7].
Regarding metopic synostosis, the occurrence of brain compression
and the benefit of decompressive surgery are controversial. While some
authors have documented intracranial hypertension [8], others, using
sophisticated imaging techniques, found no evidence of brain
compression [9]. Better developmental outcomes have been reported in
all types of craniosynostoses when surgery was performed before the
age of 1 year [10]; however, in this retrospective study, the reason why
some children were operated early, and others later, was not analyzed.
A more recent study has found that the late surgery was associated
with confounding factors susceptible to influence developmental
outcome, such as social context, prematurity, and co-morbidities [11].

23 2 3 Psychosocial Impact of Morphological Disgrace
Difficulties can arise during childhood because of the morphological
disgrace, leading to problems of self-image, taunting and even
harassment by schoolmates (and even occasionally by teachers!). The
psychological impact at school age should not be taken lightly.
Compounded with the parental stress, which children and infants feel
and absorb like sponges, this psychological burden may play a
significant role in the future life of these patients. Very rarely, the

demand for morphological correction is not expressed until adult age
[12]. Moreover, in familial cases, the demand for early morphological
correction for their child, coming from affected parents, is revealing.

23 3 Intraoperative Complications
23 3 1 Anesthesia and Installation
Complications of anesthesia and installation are the shared
responsibility of the surgeon and the anesthetist. Among these, the risk
of complications of venous and arterial catheters, and pressure sores
on the scalp or eyeballs (Fig. 23.3) must be decreased by scrupulous
attention from both teams.

Fig. 23.3 Complications of the arterial catheter (a), of peripheral venous catheters (b), of
positioning (c and d) are a shared responsibility of the surgeon and anesthetist

23 3 2 Bleeding
Intraoperative bleeding occurring, whatever the technique chosen, is
the most threatening complication during surgery, with a potential for
fatal consequences, and requires blood transfusion in a number of
patients. The importance of bleeding relates to the body proportions in
infants, with a larger head and a limited blood volume (estimated
around 500 ml at 3 months and 750 ml at 9 months) compared to
adults. Diffuse bleeding comes from the scalp, the dura-mater (in

particular arachnoid villi, which appear around 9 months) and above all
from the bone, especially at the skull base. In craniosynostosis surgery,
bleeding is increased by enlarged trans-osseous veins and intracranial
hypertension. Clotting problems can result from profuse bleeding and
hypothermia, so a high degree of vigilance and close interactions
between surgeon and anesthetist are warranted, in order to avoid
entering a fatal spiral.
Rigorous anesthesia protocols are followed in order to monitor
hemodynamics; near-infra red spectroscopy can help to determine if
and when transfusion must be decided (Fig. 23.4). In case of profuse
bleeding, supplementation with platelets and clotting factors may also
be needed. Transfusion following all the security protocols incurs
extremely low additional risk, whereas reluctance or delay to transfuse
can have fatal consequences. Although all precautions to diminish the
risk of bleeding should be taken, we consider that transfusion should
not be regarded as a complication. In consequence, the acceptance from
parent that transfusion may be needed is a prerequisite for surgery.

Fig. 23.4 Near-infra red spectroscopy can be used when the forehead is not in the operative
field (sagittal synostosis and posterior pole surgeries), and helps to determine if and when
transfusion is needed

Intraoperative blood loss is anticipated preoperatively by iron
supplementation and/or erythropoietin, and mitigated during surgery

by hemodilution and volume expansion. Meticulous hemostasis at each
stage of the operation requires precise knowledge of where the
bleeding comes from, notably the location of trans-osseous veins (Figs.
23.5 and 23.6). Permanent communication between surgeon and
anesthetist before, during, and after surgery is vital for the successful
management of this potentially lethal complication.

Fig. 23.5 Location of trans-osseous veins in metopic synostosis, numbered according to the
timing of their occurrence during fronto-orbital remodeling

Fig. 23.6 Parietal emissary veins in sagittal synostosis; (a) 3D-CT scanner and (b) Operative
view of the exposed sagittal sinus, patient in the prone position

23 3 3 Dural Tear
Even though most dural tears occur at a distance from the venous
sinuses, dural lesions, even when involving only the outer layer,
increase blood loss, and, if left unattended, can initiate a meningocele.
Bleeding can become catastrophic if a dural tear involves a venous
sinus (Fig. 23.7). The risk of dural tear is diversely evaluated, because
not all authors take note of the minimal splits of the dural outer layer.
Endoscopic techniques may not lead to more dural tears [13], but make
these more difficult to cope with. The risk of dural tear is higher in
newborns, in children with longstanding intracranial hypertension, in
craniofacial advancement [14] and in redo surgery [15], especially after
previous dural repair. Dural adherences are intense along the sutures,
in particular underneath the fontanels and epactal bones, and on the
midline of the skull base. Opening of the sagittal sinus is thus at higher
risk when the metopic suture is still patent [1]. The adherence of patent
sutures to the dura is especially tricky in unilambdoid synostosis,
because the lateral sinus is often lacking on the synostotic side [16],

and the sinus on the non-synostotic, adherent side is compensatorily
enlarged.

Fig. 23.7 Cloverleaf skull, operated on D5 of life because of life-threatening intracranial
hypertension with tonsillar herniation. (a) CT-scanner showing the lacunae and complex
sutural pattern around the lesser fontanelle. (b) Operative view showing limited dural tear
close to the posterior fontanel

Dural tear at the skull base is a not uncommon complication of the
different techniques of fronto-orbital advancement in
craniofaciosynostoses [14, 17], with a high risk of cerebrospinal fluid
leakage and meningeal infection. Although these leaks can often dry
spontaneously, intracranial dural repair is sometimes necessary (Fig.
23.8).

Fig. 23.8 Two-year-old femaleoperated for Crouzon disease with Le Fort 3 osteotomy because
of severe sleep apneas (a) coronal and (b) sagittal view. She developed rhinorrhea because of
ethmoidal dural tear (empty arrow); note intradural pneumocephalus (full arrow), which
required craniotomy for duraplasty

Partial dural tears, limited to the outer dural layer, should be
reapproximated by a few stitches whenever possible, sometimes
completed with fibrin glue. Complete dural tears must be repaired with
a running suture as watertight as possible, which may require
harvesting an epidural graft.
The prevention of dural tears involves careful dissection of bone
from permeable fontanels, and of sutures from the underlying sinuses
before using the craniotome. Use of the burr over the pterional and
asterial fontanels should be especially cautious. Dissection of the dura
from the bone can be tedious, on account of adherences and uneven
inner surface of the calvaria, as well as frequent bleeding from the
middle meningeal artery or dural veins. In very small infants with
cloverleaf malformation, patient dissection of the lacunae and epactal
bones, followed by piecemeal removal of the bone septa, often
extending deep between the sulci, is the most delicate time of
suturectomy [18].

23 4 Early Postoperative Period

23 4 1 The Emotional Shock
In the immediate postoperative days, parental distress is almost
constant [19]. In addition to the child being in pain, or drowsy and
feeding poorly on account of opioid medications, he often presents with
facial edema, of variable severity but which can be major and
complicated by chemosis, and even subluxation of the tarsal cartilage.
The child’s ordeal appeals to his parent’s feelings of guilt over their
decision to have him operated, and echoes with the guilt which is very
widespread in parents of a child with inborn diseases, especially if
genetically determined. When the edema subsides, the change in facial
features, which was the purpose of the operation, can be difficult to
cope with. The rare complaint “it’s not my child anymore” is only the
most radical expression of a widespread parental unease. To make
things worse, parental stress is absorbed by the child, so that parental
and infantile stress amplify each other in a play of mirrors. This often
translates into sleepless nights back home, regressive reactions, with
often prolonged co-sleeping. This postoperative stress should not be
overlooked and must be anticipated. Physical contact, cradling, and
cuddling should be encouraged immediately after surgery. Before
surgery, parents should be informed of the oncoming physical changes
and convinced that the child’s appearance will be “more normal,” and
that he will have “the head he should have had.” Contacts with patients’
associations can be a precious resource for these parents, who can thus
interact with others who “have been through that” before them.

23 4 2 Infection
Infection is a rare complication but can prolong hospital stay and have
dire consequences. A sepsis can result of operative site infection (OSI)
or venous or urinary catheter. However, aseptic fever is common, on
account of the large subcutaneous exposure, and should not lead to
untimely antibiotic treatments. By contrast, the reappearance of fever
and scalp edema after initial subsidence should raise alarm of OSI.
Operative site infection occurs in up to 7% [20], and can be
epidermal, dermal, or deep. OSI is sometimes elicited by the child
scratching his wound, or initiated by inflammation caused by
absorbable sutures, or skin necrosis due to tension closure associated
with ambitious calvarial expansion. It can also be a consequence of

incidental respiratory or ocular infection present at the time of surgery;
in these cases, it is wise to postpone the scheduled operation, provided
that the infection is circumstantial and not chronic, in relation with
faciostenosis, and also that the child has no menacing intracranial
hypertension. Other potential factors associated with postoperative
infection are the long duration of surgery [21], the extended incision,
opening of the facial sinuses, the creation of an epidural dead space,
skin breakdown, the presence of implanted material, especially external
distractors [22] or springs, and prolonged use of venous or urinary
catheter.
Whereas superficial scalp infection usually requires only local
measures (removal of scabs and remaining sutures plus local
antiseptics), superficial suppuration may be aggressive, the scab
protecting an ecosystem in which staphylococcus aureus thrives; in
addition to scab removal, oral antibiotics may be necessary. Deep
suppuration is rare but can be associated with septic signs, and require
debridement, drainage, and irrigation in addition to antibiotics [23].
The management of these postoperative empyema should be as
conservative as possible, because wide opening and dismantling of the
construct would devascularize the bone flaps, and bone necrosis would
have catastrophic morphological consequences (Fig. 23.9).

Fig. 23.9 Crouzon syndrome, first operated for posterior pole expansion at 6 months,
reoperated at 5 years for fronto-orbital advancement. The child presented with fistulization of
an epidural empyema, which was treated with antibiotics, prolonged drainage-irrigation, and
directed scarring (at day 16 (a), day 31 (b), day 46 (c) and day 95 (d))

Prevention of local and deep infection implies rigorous asepsis,
before, during, and after surgery, and high-quality layered closure
without excessive tension. The child must be prevented from scratching
his wound, sometimes with the help of antihistamine medications.
Prophylactic antibiotics are administered routinely during surgery,
justified by the extent of surgery, its duration, and the potential gravity
of OSI; however, protocols vary and are mostly tradition-based [24].

23 4 3 Complications of Implants and Fixation Devices
Aseptic subcutaneous granulomas can develop on absorbable sutures
and plates, and take months to disappear, but require nothing more
than reassuring words. During surgery, simple precautions can
decrease these benign but vexing complications, like avoiding to place
knots over salient facial features, cutting threads short, and burying the
knots in bone perforations. Bone fixation with wires is generally well
tolerated but can lead to skin compromise or perforation [23], as well
as migrate inward into the dura as the calvaria grows by appositionresorption, and should be used sparingly (Fig. 23.10). The same
happens with much more serious consequences with non-absorbable
plates [25], springs, and prosthetic materials [26]. Absorbable plates
are generally well tolerated but can also cause aseptic granulomas, and
migrate, both inward and outward [27, 28].

Fig. 23.10 Complications of wires: outward migration of wires (a and b) can threaten or
perforate the scalp (b), while their inward migration (c and d), caused by resorptional calvarial
growth, brings these into contact or conflict with the dura (d)

23 4 4 Scalp and Calvarial Breakdown

Skin or bone disruption generally results of excessive tension of the
scalp, after generous volume expansion; it almost never happens after
external trauma.
Skin breakdown occurs mostly in children with multisuture
synostosis, especially in older children and after redo surgery. Even
when the underlying bone is exposed, it rarely causes serious infection,
but may require prolonged directed scarring, or sometimes
reoperation. Breakdown is prevented by progressive scalp traction,
which is one of the important advances brought about by distraction
techniques. Alternately, scalp expansion using a balloon expander can
be proposed, provided that the child’s calvaria is already rigid enough
not to cave in, and surgery can be programmed some time in advance.
Bone dislocation is a rare but worrisome complication.
Cranioplasties are at best semi-rigid constructs, especially in young
infants, and the mechanical compression by scalp traction can be
enough to cause breakdown of construct. The lordosis of the frontoorbital bandeau is caused by breakage of plates [29] or bone
dislocation at the pterion, especially if the coronal suture is
incompletely fused (Fig. 23.11). The fronto-malar synfibrosis is also a
weak point, where fixation of the lateral orbital pillar can give way.
Bone breakdown also occurs in redo surgery, because regenerative
bone becomes brittle. The occurrence of “gull-winging” (the uplifting of
the parietal bone by disjunction of sutures) happens after posterior
distraction [30], as the consequence of distracting a patent or
incompletely fused suture. Anterior distraction procedures can also
cause skull base dislocation, causing optic neuropathy after monobloc
osteotomy [31], or oculomotor paralysis on account of spheno-petrous
(“Le Fort 6”) dislocation (Fig. 23.12). All these complications impose
reoperations and/or reappraisal of the surgical strategy.

Fig. 23.11 Breakdown of construct caused by dislocation of the fronto-sphenoidal suture
under the tension of scalp, resulting in lordosis of the bandeau, lifted 12 mm, with eye exposure
and pulsating exophthalmos, and requiring reoperation for refixation of bandeau

Fig. 23.12 Fifteen-months-old child with Crouzon disease, operated for fronto-orbital
advancement with transfacial pin; axial CT scanner performed on D14 of craniofacial
distraction because of abducens palsy, showed spheno-temporal (“Le Fort 6”) dislocation
(arrows)

23 4 5 Growing Fracture

Postoperative leptomeningeal cysts or growing fractures develop as a
result of untended intraoperative dural tear or postoperative dural
necrosis, with the brain herniating through the rent and preventing it
from healing. It can develop after endoscopic surgery, because dural
tear can be unnoticed or because dural repair is most uneasy [32]. The
pressure gradient causes focal hydrodynamic disturbance, with
enlarged Virchow-Robin spaces [33].
Anatomical repair of the dura and calvaria is necessary (Fig. 23.13).
Whenever possible, autologous materials are highly preferable [33, 34].
The management of postoperative leptomeningeal cysts can be
challenging because of the tension of the brain (which may require
temporary lumbar drainage); of the proximity of the dural defect to the
sinuses; of the extent of bone defect requiring a large donor site; of the
young age of the child whose thin calvaria is difficult to split. However,
modern high-speed motors and piezoelectric saws allow the splitting of
calvaria in very young children [35].

Fig. 23.13 Growing fracture (a) Seven-months male operated 2 months earlier for sagittal
synostosis (H-craniectomy with linear coagulation of the dura mater and no drainage, causing
dural necrosis). (b) Note the thickened bone margins (full arrows) due to uplifting of the
periosteal tissues; (b, c) the herniated brain tissue is highly edematous, due to expansion of
Virchow-Robin spaces; (e) The margins of the dural defect are much retracted (empty arrows),
requiring a large pericranial autograft (f). The bone defect is bridged with split calvarial
autograft (g)

23 5 Late Surgical Outcome
23 5 1 The Scar
Whatever the surgery, it leaves a scar. However much, as A. Raimondi
quipped, the infant’s scalp may be “forgiving,” the scar can be a problem
for the child’s self-image and a source of embarrassment. Its perception
is highly variable: while some children shun going to the swimming
pool for fear that their scar might show through wet hair, others glorify
it with creative hairstyle (Fig. 23.14). Like any bodily imperfection, the
scar can be a fixation point for teasing, taunting, and harassment at
school age, as well as self-depreciation at adolescence. In order to make
the scar as stealthy as possible, its curve should as much as possible
keep a 90° orientation relative to the direction of hair. When a father
has a receding hairline, his son’s incision may need to be more
posterior than usual. In complex synostoses, it should be kept in mind
that repeated surgeries may be needed in the future, and that the
bicoronal incision should be versatile enough to give access to both the
posterior and anterior poles. This may be problematic when the initial
surgery was endoscopic, with two scars, one very anterior, and the
other very posterior.

Fig. 23.14 (a) Discrete “lazy S” incision, curved in order to stay perpendicular to the natural
direction of hair, leaves the most discreet scar; (b) “Zig-zag” scar, intended to be easily hidden,
but glorified by creative haircut; (c) Early, wide, and red scar, destined to whiten with time; (d)
Persistent Keloid scar of the scalp incision and of the drain

23 5 2 Redo Operations
Reoperations can be needed, sometimes many years after the initial
surgery. The larger or lesser importance of these reoperations led
Whitaker et al. to propose a grading of surgical results as: (1) not

requiring reoperation; (2) minor reoperation proposed; (3) reoperation
less than initial surgery necessary; and (4) reoperation as large or more
than initial surgery [36]. In addition to the operative complications
mentioned above, many of which can require additional surgery, other
operations may become necessary during follow-up.
Incomplete reossification of the calvaria leaves pulsating lacunae.
These occur in about 5% of the operated cases, and appear to be more
frequent in the fronto-orbital advancement [37], and occipital pole
remodeling [38]. Lacunae most often sit close to the midline, especially
at the vertex, and occur most often after extensive midline bone
resection [39], all the more in older children. On account of their
location, calvarial lacunae present no risk of traumatic brain injury, and
no limitations should be imposed on the child’s activities. Lacunae thus
present mostly an aesthetic problem, although some children also
experience the “syndrome of the trephined,” with headaches or
learning difficulties, and changes in the cerebral blood flow have been
documented in some cases [38]. The surgical management of persistent
lacunae can be proposed after the fifth or sixth birthday, and the most
desirable technique is autologous graft by split calvaria [35] (Fig.
23.15).

Fig. 23.15 Persisting lacuna at the vertex after craniectomy at 4 months for sagittal synostosis;
repair age 4 years, using split calvaria. (a) The craniotomy for the donor site is tailored on a
template outlined around the limits of the lacuna; (b) The flap is then split using the
piezoelectric saw; (c) Both bone tables are fixed rigidly in place in order to fill the lacuna and
the donor site

Temporal hollowing is specific problem with metopic synostosis,
and can result from atrophy of the temporal muscle compounded with
excessive restoration of frontal bosses. The progressive nature of this
imperfection, which becomes more apparent with time (Fig. 23.16),
suggests that bone growth is focally disturbed by surgery, possibly
because the greater wing of the sphenoid needs the strain of muscles to
sustain its growth. Temporal hollowing can be well accepted, or lead to
a demand for esthetic correction; this is easily performed by lipofilling,
which can be repeated as needed, but should preferably be delayed
until adolescence. Different technical refinements have been proposed
in order to reduce the prevalence of temporal hollowing, like large
temporal “elephant ears” [40], or tongue-and groove bandeau
advancement, with mixed results leaving room for improvement.

Fig. 23.16 Progressive temporal hollowing after surgery for metopic synostosis

23 5 3 Other Craniofacial Operations
Other major craniofacial operations are often needed in
craniofaciostenoses, in order to correct midface retrusion or
hypertelorism. Secondary multisuture synostosis should be expected in
syndromic craniofaciostenoses [4] as well as in lambdoid synostosis
[16], but are rare in sagittal synostosis, occurring in about 2% of cases
[39], and are almost never found in non-syndromic metopic synostosis.
Secondary closure of new sutures attests of the progressive nature of
the disease, and these reoperations should not be regarded as
complications of surgery. However, this information regarding this

evolution should be given to parents as early as the first consultation, in
particular in case of prenatal diagnosis.
In addition, other relatively minor operations may be needed, such
as onlay grafts, rhinoplasty, removal of facial scars, correction of slant
eyes, or of strabismus. Ideally, all these operations, which are mostly
destined to improve cosmesis, should be performed at the end of
growth and on demand from the patient himself.
The large array of different operations, implicating different surgical
specialists, at different ages, underlines the importance of prolonged
multidisciplinary follow-up.

23 5 4 Morphological Result
Although the Whitaker classification mentioned above [36] is
convenient and widely accepted [41], this classification is focused on
reinterventions, not on morphology, and does not quantify the
preoperative dysmorphism; for these reasons, it does not evaluate
accurately morphological results. Obviously, the objective
quantification of something as subjective as morphological disgrace has
proved difficult.
The evaluation of results by satisfaction questionnaires filled by the
parents may be fraught with complacency, or by the fear of another
operation. In one study, parents were generally as satisfied as surgeons
on all items, except for syndromic cases [42], where doctors appeared
ready to accept suboptimal results, possibly because no good surgical
solution exists. Similarly, another study found a better acceptance by
doctors, compared with parents, of what is inevitable (the scar,
alopecia) or for which they have no good surgical remedy (calvarial
asymmetry, bony bumps) [41]. This discrepancy shows a mismatch
between surgeons’ and parents’ expectations; whereas parents might
have inordinately high hopes of normalization, surgeons might be more
centered on what they can expect from their usual technique. Blinded
morphological evaluation by independent surgeons avoids the
complacency bias, but not the professional one [43]: the criteria by
which surgeons judge may be at odds from what the patients expect. In
a self-declarative evaluation by adult patients operated in infancy for
non-syndromic craniosynostosis, values regarding self-esteem and
depression scores were in the normal range; these patients satisfied

themselves with all the imperfections of surgical techniques from a past
era, except asymmetry of facial features [44]. A blinded evaluation of
“attractiveness” by laypersons confirmed the negative impact of
craniofacial asymmetry [45]; the method in this study, enrolling as
evaluators independent female professionals of a daycare center, is
probably a step in the right direction. All these subjective evaluations
would also be more in line with the patients’ expectations, with the
input of patients’ associations.
Multiple efforts have been devoted recently to the creation of pre
and postoperative quantitative evaluation scales of the deformity,
much-needed tools if we want to scale postoperative results, and
compare one technique with another. The Rotterdam team has
proposed a score for scaphocephaly, summing semi-quantitative
subscores in the same spirit as the long-established Glasgow Coma
Scale [39, 46]. The evaluation by an independent panel is necessarily
based on documents, and 2D pictures are obviously misleading; for this
reason, 3D photogrammetry is a promising tool [47]. We hope that in a
near future, a consensus will emerge on quantitative morphological
scales adapted to each of the different craniosynostoses.

23 6 Clinical Outcome
23 6 1 Mortality
Overall mortality is very low in craniosynostoses, and it affects almost
exclusively syndromic cases [48]. Already from birth, some of these
patients are beyond surgical resources, and they die because of
breathing and feeding difficulties, and also possibly because of
associated tonsillar herniation. Intraoperative mortality is poorly
documented in literature, and mostly caused by uncontrolled bleeding;
this outcome, although hopefully exceptional, cannot be dismissed.

23 6 2 Development
What is the real influence of cerebral compression on development? As
mentioned above, the relation between intracranial volume and brain
compression is not linear. Furthermore, intracranial hypertension
occurs most regularly in multisuture synostoses, which have almost
always a genetic background, so that the two factors cannot be

separated. The correlation between developmental outcome and the
age at surgery might be an indication of the developmental impact of
brain compression [10, 49], but other factors, like a syndromic context,
or a lack of parental motivation for surgery are confusing factors [11].
The impact of focal cerebral compression on development is also
elusive. The Leeds group found a discrepancy between verbal and
performance IQ (VIQ PIQ) in unisutural craniosynostoses [50], which
they ascribed to parietal compression, and which could be reversed by
early surgery [49]. On the other hand, other researchers found no
correlation between the severity of deformity and cerebral
compression in metopic synostosis [8]. Shimoji found even paradoxical
results, development being more impaired in milder forms of metopic
synostosis [51]; this might suggest different referral patterns, and
confirms that the importance of trigonocephalic deformation plays a
secondary role, if any role at all in the patient’s development. Overall,
these studies suggest that the developmental impact of each type of
synostosis is a specific problem.

23 6 3 Influence of the Syndromic Context
In syndromic craniosynostoses, gene or chromosomal disorders as well
as environmental factors causing the synostosis can have a marked
impact on development. In a previous, unpublished series of 188 cases
of metopic synostosis operated over 20 years, the only significant and
independent variable impacting negatively the development was
syndromic context, which was identified in 31%. In FGFR3 mutation,
experimental models in mice have shown that a developmental impact
existed irrespective of the presence or absence of synostosis, and could
be salvaged by targeted therapy by BGj398 [52]. This suggests that the
mutation affects brain function directly, and opens exciting new
treatment perspectives.
In addition, comorbidities and complications of many syndromic
craniosynostoses are susceptible to impact on psychomotor and
cognitive development [11]. Tonsillar herniation can cause sleep
apneas, predominantly central [53], which can combine with
obstructive apneas caused by midface retrusion, compromising wake
periods and hindering learning. Hand and foot malformations in Apert
syndrome require early management in order to allow psychomotor

development [54]. Optic nerve atrophy caused by raised ICP, found in
12.3% of syndromic craniosynostoses, affects predominantly FGFRrelated diseases [55], and deafness associated with Muenke syndrome,
or resulting from tubal dysfunction in faciostenoses [56], can also both
impair learning. In addition, careful brain imaging can disclose
alterations of the cerebellar vermis and corpus callosum, which can be
the consequence of deformation as well as associated malformations,
and can impact on the child’s development [57].

23 7 The Operative Decision and the Informed
Consent
The decision to operate is taken jointly by the surgeon and the child’s
parents, based on the expected positive and adverse effects of surgery.
The aims of surgery must therefore be clearly defined, and the potential
complications well known by the surgeon and exposed to the parents.
As mentioned above, much uncertainty surrounds the natural history of
unoperated craniosynostoses, while many unknowns lay in the future
after surgery, especially in syndromic cases. Unlike in multisuture
synostoses, for which consent for surgery is comparatively
straightforward, the aim of surgery for unisutural craniosynostosis is in
a large part morphological. In that regard, the treatment can be seen as
morphological surgery with a risk of severe morbidity and even
mortality; few other fields of cranial surgery have such potential
benefit-risk imbalance. The expected improvement of morphological
appearance and better conformity with the social norm, as well as the
potentially traumatic change of their child’s facial features contribute to
make the decision to operate an agonizing process for the parents.
Although emotions are the substance of which we are made, and
society is the medium in which we live, surgeons are often poorly
trained in psychology and sociology, often wrongly dismissed as “soft
sciences.” In addition, their position as professionals, which requires
objectivity, sometimes hinders a more heartfelt approach. In this regard
also, patients’ associations can be a precious resource for these parents,
helping them to cope with the mixed feeling and stress associated with
decision-making.

23 8 The Future
The invasiveness of classical craniofacial surgery and the potentially
high morbidity prompted the development of less invasive techniques
and the boom of endoscopic surgery for craniosynostoses. However, the
abundant literature published on these techniques appears to focus
almost exclusively on easily measured outcome variables, such as
transfusion rate and duration of hospital stay, with no indication on the
long-term morphological results.
This points to the need for a consensual quantitative morphological
rating based on objective criteria, which would allow to compare the
patients pre and postoperatively, and one technique with another. A
morphological scoring proposed for scaphocephaly allows the
comparison of techniques [39, 43], and other scales are in
development.
In order to weight the other pan of the scale, we also need a
quantitative grading of complications. A classification of complications,
sorted by their timing relative to operation, and their consequences for
the patient, was proposed by the team in Leeds [58], and should
certainly be a source of inspiration.
In order to be meaningful, the two quantitative scales, results, and
complications, should not be simple lists of items, but require a
ponderation of variables. In that regard, direct interview or
collaboration of the patients themselves is invaluable to identify what
really matters to them [44]; and here again, the input of patients’
associations would be a precious help.

24 Syndromic Craniosynostosis
Rehan Zahid1, 2 , Lucia Collar Yagas1 and Faizi Siddiqi1

Keywords Syndromic craniosynostosis – Apert – Crouzon – SaethreChotzen – Pfeiffer – Muenke

24 1 Introduction
During childhood, the skull expands to accommodate the growing
brain. This growth occurs at the cranial sutures between different
bones. The paired frontal and parietal bones are separated in the
midline by the metopic and sagittal sutures, respectively; the frontal
and parietal bones are separated by coronal sutures; and the parietal
bones are separated from the single occipital bone by lambdoid
sutures. Craniosynostosis is defined as the premature fusion of one or
more cranial sutures, leading to abnormal skull shape because of a lack
of growth perpendicular to the fused sutures and compensatory growth
at the nonfused sutures. Incidence of craniosynostosis has been
estimated between 1 in 2100 and 1 in 2500 births [1].

The most common presentation is with an unusual head shape in
the first year of life. The head may be long and narrow (scaphocephaly),
triangular at the front (trigonocephaly), broad and flattened
(brachycephaly), or skewed (plagiocephaly).
Craniosynostosis occurring in conjunction with other genetic
anomalies is classified as syndromic craniosynostosis. Syndromes
commonly associated with craniosynostosis include Apert, Crouzon,
Saethre-Chotzen, Pfeiffer, and Muenke syndromes. They are usually
associated with the gain of function mutation genes related to the
Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor (FGFR) family. However, they can
occur in association with other gene variants and chromosomal
abnormalities.
The FGFRs bind to the Fibroblast Growth Factor (FGF), promoting
growth and differentiation of mesenchymal and neuroectodermal cells.
Animal studies have demonstrated that mutated FGFRs lead to a
defective FGF signal transduction which causes growth arrest of the
cranium and the midface [2, 3].
These syndromes share common features along with
craniosynostosis which lead to certain functional ramifications that
must be dealt with in a systematic manner. These patients are usually
more complicated than the nonsyndromic craniosynostosis patients
and require a multidisciplinary team to take care of their needs [4]. The
team often includes a neurosurgeon, plastic surgeon, geneticist, ENT
surgeon, sleep specialist, pediatrician, orthodontist, ophthalmologist,
speech therapist, audiologist, and psychologist.

24 2 General Considerations in Management
of Such Patients
Care of neonates and infants with severe craniosynostosis is directed
toward maintenance of the airway, support of feeding, eye protection,
treatment of raised intracranial pressure (ICP), speech and hearing
development, correcting skull deformity, and orthognathic occlusion.
Diagnostic approach for syndromic patients includes a thorough
history and physical examination. Emphasis should be given to
additional features suggesting an associated syndrome. It’s important

to evaluate whether the patient requires urgent or elective
management. Computed tomographic (CT) scan of the head with threedimensional reconstruction and CT scan of the brain are useful adjuncts
to evaluate the patency or closure of sutures and other cranial
abnormalities, as well as any associated intracerebral abnormalities
(such as ventriculomegaly or craniocerebral disproportion).
Respiratory difficulty may require urgent sleep study assessment by
specialist pediatric respiratory physicians and ear, nose, and throat
(ENT) surgeons. Patients may require either continuous positive airway
pressure (CPAP) support, nasal stenting, tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy,
choanal dilatation, early midface advancement, or tracheostomy,
depending on the anatomical cause [1].
Raised ICP associated with craniosynostosis has several different
causes, which require different treatments. Noninvasive modalities for
monitoring ICP have included radiographs, fundoscopic examination
for papilledema, transorbital ultrasound, and visual evoked potentials.
Regular follow-ups are necessary to monitor for symptoms of raised
ICP.
Elective management includes skull deformity correction,
prevention of its progression, and reduction in risk of raised ICP in the
future [1]. Early midface advancement may be necessary to address
breathing difficulties. Distraction osteogenesis is an effective technique
in addition to the more conventional methods of midface advancement.
Further description of the management options is discussed later.

24 3 Apert
Apert syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder that is caused by
specific missense mutations of FGFR2 [1]. Incidence is about 1 in
65,000 to 200,000 cases with a predominant Asian prevalence [5].
Apert syndrome is characterized by bicoronal craniosynostosis,
midface hypoplasia, and symmetric syndactyly of both hands and feet.
Frequently, cleft palate and learning disability are also present
requiring special needs.
Typically, the presentation includes an abnormally tall and broad
head shape with a prominent forehead (turribrachycephaly), proptosis,
hypertelorism, down slanting palpebral fissures, and a flattened nasal

bridge with sunken midface. Patients often have shallow orbits and risk
of corneal exposure due to restricted frontal and maxillary growth [6].
Oral findings include dental crowding, high-arched narrow palate, and
cleft anomalies in about 75% of Apert’s patients [7]. Maxillary
hypoplasia with class III malocclusion and anterior open bite
contribute to breathing difficulty and a high incidence of obstructive
sleep apnea. Such patients often have an inability to create sufficient
intraoral negative pressure that affects their feeding and swallowing as
well.
Apert patients also have characteristic complex syndactyly of
bilateral hands and feet. Syndactyly can be categorized into three
subtypes which are spade (side-to-side fusion with flat palm), mitten
(fusion of fingers resulting in concave palm), and rosebud (fusion of all
digits) [5]. Central nervous system abnormalities may exist as well
including ventriculomegaly and other structural abnormalities [6].
Furthermore hearing loss occurs in 90% of Apert patients [8]. These
patients also have a higher incidence of developmental delay.
Extracranial features also include cervical spine abnormalities and acne
vulgaris.
Airway compromise, feeding abnormalities, raised ICP, and corneal
exposure often need early intervention.

24 4 Crou on
Crouzon syndrome was first described by Louis Octave Crouzon in
1912. It is caused by mutations in the FGFR2 and FGFR3 genes with an
autosomal dominant pattern. Incidence is estimated at 1 in 60,000
newborn patients. Patients with Crouzon syndrome express a wide
phenotypic variability. Bicoronal craniosynostosis resulting in
brachycephaly, midface hypoplasia, exorbitism, hypertelorism, higharched constricted palate, beaked nose, anterior open bite, and
malocclusion are characteristic features. These patients are typically of
normal intelligence.
Crouzon syndrome has been associated with a higher risk of
increased intracranial pressure when compared to other
craniosynostosis syndromes, with up to 65% incidence. There is a
higher incidence of Chiari malformation as well requiring monitoring

throughout childhood. Other findings include conductive hearing loss,
strabismus, and hydrocephalus. Crouzon syndrome is the milder form
of the Crouzon-Pfeiffer spectrum. Initial clinical concerns are similar
requiring identification and management of airway compromise,
corneal exposure, and raised ICP [4–6, 8, 9].

24 5 Saethre-Chot en
Saethre-Chotzen syndrome (SCS) is characterized by craniosynostosis,
limb deformities, and facial dysmorphism. It was first described in
1931 by Norwegian psychiatrist Haakon Saethre and in 1932 by
German psychiatrist Fritz Chotzen.
Inheritance is autosomal dominant and caused by deletions in
chromosome 7p21.1 leading to loss of function mutations of the TWIST
1 gene. Saethre-Chotzen syndrome is one of the more common
syndromic craniosynostosis with a prevalence of 1:25,000 to 1:50,000
live births, similar to Crouzon syndrome. There is wide phenotypic
variability and incomplete penetrance among these patients and this
may lead to underdiagnosis.
The most common clinical feature is craniosynostosis and the
coronal suture is the most frequently affected, either unilaterally or
bilaterally. In some cases, the mildness of the synostosis has resulted in
delayed or missed diagnosis.
Among limb anomalies, partial cutaneous syndactyly of the second
and third digits of the hands is the most common. Others include
radioulnar synostosis, brachydactyly, hallux valgus, bifid distal phalanx
of the hallux, and triangular epiphyses of the hallux.
Facial findings include facial asymmetry, especially in unicoronal
synostosis, low frontal hairline, small ears with prominent crus,
prominent nasal bridge, eyelid ptosis, strabismus, ocular hypertelorism,
maxillary hypoplasia, mandibular prognathism and high-arched palate,
tear duct stenosis, dystopia canthorum. Other findings include parietal
foramina, vertebral anomalies, short stature, obstructive sleep apnea,
and increased intracranial pressure. Less common anomalies are
hearing loss, renal abnormalities, and congenital heart defects.
Moreover, cognitive development is usually normal, but some
patients have a mental disability, which may be related to large genomic

deletions in the Twist gene [10–16].

24 6 Pfeiffer
In 1964, Pfeiffer described a three-generation family in which eight
individuals had a syndrome consisting of craniosynostosis, broad
thumbs and great toes, and partial syndactyly of the hands and feet.
It is caused by mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor
genes FGFR-1 or FGFR-2. Inheritance is autosomal dominant but is
most commonly a result of de novo mutations. Pfeiffer syndrome is rare
with a prevalence of 1:100,000 births and affects males and females
equally.
Clinical findings include multiple suture craniosynostosis, broad
and deviated thumbs and great toes, and partial syndactyly on hands
and feet. Occasionally patients present with hydrocephalus, severe
ocular proptosis, ankylosed elbows, abnormal viscera, slow
development, Chiari type I malformation, and spinal anomalies such as
fusion of vertebrae, “butterfly” vertebra, and sacrococcygeal extension.
Pfeiffer syndrome is divided into three clinical subtypes based on the
severity of the phenotype [17, 18].

24 7 Muenke
Muenke syndrome is caused by a unique point mutation on the FGFR3
gene, that results in Pro 250 to Arg mutation. It has an incidence of 1 in
10,000 and demonstrates an autosomal dominant pattern of
inheritance.
Muenke syndrome is characterized by considerable phenotypic
variability: features may include coronal synostosis (more often
bilateral than unilateral); synostosis of other sutures, all sutures
(pansynostosis), or no sutures; or macrocephaly. Bilateral coronal
synostosis typically results in brachycephaly (reduced anteroposterior
dimension of the skull), although turribrachycephaly (a “tower-shaped”
skull) or a cloverleaf skull can be observed. Unilateral coronal
synostosis results in anterior plagiocephaly (asymmetry of the skull
and face). Other craniofacial findings typically include temporal
bossing; widely spaced eyes, ptosis or proptosis (usually mild); midface

retrusion (usually mild); and highly arched palate or cleft lip and palate.
Strabismus is common. Other findings can include hearing loss (in 33–
100% of affected individuals); developmental delay ( 33%); epilepsy;
intracranial anomalies; intellectual disability; carpal bone and/or tarsal
bone fusions; brachydactyly, broad toes, broad thumbs, and/or
clinodactyly; and radiographic findings of thimble-like (short and
broad) middle phalanges and/or cone-shaped epiphyses [19, 20].

24 8 Surgical Management
Management of syndromic craniosynostosis consists of multiple staged
procedures spanning from infancy to skeletal maturity [21]. The goal of
surgical treatment for a newly diagnosed syndromic craniosynostosis
patient is to increase the intracranial volume to reduce the risk of
increased intracranial pressure, as well as improve head shape. In this
chapter, we focus on facial dysmorphism and the specific surgical
management for syndromic craniosynostosis patients. Cranial vault
expansion techniques are described separately.
Airway compromise may need to be addressed if nonsurgical
treatment (CPAP and nasopharyngeal airway) is insufficient. Early
adenotonsillectomy, tracheostomy, and frontofacial advancement are
surgical options that are considered depending on the severity and
cause of airway compromise. There should be a high index of suspicion
for syndromic patients with close monitoring for snoring and daytime
somnolence. Formal sleep study is indicated in most of these patients.
Feeding difficulty usually accompanies airway compromise since
these patients are predominantly mouth breathers which makes it
difficult to maintain a negative intraoral pressure while feeding.
Presence of a cleft palate, enlarged tonsils, or adenoids may worsen the
feeding difficulty even further [8]. Gastrostomy tube or nasogastric
tube feeding may be needed to prevent failure to thrive. Furthermore,
tarsorrhaphy may be required to protect from corneal exposure if
needed.
Midface surgery is generally considered later in life, usually after 8–
10 years of life; however, it may be indicated earlier in patients to
address functional outcomes for airway compromise, obstructive sleep
apnea, feeding difficulty, and corneal exposure. Class III malocclusion

may be addressed with midface surgery at an earlier age of 4–7 years of
life to improve the quality of life; however, a later secondary surgery
may be warranted since maxillary growth is innately stunted in such
patients leading to recurrent malocclusion.
Midface and orbital surgery may consist of monobloc frontofacial
advancement, facial bipartition, Le Fort II and III osteotomies with
distraction osteogenesis, or rigid internal fixation. Choice of surgery
depends on the midface morphology, age of the patient, previous
surgeries carried out, and the main objective of reconstruction, keeping
in mind the functional correction, psychosocial benefit, and long-term
esthetic outcome.
Evaluation of the midface morphology in syndromic
craniosynostosis patients focuses on the position of the orbits and
supraorbital ridge when viewed from a sagittal plane, evaluation of the
maxillary, nasal, and zygomatic complex and the overall midface
concavity (often present in dual—axial and sagittal planes), width and
position of the root of the nose, presence of hypertelorism, and dental
occlusion [8, 22]. Apert and Crouzon share similar morphological
features with Apert being generally more severe with less variation in
expression [23].
Le Fort II surgery is generally indicated in patients with midface
hypoplasia involving the maxilla and nasal complex with an acceptable
position of the zygomatic complex and orbits, whereas Le Fort III is
required when the zygomatic complex is involved. Monobloc procedure
is preferred when there is a retrusive forehead as well [22]. Various
different approaches have been adopted, refined, and described by
different surgeons to address the complex abnormalities in the
syndromic patient population. The final goal is to customize the
management plan according to each patient’s clinical presentation and
needs.
McCarthy and later Cohen introduced craniofacial distraction
osteogenesis in the 1990s [24, 25]. It has become increasingly popular
and an adjunct to the conventional advancement procedure with
grafting and rigid fixation. Main advantages include producing larger
movements, decreased infectious risk, decreased relapse rate, gradual
soft tissue expansion, shorter surgery time, and less dissection. General
rule is that midface distraction osteogenesis is required for the

advancement of more than 10 mm. In this patient population, midface
growth is intrinsically inhibited which warrants overcorrection and
over distraction to compensate for the overall facial growth.
Furthermore, distraction osteogenesis has also become widely popular
for cranial vault expansion in patients with craniosynostosis.
Hopper et al. described a technique to address the unique
morphological features of Apert, Pfeiffer, and Crouzon syndromes using
Le Fort II distraction with simultaneous zygomatic repositioning [25,
26]. This technique involves a single surgery that first repositions and
fixates the Le Fort III osteotomy laterally with titanium plates to the
lateral orbital wall and frontal bone, followed by osteotomy at the Le
Fort II level to allow unrestricted movement of the central
nasomaxillary region through distraction osteogenesis. The vertical
lengthening and advancement of the central Le Fort II segment not only
corrects this biconcave deformity of Apert and Pfeiffer syndromes, but
it also creates a desirable lengthening of the nose and downward
movement of the medial canthus to improve the periorbital esthetics.
The Le Fort II segment is distracted significantly more than the zygoma
lengthening the midface and helping to close the anterior open bite.
This technique not only helps to correct the dual plane concavity but
also preserves the orbito-malar relationship and prevents iatrogenic
periorbital deformity.

24 9 Conclusion
Surgical management of syndromic craniosynostosis patients is
complex and must be tailored to each patient’s skeletal deformity and
functional requirement. Regardless of the surgical technique and timing
of operative management, the goals are directed toward restoring the
patient’s airway, increasing the intracranial volume to reduce the risk of
increased intracranial pressure, restoring orbital volume, addressing
the feeding difficulty, malocclusion, and overall esthetic outcome.
Syndromic craniosynostosis presents a spectrum of clinical
challenges. A multidisciplinary team approach is warranted for such
patients. An in-depth understanding of each syndrome and the
associated clinical problems is essential to formulate a comprehensive
long-term treatment plan.
