25 1 Introduction

Craniosynostosis (CS) is defined as a developmental abnormality of the
skull caused by premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures; the
resulting abnormal head shape depends on the sutures involved in this
process [1]. The major sutures in the skull are: the sagittal suture which
separates parietal bones; the metopic suture (also known as frontal
suture) separating the two halves of the frontal bone; the coronal
suture which divides the frontal bone from the parietal bones; the
lambdoid suture, located at the posterior part of the skull, which
separates the occipital bone from the two parietal bones. The fontanels
are mainly two: the anterior fontanel, located at the top of the skull,
which is the largest one and the posterior fontanel, at the back of the
skull [2].
From the sixth week of life, the fontanels begin to close: the
posterior fontanel closes usually within a few months after birth while
the anterior fontanel typically closes at the age of 18–24 months.
During infancy, sutures allow slight movement between the cranial
bones, which is essential for brain growth [3]. A premature fusion of
the sutures causes a perpendicular growth defect and a compensatory
parallel growth, leading to a specific skull abnormality (principle of
Virchow) [1]. CS should be differentiated from positional plagiocephaly,
due to a mechanical deformation of the skull.
Among rare diseases (defined as affecting less than 1 in 2000 live
births), CS are relatively common as a group, their incidence being
estimated as 1:2000 or 1:2500 [2]..

25 2 Classifications
Various classifications of CS have been proposed, based on different
criteria: head morphology and affected sutures; etiology; the
association with other developmental abnormalities; and CS as skeletal
disorders. These classifications can help in the diagnostic workout.

25 2 1 Head Morphology and Affected Sutures
CS can be classified based on the abnormal head shape caused by the
premature fusion of specific sutures: scaphocephaly is due to the
premature fusion of the sagittal suture and results in a long and narrow
head shape; premature fusion of coronal sutures results in

brachycephaly, characterized by a short and wide head shape;
trigonocephaly, described as a triangular or pointed forehead often
associated with hypotelorism, occurs when there is a premature fusion
of the metopic suture; plagiocephaly, characterized by an asymmetrical
and flattened head shape, is caused by the premature fusion of
lambdoid sutures; premature fusion of multiple sutures may cause a
high, tower-like appearance of the skull named turricephaly, which can
be cone-shaped (oxycephaly), or a cloverleaf skull [4]. Sagittal sutures
are involved in approximately 50% of cases, metopic sutures in about
25% of cases, coronal sutures in about 20%, and lambdoid sutures in
less than 5% of cases. Single suture fusion is seen in 78% of cases, and
multiple suture fusions in 22% [5].

25 2 2 Etiology
CS can also be classified based on etiology: primary CS are caused by
intrinsic genetic factors affecting specifically skull development while
secondary CS are due to systemic diseases affecting the developing
sutures, such as skeletal disorders (i.e., acrodysostosis;
hypophosphatasia; hypophosphatemic rickets) and metabolic diseases
with skeletal involvement (i.e., mucopolysaccharidoses).
Various etiologies have been reported for CS. A genetic cause
(chromosomal or gene pathogenic variants) is found overall in 25% of
cases [6]. Chromosomal abnormalities are found in about 20% of the
observed genetic causes, especially in patients showing syndromic
trigonocephaly or scaphocephaly and developmental delay [5]. It is
important to mention that CS can be caused also by non-genetic
etiologies such as prenatal exposure to teratogens (e.g., valproic acid,
retinoic acid, hydantoin, and fluconazole) [7].

25 2 3 Association with Other Developmental
Abnormalities
CS can be classified as syndromic (SCS), characterized by the presence
of multiple congenital abnormalities, or non-syndromic (NSCS) [8, 9].
SCS are rarer and represent around 25–30% of cases, while NSCS
account for 70–75% of cases. Neurodevelopmental problems may be
observed in both SCS and NSCS, thus blurring the distinction between
the two groups [10].

25 2 4 Nosology of Skeletal Disorders
CS are included in the last nosology of skeletal disorders (group 34:
Syndromes featuring craniosynostosis), which is based on a dyadic
naming system, associating each phenotypic condition with the causing
gene, thus taking into account either etiology or clinical manifestations
[11].

25 3 Genetic Assessment, Testing, and
Diagnosis
Patients with CS should be systematically referred to multidisciplinary
teams (MDT) including neurosurgeons, clinical geneticists, molecular
geneticists, genetic counsellors and psychologists, in order to provide a
patient-tailored appropriate genetic assessment.
The genetic consultation includes an accurate family history and, if
necessary, a clinical examination of parents or other relatives. A few SCS
and NSCS are characterized by variable expressivity (affected
individuals show a wide range of clinical severity) and/or reduced
penetrance (some individuals carrying the genetic anomaly are
asymptomatic). Proband’s history should be accurately assessed
including possible prenatal teratogenic exposure, growth, and
psychomotor development. An exhaustive clinical examination should
be performed, in order to detect possible associated dysmorphic
features, notably concerning limbs and extremities. Skull imaging (i.e.,
3D CT scan) can be performed to confirm the presence of CS. If a SCS is
suspected, cardiac ultrasounds scan (USS), abdominal USS, eye
examination, and hearing test can be performed. Skeletal X-rays can be
considered if a secondary CS is suspected. Brain MRI can be considered
in the presence of micro- or macrocephaly and/or specific neurological
signs (i.e., epilepsy; developmental delay) [5]. More than 200
syndromes presenting with craniosynostosis have been reported [5],
with various patterns of inheritance. A genetic study should be carried
out to confirm the clinical diagnosis and provide appropriate genetic
counseling; the molecular assessment depends on the clinical
phenotype. Diagnostic tools include Chromosomal microarray (CMA),
evaluating the possible presence of chromosomal imbalance (Copy

Number Variants/CNV), and next-generation sequencing (NGS),
allowing the detection of Single Nucleotide Variants (SNV) and
including the analysis of panels of genes causing CS, or whole exome
sequencing (WES) or whole genome sequencing (WGS). The genetic
assessment of SCS with no specific diagnostic hypothesis including,
notably, syndromic trigonocephaly and scaphocephaly, and multiple CS
should include CMA and, if negative, NGS. NGS can be the first choice in
all other types of CS except isolated non familial scaphocephaly and
isolated posterior plagiocephaly in which a molecular assessment is not
mandatory because of the low diagnostic rate [12].
If a molecular diagnosis is confirmed in the proband, parents should
be tested in order to evaluate possible inheritance, assess the
recurrence risk and give appropriate genetic counseling. In this respect,
it is important to emphasize that variable intra-familial expressivity has
been reported for SCS (i.e., Saethre-Chotzen, Muenke, Crouzon, and
Pfeiffer syndromes) and NSCS [13], making genetic counseling difficult.
The diagnosis should be announced in a dedicated consultation by
the MDT including ideally the clinical geneticist and the neurosurgeon.
The aim is to inform the patient and/or their legal representatives,
about the main clinical features of the disease, provide relevant
information concerning co-morbidities and prognosis, discuss
management and follow-up options, and provide genetic counseling.
Psychological support for patients and their families should be
systematically proposed. Contact details of Patients’ associations
should be provided to families. Given the complexity of the information
provided, it may be necessary to organize a second consultation a few
weeks after the diagnosis announcement, in order to further discuss
any outstanding issues with the family, with or without psychological
follow-up depending on the family’s needs.
The results of CMA and NGS can be difficult to interpret when
variants of unknown significance are found. Moreover, a systematic
genetic evaluation of NSCS patients can lead to the detection of
susceptibility factors with low penetrance, whose interpretation in
genetic counseling is difficult. These aspects emphasize the need for a
clear rationale for performing genetic tests [14]. We propose a
diagnostic flowchart in Fig. 25.1.

Fig. 25.1 Flowchart for genetic evaluation of patients affected by craniosynostosis. NGS next
generation sequencing, W S whole exome sequencing, WGS whole genome sequencing, SCS
syndromic craniosynostosis, NSCS non-syndromic craniosynostosis, CMA chromosomal
microarray analysis

Some examples of the main SCS and NSCS are summarized in the
following paragraphs.

25 3 1 SCS
SCS represent 25–30% of CS. Multiple congenital abnormalities
including dysmorphic features, limb malformations, congenital heart
defects, developmental delay, and intellectual disability can be

associated with SCS. SCS can be due to teratogenic exposure (i.e.,
valproate exposure) or genetic abnormalities: these include monogenic
disorders (around 80% of cases), with a predominantly autosomal
dominant inheritance, and predominant involvement of the coronal
suture, and chromosomal imbalance (around 20%), with a
predominant involvement of the metopic or sagittal sutures. The main
chromosomal abnormalities causing CS have already been extensively
reviewed [15]. The main features of the most frequent monogenic SCS
are summarized here.

25.3.1.1 Crouzon Syndrome (# 123500)
Crouzon syndrome is characterized by progressive coronal CS or
multiple synostosis with midface hypoplasia, without anomalies of the
extremities. Phenotypic features also include hypertelorism, eye
proptosis, and inversion of the dental articulation. Synostosis is
progressive, so signs may become more evident during infancy.
Auditory, olfactory, visual, and neurological complications
(hydrocephalus, cerebellar tonsil involvement, intracranial
hypertension) are frequent. If craniosynostosis is correctly managed,
intellectual disability is rarely observed. Crouzon syndrome is an
autosomal dominant disorder, linked to heterozygous pathogenic
variations in the FGFR2 gene. There is a particular form of Crouzon
syndrome associated with acanthosis nigricans ( 612247) due to a
recurrent mutation in the FGFR3 gene (p.Ala391Glu). The autosomal
recessive Kreiborg-Pakistani syndrome and Craniosynostosis 4 should
be considered in the differential diagnosis (see specific paragraphs).

25.3.1.2 Apert Syndrome (# 101200)
Apert syndrome is generally characterized by severe bicoronal CS
associated with moderate to severe facial involvement with maxillary
hypoplasia, inversion of the dental articulation, hypertelorism, and eye
proptosis. Soft tissue and bony syndactyly of fingers and toes are also
present, which may be total or partial and can be associated with elbow
ankylosis. Moderate to severe intellectual disability is common and
cerebral malformations can be observed. Early neurosurgical
intervention can improve intellectual prognosis. Apert syndrome is an

autosomal dominant disorder, caused by specific heterozygous
pathogenic variations in the FGFR2 gene [16].

25.3.1.3 Pfeiffer Syndrome (# 101600)
Pfeiffer syndrome is characterized by brachycephaly (bicoronal
craniosynostosis) or cloverleaf skull (pansynostosis), moderate to
severe hypoplasia of the midface, and limb abnormalities including
broad and deviated thumbs and hallux, partial syndactyly of fingers and
toes, and possible elbow ankylosis. Neurological complications are
possible (developmental delay, hydrocephalus, epilepsy). Deafness,
choanal atresia, cleft palate, and laryngotracheal anomalies can be
observed. Pfeiffer syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder due to
heterozygous pathogenic variations in the FGFR2 gene in the majority
of cases. A less severe form is caused by FGFR1 mutation p.Pro252Arg
[17].

25.3.1.4 Saethre-Chotzen Syndrome (# 101400)
Saethre-Chotzen syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder, caused
by heterozygous pathogenic variations in the TWIST1 gene or 7p21.1
chromosomal deletions including this gene. In this condition, bicoronal
or unicoronal craniosynostosis is generally observed leading to facial
asymmetry, a flat and high forehead, eyelid ptosis, possible strabismus,
and small ears with prominent crus. Limb abnormalities include
brachydactyly and partial cutaneous syndactyly of the second and third
fingers. Some patients show hearing loss, and congenital heart diseases
can be associated. Intelligence is usually normal but developmental
delay can be observed in patients carrying large 7p21.1 chromosomal
deletions encompassing TWIST1. There is considerable inter- and intrafamilial phenotypic variability [18] and mutations in TWIST1 have also
been reported in individuals showing NSCS (isolated Craniosynostosis
1).

25.3.1.5 Muenke Syndrome (# 602849)
Muenke syndrome is characterized by uni- or bilateral coronal
craniosynostosis responsible for brachycephaly, possibly associated
with macrocephaly, plagiocephaly or premature fusion of multiple
sutures. Craniosynostosis may be associated with minor limb

abnormalities (brachydactyly, clinodactyly, broad thumbs and great
toes, carpal or tarsal fusions). Strabismus and hearing loss can be
observed; intelligence is usually normal but speech delay,
developmental delay, intellectual disability, and behavioral issues have
been reported. Muenke syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder,
linked to a recurrent p.(Pro250Arg) variation in the FGFR3 gene. There
is considerable inter- and intra-familial phenotypic variability [19].

25.3.1.6 Antley–Bixler Syndrome (# 207410–# 201750)
This condition presents with several distinct clinical features including
craniosynostosis, trapezoidocephaly, midface hypoplasia, choanal
stenosis or atresia, multiple joint contractures, radiohumeral
synostosis, and in some cases, internal organ malformations and
developmental delay. CS and radiohumeral synostosis are generally
considered to be the hallmarks of this condition [20, 21].
Two different forms of Antley–Bixler syndrome have been
described. The autosomal recessive form ( 201750) is caused by
biallelic mutations in the P R gene, encoding P450 oxidoreductase,
leading to a disorder in steroidogenesis and cholesterol biosynthesis
[20]. Individuals affected by autosomal-recessive Antley–Bixler
syndrome typically exhibit less severe craniosynostosis and skeletal
manifestations; they may be at risk for adrenal insufficiency and can
present genital abnormalities; maternal virilization can be observed
during pregnancies with an affected fetus.
Autosomal-dominant Antley–Bixler syndrome ( 207410) is caused
by heterozygous mutations of the FGFR2 gene, showing a phenotypic
overlap with Pfeiffer syndrome [21]: this condition is characterized by
more severe CS and normal steroidogenesis.

25.3.1.7 Baller-Gerold Syndrome (# 218600)
The main phenotypic features of Baller-Gerold syndrome include
coronal craniosynostosis and limb anomalies, mainly radial and thumb
hypo-aplasia, metacarpal bones malformations, oligodactyly. Patients
also show short stature; lower limbs anomalies (absent patellae, genu
valgum, club feet), imperforate or anteriorly placed anus, heart and
renal malformations, skin involvement including poikiloderma, and
facial dysmorphic features. Affected individuals have predisposition to

malignancies, in particular osteosarcoma. This condition is inherited
with an autosomal recessive pattern, and it is caused by biallelic
mutations in the R C
gene [22].

25.3.1.8 Cranio-Fronto-Nasal Dysplasia (# 304110)
Cranio-fronto-nasal dysplasia is an X-linked dominant syndromic
craniosynostosis, in which girls are more severely affected than boys.
Affected individuals show coronal craniosynostosis with brachycephaly,
fronto-nasal dysplasia (marked hypertelorism, broad nasal root with
bifid nasal tip) and longitudinally grooved fingernails. Skeletal
malformations may also be present, with Sprengel deformity, scoliosis,
short and wide first toes, and brachydactyly. Other malformations have
also been described (microcephaly, cleft lip and palate, inner ear
anomalies, diaphragmatic hernia, etc.). Boys generally present with
mild clinical features and can show only isolated hypertelorism. Craniofronto-nasal dysplasia is due to pathogenic variations in the FNB1
gene, located on the X chromosome [23].

25.3.1.9 Carpenter Syndrome Type 1 (# 201000) and 2 (#
614976)
Type 1 Carpenter syndrome is characterized by multisuture CS, facial
dysmorphic features, limb anomalies (syndactyly of hands and foot,
preaxial polydactyly of toes and postaxial polydactlyly in upper limbs,
brachydactyly, broad thumbs, coxa valga, coxa vara, genu valgum),
obesity, dental abnormalities, possible mixed hearing loss, congenital
heart defects, hydronephrosis, genital abnormalities in males
(hypogonadism and cryptorchidism), and the possible presence of
developmental delay of variable severity. This condition is due to
biallelic pathogenic variants in the RAB23 gene [24].
Pathogenic variants in the M GF8 gene cause autosomal recessive
type 2 Carpenter syndrome, whose characteristics include metopic
craniosynostosis, less frequent involvement of coronal and sagittal
sutures, dysmorphic facial features, limb abnormalities, lateralization
defects, congenital heart disease, and variable neurodevelopmental
delay [25].

25.3.1.10 Kreiborg-Pakistani Syndrome (# 614188)

This autosomal recessive condition is caused by biallelic pathogenic
variants in the I 11RA gene. Phenotypic spectrum includes premature
fusion of metopic and/or coronal sutures; sagittal and lambdoid
sutures can also be involved and multisuture CS has been observed.
Some affected individuals can have a Crouzon-like appearance (eye
proptosis, midface hypoplasia, malocclusion, and prognathism). Dental
anomalies including delayed eruption, ectopic, or supernumerary teeth
have been reported, as well as minor limb anomalies (cutaneous
syndactyly, clinodactyly) [26].

25 3 2 NSCS
NSCS are the most frequent form of CS (69–75%) and involve most
often a single suture [5, 27]. Currently, the diagnostic rate of genetic
assessment in NSCS is about 13% in unicoronal, 60% in bicoronal, and
13% in metopic synostosis [28]. A few papers suggest a progressively
increasing incidence of NSCS, which currently remains unexplained [14,
29]. The availability of NGS diagnostic techniques has led to the
molecular characterization of an increasing number of NSCS and to a
“reverse” characterization of the phenotypic spectrum of these
conditions, which can include associated features such as
neurodevelopmental problems and minor limb abnormalities, thus
blurring the limit between NSCS and SCS.
Sagittal craniosynostosis is the most frequent among NSCS cases
(40–55%), occurring in about 1 in 5000 births [30, 31]. This type of CS
predominantly affects males in a ratio of 3.5:1, with most cases being
sporadic, although about 6% are speculated to be familial [27]. Various
environmental factors have been linked to sagittal NSCS, such as parity,
prematurity, intrauterine constraint, maternal tobacco, and nitrosatable
drug use [31–34].
Coronal synostosis, the second most common type, constitutes 20–
25% of NSCS cases, occurring in roughly 1 in 10,000 births. It occurs
more often in females (60–75% of cases) and is more likely to be
associated with known genetic syndromes and gene mutations. There is
a strong genetic influence noted in non-syndromic coronal synostosis,
with 8–15% of patients having a positive family history [27].
Metopic synostosis, accounting for approximately 14% of NSCS
cases, presents an incidence rate of about 1 in 15,000 births [27], with a

male-to-female ratio of 3.3:1 [27, 30]. Most cases (70%) are isolated
without other clinical malformations, although 5–10% have a positive
familial history [27, 35].
Lambdoid synostosis represents 3–5% of NSCS cases [27, 35],
occurring in about 1 per 33,000 births [27]. Its genetics are largely
unknown, and instances of a positive family history are rare [36].
Lambdoid synostosis is hypothesized to have a weaker genetic
component.
Complex craniosynostosis, involving two or more distinct sutures,
comprises 5% of non-syndromic cases [30]. Patients with complex
craniosynostosis often experience increased intracranial pressure,
leading to chronic headaches, developmental delays [4], and a higher
likelihood of re-synostosis necessitating further surgeries [37].
Overall, recurrence rates of NSCS differ based on suture type and
complexity. The genetic contribution to NSCS appears to be suturespecific, and the incidence rate among first-degree relatives varies
based on the suture type [27].
The main features of the most frequent monogenic NSCS are
summarized here.

25.3.2.1 Craniosynostosis 2: Boston Type (# 604757)
Mutations in MS 2 cause craniosynostosis 2—Boston type, an
autosomal dominant condition characterized by variable expressivity
within families and affecting mainly metopic and coronal sutures; a
multisuture involvement may occur. Main features of this syndrome
include frontal bossing, turricephaly, trigonocephaly, brachycephaly,
and cloverleaf skull in severe cases. Craniosynostosis can be associated
with brachydactyly; intelligence is usually normal [38].

25.3.2.2 Craniosynostosis 3 (# 615314)
Autosomal dominant mutations in TCF12 lead to Craniosynostosis 3,
characterized by coronal and/or sagittal synostosis possibly associated
with mild dysmorphic features including eyelids ptosis, prominent ear
crus, malocclusion, and limb abnormalities (brachydactyly, clinodactyly,
camptodactyly, and toe syndactyly). Developmental delay and learning
difficulties can be observed. Incomplete penetrance (up to 50%) has

been reported [39]. This condition should be considered in the
differential diagnosis of Muenke and Saethre-Chotzen syndromes.

25.3.2.3 Craniosynostosis 4 (# 600775)
Affected individuals can present with NSCS or Crouzon-like appearance
including midface-hypoplasia and eye proptosis. Coronal, sagittal, and
lambdoid sutures can be involved and possible multisuture
involvement has been observed. Brain imaging can detect non-specific
brain abnormalities including Chiari type 1 and dilated ventricles.
Intelligence is usually normal but learning difficulties and behavioral
problems can be observed as well as minor limb abnormalities (large
thumbs, clinodactyly and brachydactyly). This condition is caused by
heterozygous pathogenic variants in RF with an autosomal dominant
pattern of inheritance [40].

25.3.2.4 Craniosynostosis 5 (# 615529)
A
mutations are considered to be susceptibility factors for the NSCS
craniosynostosis 5. Midline involvement is observed, including
premature fusion of metopic and/or sagittal sutures. Inheritance is
autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance [41].

25.3.2.5 Craniosynostosis 6 (# 616602)
This condition is due to pathogenic variants in the IC1 gene.
Inheritance pattern is autosomal dominant. Clinical phenotype includes
premature fusion of coronal sutures (mostly bilateral) leading to
brachycephaly; lambdoid suture involvement has also been reported.
Associated features include dysmorphic features (eyelid ptosis,
strabismus), hearing loss, scoliosis, delayed closure of anterior
fontanelle, and skull defects. A neurological involvement has been
reported including speech delay, learning difficulties and autistic
spectrum disorders. Brain imaging can detect non-specific anomalies
including cerebellar anomalies (such as atrophy and Dandy-Walker
malformation), pons hypoplasia, dilated ventricles, and corpus
callosum abnormalities [42].

25.3.2.6 Craniosynostosis 7 (# 617439)

Heterozygous pathogenic variants in the SMAD gene are associated
with susceptibility to craniosynostosis 7. Phenotypic spectrum includes
midline craniosynostosis, involving metopic and sagittal sutures, and
possible developmental delay. Inheritance pattern is autosomal
dominant with reduced penetrance [43].

25.3.2.7 EFNA4 Defects
FNA variants have been rarely reported in individuals showing
coronal NSCS with incomplete penetrance [44].

25 3 3 Genetic Counseling
Depending on molecular results, it is necessary to provide clear
information about the mode of transmission to the proband and
relatives, and to offer family genetic counseling. The majority of
craniosynostosis of genetic origin is transmitted in an autosomal
dominant manner, but there are also rare autosomal recessive and Xlinked forms.
Concerning autosomal dominant CS, in the case of a de novo
mutation in the proband, parents have a low risk of recurrence for
future pregnancies (estimated at about 1% due to the risk of germline
mosaicism).
The proband has a risk of 50%, at each pregnancy, to transmit the
pathogenic variant to the offspring but the risk of craniosynostosis in
the offspring carrying the pathogenic variant depends on the
expressivity and the penetrance.
In autosomal recessive CS, the parents of an affected child are
generally heterozygote carriers of one pathogenic variant. Thus, at
conception, each sib of the propositus has a 25% chance of being
affected, a 50% chance of being an asymptomatic carrier, and a 25%
chance of being unaffected and not a carrier. An affected individual will
transmit a heterozygous pathogenic variant to all offspring, who will be
asymptomatic carriers. The risk that the offspring inherits a second
pathogenic variant depends on the genetic status of the reproductive
partner and, for rare and ultra-rare CS, can be significant in cases of
shared ancestry or close genetic relationships.
Craniofrontonasal dysplasia is inherited in an X-linked dominant
manner. Affected females have a 50% risk of transmitting an FNB1

gene mutation to offspring. Affected males have a 100% risk of
transmitting FNB1 mutation to females and no risk of transmitting to
males. As previously discussed, females are more severely affected than
males.
It is important to emphasize that while in the majority of SCS
penetrance is complete, although expressivity can be a variable, several
genes causing NSCS are characterized by an incomplete penetrance,
thus making genetic counseling challenging for these conditions.

25 3 4 Prenatal Diagnosis
In the prenatal setting, even in reference centers, detection of CS is
difficult and thus, the diagnostic rate is lower. In the absence of specific
family history, CS are often detected in the third trimester by USS.
Further imaging techniques, such as fetal CT or MRI can be performed
to better characterize skull morphology and to rule out brain, skeletal,
or internal organ abnormalities.
A molecular assessment including CMA and NSG molecular
techniques can be considered, depending on the severity of the
morphological picture, gestational age and parental request.
In the presence of specific family history with significant recurrence
risk, and a well-established molecular diagnosis, pre-implantation or
prenatal diagnosis can be considered, based on the severity of CS and
parental request. In the absence of a molecular diagnosis, close
ultrasound monitoring may be proposed (even if normal ultrasound
monitoring does not formally eliminate the risk of CS), followed by a
clinical examination of the child at birth. As previously discussed,
prenatal diagnosis should be organized within an MDT including
gynecologists, midwives, clinical and molecular geneticists, genetic
counselors, psychologists, and neurosurgeons.

25 4 Conclusion
The availability of powerful molecular tools like gene panel molecular
analysis, whole exome or whole genome sequencing has led to the
characterization of an increasing number of CS. The timely
identification of secondary CS or SCS is pivotal for managing associated
complications and improving prognosis. The genetic characterization of

primary CS has shed light on the considerable genetic heterogeneity of
these conditions, in some cases blurring the limits between SCS and
NSCS. Overall, the current detection rate of the molecular analysis of
exhaustive panels of CS causing genes and WES is about 30–40%; this
detection rate is extremely variable depending on the type of suture
involved and the possible association with other developmental
abnormalities.
The molecular characterization of CS not only leads to appropriate
genetic counseling and offers pertinent information on associated
health issues and prognosis but can also provide a reversed portrayal of
the phenotypic spectrum of these conditions. Nevertheless, a
systematic genetic assessment of NSCS patients may detect
susceptibility factors with low penetrance, making genetic counseling
challenging and prompting concerns regarding cost-effectiveness for
healthcare systems. These aspects underline the need of a clear
rationale when considering molecular testing.
Patients with CS, either syndromic or non-syndromic, should be
addressed to experienced MDT, including neurosurgeons, clinical
geneticists, molecular geneticists, genetic counsellor, and psychologists,
in order to select medically appropriate and patient-tailored
indications for performing genetic tests. Additionally, the results of
genetic tests should be discussed in multidisciplinary meetings
involving clinical and molecular geneticists, genetic counsellors, and
the referring neurosurgeon, to assess the pathogenicity and clinical
significance of gene variants.
In conclusion, genetic assessment of patients affected by SCS and
NSCS should be performed with a multidisciplinary approach and
according to a clearly established diagnostic flowchart.

26 The Role of a Psychologist on a
Craniosynostosis Team
Kathleen Kapp-Simon1, 2
(1) Shriners Hospitals for Children, Chicago, IL, USA
(2) Department of Surgery, University of Illinois at Chicago, Chicago,
IL, USA

Kathleen Kapp-Simon
Email: kkapps@uic.edu
Keywords Craniosynostosis – Psychologist – Family support –
Psychological adjustment – Neuropsychological development

26 1 Introduction
Craniosynostosis, occurring in 1 to 2000–2500 live births, encompasses
a range of conditions that vary widely in complexity and the types of
medical and psychological interventions required. Broadly speaking,
86% of craniosynostosis cases are categorized as non-syndromic,
meaning that they do not have a known genetic cause while the
remaining cases are complex multi-sutural or syndromic [1]. In its most
basic presentation, craniosynostosis involves a single fused suture
requiring a single cranial surgery. While many children with
nonsyndromic craniosynostosis go on to have typical childhoods
requiring few additional medical, psychological, or educational
interventions after a single surgery to correct the synostosis, a sizable
number of these children (30–50% depending on suture and other
factors) require ongoing medical, psychological, or educational
interventions [2–7]. Therefore, it is necessary that even children with

nonsyndromic craniosynostosis should be followed by their
craniosynostosis team until it is clear that no further intervention is
needed. Children born with a complex or syndromic craniosynostosis
almost always require frequent medical, psychological, and educational
interventions throughout childhood [7]. While the specific needs of
children with craniosynostosis may vary by diagnosis, the role of the
pediatric psychologist working with these children and their families is
similar across diagnoses and falls into four broad areas: Family support
and education; fostering child social, emotional, and behavioral
adjustment; regular screening of development including need for early
intervention, school readiness, and academic progress; and formal
neuropsychological assessment as needed. In addition to clinical
support, pediatric psychologists working in the field of craniofacial
conditions may be involved in research that examines precursors or
correlates of psychological adjustment; identifies or develops effective
interventions for social, emotional, and behavioral problems; and
clarifies the neurodevelopmental implications of the various
craniosynostosis diagnoses.

26 2 Family Support and Education
A diagnosis of craniosynostosis, regardless of whether it is a single
suture craniosynostosis or a complex syndrome, is disruptive to the
family. How a family responds to this diagnosis is influenced by their
culture; attitudes toward medicine; and family adaptability, cohesion,
and emotional health. When a diagnosis is new, families receive a
tremendous amount of information. In all but those relatively rare
instances of family reoccurrence, family members have never heard the
word craniosynostosis before and the idea that there is something
wrong with their child’s head/brain can be terrorizing. An important
role of the psychologist is to help families process the information they
have been given, support the emotional reactions they are having, and
guide them toward positive actions they can take to support each other
and their child. Helping parents to identify their strengths can be
critical. For example, is one parent better able to ask questions or
process the medical information provided while the other is better at

hands on care? Affirmation of differing roles can help parents to feel
positive about their individual contributions to their child’s treatment.
It is also vital for the psychologist to help families talk about how
they handle strong emotions. The first few months, sometimes even
years, of the child’s life can be extremely hard on a family. Parents may
have to make decisions about surgery or other treatments. The child
may have frequent or prolonged hospitalizations. Parents may have to
implement home treatments such as feeding tubes or apnea monitors.
There may be differences in the child’s appearance that draw negative
attention to the child and family when they are in public. Extended
family may or may not be supportive. One or the other of the parents
may feel guilty about, or responsibility for, the child’s condition. How
families process these emotions, the coping strategies they use, and the
ways they seek support are all important areas for discussion. A
psychologist’s role is to help families develop the psychological skills
they need to cope with the varying emotions that they are experiencing.
Treatment for craniosynostosis frequently occurs in stages from
birth through young adulthood [7]. The initial cranial vault
decompression and suture release will generally be completed by the
time a child is a year of age. Subsequent procedures are more fluid and
are recommended based on “functional, aesthetic, and psychological
needs of the patient” ([7], p9S). When there is a functional problem
(e.g., increased cranial pressure, obstructive sleep apnea), there is less
ambiguity about the need for intervention; however, when a procedure
is being considered for esthetic or psychological reasons, families need
to decide if the recommended procedure and timing are right for their
child. When the child is very young, that decision primarily falls to the
parents in consultation with the child’s medical providers; however, as
the child grows, he or she becomes an important part of the decisionmaking process [8]. A psychologist who is part of the craniosynostosis
team can help facilitate the decision-making process, particularly when
there is uncertainty, or differing opinions, as to whether or when a
procedure should be undertaken.
Clear communication between parents and medical staff and
ultimately between parents, medical staff, and the growing child
impacts the decision-making process, as well as long-term satisfaction
with outcomes [8]. Craniosynostosis teams that acknowledge the

importance of family-centered care recognize that the family is the
child’s primary source of strength and support. A child’s primary
caregivers bring expertise to treatment discussions about their child’s
needs/desires, emotional status, and coping style. Therefore, whenever
possible, caregivers’ suggestions should be incorporated into treatment
plans. The child’s perspective should also be recognized. Allowing the
child to play an active role in the decision-making process allows them
to feel empowered.
Younger children who have already had multiple stages of treatment
often want recommended procedure, but are frightened because they
know what surgery involves. Children who have had surgery in the past
may have specific fears related to needle pricks, anesthesia masks,
postsurgery nausea, or waking up alone in the recovery room. The role
of the psychologist in this situation is to work with parents to help the
child identify the source of their fears and develop coping strategies
that enable the child to successfully undergo the desired treatment.
Many hospitals provide specialized child support services, called
“called child life services,” to support young children who are having
surgery or in the hospital. If available, the team psychologist can work
with the child life therapist to facilitate implementation of the identified
coping strategies on the day of surgery.
Older children may have other reasons for resisting recommended
treatments. Resistance to a specific procedure may simply be that they
just need a break from surgery. If a specific procedure is not timedependent, a delay may not affect the long-term medical outcome but
may allow the child to feel that they have some control over their
bodies, which promotes psychological health and may ensure better
cooperation from the child when the procedure is scheduled. Likewise,
children who have frequent surgeries may find that many of their
school breaks are spent preparing for surgery, having surgery, or
recovering from surgery and they don’t want another ruined vacation.
The psychologist role in this situation is to facilitate communication
between the child and parent and work toward compromise. It may be
better for a child’s psychological health to have surgery during the
school year rather than always having surgery during the summer or
other school breaks.

A more challenging scenario occurs when parent, surgeon, and
adolescent have differing perspectives on what constitutes the end of
treatment. Many of the last stages of treatment for craniosynostosis, as
with many craniofacial conditions, focus on esthetics with possible
medical benefits (e.g., rhinoplasty, canthoplasty, cranioplasty,
genioplasty, orthognathic surgery) [7]. These are important procedures
because satisfaction with appearance has been identified as a central
factor for psychological well-being and emotional health for individuals
with craniofacial conditions [9]. Yet there are adolescents who decide
that they are not interested in these final procedures. Some parents
may be reluctant to accept the adolescent’s position because they fear
that the adolescent will come to regret this decision in the future. Other
parents feel strongly that all procedures recommended by the
adolescent’s surgeon should be completed because parents feel an
obligation to make sure everything possible’ is done for their child.
When faced with these types of disagreements, there is no right’
solution. Rather, surgeon, parents, and adolescent need to come to a
decision that is as comfortable as possible for all participants.
The team psychologist can play a valuable role in helping to resolve
this type of situation. The psychologist first needs to ensure that both
parents and adolescent are able to articulate the surgical plan including
the goals of the procedure as well as the risks related to the procedure.
Then parents and adolescent need to fully understand what influences
their own positions. A useful paradigm for assisting families with this
process is what we have called the Self-Understanding Model (SUM)
[10–12]. This model encourages both caregivers and adolescents to
identify the feelings, thoughts, physiologic reactions, and behaviors that
are associated with the recommendation for surgery. A satisfying
solution can often be found by talking about and working through the
different reactions of caregivers and adolescents.
Adolescents may state that they are satisfied with their current
appearance and not desirous of further changes. The reasons for this
lack of interest vary but may include “surgery fatigue”, after many
procedures throughout childhood, the teen has just had enough. Teens
may also be reluctant to cope with readjusting to a new appearance
after surgery or unwilling to cope with questions/comments from
peers that might be reactivated by a change in appearance [13]. Others

express the more philosophical ideas that they have worked hard to
accept their appearance and don’t see the need to change it, for
example, they’ve been told appearance is not as important as internal
characteristics, so they wonder why the adults (parents, surgeons) are
now advocating for more external changes [14]. The thoughts
associated with these scenarios range from “I just can’t handle another
surgery” to “I don’t want another change in appearance—I’ve had
enough changes”. Emotions can range from sadness to anger while
physiological reactions may include stomach pain, headaches, or a
feeling of tension throughout the body. The adolescent may react by
lashing out at caregivers or even the surgeon or they may withdraw in
depression. By working with the adolescent, the team psychologist is
able to help the patient articulate their thoughts and feelings and
subsequently modulate their physiological and behavioral reactions.
That doesn’t mean that every adolescent will agree to the
recommended procedure, but it will help the adolescent and family
understand what is driving the decision. The team psychologist assists
the adolescent in understanding, articulating, accepting, and eventually
coping with their emotional turmoil. Interventions to equip the patient
with coping skills necessary to manage the anxiety and stress
associated with another surgery are essential for supporting positive
psychological and medical outcomes.
Parents can go through a similar process when faced with a decision
about additional surgery. When an adolescent is refusing additional
procedures, parents’ reactions also range from sadness to anger. By
helping parents articulate their own thoughts and emotional reactions
to the situation, the team psychologist is able to facilitate more open
communication between the adolescent and parents. Other strategies
such as those recommended by Foster and Robin [15] and Dishion and
Stormshak [16] can be implemented as needed to foster open
communication and respect between parents and adolescent. The tools
of the SUM model can help parents understand and cope with their
emotions and stressors as well as increase their understanding of the
stresses their child faces. When surgery is advisable, motivational
interviewing strategies can empathically assist the family in coming to
terms with the challenges and ambivalence of medical decision-making
[12].

26 3 Fostering Child Social, Emotional, and
Behavioral Ad ustment
Children with craniofacial conditions, including craniosynostosis, are at
risk for social, emotional, and behavioral problems. Van der Vlugt et al.
[17] reported Child Behavior Checklist scores on 115 children between
the ages of 5 and 16 who had either single suture (N = 62) or syndromic
(N = 53) craniosynostosis. There were no significantly different rates of
psychological risk between the two craniosynostosis groups. Overall,
23% of the children were at risk for internalizing problems
(depression, anxiety, withdrawal, somatic complaints), 21% were at
risk for externalizing problems (aggression, conduct problems), and
30% fell in the at-risk range on the total problems scale (includes
internalizing and externalizing problems as well as social problems,
thought problems, and attention problems). When rates of risk were
examined based on Full Scale IQ scores, frequencies of risk for children
who had scores ≥85 were similar to the normative data. In contrast, the
children with Full Scale IQs 85 were significantly more likely to fall in
the high-risk range particularly for Internalizing and Total Problems
(Internalizing = 40%, Externalizing, 19%, and Total Problems, 50%). In
their studies of metopic and sagittal craniosynostosis, Osborn and
colleagues [18–20] reported that behavior problems were more
common in children with operated metopic craniosynostosis with
prevalence rates ranging from 27% based on objective report to 37%
when examining parent/teacher reports, for unoperated metopic
synostosis, executive functioning problems, and behavior problems
were more prevalent. Results for sagittal craniosynostosis were more
variable based on meta-analysis [20]. Speltz et al. [21] found that
approximately 1/3 of young elementary age children with single suture
craniosynostosis scored above clinical thresholds in one or more areas
(internalizing, externalizing, or total problems) compared to 21% of
control subjects based on either parent or teacher report. In another
study, children (ages 6–13 years) with syndromic craniosynostosis
were rated by a parent (generally mother) as at significantly higher risk
for internalizing, social, attention, and total problems compared to
normative data with moderate to high effect sizes [22]. Similar to Van

der Vlugt et al. [17], parents of the children with a measured Full Scale
IQ of 85 reported behavior and emotional problems at 2–3.7 times
greater frequency than parents of the children whose Full Scale IQ was
≥85 [22].
Due to this increased risk, regular screening for social, emotional,
and behavioral problems is an important role for psychologists on
craniofacial teams. This screening should include reports from multiple
informants when possible [21]. Parent, teacher, and self-reports can be
obtained by using appropriate versions of the Child Behavior Checklist
[23] or the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire [24]. Parent and
child-reported outcomes can also be assessed using the patientreported outcomes measurement information system (PROMIS)
developed through the National Institute of Health [25]. PROMIS
measures allow psychologists to monitor the physical, mental, and
social health of children through age-appropriate parent and selfreport. These three groups of measures have been used widely in
research involving children with craniofacial conditions but are also
appropriate for annual screening during craniofacial team visits.
Early literature on psychological adjustment of children with
craniofacial conditions demonstrated that social competence is related
to overall adjustment and positive feelings of self-worth [26, 27]. There
is also evidence that adolescents whose parents worried less about
their friendships and encouraged them to engage with peers displayed
greater social competence, while being teased, withdrawn, disliked, or
associating with bad friends’ was correlated with poorer social
competence [28]. Peer teasing has also been related to negative social
interactions and research shows that teasing or feelings of being
discriminated against occur with some frequency for individuals with
visible facial differences [29, 30]. Persistence of teasing rather than
isolated events may be the more important predictor of later
depression and anxiety [31–33]. There is also some evidence to
indicate that inconsistent or unpredictable negative responses to facial
differences increase negative self-evaluations about appearance as well
as anxiety and depression [34]. Finally, studies showed a relationship
between social adjustment and self-evaluation of physical appearance
for children and adults with craniofacial conditions [13, 30, 35, 36].
Building on these earlier studies, Feragen and Stock [33] postulated

that social competence is associated with a positive subjective
evaluation of appearance and social acceptance (particularly freedom
from teasing).
Satisfaction with appearance is a subjective construct influenced by
both internal and external factors as summarized in Fig. 26.1. External
factors such as cultural attitudes about appearance and social
experiences, both positive or negative, interact with an individual’s
internal cognitive processes to influence personal judgements about
body image. Interventions need to focus on making these internal
processes explicit for the individual with a craniofacial condition. The
Self-Understanding Model (SUM) described above can be useful in this
endeavor [10–12]. The psychologist can help the individual with
craniosynostosis identify a situation that one has found particularly
stressful with regard to one’s appearance. Once a stressful situation is
identified, the psychologist can guide the individual as one identifies
the thoughts and feelings associated with that situation. The individual
should then be directed to consider how one responds to that situation.
Are one’s thoughts, feelings, and reactions constructive or destructive
to one’s psychological health? Do their typical responses result in
increased satisfaction or dissatisfaction with their appearance? If the
interactions of thoughts, feelings, and behavior reactions have a
negative impact, the psychologist can help the individuals learn to use
cognitive restructuring to change their typical pattern of reaction such
that they can reduce appearance concerns and emotional distress while
improving positive feelings. Parents can also be taught to help their
children with this process so that it can be used at home. Individuals
who look different will inevitably face questions, stares, or even
negative comments from others in their environment. It is critical to the
individuals’ mental health that they learn strategies that enable them to
cope with these situations in a manner that preserves their self-esteem.
The management of these situations can directly affect an individual’s
attitudes toward one’s appearance as self-esteem has been linked to
satisfaction with appearance [37].

Fig. 26.1 Factors found to affect subjective satisfaction with appearance. (From Feragen and
Stock [9]. Used in accordance with Elsevier’s permission guidelines)

26 4 Developmental Screening
Knowing that children with craniosynostosis are at increased risk for
neuropsychological problems including intellectual ability, gross and
fine motor coordination, language, executive functioning, visual-spatial
skills, visual-motor coordination, memory, and learning means that it is
critical to regularly screen children who are seen in craniosynostosis
clinics for these problems [7, 38]. At the youngest ages, this screening
should focus on gross and fine motor skills and receptive and
expressive language as these are known areas of risk that can be
detected at younger ages [39–43]. Parent-reported screening measures
such as the Ages and Stages—3 [44] can be used as a first level of
screening. The Bayley Scales of Infant Development-4 [45] or similar,
but older tests, such as the Mullen Scales of Early Learning [46] can be
used to screen infants and toddlers through direct assessments. Early
identification of areas of concern along with referral to the appropriate
early intervention program can help young children with
craniosynostosis develop to their full potential. Developmental

screening should occur frequently during the infant to toddler years so
that new concerns are not missed.
Once children with craniosynostosis reach the preschool years,
screening should focus on a number of pre-academic skills in addition
to motor and language skills. These include progress in basic skills such
as counting, ABC knowledge, phonological awareness, and paper-pencil
control. Children struggling to master rote counting, recitation of ABCs,
having difficulty with phonological processing tasks such as rhyming,
or identification of initial or ending sounds in words or using a pencil
can be referred for more detailed evaluation.
Older children require screening in multiple areas of
neuropsychological development including memory, language,
executive functioning, visual processing, processing speed, and motor
skills as well as problems with academic achievement [47–53].
Screening via direct assessment can be accomplished for older children
by selecting subtests from the NEPSY-2 [54] that focus on areas of
suspected risk. These subtests can be used individually to screen for
neurodevelopmental risk in one or more areas including attention and
executive functioning, language, memory and learning, sensorimotor,
social perception, and visuospatial processing beginning at age 3.
Monitoring of executive functioning skills including attention,
organization, and planning can be accomplished via specialized
behavior checklists such as the Behavioral Rating Inventory of
Executive Function BRIEF [55] beginning by age 5.
As part of the evaluation process, the psychologist should educate
parents about services available through their school district. Under the
Individuals with Disabilities Education Act of 2004 [56], special
educational services are available through public schools beginning at
age 3 for children who have documented needs. Disability areas
covered by special education law include: autism, deaf-blindness,
deafness, an emotional disturbance, a hearing impairment, an
intellectual disability (formerly known as “MR”), multiple disabilities,
other health impairment (which can include ADHD), an orthopedic
impairment, speech/language impairment, a specific leaning disability,
traumatic brain injury, or a visual impairment. However, it is not
enough to have a diagnosis related to one of those areas; the school
district must determine that the disability affects educational

performance. School districts will provide diagnostic services
evaluating children for global cognitive impairment and learning
disorders and will make a determination if the named disability affects
education. Schools do not typically perform neuropsychological
evaluations and often limit themselves to an educational diagnosis of
attention deficit disorder. Children will receive services if they are
diagnosed with a cognitive disability. They can also receive speech and
language therapy, hearing impaired services, occupational therapy,
physical therapy, learning disability services, or interventions for
behavior problems. Specialized services for attention problems and
other learning challenges are provided through a designation of other
health impaired’. This designation can be useful if a child does not
qualify for services based on other criteria, but is still experiencing
learning challenges. The craniofacial team psychologist can help
families obtain required services by documenting the child’s
specialized needs. Indeed, a critical contribution of the psychologist is
to assist teachers in understanding the unique needs of their student
and to prepare parents to advocate for appropriate supports for their
child.
Currently, most school districts in the U.S. strive to provide services
for children in what’s known as multitiered systems of support (MTSS)
[57]. MTSS was developed based on experience with the earlier used
Response to Interventions (RTI) [58] and Positive Behavior
Interventions and Supports (PBIS) programs [59]. The idea behind all
of these programs is that children should receive intervention services
before they fail [60, 61]. So rather than waiting for children to fall
behind in academic areas, school districts use universal screening of all
students early in the school year to identify students in need of
services. These services are then offered in three tiered levels of
intensity such that children receive services in relationship to their
needs. Children who do not respond well to intensified small-group
instruction (Tier 2) are the ones who go on to be evaluated for special
education interventions (Tier 3). There is ongoing data collection
throughout the school year to ensure that services are appropriate and
the student is progressing. This program works well for children who
have specific needs that can be addressed with less intensive services;
however, if improperly applied, the tiered program can delay

interventions for children who have greater needs. Many children with
craniosynostosis will fall into the latter category and should receive
evaluations at the earliest point in their education career as possible.
The craniofacial team psychologist plays an important role in ensuring
that needed evaluations are completed in a timely fashion.
Psychologists working in countries other than the U.S. need to
familiarize themselves with education law and services within their
own country.

26 5 Neuropsychological Assessment
Evaluations completed through the school district may not always be
detailed enough to identify all areas of cognitive functioning requiring
intervention. Psychological and other evaluations completed by the
school personal are generally geared to determine if a child qualifies for
special education services. These evaluations are not geared to
determining if learning or behavior problems experienced by a child
are related to underlying brain function or development. For example, a
child who struggles to follow instructions in school may be labeled as a
behavior problem by the teacher because the teacher sees the child
doing something other than the work expected and therefore the first
level of intervention may be a behavior plan. However, there are other
possible explanations. Executive functioning deficits may be present
including the inability to concentrate on the directions or the inability
to keep school materials well-enough organized, either of which can
look like a behavior problem. In another situation, the child who has a
processing speech deficit is not able to complete work in a timely
fashion. It’s also possible that the child was not able to comprehend the
verbal instructions provided and so feels lost as other children begin to
work. Or perhaps, the child is not able to remember the instructions
provided. A neuropsychological evaluation is most effective in sorting
out the etiology of a problem that looks like misbehavior but is really a
neuropsychological deficit.
Similarly, reading difficulties can have multiple etiologies. A child
may misread words because of impulsivity, suggesting an attention
problem. Or a child may misread words due to poor phonological
processing abilities suggesting a learning disability. Reading

comprehension problems may occur because child speeds through text
without concentrating on what is being read, because the child cannot
decode unfamiliar words, or because the child doesn’t comprehend the
information in the text. The etiology of reading comprehension
problems can be as disparate as attention problems, problems with
phonological processing, or language impairment. Therefore, detailed
assessments are needed to sort out learning problems that have similar
presentations.
The goal of a neuropsychological evaluation is to better understand
how functions such as memory, attention, perception, coordination,
language, processing speed ability, or personality characteristics impact
learning. The profile of strengths and weaknesses that emerges from
the evaluation can help in differential diagnosis. Does the child have
ADHD or depression? Is the child’s problem with language due to
expressive/receptive language delay, difficulty producing speech,
shyness, autism, or a cognitive delay? An older child may struggle when
expectations for independent work increase. They managed well during
early elementary years, but don’t succeed when faced with more
complicated tasks or multistep projects. The neuropsychological
evaluation can identify the underlying causes of a learning problem and
help to develop an intervention plan that draws on a child’s strengths,
builds confidence, and enhances emotional functioning as well as
learning. Providing parents with information about the etiology of a
child’s learning and/or behavior problems and a detailed treatment
plan can provide guidance to teachers and ease family tensions around
a child’s learning struggles.

26 6 Research
A pediatric psychologist on a craniofacial team may be involved in
clinical research. Three broad areas of research important to the
craniosynostosis field include behavioral, social and emotional
adjustment of children, families, and adults; similarities or differences
in neurodevelopment within the differing craniosynostosis diagnoses;
and finally, the impact of medical treatments on both psychological
adjustment and neurodevelopment.

Progress has been made in understanding some of the
underpinnings related to psychological adjustment problems, though
much more data are needed to develop effective interventions that can
be used by craniofacial teams [9, 11, 27, 66]. In particular, studies need
to address issues such the validity and generalizability of the constructs
to be measured as well as instrumentation or methodology used to
measure them, ages to study, and inclusion/exclusion criteria [67, 68].
Multi-site studies that are longitudinal in nature are needed; however,
those studies are challenging both from methodological and practical
perspectives [69]. Despite the challenges, some studies have examined
longitudinal behavioral changes in children with craniosynostosis [21,
63], while other studies have examined correlates of behavioral
adjustment [17–20, 22]. Most of the comprehensive work has been
done with children who have a cleft lip and palate (e.g., Feragen, Stock
[9, 33]). While some of the principal findings may cross-reference to
craniosynostosis, additional work is needed to identify the specific
factors affecting emotional, social, and behavioral adjustment for
individuals born with craniosynostosis.
Considerable progress has been made in identifying neurocognitive
patterns in children with nonsyndromic craniosynostosis, primarily,
single suture craniosynostosis (SSC). The recent papers on SSC from the
Infant and Child Learning Project have demonstrated significant
improvements in study design including an improved theoretical basis,
a large sample size with a constrained age range, use of a control group,
and longitudinal follow-up [21, 38, 41, 42, 49–51, 63–65], while other
studies were cross sectional or longitudinal with small sample sizes but
used controls (siblings or peers) or applied current neuropsychological
theory to their research [4, 18, 20, 66]. There are fewer well-designed
studies that investigate neurodevelopment in individuals with
syndromic craniosynostosis, likely due to the lower incidence of these
disorders, which makes it difficult to acquire a large enough study
sample for longitudinal study from one site. Thus, most of the research
on craniosynostosis is based on cross sectional designs with small
sample sizes, wide age ranges, a single clinic site, and no control group.
Recent reviews of the literature on craniosynostosis have highlighted
many of the weaknesses in extant studies of these conditions [2–4, 18,
20, 22, 62]. Even when national samples are available, the number of

subjects included per diagnostic group is too small for meaningful
comparisons [22]. As recommended by the group developing standards
of care for craniosynostosis in the U.S. [7], national data bases are
needed in which social, emotional, and behavioral functioning;
neuropsychological; medical; and surgical data are systematically
collected for all children with craniosynostosis. Psychologists working
on craniofacial teams can work together to determine appropriate
constructs and instrumentation for the psychological data acquisition.

26 7 Conclusions
Individuals with craniosynostosis may have risks in multiple areas of
functioning: social experiences, dissatisfaction with appearance,
behavioral difficulties, neurocognitive function, and emotional distress.
Risks vary by diagnostic category; however, there is wide variation in
functioning among children and adults even within the same diagnostic
category of craniosynostosis [62]. A psychologist on a craniofacial team
needs to be knowledgeable about risks in each diagnostic category, but
more importantly needs to know how to screen for individual risk
when an individual presents for evaluation to the craniofacial team.
An individual with craniosynostosis presenting to a craniofacial
team will be undergoing multiple evaluations, generally within a single
day [7]. It is therefore imperative that the craniofacial psychologist
knows how to perform rapid, but effective, screenings within the time
frame available. Parent-reported and self-reported screening
instruments can be useful strategies to obtain initial information about
current concerns. Effective interview techniques can flesh out the
information provided by screening instruments. Brief interventions
such as using the SUM model to clarify issues related to surgery or
social functioning can often be performed within the context of a
craniofacial team visit. However, referrals for further evaluation and/or
intervention should be made whenever the craniofacial psychologist
identifies issues that cannot be easily resolved within the time frame of
a team visit. Medical and psychological outcomes of craniosynostosis
are intertwined. The team psychologist is an essential support for the
patient and families, a resource for educators, and an essential partner

and consultant for other members of the multidisciplinary craniofacial
team.
