27 The Role of 3D Technology in the
Neurosurgical Management of
Craniosynostosis
M. E. L. Nienhuijs1 , M. Kregel2 and H. H. K. Delye3
(1) Department of Oral-, and Maxillofacial Surgery, Radboud
University Nijmegen Medical Center, Nijmegen, Netherlands
(2) Dental School, Radboud University Nijmegen Medical Center,
Nijmegen, Netherlands
(3) Department of Neurosurgery, Radboud University Nijmegen
Medical Center, Nijmegen, Netherlands

M E L Nienhui s (Corresponding author)
Email: Marloes.Nienhuijs@radboudumc.nl
H H K Delye
Email: Hans.Delye@radboudumc.nl
Keywords Craniosynostosis – Three-dimensional imaging – Virtual
surgical planning – Surgical template

27 1 Introduction
The field of dentistry and maxillofacial surgery has always used 3D
models to accurately represent and study 3D structures. Even with very
detailed two-dimensional X-ray images or two-dimensional images
based on CT or MRI scan, it requires highly trained imaging skills from
the physician to combine this information into a mental 3D
representation of the structure at hand. The use of physical 3D models

enhances the understanding of the surgeon; it helps to study complex
cases, to practice procedures, and to teach students and patients [1].
Initially, the use of 3D models concerned an analog workflow with
physical plaster models. In the 80s, stereolithography was introduced,
which provided insight into the delicate and complex craniofacial
anatomy in three dimensions [2]. However, this method has the
disadvantage that stereolithographic models are expensive and not
reusable once physically printed. Through advances in imaging and
visualization techniques, partly driven by the gaming industry, the
workflow evolved from plaster models toward virtual 3D models [3].
Compared to physical models, virtual 3D models are faster and less
expensive to obtain. In addition, virtual 3D models enable the surgeon
to simulate different treatment plans multiple times to determine the
best surgical therapy [4]. In contrast to traditional planning, these
digital techniques require a specific set of skills to integrate computer
technology into the clinical practice. Because of the general growing
need to implement different fast developing technologies into the field
of medicine, a new training program was developed in the Netherlands
in which technical physicians were trained to approach medical
problems with a technology-driven solution. These highly skilled
technical physicians came into the view of craniofacial surgeons, and
their synergy led in our hospital to the creation of the Radboudumc 3D
lab. The 3D lab aims to improve clinical practice and patient care by
implementing innovative digital technologies. As a result, the technical
physician and the surgeon can work closely to offer the best care for
patients. In craniosynostosis (CS), a congenital deformity where one or
more cranial sutures prematurely fuse, technological advancements
enable our multispecialty team to continuously plan, modify, and
improve treatment modalities, together with the young patient and the
parents [5]. In this way, the infant will grow into an adult with a
pleasing aesthetic appearance and without functional sequelae.

27 2 Application of 3D Technology
The neurocranium rapidly expands to accommodate the growing brain
during infancy and childhood [6]. If premature closure of one or more
cranial sutures occurs, compensatory overgrowth ensues at adjacent

non-fused sutures, resulting in craniofacial deformity with associated
neurodevelopmental and social complications [7, 8]. Treatment of CS
primarily aims to halt the developing cranial abnormality and
reestablish normal growth [9, 10]. In order to satisfactorily treat CS, it
is crucial to assess the cranial abnormality objectively and precisely.
Moreover, frequent follow-ups on the infant’s head shape and size are
needed to evaluate cranial growth before, during, and after treatment
[3].
The development of 3D technology and implementation in the
treatment strategy for craniosynostosis allows for a huge step forward
in the care for CS patients.
The foci for improving the management of CS patients through the
implementation of 3D technology encompass the entire length of the
treatment process and address the four different phases of surgical and
supplemental treatment: the diagnosis, planning, surgery, and
evaluation ([11]; Fig. 27.1).
The diagnosis of craniosynostosis is critical since the clinical
outcome benefits from early and adequate detection. Although
diagnosis is based mainly on clinical examination, in selected cases
CT scanning or X-ray is still used for diagnosis. However, 3D
stereophotogrammetry combined with software algorithms can be
implemented to diagnose and classify patients with various types of
craniosynostosis without exposure to ionizing radiation [12, 13].
Preoperative, digital planning of CS surgery creates a treatment plan
individualized to the patient. This allows for the creation of a patientspecific treatment plan. The use of Virtual Surgical Planning (VSP)
has several advantages.. A patient-specific preoperative plan,
prepared by the technical physician, provides the surgeon with
different treatment options. The surgical plan with the most optimal
outcome is selected, finalized, and taken into surgery. The meticulous
preoperative planning saves time and discussion in the operation
theatre, resulting in less blood loss and shorter postoperative
hospital stays [3].
Surgery of CS can be improved using patient-specific guides and
templates. When the optimal treatment plan is virtually created, this
plan then needs to be accurately transferred to the patient amidst
surgery. Patient-specific guides can be virtually designed and

fabricated using computer-aided design and manufacturing
(CAD/CAM). 3D printed surgical guides and templates assist the
surgeon in performing a precise and rapid reconstruction of the
cranial vault according to the VSP [3]. The benefits of 3D printed
surgical guides have been proved for applications outside
craniofacial surgery, such as reconstructive trauma surgery, knee
surgery, and spinal surgery [14].
Evaluation of patients during and after treatment is critical for
monitoring the patient’s well-being. Objective evaluation of surgical
outcomes improves the entire treatment process: the diagnosis,
planning, surgery, and evaluation wherever possible (Fig. 27.1). The
objectification and evaluation of the treatment, i.e. surgery, is
Inherent in evaluating the treatment outcomes. Consequently,
continuous evaluation of the treatment is the fundamental principle
behind the evolution of the surgical and 3D techniques. In turn, this
will benefit the treatment of new patients.

Fig. 27.1 The four different interconnected phases for the treatment of CS and their
relationships

It is beyond the scope of this chapter to give a detailed description
of all above mentioned steps. The interested reader is referred to the
PhD thesis of Meulstee [11].

Nonetheless, we will focus on the application of the most commonly
used 3D tools in CS: 3D stereophotogrammetry and virtual planning
using CAD/CAM techniques.

27 3 3D Stereophotogrammetry
Conventional imaging modalities that can accurately capture
information on cranial morphology are plain radiography, CT, and MRI
[12, 15, 16]. In infants, the use of radiation and the need for sedation
raise concerns about these traditional imaging techniques [8, 17, 18].
An innovative imaging tool capable of creating 3D photos of a
patient in a fraction of a second is 3D stereophotogrammetry [19]. In a
setup with five optical pods (Fig. 27.1), it is possible to obtain 3D
images of the neurocranium, rendering this imaging modality
applicable to the management of CS [19]. The advantages of 3D
stereophotogrammetry compared to other imaging modalities are the
fast acquisition, high accuracy, and the absence of ionizing radiation
[20]. Therefore, this instrument is the preferred method for studying
the craniofacial growth of affected newborns and normative controls [3,
6, 19, 21]. In craniofacial surgery, the powerful combination of 3D
models with 3D analysis makes it possible to evaluate the cranial shape
and size objectively and accurately [19]. Longitudinal datasets of CS
patients and healthy references are collected and studied using this
non-invasive 3D imaging and analysis combination [13, 22]. Surgeryrelated outcome measurements also are more easily exchangeable and
comparable when the same imaging modality is used. Universal
implementation of 3D photogrammetric analysis will make way for the
objective comparison of treatment results and help advance the
neurosurgical management of CS.
In daily practice, we use 3D stereophotogrammetry mainly for the
evaluation and follow-up of craniosynostosis patients treated with
endoscopically assisted suturectomy followed by helmet therapy.
The goal of the endoscopic technique is to remove the fused portion
of the bone and attempt to recreate normal anatomy as soon as
possible. The helmet molding therapy then guides the multidirectional
driving force of the expanding brain, without being constrictive,
towards the region that was previously restricted in order to

compensate for the inability to surgically reconstruct the already
existing deformity at time of surgery. The growth of the brain is fastest
during the first 3–6 months postpartum, so endoscopic surgery needs
to be performed relatively early, preferably around 3 months of age
[23].
The day before surgery, a 3D photo is taken as a baseline to compare
the growth evolution after surgery. During helmet therapy, which
typically starts 2 weeks after surgery, the patient is seen every 3
months at the multidisciplinary craniofacial team. Every time, a 3D
photo is taken and compared with the previous photo and the baseline
photo. 3D photos are superimposed to measure changes in the head
shape and volume and determine the growth of the cranial vault. 3D
photogrammetric analysis enables a longitudinal radiation-free followup after endoscopically assisted craniosynostosis surgery [24]. Changes
in the head volume can be visualized for the parents and clinicians on
the spot during the clinical consultation using distance colour mapping
(Figs. 27.2 and 27.3). These maps are showing the exact amount of
growth at every position of the head that occurred between two photos,
expressed in mm. It is our experience that this is greatly appreciated
and allows for a better understanding of the treatment protocol by
parents. This information is evaluated and aids in the decision of the
remaining length of helmet therapy. Typical cephalometric
measurements giving an indication of skull growth such as the head
circumference and the cephalic index (% skull width/length) are
automatically calculated and compared to the preoperative situation
(Fig. 27.2).

Fig. 27.2 3dMD Cranial System with 5-pod configuration

Fig. 27.3 3D analysis of cranial vault using 3D stereophotogrammetry. The 3D photos can be
inspected independently using the 3D shape evaluation or superimposed to compare
morphological changes and visualize areas of growth. Also, metrices such as the cephalic index
and the head circumference can be calculated using the 3D analysis

3D stereophotogrammetry can also be used to evaluate the
treatment of larger groups of patients and to objectively compare
different treatment modalities, for example, the use of springs or
helmets. Although efforts are made to define objective criteria by which
2D photographs and 2D measurements can be used to evaluate the
results of CS surgery, still postoperative results are being evaluated by
the carpenters’ eye’ and thus biased by subjective evaluation. Using 3D
stereophotogrammetry, objective measurements of larger groups of
patients can be combined to quantify in an objective manner the actual
3D growth and evolution of the head shape after craniosynostosis
surgery for different indications.
Doing this, we evaluated our results of endoscopically treated
trigonocephaly patients and objectively showed that this treatment
results in flattening of the forehead with a clear flattening and anterior
movement of the lateral orbital bar [24].
In addition, the same technology allowed for the recent
determination of the normal head growth in infants [13]. By creating

this reference data of the normal evolution, we are now capable of not
only objectively presenting and evaluating our surgical results, but also
of comparing them to the normal growth patterns. This has led to
exciting findings considering the postoperative results of
endoscopically treated scaphocephaly patients (de Jong et al., in
preparation). In general, these reference data of the normal skull
development indicate that skull growth patterns in scaphocephalic
children tend to normalize 8–11 months after endoscopic treatment.
To conclude, it is very clear that 3D stereophotogrammetry has
become indispensable in direct clinical practice as in research to help
forward the field of CS treatment.

27 4 Virtual Planning and CAD CAM
Techniques
Endoscopic surgery is only a viable treatment option when the patient
is referred before 6 months of age. If a patient presents at an older age,
cranial vault remodeling remains the designated therapy. The
application of 3D technology in calvarial reconstruction reduces the
operative length and intraoperative blood loss, thereby reducing
postoperative morbidity and the duration of postoperative hospital
stay. The technical physician makes a preoperative (VSP) by simulating
different calvarial reconstructions on the 3D CT-scan to improve
surgical efficacy. The added value of VSP is demonstrated by three
surgical cases below.

27 4 1 Scaphocephaly Case
An age-related average healthy cranial shape is used for reference
planning of scaphocephaly. The osteotomy lines are planned and the
calvarial segments are studied to determine the optimal reconstructive
alignment using the VSP software (Fig. 27.4a). The planned final shape
should result in the desired volume increase, reduction of frontal
bossing, and widening of the skull. This individualized preoperative
plan, made by the technical physician, provides the surgeon with
different treatment options. The options are then discussed with the

surgeon, and the most optimal plan is chosen (Fig. 27.4b). Marking and
reconstructive templates are then designed and printed.

Fig. 27.4 Discussing the treatment progress with the patient’s parents using the 3D photo
analysis during the postoperative consultation

Figure 27.5 demonstrates the intraoperative workflow using 3D
VSP. During surgery, the calvaria is exposed, after which the marking
template is used to indicate the exact location of the osteotomy lines.
The cranial vault is then resected according to the osteotomy lines. The
individual bone segments are, thereafter, combined back together using

the reconstruction template via resorbable plates and sutures (Fig.
27.5). The duration of the surgery, blood loss, and comorbidity are all
reduced due to the comprehensive preoperative planning performed in
the 3D lab.

Fig. 27.5 (a) Virtual representation of the best reconstructive alignment in order to obtain the
desired increase in cranial volume for sagittal suture synostosis where cranial vault remodeling
is to be performed. (b) Using the VSP software, the exact translational and rotational
movements of the individual calvarial segments that result in the desired morphological
changes are calculated

27 4 2 Plagiocephaly Case
Figure 27.6 shows the preoperative morphology of the patients’ skull
and the VSP of the cranial reconstruction. In the 3D lab, the existing
curvature of the individual frontal bone segments is studied and used
to puzzle together until the final result is as close as possible to the
normative reference shape. When the skull is exposed in the operating
theatre, the marking template is used to transfer the planned
osteotomies onto the skull. The frontal part and the orbital bar are
taken out separately. According to the marked osteotomy lines, all parts
of the frontal bones are taken out and arranged onto the reconstruction
template. The skull elements are then fixed together with resorbable
plates. The reconstructed skull is then placed back into the patient (Fig.
27.7). In the case of plagiocephaly, it is important to recreate as much
symmetry as possible. The biggest challenge remains optimizing the

shape of the orbital bandeau. Using VSP, it is possible to estimate the
number and exact placement of the inflection points (Fig. 27.8). This
again saves a lot of time and discussion in the OR during the surgery.

Fig. 27.6 (a) The 3D printed marking template is used for transferring the locations of the
planned osteotomy lines. (b) The resected skull where the planned osteotomy lines have been
marked. (c) The individual bone segments after completion of the osteotomies. (d) The 3D
printed reconstruction template is obtained from the VSP. (e) The bone segments are
positioned in the reconstruction template. (f) The bone segments combined together according
to the 3D orientation of the reconstruction template. (g) The final reconstruction of the cranial
vault in situ

Fig. 27.7 Virtual representation of the patient-specific (a) planned osteotomy lines, (b) virtual
reconstruction in 3D, and (c) design of the marking template that will be used to mark the

planned osteotomy lines for cranial vault remodeling of plagiocephaly

Fig. 27.8 (a) 3D printed reconstruction template. (b) The individual bone segments after
osteotomies. (c) The individual bone segments positioned in the reconstruction template
according to the planned positioning of the VSP

27 4 3 Trigonocephaly Case
The fronto-orbital advancement is virtually constructed by the
technical physician using reference data of normal, unaffected skulls.
The optimal angle of the two orbital segments is again precisely
calculated using reference data of healthy individuals (Fig. 27.9). Using
VSP, the ideal angle of the orbital segments can be accurately conveyed
using the reconstruction template. The frontal bone reconstruction
template guides the fixation of the frontal bone segments. The
postoperative result shows the absence of the wedge-shaped forehead
and the forward displacement of the lateral orbital walls, which gives a
more harmonious contour (Fig. 27.10).

Fig. 27.9 The virtual surgical plan showing the exact number and placement of inflection
points

Fig. 27.10 VSP of the planned reconstruction of the two orbital segments with measurements
of the angle. The two images above present the preoperative situation of the orbita. The images

below show the virtual orbital reconstruction to improve frontal contour

In the same way that 3D stereophotogrammetry is used to evaluate
the endoscopic approach, the postoperative results of the open
reconstruction can also be evaluated. In Fig. 27.11, an example of the
growth evaluation of one individual scaphocephaly patient is shown.
The red colour shows the preoperative 3D photo, and the blue colour
displays the most recent postoperative one. The skull has widened, and
the head circumference and the cephalic index have increased. The
postoperative heat map shows that skull widening has occurred
bilaterally as indicated by the red regions.

Fig. 27.11 (a) Preoperative 3D printed model of a patient with trigonocephaly. (b) The 3D
printed marking template that will be used intraoperatively to transfer the locations of the
osteotomy lines. (c) The preoperative situation with the locations of the surgical incisions
marked on the patient’s cranium. (d) Transferring the VSP using the marking template. (e)
Resected frontal bone segments after osteotomies placed in the reconstruction template. (f)
The resected orbital bandeau placed in the reconstruction template. (g) The reconstructed skull
parts are placed back in the patient. (h) Immediate postoperative result at the end of the
surgery. (i) Preoperative frontal view of the trigonocephaly patient showing the characteristic
deformity of the forehead. ( ) Postoperative frontal view of the patient after 6 weeks, showing
the improved aesthetic contour

27 5 Conclusion
3D stereophotogrammetry enables close monitoring of the cranial
development and provides insight into the treatment effect, enabling
continuous improvement of the applied surgical techniques. In the case
of the endoscopic approach, the postoperative growth is evaluated
using superimposed 3D photos which helps clinical decision making,
e.g. how long helmet therapy is needed. A 3D preoperative VSP aids in
open craniofacial reconstruction because different surgical options are
investigated preoperatively, resulting in the most optimal operation
plan with a fast and more accurate transfer through operating
templates.

27 6 Future Perspectives
As mentioned before, early diagnosis and intervention is important as it
often leads to less invasive therapeutic options for the surgeon and
more aesthetic outcomes for the patients. In primary and secondary
health care sectors, misdiagnosis of CS still occurs due to the lack of
expertise. It was recently suggested to combine 3D
stereophotogrammetry with the modern machine learning technique
called deep learning. Deep learning algorithms can be capable of
correctly classifying the head shape of infants on 3D stereophotographs
as healthy control or as a CS patient with the subtype scaphoid,
trigonal, or anterior plagiocephaly with high accuracy [25]. 3D
stereophotogrammetry technology is rapidly evolving, enabling the use
of smartphone technology to make accurate 3D photos. This fast and
radiation-free modality for capturing the cranial shape can be used in

primary healthcare sectors, to make the correct diagnosis quickly. At
this time, progress is made on the development of a mobile phone app
for this purpose. Another perspective would be that the VSP, which is
very labour-intensive, can be automated using artificial intelligence.
Another imaging modality that holds promise is 3D ultrasound.
Current ultrasound imaging still has a relatively low detection rate of
diagnosing CS [26]. Due to advancements in 3D ultrasound technology,
preliminary results show that the detection rate for syndromic CS has
improved and is high. Through further improvements, CS could be
diagnosed in utero using 3D echoes [27].
One of the difficulties in cranial vault remodeling remains the
transfer of the VSP to the skull. That is why marking and reconstruction
templates are used nowadays. However, manufacturing such templates
is time-consuming and expensive. Therefore, investigations continue to
transfer the planning onto the patient using innovative technologies
such as augmented reality (AR). Augmented Reality (Fig. 27.12) is the
technology of blending virtual objects into the real world. AR makes it
possible to create a virtual overlay within the surgeon’s view. Image
data of a patient can be observed directly at the corresponding position
on a patient in the operation theatre. With special glasses such as the
HoloLens (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, WA, USA), the VSP could
be projected right onto the skull of the patient in the operation theatre,
while the surgery is performed [6]. Currently, the implementation of
the HoloLens in the surgical field is limited to training and educational
purposes.

Fig. 27.12 Left: the pre- and postoperative photo of a scaphocephaly case superimposed.
Right: distance map where the red color displays where the most volume increase has taken
place

Like in other specialties, robotics can be of great use in CS surgery.
The surgical bots can, more accurately than their human counterpart,
transfer the VSP onto the skull of the patient, without the use of a
template (Fig. 27.13). One could imagine that this also occurs faster and
more accurately. One can even envision that the bots will even perform
osteotomies. The use of surgical navigation techniques could become
helpful in repositioning the bone segments back into the patient. All
these future developments may eventually alter the surgeon’s role (Fig.
27.14).

the capabilities of surgical robotics

28 1 Introduction
Surgeons face the challenge of learning, planning, and performing
highly complex surgical procedures. Surgical competence requires
technical skills using three-dimensional visualization, and previously it
was only possible to train surgeons in real-life situations. Progress in
the technologies of three-dimensional (3D) printing and advanced
methods in simulation training allow us to design specific training
procedures that integrate multiple skills in a safe environment. Given
that more than 75% of neurosurgical errors are judged to be avoidable,
simulation has a significant role to play in this context [1]. A metaanalysis of McGaghie et al. (2011) has shown that simulation training
may influence translational outcomes [1].
The standards for surgical training are shifting from time-based to
criterion-based parameters that emphasize obtaining and maintaining

competencies [2]. The formation of a surgeon demands significant
dedication and effort and considerable time [3]. Currently, wellestablished methods of surgical training are being challenged as the
environment becomes increasingly competitive and litigious with
greater scrutiny of patient outcomes [3–8]. In order to increase patient
safety and improve treatment outcomes, several strategies including
problem-based learning and objective structured clinical examinations
have promoted the development of new curricula in surgical education
[9–11]. Some of these changes have been driven by events in the 1980s
and 1990s, such as medical misconduct and overworked unsupervised
resident staff, contributing to patient morbidity and mortality. This has
also coincided with a growing medical malpractice crisis.
Concerns arose about the long-established methods of training
surgical residents, and solutions were sought to reduce preventable
errors and perioperative complications [2, 12]. The airline industry,
with the development of flight simulators and pilot coaching methods,
proved to be an excellent precedent for innovation in surgical
education. Many surgical educators believe such methods are key to
accelerating the acquisition of fundamental skills and the rate of
performance improvement among surgical residents.
Neurosurgical trainees face great challenges in learning to plan and
perform increasingly complex procedures in which there is little room
for error [15]. The educator’s task becomes ever more daunting as the
number and complexity of neurosurgical procedures continue to
increase in parallel with technological developments. A Yale University
study demonstrated that criterion-based simulator training decreased
operating time by 30% and operative errors by 85% [13, 14]. The
necessity of innovative surgical curriculum development that
incorporates safe learning environments and objective skill
assessments is obvious and needs to be led by trained surgical
educators [16].
Craniosynostosis, first described by Sommerring in 1791, refers to
the premature closure of cranial sutures, leading to calvarial
deformities [17]. Thus, there is a restriction of skull growth
perpendicular to the affected suture, and the continuous increase in
brain volume, promoting the compensatory growth of the skull in the
other patent sutures, causes progressive deformity typically parallel to

the affected suture (Virchow’s law) [4]. It is essential to emphasize that
the possibilities for hands-on training of surgical techniques to treat
craniosynostosis are quite restricted. Training has been performed
preferentially on sheep heads, but with many limitations [18]. The
sheep head does not present the same pathological condition, and it is
not possible to identify the anatomical reference structures. In addition,
bone consistency is not adequate to simulate the osteotomy process,
impairing the acquisition of physical feedback. Also, emergencies such
as bleeding from the superior sagittal sinus are not reproduced.
The limitations of traditional training methods point to the high
value of developing new alternative methods. In surgical training
generally, and in training for the treatment of craniosynostosis, the
educational value of 3D printed models for teaching advanced
techniques is derived from their ability to provide the trainee with
tactile feedback and to simulate spatial relationships, thus aiding in the
memorization of the steps of the surgical procedure.
The first realistic simulator for training surgical techniques for
scaphocephaly was published in 2014, presenting a radiological
interface and a bleeding effect [19]. As an important complement of the
physical simulator, a virtual reality simulator was also developed to
emphasize the three-dimensional step by step procedure of
craniosynostosis surgical correction [20].
In this chapter, we will describe the available simulators for
craniosynostosis surgical training and the current impact of, and future
perspectives on, their use in neurosurgical education.

28 2 Craniosynostosis Realistic Simulator
Development authors with a Brazilian institute EDUCSIM (https://​
educsim.​com.​br) have worked on creating and improving synthetic
models that can provide a reliable model for craniosynostosis training.
The first realistic simulator was built with a synthetic thermoretractile, thermo-sensitive rubber which presents textures,
consistencies, and mechanical resistance similar to many human
tissues.
Regarding anatomical aspects, the skull shape was based on
computerized tomography (CT) in Digital Imaging and Communications

in Medicine (DICOM) images of a real patient (6-month-old female).
Thin slices were used to enable 3D reconstruction. A special resin, in
the shape of the skull, constituted the basic structure of the
craniosynostosis module trainer. The module contains the head (the
surgical unit, presenting a scaphocephaly type cranial malformation,
Fig. 28.1a, b) which is connected to the body by a simulated cervical
spine (acrylic composition, Fig. 28.1c). In this way, the head is locked by
a simple acrylic connection. With this, training can be performed as if it
were a real surgery (Fig. 28.1d). Due to the radiopacity of this
simulator, it is possible to perform CT scans (Fig. 28.2) and,
consequently, this simulator allows for comparison between pre- and
postoperative images.

Fig. 28.1 Realistic craniosynostosis simulator. (a, b) Craniosynostosis Surgical Unit. (c)
Connection point between the surgical unit (head) and the base of the simulator. (d)
Anatomical model ready to use

Fig. 28.2 (a–c) CT images with tridimensional reconstruction. (d–f) Hyperdensity of superior
sagittal sinus (filled with blood simulator)

There are multiple opportunities for practice using this realistic
model, including the skin incision, subcutaneous and subperiosteal
dissection, osteotomies, and cranial remodeling with absorbable
microplates. The presence of superior sagittal and transverse sinuses
filled with liquid can simulate emergency situations like bleeding (Fig.
28.3).

Fig. 28.3 (a and b) Real simulator in the operating room and delimiting the skin incision. (c
and d) Subcutaneous dissection. (e and f) Subperiosteal dissection. (g and h) Delimiting the
osteotomy. (i and ) Green-stick fracture (Renier’s “H” technique). (k and l) Cranial
reconstruction (using absorbable plates). (m and n) Skin closure

This model also can be used to practice endoscopic correction with
notable realism [20]. Surgical endoscopic treatment for a case involving
both scaphocephaly and trigonocephaly can be performed basing the
head model on a combination of real CT images obtained from
scaphocephaly and trigonocephaly patients.

28 3 Craniosynostosis Virtual Simulator
The main goal of the virtual simulator is to provide, through virtual
simulation, training that mirrors the physical platform. These virtual
models don’t allow for interaction with the trainee, but they can
stimulate the ability to mentally manipulate objects in three
dimensions, recreating the intraoperative scenario.
3D videos were developed by a graphic designer and a
neurosurgical team using 3DS Max software. They were based on
reproduction of the tridimensional anatomy of the skull and real
surgical videos [21]. The craniosynostosis virtual modules present the
scaphocephaly type and all the stages of the surgical approach by HRenier technique (Fig. 28.4).

Fig. 28.4 Craniosynostosis virtual simulator. (a–c) Patient positioning, skin incision, and
dissection by plans. (d–i) Craniotomy area definition—H Renier technique. ( ) Green stick
fracture. (k and l) Sagittal strip removal. (m and n) Use of absorbable plates

28 4 Pu le
A craniosynostosis puzzle was developed to simulate the
craniosynostosis correction (scaphocephaly type) using H Renier’s
technique [22].
The cranial model is created by 1-mm CT scans in the DICOM
format. This information is processed using a computing algorithm to
generate a 3D printed biomodel in resin. Afterward, planned
craniotomies are performed and the skull pieces are fitted with
magnets to allow real surgical simulation with the magnetic interface.
In this way, it is possible to practice the surgical technique and simulate
the cranial reconstruction step by step (Fig. 28.5).

Fig. 28.5 Scaphocephalic skull simulation, with several osteotomies. The magnetic interface of
the bone pieces makes possible the “osteotomies” and subsequent posterior cranial
remodeling, both correctly and incorrectly

The puzzle is simple to use, portable, and low cost. It can be used
many times since it is reusable and recyclable (Fig. 28.5). This is a
significant feature, as the number of attempts was proved to be
inversely proportional to the number of errors [22].
This tool may be used as a supplementary model to enhance
cognitive abilities related to anatomical recognition, allowing a variety
of degrees of immersion and realism, establishing a physical reality
learning curve, and offering symbolic, geometric, and dynamic
information, with 3D visualization.

28 5 Patient-Specific Hybrid and Augmented
Reality Models
The availability of 3D printing technology has expanded the
possibilities for developing life-like models to increase understanding
of normal and pathological anatomy [23, 24]. These models combined
with augmented reality bring new perspectives to preoperative
planning.
Augmented reality (AR) transforms virtual objects into video
images in real time, providing specific anatomical information and
elaborated metrics [25, 26]. With recent advancements, these systems
can be used not only for surgical planning, but also as tools in
intraoperative scenarios [25, 27, 28].
An innovative project was developed by Coelho et al. [29] combining
a realistic customized model and an augmented reality model for
preoperative planning of trigonocephaly correction. In the first step of
the development process, a patient-specific hybrid model was created
based on the anatomical aspects of the skull. Data were obtained from
CT DICOM thin-slice images of a real patient (a 5-month old male infant
case patient) which allowed 3D reconstruction (Fig. 28.6). The material
was composed of high-performance platinum-cured liquid silicone
components used in many applications ranging from creating skin
effects to making a variety of different tissues. After the printing
process, an artist worked manually to make the model more realistic.

Fig. 28.6 (a) Hybrid model and 3D printed models. (b) Preoperative planning using the 3D
printed and hybrid model

The surgical training using the metopic craniosynostosis model was
performed as if it were a real surgery, using surgical instruments. It was
possible to simulate the surgical approach step by step with real
instruments used to cut the skin (the silicone mimicked the tissue
accurately) and to perform the osteotomies and dissection with
appropriate tactile feedback (Fig. 28.8). As well, a customized
augmented reality model was developed for use with a smartphone app
(Fig. 28.7).

Fig. 28.7 The three layers of visualization in the AR app. (a) AR image of patient face in CT
scan. (b) Whole skull format. (c) Possibilities of AR skull creation

Fig. 28.8 Preoperative planning using the hybrid model. (a–b) Skin dissection. (c, d)
Osteotomies. (e-g) Cranial reconstruction using absorbable plates. Real surgical tools were
used in lll the stages of the preop planning

The model was considered a fundamental and valuable factor in the
multidisciplinary discussion between the neurosurgeons and plastic
surgeons. It allowed for a detailed discussion of the aspects of the
surgical planning, providing tissues with different tactile and resistance
qualities, as well as prediction of the orbit remodeling measurements

with excellent precision. The patient operated on in these conditions
presented excellent follow-up and an excellent esthetic result [ 29]

28 6 Discussion
Surgical education in the coming years faces critical challenges,
especially in training surgeons to acquire and perfect complex
neurosurgical techniques such as those required for successful
treatment of craniosynostosis. Disruptions and constraints in both local
face-to-face teaching and global mobility inhibit the transfer of
knowledge characteristic of the traditional (Halsted) model of surgical
apprenticeship and mentorship. Inadequacies in surgical education,
whether the effect of exceptional factors like regional or international
health crises, prohibitive costs, or political uncertainties, can and must
be overcome with advances in teaching technologies and methods,
among them the innovative use of highly realistic physical models that
simulate the complexities of surgical reality. Such innovations have the
further advantage of providing means for supplementary remote
training in situations where side-by-side training is impossible or
limited in scope, or would benefit from auxiliary methods.
The treatment of craniosynostosis implies extensive surgery and
presents a challenge for the surgeon. In this context, training based on
surgical simulation is extremely helpful. Multiple meta-analyses have
shown that associating simulation with conventional training results in
better performance, reduction in surgery time, reduced error rate, and
consequently, better patient outcomes [30].
Simulators can be used to facilitate assessment and objectively
provide quantifiable measures of learning using multidisciplinary
content. Many training models have been created as the initial step in
training residents and young neurosurgeons to gain experience with
surgical procedures. The majority of these have used animal models,
human cadaveric specimens, and occasionally synthetic materials.
However, procedures such as craniosynostectomy or cranial vault
remodeling can be highly complex to simulate in their entirety. In this
respect, the craniosynostosis realistic simulator provides an alternative
to the use of animal models and human cadaveric specimens.
Moreover, the realistic simulator presents some notable advantages:

1. material maintenance is convenient
2. the cranium size is appropriate and provides for realistic depth
perception
3. the simulator includes all necessary planning steps of the surgery
(from positioning to skin closure)
4. real surgical instruments can be used
5. a bleeding effect trains surgeons in the handling of emergency
situations
6. there are no ethical or location restrictions to its use
The puzzle can be considered as a complementary tool that allows
different degrees of immersion and realism. Also, it enables evaluation
of the basic competence of the resident before proceeding to real
surgery.
Despite the importance of improving technical skills, operating
room conduct, and the interpersonal abilities of those who perform
surgical procedures, few studies have examined the use of AR
technology in preoperative planning to determine the most favorable
surgical approaches [25]. With the development of an AR-based
training simulator, surgeons in training can experience realistic
simulations of surgical operations comparable to those encountered in
actual neurosurgery.
The use of a physical hybrid model and AR in planning the operative
technique involved in treating metopic craniosynostosis is particularly
noteworthy. The association of physical hybrid model technology with
the application of AR can provide a highly effective training
environment by facilitating preoperative planning while highlighting
important perspectives in medical education. The remarkable realism
of this method significantly enhances the teaching of surgical anatomy
and operative strategies in the neurosurgical field, especially during
residency training, and 3D modeling technology may provide a
complementary educational tool in any preoperative surgical planning,

enhancing the safety of the procedure and contributing to a better
outcome [29].
Practice with each of these models has particular advantages and
disadvantages that are still being elucidated in various validation
processes. The choice of the most appropriate training model should be
taken into consideration, as well as other qualities such as efficacy,
validity, cost-effectiveness, and versatility [31].
Several factors favor the increasing use of surgical simulation in
training during medical residency: restrictions on working hours;
increased supervision; more formalized educational goals; and rising
demand for increased hospital efficiency (with emphasis on the patient
and outcomes). The need for new paradigms of training and surgical
skills education has led to the development of a variety of simulation
methods that refine the technique while objectively assessing the
resident’s performance.
It is important to emphasize that there is significant evidence
demonstrating that technical skills acquired on simulated models
directly transfer into performance improvements in the operating
room, reinforcing their value in surgical training programs [32, 33]. The
ideal simulator has to be realistic in multiple dimensions. Simulation
physics, optical properties, haptic feedback, and suitability for the
required surgical tasks must be tested to ensure the quality of surgical
training.
It is also necessary to validate the ability of the simulation exercise
to teach the desired skill set or technique. The identification and
measurement of errors permit assessment of the effectiveness of
training that is specifically intended to reduce their incidence.
Additionally, to be considered a useful tool for training, a simulator
should be further evaluated regarding its overall quality. Despite a
variety of ways to do it, every simulator should meet three major
criteria: validity, reliability, and feasibility [17]. It has been suggested
that when adopting a new training paradigm such as a simulator-based
curriculum, it is important to utilize the same language and
terminology to preserve the standards of assessment [17].
The development of effective surgical simulators is a milestone in
the evolution of surgical education. Craniofacial realistic simulators
provide a safe and nonthreatening learning context that not only

promotes the development of skills, but also allows for objective riskfree testing of a trainee’s abilities prior to entering the operating room.
Beyond pure technical proficiency, the cognitive skills of anatomical
recognition, decision-making, and contingency planning can also be
developed. Additionally, these same models can be used in the process
of initial certification as well as recertification of existing practitioners
similar to performance assessment standards in the airline industry.

28 7 Conclusion
The use of simulation in teaching the operative techniques involved in
treating craniosynostosis is particularly noteworthy. The use of realistic
simulators can reduce errors, maximize sensitivity in measuring the
success of skills transfer, and improve the learning curve prior to
undertaking real surgery.
Future studies with accurate learning curve evaluation
measurements need to determine whether practice with these
described simulators translates into changes in clinical practice, such as
reduction of surgical time, complications, and length of hospitalization,
with consequent benefits in patient care.

29 Craniosynostosis: Anesthetic
Considerations—What the Pediatric
Neurosurgeon Should Know
Margaret Ekstein1 , Jonathan Roth2 and Shlomi Constantini2
(1) Division of Anesthesiology, Intensive Care and Pain Medicine, Tel
Aviv Sourasky Medical Center, Tel Aviv, Israel
(2) Department of Pediatric Neurosurgery, Dana Children’s Hospital,
Tel Aviv Sourasky Medical Center, Tel Aviv, Israel

Keywords Anesthesia risk – Anesthesia neurotoxicity in the
developing brain – Fasting guidelines in infants and children –
Positioning for craniosynostosis surgery – Blood conservation
strategies – Venous air embolism
Craniosynostosis is a premature closure of the skull sutures and is
categorized as either “single suture synostosis” (SSS) or “multi-suture
synostosis” (MSS) [1, 2]. The majority of operated CS are SSS—relating
to closure of the sagittal, or metopic sutures. The main effect of SSS is
on the appearance of the child with potential secondary psychosocial
effects; however, although debatable, some reports have stated longterm neurodevelopmental sequela. Increased intracranial pressure is
uncommon in SSS, however it may occur too.
As opposed to SSS, multi-suture synostosis is often associated with
syndromes such as Apert, Crouzon, Pfeiffer, and others. MSS impacts
the child in many aspects, such as cosmetic and various neurological
aspects: increased intracranial pressure is significantly more prevalent
compared to SSS, and Chiari malformation and hydrocephalus may

occur in about 30%. MSS often involves the skull base sutures, leading
to micrognathia and retro-maxilla, affecting the midface and upper
airway anatomy. Additionally, MSS may affect the venous outlets of the
brain, often leading to large emissary veins and excessively developed
and atypical subcutaneous venous pathways [1, 3–6].
Treatment for craniosynostosis is usually performed during the first
year of life and sometimes even during the first few months of life [7].
Thus, awareness of the anesthetic—surgical interaction is crucial for
ensuring safety during treatment.

29 1 Risk of Anesthesia in the Very Young
Patient
Recent studies have found increased risk of complications associated
with anesthesia early in life [8, 9]. This risk increases as the age of the
child decreases [10]. There has also been a plethora of animal data and
some human retrospective studies that suggest the possibility of
neurotoxicity of anesthetic agents on the developing brain [11].
Recently, prospective randomized trials have found no negative
consequences of general anesthetics on very young infants who
received a single short anesthetic [12–14]. Anesthesia for
craniosynostosis surgery is neither short nor without its own inherent
risks, and we are as yet missing data regarding toxicity of anesthesia for
craniosynostosis repair or neurocognitive impact of craniosynostosis
itself, repaired or not [15].

29 2 Preparation of the Patient
It is intuitive that preoperative optimization of associated medical
conditions of an infant before craniosynostosis surgery will be
protective. Surgery for SSS is nearly always elective. Thus, surgery
should be postponed in a child with exacerbation of underlying
pulmonary disease or a recent upper respiratory tract infection for
about 2 weeks to avoid adverse respiratory events perioperatively [16].
Optimization includes pulmonary preparation with inhaled beta
agonists and/or steroids or addition of systemic steroids in a child with

known chronic lung disease. Since multi-suture synostosis is often part
of a multi-organ system syndrome, further workup, including genetic
testing, is advised. Syndromes associated with craniosynostosis are
reviewed of Meier’s recent review [17]. Associated anomalies that
should be assessed preoperatively include whether there is midface
hypoplasia (Apert’s, Crouzon’s, Pfeiffer) or whether there is an element
of mandibular hypoplasia, or high arched palate with resultant risk of
difficult intubation. In addition to anomalous facial features (ptosis, low
set ears, hypertelorism, strabismus), there might be associated hearing
loss, syndactyly, intellectual deficits in the case of Apert’s syndrome;
and cardiovascular anomalies, obesity, hypogonadism in the case of
Carpenter’s syndrome. Preoperative neurologic assessment is
necessary for all syndromic patients, and cardiac evaluation is indicated
if cardiovascular involvement is suspected. The anesthesiologist should
review the full medical history by organ system and include: history of
prior anesthetics, allergies, medications, presence of passive smoking,
and fasting guidelines. Laboratory examination must include a full
blood count, electrolytes including glucose and renal function,
coagulation profile, and blood type and cross for transfusion.

29 3 Fasting Guidelines
It is acceptable to fast infants and children prior to general anesthesia
or sedation in order to reduce the risk of pulmonary aspiration of
gastric contents. The current European Society of Anesthesia and
Intensive Care Guidelines recommends a 1-h fast from clear liquids
defined as water, tea, juice without pulp, or carbonated drinks; a 3-h
fast from breast milk; 4 h from cow’s milk, formula and juice with pulp;
and 6 h from solid food [18]. Prolonging fasting of clear liquids has
negative consequences including risk of hypovolemia and hypoglycemia
in small infants, as well as increase in infant irritability and reduced
parental satisfaction. In the case of a delay in surgery, it is important to
feed the baby sweet clear liquids if a 2-h delay is anticipated, or start
intravenous fluid if start time is undetermined.

29 4 Preoperative Anxiety

If surgery involves infants up to 6 months of age, there is high level
parental anxiety but not yet significant situational or separation anxiety
in the infant. It is important to clearly discuss the procedures and
expectations/alternatives of general anesthesia with the parents,
answer all questions, and allay their fears. Separate informed consent
for general anesthesia including blood transfusion must be obtained.
The infant will be able to enter the operating room and undergo inhaled
induction with simple distraction techniques to keep them calm. If the
child is older than 6 months, it is helpful to administer anxiolysis. The
most common anxiolytic agent is midazolam: syrup 0.5 mg–0.7 mg/kg,
intranasal 0.2 mg/kg, or intramuscular 0.1 mg/kg. Other agents such as
dexmedetomidine, ketamine, and brevital may be given for sedation.
Narcotics and nonsteroidal medications can also be given
preoperatively for preemptive analgesia [19]. Parental presence during
induction of anesthesia is still controversial and depends on the
preference of the particular anesthesiologist and individual evaluation
of each patient and parent. If a parent is allowed to accompany their
child, it is important to prepare the parent as to what to expect and
what his/her role is while in the operating room and how he/she will
be escorted outside as per the instructions of the anesthesiologist.
There must be a staff member dedicated to care for the parent while in
the operating room.

29 5 Preparation of the Operating Room
Before arrival to the operating room, the room should be warmed to
24 °C (75 °F), the bed and intravenous fluids should be warmed, and all
equipment should be checked. A difficult airway cart should be
available, as well as ultrasound for venous and arterial cannulation as
needed. Two crossmatched units of packed red blood cells should be
checked and available. If blood loss is expected to exceed half of the
child’s blood volume, fresh frozen plasma and platelets should be
ordered from the blood bank and availability of Point of Care analysis of
coagulation should be considered.

29 6 Anesthetic Management

29 6 1 Induction and Maintenance of Anesthesia
Standard induction is via inhaled agents: oxygen with or without
nitrous oxide and sevoflurane. High concentrations of nitrous oxide are
convenient at the start of induction as it is odorless, well tolerated, and
promotes a good feeling. It can be used alone for 3 min prior to starting
a potent halogenated agent to ease comfort with the mask without
causing agitation. During surgery, however, it should be discontinued
because of risk of air embolism and N2O’s physical properties which
enlarge closed volumes of entrapped air. Once the child is under
general anesthesia, intravenous access is obtained and balanced
anesthesia follows with both inhaled and intravenous agents, including
narcotics and muscle relaxants to ease airway instrumentation and
positioning.

29 6 2 Intravenous Access
Two intravenous lines either 22 or 20 gauge comprise our standard
practice. Arterial lines are necessary for all open procedures, but can be
avoided in minimally invasive procedures in which blood loss is
anticipated to be minimal. Ultrasound is often helpful in obtaining
access in younger infants or in some in the higher weight percentiles.
Central lines are reserved for children with difficult access or in those
in whom the necessity of vasoactive agents is anticipated because of
underlying cardiac disease [20].

29 6 3 Monitoring
American Society of Anesthesia standard monitoring of ECG,
noninvasive blood pressure, pulse oximetry, and temperature is
mandatory as well as monitoring of inhaled and exhaled gases. Urinary
catheters are not placed routinely. During open craniosynostosis repair,
an arterial line is indicated. It is used for beat-to-beat blood pressure
assessment as well as for blood sampling; however, its most significant
use is its sensitivity to assess fluid responsiveness. The respiratory
variations in the arterial waveform, pulse pressure variation across the
respiratory cycle, serve as a surrogate to predict the preload’s role in
augmenting blood pressure in mechanically ventilated patients.

29 6 4 Fluid Management

Goal-directed fluid therapy has evolved from adult intensive care and
perioperative fluid management as the ideal way to guide fluid
administration. Static variables such as central venous pressure or
physical signs are unreliable as predictors of which patients will benefit
from a fluid bolus. Dynamic variables based on the heart lung
interaction are superior in assessing how fluid will impact stroke
volume and cardiac output in ventilated patients [21, 22]. While recent
literature supports the use of aortic velocity measurements by
ultrasound [22], we use systolic pressure variation during acute
hemorrhage occurring in these cases, due to its accessibility
intraoperatively, to guide transfusion and crystalloid administration.
Blood loss in these small patients is rapid and immediate replacement
is necessary to avoid complications of reduced organ perfusion, even if
it is transient. Isotonic crystalloids, either lactated ringer’s solution or
plasmalyte, should be used. Colloid solutions, such as third-generation
hydroxyethyl starch (HES 130,000 Daltons) or albumin, may also be
used [23]. While HES has been shown to increase risk of renal failure in
adults in the intensive care unit, there is no renal dysfunction or effect
on perioperative bleeding associated with HES in children at doses up
to 20 cc/kg. Administration of HES in this dose has no effect on blood
loss or transfusion perioperatively in children and is considered a safe
option for restoring blood volume quickly during surgical hemorrhage
[24].

29 6 5 Positioning
Proper positioning of the patient for cranial vault surgery is key to safe
and effective repair. Sagittal synostosis repairs at early ages (up to
about 5–6 months) are best performed in the prone, sphinx position
which allows for a full view and access to the margins of craniectomy.
Use of a vacuum-stiffened bean bag is standard for these cases [25];
other devices have also been described [26]. The neck is extended and
the bed is placed in the reverse-Trendelenburg position. Careful
attention must be made to the endotracheal tube (ETT) position as
neck extension moves the endotracheal out to a more superficial
position in the trachea. If the leak around the ETT increases, or a new
leak is heard, repositioning of the ETT to a deeper position is necessary.
Careful attention must be paid to the level of the head as compared to

the heart, as risk of venous air embolism increases with higher
differences between the surgical field and the right atrium. The arms
are positioned alongside the body. Legs are positioned flexed with
foam, lifting the feet as high as comfortable to promote venous return
from the legs (Fig. 29.1). Careful padding with foam should be provided
to prevent pressure sores during prolonged surgery. A foam cushion is
placed under the buttock and taped to the bed as a slinged hammock to
prevent the patient sliding downward in the reverse Trendelenburg
position (see Fig. 29.1). Meticulous attention should be paid to eye
protection, so no alcohol from the prep solution or debris from the field
will touch the eyes. We suggest three layers of protection: first a layer of
ophthalmologic ointment or lubricant on the corneas, then watertight
dressing on each eye covering the eyebrows, and last a sticky drape
which covers the face including the eyes and the tape fixing the ETT.
Some surgeons suture the eyelids closed or place corneal protectors,
but this is reserved for craniofacial procedures in which there is
significant preoperative proptosis typically in syndromic
craniosynostosis.

Fig. 29.1 Sketch of patient positioning for repair of saggital craniosynostosis

In anterior vault remodeling, the patient is positioned supine, with
the head supported by a horseshoe head holder. The head is flexed.
Again, careful attention must be paid to ETT position; flexing the neck
will advance the ETT deeper into the trachea and might cause a onelung intubation. Breath sounds must be auscultated in the final
position. A foam cushion is placed under the buttock as described
above and careful padding of the extremities is necessary. During
anterior cranial remodeling, there is risk of extreme neck flexion which
can kink the ETT; therefore, we place a foam collar under the neck to

prevent exaggerated flexion. Heed the oculo-cardiac reflex during
supraorbital bone reconstruction; pressure on the eyes may cause
bradycardia which will resolve with cessation of eye pressure; rarely, it
is necessary to treat with vagolytic drugs: atropine 0.02 mg/kg.

29 6 6 Venous Air Embolism
A number of factors make the risk of air embolism a particular concern
during craniosynostosis surgery, especially when operating on
syndromic craniosynostosis, in which emissary veins are more
common. Positioning is aimed at reducing blood loss and enhancing
surgical exposure to the cranial vault, thus the level of the operative
field is often higher than the heart. Bony structures have venous
channels (emissary veins) that do not collapse as other veins do. Thus,
when exposing and cutting such venous channels, the atmospheric
pressure may be higher at the level of the open vein than central venous
pressure causing entrainment of air into the right atrium, rather than
bleeding in the surgical field. Because of the size of the patient, a small
amount of air entrained into the right ventricular outflow tract can
cause hemodynamic collapse. Therefore, it is imperative that the
surgeons and anesthesiologists monitor for such an event. Monitoring
by doppler is most sensitive, but many find it to be overly sensitive, as
very small air emboli, present in as much as 82% of craniosynostosis
surgeries in one report [27], have no clinical consequence [28]. Large
centers have found the incidence of clinically significant air embolism
to be less than 5%, which is consistent with our experience, and are
detected by acute decrease in end-tidal CO2, decrease in blood pressure,
decrease in oxygen saturation, change in ECG which indicates right
ventricular strain, and abrupt increase in CVP after an initial decline.
To mitigate the risk of venous air embolism, it is best to be judicious
with positioning, diligent in fluid resuscitation, consider use of positive
end expiratory pressure (PEEP) to increase right atrial pressure, and
avoid use of nitrous oxide. If venous air embolism is suspected, the
surgeon should flood the surgical field with irrigation fluid, search for
open venous channels, use bone wax or other hemostatic measures to
occlude the entry to the venous system, lower the head of the bed to
lower the surgical field to the height of the right atrium, and tilt the bed
to the left to protect the right ventricular outflow tract [29]. It is ill-

advised to turn the patient to the left lateral position as this might
compromise sterility of the surgical field, inhibit effective chest
compressions should they be necessary, and there is no evidence that
the left lateral position has a protective hemodynamic effect [30]. Blood
pressure should be supported with fluid and pressors if needed,
increasing inhaled oxygen concentration to improve saturation.
Aspiration of air from a central line is theoretically possible, but this
author has found this strategy useful only in adults. Aspiration of air
includes air with blood, which would worsen hypotension; aspirated
blood would have to be returned after air removal which is quite
cumbersome in a small child. Sealants should be used with caution as
embolism has been described using an aerosolized fibrin sealant; if
sealants are used, it’s preferable not to deliver with a pressurized
delivery device, rather inject sealant using a manual syringe injection
[31].

29 7 Blood Transfusion and Conservation
Strategies
Open craniosynostosis surgery (as opposed to endoscopic surgery) is
associated with significant blood loss. Intraoperative blood loss varies
significantly between series and has been reported to be as high as
119 mL/kg [32]. Several factors are associated with increased blood
volume loss: length of surgery, young age, lower weight, and the cranial
suture related to repair [33, 34]. As a result of the significant
intraoperative hemorrhage, transfusion with allogeneic blood products
is often necessary during open surgery. According to the pediatric
craniofacial surgery perioperative registry, 95% of children younger
than 24 months and 79% of older children received transfusions of red
blood cells during craniosynostosis surgery. Thirty percent of the
younger group received 40 cc/kg of blood, representing 50% of their
volume and thus were considered massive transfusion patients [35].
Extent of hemorrhage and transfusion volume is associated with
perioperative morbidity. Associated complications include metabolic
acidosis, hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, coagulopathy, hypothermia,
hypoxia, and pulmonary complications, venous air embolism,

hypotension, bradycardia, and cardiac arrest, as well as longer hospital
length of stay [36]. Exposure to allogenic blood is also associated with
risks of immunologic and non-immunologic patient reactions, and in
the setting of massive blood transfusion, causes coagulopathy and
further requirements of blood products transfusion; hence, the
stimulus to initiate blood conservation strategies in this population.
Minimally invasive endoscopic surgery for craniosynostosis is
associated with a significant reduction in blood loss and transfusion
[37]. A recent review of 121 endoscopic strip craniectomies (of which
116 were for single suture craniosynostosis) reported intraoperative
blood loss to be 5.7 cc/kg; and transfusion rate 21%; intensive care was
not needed and hospital stay was a mean of 2.6 days [38]. Analysis of
data from the Pediatric Craniofacial Surgery Perioperative Registry of
North America compared endoscopic to open craniosynostosis repair.
Propensity score matching was used to normalize the inherent age and
weight difference in the groups and found that packed red blood cells
were given in 26% of endoscopic vs. 81% of open surgeries,
coagulation factors in 3% vs. 16%. Adverse events such as hypotension
requiring pressors, venous air embolism, hypothermia, and cardiac
arrest were not different; however, need for postoperative intubation,
intensive care admission, and length of hospital stay were all greater in
the open surgery group [39]. Length of surgery was significantly longer,
which plays a significant role in blood loss and transfusion volume
needed in craniosynostosis surgery [40]. In open procedures, injection
of local anesthetic with epinephrine intradermally, use of needle-tip
monopolar cautery and Raney clips for skin incision, liberal use of bone
wax during osteotomies, and use of appropriate hemostatic agents all
minimize surgical bleeding [41]. Other strategies include
administration of preoperative oral iron supplements with or without
erythropoietin 600–1000 units subcutaneously once a week for
3 weeks prior to surgery to maximize preoperative hemoglobin and
hypervolemic hemodilution with infusion of crystalloid solution
20 cc/kg before starting osteotomies [42]. Cell saver may be used but
has not been shown to be cost-effective [43]. Landmark randomized
prospective trials demonstrated effectiveness of tranexamic acid in
reducing blood loss and transfusion during craniosynostosis surgery
[32, 44]. Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic agent which depresses

the transformation of plasminogen to plasmin, thereby inhibiting
binding of plasmin to fibrin clots and reducing clot lysis. The dose of
TXA is still debated and ranges from 10 to 20 mg/kg bolus at the
beginning of surgery with or without a continuous infusion of 3–
10 mg/kg/h [44–46]. Finally, initiation of an institutional protocol using
transfusion algorithms has been shown to be effective in reducing
blood transfusion during craniosynostosis surgery [41, 47].
Management by a dedicated team of anesthesiologists has also been
associated with lower transfusion volume and blood donor exposures
[48]. Administration of fresh frozen plasma, platelets, and
cryoprecipitate should be guided by laboratory testing as well as
thromboelastography (TEG) or other point of care analysis of clot
formation [49, 50].

29 8 Postoperative Analgesia
Open craniosynostosis surgery is associated with moderate to severe
pain; inadequate pain management is not uncommon in the first 48 h
[51]. Multimodal analgesia is recommended [52]. Regional analgesia
with a scalp block is an option. This block has been used to blunt
response to head pins [53] as well as part of a general anesthetic in
children during neurosurgery and other procedures of the head [54].
Local anesthesia, 0.125% levobupivacaine, is infiltrated in multiple
sites to target the nerves that innervate the scalp: the supraorbital and
supratrochlear nerves as they emerge from the orbit; the
auriculotemporal and greater auricular nerves near the ear; the
zygomaticotemporal nerve near the zygomatic arch; and the greater,
lesser, and third occipital nerves between the inion and the mastoid
process posteriorly [53, 54]. The scalp block offers superior pain
control in the immediate postoperative period and earlier resumption
of feeding compared to morphine alone [54], but not when compared to
local anesthesia infiltration [55]. Local anesthesia infiltration with
bupivacaine and epinephrine, to reduce scalp bleeding, is our preferred
technique. Opioids are necessary for adequate pain control initially.
Intravenous morphine is used in boluses of 0.05 mg/kg as needed for
the first 24 h, then changed to oral narcotics such as oxycodone
0.2 mg/kg. Adjuvant agents including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory

drugs are given to reduce narcotic requirements and associated adverse
events. Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg syrup is given before induction in children
older than 3 months and is safe as long as the infant is well-hydrated
[56]. Intravenous acetaminophen10-15 mg/kg or dipyrone 10 mg/kg is
administered with wound closure [57], and acetaminophen is
continued around the clock every 6 h. Intravenous ketorolac 0.5–
1 mg/kg every 12 h can also be used and has been shown to have no
impact on postoperative bleeding while reducing opioid consumption
after cranial vault remodeling [58]. The FLACC pain scale (five
categories of Face, Leg movement, Activity, Crying and Consolability
each scored between 0 and 2 per for a total score of 0 = no pain to a
maximum of 10 = worst pain) is convenient and relevant for the age of
craniosynostosis repair, or another pediatric pain scale should be used
to guide titration of analgesia. A score of 4 or greater is a trigger for
treatment with analgesics.
