30 Hemostasis and Transfusion in
Craniosynostoses Surgery
Martina Messing-Jünger1
(1) Pediatric Neurosurgery Department, Asklepios Children’s Hospital,
Sankt Augustin, Germany

Martina Messing-J nger
Email: m.messing@asklepios.com
Keywords Craniosynostosis surgery – Hemostasis – Transfusion –
Tranexamic acid – Erythropoietin – Cell saver
Craniosynostosis correction is associated with a high risk of significant
perioperative blood loss, which is responsible for the majority of
complications. Most of the patients are young infants with small blood
volume and physiological anemia, e.g., in preterm babies [1]. Several
strategies to minimize blood loss are available and a variety of clinical
protocols for the reduction of transfusion rates exist. Beside patient age
and body volume, the extent of the surgical approach and the operative
time are important factors influencing blood loss and transfusion rate
[2, 3]. Significant blood loss also causes coagulopathy, which must be
avoided as well [4]. In the following chapter, techniques and strategies
to reduce blood loss in craniofacial surgery are discussed.

30 1 Preoperative Measures
A child’s preoperative hemoglobin and coagulation parameters play an
important role for the entire perioperative course in craniosynostosis

surgery. In former times, a prophylactic blood transfusion with or
without plasma substitution was often the only strategy to reduce
severe complications following significant blood loss in this patient
group with physiologically low hematocrit and hemoglobin values. In
these cases, preoperative erythropoietin (EPO) and/or ferrous sulfate
[5–8] administration elevates hematocrit and hemoglobin values and
reduces the blood transfusion rate. Abnormal coagulation parameters
must be corrected before surgery in any elective craniosynostosis
repair.

30 2 Surgical Technique
The surgical technique plays an important role for the prevention of
excessive blood loss. Skin and galea are well vascularized and local
administration of a lidocain/epinephrine-solution (up to 20 mL of
0.25% lidocaine with 1:400,000) at the incision site can reduce
uncontrolled oozing from skin edges [8]. Skin incision with a Colorado
needle tip may also help to control unnecessary bleeding. The
application of Raney clips is not advisable due to the thin and soft skin
in infants. Small curved clamps can also be used for a temporary
hemostasis of the galea.
Subperiostal dissection is performed in most craniofacial surgeries,
but sometimes causes excessive bleeding from bony perforator vessels.
Subgaleal dissection can help to reduce blood loss, e.g., in fronto-orbital
advancement [9].
The deflected galea flap may be covered by hydrogen peroxidesoaked gauzes, which control blood ooze from the tissue during
exposure.
The infantile skull bone, although very thin, is an important site of
hematopoiesis and very well perfused. The blood loss from bone edges
can be significant and sealing is important. Bone wax should not be
used since it causes bone defects and bears the risk of late infections.
Gel foam is a good hemostatic material and facilitates bone
regeneration.
Oozing from dural sinuses is frequent as well and it is advisable to
cover them with gel foam or oxidized regenerated cellulose (ORC). Gel
foam and ORC are well-established hemostyptic agents in

neurosurgery. Both materials will be fully resorbed and rarely cause
late effects. A variety of new hemostyptic products are available, but a
careful consideration of possible complications is recommended.
One of the most important blood saving factors is a short operative
time [2]. Craniofacial procedures should be performed by an
experienced team only in order to keep the exposure time as short as
possible. Minimal invasive procedures can reduce the need for blood
transfusion significantly, not only due to less soft tissue and bone
manipulation, but also due to a short operative time and should be
offered to patients as often as feasible. In their prospective
observational study, Shah et al. (2011) compared open vault
reconstruction with endoscopic strip craniectomy in sagittal synostosis.
The mean operating time for the endoscopic procedure was 88 min
versus 179 min for the open surgery and mean blood loss 29 mL versus
218 mL, respectively. Only 6.4% endoscopy cases underwent
transfusion, whereas all patients with open procedures needed
transfusion [10].
The use of specific bone cutting tools does not seem to influence the
amount of blood loss. The time of the bone incision and the subsequent
sealing of the bleeding edges or the adjacent tissues is of importance
[11].
The benefit of wound drainages in craniofacial surgery is unclear.
On one side, they may reduce postoperative swelling, on the other side
increased postoperative blood loss and infections are possible
associated complications [12].

30 3 Anesthesia Management
The anesthesia management is decisive for a good outcome in any
craniosynostosis surgery. The most important task is the prevention of
a potentially life threatening hypovolemia and anemia and to avoid
coagulopathy and a high expertise is an important prerequisite.
Several protocols to prevent hypovolemia and reduce blood
transfusion exist. In a systematic review, White et al. (2015) evaluated
18 studies; 14 were case series with controls and only four randomized
controlled trials. Several relevant aspects remained unaddressed in the
available studies. The use of erythropoietin and tranexamic acid is well

studied. Less evidence exists regarding cell saver, acute normovolemic
hemodilution, and aprotinin. Preoperative autologous donation and aminocaproic acid were not investigated. The administration of
tranexamic acid is clinically effective in reducing allogeneic blood
transfusion. Also, cell saver use and EPO show a clinical effect [13].
The Children’s Hospital of Richmond protocol includes preoperative
administration of recombinant EPO until a preoperative hemoglobin of
15 g/dL was reached, intraoperative autologous blood recycling using
small bowls of 30 or 55 mL and accepting a transfusion trigger of
7 g/dL hemoglobin. These measures significantly decreased the
transfusion rate (p 0.001) [14].
The Vancouver group published their 10-year experience of all
consecutive cases during this period. The acceptance of a transfusion
threshold of 6 g/dL hemoglobin in hemodynamically stable patients led
to an overall low transfusion rate of 24% (28% in redo cases). Seventyfive percent of transfusions occurred intraoperatively, 21%
postoperatively, and 4% intra- and postoperatively [15].
The Pediatric Craniofacial Collaborative Group (PCCG) analyzed 935
children 24 months of age with craniosynostosis and found that the
likelihood of a perioperative transfusion was 95%. The mean volume of
erythrocyte containing blood products transfused intraoperatively for
infants was 37.3 26.2 mL/kg, and the mean volume transfused
postoperatively was 16.7 9.3 mL/kg [16]. Beethe et al. (2020) started
a quality improvement initiative for reducing the transfusion rate in
craniosynostosis patients below 2 years of age and were able to reduce
a 100% into a final overall allogeneic transfusion rate of 22.7% at their
institution. The following precautions were part of the protocol: Before
skin incision, a 20 mL/kg bolus of crystalloid and a tranexamic acid
(TXA) bolus of 12.5 mg/kg were administered. Skin incision was
performed after administration of up to 20 mL of 0.25% lidocaine with
1:400,000 epinephrine. A close communication between anesthetists,
surgeons, and nurses guaranteed permanent information on bleeding
status, laboratory values, and vital parameters and ensured timely
measures. In order to maintain normovolemic conditions, a total
crystalloid administration of 30 up to 100 mL/kg was necessary. Cell
saver was used for all patients with a minimum of 25 mL returning to
the patient. Perioperative hypothermia has been avoided using air

warmers or warm blankets and increasing the operating room
temperature up to 22 °C. The intra- and postoperative transfusion
threshold was set at 7 g/dL under stable hemodynamics [8].
Escher et al. (2021) compared 21 patients without preoperative
EPO and iron administration and perioperative TXA with 15 patients
who received both treatments (study group). There were no significant
differences between groups in demographics, operative time,
intraoperative crystalloid volume, craniofacial syndromes, or sutures
affected. Preoperative Hb (13.9 1.0 vs. 12.6 0.8 g/dL, p 0.001) was
higher and intraoperative Hb nadir (7.4 1.8 vs. 9.2 1.2 g/dL) lower
in the study group. The intraoperative transfusion rate dropped to
66.7% compared to 100% in the control group (p = 0.008). The
postoperative transfusion rate was 0% versus 28.6% in the control
group (p = 0.03). The amount of packed red blood cells units dropped
as well (0.7 0.6 vs. 1.5 0.9 units) [5].
A randomised trial investigated the usefulness of prolonged TXA
administration in craniosynostosis surgery [17]. The children received
either TXA (bolus dose of 10 mL kg1 injected before surgical incision,
followed by 8 h continuous infusion of 3 mL kg1 h1). Total blood loss
dropped from a mean of 52 mL kg1 to 28 mL kg1 (P 0.001).
Intraoperative red blood cell (RBC) were reduced in the treatment
group from 14.0 mL kg1 to 8.2 mL kg1 and FFP from 13.0 mL kg1 to
7.8 mL kg1 [17].
In a retrospective international multicenter study, the Pediatric
Craniofacial Collaborative Group (PCCG) analyzed a total of 6583
patients, who had open craniofacial surgery either without
antifibrinolytic treatment or with TXA or -aminocaproic acid and
compared seizure rates. The overall seizure rate was 0.24%, with
0.20% in the no antifibrinolytic group, 0.22% in the TXA-group, and
0.44% in the -aminocaproic acid group. These results prove the safety
of TXA [18].
Krajewski et al. (2008) investigated the benefit of a blood
conserving therapy with preoperative Procrit (eopoetin alpha) together
with an intraoperative cell saver and found a significant reduction of
transfusion rates. In the study group, transfusion rates were 5% versus
100% in the control group. The volumes transfused were lower as well

(0.05 versus 1.74 pediatric units). The study group received
recombinant human erythropoietin at 3 weeks, 2 weeks, and 1 week
preoperatively resulting in a preoperative hematocrit of 56.2%. Eighty
percent of patients in the study group received cell saver blood [19].
Aprotinin, a pancreatic trypsin inhibitor with antifibrinolytic
activity, has also been tested in craniofacial surgery. Blood loss was
lower under aprotinin treatment with 3.9% of circulating blood volume
versus 22.0% resulting in a transfusion rate of 0% versus 21.1%. No
allergic or other possible aprotinin-specific complications were
observed [20].
Another study addressed the administration of fresh frozen plasma
(FFP). Prophylactic versus reactive FFP transfusion has been compared.
The prophylactic group received a significantly greater average volume
of FFP compared to the reactive group (29.7 mL kg1 versus
16.1 mL kg1; p 0.001). Coagulation parameters improved similarly;
however, there was no difference in blood transfusion requirements or
blood loss between the two groups [21].
Excessive packed red blood cells (PRBC) transfusion to maintain
target hematocrit can result in coagulopathy from coagulation factor
depletion when hemorrhage approaches 1.5 times estimated blood
volume. Perioperative monitoring of coagulation parameters is as
important as hemoglobin and hematocrit assessment [4].
Substitution of human fibrinogen concentrate is also able to
improve blood coagulation in craniofacial surgery in the case of
massive blood loss and necessary intravascular volume therapy
avoiding the need for FFP or platelets transfusion. However, no
comparative or controlled studies exist so far [22].

30 4 Postoperative Care
During the postoperative surveillance, regular hemoglobin, hematocrit,
platelet, and coagulation parameter controls are indispensable, since
postoperative blood count and coagulation changes are often seen after
craniofacial surgery. In general, a transfusion threshold of 7 g/mL
hemoglobin under stable hemodynamics is recommended, although
lower hemoglobin values may be tolerated in selected and wellcontrolled patients [15]. Thorough wound and eventual drainage

controls by the surgeon are important as well in order to detect any
postoperative bleeding complications.

30 5 Summary
Craniosynostosis surgery is associated with a high risk of excessive
blood loss and meticulous hemostasis during surgery as well as a
variety of precautions already starting before hospital admission can
help to minimize the need for blood transfusion. The usefulness of
protocols or standard operating procedures (SOP) with the aim to
reduce blood loss and transfusion rates has been proven in several
studies and the implementation of such a protocol in any institution
treating children with craniosynostoses is strongly recommended.

31 1 Principles of Endoscopic Surgery
31 1 1 Evolution of Surgical Treatment for
Craniosynostosis
Understanding the role of endoscopic approaches in contemporary
therapy requires some understanding of the history of craniosynostosis
operations and how surgical practice has changed over time. As is true
for the breadth of neurosurgery, treatment for craniosynostosis
historically carried high morbidity and mortality. The first reported
case of suture release for presumed sagittal synostosis was published in
1890. Two years later, the first report of craniosynostosis treated with

the so-called linear craniectomy’ or strip craniectomy’ was published,
though the child died only hours after the operation (attributed to the
alcohol, chloroform, and ether anesthetic used) [1]. In 1893, Abraham
Jacobi, regarded as “the Father of American Pediatrics”, detailed a series
of 33 patients treated with linear craniectomy for microcephalus at the
International Congress of Medicine in Rome. He had compiled the data
from 6 American surgeons, which had resulted in 14 deaths (42%).
Only 3 patients demonstrated “some” or “much” improvement as a
result of surgery [2]. As such, the operation fell out of favor for several
decades. These poor initial results were likely obtained due to
improper patient selection and the state of surgical and anesthetic
techniques at the time. It is likely that many of these early surgeries
were performed on patients with nonsynostotic microcephaly—strip
craniectomy would later be recounted as “ mistakenly used in the
treatment of anencephalic microcephaly and other incurable forms of
idiocy” [3]. In addition, the surgery was frequently performed far too
late in childhood after skull growth was largely completed.
There would be a call to revive linear craniectomy in 1924, but this
time as a way to prevent the late sequelae of synostosis. With improved
surgical techniques and proper patient selection, this next wave of
treatment was far more successful and led to the modern field. In
particular, it was cited as a preventative measure for vision loss and not
as a treatment for microcephalus [4]. It also became clear that the
procedure should be performed as early in childhood as was deemed
safe to do so to have the greatest impact. This was advocated for within
the first 6 months of life [3], and in 1943, was suggested to be optimal
during the first 1–3 months of life during periods of rapid skull and
brain growth [5]. This technique, with or without additional
osteotomies, was practiced for several decades. One major limitation of
the operation was suture re-ossification within several months, leading
to inadequate corrections. In attempts to combat this, many synthetic
and caustic substances were applied to bone edges [6–8], while other
surgeons advocated for removal of more extensive amounts of bone [9].
In 1968, Shillito and Matson reviewed an impressive 519 patients
treated for craniosynostosis that aided in quelling much of the criticism
of the technique’s safety (0.58% patients with lasting undesirable
sequela) and efficacy (only 2% of patients with adequate follow-up

failed to show cosmetic improvement) [10]. Other criticisms of the strip
craniectomy (as originally described) include leaving an “unprotected”
area over the vertex, and that removing a single suture will not alter the
compensatory growth at other sutures (a discovery important to the
understanding of skull growth and craniosynostosis [11]), making it
less likely to provide a satisfactory cosmetic outcome. As an alternative
to strip craniectomy, John Jane introduced an open cranial remodeling
procedure in 1978 [12]. This so-called pi procedure’ was named for the
’-shaped piece of calvarium removed for the treatment of sagittal
synostosis. Numerous variations of this procedure have since been
described, and it is significant for ushering in the era of immediate
surgical correction, as opposed to release of the pathological suture
with the hope for normalized growth over time [13]. Around the same
time, complex craniofacial reconstruction was also being pioneered for
the correction of craniofacial dysostoses (familial craniosynostosis,
generally affecting the cranial vault, base, and midfacial skeleton). Paul
Tessier described the foundations upon which current practice is
derived throughout the 1960s and 1970s [14, 15]. However, despite the
remarkable innovations introduced by these larger corrections, they
also came with significant drawbacks. First, the magnitude of surgery is
quite significant, and performing these large operations on young
infants could be a daunting task. Perhaps more importantly, creating an
ideal skull shape at surgery did not always lead to ideal long-term
results, as growth patterns over time are not normal after such major
disruption of the skull and soft tissues. This led to high frequency of
revision surgery for issues including poor cosmesis and skull defects.
Due to some of the drawbacks of large open reconstructions, we have
now evolved to an era where both reconstructive and release
techniques have a role, and it is incumbent on the craniofacial team to
understand the nuances. Indeed, modern craniofacial centers should be
able to offer both techniques based on factors including the age of the
patient, severity of the condition, and family preference (Fig. 31.1).

Fig. 31.1 Cycle of craniosynostosis surgery. This pictorial demonstrates the evolution of
surgery for the treatment of craniosynostisis, beginning with the open strip (or linear’)
craniectomy. Innovation for these early procedures plateaued around the 1950s. Open strip
craniectomy had a number of shortcomings, not the least of which was the relative infrequency
with which a satisfactory outcome was achieved. This was primarily owed to premature suture
re-ossification before optimal correction was achieved. This, along with the need to treat the
more complex craniofacial syndromes, drove innovation in calvarial vault remodeling (CVR)
procedures in the 1970s. While these techniques allowed for powerful immediate correction,
they also were fraught with high blood loss, transfusion requirements, and prolonged hospital
stays, and the results were not always durable over time. The need to minimize perioperative
morbidity combined with innovative use of endoscopic visualization allowed Barone and
Jimenez to reinvent the strip craniectomy. Their procedure used much smaller incisions, had
fewer perioperative complications, and achieved satisfactory outcomes in patients who
maintained compliance with helmet therapy after surgery. The minimally invasive strip
craniectomy is currently the procedure of choice for appropriate candidates

With several important modifications, strip craniectomy was
reintroduced as a treatment for craniosynostosis in the 1990s.
Pioneering work from Barone (plastic surgery) and Jimenez (pediatric
neurosurgery) improved upon the traditional open procedure by
introducing the minimally invasive endoscopic strip craniectomy (ESC)
with postoperative adjuvant therapy. Using an endoscope to aid with
visualization, they combined smaller skin incisions, boney removal akin
to that of the open linear craniectomy, and the concept of so-called
directed growth’ as a way to achieve the desired cosmetic result over
time. Their aim was to achieve similar outcomes as its open
counterpart, while mitigating the perioperative morbidity as well as
improving the long-term outcomes. Using these techniques, surgeons
can avoid the need for extensive removal and reshaping of bone at the
time of surgery, thereby shortening the length of the procedure and
decreasing blood loss. With directed growth, restoration of skull shape
is achieved over time by minimizing skull growth in the
overcompensated regions and promoting it in the undercompensated
regions. Current options by which directed growth is achieved is with
postoperative helmet orthoses, implanted springs, or implanted
distractors (discussed in techniques section below).
Current and historic literature regarding surgical therapies for
synostosis has been plagued by a lack of standardized nomenclature
with which techniques are described [16]. To begin, labelling the
modern variant of these procedures as endoscopic’, in truth, is a
mischaracterization. Rather, the procedure is more appropriately
described as an endoscope-assisted minimally invasive strip
craniectomy. The primary use of the endoscope for these operations is
in helping to visualize along the length of the suture that is being
removed, and ensuring the dura is free prior to removal. This allows for
the use of smaller skin incisions (and hence minimally invasive’), while
maintaining adequate visualization to assess hemostasis and adequacy
of the surgical procedure. Variations in surgical technique have also led
to variations in terminology used to describe those techniques, further
clouding the literature and the ability to compare the conditions being
treated and the efficacy of the procedures. The type and quantity of
primary osteotomy (e.g., sagittal versus bilateral parasagittal) and
adjunct osteotomies performed can vary widely, as can the size of strip

craniectomy performed (so-called extensive strip craniectomy’ or
wide vertex craniectomy’), if/how many barrel staves’ are used,
if/how many wedge osteotomies are performed, and even terminology
pertaining to removal of the ossified suture (linear craniectomy versus
strip craniectomy versus suturectomy versus synostectomy). This
variance in terminology and surgical technique further complicates
higher-order data examination such as meta-analyses.
ESC has evolved to optimally treat its own niche of patients. To say
that it is a competing therapy with open approaches is denying patients
a holistic approach to the problem. A more contemporary view would
place endoscopic surgery as a mature procedure (i.e., standard
practice), with its own appropriate subset of patients that is
complementary to open procedures. In general, ESC should be
considered over open reconstruction when patients are younger, have
fewer sutures involved, and are not syndromic, although these
techniques also play a role in syndromic patients, often as a first stage
in a treatment algorithm. Recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses
have helped us to understand the relative advantages and
disadvantages of one procedure over the other based on factors such as
age and complexity.

31 1 2 Surgical Goals
The desired clinical outcome for any craniosynostosis procedure is the
same—restoration of the cranium to a more normal configuration with
potential for normal brain growth over time. However, the
intraoperative goals and the methods by which these outcomes are
achieved are vastly different between open remodeling and endoscopic
procedures. In general, the goal of ESC is to perform a limited
craniectomy through a small skin incision to allow mobility between
the prematurely fused bones. This will allow normal growth to occur in
the previously restricted direction. The intraoperative goal is not
immediate correction of the deformity. With restoration of mobility at
the suture location, brain and directed bone growth will lead to the
desired cranial morphology. The minimal disruption of both
surrounding bone and soft tissues also allows for relatively normal
growth patterns over time and the oft detected formation of a
neosuture’, essentially a suture indistinguishable from a non-

pathological suture that occurs at the affected suture after endoscopic
release [17, 18]. This contrasts the goals of open remodeling
procedures, where surgery establishes the desired outcome at the time
of the operation, but it is more difficult to predict and account for future
growth. Since its inception, ESC has also been adapted for application to
multi-suture release and syndromic cases.

31 1 3 Outcomes
Since its introduction by Barone and Jimenez, a large body of literature
on endoscope-assisted strip craniectomy has reported cosmetic
outcomes substantially equivalent to open procedures. Smaller
incisions, unsurprisingly, have yielded smaller scars and less pruritis.
Importantly, studies that examine a variety of photographic,
radiographic, and anthropomorphic measurements also confirm
equivalent cosmetic outcomes following these procedures [19–22]. At
this point in time, the outcomes of endoscopic procedures have been
fairly rigorously scrutinized and comprise one of the most studies
aspects of craniosynostosis surgery. As such, it will be important going
forward to look at other outcome measures.
Since the cosmetic outcomes are well established, going forward it
will be important to consider neurodevelopmental outcomes among
these patients and discovering if avoidance of any potential untoward
effects imposed by premature suture closure is possible. Unfortunately,
the entire field of synostosis remains somewhat immature in this
regard, both with regard to the baseline concerns and the effects of
treatment. Data from single-suture synostosis suggest low levels of
cognitive disability including developmental delays. Early on, these
tend to manifest as psychomotor issues. Among the few studies to
include older children, some data suggest impaired neuropsychological
functions such as attention, language skills, visual spatial skills, and
processing speed [23]. While randomized trials do not exist (and likely
never will), some studies have been performed that demonstrate a
beneficial effect conferred by operative intervention. Patel et al. found
that surgery, either whole-vault cranioplasty or strip craniectomy,
before 6 months of age improved long-term neurologic outcomes
(higher scores in IQ, reading and comprehension, spelling, and math)
[24]. Other reports do not demonstrate this benefit [25]. More rigorous

studies are needed to determine any causative factors for adverse
neurodevelopmental outcomes, and which, if any, treatment option
would most successfully avoid them.
Safety outcomes are important to consider when determining
surgical approaches. It is now widely recognized that endoscopic
procedures have lower complication rates, less transfusion
requirements, lower EBL, shorter operative times, and shorter length of
stay [26–28]. As expected, many retrospective series demonstrate that
endoscopic surgeries are being performed on patients who are younger
than open surgeries. Those amenable to endoscopic correction are
done so at a much earlier age, and those who require an open
reconstruction are either captured at a later age or done so electively
when their physiology better tolerates the more demanding operation.
Of course, any surgical intervention carries risk. Many series have been
published that detail complication rates around 5–10%, with
durotomies and surgical site infections listed as the most frequent
occurrences [29–31]. When examining the National Inpatient Sample
database, Abraham et al. report risk factors for the development of
postoperative complications in patients undergoing surgery (by any
technique) for craniosynostosis (n = 6010) as advanced age (13–
36 months vs. 7–12 months vs. 0–6 months; OR = 1.32), syndromic
patients (OR = 1.92), and requiring intraoperative transfusion
(OR = 1.60) [32], all of which are known to be mitigated by endoscopic
procedures.
In contemporary medicine, additional emphasis is being placed on
healthcare costs. To evaluate the economic burden of craniosynostosis,
it is important to consider the cost of procedure itself, the hospital stay,
any postoperative travel incurred, future visitation to the surgeon or
multidisciplinary team, postoperative orthoses (when applicable), and
potentially follow-up procedures (such as the case for removal of
implanted springs). Factoring in all costs, multiple studies have
demonstrated that endoscopic correction is substantially less
economically burdensome than open cranial vault remodeling, owing to
a much shorter initial hospital stay and less ICU requirements [33–36].
One drawback to endoscopic procedures is its reliance on brain and
skull growth to achieve correction, necessitating surgery at an earlier
age. This requires patients to have their condition recognized and

referred to the appropriate practitioners for treatment expeditiously.
For the surgery to be effective, the patient also needs to be treated
postoperatively using molding orthoses or with an additional operation
for removal of implanted springs or distractors. In addition, an
important disadvantage to consider is the lack of immediate correction.
This becomes important when considering appropriate surgical
candidates for endoscopic procedures and should be discussed with the
family.

31 1 4 Patient Selection and Preoperative Evaluation
Proper patient selection is critical to achieve satisfactory results with
ESC. Several important factors must be considered, both in the patient
and the family. Patients selected to undergo endoscopic strip
craniectomy should ideally be less than 6 months of age; preferably
around 3 months. Compliance with orthosis is also important to
maximize the likelihood of achieving a good outcome. The patient and
family need to be able to tolerate wearing it for approximately
23 h/day, for at least 6 months to 1 year. It should be well understood
by the family that a good outcome is tied to compliance with this
therapy, even if optimal duration of therapy is not well understood. To
this end, they must also understand that correction is achieved over
time and not immediately.
Apart from routine preoperative workup, centers that treat
craniosynostosis should have a well-established multidisciplinary care
team [37, 38]. This is especially true when craniofacial syndromes are
present. These patients and their families often benefit from having a
craniofacial care coordinator. This coordinator is responsible for
liaising between the various specialties and helping the family to
receive appropriate, specialized, timely care for the various issues
caused by their syndrome. Table 31.1 is an example of some of the
patient care teams responsible for intervening and rigorously
monitoring their progress during development. Anesthesia care for
patients with craniosynostosis or craniofacial syndromes is a
challenging field, and it has been established that an OR and anesthesia
team experienced in the care of these patients leads to better outcomes
[39].

31 2 Techniques of Endoscopic Management
31 2 1 Intraoperative Management
Surgical techniques specific to each suture are reviewed in detail in
subsequent chapters. As a broad overview, the following framework
derived from the authors’ institutional practices can be used to inform
endoscopic management with helmet therapy.

31.2.1.1 Anesthesia
It is important to partner with anesthesia teams experienced in treating
these patients. Nonetheless, several points of intraoperative
management are important for the neurosurgeon to understand while
performing endoscopic craniosynostosis procedures. Beyond standard
anesthetic monitoring techniques (electrocardiography, noninvasive
blood pressure monitoring, pulse oximetry, and temperature
monitoring), patients should have precordial doppler ultrasonography
whenever working near the dural venous sinuses. Perioperative dosing
of prophylactic antibiotics and pain regimens differ by institution, but it
is our practice to use a single intravenous dose of a broad-spectrum
antibiotic (cefazolin 30 mg/kg). Inhaled sevoflurane with oxygen and
nitrous oxide is typically used for induction of general anesthesia, and
muscle relaxation accomplished with rocuronium at a dose of

600 mg/kg. Special attention will be needed for airways of patients
with compromised facial or laryngeal structures, and oxygenation
techniques modified accordingly. For example, Apert syndrome is
known to cause difficult mask ventilation due to midface hypoplasia,
proptosis, small nares, and choanal stenosis [40]. Ophthalmological
ointment is applied for every case.

31.2.1.2 Positioning
Ideal positioning will vary depending on intended surgical target(s).
For metopic and coronal sutures, patients will be supine on a cerebellar
headrest, whereas prone positioning may be preferred for sagittal and
lambdoid sutures. Midline, neutral to slightly flexed position is used for
bicoronal, or metopic synostoses. We prefer modified prone (sphinx)
positioning during correction of sagittal synostosis to ensure adequate
anterior-posterior access to the sagittal suture. The surgical bed will be
rotated with the head between 90° or 180° from anesthesia, giving the
surgeon the most ergonomic access. To facilitate operative efficiency,
we have our scrub tech setup on the surgeons right when possible
(right-handed surgeon) and have the endoscopic tower opposite the
surgeon’s gaze.

31.2.1.3 ncisions
Most endoscopic operations require one or two small ( 2 cm) skin
incisions perpendicular to the fused suture that will be removed. Skin
incisions are typically made using a 15 blade scalpel to gain access to
the stenosed suture. Monopolar electrocautery (needle tip) at 15W is
then used to develop the bloodless plane in the loose areolar space
between the galea and pericranium. This is then scored and stripped
with the monopolar to facilitate osseous removal.

31.2.1.4 Craniectomies
We access the intracranial space using a pediatric perforator to create a
bur hole at each incision, generally centered directly on the fused
suture, which is then enlarged with Kerrison rongeurs. A 4-mm rigid 0°
endoscope is then introduced into the epidural space. Endoscopic
visualization is crucial for safe dissection of the dura mater from the
overlying bone, typically in a bimanual fashion with the use of a

Penfield 1 or suction. The type of endoscope employed is a matter of
preference to the surgeon, though in its original description, an 0° rigid
endoscope was used during the scalp dissection, and 30° rigid scope
during dural inspection/separation. Once the dura has been freed and
hemostasis ensured, the osteotomy is enlarged longitudinally along the
axis of the suture with a combination of angled Kerrison rongeurs, bone
(pituitary type) rongeurs, and bone cutting scissors. The intended
craniectomy width used in our group is approximately 1–2 cm for any
suture involved. Osseous hemostasis is achieved with careful
monopolar cautery under direct visualization, and we leave gelfoam
lining the bone gap. The incisions are then closed with 4-0 monocryl in
a simple running fashion. As with all surgery, meticulous hemostasis
should be sought, and thoughtful communication with anesthesia
should occur throughout the case. Blood loss is usually minimal, but
failure to prepare for unanticipated losses is inadvisable.

31 2 2 Postoperative Treatment
Immediate perioperative pain is treated with administration of
intravenous morphine. The patient is started and maintained on
acetaminophen, which is often used post discharge for 2–3 days.
Typical LOS is one night. We do not routinely give postoperative
antibiotic prophylaxis.
Based on historical data, we know that suture removal by itself
often does not result in a good outcome. Unchecked compensatory
growth at the unfused sutures will continue, and the cut bone margins
may rapidly refuse, resulting in failure to obtain a corrected shape. This
was recognized when the linear craniectomy was being developed [41]
and drove subsequent advances in the field. It is now understood that
bone growth needs to be promoted in the direction that was previously
restricted. Growth should also be limited, but not prevented, in the
previously overcompensated direction. Several methods have been
studied to direct growth: use of molding orthoses, implanted spring
distractors, and standard implanted distractors.

31.2.2.1 Molding rthoses
The use of molding helmets for postoperative-directed growth for the
treatment of craniosynostosis after endoscopic suturectomy was

popularized by Barone and Jimenez [42–45]. The concept of molding an
infant’s head was not new at that time. Molding helmet use after
craniofacial surgery was described in 1986, though evidence suggests
that the practice of changing the shape of an infant’s head with external
pressure has been there since at least the Bronze age [46]. Helmet
therapy has several advantages to the other described techniques. They
can be modified over time to alter restrictions/freedoms to dynamically
achieve a desired result without any additional procedures. They can
also mold in 3 dimensions, whereas springs and distractors only work
in a single plane. Finally, there will be no need for additional surgery to
remove the device. Of course, the family needs to be compliant with the
treatment, and the helmet requires periodic adjustment, necessitating
additional travel to and from the treating facility. In addition to an illfitting orthotic, complications include reports of skin irritation and soft
tissue infection, generally at the onset of therapy [47, 48]. Some groups
report not having these issues [22, 49].
In our practice, patients are admitted to the inpatient (floor) unit
for observation overnight and discharged the following morning after
ESC. They then undergo laser scan on 3–4 days after surgery to obtain
baseline anthropometric measurements. A custom-made ethylene
copolymer helmet is then manufactured and fitted to the child within
7–10 days after surgery. Some children will gain correction with a
single helmet, but it is possible to need a second, and rarely a third
helmet as the child’s head grows and changes shape. Helmet therapy
lasts on average 7 months, and in our practice, we always discontinue
the helmet by the child’s birthday. Patients are then followed on an
annual basis until at least 6 years of age.

31.2.2.2 Spring Distractor steogenesis
Spring therapy is a relatively newer technique adapted for use with
craniosynostosis. The technique of implantable spring (nickelchromium-iron alloy) for craniofacial reshaping was first introduced by
Claes Lauritzen in 1998 [50]. They were manufactured by hand from
wire and adjusted with a pressure gauge to ensure appropriate force is
applied. Subsequent analysis of the first 100 patients treated this way
confirmed the safety and efficacy of the technique [51]. They can be
deployed either in open or endoscopic cases. One substantial benefit to

spring distraction over helmet therapy is that it does not rely on the
rapid periods of brain and skull growth. Therefore, the use of spring
distraction extends the age for which endoscopic management can be
offered. An obvious downside to their use is that it necessitates a
second operation for removal of the device. Compared to standard
distraction osteogenesis, there is also no control over the force or rate
of force applied after implantation. Complications include spring
shifting leading to suboptimal or undesirable bone movement,
dislodgement, or wound issues [51].

31.2.2.3 Distraction steogenesis
Distraction osteogenesis is a cranial remodeling technique whereby
distractors are surgically implanted and affixed to the bones after
separation. This technique requires a portion of the device to exit
through the skin to allow for subsequent adjustment. The screw is
turned daily to expand the distractor at a rate of approximately
1 mm/day. Compared to spring-assisted distraction osteogenesis for
the treatment of sagittal synostosis, operative times are longer (216
min versus 104 min), blood loss is greater (250 mL versus 82.5 mL),
and hospital stay is longer (16.9 days versus 5.5 days) [52]. Overall
complication rates are estimated to be 23%, with the majority of
complications being due to infection, scalp/wound dehiscence, and
traction pin loosening [52]. Systematic review does not demonstrate
statistically significant differences in these parameters as compared to
open cranial remodeling surgery [52]. Its use is generally reserved for
cases of advanced age where helmeted treatment will not be effective,
those with craniofacial deformities, or cases where spring therapy
would be deemed ineffective.

31 3 Summary
Endoscopic surgery for the treatment of synostosis has become a wellestablished treatment paradigm. It should be considered a
complementary treatment to open procedure, and one that any modern
craniofacial center should have competency in. As compared to open
procedures, the operation is performed at a younger age, and the
treatment is followed by a postoperative adjuvant, most commonly a

helmet, although springs or distractors can also be used. The cosmetic
and safety components of this operation are well established and
compare quite favorably to open surgery. Future investigation
comparing the neurocognitive outcomes of open versus endoscopic
surgery is a field that requires additional study.

32 Principles and Technique of
Anterior Vault Remodeling
Federico Bianchi1 and Gianpiero Tamburrini1, 2
(1) Pediatric Neurosurgery, Fondazione Policlinico Gemelli IRCCS,
Rome, Italy
(2) Universit Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Milan, Italy

Federico Bianchi
Email: Federico.bianchi@policlinicogemelli.it
Gianpiero Tamburrini (Corresponding author)
Email: gianpiero.tamburrini@unicatt.it
Keywords Craniosynostosis – Anterior vault reconstruction – Surgery
– Treatment

32 1 Metopic Craniosynostosis
Metopic craniosynostosis is nowadays considered the second most
frequent one and its distinctive features are described in detail in
another chapter of this book. This chapter will instead address the
variety of surgical techniques reported for trigonocephaly treatment.
As previously reported, surgical goal can be so summarized:
1. ICP increase prevention;
2. Cranial morphology normalization;

3. Prevention of neurodevelopmental injury;
4. Prevention of ocular movement disturbances.
All proposed techniques have a step in common, namely the
removal of the affected suture while differentiating the dealing of the
cranial deformity.
Thus, digging into the problem, trigonocephaly can be treated with
open field surgery (fronto-orbital advancement combined with anterior
cranial vault reconstruction, FOA), device-assisted procedures (DAP),
endoscopy-assisted suturectomy (EAS) followed by postoperative
cranial orthotic therapy, or mini-invasive microscope-assisted
suturectomy (MMAS). Among those options, FOA and EAS can be
considered the most used.
FOA is the oldest and more studied technique widely demonstrated
as safe and reliable in obtaining surgical goals. Nonetheless, it is
burdened by the need for larger incision, longer surgical time, the likely
need for blood transfusion, as well as supposed longer hospitalization,
increased overall health care costs, and a risk of relapse [1]. FOA user
elected this open procedure arguing better reconstruction results
obtainable in reasonable surgical times in trained hands as well as
highlighting that properly performed incisions can be easily masked
[2].
Endoscopic assisted suturectomy (EAS) are surely shorter
procedures with lesser blood loss and smaller scars but the need for
earlier surgery, postoperative helmet therapy render the result less
likely to be predict [3].
Whether the chosen technique mortality is quite low being
intravascular disseminated coagulation the major responsible. Surgical
results are usually good even though scares literature data are present.
This fact is related with long term lack of data as well as the potential
disparity between surgeon and family impression on them [3].
In the rest of the chapter for each of the previously mentioned
surgical techniques will be described what reported in the literature
about:

1. Positioning and anesthesia;
2. Exposure;
3. Bony decompression;
4. Reconstruction (FOA) vs device used (DAP) vs molding therapy
(EAS and MMAS);
5. Closure.

32 1 1 FOA (Fig 32 1)
32.1.1.1 Positioning and Anesthesia
The patient is usually anesthetized by a pediatric anesthesiologist,
using endotracheal intubation, 2 large-bore intravenous lines and or a
central line, and 1 arterial line. Further procedure consists of Foley
catheter insertion to monitor urine output. As for the position, the child
is supine with the head placed into a support. Some authors advocate
the use of a horseshoe headrest to increase head stability [4–7]. Before
incision, some authors also recommend local anesthesia with
1:200,000 epinephrine addiction to reduce soft tissue bleeding [4, 5, 8,
9]. Only Seal et al. reported the use of a different dosage using
1:400,000 epinephrine [10].

Fig. 32.1 FOA

32.1.1.2 Exposure
FOA approach always starts with a bicoronal incision posterior to the
anterior fontanelle whose fashion varies among authors. In fact, some
of them prefer a sinusoidal cut [8], while others prefer zig-zag ones [4,
6, 11–15] or double opposing lazy S incision [16], scalloped pattern one
[17], lazy W incision [9, 18], and finally straight incision at the vertex
with zig-zag pattern on the temporoparietal surface [10, 19].
Independently from the chosen fashion, the cut is customed to reduce
esthetic trouble from a wide scar. Most of the authors prefer monopolar
diathermy to reduce bleeding with or without previous shallow 15blade epidermis cut. Manikas et al. also suggest to incise the skin in an
oblique fashion to reduce hair follicle damage [20].
After incision, exposure proceeds with scalp flap blunt dissection
preserving the periosteum in order to create large enough flap to cover
the future osteotomies. The aforementioned periosteum flaps extend
till 1.5 cm above the superior orbital rims where a different incision,
including the external fascia of the temporalis muscle bilaterally,
permits the exposure of both the frontal and pterional regions, the

lateral margins of the orbits (down to the fronto-zygomatic suture), the
superior orbital ridge, and the upper part of the nasal bones, preserving
the frontal branches of the supraorbital nerves [5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 17, 20,
21]. Smaller variation of the reported procedures are the ones from
Bennet et al. in which the area of periosteum overlaying the metopic
suture is removed in order to cancel tissue memory in this region [8]
and the ones from Braun et al. (2018) whose technique uses
subperiosteal dissection [11].

32.1.1.3 Bone Decompression
Once uncovered the cranial vault and the orbital region, the
decompression phase can be started. This phase can be actually divided
into two segment, cranial vault decompression and orbital
advancement.
While most of the authors concord in the use of a bicoronal
craniotomy for vault decompression, many different techniques are
reported in the orbital advancement.
Starting with bicoronal craniotomy, it usually extends from
posterior the anterior fontanelle till 1.5 cm above the orbital rim to
ensure successive orbital advancement. There are a few differences in
the bicoronal craniotomy according to the number of flaps collected. In
fact, while most of the authors chose to harvest a single bone flap [5, 6,
10, 12], others prefer to divide it into two or more pieces [8].
Some authors also suggest to split the calvarial bone in order to
obtain more pieces for reconstruction [8].
As for the orbital bandeau, it is usually created performing
osteotomies of the orbital roofs, the medial and lateral orbit walls, and
zygomaticofrontal sutures. In removing the bandeau, care must be
taken into preserving the supraorbital nerve that might be elevated
from its notch or freed from its foramen [4–6, 8, 12, 17]. The
aforementioned osteotomies can be carried out completely offering an
en-bloc bandeau or trough green-stick fracture according to the
surgeon preferences and depending on the severity of the cranial
malformation. Surgical instrument useful in performing the orbital
bandeau are: the reciprocating saw [8, 18], the piezosurgery scalpel
[14, 22, 23], a craniotome or a trephine [24], the chisel [5], and a highperformance ultrasonic aspirator [13].

32.1.1.4

econstruction

The reconstruction phase in FOA is definitely the most variable among
authors. In fact, either talking about cranial vault reconstruction or
orbital bandeau advancement, there are a lot of different opinions.
Starting from the orbital bandeau reconstruction, the supraorbital
bar can be remodeled either through green-stick fracture or transecting
it and plating it back together in a more anterior position [25].
Complete bandeau advancement supporter argues that, using a freeflap, it is possible to obtain a wider enlargement of the anterior cranial
fossa and of the orbits. On the other hand, green-stick fracture
supporter states that the central portion of the bandeau is already in
the ideal position granting the possibility in trigonocephalic patient to
expand only laterally the anterior cranial fossa and the orbits. In
addition, bending of the supraorbital bandeau can be added to reach a
more spherical contour [8].
Regardless the choice, the new bandeau has to be strongly fixated
not to lose the desired correction. Furthermore, most of the authors
highlight the importance of hypercorrection in order to compensate for
the physiological retrusion of the new construct once the skin flap is
closed and to reduce the risk of recurrence.
To obtain such fixation, there are several techniques involving
sutures [9], reabsorbable plates [4–6, 20, 21, 24], titanium ones and
stainless steel wires [21], and bone grafts [26].
As for cranial vault reconstruction, there are several shapes in
which the bone flap can be molded as a way to cover as better as
possible the area of craniolacunia. Furthermore, most authors suggest
to rotate the bone flap of 180° to use the optimal contour of the parietal
bones to reconstruct the forehead. Examples of modeling are the
Christmas tree foreheadplasty [16], the shell technique [12], or the
cathedral dome procedure [6]. The fixation of the molded flap can be
achieved with sutures, reabsorbable plates [10, 20], and stainless steel
wires [15, 16, 21]. Some authors also suggest the use of bone
particulate and graft to widen even more dural covering [4, 11, 26].
Others also supported the implant of acellular dermal matrix to
enhance ossification [27].

32.1.1.5 Closure

In the end, FOA skin flap closure start repositioning the temporalis
muscle that has to be advanced to cover for the hollowness left by
cranial advancement. Vycril sutures are usually used for the task [4, 8,
28]. Another important step in completing the surgery is the sewing of
the periosteum as a lead in future ossification [12, 16]. After that the
skin flap is closed in layers using skin suturing reabsorbable stiches,
sometimes leaving a subcutaneous drain according to bleeding levels.
Nonetheless, some authors still use staples, even though in kids it might
be difficult to remove them [9].

32 1 2 Device-Assisted Techniques
Device-assisted techniques resemble FOA in many aspects of the
procedures. Positioning, anesthesia, exposure, and closure are
practically overlapping, while some differences regard the extent of
bony decompression and of course the chosen device. While most of the
authors who use this kind of surgery add the device to a standard FOA
decompression, others like Bhatti-So fteland et al. prefer to carry out
barrel stave osteotomies perpendicular to the coronal suture in the
anterior parietal region [29]. Fawzy et al., on the other hand, create
fronto-orbital osteotomy without separating the bandeau [30]. Finally,
some authors prefer to perform a strip craniotomy along the fused
suture leaving the distraction to the device [31–33].
Coming to the more commonly implanted devices, it is necessary to
distinct among classic distractors [30, 33–35] and springs [29, 31, 32,
36]. Both surgical choices aim to reduce the intraoperative work in
exchange for a more prolonged distraction. Supporters of the technique
underline the importance of shorter surgical timing and scarring and
the possibility of major distraction compared with classical FOA. On the
other hand, it is important to remember the added device-related
complication as well as the need to remove the device once distraction
is completed.

32 1 3 Endoscopic Techniques
Apart from FOA, endoscopic treatment of trigonocephaly represents the
second most common surgical procedure. A peculiarity of the technique
resides in the need for very malleable bone and, for this very reason,
children are usually operated on earlier in comparison with FOA. Most

authors refer the age of 3 months as the ideal one for endoscopic
treatment. As previously done for FOA, each of the surgical step of the
procedure will be covered.

32.1.3.1 Positioning and Anesthesia
Similarly to what happen in FOA, the child is supine with the head
located in a cushion or in a pediatric cerebellar head rest [37–40]. Some
authors also suggest to infiltrate the skin with a solution of SSF, 25%
bupivacaine, and adrenaline 1:1 to reduce bleeding [37, 39].

32.1.3.2 Exposure
Most of the authors perform a small incision, around 3 cm width,
behind the hairline posterior to the anterior fontanelle [11, 40, 41],
while others prefer to do it anteriorly [37, 42, 43] or over it [38, 44]. In
addition to the previously described incisions, some authors add
further ones, namely tarsal and periauricular incisions, in order to
better reach the lateral orbital aspects, especially in older children [43,
44].
Once completed, the skin opening subgaleal dissection over the
metopic ridge is carried above and down from the anterior fontanel to
the nasion and frontonasal suture with endoscopic assistance and
electrocautery [39, 43].

32.1.3.3 Bone Decompression
Endoscopic bone decompression starts preparing specular burr holes
along the midline. Freeing the upper part of the superior sagittal
sinuses. The dura is then detached from the intracranial aspect of the
suture under 0° straight rigid endoscopic guidance, thus passing onto
the suturectomy. Suturectomy can be performed using rongeurs, mayo
scissors, piezosurgery, drill, or Leksell [11, 37–39, 42, 43]. Extra care
has to be taken in controlling bleeding coming from bridging vein from
the superior sagittal sinus, especially in the more nasofrontal portion of
the metopic suture. Further osteotomies can be performed
transversally to the suturectomy to promote frontal widening [11, 18].
Some authors also change the endoscope optic, preferring a 30° one, to
perform osteotomies of the nasofrontal junction [41].

Whenever accessory incisions are performed, bone decompression
is also carried out through them. In particular, endoscopic-assisted
osteotomies of the orbital roof until anterior cranial fossa, cribriform
plate, and lateral orbit walls are reached at the level of pterion and
frontomalar union are carried out [43].

32.1.3.4 Molding Therapy
Trigonocephaly endoscopic treatment uses the high malleability of the
younger bone together with brain growth to remodel the cranial vault
and orbital region. In order to harvest the best result, no endoscopic
treatment can be done without planning postsurgical head molding.
Children operated on are in fact supposed to wear a helmet for at least
23 h a day for at least 6–9 months after surgery [39, 40, 42, 44]. Such a
need represents without a doubt one of the major concerns for
surgeons disliking this procedure. The second one resides in the young
age needed to successfully perform the technique. Furthermore, it
seems more difficult to predict long-term results, also considering the
high therapy drop-out rate due to patient discomfort.

32.1.3.5 Microsurgical Mini-in asi e Techni ues
Finally, a further mini-invasive technique is represented by the
microsurgical suturectomy. This technique has a lot in common with
the endoscopic resection as it is performed through small incision and
requires postsurgical molding therapy. The difference resides in fact in
the use of the microscope instead of the endoscope. Truth be told the
only to paper regarding such a technique are quite old being from an
era in which the endoscopic learning curve was still at its prime for
metopic suturectomy [45, 46].

32 1 4 Unicoronal Synostosis
32.1.4.1 ntroduction
Unicoronal synostosis (UCS) represents distinct challenges compared
with other single-suture craniosynostoses from a surgical point of view.
In fact, it represents the form of craniosynostosis in which the cosmetic
correction has the highest impact, seen the secondary associated
deformation of the orbit and face [47], which is almost invariably
progressive in untreated children and destined to have a major

psychological impact on the growing child and his family. It is also not
negligible the role of surgery in contributing to the correction of ocular
movement deficits. In fact, repairing orbital asymmetry contribute in
inmproving the impaired ability to fix and follow and visual field
defects in these children [48].
Concerning intracranial pressure (ICP), abnormal ICP values have
only been seldomly reported in children with unicornal synostosis [49],
a finding which is easily explained by the fact that the intracranial
volume in UCS overlaps normal volumes of unaffected children up to
18 months of life and that most of the normal ICP recordings which are
present in the literature refer to toddlers up to 1 year of age.
Conversely, Eley et al. have reported abnormally increased (42%) or
borderline ICP values (29%) in unoperated children with mean age of
3.5 years [50]. In spite of the small size of the series (7 cases), results
reported by these authors confirm that the risk of increased ICP in
unoperated children with craniosynostosis is growing with the child
growth. Timing of surgery is a matter of debate. Whereas some author
advocate early correction of the deformity (1–4 months) using less
invasive techniques, profiting in this case of the malleability of the bone
[51], but at the cost of a too early re-ossification and higher
intraoperative infectious and hemorrhagic complication rates, other
neurosurgeons prefer to operate later on, generally between the fourth
and the eighth month of life, to achieve more stable results, but at the
cost of an higher rate of bone defects [52].

32.1.4.2 Goals of the Surgery
The goals of the surgical corrections are to restore the shape of the
forehead and the orbit, to increase the volume of the ipsilateral anterior
cranial fossa and orbit, and to redirect the vectors of growth of the
skull, with the final aim of minimizing the facial asymmetry and the
neurological and ophthalmological changes. Many techniques are
currently available to achieve these goals [6, 16, 53–56].

32 1 5 Surgical Technique: Open Surgery
32.1.5.1 Surgical Steps Specific for nicoronal Synostosis
(Fig. 32.2)

Surgical considerations for anesthesiology and skin incision are similar
to what has been reported for metopic synostosis. Similarly, the goal of
this step is to expose both the frontal bones (and part of the parietal
and the temporal bones), the nasofrontal junction, both the orbits, and
the fronto-zygomatic sutures. The bilateral exposition is meant to favor
a symmetrical frontal reconstruction, even when the fronto-orbital
craniotomy is unilateral. The pericranium is incised parallel to the
affected orbit (at least 1 –2 cm above the supraorbital rim to preserve
the supraorbital nerve main branch and the vessels), to the metopic
and the coronal suture. After a subperiosteal dissection, the
pericranium pedunculated on the temporal muscle is overturned
toward the ear. In case of a unilateral approach, the dissection of the
periosteum, though being substantially unilateral from the affected
frontal side, should be extended over the midline for 2 cm; this in order
to gain a sufficient amount of tissue to cover the advanced orbital roof.
Downward, the dissection is carried out over the supraorbital ridge,
extending medially up to the front-nasal junction and, laterally, to the
lateral orbital canthus down to the zygomatic body: as a result, the
medial, superior, and lateral walls of the orbit are exposed. During this
phase of the dissection, the periorbital fascia is separated from the
orbital roof taking care to not damage the lacrimal gland. Downward
care should be taken to free the supraorbital nerve from its groove or
foramen, when closed; in fact, the supraorbital canal is commonly still
opened in its inferior border in the great majority of children below
1 year of age. When the canal is closed, sparing of the supraorbital
nerve is not always possible, but a spontaneous functional recovery has
been observed during the follow-up in the majority of cases [57]. Once
this phase is completed, an ipsilateral frontal bone flap is designed
according to the frontal flattening and the severity of the retrusion.
Templates may be used to better design the flap as well as software
designed to preplan the flap using virtual reality or 3D preprinted
models are available for this purpose. As a common rule, the bone flap
is extended 1 to 3–4 cm beyond the midline which allows to improve
remodeling profiting of the contralateral convex frontal bone shape. For
a similar purpose, the posterior border of the flap is variably placed a
few centimeters behind the affected coronal suture. The anterior limit
of the flap is set 1.5–2 cm above the supraorbital rim. The number and

location of the burr holes are defined according to the planned
craniotomy and the available instrumentation. If the anterior fontanel
(AF) is still opened, two burr holes only are needed, the first at the level
of the pterional region, the second at the lower medial limit of the
frontal bone flap, 1.5-2 cm, above the fronto-nasal-orbital junction. In
case of closure of the anterior fontanel, an additional burr hole is
placed midline at the frontoparietal junction. Craniotome is used to join
the burr holes, substituting it with ultrasonic bone cutting devices (i.e.,
Piezosurgery ) if available at the inferior border, main advantages
being a reduction of the risks of damaging the dura mater as well as a
consistent higher possibility to spare bone tissue. The bone flap is
elevated after careful dissection from the dura mater and the coronal
suture. The thickened pterional bone is removed with rongeur or it is
cut with ultrasonic saws along the temporal fossa to unlock the locally
restricted regional bone growth.

Fig. 32.2 Surgical steps specific for unicoronal synostosis

Bilateral frontal craniotomy, originally proposed by Tessier in 1967,
has been alternatively used to unilateral frontal bone flaps. In a
bilateral approach, the bilateral frontal flap is realized cutting the bone
anteriorly at least 1 cm behind the orbital rim and posteriorly 1 cm
behind the coronal suture.
Orbitotomy represents the second step of the surgery. In case of a
unilateral approach, the orbitotomy is carried out by cutting the lateral
orbital wall at the level of the orbito-zygomatic suture and the roof 1
cm posteriorly and parallel to the superior orbital ridge reaching the
upper aspect of its medial wall. Both microdrill and ultrasonic cutting
devices may be used for this purpose. The medial wall of the orbit
(orbito-nasal surface) is left intact constituting the pivot for the lateral
advancement of the superior orbital ridge obtained by means of a green
stick fracture at its level. The orbit is recontoured manually, with
rongeurs or Tessier bender orbit in a way to make it more arched and
more convex anteriorly, mimicking the normal border of the opposite
side.
Finally, the orbital ridge is advanced and placed in a hypercorrected
position in order to avoid an early postoperative retrusion and it is
done both in the sagittal (anteriorly) and in the coronal plane with the
objective of overlapping the position of the contralateral orbit; the final
position is stabilized with the use of a resorbable plate, fixed on the
pterional region proximally and on the lateral border of the orbit
distally. Among the several changes that have been proposed, the most
common is harvesting a complete (bilateral and in one piece)
supraorbital bar [58]. The osteotomies in this case are carried out
asymmetrically, ending at the fronto-malar suture on the healthy side
and extending to the lateral orbital process of the malar bone on the
synostotic side. The bandeau is then contoured to achieve a smooth
curved symmetrical contour. One resorbable plate for each side is hence
used to fix the orbital bar to the two temporal regions; in order to
obtain an adequate correction, the orbital bar is placed obliquely with
its higher point in the contralateral side and lower point in the affected
side.
Barrel stave osteotomies and greenstick fractures, to weak the bone,
and by Tessier bender are used to achieve the right curvature of the

frontal bone which is defined case by case based on preoperative
imaging, templates, or 3D printed models [10, 59–61].
The bone flap is then replaced, usually rotated by 90 or, less
frequently, rotated by 180 or not rotated, according to which rotation
assures the best reconstruction [6, 16, 54–56]. The modified frontal
bone flap is finally fixed to the advanced orbital bandeau with titanium
or biodegradable plates or alternatively sutures.
Concerning sutures, resorbable stitches are preferred to silk for
their lower risk to cause granulomatous reactions. In case they’re used,
the advanced orbit and frontal bone must perfectly fit to maintain their
position, in order to reduce the risk of postoperative retrusion. A tip in
this case is to buttress a tongue-in-groove bone fragment between the
orbit and the sphenoid wing/temporal bone [10].
Titanium miniplates and screws, widely diffused, easy to use,
malleable, and relatively cheap, ensure the best rigid fixation and the
lower rate of recurrence. However, they are burdened by the higher risk
of complications such as disturbance of the growth of the skull,
rupture/pull out, skin erosion, and inner migration [62–64]. The inner
migration is the main disadvantage of using metallic fixation in
craniosynostosis surgery, since a second operation is needed to remove
the plates and the screws in cases of their migration, that, due to its
relatively high rate of occurrence, is actually suggested for prophylactic
purposes to prevent such a complication. Absorbable mini-plates and
screws are actually considered to offer the best compromise between
reabsorption (Vycril suture) and rigid fixation (titanium). Transient
visibility up to their resorption and granulomatous reactions, reported
with an incidence of up to 15%, are the main reported complications of
these devices [65–67], though their incidence is significantly reduced
by the recent improvement in the materials. Actually, in a large
multicenter review (1883 patients), device instability rate was as low
as 0.3%, the infection rate 0.2%, and the granuloma occurrence rate
0.7% [68]. Actually, the main limitation of absorbable plates is their
elevated cost.
Once the bone fixation is ended, the periosteal flap is sutured to
cover as much as possible the osteotomies, especially in the orbital
region, to drive a good re-ossification.

32 2 Bicoronal Synostosis (Brachycephaly)
Brachycephaly is the definition of the cranial shape that commonly
results after premature closure of both sides of the coronal suture. As a
consequence of this premature fusion, the anterior fossa adopts a
characteristic deformation, broad and short, and there are retruded
frontal bones and orbital rims with a vertical, broad, flat forehead and a
high bregmatic point. Bicoronal synostosis may appear as an isolated
synostosis and has then a favorable prognosis. More often, however, is
the clinical manifestation of different syndromic craniosynostoses that
share a premature closure of bicoronal sutures and similar phenotype
(like Saehtre-Chotzen or Pfeiffer type I syndromes).
Surgical treatment and technique do not differ significantly from
what has been previously described for unicoronal synostosis with a
bilateral approach. A bilateral skin incision back to the coronal suture
and bilateral periosteal flap precede a bilateral frontal craniotomy 2 cm.
above the two orbital roofs. A tongue in groove orbital bar is created
with similar principles as for the orbital bar, when performed, in
unicoronal synostosis. The frontal bone flap is remodeled with radial
cuts and reversed more commonly 180° to get the more rounded
frontoparietal region to represent the frontal prominences. A
recontouring of the orbital bar gaining an adequate curvature follows,
with its fixation to the temporal region on the two sides, with special
attention to invert the concave curvature as much as possible to make it
convex. Suture of the bone flap to the orbital roofs, closure of the
periosteal flaps before skin closure, follows the same principles cited
above.

32 3 Endoscopic Treatment of Coronal
Synostosis (Fig 32 3)
As for metopic synostosis, endoscopic treatment has been considered
as an alternative to open FOA also for coronal synostoses. Indications
and limits, including the need of a postoperative helmet, are shared.
The technical and directly related points are:

1. 3 cm skin incision 1 cm. back to the coronal suture
2. 1 cm incision lateral 3 cm above the fronto-orbital junction
3. Release of the coronal suture through a 1–1.5 cm. in
anteroposterior diameter craniectomy that starts from the midline
and it is extended downward and laterally to reach the frontoorbital junction.

Fig. 32.3 Endoscopic treatment of coronal synostosis

33 Principles and Techniques of
Posterior Vault Remodeling

de Lyon, Lyon, France

Keywords Posterior skull vault – Distraction – Springs mediated
