33 1 Principles: Rationale, Indications, and
Risks
Posterior cranial deformities can be either asymmetrical (posterior
plagiocephaly) or symmetrical (brachy-turricephaly) [1].
Isolated fusion of the lambdoid suture is the rarest form of
craniosynostosis: it represents less than 1–5.5% of all cases of
craniosynostoses. Its incidence has been considered to be increased up
to 8.2% in the last decades because of the “Back to Sleep campaign” of
the American Academy of Pediatrics in 1992 to prevent the sudden
death of neonates, which has participated actually to increase the

incidence of positional calvaria deformations with which the true
lambdoid synostosis is misdiagnosed.
True lambdoid craniosynostosis is characterized by the homolateral
occipitomastoid bulge with shifting of the ear inferiorly and posteriorly
and a contralateral parietal and ipsilateral occipitomastoid bossing
which makes the head wider posteriorly than anteriorly, resulting in a
trapezoid head shape when viewed from above.
It is estimated that 15% of cases of lambdoid craniosynostosis are
bilateral [2]. This condition is characterized by the flattening and
widening of the occipital region associated with elongation of the
vertex resulting in a brachi-turricephalic aspect of the cranium. The
ears are displaced anteriorly and inferiorly.
These aspects can be found in association with synostosis of the
sagittal suture in the so-called “Mercedes-Benz syndrome” or be part of
a complex, multi-suture syndromic synostosis [3].
The growing brain is the force that guides the neurocranium
growing: the calvaria bone is separated and then the osteogenesis
process progressively fills the gap [4].
The change in intracranial volume with age is not clearly linear: we
can recognize three main period each lasting approximately 5 years (0–
5, 5–10, 10–15), characterized by a linear growth of intracranial
volume, although the rate of growth differs between these periods.
In 1999, Sgouros et al. showed that in the first few months of life,
the intracranial volume is on average 900 cm3 in boys and 600 cm3 in
girls and that at the age of 2 years it reaches 77% of the volume that il
will have at 15 years and at 5 years the 90%. They further
demonstrated that patients with craniosynostosis born with a
significantly smaller intracranial volume, about 500 cm3 at the age of
1 month, but at around the age of 6 months the total cranial volume is
normalized and since that age they follow the normal head growth
pattern. Consequently, any negative constricting effects from
craniosynostosis are most likely to occur during the first months of life
when the difference in intracranial volume between normal and
craniosynostosis patients is maximal [5, 6].
An underdeveloped posterior cranial fossa and a consequent
craniocerebral disproportion due to the premature fusion of the cranial
sutures in children with syndromic or multi-sutural craniosynostosis

can be predisposed to a raised intracranial pressure (ICP) with various
associations with hydrocephalus or a Chiari type 1 malformation [7, 8].
An incidence of Chiari malformation is described up to 72.2% in
children with Crouzon syndrome and between 1.1 and 3% in nonsyndromic craniosynostosis [7, 9].
Progressive hydrocephalus has been reported to occur in 9–26% of
Crouzon patients and 28–64% of patients with Pfeiffer syndrome. Its
origin has to be considered multifactorial, with one of the main
recognized mechanisms being crowding in the posterior cranial fossa
leading to functional obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid outflow within
the cerebral aqueduct [7, 10].
As previously mentioned, the problem of craniocerebral
disproportion in craniostenosis, with few exceptions like FGFR2-related
craniosynostosis, is maximum in the first month of life, [5, 11] so it
cannot be the only mechanism that contributes to increase of
intracranial pressure in these patients: airway obstruction [12] and a
venous engorgement [13–15] play a non-marginal role in the
development of this sequelae which can be considered therefore as a
complex and multifactorial pathology (Fig. 33.1) [13].

Fig. 33.1 The complex relationship between the factors concurring to a raised intracranial
pressure. (Adapted from: Protzenko T et al. Venous anomalies in hypoplastic posterior fossa:
unsolved questions. Childs Nerv Syst. 2021;37(10):3177–3187)

These patients present a high incidence of anomalies of venous
drainage, namely the stenosis of the sigmoid-jugular complex and the
transverse sinus agenesis, in particular the one homolateral to the
stenosis, associated with various degree of collateral venous collector
and in some cases associated with a hypertrophy of the contralateral
transvers sinus which can make surgery challenging because of the risk
of damage during the dural dissection (Fig. 33.2) [16, 17].

Fig. 33.2 Transversus sinus asymmetry in Crouzon syndrome

Recent genetic studies speculate on the role of an intrinsic vascular
problem associated with the intracranial hypertension.
Immunohistochemical examination detected FGFR gene expression
products both in synostosic sutures and cranial vascular endothelium:
they would stimulate a premature endothelial proliferation resulting in
stenosis of these vessels [18]. Loss of expression of the Twist 1 gene
seems to have the same implications [19], though clinically SaethreChoitzen patients do not display the same degree of vascular anomalies
than patients with Crouzon or Pfeiffer syndrome.
Venous compression and malformation can also have an impact on
surgery: according to the literature, the most exuberant collateral

circulation in patients with syndromic craniosynostosis occurs in the
posterior fossa, making adequate preoperative planning essential.
Rollins’ studies on cerebral venogram find functional stenosis of the
jugular foramen in 100% of patients affected with Pfeiffer syndrome, in
62% with Crouzon syndrome, in 50% with Apert syndrome, and in
83% with complex craniosynostosis [20].
Exuberant emissaries are found in 100% of patients with Pfeiffer
syndrome, 74% in Crouzon, 36% in Apert, and 33% in SaerthreChotzen; occipital and mastoid emissaries are the most common. The
persistence of fetal sinus is described in Crouzon and Pfeiffer
syndrome, in particular the occipital sinus and the marginal one [21].
The two main objectives of surgery for craniosynostosis are to
expand the cranial vault volume to prevent or reduce the raised
intracranial pressure and to correct the morphological impact on the
anterior cranium [22].
For decades, fronto-orbital advancement (FOA) for cranial vault
expansion has been the standard treatment to correct the typical
exorbitism, the forehead, and supraorbital bar recession of
brachycephaly and to increase the volume of the intracranial cavity.
The high reoperation rate due to the failure in restoring the
intracranial pression and the inadequate correction of brachyturricephaly deformity, described up to 100% in Apert patients, 26% in
Crouzon, 38% in Pfeiffer, and 65% in patients with Saethre–Chotzen
syndrome, [23] with a reoperation rate of 8.2%, raising to 16.7% in
Apert syndrome, even higher if fronto-orbital advancement (FOA) is
performed before 6 months of age, stimulates the development of
surgical procedure for the direct expansion of the posterior cranial
vault. Choi’s study effectively shows that these procedures can reach
intracranial volume expansion approximately 35% greater than
anterior cranial vault advancement procedures [24].
The procedure should be made early enough to prevent negative
effects on brain development and further progression toward
turricephaly, but in case of syndromic craniosynostoses the surgical
reconstructions are associated with a higher rate of relapse when
performed in very very young children [24]. Thus, the surgical timing is
a compromise between developmental stage compatible with safe
general anesthesia and surgery and the stage of maximal craniocerebral

disproportion to prevent also a supranormal correction of intracranial
volume. In practice, this puts the preferred timing between the age of 3
and 6 months [4, 6].

33 2 Surgical Techniques
The posterior cranial vault may be expanded by posterior cranioplasty
or by less invasive methods based on gradual posterior cranial vault
expansion or distraction [22].
The common goal of all these procedures is to prevent the
developing of intracranial hypertension, the progression toward
turricephaly, and to reduce any local brain compression within the
posterior cranial fossa by increasing the intracranial volume [4].
Posterior skull vault remodeling can either use a single procedure
that is necessary in case of pure lambdoid or Mercedes-Benz synostosis
or represent the first step of a multistage operative management in
cases of complex syndromic craniosynostoses [25].

33 2 1 Fixed Posterior Cranial Vault Expansion (PCVE)
The “conventional” PCVE implies parieto-occipital bon flaps
osteotomies, active remodeling, repositioning, rearrangement,
reconstruction, advancement, and enlargement plus their fixation,
usually elevated from the dura. It is a surgical option suitable for
syndromic and non-syndromic unilateral or bilateral lambdoid
synostosis, Mercedes-Benz pattern, secondary craniosynostosis due to
an over drainage in shunted patients, and correction of scaphocephaly
with a severe occipitoparietal narrowing and prominent inion [26]. It
has also been proposed in case of severe positional plagiocephaly in
which every corrective noninvasive measure applied has failed [27].

33.2.1.1 PC E Surgical Techni ue
Several technical nuances are described in literature; [1, 28, 29] here
we describe the “Lyonnaise technique” which combines the Tiaratechnique, a remodeling procedure described by Goodrich, and the
Meander technique, a volume increasing tongue-in-groove procedure.
The patient is in prone position, with the head slightly flexed in a
horseshoe headrest. It is very important to pay attention to the

positioning of face and eyes to avoid decubitus and pressure damage: a
“hellenic helmet” (Fig. 33.3) can be used with this scope [25].

Fig. 33.3 The “hellenic helmet”

The German group suggests the use of a fixed pediatric headrest
system and the spatial registration of patient radiological images with a
neuronavigational system to define the position of posterior sagittal
and transverse sinuses [1].
A standard ear to ear bicoronal incision is performed. Its location is
very important for the further bon exposition: it should be enough
anteriorly to permit a large skin flap allowing a resistant coverage of
the expanded bone flap and anticipate at the same time the possible
need for a secondary frontal surgery.
A subgaleal flap is then elevated posteriorly until the nuchal line,
and a periosteal flap is dissected and elevated down to the insertion of
the nuchal muscles: the posterior part of the parietal bones and the
superior part of the occipital bone are exposed.
The lateral exposure reaches the posterior part of the temporosquamosal suture and asterion, while, inferiorly, the dissection reaches
the external occipital protuberance.
In case of skull lacunae and potential venous anomalies, care must
be taken in order to avoid any dural bleeding and emissary vascular

damage. Bone bleeding is controlled with bone wax, if needed.
When the posterior cranial vault is enough exposed, the osteotomy
line can be drawn according to the preoperative plan: attention must be
taken in case of forehead associated anomalies to spare the temporal
region if a secondary distraction surgery of anterior cranial vault could
be required.
A carefully dissection of dura mater is made with the help of blunt
dissection through the sagittal suture itself or by directly passing
through bony lacunas if present. The risk of dural adhesion, and a
consequently dural damage, is higher when the lambdoid suture is
present and in case of bony spicules that can be embedded extremely
deeply within the dura and the parenchyma. Furthermore, particular
attention must also be paid because hypertrophic transverse sinuses
are described predominantly on the side of the permeable suture [16,
17]. If needed, burr holes are drilled to allow a proper dissection of the
epidural plan: a median burr hole on the vertex on the sagittal suture or
two paramedian burr holes to protect the sagittal sinus, and a burr hole
on the asterion on each side can help a safer dissection.
At this point, in the “Meander technique”, four to five tongues with
about 2–3 cm of breadth and 10–15 cm of length are created parallel to
the sagittal sinus in the technique described by Wagner [29] or
perpendicular to the sagittal sinus in the midline in the case of
symmetrical brachycephaly or towards the respective side in case of
posterior plagiocephaly [1]. The tongues are then elevated from the
dura mater and distracted away from the contralateral ones to
progressively expanding the convexity of the calvarium and creating
additional sub-calvaria, extradural space. The calvaria tongues are then
connected in their distracted position [1, 29].
The Lyonnaise technique involves, first, the creation of bony band
1.5 cm width, a “Tiara”, from the vertex down to the asterion on both
sides that will be used later to enlarge the occipital region, and second,
the realization of parietal and occipital osteotomies with the help of
craniotome or piezosurgery (Fig. 33.4a).

Fig. 33.4 Schematic representation of osteotomies (a, b) and of the final reconstruction (c).
(Adapted from: Di Rocco et al. Fixed posterior cranial vault expansion technique. Childs Nerv
Syst. 2021;37(10):3137–3141)

A better control of potential emissary veins at occipital bone level
can be reached with the help of rongeurs instead of craniotome.
According to the operative plan, the occipital osteotomies can be
carried out up to or even beyond the transverse sinuses.
After completing the dural dissection, the bone flap can then be
elevated, the hemostasis controlled, and any eventually dural tear
repaired.
At this point, multiple occipitoparietal bone cuts perpendicular to
transverse sinus are done with the osteotome or piezosurgery: this
maneuver creates occipital bone segments to be bent externally,
resulting in a further increase of the skull expansion and intracranial
volume increase (Fig. 33.4b) [25].
Finally, the reconstruction step can start. The “parietal-tiara” is
placed occipitally and fixed with absorbable plates or absorbable
stiches to the skull, creating a dead space allowing the posterior
cerebral expansion: normally the bandeau needs a minimal reshaping
to achieve a correct morphology, and furthermore, its consistency is
hard enough to allow the child to rest on the head subsequently.
The remaining posterior parieto-occipital bone flap is reshaped and
replaced over the dura in anatomical position or turned 180° if there is
a great asymmetry to correct. Its fixation to the bandeau is usually
performed with resorbable stitches. One or several absorbable plates
can be used to maintain the posterior expansion and avoiding the bone
flap to fall when closing the soft tissues (Fig. 33.4c).

Once the bone flap has been fixed, bone powder and bony chips can
be added to favor the postoperative ossification [25].
A closure layer by layer is performed; the skin tension can be
reduced by an anterior subgaleal undermining.
A subgaleal drain can be placed and removed after 24 h.

33.2.1.2 Ad antages and imits
The fixed posterior vault expansion technique allows an immediate and
single-step correction of the deformation and usually permits to reach
the exact shape that is planned in the preoperative period. The use of a
fixed and rigid occipital bandeau permits the children to rest on the
back without modifying or damaging the construct.
Furthermore, in case of raised intracranial pressure, it can offer an
immediate control.
The drawback is the impossibility to correct the obtained surgical
skull expansion and influence the morphological remodeling in the
postoperative phase, because of the “fixed” cranial reconstruction.
Perioperative risks are the dural tearing particularly high in case of
craniosynostoses associated with severe cranial bone dysplasia and the
hemorrhagic risk due both to a large bone osteotomies and remodeling
and to a direct damage of emissary veins or of sinuses secondary to a
dural tear.
Although the infection risk is very small, as there are no external
devices, the displaced bone, detached from its blood supplies, acts as a
not-vascularized bone graft in the immediate postoperative period time
and it could interfere in the medical management of infection because
the diffusion of antibiotics in the bone is reduced [25].

33 2 2 Free Floating Parieto-occipital Cranial Vault Release
The free-floating parieto-occipital cranial vault release exploits brain
growth in infants as a driving force for spontaneous and gradual
displacement of the free-floating occipital bone flap for posterior
cranial vault expansion.

33.2.2.1 Free Floating Parieto-occipital Cranial ault
elease Surgical Techni ue

The first historical report dates to 1996 with two techniques described,
both included in the multistaged management protocol with the aim of
postponing fronto-orbital advancement: the first one consisted in a
single bone flap extended 2 cm above the lambdoid sutures with lower
limit at the torcula sigmoid sinuses junction (Fig. 33.5a) and the second
one in a biparted double bone flap with a midline bone strip
craniectomy along the lower third of the sagittal sinus (Fig. 33.5b) [30].

Fig. 33.5 Schematic representation of free-floating craniectomy. (a) Single bone flap above the
lambdoid sutures. (b) Biparted double bone flap with a midline bone strip craniectomy along
the lower third of the sagittal sinus. (Adapted from: Sgouros S et al. Posterior skull surgery in
craniosynostosis. Childs Nerv Syst. 1996;12(11):727–733)

The procedure can be performed in the prone or semi-sitting
position. A posterior bilambdoid [31] or a bicoronaric [4] skin incision
is performed to expose the cranial posterior vault in the subgaleal plane
to minimize blood loss and avoid injuries to the dura mater protruding
through the lacunae. If the coronal suture is involved, the subgaleal
dissection can be extended to the bregmatic fontanel and laterally to
the pterional region [16, 17].
A carefully dura mater dissection till transverse and sigmoid sinuses
is made: in case of children with a honeycomb structure of the bone, the
existing holes are used as a pathway to release the bone from the dura
dissecting bone limits around the lacunae from the dura by incising the
periosteum, while in patients with more compact bone structure, two
parietal drill burr holes can be performed 1 cm from the midline and
two further burr holes at the level of the lateral third of the transverse
sinus [31]. In very young babies, spatula or the cutting edge of the
rounded Obwegeser rugine can be used to make the holes [16, 17].
A craniotomy, with craniotome or piezosurgery, is then performed
in front of both lambdoid sutures and down to the asterion, and it can
be continued caudally under the torcula to the foramen magnum.
The bone is then completely detached from the dural plane except
at the level of sagittal sinus, where it is left in place as an anchor point
for the bone. If a great venous hypertension is remarked, the flap can be
divided into two to protect the sagittal sinus and/or the torcula and
reduce the risk of transosseous vein damage [31].
No subcutaneous drain is left in place and a layer-by-layer closure is
done. Sometimes an extended subgaleal dissection is needed to have
enough tissue for closure [32].

33.2.2.2 Ad antages and imits
Surgical time reduced compared to a conventional PVCE; the minimal
blood loss and the immediate relieve of intracranial hypertension make
this procedure suitable even for the youngest patients with severe
craniostenosis: a recently published series shows safe results of this
technique in a cohort of patients aged from 6 days to 6 months [16, 17].
Another advantage is the minimal surgical manipulation which
minimizes the risks for dural tears.

Very small babies have great potential of re-ossification, but the risk
of relapse and incomplete ossification is quite high in case of complex
craniosynostosis with an “honeycomb” bone-structure.
Its main limitation is related to the mandatory positioning in the
postoperative period: alternate lateral positioning is required for a
posterior expansion to occur at an age in which there is still a risk of
sudden death in the prone position. Indeed, the supine positioning of
the infant during the postoperative course could prevent the posterior
expansion and could even result in brain compression.
Another limit is the relative ineffectiveness of the technique in
correcting the abnormal position of the petrous bone and the
deformation of the frontal and facial bones that are present in severe
positional plagiocephalies and in all synostotic ones [32].

33 2 3 Spring-Assisted Posterior Vault Expansion (SAPCVE)
The challenging skin closure using rigid posterior vault expansion
incentivized the introduction of gradual and dynamic expansion of
posterior vault using devices to support. The use of subcutaneous
springs was first described by Lauritzen [33].
The springs can be used alone in case of open lambdoid sutures or
in combination with a large osteotomy to obtain a bone flap that will be
displaced progressively by the springs in case of closed sutures.

33.2.3.1 Springs Manufacture
The springs are Omega-shaped tools in strainless-free wire introduced
in the 1970s for craniofacialsurgery and Lauritzen introduced their use
in cranial vault remodeling in late 1990s.
Initially, their wire-form was bent intraoperatively into the desired
U shape, and only in 2007, a group of surgeons and engineers of the
Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children (GOSH), of London, tried to
standardize the device.
Springs are composed by a central loop which extends into two
longer arms which end in a footplate that is used to anchor the spring
to the bone cuts performed during the surgery. The distance between
the tips (“inter-foot distance”) is 60 mm at rest and before implantation
and the central loop diameter is 10 mm.

When positioned, the opening of the spring narrows its end points.
Three standardized models with different thicknesses, which
correspond to a different force, are now currently used: model S10—
1.0 mm wire thickness, model S12—1.2 mm thickness, and model S14
—1.4 mm thickness [34].
The force at implantation is 11.4 4.3 N for the anterior spring and
11.8 4.1 N for the posterior spring, and studies demonstrate that it
takes 10 days from day of surgery for the springs to open completely
[35].

33.2.3.2 SA-PC E Surgical Techni ue
The patient is positioned prone with the neck in a neutral or slightly
flexed position.
A bicoronal incision is done until the subgaleal plane and the skin
flap is then reflected posteriorly until reaching the confluence of the
lambdoid sutures paying attention to the emissary veins and to the
subcutaneous venous anatomy. A pericranial flap is then dissected
leaving the temporalis muscle in situ and a subperiosteal plane is
created in the retromastoid area at the level of foramen magnum, while
the extracranial soft tissue over the torcula is left in situ.
A curved bicoronal osteotomy is done about 5 cm posterior to the
skin incision and taken through the soft tissue tunnel towards the
foramen magnum (Fig. 33.6a, b).

Fig. 33.6 Schematic representation curved osteotomy (a–c) and springs placement along the
osteotomy line (b–d). (Adapted from: Breakey RWF et al. Spring-assisted posterior vault
expansion-a single-center experience of 200 cases. Childs Nerv Syst. 2021;37(10):3189–3197)

Along the osteotomy line, burr holes are previously made and the
ones in the retromastoid areas are expanded into a small craniotomy to
allow visualization of the transverse sinus and to permit the dural
dissection towards the foramen magnum under direct vision.
Once the osteotomy is completed, the dura is dissected and stripped
from the inner table a few centimeters anteriorly and posteriorly to
permit a certain degree of motion of the posterior bone flap: if the flap

remains rigid, the osteotomy can be extended towards the torcula and
foramen magnum, or the dural dissection can be widened.
When the bone mobility is considered sufficient, the springs can be
placed across the osteotomy lines (or across the lambdoid sutures
when present) [36].
Three different wire diameters are available, resulting in three
different spring stiffnesses: normally, younger the child is, the weaker is
the spring needed for surgical correction. Two, or occasionally more,
springs, if two springs are felt to be insufficient, are placed along the
osteotomy line facing each other around 2 cm from either side of the
midline into prepared grooves that ensure to lock the spring footplates
in position (Fig. 33.6c, d). A resorbable suture is used to anchor the
midpoint of the springs to the periosteum to prevent their
dislodgement.
The pericranium is closed over the springs. This gives stability to
the construct and permits to see how the soft tissues will drape over
the springs: any spring protrusion or bony prominence should be
overcome at this stage.
The closure of scalp should be done with the compressive help of an
assistant, who ensures one hand on the occiput and one on the
forehead to avoid compression of the face and eyes.
Once the skin is closed, the springs will begin their expansion.
The treatment time is customized, ranging from some weeks to
several months with a mean time of 9 months [37].
Spring removal is done under general anesthesia. The positioning is
the same of the insertion and the original scar is reopened. The springs
are uncovered using monopolar cautery. Generally, most of the bone
gaps have ossified by this time, but careful dissection has to be done to
avoid dural tears.
Once the springs are exposed, they are removed with a combination
of Mitchel’s trimmers, a Tessier periosteal elevator, and a pair of heavy
forceps. Care is taken when removing the footplate not to catch any
dura in the tip.
The wound is closed layer by layer, and no drain is used [37].

33.2.3.3 Ad antages and imits

SA-PCVE provides a correction of cranial shape based on forces applied
to the calvarium rather than on rearrangement of separated bone
fragment, reducing the need for multiple osteotomies and thereby the
bleeding and surgical time.
The main criticism is the lack of the control over vectors forces and
on the degree of bone fragments separation. Furthermore, the largest
distraction force is at the beginning, after the force decreases with
expansion of the springs: this could cause incomplete ossification, but it
appears to be mostly an age-related complication than a technique one
[38].
The great ossification capability of the younger has the drawback to
make them the group that more likely needs repeat SA-PCVE. The
incidence of repeated SA-PCVE is maximum in Apert population,
followed by Crouzon-Pfeiffer, and multi-suture craniosynostosis [37]. A
study on rabbits shows that 80% of cranial vault expansion is achieved
by 2 weeks and 90% by 3 weeks of springs-distraction: at this point of
expansion, the residual spring force is 28% of the original one. It shows
also that the craniofacial biomechanics modify the expansion curve as
the spring force decays; this could explain the relapse if the springs are
removed too early, [39] underlying the importance of a close follow-up
with serial craniometric studies.
Like all prostheses, they have a non-negligible risk of infection,
theoretically reduced by the fact that they are completely subcutaneous
(up to 30%, [37]), a risk of dislodgement, skin penetration, LCR
leakage, and pressure sores (about 3% in Lauritzen’ cohort) [33].

33 2 4 Distractors Osteosynthesis (DO-PCVE)
Transcutaneous distractors’ use for cranial vault expansion is based on
gradual and controlled separation of bone fragments created by an
osteotomy, with a distraction rate that allows a progressive bone
formation.

33.2.4.1 Distractors Manufacture
The concept of Distraction Osteogenesis has been directly adopted from
orthopedic practice.
The most important characteristics of devices used for distraction
osteogenesis are their capacity to transfer distraction forces directly to

the bone, and second, the strength to offer the adequate rigidity for
osseous consolidation to occur.
The first experimental investigation on cranial osteodistraction was
performed in 1957 by Polezhaev and colleagues. Now a variety of plate
designs are available to fit your patient’s anatomy and your surgical
needs.
The main components, all made in lightweight titanium, are the
central distractor, the fixation meshes, and the activation arms, which
permit the movement of central arm, and so the bone distraction when
turned by a screwdriver.

33.2.4.2 D -PC E Surgical Techni ue
The patient is prone-positioned and a bicoronal scalp subgaleal incision
is required.
Two types of craniotomies can be used: supratorcular parietooccipital craniotomy or infratorcular craniotomy below the venous
torcular. The choice is determined depending on the crowding of the
posterior fossa, presence of tonsillar prolapse, preoperative assessment
of the venous anatomy, and perioperative surgical findings [40]. For a
maximal volume gain, the vertical part of the osteotomy should be
placed at the level of maximal vertical cranial circumference and the
horizontal osteotomy as low as possible (Fig. 33.7). The osteotomy is
performed with a motor drill or bone rongeur without elevating the
cranial bone from the dura matter. Two to four distractors are applied
depending on the age of the patient and the vector direction of the bone
flap [4, 40].

Fig. 33.7 Schematic representation of distractors positioning

In the original White’s paper, the horizontal osteotomy is placed
below the level of the torcula paying attention to the trans-osseous
communicating veins to decrease the risk of intraoperative bleeding.
The distractors are positioned and fixated with titanium screws in
each temporal region and a superior paramedian to avoid the sagittal
sinus [41].
The two types of craniotomies show no significant differences in
term of clinical or radiological efficacy. Increasing the number of
distractors can enhance construct stability but, at the same time, it
increases the risk of wound-related complications and may introduce
conflicting vectors. In most cases, two distractors are showed sufficient
to allow good expansion [40].
It is possible to leave at this early stage few millimeters of
distraction, to achieve some degree of distraction.
The direction of the vector will dirige the expansion of the cranial
vault: posterior vectors are indicated for cephalo-cranial disproportion
with the acceptable overall shape; posteroinferior vectors for

turribrachycephaly, bilateral vectors for shunt-related slit ventricle
syndrome [42].
Barrel stave osteotomy can be made at inferior occipital segment to
expand the cranial vault below the horizontal craniotomy to increase
the gain volume [43].
Prior to skin closure, the soft tissues around the activation arms,
especially the periosteum, are checked and adapted, if necessary, to
avoid pinching them in the rotating parts of the devices during the
activation period. The wound is then closed layer by layer, and no drain
is used.
After a latency phase of 2–7 days, the distraction phase is
characterized by distraction rate of 1 mm/day, divisible once or twice
per day. Ong et al. propose a latency period and a distraction rate in
function of age: shorter latency period with higher distraction rate for
the younger and a longer latency period with smaller distraction rate
for the older patients [42].
The distraction is carried out till reaching a slight overcorrection of
the preoperative brachycephaly: periodic plain radiographs of the skull
are used to monitor the progress of distraction and re-ossification.
Normally, the consolidation period is on average twice as long as the
period of activation, but it has to be individualized to each patient [40,
41, 44].

33.2.4.3 Ad antages and imits
Distractors can be used at every age with satisfactory results, but they
have to be preferred for infants with a sufficiently thick calvarium.
Goldstein in his cohort of patients aged from 0.3 to 14.1 years
documented an overall average volume change of 21% over
preoperative intracranial volume measurements, while in patients
younger than 12 months the volume increases up to 29%. Furthermore,
when the low occiput is included in the distraction segment, it could
influence the volume of the posterior cranial base, potentially
decompressing a Chiari malformation [44].
Distractors allow a gradual distraction of 0.5–1 mm a day which
results in an osteogenetic effect, reducing the risk of severe lacunas
[38].

In case of thin bone, the fixation of the distractor may be complex. In
order to try and avoid a dislocation while activating the system and
reducing the risk of dural tears while positioning the distractor, the use
of metallic stainless-steel wires to stabilize the internal distractor has
been proposed [45].
Risk related to the device is dislocation or dysfunction; the injury of
the underlying dura mater during the placement or fixation of screws
and pins in areas of limited bone stock may be up to 10% [4, 40].
Lastly, percutaneous component of the distraction can carry a
potential infective risk due to the percutaneous with a tax of infection
up to 30% [46].

33 3 Comparison and Conclusions
All these techniques have been proven to permit a satisfying
intracranial volume increasing without major significative differences
in volume: 13–24% for the free posterior flap, 18–25% for the trans
lambdoid springs, 26% for the fixed posterior cranial vault expansion,
and 22–29% for the distractors [4, 14, 47].
Not only posterior vault remodeling improves the supratentorial
vault volume and skull shape, but posterior cranial vault expansion has
shown to permit a complete resolution of Chiari malformation and an
accompanying syringomyelia [48].
Internal distractors allow a gradual distraction, resulting in an
osteogenetic effect while springs give the largest distraction force in the
beginning, and then the force decreases, and this could cause
incomplete ossification in older patients because the ossification rate
decreases with age [47]. On the other hand, De Jong et al. showed that
the spring distraction technique permits larger increase of
anteroposterior length in a shorter measurement interval (6.1 versus
8.5 months) when compared to the fixed distraction technique. They
concluded that springs permit a larger expansion to the fixed cranial
vault expansion, [38] but the fixed cranial vault expansion technique
has been shown to have a non-negligible learning curve [47] and it can
be a bias in the comparison.
Free floating parieto-occipital cranial vault release could be used in
the most unfavorable conditions (tiny honey-comb internal bone

structure, severe constriction of intracranial structures) in the very
young patient with a reduced surgical time and reduced blood loss. The
surgical time is also reduced in all the osteogenic techniques when
compared to fixed cranial vault expansion, which has also a higher risk
of blood loss [49] and dural tears due to the elevation of the bone flap.
The main drawbacks of springs and distractors are the infectious
risk, the device failure, and the need of a second surgery to remove
them. Free floating parieto-occipital cranial vault release and springassisted expansion share the risk of failure due to the necessity to avoid
the dorsal position. On the other hand, fixed posterior cranial vault
expansion permits a free posterior postoperative decubitus with the
strength and defect of not allowing to adapt the postoperative result.
All the techniques offer good results with good security profile. For
the best correction, surgical decision should be based on clinical
presentation, age, sutural pattern, and syndromic context.

Keywords Craniosynostosis – Technical tips – Complications – Surgical
approach – Older children

34 1 Introduction
Most children with craniosynostosis are identified and managed in
infancy. There is, however, a subset of patients in whom the diagnosis of
craniosynostosis is delayed, either through a lack of recognition or
because they lack some or all of the sentinel cranial shape changes. In
addition, revision surgery may be required in some patients to address
persistent or recurrent issues of cranial shape and/or volume.
Nevertheless, the indications for surgical correction remain the same as
for the younger cohort: cranial shape/appearance and the possibility of
intracranial hypertension. Surgical assessment and intervention in
older patients present a unique set of challenges when compared to the
treatment of younger patients. The epidemiology, pathophysiology, and
key treatment considerations are the subject of this chapter.

34 2 Epidemiology and Pathophysiology
The incidence of nonsyndromic craniosynostosis, defined as abnormal
or premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures, is 1 in 2000 live
births. Craniosynostosis typically results in characteristic changes in
cranial form and volume that herald the presence of the condition, and
these changes may lead to adverse effects on cerebral growth and
function. Most studies support early intervention to help mitigate these
undesirable outcomes, but only 75% of affected patients will be
referred to neurosurgery and receive treatment within the first year of
life [1, 2]. The underlying causes for delayed treatment are
multifactorial and include failure to diagnose or refer in a timely
fashion, impaired access to care, or more rarely, development of latent
suture fusions [3–6]. The latter category is rare but can result from
postnatal environmental influences including: metabolic bone diseases
such as rickets, hypophosphatasia, pseudohypoparathyroidism,
osteopetrosis, and mucopolysaccharidosis [7]; mechanical forces [8]; or
natural population variability in suture closure patterns [9]. Children
with rickets have an increased incidence of craniosynostosis (both

single and multiple sutures) and are more likely to suffer from
increased ICP when compared to other patients with craniosynostosis
[10]. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) shunts have also been associated in
certain studies with development of secondary craniosynostosis in
nearly 50% of patients [8]. Furthermore, recent studies of children
evaluated for head trauma demonstrate that approximately 7% of
normal infants with otherwise normal head shape will have developed
fusion of the sagittal suture before the age of two [9]. While the effect of
these latent forms of craniosynostosis on cranial shape and volume can
be minor or negligible, increased intracranial pressure has been
reported and careful clinical oversight is necessary [11].
Revision surgery is also more likely to be performed in older
patients. The indications for revision surgery are esthetic concerns or
elevated intracranial pressure, which can occur due to inadequate
primary surgery or insufficient cranial growth after an adequate
reconstruction. Risk factors include a syndromic diagnosis, surgery
before age 6 months, and the number and type of suture fusions
(sagittal highest of single suture fusions) [12–16]. Revision surgery
may involve longer operating times, greater overall blood loss, and
more intraoperative complications related to existing bone defects,
scarring of the dura, or elevated intracranial pressure.

34 3 Clinical Presentation
The clinical presentation of patients who present with craniosynostosis
later in life varies significantly depending on the reason for the delay.
Patients with latent fusion (postnatal) may have little or none of the
characteristic changes in cranial shape. These patients can be nearly
impossible to identify clinically and are often detected only by
fortuitous imaging or other findings. Patients with characteristic cranial
shape changes in whom diagnosis was made later in life tend to have
more pronounced craniofacial abnormalities, especially at the cranial
base, secondary to compensatory calvarial growth, and appear to have
an increased risk of increased intracranial pressure (ICP) and
developmental delay [11, 12, 17, 18]. Typical signs and symptoms of
elevated intracranial pressure such as headaches, nausea/vomiting,
and/or vision changes/papilledema are often absent in older children

with craniosynostosis [12]. Workup should include a detailed history
and physical exam which includes the trajectory of head circumference
growth since birth, a fundoscopic examination, and a low threshold for
radiographic evaluation (CT, MRI) to assess subtle changes consistent
with increased pressure. ICP monitoring may be indicated for patients
who manifest minor changes to cranial shape or in whom the decision
to proceed with surgical correction is predicated on the presence or
absence of intracranial hypertension (e.g., older with reasonable head
shape and volume, or parental uncertainty).
The presence of elevated intracranial pressure is an absolute
indication for cranial vault expansion, but the beneficial effect of
surgery on long-term neurocognitive outcomes is less clear.
Developmental delay and neurocognitive deficits have been well
demonstrated in older children with untreated synostosis by several
groups; up to a three to fivefold increase in risk in some studies [17–
21], but a few studies have documented that surgical intervention
improves these parameters, especially in older children. A study by
Starr et al. also demonstrated significant delay both before and after
surgery in patients with isolated single-suture synostosis [22]. Even
when these patients have normal IQ scores, they tend to have
significant learning disabilities secondary to impairments in executive
dysfunction [20]. Functional imaging studies have confirmed altered
neural connectivity in patients with sagittal synostosis [23] and
surgical intervention prior to 6 months of age has been shown to
improve longitudinal outcomes in these kids and has led many to
recommend correction at an early age [24]. However, a small
prospective study by Fontana et al. has shown developmental
improvement even in older patients undergoing cranial vault
remodeling encouraging craniosynostosis repair in this cohort [17].

34 4 Surgical Considerations
Treatment of craniosynostosis addresses two concerns: cranial shape
and intracranial volume. The choice and timing of treatment depend on
many variables including patient age and comorbidities, the number
and type of fused sutures, prior cranial vault procedures, presence or
absence of intracranial pressure, and others.

1. Blood oss
The increased thickness of the scalp and bone in an older child may
increase the risk of bleeding. Use of meticulous surgical technique,
perioperative tranexamic acid (TXA) or aminocaproic acid, and a
well-coordinated team effort to minimize operative time can
mitigate the need for blood transfusion. This is especially important
in revision surgery. Through these measures, our transfusion rate
for patients over 2 years of age undergoing cranial reconstruction
has been less than 50%. Although rarely used in our center,
preoperative use of virtual surgical planning (VSP) can also aid in
optimizing the final calvarial shape and reduce surgical time with
the help of printed 2D templates to guide osteotomies [25, 26].
2. Bone Contouring and Stabilization
Bone of older children is thicker and more brittle than in infants
and often requires more releasing cuts to permit remodeling or
shape changes. This can result in bone edges that may be visible or
palpable postoperatively, and smoothing of any rough or prominent
bone edges with a burr is recommended. We typically use
resorbable plates on the endocortical surface to maintain the new
bony contour and to stabilize any bony advancement. Although
titanium plates are a reasonable option in older children, we prefer
resorbable hardware if possible. There are less issues in the long
run with prominent plates, etc.
3. Bone Defects
After the age of 18–24 months, the chance of spontaneous healing
of significant residual cranial defects decreases dramatically [19,
27]. We routinely cover all areas of exposed dura with autologous
particulate graft and this practice has reduced the rate of residual
bone defects and need for secondary cranioplasty at our center to
nearly zero. The technique has been well-described and uses a
Hudson brace and D’Errico bit to obtain the bone graft from the
endocortical surface of any removed bone segments or the
ectocortical surface of the intact calvaria (Figs. 34.1a–c and 34.2).
4. Hydrocephalus

It is important to assess any degree of cerebral ventriculomegaly
and the possibility of hydrocephalus. While ventriculomegaly can
contribute to an increase in the ICP, draining the ventricles with a
shunt may reduce cerebral growth and internal support for the
bony reconstruction, and potential lead to fusion of other cranial
sutures. A shunt or CSF diversion should be reserved for the patient
with clearly demonstrable hydrocephalus. A progressive Chiari
malformation or the presence of syringomyelia may offer potential
clues in this regard. One of the most helpful tools is evaluating
changes in head circumference percentile. Patients with restricted
calvarial growth (due to craniosynostosis) will usually manifest a
decreasing percentile over time, whereas the patient with
hydrocephalus demonstrates the opposite with an increasing or
stable head circumference percentile.
5. Infection
The risk of infection is also increased in these patients. This
increase is mainly twofold: due to increased exposure and longer
operative times required for the more extensive surgery, but also
due to the potential pneumatization of the frontal sinus in the older
patient. In a study looking at over 8000 children undergoing
craniosynostosis repair at multiple locations, Bruce et al.
demonstrated an increased risk of all complications, including
bleeding and infection in children undergoing a repair after
12 months of age. The conclusions held true even after they control
for procedure type and presence of comorbidities [2].
6. Relapse
Multiple studies have confirmed that surgical correction of
craniosynostosis in very young infants (i.e., 6 months of age) or in
patients with certain craniosynostosis syndromes results in a
higher likelihood of relapse and need for revision surgery [16].
Most surgeons compensate for this by overcorrecting the bone
movements during the cranial reconstruction. Since older children
are further along in their cranial growth, the need for
overcorrection and likelihood of relapse of the deformity are much
smaller. The surgeon should consider the amount of cerebral
growth remaining in determining how much to increase the

intracranial volume or advance the bone segments. This is
especially important in fronto-orbital advancement surgery where
overcorrection of an older patient can lead to a disfiguring or
stigmatizing result as well as difficulty in closing the surgical flap
and increasing the likelihood of wound breakdown or infection.

intradiploic bone fragments which will be used for bone particulate cranioplasty material. (b) A
relatively large amount of particulate bone graft may be harvested from the extra/intracranial

34 5 Reconstructive Techniques for Common
Forms of Craniosynostosis
While there are multiple approaches in dealing with the older patient
with craniosynostosis, ranging from simple radial osteotomies to
external distraction, general principles of positioning, anesthetic
considerations, minimizing morbidity/blood loss, and ultimately having
a defined and cogent reconstructive plan are critical components to a
successful surgery. At the outset, one must decide on the principal
indication for surgery: cosmesis or increased intracranial pressure, or
the frequent presentation of both. Patients presenting at an older time
frame often have significant calvarial distortions as well as evidence for
increased ICP (thinned calvarium, papilledema, decelerating head
circumference percentile, headache, or cognitive decline). Thus, the
goal of reducing ICP by increasing skull volume is often intertwined
with a desire for an improved morphological appearance. It doesn’t
take a significant increase in calvarial volume to markedly reduce the
patient’s ICP and the extent of volumetric expansion will be dictated by
the patient’s age. Patients approaching 5–6 years of age are unlikely
(but still seen on rare occasions) to need additional volumetric
expansion for purposes of intracranial pressure, whereas the younger

patients (2–4 years) will need to be followed closely, especially in the
setting of multi-suture synostosis. For the younger patient, every
attempt is made to maximize the increase in volume (e.g., frontal
advancement for bifronto-orbital conditions), but this is often limited
by the ability of the scalp to accommodate 2 cm frontal advancement.
For reasons that remain unclear, older patients most often present
with scaphocephaly and may be at the highest risk for increased ICP for
single-suture craniosynostosis. Bilateral coronal synostosis is the
second most frequently seen condition, whereas single coronal suture
or even metopic suture synostosis usually presents earlier due to the
significant calvarial asymmetry seen at an early age. While both types
may require a need to increase the calvarial volume, methods to do so
vary markedly and ultimately offer different esthetic considerations.

34 5 1 Fronto-orbital Advancement: Metopic Synostosis
While the presence of increased ICP may be less common in the delayed
presentation of metopic or coronal synostosis and cosmetic
considerations may be paramount, an adequate advancement of the
fronto-orbital bar will usually accomplish both goals of improving
appearance while simultaneously increasing intracranial volume if
there are any concerns about pressure. Fronto-orbital advancement is
the most predictable surgical option in older patients with
trigonocephaly. This method has predictably good outcomes in older
children if done correctly. With the patient in the supine position, the
frontal bones and orbital bandeau are removed.
The greatest challenge in these kids may be the presence of a frontal
sinus, although this usually develops after 7–8 years of age. In the event
that the frontal (or ethmoidal sinus) is encountered, then it is critical to
adequately remove all sinus mucosa (exenteration) and seal off this
extracranial compartment from the intracranial cavity. This may be
accomplished by using bone fragments harvested during the
craniotomy and small pieces of temporalis muscle to plug the
nasofrontal duct (or adjacent bony defects) and subsequently using
fibrin glue to hold the matrix in place. It is often prudent to leave the
pericranium intact during the exposure, to potentially use this as a
vascularized pedicle to overlie the area (Fig. 34.3). This will help
promote healing of this graft and lead to a true sequestration of the

extra from intracranial compartments. The additional time and
morbidity are minimal compared to the added potential of a wellhealed site (Fig. 34.4a–d).

Fig. 34.3 (a, b) Exposure of the frontonasal duct and ethmoid sinuses via a recently aerated
frontal sinus. A portion of pericranium has been preserved to be used as a vascularized pedicle
covering the exposed sinus which has been cleared of all mucosa and walled off from the
extracranial compartments (with bone fragments)

Fig. 34.4 (a–d) After the frontal bandeau is removed, its shape may be reconfigured by
performing osteotomies to facilitate bending the lateral structures as well as the midline.
Absorbable plates are used on the endocortical surface to maintain the desired new
configuration. When the newly shaped frontal orbital bandeau is returned to its original
position, one can appreciate the significant change in the new position (and shape) relative to
the preexisting frontal lobes

The V-shaped bandeau is expanded, and if necessary, the flat lateral
segments are contoured to increase the convexity. In severe cases, the
expanded bandeau may require a midline separation and leveling of
each half. If this creates a gap, it can be filled with a trapezoidal or
triangular bone. The nasal process of each frontal bone is long and
should be shortened. The bandeau is intentionally overcorrected in the
temporal areas and fixed with resorbable plates. The coronal gap can be
filled with a rectangular piece of bone harvested from the vertex to
stabilize the bandeau, provide bony continuity, and prevent any
possibility of collapse. While the frontal elements are off, a particulate
bone graft can be harvested from the inner table and stored in a bloodfilled container on the back table (see Fig. 34.1). This will provide bone

graft to repair any defects created by the advancement or harvest of
full-thickness bone graft. Each frontal bone is then remodeled with a
shaping burr or radial osteotomies and then orthotopically or
heterotopically affixed to the bandeau. The frontoparietal segments can
be affixed to the bandeau with resorbable plates or secured with wires
or sutures. To create a smooth transition with the widened frontal
segments, the parietal bones laterally should be out-fractured using
horizontal barrel staves and stabilized to the frontal elements with
absorbable plates. Although the lateral bone gaps between the frontal
and parietal segments could be left to heal spontaneously, repair with
full-thickness cortical bone harvested from the vertex provides bone
continuity and reduces the likelihood of depression (temporal hollow)
in this area. The temporalis muscle should be advanced anteriorly and
resuspended. If the soft tissue closure is tight, the galea can be scored
to reduce tension on the repair. This should not induce alopecia if done
properly—the scoring must not enter the fat layer where the hair
follicles reside.
The older patient often has many areas of calvarial deficiencies after
any frontal advancement or bilateral parietal expansion. It is best to
ensure that the frontal and other areas of cosmetic priority have
adequate bony reconstruction in these regions. Additional bone may be
harvested by using split-calvarial cranioplasty as well as using
particulate bony matrix harvested from the inner table using a Hudson
brace [28]. This technique affords a considerable amount of graft
material which when mixed with fibrin glue (Tisseel) will fill in many
leftover defects and provides a solid fusion construct most of the time.
Other challenges unique to the added fronto-orbital length include
the frequent difficulty of closing an older and less compliant scalp over
a greater volume (especially when advancing more than 2 cm). A
number of techniques can be employed to facilitate this often late in the
course of surgery challenge. The simplest is to use a through and
through heavy duty stitch at three to five locations through the scalp to
approximate the skin edges as best as possible and then to use a
smaller subcutaneous suture to gradually bring the edges together
much like a zipper before using a final and superficial skin closure with
3-0 monocryl (absorbable) or nylon suture. This will usually work for
most significant advancements if done gradually and carefully.

However, one must be cognizant of the amount of tension on the skin
edges and the possibility of wound breakdown contributing to a greater
chance of infection as well as development of a hypertrophic scar. If this
is unsuccessful or if the skin edge tension appears problematic, another
approach is to score the galea on the inner surface of the flap, being
careful not to extend this too close to the surface or to compromise the
dermal vascular layer of the flap. This will also offer greater relaxation
of the flap and potentially minimize any later healing problems.
Subgaleal drains are universally used with a catheter on each side of
the head (in case one falls out) and have been seen to reduce postop
pain and swelling and decrease the length of stay. It is also important to
use generous postoperative intravenous steroids to minimize any
fronto-orbital swelling that is not only uncomfortable, but can also
compromise healing of a flap under tension. We usually start the
steroids at the time of induction and use the steroids for 3 days with a
diminishing dose each day. To date, we have not seen any added
morbidity from a short course of modest steroids, but have seen
significant improvement in pain as well as universal discharges to home
by postop day 3.

34 5 2 Fronto-orbital Advancement: Unilateral Coronal
Synostosis
After the removal of the frontal bones and bandeau, each is remodeled.
The frontal bone is remodeled using radial osteotomies, or selective
fractures are performed to achieve the desired form. The bandeau is
contoured to increase the convexity of the flattened side. A resorbable
plate placed on the endocortical surface is excellent for maintaining the
bandeau shape. There is a tendency for the correction to relapse in
younger children who are still growing, so many surgeons advocate
recontouring and sagittal overcorrection of the bandeau and frontal
bone on the side of the fusion. Some authors have recommended using
an onlay bone graft over the orbital rim on the ipsilateral side to help
accentuate the sagittal projection, but it is the authors’ experience that
onlay grafts resorb. The bandeau repositioned with ipsilateral overadvancement and affixed to each temporal fossa with resorbable plates
is, in our opinion, a better option. A full-thickness rectangular bone
graft behind the bandeau will help prevent postoperative collapse and

ensure bony healing. The frontal bone plates are reattached to the
orbital bandeau with resorbable plates. The frontal bones should be
attached to the parietal segments with absorbable plates to prevent
collapse during the redraping of the coronal flaps. Full-thickness bone
grafts harvested from the vertex can be used to fill the lateral coronal
gap, especially on the more advanced side. Particulate cranial bone
graft harvested from the endocortex of the frontal elements, or
ectocortex of the parietal bones, can easily cover all remaining bone
defects. The asymmetry of the palpebral fissure can be corrected with a
lateral canthopexy on the side of the fusion.

34 5 3 Total Cranial Vault Remodeling: Sagittal
Surgical correction for delayed recognition of scaphocephaly more
often may be undertaken for concerns regarding increased ICP,
although morphological constraints may also be significant contributor
as an indication (Fig. 34.5).

Fig. 34.5 Five year-old male with untreated scaphocephaly referred because of teasing in
school. Note the significant skull base changes as well as the narrow face

Thus, this approach needs to adequately increase the intracranial
volume while concomitantly improving the cephalic index. Many of the
usual principles for a safe and effective cranial reconfiguration will
apply here, but there are a few concerns to consider differently in this

cohort. With careful dissection during the bicoronal incision (leaving
the periosteum intact on the bone), in addition to controlled systemic
hypotension (55–60 mmHg) as well as preoperative administration by
anesthesia of TXA/Amicar, one should be able to minimize bleeding
during the opening to less than 50 cc. Starting off with a minimal blood
loss during the opening increases the likelihood of not needing any
transfusion for these cases and our transfusion rate routinely runs
between 25–40% for the older patient. The most important factor is
performing a meticulous dissection and watching for the innocuous
slow oozing occurring under the towels or in a pocket of the flap. One
can lose a large amount of blood over an extended period of time
without truly appreciating the loss due to the slow and unimpressive
volume at the outset.
In the older child, the degree of anterior-posterior shortening that is
safe is considerably less than in a young infant and it is usually not
necessary to do any frontal advancement. One may leave the frontoorbital bar intact, which greatly facilitates the operation as well as
reduces postoperative morbidity. The primary goal is to increase the
intracranial volume while expanding the biparietal diameter. This is
best facilitated by performing a “sunrise” series of frontal osteotomies
leaving the fronto-orbital base predominantly intact but expanding the
lateral and posterior portions of the frontal bone while expanding both
parietal bones hinged off the intact and midline sagittal strut (Fig.
34.6a, b).

Fig. 34.6 (a, b) Sunrise technique for calvarial vault reconfiguration in the setting of delayed
presentation of sagittal synostosis. The frontal bone is left in place, but the lateral and posterior
components are opened up by radial osteotomies to expand the width of the frontal bone.
Partial thickness osteotomies are represented by the dotted lines, whereas the full thickness

osteotomies are planned along the solid lines. The midline bone overlying the sagittal sinus is
left in place to protect the sinus as well as being used as a scaffold for fixation of the new
calvarial bone flaps

Total vault remodeling for sagittal synostosis requires exposure
from the glabella anteriorly to the posterior cranial base. Supine
positioning on a cerebellar head holder is the senior author’s preferred
position for addressing all types of craniosynostosis as it permits full
exposure of the entire cranium and eliminates some potential
complications with prone positioning. The entire occiput is easily
accessed by simply turning the head to one side or the other. Frontal
bossing has been shown to correct naturally with growth and, thus,
does not require setback or manipulation. Low temporal and parietal
regions barrel stave osteotomies are performed, and the segments are
out-fractured. This expands the parietal width and provides a complete
release. The cone-shaped occiput is remodeled with radial osteotomies
and bending to give a more gradual convex curvature. The bifrontal
fragment is radially osteotomized and similarly reshaped. Shortening
the anteroposterior length is not usually required. However, this can be
accomplished by resecting a portion of the frontal and parietal bones at
the midline. The remaining parietal bone fragments are remodeled to
increase the lateral convexity. Once the bone fragments are remodeled
satisfactorily, they are secured in a more lateralized position with
absorbable plates. The exposed dura is covered with particulate bone
graft that can be harvested from the endocortical surface of the parietal
bones. Plate stabilization assures that the expansion and shape
correction achieved intraoperatively will not relapse or collapse
postoperatively (Fig. 34.7a–c).

Fig. 34.7 (a–c) After the frontal osteotomies, the expanded frontal width is now configured to
the newly expanded biparietal flaps (also with radial osteotomies) to increase the total width of
the head as well as offer greater intracranial volume. The construct is maintained using
absorbable plates

34 5 4 Cranial Vault Distraction
The distraction of the cranium is a newer technique that has shown
promise for certain types of craniosynostosis (e.g., bicoronal
craniosynostosis), but is used more liberally by some surgeons for all
types of craniosynostosis. Distraction can be used for patients of all
ages and allows large movements of cranial bone that would be
difficult, if not impossible, to achieve with minimally invasive or open
cranial remodeling procedures. Because this is a gradual process,
ossification of the bone gaps is quite good. But this procedure does
require a significant open dissection comparable to a conventional
open vault operation to perform the craniotomy and place the

distractors. It requires a second procedure to remove the device. The
greatest limitation for distraction in single suture fusions is that each
distractor moves the bone segment in one direction and there is no
capacity for bone remodeling or complex three-dimensional shape
changes. Thus, its utility and benefits for most types of single-suture
craniosynostosis are dubious at best. In the case of bilateral coronal
craniosynostosis, some centers have begun to emphasize early
posterior expansion, often using distraction and a later staged anterior
procedure to improve frontal shape. Advocates suggest that this
approach provides the neurocognitive benefits of early decompression,
avoids the development of compensational turribrachycephaly, and
permits a later anterior reconstruction (presumably less relapse). The
disadvantage of this algorithm is that it requires three procedures early
in life, including a relatively large procedure to create the posterior
osteotomies and place the distractors, another minor procedure to
remove the distractors, and the frontal procedure at some time in the
future. The procedure also results in the closure of the normal
lambdoid sutures—the effect of this is unknown.

34 6 Conclusions
Most children with non-syndromic craniosynostosis present to
neurosurgical attention in early infancy and undergo surgical repair
prior to 1 year of age. However, a subset of patients may present in a
delayed fashion due to several factors and often present unique
challenges for the craniofacial team. These children are at risk for
presenting with increased ICPs and may manifest developmental delay
from the growth restriction placed on the skull and brain in infancy.
They also tend to have more craniofacial abnormalities and require
more extensive surgery with an increased risk of potential
complications. However, with detailed preoperative planning and a few
key considerations, these patients can safely undergo repair for both
aesthetic purposes and alleviation of any increased ICP as well as
potential improvement in any cognitive deficits.
Pearls and Pitfalls

One must look carefully for any possible sign of increased ICP in the
older patient, even those of a single suture synostosis. This entails a
detailed history and exam (the HC trajectory is a critical piece of
information) as well as radiographic evaluation (CT, MRI) and
funduscopic evaluation to look for subtle changes consistent with
increased pressure. It may also be necessary to place an ICP monitor
for those patients who remain less than clear with respect to their
ICP.
The use of TXA or Amicar at the time of induction (before surgery
has started) in addition to keeping the mean systolic BP between 55–
60 mmHg has been shown to significantly reduce the need for
perioperative transfusion and has allowed our transfusion rates to be
50% in the older kids. Unpublished data from our institution
comparing both agents have demonstrated equal efficacy between
the two agents.
For the patient with cerebral ventriculomegaly or suspected
hydrocephalus, a shunt or CSF diversion should be reserved only for
the patient with clear-cut hydrocephalus (over time); with a
progressive Chiari malformation (can also be seen with
pansynostosis) or syringomyelia as potential clues.
The older patient often has many areas of calvarial deficiencies after
any frontal advancement or bilateral parietal expansion. It is best to
ensure that the frontal and other areas of cosmetic priority have
adequate bony reconstruction in these regions. Additional bone may
be harvested by using split-calvarial cranioplasty as well as using
particulate bony matrix harvested from the inner table using a
Hudson brace. This technique affords a considerable amount of graft
material which when mixed with fibrin glue (Tissel) will fill in many
left over defects and provides a solid fusion construct the majority of
the time.
It doesn’t take a significant increase in calvarial volume to markedly
reduce the patient’s ICP and the extent of volumetric expansion will
be dictated by the patient’s age. Patients approaching 5–6 years of
age are unlikely (but still seen on rare occasions) to need additional
volumetric expansion for purposes of intracranial pressure, whereas
the younger patients (2–4 years) will need to be followed closely,
especially in the setting of multi-suture synostosis.

Subgaleal drains are universally used with a catheter on each side of
the head (in case one falls out) and have been seen to reduce postop
pain and swelling and decrease the length of stay.
In the event of a challenging effort to reapproximate bicoronal skin
flaps after a significant frontal advancement, one may score the galea
on the inner surface of the flap, being careful not to extend this too
close to the surface or to compromise the dermal vascular layer of
the flap. This will offer greater relaxation of the flap and potentially
minimize any later healing problems.
