35 1 Aetiology
The impaired growth capacity of the cranial vault due to
craniosynostosis—especially in the event of multiple fused cranial
sutures—results in a situation termed “cephalo-cranial disproportion”
which is characterized by insufficient intracranial volume increment for
the developing brain and subsequently chronic elevation in intracranial
pressure (ICP) [1, 2]. In the case of insufficient volume development of
the posterior fossa, this disproportion may further adversely impact the
CSF circulation and contribute to a developing hydrocephalus. Tonsillar
herniation (Chiari malformation) is a further known manifestation of
the cephalo-cranial disproportion affecting the posterior part of the
cranial vault and the posterior fossa. In one large series about 8% of the

children with craniosynostosis (29/329) presented with Chiari
Malformation. The incidence was highest for children with
multiple/syndromic craniosynostosis with 35% (14/40) and with
isolated lambdoid synostosis (56%, 6/9). The average area of the
foramen magnum has been demonstrated to be smaller in children
affected by syndromic craniosynostosis and a correlation between the
area of the foramen and the size of the ventricular system has be shown
by Rijken et al. [3]. In accordance with Coll et al., a correlation between
smaller size of the foramen magnum and hydrocephalus as well as an
association of hydrocephalus and tonsillar herniation was observed [4].
Several factors contribute to a disturbed circulation of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) resulting in a hydrocephalic condition [5]. In
craniosynostosis, relevant factors are restricted skull growth with
possible secondary displacement of intracranial structures and
impaired venous outflow, which may result in CSF resorption
impairment as a possible contributing factor for CSF circulation
disturbance.
Anatomical displacement will more often be seen in multiple
synostosis conditions most likely due to decreased volume of the
posterior fossa. This may lead to major CSF pathway occlusion at
locations such as the Sylvian aqueduct or the outlets of the fourth
ventricle. Secondary tonsillar herniations may obstruct the foramen
magnum, which might reduce the transmission of CSF pulsation
between the intracranial and the spinal compartment in which the dura
is imbedded in epidural fat tissue. This spinal dural elasticity normally
enables to balance the pulsatile ICP wave which is impaired in
condition of tonsilar herniation. In addition, impaired absorption
capacity of the CSF back into the venous system secondary to
intracranial venous hypertension is caused by altered skull base growth
and compression of venous sinuses within the posterior fossa—both
leading to increased venous outflow resistance [6, 7]. Possible
obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) secondary to impaired midfacial growth
or brainstem compression causing CO2 retention and thereby increased
intracranial blood volume has been furthermore discussed as a
contributing factor for ICP elevation [8–10] (Fig. 35.1).

Fig. 35.1 The ventricular system as well as the external CSF spaces may show disbalance in
circulation more often in the context of multiple craniosynostosis affecting the posterior fossa
growth. Possible contributing factors for CSF circulation disturbances may be major CSF
pathway obstruction at the outlets of the fourth ventricle or the foramen magnum, venous
outflow disturbances, and CO2 retention due to sleep apnea or comorbidities contributing to
hydrocephalus development

35 2 Epidemiology
The prevalence of hydrocephalus in children with craniosynostosis
depends on the underlying aetiology of craniosynostosis. In nonsyndromic children with single suture craniosynostosis, the prevalence
is reported to be rare—between 0.28 and 1.8% (4/1447—5/275) [11,
12]. Some of the reported children in those series were furthermore
affected by concurring comorbidities known to predispose
hydrocephalus (e.g. previous haemorrhage, myelomeningocele). Thus,
primary CSF circulation disturbances due to single suture synostosis
alone may even be less frequent. On the contrary, the incidence of
hydrocephalus in children with multiple or syndromic craniosynostosis
is reported to be significantly higher and will certainly dependent also

on the underlying genetic precondition. Although inconsistently
discussed in the literature, several authors differentiate between
hydrocephalus requiring surgical treatment and non-progressive
ventriculo- or subarachnomegaly (Fig. 35.1).
The prospectively collected data of the Hydrocephalus Clinical
Research Network confirm the disparity of the incidence of
hydrocephalus between non-syndromic and syndromic children—in
this cohort of children who were treated for hydrocephalus (n = 6152),
only 42 children were affected by craniosynostosis. Of those, 79%
(33/42) presented with multiple craniosynostosis and the remaining
21% (9/42) with single-suture craniosynostosis (3 with unilateral
coronal, 3 with sagittal, and 2 with lambdoid suture craniosynostosis).
For the majority of children (90%, 38/42), an underlying craniofacial
syndrome was identified (the largest share being Crouzon Syndrome in
42% (16/38)) [13].
For children with Crouzon syndrome, the rates of hydrocephalus are
reported to be 15.9% (10/63) and of ventriculomegaly to be 35%
according to Collmann et al. [11], 16.6.% for hydrocephalus and 33.3%
for ventriculomegaly according to Noetzel et al. [14], and 29% (4/14)
for hydrocephalus according to Coll et al. [4]. For children with Pfeiffer
Syndrome, even higher rates are reported—60% (9/15) with
hydrocephalus and further 15% (3/15) with ventriculomegaly
according to Collmann et al., 40% (2/5) according to Noetzel et al., and
33% (2/6) according to Coll et al. On the contrary, the rates of
hydrocephalus are low in children with Apert Syndrome—between 0
and 8.3%. Nevertheless, the rate of ventriculomegaly without the
necessity for a surgical intervention is reported to be substantial at 43–
100% [4, 11, 14, 15].
For children with a combination of bilateral lambdoid and sagittal
suture synostosis (“Mercedes-Benz-Pattern”), a 5.1% rate of
concomitant hydrocephalus and 28.8.% rate of ventriculomegaly have
been reported [16].
For other craniofacial syndromes, the incidence of hydrocephalus
seems to be negligible—none of the children affected by MuenkeSyndrome (n = 24) of Saethre-Chotzen-Syndrome (n = 37)
demonstrated features of hydrocephalus [11].

35 3 Diagnostics
For children with syndromic craniosynostosis, a correlation between
occipito-frontal head circumference and intracranial volume has been
documented and underlines the value of repetitive head circumference
measurements to detect insufficient growth [17]. In infants, the open
fontanelle allows an indirect but easy assessment of the ICP and by
means of transfontanellar ultrasound, the imaging and repetitive
monitoring of the dimensions of the ventricular system and Doppler
sonography for “resistance index” evaluation, which may indicate an
increased ICP via decreased end-diastolic flow.
However, the higher quality imaging modes for the evaluation of the
intracranial compartment are CT and MRI. Although both methods
allow assessment of the dimensions of the ventricular system, the
repetitive utilization of CT should be deferred in favour of MRI because
of the documented increased life-time risk for smaller children to
develop a malignancy after exposure to ionizing radiation [18, 19].
Furthermore, the MRI offers the better soft-tissue differentiation and
the possibility of dynamic CSF circulation studies including T2sequences in three dimensions, venous MR angiography and sagittal
midline CISS sequence for evaluation of the cisternal and
intraventricular membranes and superior evaluation of a possible
tonsillar herniation and thus may be considered as diagnostic measure
of choice [20].

35 4 Treatment Options
(a) Craniofacial Treatment Options
Children with craniosynostosis and concomitant
hydrocephalus constitute a difficult and complex situation,
because utilized treatment steps may favourably or adversely
impact various aspects of the primary pathology. Clinical outcome
and consecutive treatment.
As a basic rule, both aetiology and pathophysiology of the
existent hydrocephalus as direct result of intracranial volume
reduction should be taken into consideration to establish the
appropriate order of treatment steps. If ever possible, treatment

should attempt to reverse the underlying aetiology of
hydrocephalus. In this regard, one of the first questions to answer
is whether the development of the intracranial volume so far has
been and will presumably remain sufficient. In a child with
obvious cephalo-cranial disproportion with cranial restriction and
hydrocephalus, an expansive cranioplasty to enlarge the
intracranial volume should be performed at first step if clinically
feasible. That will always be preferable to any CSF diverting
measures, since a shunt system constitutes a risk of overdrainage
and may even further diminish calvarial growth or compromise
previous expansion results.
Posterior calvarial expansion may play a relevant role to
influence CSF circulation since it seems to more effectively
increase intracranial volume (by 35%) than anterior calvarial
vault expansion—as demonstrated for three simulated
translational and similar distances of advancement [21].
Furthermore, posterior cranial vault expansion addresses the part
of the calvarium in anatomical relation to the disturbed CSF
circulation such as the foramen magnum, tonsillar herniation,
draining veins and sinuses, and the compressed fourth ventricle.
Therefore, the suggested order of cranial vault enlargement in
cephalo-cranial disproportion with secondary signs of increased
ICP is a posterior vault cranioplasty at the age of 3–6 months
followed by later anterior advancement (e.g. by fronto-orbital
advancement) at 10–12 months [22, 23].
Several techniques of posterior cranial vault remodeling
(PCVR) have been published, allowing increase of the intracranial
volume between 13 and 29% [24–27]. As an advantage, a PCVR
procedure allows the treatment of a Chiari Malformation—a
possible contributing factor for hydrocephalus—by a suboccipital
craniectomy (and laminectomy C1, if necessary) [28, 29]. One
published series compared the influence of the applied
cranioplasty technique: regarding the rate of hydrocephalus, no
difference was demonstrated between posterior vault distraction
osteogenesis (PVDO, n = 49) without however involving the
foramen magnum and calvarial vault remodeling (CVR, n = 23).
The rate of developing tonsillar herniation was significantly lower

after PVOD compared to CVR, possibly due to the larger achievable
expansion distance after PVDO [30]. In a series of 41 patients
receiving posterior cranial vault expansion, five hydrocephalus
surgeries were done before the expansion surgery including four
VP shunt implantation. During mean follow-up of 18 months (3–
72), none of the patients needed any VP shunt implantation while
only 2 had additional ETV surgeries [27] (Fig. 35.2).

Fig. 35.2 9.5 year old boy with pansynsotosis who received early total calvarial vault
remodeling externally with secondary pansynositosis, brachycephaly, and severe
headaches (a, b). Parieto-occipital expansion was performed, which enhanced the
posterior cranial vault curvature (c). In follow-up MRI, the relief of posterior fossa and
establishment of CSF flow anterior to the tonsils can be appreciated (d), which resolved
the headaches

The recommendation to consider and perform a cranial vault
expansion prior to the insertion of a CSF diverting shunt is based

on the obvious risk that a CSF diversion may further adversely
affect cranial growth and may aggravate cephalo-cranial
disproportion. In a series by Nilsson et al., significantly smaller
head circumferences were observed in children (age 2–3 years)
who underwent a shunt insertion during their first year of life
compared to children without a shunt. Furthermore, chronic
shunt-induced overdrainage has been reported to induce
secondary craniosynostosis. Especially in the setting of tonsillar
herniation and pre-existing cephalo-cranial disproportion, a shunt
insertion may have deleterious effects [31–33].
(b) CSF Diverting Treatment Options
In addition to the discussed specific cranial expansion
treatment options, all possible established CSF diverting
treatment options remain available for children affected by
craniosynostosis and concomitant hydrocephalus if necessary.
Depending on the underlying pathophysiology, the primary
treatment option may be the endoscopic third ventriculocisternostomy (ETV) to establishing an alternative intracranial
CSF pathway in the setting of a non-communicating
hydrocephalus. Extracranial CSF diverting shunt implantation
remains appropriate for communicating hydrocephalus if
alternative options are not available.
For both treatment options for hydrocephalus, a substantial
amount of data in children without craniosynostosis have been
published. The reported revision-free survival after ETV in a
pediatric cohort of 336 children with hydrocephalus of all causes
(median age of 6.9 years, IQR 1.7–12.6 years) was 64.8%, 61.7%,
and 57.8% after respective 6 months, 1 year, and 2 years [34].
After shunt implantation in a large cohort of 1036 children (mean
age of 131 228 weeks, among them 56% less than 6 months
old), a revision rate of 33% and an infection rate of 7.6% after a
median follow-up of 264 days were documented [35]. The
treatment of hydrocephalus in the context of craniosynostosis was
evaluated by data of the prospective registry of the Hydrocephalus
Clinical Research Network [13]. The median age of the 42 treated
children was 0.6 years (IQR 0.3–1.7 years) at the time of the first
craniosynostosis surgery and 1.2 years (IQR 0.5–2.5 years) at the

first hydrocephalus surgery—thereby underlining the suggested
order of antecedent craniosynostosis intervention before
hydrocephalus surgery. Only 28% of the treated children
underwent hydrocephalus treatment prior to craniosynostosis
intervention. Hydrocephalus treatment was performed via shunt
insertion in 2/3 of the patients (28/42); the remaining third
underwent endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV). After
12 months, in total 34% of the children (14/42) required revision
surgery—8 (28.6%) after shunt insertion and 6 (42.9%) after ETV.
After a follow-up of 5.2 years (range 0.1–9.7 years), in total 50% of
the patients (21/42) required an operative revision—there was
no significant difference between the success rate of shunt
insertion and ETV which supports the author’s statement that
ETV must be considered as a relevant alternative to shunting in
this group of patients. This is in accordance with prior reports of
success rates of ETV of 63.6% (7/11) children in children with
craniofacial syndromes [36] (Fig. 35.3).

Fig. 35.3 1 year 4 months old patient with Crouzon syndrome showing ventricular
enlargement and Chiari malformation while cranial expansion surgeries were already
accomplished (a, b). An endoscopic third ventriculostomy was performed in condition of
relative ventricular enlargement. MRI at 2 years follow-up (age: 3 year 4 months)
showed decreased ventricular size and a patent ETV stoma due to stabilized CSF
circulation disturbances (c, d)

The choice of ETV over extracranial CSF diversion is especially
supported by the typical signs of an existing pressure gradient
between the internal CSF spaces and the external CSF spaces—
including outward bulging membranes of the third ventricle such
as the floor of the third ventricle, the lamina terminalis, and the

pineal recess on sagittal midline MRI. In the absence of those signs
and if cranial vault expansion is not necessary because of
sufficient intracranial overall volume, extracranial CSF diversion
may become unavoidable. In these situations, the shunt system
and its valve should be chosen with the possibility to avoid
overdrainage at all measures. A recent review has more precisely
defined the possible signs of CSF overdrainage such as postural
dependent headache, vomiting and mood change/irritability,
sunken fontanelle (if present), decreasing head circumference,
and/or radiological signs as slim ventricles/complete ventricular
collapse, subdural hygroma/haematoma, and overriding or fused
cranial sutures [37]. In order to avoid these conditions, we
strongly recommend the use of any overdrainage protecting units
such as anti-gravitational units or any alternative effectively
counteracting the hydrostatic effect in standing position. In
addition, the adjustability of the valve resistance furthermore will
allow patient-specific adaptation of valve drainage without the
need for surgical shunt revision in a situation of overdrainage. The
resistance in the entire valve system should be adjusted
principally at a higher level compared to other hydrocephalus
entities since the expected amount of required CSF diversion will
be relatively low.
In infants with adjustable valves implanted within the first
year of life, the option to adapt the setting of the valve was utilized
in 31% and 42% of the children after 1 and 2 years and in a
majority of 61% of the children by the time of the latest follow-up
[38]. Concordantly, in older children (n = 53, mean age of
7.3 years), 35.8% underwent adaptation of valve settings after
shunt insertion within a mean observation period of 15.2 month
[39] which could be supported in subsequent reports with the
same shunt system [40, 41]. Alternatively to adjustable valves
with anti-siphoning units, flow-regulated valves demonstrated
low primary overdrainage situations [42] (Fig. 35.4). Regarding
the entry point of the ventricular catheter—the parietal entry
offers the advantage that it might interfere less with later frontofacial advancements and the necessary internal or external
distraction devices. However, in the author’s experience with

exclusively frontally inserted ventricular catheters, no significant
problems secondary to catheter location have been encountered.
The site of the catheter entry is usually not incorporated in the
advanced part of the forehead and meticulous dissection as well
as anti-infective measures ensures that secondary damage or
infection of the shunt system is avoided.

Fig. 35.4 One year old girl with Crouzon syndrome, received fronto-orbital
advancement at an external center including VP shunt insertion (Codman hakim valve
plus shunt assistant (SA) at 3/ 20 = 3/23 cmH2O with overdrainage showing the SA not
in strict vertical position (a–c)). A craniocervical decompression and shunt valve
exchange with higher valve resistance (proV and proGAV: 20 10/ 30 = 30/60 cmH2O)
were performed followed by occipital expansion and later cranio cervical
decompression establishing a better harmony in head shape and ventricular appearance

It remains essential that in any child after treatment of
hydrocephalus, close clinical and radiological follow-up with 3D
photography, head circumference measures, and serial MRIs are
mandatory to observe long-term effects to the ventricular system
and the related anatomical structures.

Bullet Points
Different pathophysiological mechanisms contribute to disturbed
CSF circulation in craniosynostosis patients such as venous outflow
impairment and major pathway obstruction, especially in volumedeficient posterior fossa anatomy mainly in children with multiple
suture craniosynostosis.
Avoid primary extracranial CSF diversion, if ever possible and
clinically acceptable. Consider cranial expansion and/or foramen
magnum decompression prior to any extracranial CSF diversion.
Posterior cranial vault remodeling possibly has a more advantageous
effects on disturbed CSF circulation than anterior advancement. The
staged combination of both will effectively increase the intracranial
volume with beneficial effects on CSF circulation and venous outflow.
Consider ETV as appropriate first choice before any extracranial CSF
diverting shunt especially in enlarged ventricles and posterior fossa
crowding.
If shunt implantation becomes unavoidable, consider the selection of
relative high differential pressure settings in combination with
counteracting the hydrostatic effect in upright position by the use of
antihydrostatic units (gravitational/anti-siphoning units) to reduce
the risk of overdrainage.
Consider the use of adjustable valves to establish the option to alter
valve resistance if clinical or radiographic signs of overdrainage are
observed during follow-up.
Maintain close clinical follow-up to assure sufficient shunt function
and to identify possible overdrainage at early stages.

36 Management of Hydrocephalus in
Patients with Craniosynostosis
Eduardo Jucá1 and Carolina Carmona Pinheiro Machado1
(1) University of Fortaleza, Fortaleza, Brazil

Keywords Craniosynostosis – Hydrocephalus – Neuroendoscopy –
Endoscopic third-ventriculostomy

36 1 Contextuali ation and Epidemiology
Interest in the challenges posed by the association between
craniostenosis and hydrocephalus dates back to the 1970s and 1980s,
coinciding with a period of exponential progress in the understanding
and development of operative techniques for the management of
craniostenosis. In fact, as they represent two of the most important
diseases faced by pediatric neurosurgeons and both have the risk of
intracranial hypertension leading to neurodevelopmental delay and
cognitive impairment, the two entities entail particularities and specific
challenges in their treatment when combined [1, 2].
More specifically, while the incidence of hydrocephalus seems to be
fortuitous and anecdotal in nonsyndromic craniostenosis involving
early closure of one or more cranial sutures, most cases of association
affect children with syndromic craniostenosis in all reported series.
Back in 1985, in a study that actively researched hydrocephalus and
cognitive impairment in cases of craniostenosis, Noetzel et al. found no
cases of hydrocephalus in 27 cases of nonsyndromic craniostenosis, but
identified 5 occurrences in 23 cases of syndromic craniostenosis,
including cases of Crouzon syndrome, Pfeiffer syndrome, and cloverleaf
deformity [2].

Golabi et al. also reported in 1987 a series of 10 patients with
hydrocephalus in a total of 250 patients treated for craniostenosis in 5
consecutive years. Of these, four had Pfeiffer’s syndrome, three had
Crouzon’s syndrome, two had syndromic features but without a defined
syndrome, and only one patient had a single suture craniostenosis, a
case of scaphocephaly due to sagittal suture closure. The origin of
hydrocephalus in the latter case was associated with prematurity;
therefore, there was no causal association between the two entities [1].
In 2010, Di Rocco et al. described a series of 2194 cases conducted
at the craniofacial surgery unit of the Necker Hospital in Paris between
1995 and 2008, with the identification of 293 patients with syndromic
craniosynostosis and 46 of these cases (15.69%) with progressive
hydrocephalus in need of surgical treatment [3].
Overall, the incidence of hydrocephalus was estimated at 12.1% of
cases of syndromic craniostenosis and 0.3% of cases of isolated
craniostenosis by Cinalli et al. in a study in 1998. In this large survey
involving 1727 patients, the authors advanced in order to suggest
which syndromes present a higher risk of developing hydrocephalus
among affected patients. According to the report, patients with
cloverleaf deformity have hydrocephalus as a typical feature, whereas
patients with Crouzon syndrome have a higher risk of hydrocephalus
than patients with other syndromes, and patients with Appert
syndrome have overall increased ventricular dimensions, but without
progressive character and with less need for surgical treatment [4].
All this background in the literature and the questions still to be
answered regarding the best way to manage cases of association
between craniostenosis and hydrocephalus demonstrate the need for
additional studies that elucidate the contribution of each pathological
entity in the clinical picture of affected children, so that the better
treatment for controlling intracranial hypertension and preserving the
cognitive development potential is achieved.

36 2 Pathophysiology
The pathophysiological mechanisms that lead a patient with
craniostenosis to develop progressive hydrocephalus are unclear.
Understanding these factors is very important for therapeutic planning.

There are some clues to the marked predominance in cases of
syndromic craniostenosis and also to the greater risk in certain
syndromes over others. Although the literature on the subject is not
very extensive, several hypotheses have already been raised to explain
the development of hydrocephalus in patients with craniostenosis.
Certainly, a distortion of the anatomy manifested in different ways
in a syndromic cases leads to obstruction of the cerebrospinal fluid
flow. In this context, a tight posterior fossa that causes herniation of the
cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum with obliteration of the
fourth ventricle outflow ways, compression of the aqueduct of Sylvius,
and venous return difficulties based mainly on the narrowing of the
jugular foramina seem to play a key role [3].
Among these structural alterations, impaction or even herniation of
the cerebellar tonsils in the foramen magnum seems to be of special
importance, obliterating the outflow ways of the fourth ventricle
through the foramina of Luschka and Magendie. In fact, Chiari type I
alteration is present in most cases of syndromic craniostenoses (Fig.
36.1). An additional argument in favor of this pathophysiological
mechanism in the development of hydrocephalus is the fact that the
surgical treatment of space restriction in the posterior fossa, either in
the classic way with suboccipital median craniectomy, or with posterior
cranial enlargement through implantation of distractors, is capable, in
many cases, of controlling the progression of ventricular dilation and
avoiding the indication of ventricular shunting. On the other hand,
Chiari type I malformation is present in 90% of children with
hydrocephalus and syndromic craniostenosis, as highlighted by
Frassanito et al. Synergistically, hydrocephalus and Chiari I could be
part of a cyclical mechanism in which one entity could worsen the
evolution of the other: the impaction of the tonsils impairing the flow of
cerebrospinal fluid and hydrocephalus functioning as a downward force
promoting the passage of tonsils through the foramen magnum [5].

Fig. 36.1 Magnetic resonance imaging of a child with Crouzon syndrome showing herniation of
the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum (Chiari I) and supratentorial ventricular
dilatation

Compression of the cerebral aqueduct can also be included in the
general picture of conflict between continent and content in the
posterior fossa, reproducing obstructive hydrocephalus with the
possibility of treatment by endoscopic third ventriculostomy. Although
it is currently difficult to define the exact topography of the obstruction
to cerebrospinal fluid flow, the possibility of improving this topographic
localization in the future may serve as a basis for improving the choice
of therapeutic modality.
In addition to structural abnormalities and anatomical distortions
with mechanical consequences, there is evidence of functional elements
that contribute to the blockade of CSF absorption with consequent
progressive ventricular dilation. Among these factors is the difficult
passage of CSF through hypoplastic subarachnoid spaces in syndromic
craniostenosis and also the difficulty in venous return due to the
alteration of the venous sinuses anatomy and the characteristic

narrowing of the jugular foramina in these patients. Thus, one of the
causal factors for the appearance of hydrocephalus would be the
impairment of the full return of CSF to the venous compartments due to
the slowing of the venous return flow [3, 5].
In practice, all these possibilities may be combined in the genesis of
hydrocephalus related to syndromic craniostenosis. In fact, a possible
common origin for most of these pathophysiological processes would
be the early fusion of the basiooccipital and lambdoid sutures, leading,
at the same time, to the narrowing of the jugular foramina with
overlying venous hypertension and to hypoplasia of the posterior fossa
leading to mechanical constriction of the cerebrospinal fluid flow. An
important argument in favor of this theory is the higher incidence of
hydrocephalus in FGFR-2 gene-related craniostenosis, reaching 88% of
cases in Pfeiffer syndrome. Furthermore, a difference in the osteogenic
action of the FGFR-2 gene in the early fusion of intraoccipital
synchondrosis in Crouzon and Appert syndromes could explain the
higher incidence of hydrocephalus in patients with Crouzon syndrome
[5].
Indeed, in Appert syndrome, it is common to find ventriculomegaly
without evidence of progression or intracranial hypertension that
requires surgical treatment with shunt. This situation can also occur
with other forms of syndromic and even nonsyndromic craniostenosis,
since a child with isolated suture fusion is also subject to factors such as
prematurity or the coexistence of other causes of hydrocephalus such
as aqueductal stenosis.
Another way in which a disturbance of CSF circulation can occur in
patients with craniostenosis, in addition to hydrocephalus, is the
identification of subdural collections, also known as pericerebral
effusions. This topic was addressed by Usami and colleagues in a very
focused study in 2021 with patients diagnosed with scaphocephaly. In
this survey of 63 children, 57% had pericerebral effusions greater than
expected for their age, 57% had ventriculomegaly according to the
Evans index greater than 0.3 criterion, and 46% had both conditions.
The main hypothesis raised for this increased risk of subdural
collections in patients with scaphocephaly was venous hypertension
caused by compression of the superior sagittal sinus by the synostotic
sagittal suture. Supporting this possibility is the fact that most patients

had regression of measurements of both the subdural space and the
ventricular dimensions after surgical correction, which included
sagittal suturectomy in the technique with release of the superior
sagittal sinus from eventual compression. This postulation makes the
surgical indication even stronger in isolated craniostenosis, in addition
to the aesthetic, structural, and control of intracranial hypertension
aspects [6]. Although the aforementioned study focused only on
patients with scaphocephaly, this situation can potentially be
reproduced with other types of nonsyndromic craniostenosis involving
the superior sagittal sinus, such as brachycephaly or trigonocephaly, as
shown in Fig. 36.2.

Fig. 36.2 Computed tomography scan of the skull of a 3-month-old child showing
trigonocephaly and frontal pericerebral effusion

Finally, a specific situation of combined hydrocephalus and
craniosynostosis that may require the attention of the pediatric
neurosurgeon is craniosynostosis secondary to treatment of
hydrocephalus with a ventricular shunt. In this case, the

pathophysiological sequence is inverted and the drainage of the
cerebrospinal fluid for the treatment of hydrocephalus is the cause of
the fusion of one or more cranial sutures. The mechanism underlying
this phenomenon would be a decrease in intracranial pressure leading
to loss of stimulus for skull expansion, which is based on osteogenic
proliferation mainly on the cranial sutures [7, 8].
In a 2021 study, Bryant and colleagues studied with computed
tomography (CT) and 3D reconstruction a population of 125 children
treated for hydrocephalus with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt. Almost
half of the patients presented fusion of one or more sutures in exams
performed on average 26 months after shunt surgery. The influence of
these image findings on cranial growth and the development of
intracranial hypertension, however, was unclear [7].
In fact, it is necessary to identify early cases in which a secondary
craniosynostosis may represent only an image finding and situations in
which there is cranial deformity or worsening intracranial
hypertension as consequences. Golinko et al. described a series of 13
patients with ventricular shunt-induced craniostenosis in which
surgical skull remodeling was performed. The criteria adopted for the
indication of cranial remodeling in this series were the existence of
cranial deformity, clinical or radiological evidence of intracranial
hypertension, evidence of suture fusion in image studies, and absence
of shunt malfunction signs [8].
Knowledge about all these pathophysiological variables is very
important for adequate guidance during patient assessment and for
adequate therapeutic decision-making. The management options in the
face of the association between hydrocephalus and craniosynostosis
can range from ventricular shunt to endoscopic third ventriculostomy,
including or not skull remodeling procedures. Understanding the
mechanisms underlying the clinical picture and the structural changes
should contribute to the best choice for the management of each
individual case.

36 3 Assessment
The assessment, both clinically and by neuroimaging, of cases involving
the association of hydrocephalus and craniostenosis imposes

difficulties related to the manifestations of each entity and the specific
contribution to the clinical presentation of each patient.
In the case of nonsyndromic craniosynostosis involving fusion of
one or more sutures, incidental cases of hydrocephalus can be
identified based on the usual clinical presentation of the disease in
infants, which includes increased head circumference outside the
expected curve for age, fontanelle bulging, and neurodevelopmental
delay. CT or MRI shows increased ventricular dimensions with
occasional indirect signs of intracranial hypertension, such as
ependymal transudation and effacement of sulci and cisterns. Special
attention must be paid to these clinical and radiological signs in cases
of risk factors for hydrocephalus, such as prematurity.
In cases of syndromic craniostenosis, given the considerable
percentage of patients who develop hydrocephalus, it is necessary to
actively seek clinical and radiological manifestations, since one in eight
patients will need surgical treatment for hydrocephalus. Thus, from the
diagnosis of craniostenosis and the related syndrome, it is necessary to
look for clinical manifestations of intracranial hypertension and for
radiological signs of progressive ventricular dilatation. The initial
assessment is performed by means of CT of the skull, and the same
exam used to study the sutures and cranial conformation already allows
the observation of ventricular dimensions and signs of hydrocephalus.
However, the need for more detail and the search for causal factors in
each specific case should lead to obtaining a brain MRI.
In addition to assessing the size of the ventricles and the use of
objective criteria such as the Evans index, it is necessary to observe
other factors on MRI, potentially related to the origin of hydrocephalus:
descent of the tonsils through the foramen magnum, size of the fourth
ventricle, tight appearance of the posterior fossa, compression of the
aqueduct of Sylvius, distortion of the position of the floor of the third
ventricle, and alteration in the anatomy of the venous sinuses [3].
In a complementary way, obtaining a CT angiography, especially
when planning a surgical approach to craniostenosis with anterior or
posterior remodeling and distractions, can help in the planning of
osteotomies in order to respect and preserve venous drainage,
preventing possible damage to the venous network that could cause an
additional increase in intracranial pressure by impairing venous return.

Although all the mentioned clinical manifestations and radiological
findings are important in the global assessment of children with
craniostenosis at risk of developing hydrocephalus, it must be
recognized that the main question to be answered is whether there is
intracranial hypertension that leads to the indication of a specific
treatment for hydrocephalus. Some initiatives have already taken place
to directly assess intracranial pressure in patients with craniostenosis
through the intracranial implantation of specific catheters for this
purpose, both preoperatively and intraoperatively [9, 10]. Thompsom
and colleagues found intracranial hypertension in 28 out of 53 cases of
syndromic craniostenosis, but also in 20 out of 83 cases of
nonsyndromic cases [9]. Although direct measurement is the most
reliable method, this can be invasive and costly, even requiring the child
to be hospitalized for a few days for an adequate study to be carried
out.
To make the estimation of intracranial pressure more practical,
without the need for hospitalization, less invasive methods have been
developed. An assessment technique that has gained prominence is the
measurement of pulse waves by a sensor fitted close to the skull (Fig.
36.3). This method quantitatively evaluates the relationship between
the various components of pulse waves and suggests that there is a loss
of intracranial compliance caused by hypertension when there is an
increase in the P2 component in relation to the P1 component, with a
P2/P1 ratio predominantly above 0.8. The strategy has already proved
to be useful in cases of hydrocephalus not associated with
craniostenosis and could be applied with a view to decision-making in
cases of association between the two diseases [11].

Fig. 36.3 Monitoring screen and sensor used to assess intracranial compliance by measuring
pulse waves and the P1/P2 ratio

All assessment strategies described, including clinical, imaging, or
functional phenomena, must be globally taken into account to support
the choice of the best management in cases of hydrocephalus
associated with craniostenosis. Since there is no repetition of a single
pattern between cases, all information needs to be collected, so that the
best decisions are reached.

36 4 Treatment
Clinical evaluation of active hydrocephalus in the craniostenosis context
is difficult, the patient may present with nonspecific symptoms and the
condition may be masked by the craniostenosis deformity. In addition,
ventricular dilation is often only identified after decompression surgery
[12]. Because of the complexity and multifactorial aspect of the etiology
of hydrocephalus, there is still discussion about which would be the
best treatment choice [5].
Craniosynostosis is treated with combinations of techniques that
involve suturectomy, decompressive craniectomy, and bone remodeling.
The procedure itself can stabilize and improve intracranial pressure
and ventricular dilation by providing space for the brain to expand.
Even so, patients with syndromic craniosynostosis, who have a higher

incidence of progressive hydrocephalus, may develop ventricular
dilatation after surgery, threatening the life of these patients and
requiring immediate resolution [2].
The pathophysiology of hydrocephalus in syndromic craniostenosis
is still under study; however, it is known that jugular stenosis and
posterior fossa constriction are important factors. According to
Frassanito et al., there are three scenarios for the occurrence of
hydrocephalus such as (1) ventricular dilation begins to progressively
worsen before surgery, and then, there is surgical intervention to
reduce intracranial hypertension. (2) Hydrocephalus is only apparent
after decompression surgery as a complication of CSF leakage. (3)
Patients with stable ventricular dilatation and/or nonspecific signs of
intracranial hypertension who improve with decompressive surgery
[5].
The current recommendation is: if there is no accurate and
confirmed diagnosis of active hydrocephalus, surgery to correct
craniostenosis should be chosen as a first step, observing ventricular
development and monitoring intracranial pressure afterwards. If
hydrocephalus is evident prior to decompressive surgery, primary
resolution of hydrocephalus should be chosen, as the patient’s
condition may worsen with increased intracranial pressure after
craniostenosis surgery [13].
Figure 36.4 illustrates the management of a personal case of the
author of this chapter, in which a 14-month-old boy, 29 weeks’
gestation premature, presented with increased head circumference and
ventricular dilatation, while he had a craniofacial deformity compatible
with left anterior plagiocephaly. An option was made for initial
correction of craniostenosis and cranial decompression was sufficient
to contain the progression of hydrocephalus and to stabilize the growth
of the head circumference in the curve (Fig. 36.4).

Fig. 36.4 Preoperative image of a child with anterior plagiocephaly showing significant cranial
asymmetry (a) and ventricular dilatation (b). 3D tomography after surgical correction of
craniostenosis (c). Reversal of disproportionate growth of head circumference after correction
of craniostenosis

Over the past 70 years, the ventriculoperitoneal shunt has been the
method of choice for the treatment of hydrocephalus due to its
effectiveness, cost and clinical benefit. However, the technique has been
questioned due to frequent complications. Device-related morbidity is
higher in syndromic craniosynostosis, and the risks of hemorrhage,

infection, and device dysfunction are some of the related factors. The
ventriculoperitoneal shunt may also impair skull growth by excessively
decreasing pressure from the inside to the outside and may excessively
drain the CSF, causing hypotension and impairing bone remodeling
(secondary synostosis), especially in patients with multiple suture
craniosynostosis. In addition, an increase in epidural dead space may
occur, which increases the risk of infections.
Bonfield, in a 2021 article, points out that 50% of patients with a
shunt for hydrocephalus and craniostenosis need shunt revision,
especially those with syndromic craniosynostosis, because of their
more challenging anatomy, which can lead to infections, dysfunctions,
and failures. The same study reports similarity of results between
ventricular shunt and third ventriculostomy, making the use of the
endoscopic method advantageous [14].
ETV can minimize risks by maintaining intracranial CSF flow and
preventing hypotension, in addition to being effective in cases of
obstructive hydrocephalus due to anatomical variations or Chiari
malformations.
In a 2010 study, DiRocco et al. described a series of 11 cases of
syndromic craniosynostosis with hydrocephalus treated with ETV (Fig.
36.5). All cases presented features such as aqueduct obstruction, tight
posterior fossa, and mechanical conflicts in the cisterna magna and
foramen magnum. The presence of jugular stenosis in nine patients was
not a contraindication for ETV. Four patients needed to receive a
ventriculoperitoneal shunt after ETV failure. In eight patients,
endoscopy was effective with disappearance of symptoms and signs of
intracranial hypertension and reduction of ventricular dimensions.
Among the children with implanted shunts, one had shunt associated
infection and the other had mechanical dysfunction [3].

Fig. 36.5 Preoperative image (a), view of intraoperative anatomy (b, c) and postoperative
image with flow sign through the floor of the third ventricle (d) of a patient with Crouzon
Syndrome and hydrocephalus treated with endoscopic third ventriculostomy. (From di Rocco et
al., 2010, with permission from the authors)

Thus, endoscopic treatment would be preferable in cases with
favorable anatomy. Even when there is a subsequent need for shunt
implantation in some cases, it is possible to spare a considerable part of
patients from the definitive installation of a shunt.
When ventricular shunt cannot be avoided, systems including
adjustable valves and antisiphoning devices should be preferred in
order to reduce the risk of excess CSF drainage. If, during cranial
reconstruction surgery, there is a complication with the development of
active hydrocephalus, an external shunt can be put in place for primary
containment of the problem and subsequent assessment of the need for
a shunt.
Finally, for both nonsyndromic and syndromic craniosynostosis, the
decision-making regarding the primary treatment or not of
hydrocephalus must be carefully planned, individualizing each case
with their particularities and issues such as age, general condition of
the patient, severity of craniosynostosis, and neurological impairment.

37 Postoperative Management and
Long-Term Follow-Up After Surgery for
Craniosynostosis
Elena Kurudza1 and John R. W. Kestle1
(1) Department of Neurosurgery, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT,
USA

John R W Kestle
Email: neuropub@hsc.utah.edu
Keywords Craniosynostosis – Postoperative management – Intensive
care unit – Helmet therapy – Endoscopic-assisted craniectomy – Cranial
vault remodeling – Distraction osteogenesis – Spring-assisted
cranioplasty – Long-term follow-up

37 1 Introduction
The postoperative management of children after craniosynostosis
surgeries depends predominantly on the surgical technique used. This
chapter will discuss general early and late postoperative management,
as well as specific variations in management associated with each
surgical technique.

37 2 Early Postoperative Management
Regardless of the surgical technique, the immediate postoperative
management should be geared towards early identification of potential
immediate postoperative complications. Typically, this should include

monitoring of neurologic status, hemodynamics, feeding, and pain
control. Although the following complications are rare, a high clinical
suspicion should always be maintained for hematoma, seizure, and
cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak in the immediate postoperative setting
[1]. A patient’s length of stay, level of care, need for blood transfusion,
and drain management, among other factors, depend on surgical
technique and will be discussed further below.

37 3 Technique-Specific Postoperative
Management
37 3 1 Endoscopic-Assisted Craniectomy
37.3.1.1 ength of Stay and e el of Care
Children treated with endoscopic-assisted craniectomy usually do not
have syndromes or significant systemic illness. Their postoperative care
is therefore less complicated, and most do not require admission to an
intensive care unit (ICU). Length of stay is typically shorter in
endoscopic-assisted craniectomies when compared with cranial vault
remodeling. Centers have reported a mean length of stay of 1–2 days
and the majority of patients were managed on the surgical ward
postoperatively [2–4]. For example, in a retrospective study of 225
patients by Dalle Ore et al. [5], the median length of stay for
endoscopic-assisted craniectomy was 1 day, with 216 (96%) patients
admitted directly to the surgical ward postoperatively. Of the 8 patients
that were admitted to the ICU postoperatively, 7 had preexisting
medical conditions that the team had identified preoperatively as
necessitating a planned ICU admission.

37.3.1.2 Special Postoperati e Considerations
The main considerations in the postoperative setting for endoscopicassisted craniectomy include monitoring for blood loss, pain control,
and adequate oral intake. As noted above, most patients are able to
meet discharge criteria within 1–2 days postoperatively. Typically,
subgaleal drain placement is not necessary; however, postoperative day
1 hemoglobin and hematocrit levels are routinely checked. Although
transfusion threshold varies, multiple studies have reported

significantly lower rates of transfusion after endoscopic-assisted
craniectomy, ranging from 6.4 to 26% [2, 4, 6], when compared with
cranial vault remodeling.
Pain management varies depending on which suture has been
treated. Children who undergo endoscopic-assisted craniectomy on the
sagittal suture usually experience more discomfort than those whose
treatment addresses the metopic or coronal sutures, and they often
require oral or intravenous (IV) narcotics overnight. Most of them feel
much better the next day and are comfortable on over-the-counter oral
pain medications such as acetaminophen. Patients are usually able to
tolerate oral intake within a few hours of surgery. Overall, discharge
readiness is determined by postoperative hemoglobin and hematocrit
levels, pain control on oral medications, and ability to tolerate oral
intake. Imaging is not routinely obtained for these patients, but specific
instances will be discussed further below.

37 3 2 Cranial Vault Remodeling
37.3.2.1 ength of Stay and e el of Care
Compared with endoscopic approaches, open cranial vault approaches
are associated with a longer hospital stay, with reported averages of
approximately 4 days [2, 4]. Although practice varies by institution, in a
multicenter study, 24 out of 29 institutions routinely admitted patients
undergoing open cranial vault procedures to the ICU, with a median
length of ICU stay of 2 days [4]. Despite these findings, there is recent
literature that demonstrates that routine ICU admission may not be
necessary in the majority of cases [7].

37.3.2.2 Special Postoperati e Considerations
As with endoscopic approaches, the postoperative management for
open cranial vault surgeries involves monitoring neurologic status,
need for postoperative transfusion, and pain control; however, in
addition to the aforementioned discharge readiness requirements,
special considerations for open cranial vault surgeries include drain
management, postoperative antibiotics, postoperative imaging, and
hemodynamic monitoring.
Open cranial vault surgeries are associated with a higher rate of
blood transfusion when compared with endoscopic approaches, with

reported rates of intraoperative transfusion in 81% of cases and
postoperative transfusion in 25.1% of cases, according to one
multicenter study [4]. In addition, 16% of patients received coagulation
blood products (defined as platelets, fresh frozen plasma, or
cryoprecipitate) [4]. Other studies report an even higher frequency of
postoperative blood transfusion [2].
When it comes to pain control, multimodal analgesia remains the
mainstay; however, in contrast to endoscopic approaches where
patients’ pain is routinely controlled on oral medications, open cranial
vault surgeries are associated with more frequent use of IV analgesics,
including IV acetaminophen and IV opioids [8, 9]. In a recent review,
Brown et al. [8] proposed an increasing role for dexmedetomidine to
minimize IV opioid use.
Unique postoperative considerations for open cranial vault
surgeries include drain management, antibiotic use, hemodynamic
monitoring, and postoperative imaging. Again, while practice varies per
institution, it is common practice at our institution to leave a subgaleal
drain in place postoperatively. In a survey of 19 American craniofacial
teams, 63% reported using a drain [9]. The timing of removal as well as
indications for removal are not well established in the literature, but in
our practice, drains are commonly in place for 2 to 3 nights unless
drainage is minimal before that. In the same survey, 75% of teams
reported routine use of arterial lines for postoperative hemodynamic
monitoring in the ICU setting and 75% reported using prophylactic
antibiotics postoperatively [9]. Finally, there is additional variation
between institutions regarding postoperative imaging. Shah et al. [2]
reported that nearly all patients that underwent open cranial vaults in
their prospective study had a computed tomography (CT) scan before
discharge, but Binning et al. [10] reported no significant association
with postoperative events, including seizures, prolonged ICU stay, or
reoperation in patients without shunts who underwent CT, although
there was an increased rate of identifying shunt malfunction in patients
with shunts. Thus, at our institution, we only obtain CTs as clinically
indicated.
Discharge readiness is determined by stable hemoglobin and
hematocrit levels, ability to tolerate oral intake, and pain controlled on
oral medications. Discharge typically requires at least twice the number

of hospital days on average to meet this in comparison with endoscopic
surgeries. At our institution, patients usually spend 3 to 4 nights in the
hospital before discharge.

37 3 3 Distraction Osteogenesis
37.3.3.1 ength of Stay and e el of Care
Overall, standard distraction osteogenesis is considered a less invasive
option compared with cranial vault reconstruction and is thought to be
associated with shorter operating times and less blood loss when
compared with cranial vault remodeling, although this difference was
not statistically significant in a systematic review including 181 cases
[11]. Additionally, the use of distraction osteogenesis rather than
cranial vault remodeling does not translate to a significant difference in
postoperative management, as the two procedures have similar
transfusion rates, postoperative ICU length of stay, and overall hospital
length of stay [11–13]. Additionally, like patients who undergo cranial
vault remodeling, most patients who undergo distraction osteogenesis
require IV medication for pain management.

37.3.3.2 Special Postoperati e Considerations
Unique considerations in the postoperative setting for distraction
osteogenesis include the importance of caregiver education in regard to
operating the distractor. Distractors are also associated with higher
rates of dural tears intraoperatively [12, 14]. As such, special attention
should be paid to early detection of CSF leak in the postoperative
setting. Distractors are also associated with higher rates of infection,
wound dehiscence, and device failure, so there should be routine
monitoring in place for these complications [14]. At follow-up, it is also
common practice for the patient to undergo routine three-dimensional
CT imaging as often as every 1–3 weeks to monitor progress after
activation [15]. Finally, it is important to consider that unlike
endoscopic strip craniectomies and cranial vault reconstructions,
distractor osteogenesis requires the patient to return for a second
surgery for removal.

37 3 4 Spring-Assisted Cranioplasty

37.3.4.1

ength of Stay and e el of Care

Breakey et al. [16] performed a retrospective review of 200 cases at
their institution and found that the median length of hospital stay for
spring-assisted cranioplasty was three nights; however, there remains
variability among institutions regarding the level of postoperative care
for patients undergoing spring-assisted cranioplasty. As with open
vault surgeries, most patients are admitted to the ICU postoperatively,
but in a single-center retrospective study, the average length of stay in
the ICU was 30.9 h, which is shorter than that of patients who have
been treated with open cranial vault procedures [17]. In addition,
Malmqvist et al. [18] performed a small observational study during
which they used a simplified protocol for postoperative pain
management. They found that there was no significant difference in the
number of patients with FLACC (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability)
pain scores 4 with intermittent injections of morphine and clonidine
rather than a morphine infusion [18]. This made it possible for their
patients to avoid an ICU admission, which many centers are starting to
avoid.

37.3.4.2 Special Postoperati e Considerations
Monitoring hemoglobin and hematocrit levels is crucial because
transfusion is common in the postoperative setting in spring-assisted
craniectomy [17]. In their study, Breakley et al. [16] found that the most
common complications were related to infection, so special attention
should be paid to wound healing at follow-up. Finally, as with
distractors, this technique requires that the patient return for a second
operation for removal, usually between 4 and 6 months later.

37 3 5 Imaging
There are undefined postoperative imaging protocols for
craniosynostosis surgery, and practice varies widely by institution. In a
retrospective study of 1150 patients who underwent cranial vault
reconstructions across the United States, 28.4% of patients underwent
routine postoperative CTs. Of those that underwent a CT, only 7.1%
were found to have an associated intracranial hemorrhage [19]. At our
institution, we do not routinely obtain immediate postoperative
imaging.

During long-term follow-up, the majority of patients who
underwent cranial vault reconstructions underwent a CT within 1 year
of surgery and 95% had undergone a head CT for follow-up within
6 years [19].

37 4 Long-Term Follow-Up
Special consideration for follow-up must occur in the cases of helmet
therapy associated with endoscopic-assisted craniectomy as well as
spring-assisted craniectomy. In the case of endoscopic-assisted
craniectomies, most patients are fitted for a helmet within 4–5 days
postoperatively and begin wearing the helmet about 2 weeks
postoperatively. They are then followed by the orthotist every 2–
3 weeks over the first 3–6 months to monitor growth and to have
helmet adjustments. The surgical team also sees them when they first
get the helmet (about 2 weeks postoperatively), then 3, 6, 9, and
12 months after surgery, and then yearly to 5 years of age. It has been
demonstrated that peak cephalic index is reached at 7–9 months.
Prolonged helmet therapy beyond this did not demonstrate any clear
benefit [20, 21], but longer follow-up is recommended to monitor head
growth, development, and the rare occurrence of symptoms of raised
intracranial pressure.
Distractors typically are used beginning 3–5 days postoperatively
and are turned one to two times daily for 2–3 weeks. Caregivers are
instructed on how to operate the device before discharge, and patients
are seen in the clinic with skull X-rays each week. Patients typically
return for a second surgery at 3 months for removal of the distractors.
For patients who undergo open cranial vault procedures, the time to
first follow-up varies based on institution. At our institution, we
typically schedule an initial postoperative follow-up appointment for 4–
6 weeks after discharge.
At follow-up visits for all procedures, special attention is paid to
head shape, cranial index, signs of high intracranial pressure, and signs
of infection/wound breakdown and bony defects. The mean length for
follow-up is reported to be just over 2 years [21]; however, Ridgway et
al. [21] proposed follow-up should last until at least 6 years of age to
allow for completion of intracranial growth.

In our practice, regardless of the surgical technique, we continue
annual clinical follow-up for a minimum of 5 years. Patients are
evaluated for symptoms, particularly problematic headache, cranial
shape, and or defects. We also monitor patients’ developmental
progress. We do not routinely obtain imaging of patients unless they
present with problematic headache, flattening of the head
circumference percentile, or a new deformity that would suggest
delayed fusion of previously untreated sutures. In those patients, we
would have an ophthalmology evaluation of their fundi, a new threedimensional CT scan, and, in those with a developmental concern, a
formal developmental assessment. Nonsyndromic children who have
no issues after 5 years of follow-up are then seen on an as-needed basis,
but syndromic children and those with issues described above are
monitored and treated as appropriate. In rare situations where the
symptoms are out of proportion to the other findings, we have used
intracranial pressure monitoring to assess these children.
One report describes very long follow-up of isolated sagittal
synostosis patients [22]. At a mean of 26.5 years’ postoperative followup, these patients were as happy with their facial appearance as were
age- and gender-matched controls. Socioeconomic situation and
general health were also similar to those of controls.
As with so many other aspects of pediatric neurosurgery,
craniosynostosis has lifelong implications, and adequate follow-up and
availability of pediatric neurosurgical care are essential.

38 Sagittal Suture Synostosis:
Endoscopic Approach, Key Points for
the Neurosurgeons
Nikita Alexiades1, 2 and John R. W. Kestle1
(1) Department of Neurosurgery, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT,
USA
(2) Department of Neurosurgery, University of Arizona College of
Medicine – Phoenix, Phoenix, AZ, USA

John R W Kestle
Email: neuropub@hsc.utah.edu
Keywords Sagittal synostosis – Endoscopic approach – Strip
craniectomy – Parietal wedge osteotomies – Helmet

38 1 Introduction
Since its introduction by Jimenez and Barone in 1998, the endoscopic
minimally invasive approach to sagittal suture synostosis has gained
wide acceptance [1]. It has proven to be a safe and effective technique
that minimizes operative time, blood loss, transfusion rates, cost, and
the length of hospital stays while resulting in excellent and durable
surgical results compared with open cranial vault remodeling when
done in patients under 6 months of age [2–7]. This approach, called the
strip craniectomy, entails a craniectomy encompassing the entire length
of the fused sagittal suture with or without wedge osteotomies,
followed by the postoperative use of a custom-made cranial molding
helmet. This approach can be broken down into two subtypes, a wide

(4- to 6-cm) strip craniectomy with parietal wedge osteotomies as
described by Jimenez and Barone or a narrow (2-cm) strip craniectomy
without additional osteotomies. The wide approach pioneered by
Jimenez and Barone has a more robust body of the literature
supporting it, but a number of studies have demonstrated similar
outcomes with the narrow strip approach [8–10].
In a recent retrospective multicenter study of outcomes, open
cranial vault remodeling and strip craniectomies showed satisfactory
postoperative cephalic indices, but wide strips were associated with a
greater improvement in the cephalic index (CI) than narrow strips [10].
It is our practice to perform the wide strip approach with small
biparietal wedge osteotomies. Our operative approach is detailed below
and can be modified easily to a narrow strip approach by planning a
smaller craniectomy and forgoing wedge osteotomies.

38 2 Preoperative Planning
It is our practice to perform low-dose computed tomography (CT) scans
with three-dimensional reconstruction on all patients as part of our
preoperative evaluation. Special attention should be paid both to bony
defects within the planned dissection area and the bony anatomy of the
suture overlying the sinus, particularly at its posterior extent. A
preoperative hematocrit value should be obtained to guide decisionmaking regarding the need for intraoperative or postoperative
transfusions. A blood type and cross match should also be performed,
and blood should be readily available even though it is often not needed
with this approach.

38 3 Anesthetic Considerations and
Positioning
Proper positioning coupled with excellent communication between the
surgical team and anesthesiologist are vital to surgical success.
Adequate intravenous access should be obtained prior to positioning as
it is essential in the event of significant blood loss and the need for fluid
resuscitation. We employ the sphinx position to provide sufficient

access to the entirety of the sagittal suture. To facilitate airway
management in this position, nasotracheal intubation is performed and
the tube is secured using a silk purse string suture through the nasal
septum. It is essential to confirm that all bony prominences, including
the chin, are well padded to prevent pressure necrosis and ensure that
the neck remains supple in extension. We use gel bolsters under the
chest along with a beanbag wrapping under and around the neck and
shoulders. The patient is then taped securely in place using silk surgical
tape.

38 4 Operative Procedure
After the patient is appropriately positioned, the skull is palpated to
identify the anterior fontanelle, sagittal suture, and lambda. Two 4- to
5-cm transverse incisions are marked, one anteriorly several
centimeters behind the anterior fontanelle and one posteriorly several
centimeters in front of the lambda, each centered on the midline. Each
incision is infiltrated with an appropriate amount of local anesthetic for
the patient’s weight, and sterile prepping and draping is completed. An
incision is made with a 15 blade through the dermis and into the
subcutaneous fat. A monopolar cautery is used to further dissect
through the galea and then to widely dissect subgaleally in the loose
areolar tissue. It is important to leave the periosteum in place to
minimize unnecessary blood loss from diploic venous channels. Once
the subgaleal dissection is adequate and the incisions are in
communication, the craniectomy is planned. We prefer a rectangular
craniectomy 5 cm in width spanning the anterior fontanelle to the
lambdoid sutures. The monopolar cautery is used to mark planned burr
hole sites 2.5 cm lateral to the midline bilaterally in line with both the
anterior and posterior incisions. We then mark oblique, medially
oriented cuts on either side from the anterior burr holes to the anterior
fontanelle. Posteriorly, our cuts are marked bilaterally from the burr
holes to the lambdoid sutures. Figure 38.1 demonstrates the planned
craniectomy and osteotomies.

Fig. 38.1 Illustration of the planned craniectomy and wedge osteotomies along with the
locations of planning incisions

The craniectomy is begun by making the anterior burr holes using a
7-mm perforator bit, bony edges are waxed, and a Penfield 3 dissector
is used to strip the dura first anteriorly towards the fontanelle and then
gently across the midline. The craniotome is then used to make the
anteriorly directed cuts and then to cross the midline and connect the
two burr holes. At this point, the bone fragment will still adhere via
fibrous tissue to the anterior fontanelle. The bone is hinged forward
under gentle traction and then cut at its attachment using Mayo
scissors. Hemostasis from bone edges is achieved using the monopolar
cautery with cotton patties to protect the dura along with bone wax as
needed. The bipolar cautery is used to gently coagulate any dural
vessels and the fibrous tissue at the anterior fontanelle. Next, in a
similar fashion, burr holes are made at the posterior incision and
stripped with a Penfield 3 dissector, and the craniotome is used to make
the posteriorly directed cuts towards the lambdoid sutures and then a
cut connecting the burr holes. Care must be taken in stripping the dura
in the midline here because it can be densely adherent or overgrown
with bone (Figs. 38.2 and 38.3). If needed, we will perform small
bilateral craniectomies here to allow for direct visualization of the
midline dural dissection. Once all posterior cuts are made, the bone is
reflected and hinged at the lambdoid sutures and cut with Mayo
scissors. Dural bleeders are then coagulated with bipolar cautery, and
bony hemostasis is achieved with monopolar cautery and bone wax as
needed.

Fig. 38.2 Coronal bone windowed CT scan demonstrating bony overgrowth with investment of
the posterior sagittal sinus within it

Fig. 38.3 Operative photo of bone that was overlying the posterior sagittal sinus showing
evidence of ingrowth

Once the anterior and posterior bone windows have been created,
we next perform an endoscopic dissection along the remaining bone
flap. The surgeon is seated for this portion of the procedure. A 2-mm

rigid 30° endoscope is advanced lateral to the midline from the anterior
incision to the posterior bony opening. A suction device is used in the
surgeon’s other hand and advanced just in front of the endoscope to
maintain visualization and provide gentle downward pressure to strip
the dura. With the room lights lowered, the progress of the endoscope
can be tracked via transillumination through the skull and skin. Once
the posterior bony opening is reached, the endoscope is retracted and
gently swept laterally to provide additional dissection for wedge
osteotomies. The same maneuver is then repeated on the contralateral
side, and the endoscope is angled medially to visualize the full dissected
epidural space overlying the sagittal sinus. Curved Mayo scissors are
then used to fashion the lateral bony cuts. Our preferred maneuver is to
place the nondominant hand at the corner of the posterior opening and
gently advance the Mayo scissors with the concavity directed medially
towards the posterior opening. The cut is repeated on the contralateral
side, and the bone fragment is gently removed; care is taken to not
allow the posterior margin to drive into the exposed dura in the
process. A lighted retractor is then used to retract the scalp, and any
bleeding dural vessels are coagulated with the bipolar cautery. Bone
edge hemostasis is achieved by using the monopolar cautery with
cotton patty protection and bone wax as needed.
Our plastic surgery colleagues then perform two sets of parietal
wedge osteotomies just behind the coronal suture and just in front of
the lambdoid suture. Once these are completed and bony hemostasis is
assured, a large piece of dry compressed Gelfoam is cut to size and
placed in the epidural space. The incisions are then closed by using
inverted, interrupted 4-0 monocryl sutures in the galea and a running,
nonlocking 5-0 Rapide suture in the skin. The incisions are cleaned, and
dry sterile dressings are placed. The patient is then carefully removed
from the sphinx position, and care is returned to anesthesia for
extubation.

38 5 Complications
Complication avoidance begins with good positioning and anesthesia
preparation. Adequate intravenous access is critical in the event of
significant blood loss, as is the ready availability of cross-matched

blood. Communication with the anesthesia team is critical as soon as
any significant bleeding is encountered. Injury to the sagittal sinus is a
real risk, and the low circulating blood volume in these patients can
rapidly lead to hemorrhagic shock. The modified sphinx position and
extensive bone work puts these patients at risk for venous air emboli. If
encountered, the field must be immediately flooded with saline, and the
head of bed lowered. If needed, the patient must be rapidly turned
supine and flat. We limit the use of irrigation during our bony opening
to readily identify any dural tears. If cerebrospinal leakage is identified,
any tears should be promptly closed to prevent the development of
large pseudomeningoceles, given the extensive dead space under the
scalp.

38 6 Postoperative
Patients are monitored in the hospital overnight. We check a repeat
hematocrit level the morning after surgery. Patients are discharged
once they are feeding normally and pain is controlled with only oral
pain medications.
Key Points
The modified sphinx position requires meticulous attention to detail.
We employ nasal intubation secured via suture, given the lack of easy
access to the oropharynx once positioned. Particular attention should
be paid to the degree of neck extension and appropriate padding of
the chin in addition to the more commonly addressed bony
prominences.
We obtain preoperative a low-dose CT scan on all patients. In some
instances, varying degrees of bony overgrowth around the posterior
sagittal sinus may be observed. In such cases, piecemeal removal of
the bone to obtain adequate visualization for sinus dissection is key.
We will occasionally leave an island of bone on the sinus if needed,
with our craniectomy extending to the lambdoid suture on either
side of the midline.
Awareness of the starting hematocrit level and careful attention to
hemostasis will decrease the need for intraoperative and
postoperative transfusions.

During initial dissection, leaving the periosteum in place aside from
planned bony cuts will limit unnecessary blood loss from diploic
veins.
Care should be taken to not cross the midline initially when
performing epidural dissection using the endoscope.
Transillumination of the scope through the skin can guide the
dissection.
In some older children with thicker bone, Mayo scissors may be
insufficient to make the lateral bony cuts. We have occasionally used
sternotomy scissors to accomplish this.
The large bone fragment must be removed gently without levering it
into the underlying dura and brain. If necessary, it should be removed
in pieces.
A handheld lighted retractor can be particularly helpful once the
bone is removed to evaluate the craniectomy and obtain hemostasis.
There are often midline veins emerging from the sinus at its
posterior extent that require gentle bipolar cautery to obtain
hemostasis.
