Keywords Craniosynostosis – Synostosis – Sagittal suture – Cranial
vault remodeling – Scaphocephaly – Dolichocephaly – Barrel stave
osteotomies – Radial osteotomies

39 1 Introduction
39 1 1 Background
Sagittal craniosynostosis is an anatomical condition resulting from
premature fusion of the sagittal suture that causes abnormal calvarial
formation and potential limitation of underlying brain growth. Of all the
cranial sutures, sagittal synostosis is the most commonly affected by
early fusion, comprising more than half of patients with nonsyndromic
synostosis and 2:1 ratio for males:females [1]. Over the past few
decades, several different surgical approaches have been employed to
treat this condition. The two principal treatments are strip craniectomy
and cranial vault reconstruction with each procedure having multiple
technical variations. Endoscopic strip craniectomy is most effective in
children under 4–6 months of age while open cranial vault
reconstruction has historically been the standard of care and an
alternative approach employed when the patients are older or there are
multiple sutures involved. Open vault surgery is characterized by an
open craniotomy with strategic osteotomies to expand the cranial vault,
reduce intracranial pressure (ICP), and improve calvarial symmetry as
well as cosmesis. In this chapter, we will review the preoperative
planning objectives, surgical techniques, postoperative care, and
complications associated with open vault surgery in the pediatric
population.

39 2 Clinical Presentation
Infants (age 12 months) presenting with craniosynostosis are most
often referred for abnormal head shape. Sagittal synostosis may be
identified by a scaphocephalic head shape such that the biparietal
diameter is narrowed compared to an elongated occipitofrontal
diameter. This ratio is defined as the cephalic index. Normal cephalic
indices fall between 75 and 80. Values less than 75 are predictive of
sagittal synostosis. Additional characteristics may include ridging of the
sagittal suture as well as prominent bulging of the frontal and occipital
regions (Fig. 39.1).

Fig. 39.1 An infant with sagittal synostosis characterized by a scaphocephalic head shape with
frontal and occipital bossing

Of note, breech positioning in utero may mimic a scaphocephalic
head shape with overlapping parietal bones being mistaken for a ridge.
This condition will typically resolve within a few days of birth
compared to sagittal synostosis that will persist and/or worsen with
time. Another mimic of scaphocephaly includes persistence of the
mendosal suture that produces a bathrocephalic head shape in addition
to an occipital protuberance. This condition has no effect on brain
growth and should not undergo surgical treatment [2]. One also has to
consider secondary scaphocephaly related to prematurity or lack of
overall brain growth. In this setting, the scaphocephaly is not related to
premature fusion of the sagittal suture but rather to biparietal brain
growth.
Older children tend to present with more subtle calvarial
abnormalities and may manifest mild neurocognitive difficulties. While
IQ scores tend to fall within a normal range, up to 50% of patients with
single-suture sagittal synostosis may have learning disabilities
secondary to impairments in executive functioning [3]. Functional
imaging studies have confirmed altered neural connectivity in patients
with sagittal synostosis [4]. The etiology behind these deficits has not
yet been elucidated, though restricted brain growth due to an abnormal
skull shape has been proposed to play a role. For the same reason, older
patients may also present with symptoms of elevated ICP, such as
headache, nausea/vomiting, and vision changes. Unlike coronal and
metopic synostosis, ophthalmic dysfunction is less common in sagittal

synostosis; however, routine preoperative ophthalmologic evaluation
may be helpful in identifying elevated ICP [5].

39 3 Pathophysiology
Regarding factors that contribute to the act of bony fusion, there are
both intrinsic and extrinsic conditions that may occur in utero, with
primary craniosynostosis, or postnatal, with secondary synostosis. It is
critical that the treating physician appreciate these factors and
determine whether the craniosynostosis is primary versus secondary.
Environmental exposures such as parental age as well as a mother’s
smoking status, medications, and vitamin consumption carry variable
risks across all types of craniosynostosis [6]. Regarding sagittal
synostosis, thyroid dysfunction during pregnancy and the action of
thyroid hormone on osteogenesis in utero has been observed with a
positive association. Postnatal, metabolic bone disorders such as,
rickets, hypophosphatasia, pseudohypoparathyroidism, osteopetrosis,
and mucopolysaccharidosis, may also play a role in sagittal synostosis
[6].
Genetic factors have been more clearly identified in syndromic
craniosynostosis, which in turn have a higher likelihood of increased
ICP as well as greater chance of needing additional surgery in the long
run. Alpert’s, Pfeiffer’s, and Crouzon’s have all been strongly linked to
fibroblast growth factor genes. With respect to single-suture
craniosynostosis, Clark et al. identified causative genetic factors in just
15% of 391 patients presenting with single suture synostosis [7]. In an
even smaller percentage of patients (3.8%), sagittal synostosis suggests
familial inheritance [8]. The increased incidence of sagittal suture
synostosis in males supports a genetic component. Despite these
observations, there are no enough data to warrant genetic testing in
this population unless there is concern for an underlying syndrome.

39 4 Diagnosis and Treatment
(a) Diagnostic imaging

(b) Surgical management
Physical exam, as described previously, has been shown to
accurately diagnose sagittal craniosynostosis alone [9]. However, it is a
typical practice to obtain radiographic confirmation in patients with
strong suggestive features. Computed tomography (CT) will show a
fused sagittal suture in addition to other anatomical features that are
helpful for preoperative planning. In 3–5% of patients, an additional
fused suture may be identified on imaging that ultimately affects
management [10–12]. Once confirmed, the family should be counseled
on their treatment options.
Prior studies focused on the natural history of sagittal synostosis
indicate that the skull deformity is likely to worsen without
intervention [13]. Although still controversial, there are some data to
support that patients with neurocognitive deficits may demonstrate
improvement with surgical intervention [14]. If the patient is less than
4–6 months of age, an endoscopic strip craniectomy may be offered. If
the patient is older than 4–6 months or there are barriers to complying
with helmet therapy, other surgical options, including open cranial
vault surgery, may be offered (discussed below).

39 5 Preoperative Planning
Surgical treatment aims to provide an optimal long-term aesthetic and
neurocognitive outcome. As sagittal synostosis often presents with a
wide variety of deformities (frontal vs occipital bossing,
scaphocephaly), the surgical approach will be tailored to correct the
most salient deformity. The specific technique will also differ based on
anatomical features such as bone quality, volumetric analysis, and
venous anatomy, particularly in the occipital region.
Three-dimensional, computer-aided planning with CT may assist
with surgical planning. The placement of osteotomies and repositioning
of bone flaps can be strategically planned for the safest desired
outcome as well as to decrease operative time and morbidity.
Experimental growth models have also been studied to predict skull
morphology based on planned surgical technique [15–17]. A majority
of patients require remodeling of the anterior 2/3 of the cranium. Some

patients also require posterior cranial remodeling of the occiput.
Recontouring of the occipital region increases the element of morbidity
especially in the vicinity of the transverse sinus and often addressing
the anterior 2/3 of the calvarium improves the aesthetic appearance
adequately to obviate the need for a posterior operation. If needed
(rarely) this can be addressed by a later operation. Calvarial growth
over time often self-corrects this issue. Other variations of cranial vault
reconstruction that are used less often but have efficacious value are
the pi and reverse pi procedures.
Patient age and comorbidities should also be considered prior to
surgical intervention. The ideal timing of surgery has been debated.
Studies focused on neuropsychological outcomes advocate for surgical
correction prior to 6 months of age [18]. While surgery performed at a
younger age minimizes growth restriction of the developing brain,
there is a higher likelihood of postoperative bony growth requiring
reoperation. Open cranial vault surgery is also associated with longer
operative times and higher estimated blood loss than endoscopic
approaches. The effects of anesthetic and blood loss may be significant
in a young patient population. Preoperative volume status should be
optimized. Administration of erythropoietin (EPO) 7–10 days before
surgery or tranexamic acid (TXA) or aminocaproic acid (Amicar) at the
start of surgery should be considered to decrease intraoperative blood
loss with significant literature supporting its efficacy [19, 20]. The
patient should also be type and crossed and blood products made
available for administration intraoperatively with donor-designated
blood as an option.

39 6 Operative Technique
(a) General principles
(b)

and modified

procedures

(c) Foreshortening and lateral expansion of the cranium
activated by gravity (FLAG)

(d) Open cranial vault remodeling
An observational study by Baker et al. demonstrated that operative
techniques for the treatment of single suture sagittal synostosis vary
widely and additional studies are necessary to determine best
outcomes [10]. The goal of this section is to describe the most
commonly adopted principles, including the modified Π procedure,
foreshortening and lateral expansion of the cranium activated by
gravity (FLAG), and current approaches to open cranial vault
remodeling techniques.
In most cases, the patient is typically positioned in a supine or
prone position to achieve exposure of the calvarium that extends from
the forehead to the lambdoid suture. A bicoronal incision is planned to
mitigate and obscure resultant scarring and hair loss [21]. Subgaleal
dissection is carried out both anteriorly and posteriorly with
preservation of the periosteum (this helps to minimize bleeding).
Exposure typically extends anteriorly to the orbital rims and
posteriorly to the occiput, depending upon the preop planning. Careful
attention should be paid to preserving the superior temporal artery
during exposure and preservation of the supraorbital vessels and
nerves if possible.
The extent of bony removal is dependent on the degree of deformity.
Great care should be taken separating the bone from its underlying
dura so as not to inadvertently injure underlying brain or vascular
sinus, if exposed. Any opportunity to stay clear of the sinus should be
undertaken. Hemostasis is periodically achieved from bleeding points
on the dura using bipolar electrocautery or bone edges using bone wax.
The craniotomy and reconstruction are then performed based upon the
surgical technique employed. During closure, deep galeal and
epidermal sutures are placed in a standard fashion. If skin closure is
under significant tension due to significant cranial expansion, galeal
scoring may assist with approximation as well as additional subaleal
dissection. A surgical site drain is used at the discretion of the surgeon
and absorbable sutures are used at the surface.
The Pi (Π) procedure was first proposed by Jane et al. [22, 23] as a
total cranial value reconstruction for the treatment of sagittal
synostosis and typically performed between 6 and 9 months of age. The

technique was named because of the shape of the bone removal to
address the primary stenosis as well as the resultant deformity of the
cranial vault (Fig. 39.2). In this technique, the patient is placed in a
prone position and the bone is removed with a craniotome roughly
outlining the Greek letter pi (Π). The parietal bone removal is made
anterior to the lambdoid and posterior to the coronal sutures and down
as far as possible towards the squamosal sutures in the temporal
region. Minimizing any interruption of the coronal or lambdoid sutures
may help in avoiding delayed craniosynostosis of these sutures in the
future. The bone can be removed in one piece or as two pieces, as in the
letter “L,” to avoid dissection of the anterior sagittal suture. The
anterior-posterior (AP) diameter is then shortened using two Neurolon
sutures from the frontal bone and remaining overlying piece of bone
over the sagittal sinus. Leaving the stenosis sagittal suture in place does
not jeopardize normalization of the calvarial growth. Care is taken not
to tighten this gap too much ( 1 cm), to avoid any potential
compression of the underlying sagittal sinus. When the remaining
sagittal strip is brought forward ( 1 cm), the lateral pieces of parietal
bone often move in more lateral direction and often requires the
parasagittal osteomy to made wider than the frontal and occipital cuts,
to facilitate skin closure due to the newly expanded parietal bones. The
parietal bone removal is made anterior to the lambdoid and posterior
to the coronal sutures and down as far as possible towards the
squamosal sutures in the temporal region.

Fig. 39.2 Intraoperative photographs of a Π procedure. (a) An axial view of the planned bony
removal with anterior and posterior boundaries. (b) A close-up view of the remaining sagittal
suture that is left in place following the previously outlined cuts and biparietal widening. (c) An
image of the bone flap removed with a distinct shape for which the procedure is named

The Pi procedure has undergone many variations and modifications
over time. The modified Π procedure was described by Jane et al. to
address the variations in phenotypical patterns seen in sagittal
synostosis and typically performed in children older than 3 months of
age [22]. In this technique, sagittal, bilateral coronal, and lambdoid
sutures are first removed, and the parietal bones are out-fractured to
increase the biparietal diameter. The sagittal suture is then cut and
used as strut grafts to maintain the outward position. Depending on the
phenotypic variation, frontal bossing is corrected by performing a
bifrontal craniotomy and radial barrel staves for contouring. Similar
craniotomy and radial barrel staves are performed in the occipital bone
for occipital bossing with careful attention to dissecting where the
dural sinuses are located. The additional osteotomies add to the
complexity and morbidity of the surgery and the long-term outcomes
remain lacking.
The FLAG procedure was first described by Amm et al. as a
technique for sagittal synostosis correction that avoids the use of
hardware in infants between 6 and 12 months of age [24]. In this
procedure, the patient is positioned prone in order to expose the

occipital bullet. A bicoronal incision is performed, and subperiosteal
dissection exposes the fused sagittal suture and the occipital
prominence. A 3-cm parietal craniectomy is performed encompassing
the sagittal suture (Fig. 39.3). Closing wedge osteotomies are resected
posteriorly over the lambdoid sutures. Lateral barrel stave osteotomies
are then performed behind the coronal sutures, out-fracturing the
parietal bones to allow for a widened biparietal diameter. A trough is
then drilled to thin the lower aspect of the occipital bone and allow it to
hinge anteriorly with digital pressure. The parents are instructed to
keep the infants strictly supine for 3 weeks during recumbence to allow
flattening of the occipital prominence.

Fig. 39.3 Example of the FLAG procedure in a 5-month old child. (a) Preoperative axial CT
diagnosing sagittal synostosis with a fused sagittal suture and an elongated frontooccipital
length. (b) Preoperative photograph of patient in prone position with planned cranial incision.
(c) An intraoperative photograph showing biparietal craniectomy including with posterior
wedge osteotomies and bilateral parietal barrel stave osteotomies. No hardware is necessary.
(d) A postoperative axial CT demonstrating improved CI without restenosis

At Children’s National Hospital, variations of the open cranial vault
remodeling surgery are employed; more specifically, cranial vault
remodeling for sagittal synostosis diagnosed beyond 4–6 months of age
(Fig. 39.4).

Fig. 39.4 An example of open cranial vault remodeling surgery. (a, b) Axial and sagittal views
of the planned cuts to include parietal craniectomies and radial barrel stave osteotomies (c)
Image following parietal craniectomies and posterior barrel stave osteotomies. Note that the
sagittal suture is left in place. (d) Photo showing replacement of the parietal bone flaps in a
position that increases biparietal diameter. The flaps are anchored to the sagittal suture and
native occipital bone with absorbable plates and screws. (e) Native bone and particulate bone
graft are used to fill the gaps created by widening the skull

In these cases, calvarial remodeling is initiated with burr holes just
lateral to the fused sagittal suture. Parietal bone flaps are removed, and
lateral osteotomies are performed above the squamosal sutures to
increase the biparietal diameter. A sagittal bar is maintained over
midline as an anchoring point for reconstruction, while minimizing the
risk to the sagittal sinus. Radial barrel staves are performed in both
anterior and posterior directions to promote greater frontal and
occipital width. Finally, the parietal bone flaps are affixed to the native
skull as well as the intact midline bone over the sagittal sinus and
positioned in a configuration to increase the biparietal diameter. The
cranial bones are secured using absorbable hardware. Endocortical
particulate bone graft is harvested using the Hudson brace from the
parietal bone flaps, and any bony gaps or larger deficits are

subsequently filled with this bone material affixed by fibrin glue over
the area of defects.

39 7 Postoperative Care
Those patients who have had Pi or FLAG procedures are generally
monitored in a skilled postop nursing unit and are usually ready for
discharge to home the next day after their drains are removed and their
hemacrit/hemaglobin is stable. Antibiotics and routine analgesia is
given in the postoperative period.
Patients having undergone open vault reconstruction for sagittal
craniosynostosis should receive routine postoperative monitoring in a
pediatric intensive care unit with neurological monitoring for 24 h.
While it has been demonstrated that intensive therapy is generally not
needed in a healthy, nonsyndromic patient [25], it is still important to
perform frequent neurologic exams to assess for potential intracranial
complications. In the event of a neurologic change, imaging should be
obtained. Given the risk of significant blood loss, hemoglobin and
hematocrit should be trended in the postoperative period and blood
products transfused as needed. Drains are removed when the
hematocrit is stable and output from the drains is less than 30 cc over
8 h. Antibiotics are given for 24 h (until the subcutaneous drains are
removed) and routine analgesia is provided. Patients are discharged
home when they have established neurological and hemodynamic
stability, have adequate pain control and demonstrate stability of any
anticipated postop edema. The mean length of hospital stay in patients
undergoing cranial vault reconstruction is 3 days [10].

39 8 Complications Outcomes
Overall, cranial vault surgery for sagittal synostosis has a low
complication rate [20, 26]. However, when complications occur, they
can have devastating consequences and attention to technique should
be paid to avoid these outcomes. Blood loss may occur from multiple
cuts through cancellous bone. Hemodynamic monitoring along with
adequate intravascular volume replacement and meticulous hemostasis
should be employed to avoid significant blood loss, especially in

younger children. Although uncommon, blood transfusion reactions
may also occur. In addition, osteotomies in the bone increase risk for
venous air embolism and this should always be considered, especially if
there is a sudden change in blood pressure or in end-tidal CO2. Patients
should have an optimized circulating volume prior to surgery and
systolic blood pressure should be well-controlled during osteotomies. A
precordial doppler may be placed and carbon dioxide monitoring
should be employed throughout the operation in order to detect an
intraoperative venous air embolism but the practice of placing a central
line is seldom done due to the rarity of such an event. Venous sinus
injury is a rare but potentially severe complication and always should
be kept in mind. Major venous structures should be identified on
preoperative imaging and the steps of bony removal incorporated to
avoid injury. Wound infection rate ranges from 2.5 to 12.1% [27] and
increases with patient age and lower weight [28]. Pneumonia is an
additional postoperative complication found to occur more often in
patients 12 months [26].
Patients are followed over the long term (till 10 years) for
morphological and developmental progress and monitored for delayed
complications. The symmetry of the calvarium and cranial index are
trended clinically as well as the head circumference percentile. While
the utility of cranial index as a measure of surgical success has been
debated, it is still widely used to assess deformity correction. Any time
the head circumference percentile decreases or the cephalic index
deteriorates, it is reasonable to check for any potential increased ICP by
utilizing a head CT (to evaluate the calvarial bone) as well as an
ophthalmological exam of the fundus to rule out papilledema. Cranial
vault reconstruction tends to result in more dramatic CI changes from
baseline compared to strip craniectomy with an average associated
improvement of 0.11 [10]. Long-term complications include restenosis
and delayed intracranial hypertension. When an open approach is
indicated for sagittal synostosis, the rate of reoperation ranges 5.2–
16.7% [29–31]. Alternatively, some patients require reoperation for
cranioplasty to address persistent cranial defects [32], although we
have found this issue to be uncommon in our practice. There is ongoing
research investigating long-term neurocognitive outcomes with some

data that favors cranial vault reconstruction to alternative methods for
improvement in cognitive function [33, 34].

39 9 Conclusion
(a) Summary of key points, important considerations
(b) Future directions for research and treatment
Open cranial vault reconstruction for the treatment of
nonsyndromic single suture sagittal craniosynostosis is an important
tool with various techniques to suit a patient’s particular deformity. For
older patients and those with significant deformity, it may be the most
effective treatment available. Given the extensive nature of this
operation, it is important to consider the operative time and expected
blood loss in a younger patient population. Complication rates are low
but special attention should be paid to preoperative anatomy to avoid
any devastating vascular sinus injury. Long-term follow-up (10 years)
should be undertaken to monitor for recurrent cranial deformities and
possible intracranial hypertension. Research that explores genetic
contributions and neurocognitive outcomes may aid in surgical
selection and timing. The utilization of advanced imaging techniques
and predicted growth models will also contribute to optimized surgical
outcomes.
Pearls and Pitfalls
It is important to differentiate between primary and secondary
scaphocephaly. A CT scan will demonstrate fusion of the sagittal
suture in the setting of normal appearing brain. Whereas secondary
scaphocephaly will show an underlying element of lack of cerebral
development.
Recontouring of the occipital region increases the element of
morbidity especially in the vicinity of the transverse sinus and often
addressing the anterior 2/3 of the calvarium improves the aesthetic
appearance adequately to obviate the need for a posterior operation.

If needed (rarely), this can be addressed by a later operation.
Calvarial growth over time often self-corrects this issue.
For the Pi procedure, the parietal bone removal includes up anterior
to the lambdoid and posterior to the coronal sutures and down as far
as possible towards the squamosal sutures in the temporal region.
Minimizing any interruption of the coronal or lambdoid sutures may
help in avoiding delayed craniosynostosis of these sutures in the
future.

40 Sagittal Suture Synostosis:
Distraction Osteogenesis, Key Points for
the Neurosurgeons
Kyu Won Shim1 and Eun Kyung Park1
(1) Department of Pediatric Neurosurgery, Severance Children’s
Hospital, Yonsei University College of Medicine, Seoul, South Korea

Kyu Won Shim (Corresponding author)
Email: shimkyuwon@yuhs.ac
Eun Kyung Park
Email: estherpark@yuhs.ac
Keywords Craniosynostosis – Sagittal – Distraction – Psychomotor –
Distractor

40 1 Introduction
Sagittal synostosis is the most common form of craniosynostosis.
Dolichocephalic cranial morphology is a distinguishable characteristic
that allows a clear diagnosis of sagittal synostosis [1]. The surgical
treatment is inevitable, and various techniques (total skull remodeling,
pi-plasty or modified pi-plasty, endoscopic suturectomy, and distraction
osteogenesis) have been used [2–5]. In younger patients (4–6 months)
with the innate capability of early reossification, corrective methods
include removing the pathologic sagittal suture and waiting for natural
reformation following brain growth [6]. Cranial molding helmets have
also been used to support realignment [4].

The brain volumetric growth will transmit the tensile strains to the
sutures and stimulate the bone deposition at the cranial vault suture
[7]. The functional matrix theory insists that the functional
enlargement or development of an organ system is the primary force in
changing its overall shape and determining its final form. Brain
enlargement is clearly the engine of skull remodeling and the vault
suture plays a critical role in the development of the skull pathology
associated with craniosynostosis [8].
Sagittal craniosynostosis can notably distort and deform the cranial
vault and the underlying brain parenchyma. Intracranial pressure (ICP)
and neurocognitive impairment are reasonably assumed that there is a
probable linear relationship with skull deformation or distortion.
Neuroanatomical changes resulting from the interaction between the
growing skull and the developing brain can extend beyond the region
directly beneath the fused suture [9]. The development of the brain and
skull is quite independent and follow different trajectories. The growth
of brain does not correlate with the morphology of skull. The
deformational stress on the cerebral cortex affects subcortical
structures and also affects the overall spread throughout the brain [10,
11]. Sagittal craniosynostosis usually shows cognitive impairment, and
there have been several studies suggesting that the occurrence of
cognitive impairment is directly due to cranial deformation [12]. Skull
growth is regionally restricted [13], but the brain volume in these cases
is usually within [14, 15] or exceeding [15] normal limits. Our recent
data are consistent with these findings regarding the intracranial
volume. A smaller preoperative intracranial volume might suggest a
low developmental score compared to the normal volume, although in
most cases, the volume is not smaller than the age-matched average
[16].
At school age, learning disabilities or related problems associated
with neurocognitive impairment do become apparent, because of the
fact that children are positioned into more intellectually demanding
surroundings, combined with higher expectancies of social interaction
[17]. A comprehensive and team-based close follow-up should be
needed.

40 2 Positioning
All procedures are performed by plastic and neurosurgery
professionals [16]. In each instance, “a baseline circumferential
osteotomy” is performed starting 5 mm above the supraorbital rim and
connecting the near inion. Midsagittal and horizontal bicoronal
osteotomy lines are variably implemented (Fig. 40.1).

Fig. 40.1 Intraoperative photo (a) and schematic diagram (b) of anteroposterior compression
with the bitemporal expansion technique. Craniotomy lines are shown (frontal-vertex-occipital
and bitemporal-vertex), dividing the hemisphere into quadrants. An additional hairbandshaped craniectomy line (bitemporal vertex) is made for anteroposterior compression as
needed

For this basic surgical scheme, the supine position has been used at
our institute (Fig. 40.2). To address both anterior and posterior aspects
of the skull without the need for repositioning, modified prone position
is recommended [18]. This modified prone position has been used for
whole cranial vault remodeling surgery. However, our circumferential
craniotomy technique does not require “the easy access to the area of

inion and posterior inferior part of cranium.” Our technique needs only
a small gap or space between surgical table or head rest/horse shoe
and patient’s head to be passed by electrical craniotome to make a
craniotomy line. This standard supine position is very comfortable for
patients as well as anesthesiologist to access the patients, but it may be
uncomfortable to surgeons (Fig. 40.2). In case of emergency situation
like a hypovolemic shock, supine position will be tremendously
beneficial for patient’s safety. When an operator is making craniotomy
line at posterior parietal bone and occipital bone which is very
dependent position and narrow access to the field reverse, the
Trendelenburg position of 15–30° will give a better approach angle
toward the surgical field.

Fig. 40.2 Supine position. A small gap or space between surgical table or head rest/horse shoe
and patient’s head will be enough to be passed by electrical craniotome to make a craniotomy
line

40 3 Incision
Main skin incision is curvilinear wave pattern along to the coronal line
to minimize the visualization of scar. Curvilinear wave pattern incision
will be covered and a scar exposure will be minimized by hair growth.

Small multiple additional incisions for the outlet of distractors are
needed. The author’s institute uses two types of distractors, which are
internal and external type. Small additional incision for their outlet will
be adjusted according to the position and type of distractors. For the
external distractor, additional skin incision for outlet will not be
necessary. However, the internal distractor usually has another outlet,
so additional skin incision is necessary. As you can see in Fig. 40.4, the
shape of the internal distractor distal half of distractor is flexible and
long tailed. When the fixation of distractor, the outlet and direction of
that should be considered to minimize the additional incision and scar
(Fig. 40.3).

Fig. 40.3 Sagittal craniosynostosis with moderate plagiocephaly. An incision is curvilinear
wave pattern along to coronal line and multiple additional incision for exit of internal
distractors. Only internal distractors were used for this case. This case used three internal
devices for midline distraction

40 4 Instrumentation
Distraction devices [19] are developed by plastic surgeon of the
author’s institute. The internal and external distractors are shown in
Fig. 40.4. The internal device consists of two parts, proximal rigid which
has two foot plates for fixation on craniotomy edges with eight holes for
screw and distal flexible parts covered by silicon sheath (Fig. 40.4a).
This distal flexible part is useful for exiting skin through additional

incision and hiding inside dressing. This internal device can be used for
distracting and compressing. The internal device is not so tough to
withstand hard distraction or compression, so an external device is
useful for hard distraction. Hard distraction shall be applied to distract
two big bone flaps in the middle of two parietal bones. Our institute
uses three external devices for distracting midline bones of sagittal
craniosynostosis because the distracting line is too long for single
distractor. An external device is strong enough to hold and distract
thick and large bone flaps (Fig. 40.4b, c). It has large profile and is
heavier than the internal device, but no additional incision is needed.
Both distraction devices can distract or compress by a linear vector.
There is another one for curved vector distraction (Fig. 40.4d, e). The
main body of this distractor is malleable so that the operator can adjust
the curvature of the distractor, as shown in Fig. 40.4d.

Fig. 40.4 Distraction devices which the authors developed. (a) Internal device, (b, c) external
devices, and (d, e) malleable distractor

40 5 Position of Surgical Team
Surgical procedures are performed by engaging a team of professionals
(i.e., plastic surgeon, neurosurgeon, anesthesiologist, geneticist, and
pediatric psychologist). Figure 40.5 clearly shows operating theater and
the position of surgical team. The anesthesiologist team dedicated to
pediatric craniofacial surgery is prepared all about anesthesia inside of
the room. As shown in Fig. 40.5, the patient is positioned supine next to
the anesthesiologist. The area of patient’s head is freely open for
surgeons to ensure full access to the whole area of the calvarial bone.

Surgical instruments are kept ready which are perpendicular to the
surgical table. Scrub nurse can access surgical instruments and assist
surgeons simultaneously at the corner of the patient’s and instrument
table.

Fig. 40.5 The panoramic view of the operating theater. Anesthesiologist is usually on the left
side of patient, i.e., deep inside of the operating room. Green chair at the left lower corner is for
surgeon. Surgical instruments are positioned at the right side of patient’s foot. The black round
chair is for scrub nurse

40 6 Intraoperative Monitoring
The author’s institute has not done with any type of intraoperative ICP
monitoring. The reason is the main purpose of the surgical correction
of craniosynostosis is not ICP control. And also, we did a study of
preoperative measurement of ICP through a lumbar puncture while the
patients are on the general anesthesia and ophthalmologic exam for
papilledema (unpublished). There has been no clear evidence for those
parameters that could be essential for patients to be decided for
surgical treatment or surgical extent so far. Elevated ICP may be one of
the considerations for decision-making although the normal variation
of ICP with age is not well delineated. And only small portion of singlesuture craniosynostosis patients show elevated ICP [19]. Recently,
Brendan et al. [20] did an intraoperative ICP monitoring before and
after craniectomy or craniotomy using a flexible ICP fiberoptic probe.

They reported that in the mean precraniectomy ICP, there was no
significant difference between syndromic and nonsyndromic patients
(17.68 vs. 15.58 mmHg, p = 0.239). In regard to postcraniectomy ICP,
there was no significant difference between syndromic and
nonsyndromic patients (8.68 vs. 8.96 mmHg, p = 0.820) [20].
Distraction osteogenesis shows statistically significant decreased
blood loss and reduced amount of blood transfusion [21]. However, the
absolute amount of blood loss is still large for infant. In the author’s
institute, a standardized anesthesia protocol has been used and
bleeding monitoring was published, which was developed by an
anesthesiology team [22]. At the author’s institute, the following
standardized general anesthesia protocol is used: induction with
2 mg/kg propofol and 1 g/kg fentanyl, neuromuscular blockade with
0.6 mg/kg rocuronium bromide, maintenance with desflurane or
sevoflurane in an oxygen-air mixture (fraction of inspired oxygen, 0.5),
and administration of intermittent bolus doses of fentanyl and
rocuronium. A central venous catheter is placed in the femoral or
internal jugular vein, whereas an arterial catheter is placed in the radial
artery. Urine output is monitored using a urinary catheter. Rectal
temperature is measured and maintained at normothermic levels with
a forced-air blanket throughout the surgery. Due to the inaccuracy in
estimating blood loss during surgery, blood loss is calculated by the
anesthesiologist using a previously adopted formula for this patient
population [23–25]: estimated red cell volume
(ERCV)lost = ERCVpreoperative ERCVtransfused ERCVpostoperative where
ERCV is estimated blood volume (EBV) Hct/100. EBV is 80 mL/kg for
infants younger than 12 months and 75 mL/kg for children older than
12 months. ERCVtransfused is calculated as follows:
ERCVtransfused = transfused volume of packed RBC (mL) Hct of packed
RBC/100 Hct of packed RBC is estimated to be approximately 60% by
the local blood bank. Therefore, EBVlost is calculated as follows: EBVlost
(mL/kg) = ERCVlost (mL)/[Weight (kg) Hctpreoperative/100]. Routine
fluid management during surgery consisted of continuous
administration of balanced crystalloid with additional SD 1:4 solution
(0.2% NaCl with dextrose). The amount of fluid administered is
determined based on preoperative fasting time, intraoperative deficits,

and basal fluid maintenance. Colloid (hydroxyethyl starch (6%,
130/0.4) in a balanced electrolyte solution, Volulyte; Fresenius Kabi,
Schelle, Belgium) up to 20 mL/kg/day is administered in case of acute
and massive perioperative blood loss prior to the initiation of blood
product preparation and transfusion. Controlled hypotension is not
performed during surgery.
TXA-induced hemostasis involves the inhibition of plasminogenplasmin interactions on the surface of fibrin, thereby preventing fibrin
degradation [26]. The antifibrinolytic activity of TXA resulted in
reduced transfusion requirement until postoperative day 2 in our
institute [22].

40 7 Hemostasis Control
Tranexamic acid (TXA) is effective for reducing blood loss and the need
for transfusions during surgeries [22, 26]. TXA is administered as an
intravenous loading dose of 10 mg/kg over 15 min, followed by
continuous intravenous infusion at 5 mg/kg/h from the beginning of
the surgery until skin closure [22, 27].
The initial skin incision starts when blood transfusion is ready. A
local infiltration of local anesthetics along the incision is commonly
used to minimize bleeding. Small size scalp clip for pediatric patient is
applied to reduce the bleeding from the open scalp wound during
operation.
There are many active possible bleeding points while performing
craniotomy. Supraorbital bony sinus or bone marrow, pterional
meningeal artery, and bone bleeding around the anterior fontanelle are
main sites of bleeding. Bleeding along the coronal craniotomy site is
frequently encountered as well as from sagittal venous sinus. There are
many commercially available hemostatic materials with various
application techniques such as Bone wax, absorbable hemostat
(Surgicel fibrillar), microfibrillar collagen hemostat (Avitene ), fibrin
sealant patch (Tachosil ), and hemostatic matrix (Floseal ), etc. These
materials are unique feature of hemostatic mechanisms, so surgeons
can choose several of them according to the nature of bleeding and
oozing.

40 8 Bone Opening
Under general anesthesia, the patient is placed in the supine position
on a horse-shoe head rest. A curvilinear wave pattern incision is made
along the scalp as a bicoronal line. Subperiosteal dissection is done to
the supraorbital rim anteriorly and below the inion posteriorly. In each
instance, a baseline circumferential osteotomy is carried out, starting at
a point 5 mm above the supraorbital rim and connecting the near inion.
Two additional straight osteotomy lines are variably implemented as
needed; the first is a mid-sagittal line, and the second is a horizontal
bicoronal line. Furthermore, bicoronal strip ostectomy (width, 10–
20 mm) is performed along the bicoronal osteotomy line. Once
removed, internal distraction devices are applied for fronto-occipital
compression, incorporating vectors of frontal bossing. Along the midsagittal osteotomy, two or three distraction devices are then applied for
bitemporal expansion (Fig. 40.6) [12].

Fig. 40.6 Intraoperative photographs and schematic diagrams of surgical techniques for each
therapeutic group. The arrows indicate the distraction direction, and the shaded area
represents the cranial segment removed. The dotted line in the bitemporal distraction
procedure denotes the craniotomy line, which was performed when anterior and posterior
cranium expansions differed. Group 1, anteroposterior compression with bitemporal expansion
(left); group 2, bitemporal expansion (center); and group 3, anteroposterior expansion with
bitemporal expansion (right) [12]

For safe and efficient craniotomy, initial burr hole should be
carefully made at critical point along the designed craniotomy line. At
the age of 1 year, the sutures are tight and ligamentous nature, so they
are not easy to directly cross with craniotomy burr. For effective
correction of sagittal craniosynostosis, circumferential craniotomy to
detach calvarial bone from the skull base should be made. Coronal
sutures, pterion, squamosal suture, and lambdoid sutures are crossed
for basal circumferential craniotomy. If a suture is too tough to directly
cross, dissecting burr can be helpful to cross the suture and also the
removal of tight ligamentous tissues. However, the pterion crossing the

internal bony ridge is problematic and craniotome is used to be stuck. A
gentle “to and fro” maneuver of craniotome may cross the internal
ridge, otherwise dissecting burr should be used carefully to remove the
internal bony ridge. Frontal base craniotomy is little challenging
because usually there is an internal sharp bony ridge. And also, there is
long and tough midline ridge underneath the midline of the frontal
bone. For a patient who has prominent frontal bossing, this midline
frontal craniotomy is needed. Most of the midline internal ridge is not
so high to be removed by simple craniotomy. A gentle “to and fro”
maneuver of craniotome and feeling the “grinding out of the ridge” will
help to overcome this ridge. Posterior 2/3 of the midline is quite
challenging due to the position of the patient and very tight dura
around the lambdoid suture. Similar principle can be applied. A gentle
“to and fro” maneuver of craniotome and feeling the “grinding out of the
bone” will help. For tight lambdoid suture, dissecting burr should be
used not to injure the sagittal sinus. Craniotomy for occipital bone is
very difficult for the surgeon because patients are supine and
craniotomy line is in dependent position.
In group 1, a bicoronal strip ostectomy (width, 10–20 mm) is
performed along the bicoronal osteotomy line. Once removed,
distraction devices are applied for antero-occipital compression,
considering frontal bossing vectors. Two or three distraction devices
are then applied along the midsagittal osteotomy for bitemporal
expansion (Fig. 40.7) [12].

Fig. 40.7 Anteroposterior compression procedure for distraction osteogenesis in
dolichocephalic sagittal synostosis. Sagittal synostosis noted preoperatively with intact coronal
and lambdoid sutures (left). Devices were applied at craniotomy sites for anteroposterior
compression and bitemporal expansion to perform distraction in distinguishable vectors
(second from left and second from right). Correction of scaphoid cranial shape and excessive
frontal bossing were confirmed, and newly generated calvarial bone was verified at the sagittal
suture point (right)

In group 2, a midsagittal osteotomy is performed, and two or three
distraction devices are applied along the midsagittal osteotomy for
bitemporal expansion. A bicoronal osteotomy was performed to correct
disparate front-to-back width, applying distraction devices to each flap
(Fig. 40.8) [12].

Fig. 40.8 Bitemporal expansion procedure for distraction osteogenesis in sagittal synostosis,
with a cranial index of 75–80. Sagittal synostosis was noted preoperatively, with intact coronal
and lambdoid sutures (left). Devices were applied at craniotomy sites for bitemporal expansion
to perform distraction (second from left and second from right). Correction of constricted
cranial growth at midline was confirmed. Newly generated calvarial bone was verified at the
area of the former sagittal suture (right)

In group 3, midsagittal and bicoronal osteotomies are performed,
and distraction devices are placed along osteotomy lines to expand in
the bitemporal and antero-occipital directions (Fig. 40.9) [12].

Fig. 40.9 Anteroposterior and bitemporal expansion procedure for distraction osteogenesis in
nondolichocephalic sagittal synostosis. Sagittal synostosis was noted preoperatively, with intact
coronal and lambdoid sutures (left). Devices were applied at craniotomy sites for
anteroposterior and bitemporal expansion, and distraction was performed in the expansile
vector (second from left and second from right). Correction of nondolichocephalic cranial shape
was confirmed, and newly generated calvarial bone was verified at the distraction site (right)

40 9 Postoperative Drain
The scalp is closed with resorbable sutures, and a compressive dressing
is applied. Whole calvarial bone is usually exposed, so two silicone
vacuum drainage bags are inserted anteriorly and posteriorly. While
patients are monitored in the neurosurgical intensive care unit for 1–
2 days, the drains are monitored hourly. Usually, the drainages are
maintained for 3–4 days postoperatively. Removal of drainage depends
on the amount of drainage.

40 10 Postoperative Dressing and Surveillance
The patients are monitored at recovery room immediately after
operation until patient’s vital signs and general condition are

considered stable. In most of the patients, chest X-rays are taken at the
recovery room to monitor the volume status, because the infused fluids
including blood products are plenty. The anesthesiologist and
neurosurgeon decide to transfer the patient to the neurosurgical care
unit. A 3D head CT is usually performed if the patient’s condition
permits, while the patient is being transferred to the neurosurgical care
unit.

40 11 Postoperative Intensive Care at
Neurosurgical Care Unit
Patients are monitored in the neurosurgical intensive care unit for 1–
2 days. Heart rate with electrocardiography, respiration rate, blood
pressure with arterial line and oxygen saturation. After patients are
stabilized at the neurosurgical care unit, a dressing is changed to
inspect the undetected hematomas collection and active bleeding from
distractor exit sites, usually 6 h after the end of operation. One hour
before midnight, a dressing is inspected by the plastic surgeon and
neurosurgeon to check bleeding or oozing. Complete blood counts and
coagulation profiles are checked. Other routine chemistries are also
checked. Additional infusion of volume expander or transfusion of
blood is decided according to the results of laboratory test and the
amount of drainage.
The next day after the operation, most of the patients are sent to the
general ward to proceed the rest of the postoperative care and take an
instruction for distraction and wound care at home.

40 12 Outpatient Clinic Follow-Up
Five days after the procedure, distraction is initiated at a rate of 0.5–
1.0 mm/day and continued until the shape of the skull is satisfactory by
appearance and on radiographic images. Overall perioperative
management adhered to critical pathways of the institute for
craniosynostosis patients. Seven days after admission, guardians may
make adjustments to distraction on an outpatient basis. In outpatient
clinic, the status is checked at 1–2 week interval with skull X-ray and

visual inspection until they reach the planed shape of expansion and
compression. Usually, 3–4 weeks are enough for distraction and
compression.

40 13 Removal of Instrumentation
After completion of distraction or compression, a consolidation period
is given for 8–12 weeks according to the status of the skull and patient’s
age. The devices are removed under general anesthesia after
consolidation. Absorbable plates are placed on each expansion site to
maintain distracted gaps, which help retain stability and overcome
adjacent soft-tissue pressure until complete reossification is achieved.

40 14 Postop Helmet
As shown in Figs. 40.7, 40.8, and 40.9, cranial indices are much
improved. But there are usually certain amount of bone gaps/defects
and skull growth is still taking place after the completion of distraction.
Helmet orthosis can assist symmetrical growth of skull and provide a
guidance for proper filling of the bone defect. The duration of helmet
assist depends on the postoperative status of patients.

40 15 Neurosurgeon s Perspectives
Dolichocephalic sagittal craniosynostosis can be treated effectively by
circumferential cranial reformation, strategically using distraction
osteogenesis for maximal benefits. Sagittal craniosynostosis with a
normal intracranial volume is corrected through distraction
osteogenesis in combination with antero-posterior compression and
bitemporal expansion. These procedures resulted in
neurodevelopmental improvement, demonstrating the validity of
expansion linked with a compression technique [12, 16]. Most of
nondolichocephalic sagittal craniosynostosis showed subnormal
intracranial volume. The preoperative psychomotor developmental
index is mostly lower than dolichocephalic sagittal craniosynostosis
[12]. Table 40.1 shows the assessment results of neurodevelopmental
outcomes (unpublished data). The “Golden Time” for surgical

correction is 4–6 months old [28]. According to studies of patients with
sagittal synostosis, early surgery (i.e., 6 months of age) with a more
comprehensive approach yielded a better neurological outcome than
strip craniectomy (endoscopic or otherwise) before 3 months of age
[29, 30]. Distraction osteogenesis has advantages of larger volume
expansion and effective correction of the vault shape [21].

41 1 Introduction
Nonsyndromic sagittal craniosynostosis (SCS) causes an abnormally
long and narrow head shape. Surgical management for SCS can be
classified into two general approaches such as (1) traditional open
cranial vault remodeling (CVR) and (2) early management with lessinvasive techniques. While these approaches are vastly different, they
share the same fundamental goals such as (1) to restore normal cranial
appearance and (2) to prevent future neurocognitive impairment. CVR
techniques are performed around after 6 months of age through an
open bicoronal approach, whereby the affected skull is removed and

reshaped into a normal form at the time of surgery. While CVR enables
immediate and consistent outcomes, the benefits are negatively
weighted by the risk of intraoperative blood loss, larger scar burden,
need for postoperative critical care, and length of stay in the hospital.
To overcome these limitations, less-invasive alternatives were
developed wherein the sagittal suture is surgically “released,” followed
by postoperative reshaping with either an external cranial orthosis or,
more recently, internal stainless-steel springs.
In 1998, Jimenez and Barone pioneered endoscopic-assisted strip
craniectomy (ESC) for early treatment of SCS around 3–6 months of age
[1]. Unlike CVR, cranial shape is not corrected at the time of ESC.
Instead, head shape is passively molded by rapid infantile brain growth
and an external cranial orthosis. The cranial orthosis is worn 23.5 h
daily for 6–9 months. Noncompliance with the intense, prolonged
treatment course leads to less predictable outcomes.
In 2008, spring-mediated cranioplasty (SMC) was popularized in
the literature by Lauritzen and colleagues after reporting the results of
the first 100 cases [2]. Strip craniectomy is performed; however, in lieu
of postoperative helmet therapy, correction is achieved with internal
stainless-steel springs. Like ESC, head shape is not corrected at the time
of surgery. Parietal bone widening occurs over the course of several
weeks as expansile and resistive forces reach equilibrium. Springs are
removed in 3–4 months after bone consolidation. The primary
challenges of SMC are (1) understanding the nuanced interplay
between spring attributes and the viscoelastic properties of the
pediatric skull and (2) how can we apply this knowledge for guiding
surgical decision-making to achieve consistent results across the
phenotypic spectrum of SCS. As such, there is a learning curve when
first incorporating SMC into practice.
Over the last 25 years, more and more craniofacial treatment
centers have adopted less-invasive techniques to treat patients with
sagittal craniosynostosis. The growing body of the literature
demonstrates that ESC and SMC are effective alternatives to CVR. The
more favorable perioperative risk profiles have led some to prefer ESC
and SMC as first-line treatments. Despite the growing popularity of
SMC, however, there is wide variability in technique and other factors
important to surgical decision-making [3]. These issues are addressed

in the following sections describing preoperative evaluation, patient
selection, surgical planning, and technique variations with respect to
incisions, spring implantation, and strip craniectomy.
In this chapter, we define which patients are appropriate candidates
for SMC, highlight factors important for surgical decision-making, and
illustrate SMC with detailed step-by-step notes.

41 2 Eligible Surgical Candidates
SMC is indicated for infants with isolated SCS prior to 6 months of age.
Surgery is typically performed between 3 and 6 months of age. Children
younger than 3 months are less tolerant to surgical blood loss due to
the physiologic nadir of hematocrit [4]. Their relatively thin skull also
makes spring use unfavorable. Surgical timing should consider
gestational age; SMC is delayed for children born preterm until they are
3–6 months from the term date. Patients with contraindications at a
young age (major comorbidities) or those older than 6 months of age at
the time of presentation are monitored and later treated with CVR.

41 3 Patient Evaluation
Infants with suspected SCS undergo a detailed craniofacial assessment.
The degree of scaphocephaly, frontal bossing, biparietal narrowing, and
occipital bulleting is noted. Ridging of the sagittal suture is often
present. The cephalic index is measured with calipers. It is important to
perform a full history and physical examination to identify extracranial
comorbidities or syndromic manifestations. Preoperative threedimensional (3D) photographs serve as a useful baseline assessment of
morphologic shape allowing for objective analysis of future cranial
growth. A low-dose 3D CT scan is performed to confirm SCS, evaluate
patency of other cranial sutures, evaluate bone thickness, and rule out
any intracranial abnormalities.
Comprehensive evaluation should be performed by a
multidisciplinary team consisting of plastic surgery, neurosurgery,
ophthalmology, and genetics. Dilated ophthalmologic exam, visualevoked potential (VEP) and/or optical coherence tomography are
performed to assess for signs of elevated intracranial pressure, which

are rare in infants, but provide a useful baseline for future comparisons.
Routine preoperative laboratory assessment includes a complete blood
cell count, electrolyte panel, type and crossmatch, and prothrombin
time to screen for bleeding disorders.
Parietal bone thickness of 0.5–1.5 cm from the suture line, along the
strip craniectomy site, may predict perioperative outcomes. Thicker
bone, but not patient age, has been reported to be associated with
increased surgical blood loss, need for transfusion, and hospital length
of stay [5], although this may vary based on technique.

41 4 Surgical Decision-Making
The long-term goals of SMC are to (1) restore normal cranial
appearance and (2) prevent future neurocognitive impairment. The
technical goals are to implant springs sufficient to slowly widen the
parietal bones such that cephalic index is normalized over the
subsequent weeks following surgery. Surgical outcomes ultimately
relate to a combination of patient age, phenotypic severity, spring
characteristics, and surgical technique. While our understanding of
these factors is still incomplete, we discuss considerations for surgical
decision-making.

41 5 Patient Age
Many techniques typically describe performing surgery between 3 and
6 months, because treatment efficacy wanes with older age. One
retrospective study reported that for every month increase in age, the
change in the cephalic index decreased by 1.3 [6]. Bone thickness
increases and viscoelastic compliance of the skull decreases during this
time, which counterbalances the expansile forces of the springs.
Implanted springs stop expanding once force equilibrium is reached
against resistive forces of the skull. Patients presenting for surgery
closer to 6 months of age benefit from technique modifications to
increase force exerted across the craniectomy.
The most dramatic changes to the cranial shape occur over the first
several weeks as the skull is actively expanded transversely. However,
postoperative improvements to forehead and occiput aesthetics are

observed over subsequent months, even after the springs have been
removed. Bearing in mind that SMC primarily addresses the midvault in
the transverse dimension, changes to the forehead and occiput rely on
postoperative brain growth after brain matter is restored to its normal
distribution within the transversely expanded vault. As such, it may be
prudent to treat children with severe phenotypes around 3 months of
age to maximize the secondary molding benefit of the brain. However, a
limiting factor is that bone in younger patients is thinner, more fragile,
and at risk for fracturing under the pressure from springs. Spring force
should be adjusted accordingly. If preoperative CT images demonstrate
especially thin bone (Fig. 41.1), the treatment team may consider
postponing surgery or alternative treatment with ESC and
postoperative cranial orthosis. During the informed consent process,
regardless of bone thickness, parents should be informed of the
possibility of intraoperative bone fracture and the need to switch to ESC
with postoperative helmeting.

Fig. 41.1 Sagittal (upper) and coronal (lower) computerized tomography 3D bony
reconstructions, highlighting both the sagittal synostosis and the bony thinning that may
warrant consideration for spring placement versus postoperative helmeting

41 6 Spring Design

Generally, two or three U-shaped stainless steel springs are used [7–
10]. Standardized, prefabricated springs are commercially available
(OsteoMed SmartFlex, Acumed; Fig. 41.2). Springs exert expansile
forces across the craniectomy site to slowly widen the parietal bones
and, thereby, normalize cephalic index. The two most important factors
for increasing CI are spring expansile force and spring excursion [10].
Indeed, while there is some minimum spring force that is required to
overcome the intrinsic resistive forces of the bone and scalp,
maximizing spring force may counterintuitively decrease total skull
expansion. With commercially available springs, spring force is
inversely proportional to arm length. Higher force springs have shorter
arms and, consequently, less excursion potential when compared to
lower force springs. Additionally, high-force springs increase bone
contact point-force and may erode through the bone rather than
pushing the bone, decreasing total biparietal expansion.

Fig. 41.2 The appearance of a typical spring. Arm length and force dynamics are factors that
can be modified to fit the procedure, as discussed in the text

Custom-made springs can be fabricated by the surgical team to
modify spring characteristics. However, the biomechanical relationship

between springs and cranial expansion is complex, still poorly
understood, and requires further systematic clinical investigation.
Nonetheless, there are several modifiable spring characteristics that
impact the cumulative force translated to the parietal bones, including
number of springs used, opening angle, wire thickness, spring
compression, and arm length.
Generally, 2–3 springs have been used with intrinsic forces of each
ranging between 5 newtons (N) and 10 N [7–10]. Posterior bone is
thicker and often fitted with a larger force spring. Use of three springs
enables a larger total force to be applied compared to two springs by
distributing the force more gradually and reducing point-force along
bone contact points. While reducing the risk of bone erosion,
implanting additional springs can also be problematic due to spring
overcrowding, interlocking, spring dislodgement, and undue soft tissue
tension. The intrinsic force of the springs can also be modified as
desired. A wider “U” bend generates greater distracting force versus a
narrower bend independent of spring length. Heavier gauge wire
generates even greater distracting force when compared to alterations
in the spring “U” bend independent of spring length and width. The
strip craniectomy can be designed to exploit the inherent properties of
springs. Springs compressed to a narrower defect width (e.g., 10 versus
40 mm) exert a greater distracting force: per Hooke’s law, the
distraction force correlates to degree of compression at the time of
implantation across the suturectomy width. Maintaining a narrow strip
craniectomy is, therefore, advantageous to maximizing spring-mediated
skull expansion, and we recommend keeping this width to no more
than 10–15 mm.
Finally, biparietal widening can be maximized using long-arm
springs because the length of the spring arm dictates the maximal
spring excursion. Longer arm springs exert a slower, more uniform
expansion with less initial distracting force when compared to shorter
arm springs (e.g., 60 versus 40 mm), which exert an accelerated
expansion initially but reach their maximal opening earlier. Thus, there
is less relative expansion immediately after placement of longer springs
but greater expansion in the longer term [10]. Because spring length is
inversely related to force, longer springs are less likely to fracture the
skull. Taking these caveats together, the greatest amount of distraction

is typically achieved when utilizing multiple wide, thick, long-armed
springs, and a narrow strip craniectomy width.

41 7 Operative Technique: Spring-Mediated
Cranioplasty
41 7 1 Overview
We find that a simple, standardized approach to patient selection, strip
craniectomy, and spring selection reliably corrects cephalic index by
0.1–0.15. Most children who present with a cephalic index ranging from
0.6 to 0.7 benefit from the approach described below without major
modifications. Surgical timing, spring force, and spring arm length may
be modified for patients with CI outside of this range.

41 7 2 Surgical Timing
Surgical timing for spring meditated cranioplasty must weigh the
benefits of rapid head growth early in infancy with increasing bone
integrity, and thus spring function, with age. Although SMC has been
described in patients ranging from 3 to 6 months of age, in our
experience, the ideal time for spring placement is 4 months of age
(corrected for any prematurity). At this age, the brain growth trajectory
is still rapid, but skull thickness has increased enough that springs can
be placed with low concern for footplate-induced bone fractures.

41 7 3 Implants and Instrumentation
Two prefabricated 0.051″ thick stainless steel U-shaped cranial springs
are selected (OsteoMed SmartFlex, Acumed). Instruments are shown in
Fig. 41.3. The 30° endoscope is used with the optical dissector (Karl
Storz, Germany). The fenestrated spatula at the distal end of the optical
dissector retracts the scalp and prevents blood from obscuring the
camera.

Fig. 41.3 Typical instrumentation used during the SMC procedure

41 7 4 Anesthesia Considerations
Anesthesia is delivered by experienced anesthesiologists well-versed in
craniofacial surgery. Two intravenous (IV) catheters are placed. One
catheter delivers IV fluids and medications while the other delivers
tranexamic acid (loading dose: 10 mg/kg; continuous infusion:
5 mg/kg/h) to reduce blood loss and need for transfusion [11]. Unlike
more invasive open CVR procedures, early aggressive fluid resuscitation
is unnecessary with meticulous hemostasis. For this reason, SMC can be
safely performed without an arterial line or Foley catheter [12].
Precordial Doppler monitoring is not routinely used. Weight-based IV
prophylactic antibiotics are administered. Cross-matched blood is
immediately available in the operating room.

41 7 5 Patient Positioning and Preparation
The operative table is turned 180° away from the anesthesia team.
While SMC can be performed with the patient positioned supine, prone
positioning facilitates more efficient access to the mid- and posterior
vault, especially in cases of severe scaphocephaly. The forehead and
cheeks are padded with Reston foam to prevent pressure-indued injury
of the face and orbits. The scalp is shaved, scrubbed with a
chlorhexidine brush, and then infiltrated with local anesthesia (0.25%
bupivacaine with epinephrine 1:200,000). The surgical field is sterilely
prepped with povidone-iodine solution and draped with a craniotomy
drape.

41 7 6 Scalp Incision
The anterior fontanelle and lambda are demarcated on the skin with a
marking pen. A midline 2–3 cm incision is marked slightly dependent to
the midpoint between the prior markings (Fig. 41.4). The scalp is
incised with a 15 blade 10 min after local anesthetic injection
allowing the epinephrine hemostatic effect to develop. The galea is
bluntly separated from the pericranium with Metzenbaum scissors. The
sagittal suture is exposed with minimal undermining creating a
subgaleal tunnel between the anterior fontanel and the lambdoid
sutures. A 1-cm wide strip craniectomy is demarcated by scoring the
periosteum (centered on the midline) with electrocautery.

Fig. 41.4 Upper: The skin incision and schematic of the intended spring placement on typical
procedure. Lower: Multistep schematic of the various steps in bone removal and spring
placement and the resultant remodeling dynamics that contribute to the ultimate cranial
reshaping

An alternative skin incision commonly used involves two transverse
incisions near the anterior fontanelle and lambdoid sutures. We prefer
a single vertex incision as described above to minimize scar visibility,
especially in the case of males due to the possibility of a receding
hairline with aging. The trade-off, however, is that endoscopic-assisted
surgery can be technically more challenging. In our early experience,
we found the endoscope to be unwieldy when performing the anterior
strip craniectomy. The operating surgeon is forced to operate in the
opposite direction of the camera (i.e., reverse alignment “mirror image”
visualization). We found that by placing the 2–3 cm incision in a slightly
dependent manner, we can avoid this situation without lengthening the
scar or compromising surgical efficiency. The anterior bone is removed
comfortably and expeditiously under direct visualization using a lighted
retractor. The endoscope is often only used when performing the
posterior strip craniectomy, which is straightforward because the
camera faces in the same direction as the operating surgeon. For severe
cases that require extensive anterior and posterior visualization, we
use endoscope monitors at both the head and foot of the patient to
allow normal viewing orientation in both directions.

41 7 7 Strip Craniectomy
A parasagittal burr hole is drilled while carefully avoiding the sagittal
sinus. Dura is dissected free from adjacent bone with a modified
Penfield 4. The craniectomy is initiated at the burr hole with a Kerrison
rongeur and proceeds in the dependent direction to avoid pooling of
blood in the operative field. If the patient is prone, the anterior strip
craniectomy is performed first with a small rongeur and lighted
retractor. Sequential dural dissection is performed as the craniectomy
continues anteriorly until it is continuous with the anterior fontanelle.
In cases of severe scaphocephaly, a straight Blakesley Thru-Cut forceps
is used to complete the distal craniectomy.
The strip craniectomy proceeds posteriorly in similar fashion with a
small rongeur and a lighted retractor until it becomes ergonomically
unfavorable. The lighted retractor is exchanged for a 30° endoscope
with optical dissector and attached irrigation syringe. A short-angled
drill attachment (Stryker, Kalamazoo, MI) and a 4-mm coarse diamond
round drill bit is used to obliterate the outer cortex (Video 41.1). The

coarse diamond bit simultaneously cauterizes bone controlling
hemostasis, which is particularly helpful if there is a thick midline
ridge, which is common posteriorly (Fig. 41.5). A suction tip is used to
protect the dura while simultaneously clearing irrigation. The inner
cortex is removed with Thru-Cut forceps extending to the lambdoid
sutures while also ensuring that the craniectomy width is minimal.
Once the entire fused suture is removed, the parietal bones will be
“unlocked” and independently mobile. Adequate mobility is confirmed
by alternating manual depression of the scalp over the parietal and
occipital bones while simultaneously visualizing the lambdoid suture
with the endoscope. If the bony plates do not move independently
across the lambdoid suture, dura is dissected from the proximal
lambdoid sutures and additional bone is removed until mobility is
satisfactory. Hemostasis at the bone margins and the dura are obtained.

Fig. 41.5 Upper: Endoscopic view, showing the periosteal incision and endoscope-mediated
visualization of the posterior sagittal suture. The dura is protected with a suction in
preparation for additional bone removal. Lower: The thick midline keel is thinned down using
a short-angled drill and a 4-mm coarse diamond burr, and then removed with a Thru-Cut
forceps. This step is repeated until the lambdoid suture junction is reached. Right- and left-

angled forceps are sometimes used to remove bone at the sagittal/lambdoid junction to obtain
free mobility of posterior parietal bone plates

41 7 8 Spring Insertion
Two stainless steel U-shaped springs with hooked footplates are
selected (0.051-inch wire diameter; OsteoMed SmartFlex, Acumed).
Matched osteotomy notches are made using a 1-mm Kerrison rongeur
along each margin of the strip craniectomy where the footplates will
engage, approximately 1–2 cm posterior to the coronal sutures and 1–2
cm anterior to the lambdoid sutures. Springs are then prepared for
implantation. For the majority of 4-month-old patients who fall within
the 0.6–0.7 range of cephalic index, 7 or 7.5 Newton Smartflex springs
are chosen. First, the spring opening angle is manually widened to
increase the distance between the footplates to 70–75 mm from the
“out-of-package” resting state of 55–65 mm. This step is critical to
maximize the potential skull expansion. Second, spring implantation
through the small scalp incision is facilitated by using a 4–0 Vicryl
suture to secure the footplates to within 1 cm of each other (Video
41.1). The spring is positioned such that the footplates engage with the
osteotomy notches and, while the dura is protected with a wide
malleable, the suture is cut with scissors releasing the spring. At this
point, it is important to confirm that the (1) long axis of the spring is
parallel to the strip craniectomy to ensure symmetric transverse
expansion of parietal bones; (2) springs are not interlocking such that
one spring prevents full opening excursion of the other; and (3) spring
footplates are firmly engaged with bone to prevent migration.
Generally, we like to see widening of the strip craniectomy by up to 1
cm at this point. Springs are then secured to the periosteum with a 4–0
Vicryl suture on each side where springs overlap.

41 7 9 Incision Closure
The skin is closed in two layers. The galea and dermis are captured in a
single pass using 3–0 Vicryl suture. Skin edges are approximated with a
running subcuticular 4–0 Monocryl suture. Subgaleal drains are not
used. The incision is covered with bacitracin and xeroform, and a
craniofacial head wrap is placed.

41 7 10 Postoperative Monitoring

Patients are monitored for one night on a regular inpatient surgical
floor. Surveillance in the intensive care unit is not necessary unless
otherwise warranted by patient comorbidities. In the rare instance that
a blood transfusion was required, a Complete Blood Count is collected
the following morning. Four-view skull X-rays are obtained prior to
discharge (Fig. 41.6). The head wrap is removed on postoperative day
two at home.

Fig. 41.6 Immediate postoperative (left) and 3-month follow-up (right) x-rays in a child who
was 5-months of age at the time of surgery, illustrating the degree of spring expansion and
resultant cranial expansion that can be achieved. CI has normalized from 0.69 to 0.82 during
this interval

The degree of cranial expansion observed 1-month postoperatively
serves as a gross clinical endpoint of expansion. If long-arm springs are
used, expansion may take longer (up to 2–3 months). Ongoing
remodeling of frontal bossing or occipital bulleting can be clinically
observed for several months, even after springs are removed.

41 8 Operative Technique: Spring emo al
41 8 1 Overview
Springs are removed 4 months after implantation to allow
consolidation of bone. X-ray is performed to document expansion width
and evaluate interpositional bone formation.

41 8 2 Patient Positioning
The surgical table is turned 180° away from the anesthesia team. The
patient is positioned supine with a Mayfield head rest. The scalp is with
scrubbed a chlorhexidine brush, and then infiltrated with local
anesthesia (0.25% bupivacaine with epinephrine 1:200,000). The
surgical field is sterilely prepped with povidone-iodine solution and
draped with a craniotomy drape.

41 8 3 Spring Removal
The existing scalp scar has often widened due to the transverse spring
forces on the soft tissues during distraction. As such, the scar is revised
with full-thickness incision. Cranial springs are easily accessed through
this incision. Metzenbaum scissors are used to bluntly separate the
galea from the springs. The springs are freed from adherent soft tissues
with an elevator. A Kirschner wire cutter is used to divide both springs
at their apex. At this point, spring segments should be easily
manipulated with minimal resistance from adherent soft tissues. Each
segment is removed separately with a simple two-step maneuver. First,
a heavy needle driver is used to rotate the spring segment in the axial
plane away from midline so that the footplate is retracted from its
subcranial position. Second, the spring is rotated in the coronal plane
away from the midline and then removed. These steps are repeated for
each leg. The incision is closed in the same manner as the initial
operation. Patients are discharged home the same day.

41 9 Complications and Pitfalls
SMC is a relatively safe procedure when performed by experienced
craniofacial surgeons. Nonetheless, there are potential serious

complications, particularly during the midline strip craniectomy. Lifethreatening bleeding is the most serious complication. Sizable bridging
veins between the dura and bone may be encountered and should be
addressed in controlled fashion. Wax is applied as bone is sequentially
removed to minimize bleeding and the risk of air embolism. Caution
must be exercised to avoid tearing as the dura is separated from
overlying bone without excessive traction.
The most common complications are minor, including delayed
wound healing and surgical site infection. Hardware removal or
additional surgical intervention are rarely necessary. There are several
potential pitfalls to avoid during spring placement. The number of
springs should be minimized to avoid overcrowding, spring
interlocking, undue soft tissue tension, and skin erosion. Generally, only
two springs are necessary to adequately widen the skull. In severe
cases, the surgeon can use longer, higher force springs and a narrower
strip craniectomy to maximize expansion without adding a third spring.
A third spring also increases the probability of spring dislodgement and
interlocking, both of which can result in inadequate expansion. Springs
should be secured to the periosteum with suture while ensuring the
planes of expansion do not overlap. Spring footplates are positioned
such that the long axis of the spring is parallel to the strip craniectomy
defect; otherwise, asymmetric cranial expansion will occur. Finally, thin
bone is less tolerant to the point-force of springs and can result in
erosion of the spring through parietal bone. When excessively thin bone
is noted intraoperatively, surgery is converted to strip craniectomy only
followed postoperative helmet molding.
