42 1 Introduction

Sagittal craniosynostosis (SCS) is the most common type of premature
cranial suture fusion, occurring in approximately 1 in 2000 people [1].
Historically, a wide variety of techniques have been used for surgical
correction of this malformation, with varying degrees of success and
risk to the patient depending on surgical timing, team composition and
experience, and technique [2–7]. Initial correction of craniosynostosis
was first described by Lane in 1892, but surgery for this fell out of favor
for a time due to high complication and mortality rates owing to long
surgeries and high blood loss early on. A more minimally invasive
technique was developed in the form of strip craniectomy, which
removed the affected suture, but frequently led to inadequate
correction. In the 1960s, Paul Tessier established the first
multidisciplinary craniofacial team in Paris, and was able to
demonstrate effective and safe open cranial vault remodeling
procedures [7].
Since this time, improvements in the surgical technique and
anesthetic management have made what was once a difficult surgery
with high risk into a relatively routine procedure at high-volume
craniofacial centers. At Seattle Children’s Hospital, the management of
craniosynostosis is provided by a multidisciplinary team, with patients
placed in a treatment pathway that sees them through initial
consultation to eventual discharge following surgical correction [8–10].
Corrective techniques are tailored to the age and affected suture(s) of
each patient [11]. For sagittal synostosis, patients younger than
9 months old are treated via a modified pi procedure; for those
diagnosed after 9 months old, total cranial vault expansion is the
preferred method of surgical correction.

42 2 Preoperative Evaluation
Initial diagnosis of isolated sagittal synostosis or multisuture synostosis
involving the sagittal suture involves a multidisciplinary team at our
institution. This team includes a pediatrician trained in craniofacial
deformity and syndromes, craniofacial plastic surgeon, and pediatric
neurosurgeon. When patients present with multisuture synostosis or
concern for an underlying syndromic cause, the team is expanded to

include geneticists, otolaryngologists, dentists, ophthalmologists, and
other needed specialties.
Diagnosis is typically made by physical examination by the primary
craniofacial team and confirmed by preoperative CT scan with 3D
reconstructions. This aids in diagnosis as well as in reconstruction
planning, and serves as a baseline to assess morphologic calvarial
change longitudinally. Preoperatively, consultation with an experienced
anesthesia team is of utmost importance. During this consultation, the
team reviews family and medical history, physical exam, and a thorough
preop laboratory workup is performed as well as discussion of
anesthetic risks. Critical preoperative lab workup includes CBC, CMP,
analysis of coagulation status, and preoperative type and screen for
transfusion planning.

42 3 Intraoperative Considerations
Operating room set up is an important consideration for streamlining
these surgeries. The OR team consists of a pediatric anesthesiologist
who is a member of the craniofacial group, typically a fellow, resident,
or CNA under their supervision, a craniofacial plastic surgeon and
pediatric neurosurgeon and their respective assistants, a surgical scrub
nurse with experience in these procedures, and one to two circulator
nurses. Patients are brought in under the care of the pediatric
anesthesia team. After induction, IV access is obtained with two large
bore peripheral catheters as well as an arterial line for continuous BP
monitoring. An endotracheal tube is placed (in those patients with
syndromic conditions and other craniofacial anomalies, often via
fiberoptic intubation) and secured with a silk circum-mandibular
suture. A continuous end tidal CO2 monitor is placed as well as a
precordial Doppler to monitor for air embolism during the case. All
pressure points are padded. Appropriate preoperative antibiotics are
infused and redosed at appropriate intervals throughout the case. For
cases of isolated sagittal synostosis, patients are typically positioned
prone with the head resting on a Mayfield horseshoe headrest in order
to facilitate middle and posterior vault expansion. However, depending
on which other sutures are affected and based on the preoperative plan
made by the reconstructive team, supine positioning may be necessary

(i.e., if patients also require fronto-orbital advancement or another
form of anterior/middle vault expansion). Padding around the face and
eyes is placed, and a precordial Doppler is secured in place and padded
prior to flipping the patient over.
The head of the bed is turned 90 degrees with the surgical team at
the head, anesthesia and scrub technician on either side of the bed, and
bulky equipment (suction towers, etc.) at the foot. Hyperventilation is
typically initiated to reduce intracranial pressure prior to the start of
the case. Cross-matched packed red blood cells and fresh frozen plasma
are available in the room prior to incision. Unless otherwise indicated,
transfusion of the first units of pRBCs and FFP is initiated around the
time the first burr hole is placed for intracranial access. Further blood
product administration is based on the anesthesia team’s careful
monitoring of vital signs, serial hematocrits, and other indicated labs.
Intraoperative autotransfusion is typically not utilized at our institution
given prior studies showing minimal benefit [12]. Intraoperative
steroids are typically used for nausea control by the anesthesia team
but are typically not required for specific intracranial effects.
Tranexamic acid is routinely used at our institution for open cranial
vault remodeling.
The head is fully shaved prior to positioning and corneal protectors
placed. A coronal incision is marked out in a zig zag pattern in order to
reduce tension on the scalp wound and camouflage the future scar (Fig.
42.1). The incision is infiltrated with local anesthetic. The patient is
prepped and draped in sterile fashion with the entire head, face, and
ears visible. The scalp is reflected in the subperiosteal plane using a
combination of monopolar cautery and blunt/sharp dissection. The
anterior flap includes the temporalis muscle, the posterior flap is
dissected laterally past the squamosal sutures (Fig. 42.2a). Following
exposure, the outline of the craniectomies is drawn onto the bone using
pencil (Fig. 42.2b). The neurosurgery team then undertakes burr hole
craniotomy for intracranial access.

Fig. 42.1 A zig-zag coronal incision is our preferred approach for exposure (left). The zig zag
incision facilitates easy closure (middle image) results in a less conspicuous scar after healing
(right)

Fig. 42.2 Initial exposure is completed in the subpericranial plane. A pericranial flap (left) can
be developed as a separate layer if needed (e.g., to cover shunt hardware). The skull exposure is
completed 2 cm anterior to the coronal sutures, just past the squamosal sutures laterally, and
just past the external occipital protuberance posteriorly (middle). Once the exposure is
completed, the craniotomies are marked using a sterile pencil (right). The craniotomy patterns
are based upon the morphology to be treated, but typically include parietal and occipital cuts,
as well as liberation of the central strip containing the fused sagittal suture

Burr holes are placed with an acorn drill bit parasagittally along the
marked strip of bone, typically three per side. These are then widened
with a Kerrison rongeur until a Penfield 3 can be used for epidural
dissection. Two additional burr holes are made on each side laterally in
the parietal bones. Following this, the acorn is swapped for a
craniotome drill bit to complete the parasagittal cuts along the marked
lines. Throughout this portion, the dura is protected under direct

visualization. The dura is stripped from the lambdoid sutures
bilaterally as well as the occipital bones. Wing osteotomies are made to
remove the occipital bones and the prior marked cuts are used to
remove the parietal bones bilaterally as well. Careful dissection is used
to free the midline sagittal strip of bone from the underlying dura,
taking care to protect the sagittal sinus underneath. Depending on the
degree of correction needed, the sagittal bone strip is either removed as
well or can be reshaped in situ using a Tessier rib bender. The dura is
thoroughly checked for any defects that might require repair, and these
are addressed in the appropriate fashion (Fig. 42.3a). At this point, the
craniofacial plastic surgery team proceeds with the reconstruction.

Fig. 42.3 Bur holes are drilled and a complete epidural dissection is completed. The
craniotomies are then completed and the bone flaps removed. The dura is then inspected to
verify its integrity (left). The bone flaps (middle) are then taken to the back table for
contouring. It is not uncommon to see evidence of intracranial hypertension, such as
thumbprinting of the bone flaps (right)

Reconstruction is achieved primarily off the surgical field on a back
table. The removed segments of the skull are reshaped using a
combination of radial osteotomies with a reciprocating saw for
aggressive out-fracturing or the Tessier rib bender for more gradual
correction. Prior to reshaping them, a particulate bone is harvested
from the endocranial surface with a cortical bone scraper. The ultimate
goal of recontouring is to achieve satisfactory biparietal widening,
occipital flattening, increase in vertex height, and shortening of AP
dimension. Once this is complete, the bone is secured in situ using a
combination of resorbable plates (KLS Martin SonicWeld ,
Jacksonville, FL) laterally and 3–0 PDS suture medially (Fig. 42.4) After
thorough irrigation, the harvested cortical bone particulates are mixed
with fibrin sealant and interposed in the gaps created by the expansion.

Throughout the procedure, hemostasis is achieved using a combination
of bone wax (particularly important during the initial scalp flap
advancement to stop bleeding from the calvarium), gel foam and
sponges soaked in thrombin, and liquid gel foam (applied liberally to
the dura to prevent microhemorrhages).

Fig. 42.4 (Left) Central strip recontouring to achieve appropriate vertex position and height,
(right) parietal and occipital bone flaps are contoured by creating radial osteotomies and
bending the done using rib benders. They are then affixed using resorbable plates and sutures.
The interpositional gaps created by the expansion are filled with cortical and particulate bone
graft mixed with fibrin sealant. No exposed dura should remain following grafting

Once reconstruction is complete, hemostasis is again verified and a
drain is placed. Typically, a single flat Jackson Pratt drain is placed
subgaleally in the posterior aspect of the wound bed and tunneled out
behind the ear and secured with suture. The team then turns their
attention to closure, with a typical layered scalp closure that
reapproximates the galea in interrupted fashion and then the skin with
running absorbable suture (Fig. 42.1b). Following this, the scalp is
examined to ensure adequate vascularization. Should excessive tension
on the scalp be a concern, regular slashes in the galea can be made in
order to provide scalp advancement, which may be more of a concern
in older children. The skin is cleaned and dried and antibiotic ointment
liberally applied to the incision . The patient is the carefully
repositioned supine and turned over to the anesthesia team for

extubation following removal of the suture securing the ET tube.
Occasionally, at the discretion of the anesthesia team depending on
procedure length and patient anesthetic tolerance, extubation may be
deferred immediately postop.

42 4 Postoperative Care
Following extubation, the patient is taken by the anesthesia and
surgical teams for an immediate postoperative head CT (Fig. 42.5),
again with 3D reconstructions included. This serves the dual purpose of
ensuring that there are no immediate postoperative concerns regarding
hematoma formation or intradural injury and serves as a new baseline
for longitudinal assessment of calvarial remodeling. The patient is then
transferred to the pediatric ICU for close monitoring and further
resuscitation if needed.

Fig. 42.5 (Left) Preoperative imaging demonstrating sagittal craniosynostosis with biparietal
narrowing and occipital constriction. (Right) Postoperative appearance after open cranial vault
expansion with parietal and occipital craniotomies, reshaping using radial osteotomies, central
strip recontouring to achieve appropriate vertex height, and placement of calvarial bone graft
into interpositional defects

There exists at our institution as part of the surgical pathway for
craniosynostosis patients a standardized postoperative order set [10].
This includes immediate postoperative CBC, INR, PT, PTT, fibrinogen
level, and electrolyte panel. Patients with hematocrits less than 25
postoperatively receive further blood products in the unit. CBC is
further checked following additional transfusion and the morning of
POD 1. JP drain output is carefully monitored, and the surgical team is

alerted for outputs greater than 50 cc/h for the first 2 h, then 100 cc/h
following this initial interval, which may indicate an active bleeding
process that may require surgical intervention. Continuous pulse
oximetry is performed while in the PICU, which may help to detect rare
delayed venous sinus embolism. Continuous isotonic IV fluids are
administered until the patient can tolerate sufficient PO intake, which is
encouraged as soon as possible following the operation. The head of
bed is adjusted initially to 30 degrees to promote resolution of
postoperative facial and scalp edema. Perioperative antibiotics are
continued for 24 h postop, and pain is closely monitored and controlled
using IV and PO medications. NSAIDs are typically avoided within the
first 24-h postoperatively, and a scheduled postoperative bowel
medication regimen is implemented.
Following 24 h of ICU monitoring, as long as there are no
contraindications, the patients are transferred to an acute care surgical
ward. Patients remain in the hospital until their JP drains are removed
(typically once outputs at 20 cc per day), their pain is controlled on a
PO regimen and they are tolerating feeds without bowel/bladder
issues, and their postoperative periorbital edema has improved to the
point where they are able to open one or more eyes. Typical length of
stay is usually 3–4 days in uncomplicated cases. Antibiotic ointment is
applied to the incision twice a day for a total of 7 days postoperatively.
No helmets are provided either for protection or remodeling in cases of
total vault reconstruction.
Longer term, the patients return for a 2–4-week postoperative
wound check. If no immediate issues are identified, they will then
follow-up at a 1-year interval with a repeat 3D reconstructed CT scan at
2-years postoperatively (Fig. 42.6). At this point, several issues are
evaluated, including skull shape and contour, presence of large
( 3 3 cm) calvarial defects, issues with scar formation/healing, and
any other concerns for an underlying syndromic cause that might
require further genetic testing if not already performed. Assuming that
there are no issues identified that might require surgical revision,
patients then have further follow-up with serial imaging at 2-years
postop, and at 5–6 years of age [10].

Fig. 42.6 Preoperative (top), immediate postoperative (middle) and 2-years postoperative
(bottom) three-dimensional computed tomographic images for a patient treated at 2 years of
age for sagittal craniosynostosis

43 Metopic Suture Synostosis:
Endoscopic Approach, Key Points for
the Neurosurgeons
Yusuke S. Hori1 and Mark R. Proctor1
(1) Department of Neurological Surgery, Boston Children’s Hospital,
Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA

Yusuke S Hori
Email: Yusuke.Hori@childrens.harvard.edu
Mark R Proctor (Corresponding author)
Email: Mark.Proctor@childrens.harvard.edu
Keywords Craniosynostosis – Endoscope-assisted repair – Metopic
synostosis

43 1 Background
Children with pathologic metopic craniosynostosis present with a
characteristic head shape known as trigonocephaly. This needs to be
distinguished from normal early closure of the metopic suture, as it
closes in many normal babies by 3 months of age, with either no
sequelae or just a simple ridge associated with a normal forehead
shape, which does not require treatment. To date, studies have
not shown a clear association between severity of trigonocephaly and
cognitive development [1], although several reports have shown that
patients with metopic synostosis and associated trigonocephaly may
develop cognitive impairment and behavioral disturbances [2, 3]. As a

definitive treatment, surgical correction is recommended not only to
improve appearance, but also because it has the potential to improve
the neurodevelopmental outcomes, although the data on this latter
point remains unclear [4].
The mainstay of the surgical treatment has been open surgery near
the maturation of skull shape development in the range of 8–
12 months, at which point, trigonocephaly correction requires a fairly
extensive and invasive procedure [5]. Endoscope-assisted repair was
introduced in the early 2000s, and studies have shown its safety and
effectiveness [6–8]. Jimenez et al. have reported the largest case series
with the mean estimated blood loss of 35 mL, mean operative time of
56 minutes, and the total transfusion rate of 4.3% [7]. Lajthia et al. have
reported the effectiveness of this procedure in patients with severe
trigonocephaly [8]. Furthermore, several studies have shown the
comparative results of open vs. endoscope-assisted repair [9–11]. The
results have demonstrated that endoscopic repair had significant better
perioperative outcomes including estimated blood loss, transfusion
rate, operative time, and hospital LOS [9, 10], while
maintaining comparable postoperative morphological results [11].

43 2 Institutional Experience at Boston
Children s Hospital
In our institution, we introduced endoscope-assisted metopic
craniosynostosis repair in 2006, and since then, over 130 cases have
been treated with this minimally invasive technique. The cumulative
results have shown its effectiveness in both safety and cosmetic
outcome. As a brief summary, our institutional data showed the mean
age was 14 weeks at the time of treatment with the mean weight of 6
kg. Approximately 80% of the patients were male and 20% were
female, similar to other large series [7]. Perioperatively, the transfusion
rate for the last 10 years was 6.7%, also comparable to the previously
reported rate [7]. Postoperatively, no patients experienced recurrence
of metopic synostosis requiring operative repair, with one minor
revision for a bony prominence that was drilled down for cosmetic
reasons.

43 3 Procedure
Our preferred age for treatment is 10–12 weeks, with a minimum
weight of 5 kg. We do not routinely obtain preoperative imaging,
although many patients present to our clinic with a CT scan, and on rare
occasions, we obtain one if there is question of a syndromic diagnosis.
The patient is taken to the operating room and two intravenous (IV)
lines and routine cardiorespiratory monitors are placed. General
endotracheal anesthesia is employed. We do not routinely use an a-line,
but often employ tranexamic acid to aid with hemostasis. Precordial
doppler to monitor for air embolism is routinely employed. A baseline
blood specimen is obtained to assess the hematocrit and hemoglobin,
which is repeated at the end of the case to assess the blood loss. The
patient is placed in a spine position, and the fused metopic suture is
confirmed by palpation for surgical planning. The incision is outlined,
directly at the hairline, and then, hair is clipped (Fig. 43.1a). Sterile
prep is performed with betadine scrub and paint. Standard surgical
drapes are applied (Fig. 43.1b). A single dose of antibiotics is
administered 30 min prior to the incision, and cefazolin is our
preferred antibiotic.

Fig. 43.1 Presurgical preparation. Incision is outlined (a) and standard surgical drapes are
applied (b)

After surgical time-out, local injection is performed using
bupivacaine with epinephrine (Fig. 43.2a). A small 5-mm incision is
placed at the edge of the preplanned incision site with a 15 blade
surgical scalpel (Fig. 43.2b). The incision is extended with a platinum
tipped microdissection needle to open in a bloodless fashion while
minimizing skin injury (Fig. 43.2c). The deeper layer is then explored
while preserving as much periosteum as possible (Fig. 43.2d), as it
seems helpful to minimize soft tissue disruption. The planned burr hole
site is cauterized at the midline, with further dissection performed
under the periosteum, which is elevated with a retractor. A small
midline burr hole is carefully created using the high-speed drill (Fig.
43.3a and b), and then expanded with curettes and Kerrison rongeurs
until an approximately 1 cm gap is achieved.

Fig. 43.2 Local injection with bupivacaine with epinephrine (a). A 5-mm incision is placed (b)
extended with a platinum tipped microdissection needle (c). Deeper layer is then explored
while preserving periosteum (d)

Fig. 43.3 A small burr hole is created using the high-speed drill (a). A tiny dural exposure is
observed at the center of the hole (b)

At this point, suture removal is directed towards the anterior
fontanelle using the rongeur, and a dissector is used to strip the
periosteum off the external surface of the bone to the fontanelle (Fig.
43.4a). A zero-degree endoscope is introduced to help dissect the dura
off the undersurface of the bone (Fig. 43.4b). After confirming that we
have reached the anterior fontanelle and the dura is sufficiently
stripped, bone-cutting scissors are used to complete the strip
craniectomy extending to the fontanelle (Fig. 43.4c–e).

Fig. 43.4 Stripping the periosteum off the external surface of the bone using dissector (a). A
zero-degree endoscope is introduced to help dissect the dura (b). Bone-cutting scissors (c) are
used to complete the strip craniectomy (d). Absorbable gelatin sponges are placed along the
removed suture (e)

Once the superior portion of the bone is removed, the suture
removal is next directed towards the inferior portion. Similar to the
superior site, the periosteum and dura are stripped off the
undersurface of the bone with a Penfield 1 dissector. Bone is initially
removed with a Kerrison rongeur, but as one dissects inferiorly the
bone rapidly becomes quite thickened (Fig. 43.5a) in most children and
is not easily amenable to cutting with scissors. After careful dissection
and coagulation of the midline emissary views, usually one on either
side of center, an ultrasonic bone aspirator is used to dissolve the bone
all the way down to the nasofrontal junction (Fig. 43.5b). At the
completion, the surgeon should confirm that the two frontal bones are
completely disconnected by physically moving them and being sure
they move independently (Fig. 43.6a). At the completion, a gap between
the frontal bones is observed with a width of approximately 1 cm.

Fig. 43.5 Thickened bone is typically observed inferiorly (a) and an endoscope-assisted
ultrasonic bone aspirator is used to dissolve the bone all the way down to the nasofrontal
junction (b)

Fig. 43.6 Confirming that the two frontal bones are completely disconnected by physically
moving them (a). Wound irrigation with betadine (b). Subcutaneous (c) and skin (d) layers are
closed with absorbable sutures

Absorbable gelatin sponges are placed along the removed suture to
help hemostasis. The wound is meticulously irrigated with bacitracin or
betadine, along with saline (Fig. 43.6b). After confirming hemostasis,
the incision is closed in subcutaneous (Fig. 43.6c) and skin (Fig. 43.6d)
layers with absorbable sutures. A sterile dressing and a pressure wrap
are applied. The patient is transferred to the anesthesia recovery room.

43 4 Postoperative Course
A hemoglobin and hematocrit is sent at the completion of the case, with
a typical hematocrit decrease of 7% comparing pre- vs. postoperative
specimens. A very low percentage of infants require transfusion as
described in our institutional experience section. The patient is
observed overnight on the neurosurgical floor. Pain control might
require a dose or two of narcotic, with IV morphine 0.1 mg/kg being
our preferred drug, but with rapid transition to acetaminophen, which
is the only discharge medication. The vast majority of patients are
discharged on postoperative day 1 after confirming that pain is well
controlled and oral intake is sufficient. Helmet fitting is performed 2–
4 days after surgery, with a goal of instituting helmet therapy by day 7.
The patient is followed up at the outpatient clinic in 1 month. The
family is informed that helmet therapy may continue until 1 year of age,
but the typical duration of the helmet therapy is less than 7 months.
Completion of helmet therapy is not a specified duration but based on
response.
As for any patient with synostosis, it is important that these
children be followed for at least 5 years. This corresponds to the
essential completion of brain growth, as brain weight and size reach
maturity at 5–6 years [12]. Routine follow-up should always include
annual head circumference measurement, and routine eye exams to
rule out papilledema. Although the reoperation rates for metopic
synostosis are exceedingly low, any child with synostosis is at risk for
refusion of the original suture, or other sutures, prior to full brain
maturity. Specific to metopic synostosis, the family and surgeon will
notice an indentation where the prominence had been over the first
year or two. The goal of the therapy in the first year is to achieve lateral
frontal growth and a normalized forehead shape (Fig. 43.7). It will still
appear slightly indented in the midline and have some slight angularity
at the release site at 1 year of age. This improves over the next few
years as the bone gap completely fills in and the surrounding frontal
bones thicken.

Fig. 43.7 Representative laser scan images demonstrating significant improvement of
trigonocephaly. Immediate postoperative (a, 3 days after the procedure) and 6-month follow-up
(b)

It is our experience that children with metopics synostosis tend to
have a slightly narrower forehead than the average population after
treatment, which this is true with both endoscopic and open
operations. This is why some surgeons have advocated for extreme
hypercorrection when they do a frontal orbital advancement [13]. That
said, children with this condition have slightly narrow facial features, so
that if you overly widen the forehead it actually appears to be a
mismatch between the forehead and frontal region, and in our view,
this is not advised.
For some forms of synostosis repair, it is the opinion of the authors
that the endoscopic outcomes are actually superior to the open cranial
reconstructions due to minimization of scar and excellent skull
morphology. Although the literature often notes very comparable
anthropometric outcomes for open and endoscopic procedures metopic
synostosis, and in our experience patient and family satisfaction rates
have been very high, we do believe that the open operations often
achieves a slightly wider forehead configuration. With that caveat, in
the authors’ experience, a family has never requested a repeat
operation after endoscopic metopic suture release, and they have been
very happy that they chose the minimally invasive technique.

43 5 Conclusion
Endoscope-assisted repair is a safe and effective treatment for metopic
synostosis. The estimated blood loss is much less and the operative
time is significantly shorter when compared with open procedures.
This procedure rarely require intra- or postoperative transfusion. The
cosmetic outcome of the treatment is comparable to open repair with
very high rates of family satisfaction. This chapter details the actual
procedure as a reference for those considering endoscope-assisted
metopic suture repair, which should be part of the treatment algorithm
for a complex craniofacial center.

44 Metopic Suture Synostosis: Open
Vault Surgery: Key Points for the
Neurosurgeon
Vijay M. Ravindra1, 2, 3, Barbu Gociman4 and John R. W. Kestle1

USA

Keywords Single-suture craniosynostosis – Metopic suture –

44 1 Introduction
Premature closure of the metopic suture accounts for about 15% of all
single-suture fusion cases [1–8]; it occurs in 1 in 2500 to 1 in 70,000
live births in the U.S [9, 10].Typically, closure of the metopic suture
occurs by 9 months of age, although the suture may remain patent until
2 years of age, which allows for growth of the frontal bones [11]. In
some cases, however, physiologic closure may occur by 3 months.

Premature fusion of the metopic suture results in restriction of the
normal growth of the frontal bones. When clinically significant fusion is
present, it is theorized to occur during intrauterine development,
although some fusion may occur after birth [12, 13]. Most diagnosed
cases of metopic synostosis are single-suture conditions without
syndromic involvement, although syndromic cases may appear in
conjunction with Opitz C syndrome, Say-Meyer syndrome, or Frydman
syndrome [10, 14, 15]. Most cases of metopic synostosis occur in males,
who make up 65–85% of cases [4, 16, 17].
The clinical presentation of metopic synostosis includes
trigonocephaly—a wedge-shaped frontal region with significant ridging
(Fig. 44.1), hypotelorism, and temporal narrowing [18]. It is important
to realize that not all patients who experience premature closure will
develop trigonocephaly. The wedge-shaped frontal bones also result in
prominence of the lateral supraorbital rims. With metopic synostosis,
the orbits are medialized in position, which results in hypotelorism. In
addition to the cosmetic effects of premature metopic suture fusion,
there is the possibility of cognitive deficits or elevated intracranial
pressure (ICP) [2, 19], and there are often intracranial abnormalities,
such as congenital anomalies, extra-axial fluid collections, and so-called
“copper beaten” skull [20].

Fig. 44.1 (a, b) Three-dimensional computed tomography (CT) reconstruction (left anterior
view, right superior view) demonstrating a mild metopic ridge with no significant narrowing of
the anterior cranial fossa; a child with this type of deformity does not require surgery. (c) In
contrast, a 3D CT reconstruction of a child with significant metopic synostosis and
trigonocephaly and axial brain (d) and bone (e) window images demonstrate an example of a
narrow anterior cranial fossa in metopic synostosis

44 2 Choice of Surgical Procedure Goal of
Surgery
The two main indications for surgical treatment of craniosynostosis are
to correct the skull shape for both cosmetic and psychosocial
considerations and to ensure there is adequate room for normal brain
growth and development. As with any craniosynostosis correction, the
goal is to achieve the most durable and best cosmetic result possible
while keeping the risk profile low. For mild cases, observation alone
may be warranted. Otherwise, when choosing the type of surgical
correction, the age of the patient is the most important factor. For

infants younger than 3 months of age, endoscopic correction with
subsequent prolonged helmet therapy may be applied. For older
children, open vault surgery is necessary. In this chapter, we focus on
the key aspects of open vault surgery, but knowledge of additional
treatment options is important.

44 3 Preoperative Evaluation Surgical
Planning
The diagnosis of metopic synostosis is most often made during a
clinical examination. Preoperative computed tomography with threedimensional (3D) reconstruction of the skull can be useful for
identification of additional suture involvement or preoperative
planning, but this imaging is not necessary for diagnosis and rarely
alters surgical plans [20]. Surgical planning is often performed in
conjunction with craniofacial surgeons as part of a multidisciplinary
team.
The decision to operate on affected children is based on the degree
of deformity of the forehead and anterior fossa and also on the risk of
raised ICP. At one extreme on the spectrum of severity of deformity,
there are children with a virtually normal forehead contour with a
simple ridge superimposed on the metopic suture. These children do
not need intervention (Fig. 44.1a and b). At the other extreme are
patients with severe trigonocephaly with reduced anterior fossa
volume (Fig. 44.1c–e) who clearly need corrective surgery. Between
these two scenarios, there are various degress of deformity, and
surgeons vary in their threshold for suggesting corrective surgery.
Surgery for mild deformity has been advocated [21, 22] but is
controversial [23, 24]. Birgfeld et al. [25] proposed some criteria to
differentiate between true metopic synostosis and a simple metopic
ridge. They suggested that the relationship between the lateral frontal
bone and lateral orbit is helpful in distinguishing the two and that CT
can be helpful not to confirm suture closure but rather to investigate
other characteristics of metopic craniosynostosis including upsloping
of the superior orbital rim, absence of pulled anterior fontanelle,

position and shape of lateral frontal bone, frontal bone tangent to
midline, and orbital/intraorbital narrowing.
Generally, patients with single-suture synostosis demonstrate a low
rate of elevated ICP, and the mean ICP for children with metopic
craniosynostosis in a study by Kalmar et al. [26] was 12.5 mmHg,
significantly lower than in their unicoronal or sagittal counterparts; in
addition, no children had an ICP measurement of ≥20 mmHg. In this
study, including children with single and multisuture synostosis with
syndromic and nonsyndromic disease, the authors found that
syndromic status, older age at intervention, and multiple suture
involvement were associated with elevated ICP. Although the
relationship among bony abnormality, ICP, and neurocognitive outcome
has been questioned [27], Starr et al. [28] found that children with
metopic synostosis had neurodevelopmental scores 0.9–4.5 points
worse than those of children with sagittal synostosis. Similarly, Baird et
al. [29] found that children with metopic suture have the highest rate of
cognitive impairment among the single-suture synostoses. For further
detailed discussion of these issues and the indications, see Chap. 8.
If there is no concern for high ICP and the child presents outside the
window for endoscopic release, then open vault surgery is typically
delayed until the child reaches at least 6–12 months of age. This allows
the circulating blood volume in the child to increase and enables the
child to deal better with the stress of a cranial vault operation [30]. All
children undergoing cranial vault remodeling should be prepared for
blood transfusion; family is given the option to donate before surgery in
most cases.

44 4 Positioning
For open cranial vault remodeling surgery, the patient is placed supine
on a horseshoe headrest with even pressure distributed through the
scalp (Fig. 44.2). A bicoronal incision, which can be linear, wavy, or
zigzag, is planned. Skin preparation is undertaken well behind the
coronal incision posteriorly and anteriorly/inferiorly to the eyebrow
and to the skin of the upper eyelids. The use of 5% povidone-iodine
ophthalmic ophthalmic solution allows prepping near the eyebrows
with corneal guards. Extending the prep inferiorly helps post-

correction visualization of the fronto-orbital, supraorbital advancement
by allowing full view of the structures from an anterior, lateral, and
superior view after reconstruction is completed [30].

Fig. 44.2 Photograph (superior view) of a child with trigonocephaly. Characteristic findings
include a frontal keel, bitemporal narrowing, coronal sutures displaced anteriorly (not
pictured), compensatory bulging of the parieto-occipital region, bizygomatic narrowing, and
posterior displacement of the superolateral orbital rim (not pictured)

44 5 Blood Loss
Standard measures should be taken to minimize blood loss during
cranial vault surgery. Adequate intravenous access with accurate
monitoring of blood loss is essential to safe reconstruction. The use of
central venous access and precordial Doppler ultrasound placement is
at the discretion of the pediatric anesthesia provider and surgical team.
Significant bleeding may occur during scalp incision and
osteotomies. Meticulous attention to hemostasis is important to
minimize the need for transfusion. A needle tip Bovie electrocautery
can be used to complete the scalp incision and elevate the scalp flap to
prevent blood loss. The use of tranexamic acid can decrease the rate of
transfusion in cranial vault remodeling [31].

44 6 Bifrontal Craniotomy
The scalp is elevated in the subgaleal plane as an anterior flap and a
posterior flap. The anterior flap dissection is carried on to
approximately 2 cm from the brow. A large anteriorly based pericranial
flap can then be elevated based on the supraorbital and supratroclear
arterial blood supply. The flap is elevated past the brow, into the orbits.
At the end of surgery, this flap will help to cover the entire
reconstructed anterior cranial vault and provide good blood supply to
promote bony healing (Fig. 44.3). The bony portion of the procedure
begins with the neurosurgical team performing a bifrontal craniotomy.
The posterior margin is just behind the coronal sutures. Anteriorly, the
craniotomy cut goes across the inferior frontal region, leaving a
supraorbital bar at least 1 cm in width attached to the orbits (Fig. 44.4).
Burr holes are placed at the temporal regions bilaterally, and in the
midline posterior to the coronal suture and adjacent to the midline
anteriorly, just above the orbital bar. The burr holes should be placed so
that the orbital bar is spared in its entirety to facilitate the
reconstruction. Dural separation is then carefully performed through
these burr holes using Penfield dissectors. The dura may be quite
adherent under the normal coronal sutures, and if dissection from one
direction is difficult, another burr hole and approach to the adherent
area should be attempted. In addition, there is frequently in-folding and
invagination of the dura into the metopic ridge and a midline ridge on
the inner table of the skull just above the orbital bar. All of these should
be carefully dissected. It is very common to find a pair of large diploic
veins low down, near the orbital bar on either side of the midline. If
these bleed, the area should be packed with surgical foam while the
craniotomy is opened. Finally, great care should be taken in dissecting
the dura and sinus from the bone at the posterior margin of the
craniotomy. Two burr holes, one on either side of the midline, may be
needed to do this safely. Once the dura is clear, the craniotomy is cut
circumferentially and elevated from posterior to anterior. As it is
elevated, the dura should be visualized and bleeding points coagulated.
An approximately 5-cm-wide parietal craniotomy is then made. This
allows for complete reshaping of the anterior vault and provides ample

bone graft for the reconstruction. In the unlikely event of a dural tear,
primary closure can usually be done with an absorbable 4–0 suture.

Fig. 44.3 Dissected pericranial flap (superior view). This flap can be useful to cover the entire
reconstructed anterior cranial vault and provide good blood supply to promote bony healing

Fig. 44.4 Intraoperative photographs after reflection of the scalp demonstrating the margins of
cranial bone removal. (a) Anteriorly, the craniotomy cut goes across the inferior frontal region
(marked line indicating the delineation between the frontal bone and supraorbital bar). (b) A
supraorbital bar about 1 cm in width attached to the orbits (lateral view). (c) Superior view
demonstrating the posterior aspect of the craniotomy well behind the coronal suture and

parietal bone to facilitate reconstruction and remodeling (marked line delineating the posterior
aspect of the bone removal)

The dura is then dissected from the floor of the anterior fossa and
the anterior aspect of the middle fossa bilaterally. In the midline, the
dura should be elevated down to the nasofrontal suture (Fig. 44.5).
Dissection of the periorbita of the supraorbital rim is carried out and
extended at least 1–1.5 cm off the orbital roof bilaterally. Next, a sagittal
saw or a piezoelectric bone cutter is used to create an osteotomy in the
orbital roof from medial to lateral. Very gentle retraction is placed on
the frontal lobe dura and periorbita. Typically, no augmentation for ICP
is needed or recommended at this point. The osteotomy is extended
laterally to the greater wing of the sphenoid bone. In the midline, the
osteotomy is completed anterior to the foramen cecum with a small
osteotome or the piezoelectric bone cutter, and the orbital bar is
removed (Fig. 44.6).

Fig. 44.5 (a) Intraoperative photograph (anterior view) demonstrating exposure of the dura to
the level of the nasofrontal suture and orbital contents after removal of the frontal bone
bilaterally and the orbital bandeau. (b) Lateral photograph demonstrating the inferior aspect of
the bone removal as well as clear exposure of the orbital contents indicating the amount of
bone removal needed for full mobilization of the orbital bandeau and bone removal well behind
the coronal suture over the parietal dura. (c) Superior view showing the entire extent of frontal
and parietal craniotomies

Fig. 44.6 Intraoperative photographs demonstrating the removed bony segments from the
frontal bone and orbital bandeau (a, front view) and supraorbital bar/orbital bandeau (b,
superior view)

44 7 Reconstruction
44 7 1 Fronto-Orbital Advancement Technique
The goals of the reconstruction are to increase the volume of the
anterior cranial fossa by advancing and widening the forehead and to
reshape the orbits. This is achieved by straightening and widening the
orbital bar. To straighten the bar, the inner table is removed just lateral
to the level of the lateral orbital wall, which makes the bone more
malleable and allows for reshaping. The supraorbital bar can be split at
the midline and then reshaped and widened with an interposition bone
graft to correct the hypotelorism. The orbits are burred as needed to
achieve a harmonious and symmetrical shape (Fig. 44.7). Prior to
reattachment of the reconstructed orbital bar, barrel staving of the
temporal bone bilaterally is done to further enlarge the anterior cranial
fossa in the transverse dimension. The staves are made approximately
2 cm in width and 4 cm in length and greenstick out-fractured to
preserve their viability (Fig. 44.8). The supraorbital bar is advanced
approximately 1–2 cm anteriorly from its original position and secured
to the temporal bone and the lateral orbital walls at the level of the
frontozygomatic sutures using a resorbable plating system. Any gaps
present at the level of the bar fixation points are filled with well-fitted
bone grafts to prevent dislodgement. No plating is done at the level of

the nasal bone. The bar is placed over the nasal bone for a overlap
distance of approximately 2 mm in the vertical dimension. The inner
table of the bar is removed with a burr at the level of the overlap to
prevent any significant prominence (Figs. 44.8 and 44.9).

Fig. 44.7 Intraoperative photographs (a, front view; b, superior view) demonstrating the
technique of splitting supraorbital bar at the midline and reshaping and widening it with an
interposition bone graft to correct the hypotelorism

Fig. 44.8 Inset of the supraorbital bar showing the increase in volume at the level of the
anterior cranial fossa (a, anterior view; b, lateral view; c, superior view). The bar is advanced
approximately 1–2 cm anteriorly and secured using a resorbable plating system to the temporal
bone and the lateral orbital walls at the level of the at the frontozygomatic sutures. Any gaps
present at the level of the bar fixation points are filled with well-fitted bone grafts to prevent
dislodgement. No plating is done at the level of the nasal bone. In b, the barrel staving
technique of the temporal bone bilaterally is done to further enlarge the anterior cranial fossa
in transverse dimension. The staves are approximately 2 cm in width and 4 cm in length and
greenstick out-fractured to preserve their viability

Fig. 44.9 Intraoperative photographs of case 1 (a, anterior view; b, lateral view; c, superior
view) demonstrating the technique of splitting the frontal bone flap and rotating the halves to
obtain a broader contour of the forehead. The contour of the frontal bone can be achieved with
a bone bender or radial osteotomies (if the bone is too rigid). To enlarge the anterior cranial
vault, the parietal bone flaps are split at the level of the diploic space using osteotomes. The
resulting bony pieces are used to reconstruct the anterior cranial vault by enlarging it and
giving it a well-proportioned shape. All of the pieces are secured using resorbable plates and
screws, and no defects are left ungrafted

The frontal and parietal bone flaps are typically split down the
middle. Each half of the frontal bone flap is rotated to obtain a broader
contour of the forehead. The contour of the frontal bone can often be
achieved with a bone bender in younger patients, but if the bone is too
rigid then radial osteotomies can be performed. To enlarge the anterior
cranial vault, the parietal bone flaps are split at the level of the diploic
space using osteotomes. The resulting bony pieces are used to
reconstruct the anterior cranial vault by enlarging it and giving it a
well-proportioned shape. All of the pieces are secured using resorbable
plates and screws, and no defects are left ungrafted. Every
reconstruction is unique based on the malleability or rigidity of the
bone flaps and the size and quality of the split calvarial bone grafts, as
illustrated by the three different cases presented (Figs. 44.9, 44.10, and
44.11). An alternative to split calvarial bone grafting is filling of the
bony defects with inner table bone shavings obtained by using a burr or
a bone scraper. It is imperative to reflect the scalp over the correction
intermittently to ensure the desired cosmetic result is being achieved,
specifically at the end of the correction (Fig. 44.12).

Fig. 44.10 Intraoperative photographs of case 2 (a, anterior view; b, lateral view; c, superior
view) demonstrating the potential reconstruction based on the malleability of the bone flaps
and the size and quality of the split calvarial bone grafts

Fig. 44.11 Intraoperative photographs of case 3 (a, anterior view; b, lateral view; c, superior
view) demonstrating another unique reconstruction based on the malleability of the bone flaps
and the size and quality of the split calvarial bone grafts

Fig. 44.12 Intraoperative photograph demonstrating skin closure over the newly contoured
bone structure of the frontal bones and orbital bandeau

44 7 2 Single-Segment Reconstruction
Fearon et al. [32] described an alternative method of remodeling the
frontal bone using a single-segment bone flap (Fig. 44.13). The
reconstruction method involves harvesting an appropriately sized
biparietal bone flap after measurement of the nonhair-bearing
forehead skin to correctly size the repair.

Fig. 44.13 Image demonstrating single-piece reconstruction using a biparietal harvested bone
flap for re-creating the supraorbital bandeau and frontal bone. The technique described by
Fearon et al. [32] involves rotation of the harvested parietal flap 180 degrees, so the posterior
aspect of the flap becomes the inferior aspect of the supraorbital/frontal bone. (From Fearon
JA, Ditthakasem K, Castro Garcia J, Herbert M. Adandoning the Supraorbital Bandeau in Anterior
Craniosynostosis Repairs, for a Single-Segment Reconstruction. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2018
Sep;142 (3):334e-41e)

The exposure reaches the level of the supraorbital rims, but no
intraorbital dissection is necessary. Once the scalp is reflected using a
coronal incision, further donor-site inspection is required to harvest
the most appropriately shaped bone graft that will match the curvature
for reconstructing the forehead as a single unit. On the basis of their
experience, Fearon et al. [32] noted that this often comes from the
posterior half of the parietal bone.
A frontal craniotomy is performed, and the low supraorbital region
is excised to the level of the floor of the anterior fossa; the orbital roof is
left undisturbed. All bone removed is then split on the back table, and
forehead reconstruction proceeds with fixation of the biparietal bone
flap (Fig. 44.12), which is often rotated 180 degrees, so the posterior
aspect of the harvested flap becomes the most inferior portion of the
supraorbital/frontal bone. The flap is secured in the midline with a Ushaped suture that is secured through two holes in the glabella, and the

lateral outer aspects of the donor flap are advanced on either side. The
single-piece reconstruction replaces the bandeau and frontal bone with
the most anterior inferior aspect, giving rise to the new supraorbit.
After the new frontal bone has been secured in place, removal of bone
in the temporal region is undertaken, which permits bone-to-bone inset
of the posterolateral aspects of the new frontal bone, similar to the
traditional fronto-orbital advancement procedure described above.
Once the contour and reconstruction are cosmetically suitable, the
posterior parietal bone donor site is reconstructed with the former
frontal bones, supraorbital bone, and split calvarial grafts. The
outcomes for this method are comparable with the traditional
supraorbital bandeau method with respect to surgical time, blood loss,
and complication rates, and there is some evidence of lower
reoperation rates (0 vs. 2.7%) and improved aesthetic outcomes [32].

44 8 Postoperative Care
The most immediate concern after surgery is acute blood loss anemia.
Serum hemoglobin is usually drawn 4–6 h postoperatively and the next
morning. Transfusion thresholds may vary, but a hemoglobin level less
than 8 g/dL should trigger consideration of transfusion. The presence
of significant periorbital edema is normal between postoperative days
1 and 3 and is often accompanied with emesis and fever. The most
common postoperative complication is fever [33], and this is usually
self limiting.
When absorbable cranial plating systems are used, there can be
painless scalp swelling approximately 9–12 months after surgery that
coincides with plate resorption [34]. Reassurance should be provided
to the family during this time.

44 9 Complications
44 9 1 Intraoperative Sagittal Sinus In ury
Injury to the superior sagittal sinus should be extremely rare if dural
dissection and craniotomy cuts are done carefully. Bleeding from the
sinus can be mitigated with gentle pressure and often closed primarily
with a suture. Care should be taken while doing this to avoid air

embolus, so the head should be flat, and the assistant should provide
irrigation while the suture is placed. More severe bleeding may require
placement of a dural patch, or in extreme circumstances, sacrifice of the
sinus. Ligation of up to one third of the anterior sagittal sinus can be
performed with low risk of venous infarction but should be reserved for
the extremely rare severe sinus injury that cannot be controlled by
other means.

44 9 2 Postoperative Infection
Infection is an uncommon complication after craniosynostosis surgery,
with mean infection rates reported to be 2% [33], but should be
identified and dealt with in a similar manner as other postcraniotomy
infections. Superficial or incisional infections may be treated with local
wound care and antibiotic therapy, but deep infection may require open
debridement. If there is concern for or evidence of osteomyelitis, then
removal of the flap is required with prolonged antibiotic therapy.
Although bone flap removal is not ideal, a period of observation is a
reasonable option before planning any secondary flap replacement or
reconstruction because bone gaps may fill in on their own in very
young children.

44 9 3 Poor Postoperative Cosmetic Outcome
The long-term success with open reconstruction is more than 90% in
patient with nonsyndromic metopic synostosis [16, 35–39]. The
cosmetic outcomes are highly dependent on the severity of the
preoperative deformity. Overall, rates of new metopic ridging or
progression are very low, although reoperation may be necessary [40].
An additional source for potential reoperation arises from temporal
hollowing, which can occur in 15% of patients [41].
Decisions to intervene or reoperate should be made with the
knowledge that each additional surgery carries an increased risk of
dural injury, vascular injury, bleeding, and potential for no appreciable
improvement in cosmetic deformity. Ideally, a shared, multidisciplinary
decision-making approach should occur.
As mentioned above, the use of a single-segment bone flap has been
described with similar results to conventional fronto-orbital
advancement [32, 42]. At present, the selection of the method for

reconstruction should be based on surgeon experience and outcomes
because further head-to-head study is needed to compare these
techniques.

44 10 Conclusion
Premature closure of the metopic suture is usually a single-suture
pathology but rarely can be seen in the setting of syndromic conditions.
Open vault surgery is typically performed after 6 months of age with
the goal of correcting the associated trigonocephaly, hypotelorism, and
temporal narrowing with abnormal shape of the supraorbital rim. Open
surgical treatment usually includes a 1-cm fronto-orbital advancement
with recontouring of the frontal bones and widening of the orbital rim.
An alternative single-segment reconstruction has been proposed.
Correction should be tailored to the nature of the deformity. Careful
neurosurgical dissection of the dura and hemostasis will avoid many of
the potential complications that might otherwise occur.

45 Unicoronal Suture Synostosis:
Endoscopic Approach for the
Neurosurgeons
David F. Jimenez1, 2
(1) Department of Neurosciences, Pediatric Neurosurgery, El Paso
Children’s Hospital, El Paso, TX, USA
(2) Neurosurgery Department, University Medical Center, El Paso, TX,
USA

Keywords Craniosynostosis – Coronal – Suture – Dystopia –
Endoscopy – Strabismus

45 1 Introduction
Premature closure of the coronal suture leads to a number of significant
deformations of the facial and cranial skeleton. The phenotypic clinical
presentation includes the following findings:
1. Disorbitism in the primary form of vertical dystopia.
2. Strabismus.
3. Ipsilateral frontal plagiocephaly.
4. Nasal tip deviation to the contralateral side.
5. Ipsilateral proptosis.

6. Cranial scoliosis and sagittal cranial and facial imbalance.
Altogether, these findings present the neurosurgeon and his/her
craniofacial team with a major treatment challenge. The classical and
common way of treating this condition is with an orbitofrontal
advancement, which is typically done between the ages of 9 and
12 months. The problem with this approach, in my view, is that the
cranial-facial skeleton settles in the specific level of deformity and
correction of the aforementioned issues become extremely difficult. For
example, repositioning of the entire orbital osseous complex to correct
the vertical dystopia becomes an impossibility. Simply moving forward
the supraorbital rim and forehead does not address the sagittal
imbalance, nasal deviation, or vertical dystopia. On the contrary,
releasing the stenosed suture at an early age allows the brain to correct
all of these complex deformities, as will be shown in this chapter.

45 2 Procedure
Given the simple and uncomplicated nature of the endoscopic release of
the stenosed coronal suture, minimal preoperative preparation is
needed. The diagnosis is simply a clinical one and no CT scan, X-rays, or
unnecessary radiation exposure to the patient is needed if the patient
has the classical phenotype presentation. The only laboratory value to
obtain is a hemoglobin/hematocrit level after the patient is placed
under anesthesia. No arterial or central venous lines are placed. No
Foley is used, and only one or two peripheral intravenous lines are
inserted. The table is rotated 180° from the anesthesiologist and the
head is placed on a cerebellar horseshoe headrest. Lubricated corneal
shield protectors are placed under the eyelids. A precordial Doppler is
placed over the heart to auscultate for possible venous air emboli
during the procedure. The head is slightly rotated to the contralateral
side in order to expose the entire affected suture (Fig. 45.1). A small
strip of hair is shaved at the proposed incision site. The incision is made
half way between the anterior fontanelle and the squamosal suture
immediately in front of the ear (Fig. 45.2). The head and face are
prepped with povidone-iodine solution, and a single dose of antibiotics
is given 30 min prior to skin incision.

Fig. 45.1 A patient with right coronal synostosis is placed on the cerebellar horseshoe
headrest with the head slightly rotated to the left side for improved surgical access

Fig. 45.2 The location of the incision is placed midway between anterior fontanel and pterion.
(a) The stenosed coronal suture (c) is denoted by the dotted line. A strip of bone (4 mm width)
shown and marked (b), is located behind the stenosed suture and must reach the squamosal
suture (d). (e) Denotes the precordial Doppler

The incision ( 2 cm) is made with the monopolar electrocautery
unit using the needle tip set at 10 W on the cut mode. Once the dermis
is opened, the rest of the opening through the galea is done using the
coagulation mode at 20 W of energy. A rhinoplasty hand held lighted
retractor is used to elevate the galea and develop the subgaleal plane
towards the anterior fontanelle. A zero-degree rigid endoscope can also
be used to perform this dissection. A craniotome with a 7 mm
perforator is used to create a burr hole at the incision. A Woodson
elevator is used to dissect the dura around the burr hole. A 4 mm
Kerrison rongeur is used to remove bone towards the fontanelle for

about a centimeter. This maneuver allows the introduction of a 30°
rigid endoscope with the angled end aimed at the bone. A small, 7
French suction is inserted and advanced in tandem with the endoscope,
developing the epidural plane until reaching the fibers of the anterior
fontanelle (Fig. 45.3). Using bone biting pituitary-like rongeurs, a 4 mm
osteotomy is created by removing the bone, in a piece-meal fashion
under visualization. Once the frontal bone is released from the parietal
bone, the diplo is cauterized with suction coagulator. Gentle
manipulation of the frontal and parietal bones will demonstrate release
and disconnection of these bones (Fig. 45.4).

Fig. 45.3 Endoscopic view of the anterior fontanelle (a). After dissecting the epidural plane
medially. The frontal bone (b) and parietal bone (c) are visualized. The dura (d) and the
section-dissector (e) are also seen

Fig. 45.4 The osteotomy/craniectomy (O) has been extended all the way to the anterior
fontanelle. The arrows denote the edges of the osteotomy. The frontal bone (F) has been fully
detached from the parietal bone (P) medially

Once the medial release has been done, attention is directed
towards the greater wing of the sphenoid bone and pterion. The
subgaleal plane is developed above the temporalis muscle with blunt
dissection using a dissector (Fig. 45.5). The endoscope is inserted
under the bone and advanced toward the greater wing of the sphenoid
(Fig. 45.6), pterion, and the open squamosal suture is identified (Fig.
45.7). The temporalis muscle can be elevated and mobilized from the
temporal and parietal bones using the 1 Penfield dissector. The bone
biting rongeur is used to create a 4 mm osteotomy all the way down
past the squamosal suture (Fig. 45.8). This completes the separation of
the fronto-orbital complex from the parietal bone (Fig. 45.9). The
diploic space is coagulated using suction electrocautery in order to
obtain full homeostasis. Surgiflo is sprayed along the osteotomy. The
galea is closed with 4.0 monocryl suture. The skin is sealed with
Mastisol and Steri-strips, which are removed 6 days later.

Fig. 45.5 Having completed the osteotomy medially from the fontanelle, attention is directed
towards the pterion. A right endoscope is on the surgeon’s left hand, and a dissector is used to
develop the epidural space with the right hand. The assistant elevates the scalp with a lighted
retractor

Fig. 45.6 Endoscopic view of the greater wing of the sphenoid (S), the dura of the frontal lobe
(F) and temporal lobe (L). The sphenoid wing must be first identified as a primary landmark
prior to moving the endoscope posteriorly to look for the squamosal suture

Fig. 45.7 The endoscope has moved posteriorly and inferiorly. The open squamosal suture (S)
is identified as pointed by the arrows

Fig. 45.8 The osteotomy (O) is taken to and past the squamosal suture (SS) to make sure that
the frontal and parietal bones have been fully disarticulated

Fig. 45.9 Immediate postoperative lateral skull radiograph shows the 4–6 mm osteotomy (O)
extending from the anterior fontanelle to the pterion

The patient is admitted to the hospital for a 23-h observation period
and discharged the next morning. Pain is controlled with alternating
doses of acetaminophen and ibuprofen every 3 h for 3 days. On postop
day 4, the patient is scanned for a postoperative cranial orthosis, which
is manufactured the same day and fitted on the following day. The
patient wears the cranial orthosis until correction of the vertical
dystopia, advancement of the ipsilateral supraorbital rim, and nasal
deviation corrects, usually 6–9 months. The last to correct is the frontal
plagiocephaly, which may take several years to fully correct.

45 3 Outcomes
We have the longest and largest series of unicoronal synostoses treated
with endoscopic assisted, minimally invasive techniques. The series
expands over 26 years (1996–2023) and comprises a total of 182
patients. There were 112 females (69.3%) and 70 males (30.7%). The
median age of the surgery was 4.1 months (0.5–10 months). Median
estimated blood loss for the entire cohort was 15 mL. There were no

intraoperative blood transfusions and only one patient was transfused
postoperative for a 0.7% transfusion rate. The mean surgical time was
43 min. All patients were discharged the morning following the surgery.
No patient required the surgery to be converted from endoscopic to an
open procedure. Anthropometric analysis with the craniofacial
software analysis from the cranial orthosis unit demonstrated marked
and significant improvement of the preoperative deformities. Fifty one
percent of the patients demonstrated 100% correction of the vertical
dystopia and over 2/3 if the patients had over 80% correction of this
major deformity (Figs. 45.10, 45.11, 45.12, 45.13, 45.14, 45.15, 45.16,
and 45.17). Eighty one percent of the patients presented with sagittal
deviation and cranial scoliosis. Following surgery at a 2-year follow-up,
77% of the patients achieved 100% correction, 4% of the patients
achieved correction between 80% and 90%, 8% of the patients
achieved 70%, and 12% of the patients achieved less than 70%
correction. There were no mortalities. Strabismus is a very common
presenting finding and in our patient cohort, 84.3% of the patients
presented with strabismus (Figs. 45.18, 45.19, 45.20, 45.21, 45.22,
45.23, 45.24, 45.25, and 45.26). At 3-year follow up, only 3.7% of the
patients required strabismus correction surgery. This means that there
was an 88.9% correction of the strabismus with a simple craniectomy
done at an early age.

Fig. 45.10 Patient A preoperative photograph of the 3-month-old female with left coronal
craniosynostosis and severe vertical dystopia affecting the left eye/orbit

Fig. 45.11 Patient A 2 years postoperatively, the same patient shows that the orbits have
realigned along the horizontal exo-endocanthal axis after endoscopic release

Fig. 45.12 Patient B 4-month-old male with right coronal synostosis and severe vertical
dystopia

Fig. 45.13 Patient B already at 6 months, he demonstrates significant inferior displacement of
the right orbit and improvement of the dystopia

Fig. 45.14 Patient B, 3 years after surgery, the patient demonstrates complete realignment of
the eyes along the horizontal axis and no vertical dystopia

Fig. 45.15 Patient C 2-month-old female with left sided coronal synostosis and vertical
dystopia

Fig. 45.16 Patients C, 1 year after surgery demonstrates a complete correction of the dystopia

Fig. 45.17 Patient C, 2.5 years after surgery continues to show complete and persistent vertical
dystopia correction

Fig. 45.18 Patient D, 10-week-old male presenting with right coronal craniosynostosis and
right eye exotropia

Fig. 45.19 Patient D, 1 year following endoscopic release of the right coronal suture. The
strabismus has fully corrected without the need for surgical corrections

Fig. 45.20 Patient E, 9-week-old male with right coronal synostosis and left exotropia

Fig. 45.21 Patient E, 1 year after surgery patient shows complete correction of the strabismus
without the need for ocular surgery

Fig. 45.22 Patient F, 10-week-old male with right coronal synostosis and right exotropia

Fig. 45.23 Patient F, 4 years after endoscopic craniectomy, no strabismus, no ocular surgery

Fig. 45.25 Patient G, 6-years postendoscopic surgery the patient has fully corrected the

Fig. 45.26 Patient G, 16 years after surgery shows no dystopia, strabismus or midsagittal
imbalance correction

45 4 Discussion

Presented in this chapter are the results treating patients with
unicoronal craniosynostosis using minimally invasive techniques. This
series is the longest (26 years) and the largest (182) reported in the
literature. The basic underlying principles supporting this approach are
simple. Brain growth doubles in size in the first 6 months. Average
brain weight at birth is 400 g, at 6 months the weight doubles to 800 g.
This extremely rapid brain growth phase provides an opportunity for
the brain to reshape the cranial and facial skeleton once the root cause
of the problem is removed by fully releasing the stenosed suture. The
results of this series prove that to be the case. Once the suture is
released, the ipsilateral frontal lobe, which has been retained in a
posterior and superior position in relation to the contralateral lobe, is
allowed to resume its normal and preferred position. The brain
advances forward and inferiorly. As such, the forehead and supraorbital
rim move forward. The orbit moves forward and inferiorly, thereby
correcting the sagittal imbalance and cranial scoliosis. The goal of the
fronto-orbital advancement surgery is to move the ipsilateral forehead
and supraorbital rim about 2–3 cm forward. We have found out that the
same can be done with the endoscopic procedure and cranial orthosis
without having to do major open surgery (Fig. 45.27a–c).

Fig. 45.27 (a) Immediate skull ray of a patient with right coronal synostosis who underwent
and endoscopic 6 mm craniectomy. Notice the elevation of the right orbital roof in relation to
the left. (b) 7 weeks post-surgery, the lateral radiograph shows internal fronto-orbital
advancement of 11 mm. The right orbital roof has lowered. (c) 16 weeks after surgery, the
suturectomy has increased to 3.1 cm and both orbital roofs have aligned without the need for a
front-orbital advancement

Furthermore, preliminary unpublished data show there is a mild to
moderate elevation of the intracranial pressure which normalizes
immediately following the craniectomy. Fundoscopic examination in
our patients preoperatively is showing significant abnormalities to
include segmental papilledema and retinal vascular abnormalities,
which resolve as early as 2 months postoperatively.
Neuropsychological testing done before and after surgery show all
of our patients to be average or above average. We have found no
underperformers or abnormal patients. We believe that short surgical
times (43 min) with minimal exposure to general anesthesia, excellent
blood pressure control, and brain perfusion pressures and lack of need
for significant blood transfusions (as in calvarial vault surgery) underlie

these superb results. Endoscopic treatment of unicoronal
craniosynostosis, done at an early age is an excellent option that should
be given to all of the parents of those affected children.
