46 Unicoronal Suture Synostosis: Open
Vault Surgery, Key Points for the
Neurosurgeons
Federico Di Rocco1
(1) Department of Pediatric Neurosurgery, French Referral Center for
Craniosynostosis of Lyon, ERN Cranio, INSERM 1033, Université de
Lyon, H pital Femme Mère Enfant, Hospices Civils de Lyon, Lyon,
France

Federico Di Rocco
Email: federico.dirocco@chu-lyon.fr
Keywords Anterior plagiocephaly – Coronal suture – Fronto-orbital
advancement – Orbital surgery

46 1 Introduction
The early fusion of one hemicoronal suture leads to a complex
combination of bone anomalies of the cranial basis, the cranial vault,
the facies and, in most severe cases, of the upper axis. While the
anomalies of the cranial vault and the orbit are satisfactorily corrected
by an appropriate surgical treatment those of the face, namely, the
deviation of the nasal pyramid and the mandibular asymmetry are
faced by the surgeon only when extremely severe and disfiguring. In
most cases, they are not addressed due to their limited functional
impact (Fig. 46.1).

Fig. 46.1 Phenotype of anterior plagiocephaly. The early fusion of the right hemicoronal suture
determines several developmental bone anomalies: the flattening and posterior displacement
of the right hemifrontal bone (1), the flattening of the orbit with secondary ocular proptosis (2),
the flattening and elevation of the right supraorbital ridge (3), the contralateral deviation of the
nasal pyramid (4) and mandibula (5), the anterior displacement of the temporal pyramid (6),
the volumetric asymmetry of the lateral masses of the first cervical vertebrae associated to an
opposite volumetric modification of the occipital condyle resulting in a torticollis (7). Because
of the ocular proptosis in the affected side, the normal eye appears smaller. Squint is nearly
always associated (8)

The anomalies of first vertebra consist of the volumetric
combination of the hypotrophy of the lateral mass on the side of the
early fused hemicoronal suture and the hypertrophy of the
controlateral one. Opposite volumetric changes involve the occipital
condyle, being hypertrophic the one on the side of the early affected
hemicoronal suture and hypotrophic the contralateral one. These
“crossed” changes account for the oblique orientation of the
craniovertebral junction on the horizontal plane that is responsible of

the torticollis which characterizes the most severely affected subjects.
The depending functional disturbance is rarely addressed surgically
because of the limitations of the techniques currently available.
Consequently, when necessary, most of the affected children undergo
specific physiotherapic treatments. Also, the peculiar type of
strabismus and other abnormalities of ocular movements that can be
noticed in many of the infants with anterior plagiocephaly secondary to
the alterations in volume and shape of the orbit on the side of the
precociously fused hemicoronal suture are rarely treated surgically
during infancy [1, 2]. Indeed, the early surgical correction is required
only in children with significant functional impairment. Similar
considerations can be made for the other bone anomalies that do not
cause an evident cosmetic defect or do not bear an important
functional impact, e.g., the anterior displacement of the petrous bone in
the affected hemicranium or the asymmetry of the mandibula that
depends on the anterior displacement of the mandibular articulation
on the synostotic side (Fig. 46.1).
On the other hands, some of the osseous anomalies in the coronalfrontosphenoidal, sphenoethmoidal, and frontozygomatic suture
associated with the early fusion of the hemicoronal require a prompt
surgical correction both to correct the cosmetic defect secondary to the
already established bony anomalies and to prevent their further
aggravation. This is the case of the hypoplasic and posteriorly displaced
hemifrontal bone that may impair the normal growth of the brain and
the reduced volume of the abnormally shaped orbit resulting in the
typical drop or “harlequin” type deformity and ocular globe proptosis.
Indeed, besides the possible functional abnormalities, the frontal
and orbital deformation impact on the facial development of the
affected child that might influence the self-perception or social
acceptance, so impairing the normal psychomotor development. A
similar motivation may encourage the craniofacial surgeon to surgically
manage the deviation of the nasal pyramid during adolescence in cases
where it aggravates the cosmetic appearance of the C-shaped and
twisted face, typical of the condition, already visible in the first months
or years of life.

46 2 Surgical Considerations
The surgical management of unilateral coronal synostosis should be
modulated, taking into account the degree of severity of the condition
in various children. In such a regard, the classification that subdivides
the affected population in three main types according to the anomalies
of the cranial base as shown by the radiological investigations offers a
valid and practical tool both for the surgical indication and the
prediction of the surgical outcome (Fig. 46.2).

Fig. 46.2 Classification of coronal synostosis according to skull base alterations. (Adapted from
Ref. [3])

In Type I, the bone anomalies do not involve the anterior skull base.
Only the frontal bone on the side of the early fused hemicoronal suture
is flattened and displaced posteriorly together with the supraorbital
rim. The vomer bone maintains its midline position as well as the nasal
pyramid.
In Type II, the posterior displacement of the hemifrontal bone on
the affected side is associated to a deviation of the vomer bone towards
the fused suture and to a moderate contralateral deviation of the nasal
bones. Type II can be further subdivided into Type II A and Type II B
according to the absence or presence of anterior rotation and
displacement of the homolateral temporal petrous bone.
Type III is characterized by the obvious anterior displacement of the
temporal pyramid, the marked homolateral attraction of the vomer
bone towards the affected side and the more pronounced retrocession
of the hemifrontal bone, all contributing to a further volumetric
reduction of the anterior hemicranial fossa. Also, the contralateral

deviation of the nasal pyramid is more obvious. In most severe cases
even the occipital fossa is affected with the homolateral deviation of the
posterior half of the median basal axis of the skull.
Such a classification is quite useful to anticipate the family’s
expectations as the surgical result is very satisfactory in Type I and
limited in type III. Intermediate results can be expected in Type II
anterior plagiocephaly [3, 4].
When planning the surgical management of anterior plagiocephaly
synostosis is necessary to take into account the potential underlying
genetic condition, e.g., Muenke, TCF12 or Saethre-Chotzen syndromes
that are phenotypically expressed as unilateral coronal synostosis in
some infants. Indeed, the presence of genetic anomalies is associated to
a high risk of recurrence or incomplete cosmetic results that should be
anticipated to the parents.
The surgical management starts from a careful analysis of the
available imaging in order to anticipate how the vascular structures are
displaced. Indeed, the superior sagittal sinus will not be on the midline
due to the skull scoliosis (Fig. 46.3). The superior sagittal sinus is
usually deviated contralaterally to the closed coronal suture and
generally it is deviated contralaterally to the closed coronal suture [5].

Fig. 46.3 Projection of the superior sagittal sinus position on the skull vault. (Adapted from
Ref. [5])

In the past, the surgical correction of anterior plagiocephaly
consisted of large strip craniectomies with the resection of the early
fused suture that proved to provide only a limited release of the frontal
bone and failed to counteract the recession of the superior orbital ridge.
Strip craniectomies were also associated with a high incidence of
relapse, even when the linear craniectomy was extended along the
lateral wall of the orbit the inferior orbital fissure in the attempt of
addressing the synostosis involving the skull base too [6]. Even the
introduction of some technical variations such as the lateral canthal
advancement [7] or the apposition of a piece of bone between the
surgically advanced lateral canthus and the anterior border of the
parietal bone failed to prevent relapse in a significant proportion
operated on patients [8]. Surgical failures of linear craniectomies have
led to a more aggressive surgical approach, in which a free and
advanced forehead is separated from the face and the cranial vault, the
so-called “floating forehead” [9, 10].

46 3 Goals and Modalities of the Surgical
Correction
The basic aim of the surgical correction of the early fusion of the
hemicoronal suture is to advance the anterior cranial vault and the
superior orbital rim on the affected side in order to reestablish a
normal volume of the anterior cranial fossa and the orbit To assure a
cosmetically rewarding surgical outcome, the advancement of these
bone structures is associated to their remodelling to assure a
cosmetically rewarding surgical outcome that can be better obtained
with an open surgical approach.
The open surgical approach is usually well tolerated by an healthy
infant. Nevertheless, the associate blood loss should not be
undervalued especially when the operation is carried out in early
infancy to profit of the more malleable bone and the pushing of the
developing brain, postoperatively.

46 3 1 Open Surgical Technique: Key Points
The open surgical approach allows the direct access to the malformed
anterior frontal bone and superior orbit that facilitates the removal of
the flattened and retruded hemifrontal bone, containing the early fused
hemicoronal suture, and the frontal bandeau containing the flattened,
retruded, and superiorly displaced orbital rim. These free bone flaps so
obtained are then remodeled prior to their replacement by greenstick
fracture of the supraorbital rim to recreate its normal anterior convex
shape and by parietal linear bone cuts of the frontoparietal flap to
favour the late normalization and possible expansion under the force of
the growing brain to compensate for the restricted volume of the
anterior cranial fossa.. The remodeled bones are repositioned in a more
advanced position to assure sufficient space for the normal cerebral
growth (frontoorbital advancement). In most cases, the frontal bone
flap is replaced after an appropriate rotation to exploit the curvature of
its less flattened superior half in order to create a “normal” frontal
bossing similar to that of the contralateral intact hemifrontal bone [6–
8]. Spatial overcorrection is often selected by replacing the superior
orbital ridge and the frontal bone in a more advanced position as

compared to the contralateral intact side to favor a symmetrical aspect
in the subsequent late developmental phases and the risk of relapse of
the condition [11, 12]. Such a risk is high in cases of syndromic
synostosis.
The necessity to count on thick enough but still pliable cranial
bones to be remodeled and a stable reconstruction of the anterior skull
explains the reason to operate on the affected children between 9 and
12 months of age. However, some authors advocate an earlier
correction to fully exploit the action of the developing underlying brain
and its ability to mold more compliant bones.
A reliable stabilization of the bone segments utilized for the cranial
reconstruction is mandatory to prevent recurrence of the cosmetic
defect and, even more important, brain damage related to their
postoperative mobility. In the past, metallic screws and plates were
utilized for such a purpose. They were abandoned after the
demonstration of their migration through the bone in late
postoperative radiological controls. Nowadays, biodegradable
resorbable plates and screws made from polylactide polymers are
commonly utilized, placed whenever possible on the internal face of the
bone segment. Resorbable plates and screws provide a rigid fixation for
the first 2–3 months up to for 6–9 months before biodegrading around
the end of the first postoperative year [13, 14].
The main advantage of the open surgical approach is the immediate
correction of the malformation. The main disadvantages are
represented by the relative severity of the operation, the perioperative
haemorrhagic risk. A further significant disadvantage compared to
minimally invasive techniques is the postoperative obvious scar [15–
20].

46.3.1.1 Surgical Procedure
The hair is prepared with antiseptic shampooing. The child is then
placed supine on the OT, the head resting on a horseshoe headrest. The
skin of entire frontoparietal regions and face are prepped with betadine
solution, and the head and face are draped up just below the nose. The
hair is combed or it might be shaved minimally for a coronal strip, 1 cm
in width, from one ear to the other. A zig-zag bilateral coronal incision
of the scalp is designed with the end points at 2 cm above the ear of

each side. The zig zag incision should be preferred to minimize the risk
of enlarging postoperative scar faced by a linear straight incision in
case of an excessive tension secondary to the expansion of the frontal
lobe. The zig zag incision is thought to better distribute the force
vectors in multiple directions. Furthermore, this type of incision is
more effectively hidden by the hair even when wet, in children with
straight hair too. The scalp incision is then carried out after having
infiltrated the subcutaneous tissue and galea with a solution of
Lidocaine and Epinephrine in order to reduce blood loss. Hemostasis of
the scalp is obtained using the bipolar coagulation, the Colorado needle
and/or clips.
A blunt dissection of the galea from the underlying periosteum is
then made to reflect the cutaneous flap anteriorly and expose the
frontal region. The dissection can also be undertaken directly
subperiosteally leaving the periosteum adherent to the skin flap. In all
cases, the preservation of the periosteum is important to retain the
bone production capacity. The folded frontal flap is reflected anteriorly
using elastic bands and protected during the operation by the topic
application of wet abdominal pads. Matrix hemostatic sealants might be
utilized throughout the operation to favour hemostasis. The periosteum
is then incised along the anterior border of the temporal muscle. The
muscle is then transected horizontally together with the underlying
periosteum at about 1 cm from its proximal insertion on the skull and
reflected off the temporal fossa left attached to the scalp flap. The use of
electrocautery and accurate hemostasis minimize the blood loss. The
incision of the periosteum is then continued inferiorly to expose the
lateral orbital rim down to the body of zygomatic bone, approximately
at 1 cm posteriorly to the fused hemicoronal suture up to the midline.
By contouring the lateral borders of the anterior fontanel the incision is
extended anteriorly along the midline ending at 2 cm above the
supraorbital ridge to be then continued at this distance parallelly to the
inferior border of the frontal bone to reach the periosteal incision in the
temporal region. Successively, the frontal incision of the periosteumis
extended on the contralateral frontal region to facilitate the anterior
reflexion of the membrane above the frontal folded scalp. The
nasofrontal suture and the supraorbital notch are exposed. In case
when the nerve is running in a groove, it should be made free using a

bone scalpel with a delicate manoeuvre meant at preserving its
anatomical and functional integrity to avoid postoperative sensorial
deficit. The superior surface of the ocular capsule is then detached from
the overlaying inferior surface of the orbital roof and the palpebral
ligament from the frontozygomatic suture. The intraorbital dissection
of the periorbita is extended to the lateral orbital rim and down to the
junction of the inferior orbital rim.
The osteotomy design is performed (Fig. 46.4).

Fig. 46.4 Osteotomy design to correct a left coronal synostosis. Note that the forehead is
planned to be tilted inferiorly on the left side in order to correct the asymmetry of the frontal
bossing

The osteotomy plan aims at identifying the orbital bandeau and the
future frontal bone. The donor site for the new frontal bone will be
adapted to the patient anatomy and degree of deformation. The same
forehead might be used after a minor remodeling in case of mild
deformation whereas, in case of sever deformation, the forehead must
be obtained by a different anatomical region.
The hemifrontal craniotomy is performed after the appropriately
blunt dissection of the periosteum along the outlined borders of the
osteotomy plan.
One or several burr holes might be performed in order to get an
access to the epidural space and separate the dura from the bone that

will be cut with a craniotome.
The bone flap can also be obtained using directly an ultrasonic
piezosurgery bone scalpel which allows to spare bone and reduces the
risk of dural tears or damaging the soft tissues (Fig. 46.5).

Fig. 46.5 Frontal bone osteotomy using piezoelectric

bone scalpel

A blunt dissector can be the used through the burr holes to detach
the dura from the overlying inner cranial surface along the line of the
designed craniotomy to facilitate the careful lifting and removal of the
frontal bone flap. Care must be taken when dissecting the pterional
region in the affected side where the dura can makea fold within the
elevated sphenoid ridge. A supraorbital bar is then prepared by
removing the inferior border of the frontal bone and the upper part of
the nasal bones and cutting the mesial supraorbital ridge anteriorly to
the foramen cecum: completely, if the removal of the fronto-orbital bar
is planned, or partially in case where only the anterior rotation of the
bar is decided by pivoting it on this level after fracturing the residual
bone at the mesial superior angle of the orbit. Eventually, the
craniotomy can continue laterally and the lateral pillar of the orbit can
be included in the bandeau (Fig. 46.6).

Fig. 46.6 The lateral wall of the right orbit is included in the bandeau advancement. Note that
the periosteum is attached to the skin flap

The bone cut is then continued across the orbital roof remaining at
about 1 cm posteriorly to the superior orbital ridge by retracting the
dura mater and the underlying frontal lobe using malleable retractors
to protect the brain as well as the capsule of the ocular globe. Laterally
the cutting is extended posteriorly and inferiorly, on the lateral wall of
the orbit paralleling the zygomatic arch in the region of the
frontosphenoidal and frontozygomatic sutures, to create a rectangular
“tongue” to be used to advance and lowering the supraorbital bar.
The supraorbital bar is first drilled to obtain symmetrical orbital
roofs; then, it is replaced on the skull. It is held in place in the new
advanced position with transosseous sutures with PDS or vicryl, and/or
bio-resorbable plates and screws. The degree of advancement is related
to the severity of the malformation. Usually, the supraorbital bar
advancement overcompensates the contralateral side to favour the late
outcome [1–12]. The degree of over overcorrection when replacing the

supraorbital and the frontal bone is limited by the need of performing a
scalp closure without tension. The abnormal superior orbital roof
homolateral to the synostosis can be corrected with a greenstick
fracture and using a bone bender at this stage.
The supraorbital bar is then replaced, inclined in a ventral direction
to correct the usual more vertical and backward slanted development
of this structure, so to reestablish the normal angle and assure an
immediate better cosmetic reconstruction. The “tongue in groove”
portion of the supraorbital bar advanced within the parietal groove
assures a stable new position that can be further reinforced by the
replacement of the frontal bone flap, appropriately reshaped and
rotated (usually by 180°), anchored to the contralateral frontal bone
mesially and to the border of the parietal bone superiorly. The
reshaping of the frontal bone flap, by means of the bone bending
forceps is facilitated by radial cuts that decrease the bone resistance
consequently facilitating the action of the instrument. When the
anterior portion of the parietal bone is abnormally restricted, it can be
enlarged with the same tool after having carried out radial bone cuts.
In case of marked protrusion of the temporal fossa, which is often
the case in FGFR3 related plagiocephaly, some remodeling of the
temporal bone can also be performed (Fig. 46.7).

Fig. 46.7 Different types of remodeling of the temporal region

Because of the reduced dimensions of the replaced frontal bone,
small areas of cranial defects will result from the procedure that
increases the volume of the anterior cranial fossa (Fig. 46.8).

Fig. 46.8 Initial and late intraoperative pictures showing the correction of a left anterior
plagiocephaly. Note the overcorrection on the left side

The defects reossify spontaneously in nearly all the cases previous
the accurate reconstitution of the periosteum and repositioning of the
temporal muscle. The elevation of the temporal muscle en bloc with the
scalp flap and eventually the suturing of its superior end to the
periosteum of the parietal bone and/or the replaced frontal bone flap is
quite useful to fill the hollow due to the advanced frontal–orbital bone
The scalp is sutured in two layers; a subgaleal drainage might be left in
place may reduce the volume of postoperative effusions, so allowing a
faster and safer healing of the surgical wound.
Intraoperative and postoperative (from the postoperative drainage
or within the subcutaneous space) surgical losses range between 50
and 400 mL, with a mean value around 200 mL. Intraoperative blood
transfusion is required in nearly half of the cases. The operative time
commonly range between 2 and 3 h.
After the operation, the child is observed in the pediatric intensive
care department for 24 h with monitoring of the hemodynamic and
neurological condition. The postoperative hospitalization is about 4–
5 days.
Postoperative 3D-CT scan can be used to evaluate the reconstructed
skull. However, in most cases, the immediate postoperative result is
based on the mere clinical observation to avoid further irradiation.

47 Bicoronal Sutures Synostosis
Ricardo Santos de Oliveira1 and Matheus Ballestero2
(1) Division of Neurosurgery, School of Medicine of Ribeir o Preto,
University of S o Paulo, Ribeir o Preto, SP, Brazil
(2) Medicine Department, Federal University of S o Carlos, S o Carlos,
SP, Brazil

Keywords Craniosynostosis – Nonsyndromic – Brachycephaly –
Coronal sutures – Bicoronal

47 1 Introduction
Bicoronal sutures synostosis is a skull deformity characterized by a
shortened anteroposterior skull length and a widened biparietal
diameter. This condition may be nonsyndromic, or syndromic. Accurate
diagnosis of the type of brachycephaly is paramount in deciding the
appropriate treatment options.
The treatment of bilateral coronal synostosis skull deformities is
challenging. It is directed at increasing the anteroposterior dimension
of the skull, reducing its superior-inferior dimension, releasing the
fusion of the coronal sutures, and advancing the supraorbital rims
bilaterally. Although helmet therapy is promising [1], surgical
intervention is the cornerstone of treatment [2].
Bilateral coronal craniosynostosis gives rise to the so-called
brachycephaly, a short and wide head shape due to the fusion of the
coronal sutures, restricting anteroposterior growth (Fig. 47.1). The
compensatory growth occurs sideways, resulting in upper and midface
hypoplasia [3, 4]. Neurosurgeons also must be aware that patients with
brachycephaly should be evaluated by a clinical geneticist in order to
exclude a syndrome [5].

Fig. 47.1 Superior (a), lateral (b), and frontal (c) preoperative view of a brachiocephalic child,
showing bilateral coronal synostosis. A typical frontal appearance of brachiocephalic with a
short and wide head shape due to the fusion of the coronal sutures, restricting anteroposterior
growth

47 2 Surgical Strategy
47 2 1 Recommendation
Once the diagnosis of craniosynostosis is confirmed, the treatment
should be surgical, based on three factors:

47.2.1.1 Brain Compression
The main indication for surgical treatment of craniosynostosis is the
risk of chronic intracranial hypertension, and consequent cerebral
suffering due to chronic hypoxia, thus leading to cognitive alterations
and regression of neuropsychomotor development.
Accelerated brain growth, especially in the first year of life,
associated with bone restriction resulting from synostosis, can lead to
intracranial hypertension.
In 1982, Renier et al. [6] demonstrated the effects of increased
intracranial pressure (ICP) in children with craniosynostosis
undergoing surgical correction through pre-and postoperative records.
The authors confirmed that even isolated craniosynostosis could
present high levels of ICP.
ICP measurement has become an important tool for pre-operative
assessment of craniofacial abnormalities prior to calvarial remodelling,
as well as postprocedural screening for suspicion of raised ICP in
syndromic craniosynostosis. ICP monitoring may also be of value to
both the parents and surgeon in cases of mild deformity where there

may be doubts as to the need for surgery on a cosmetic basis in
addition to concerns about the functional effects of chronic intracranial
hypertension [7].

47.2.1.2 Aesthetics

epair

Psychological studies in patients with nonoperated craniosynostosis in
childhood confirm the loss of self-esteem, difficulty in accepting the
child by society, by the parents, relatives, and by himself, so the surgical
indication should be made in order to repair the installed craniofacial
deformity [8].

47.2.1.3

phthalmologic mpairment

Orbital alterations are present in some types of nonsyndromic
craniosynostosis, such as brachycephaly, oxycephaly, anterior
plagiocephaly, and trigonocephaly. Ocular proptosis can lead to corneal
exposure, trauma, and consequent visual loss. The involvement of skull
base sutures in brachycephaly and oxycephaly (frontoethmoidal and
frontosphenoid) may be associated with the appearance of important
orbital deformities.

47 2 2 Surgery Time
For the reasons presented, it becomes evident that the surgical
indication must be early. In nonsyndromic brachycephaly, surgery is
recommended, preferably between 6 and 12 months.
Some factors are essential for the success of the procedure in
children under the age of 1 year: the child’s weight is sufficient to
support a major surgery ( 6 kg); neuroanaesthesia, preparation of
blood products before the beginning of the procedure and intensive
care in the postoperative period (preferably in the pediatric ICU).

47 2 3 Surgical Technique
47.2.3.1 Preparation
The child should preferably be positioned in the supine position, so that
the anesthesiologist has easy access to the endotracheal tube, if
necessary, during the surgical procedure (Fig. 47.2).

Fig. 47.2 Photography of a brachycephalic child in supine position using horseshoe pad. (a) A
free and accessible endotracheal tube and cautious protection to the eyes are shown. (b)
Illustration showed a zig-zag bicoronal scalp incision for cranial-facial surgical correction

Before starting the surgical procedure, a check must be made
regarding:

Presence of the informed consent for surgery
Proper and safe patient position
Eyes closed and protected
Free access to the endotracheal tube
Adequate venous access with blood products in the operating room
ready for infusion
Invasive (intraarterial) blood pressure, when possible
Photographic documentation

47.2.3.2 ncision
In all types of craniosynostosis, a bicoronal zigzag incision can be made
(in a straight or curvilinear way), in order to minimize the effects of late
healing. A scalpel with monopolar needle coagulation (Colorado
microdissection) is essential for dissection of superficial planes to
minimize blood loss and. Raney clips may also be used, sometimes
along with a surgical compress, to make the scalp thicker and archives a
more effective compression hemostasis. At the end of the surgery, an
aspiration drain is placed to prevent postoperative periorbital
hematomas and edema, a suture absorbable line is fixed in the suction

drain’s exteriorization point, in order to close it with a surgical knot
when removing the drain (Fig. 47.3).

Fig. 47.3 Preoperative photography of a brachicefalic child. (a) Lateral view of a bicoronal zigzag incision. (b) Illustration of a suction drain position and exteriorization

47.2.3.3 Cranial ault emodeling
The recessed and abnormally wide supraorbital bar is lifted with a
bilateral temporal tenon, reshaped and replaced with a bilateral
advancement. The upper forehead is usually constructed from the
existing forehead (Fig. 47.4), which is fixed back onto the supraorbital
bar in its new position. The bulging of the temporal fossae is corrected
by lifting a small bone flap and putting it back with the concavity
outward. In infants younger than 6 months, the forehead is fixed in the
advanced position only at the root of the nose and lateral orbital walls,
without any fixation to the posterior cranial vault. This allows the brain
to push freely on the forehead, realizing what we have called the
“floating forehead” [9, 10]. Bony defects should be filled in by bone
grafts fixed with fibrin glue (Fig. 47.5).

Fig. 47.4 (a) Marchac frontal patterns and instruments. From the left to right ruler, frontal
model in two sizes and orbital model [11]. (b) Surgical planning

Fig. 47.5 Surgical photographs for brachycephaly deformity correction. Main surgical steps
showing a cranial vault remodeling technique. (a) Superior view of complete exposition of
supraorbital rim and craniofacial bones. (b) Craniotomy planning drawn on bone surface. (c)
Planning of the supraorbital advance. (d) Reconstructed and fixed (steel wires) frontal. (e)
Lateral view of final cranial vault remodeling and bilateral fronto-orbital advancement. (f)
Superior view of final cranial vault remodeling

The fixation of the frontal and the supraorbital bar can be obtained
with absorbable plates, when available, or through steel wires
(Aciflex ) (Fig. 47.6). Currently, the preference to stabilize the frontoorbital bar and the new frontal are the absorbable plates.

Fig. 47.6 Intraoperative photographs. (a) Absorbable plate (yellow arrow) and Raney Clip
(green arrow) used for skin hemostasis. (b) Screwdrivers and screws used to fixate the
absorbable plates (mechanical on the left and ultrasound assisted on the right)

Fronto-orbital advancement allows eye protection in cases where
there is marked proptosis, in addition to allowing adequate cerebral
decompression, minimizing the risk of intracranial hypertension. The
bulging of the temporal region is corrected through the inversion of the
temporal bone flap.

47 3 Postoperative Outpatient Follow-Up
At least 24 h of monitoring in the pediatric intensive care unit (UCI) is
important to verify the hemodynamic stability, bleeding and to control
the hematimetry. On the first or second postoperative, depending on
the output, the suction drain must be removed and the exteriorization
point sutured. Prescription of intravenous and/or oral analgesia on a
regular basis should be recommended.
In general, children remain hospitalized after surgery for a total
period of 3 days. After 1 week, the surgical scar should be evaluated on
an outpatient basis. The use of absorbable polyglactin 910 4-0 (Vicryl
Rapide ) sutures should be encouraged.
A postoperative 3D CT can be performed in selected cases. However,
periodic photographic documentation is essential for late assessment of
the result (Figs. 47.7 and 47.8).

Fig. 47.7 Photography in 4 months follow-up after brachycephaly surgical correction. (a)
Frontal view. (b) Lateral view. There is no visible scar because of zig-zag incision. A gradual
normalization of the cranial was observed

48 Lambdoid Suture Synostosis:
Endoscopic Approach, Key Points for
Neurosurgeons
David F. Jimenez1, 2, 3
(1) Department of Neurosciences, El Paso Children’s Hospital, El Paso,
TX, USA
(2) Pediatric Neurosurgery, El Paso Children’s Hospital, El Paso, TX,
USA
(3) Neurosurgery Department, University Medical Center, El Paso, TX,
USA

David F Jimene
Email: drj@nexusneurosurgery.com
Keywords Craniosynostosis – Endoscopy – Lambdoid – Suture –
Plagiocephaly

48 1 Introduction
Although it is the least common of all craniosynostosis, lambdoid
synostosis can be difficult to diagnose and may be easily confused with
positional plagiocephaly by many primary care providers unfamiliar
with its clinical presentation [1–10]. However, the diagnosis should not
be difficult to make for those surgeons and centers that treat
craniosynostosis. For the most part, isolated single suture
nonsyndromic craniosynostosis is a clinical diagnosis. A well-versed
clinician can make the diagnosis by simply observing the patient while
doing the physical exam. As such, it is our policy not to obtain CT scans

and unnecessarily expose patients to radiation. However, lambdoid
synostosis is the exception and as such, we obtain CT scans in all
patients suspected of lambdoid synostosis. We do this to rule out
positional plagiocephaly and to document the extent of the synostosis.
In brief summary, lambdoid craniosynostosis presents clinically as
follows: (a) occipital plagiocephaly ipsilateral to the craniosynostosis
(Fig. 48.1), (b) inferior displacement of the mastoid process on the
affected side (Fig. 48.2), (c) inferior downward displacement of the
ipsilateral ear, (d) a bony ridge along the stenosed suture (Fig. 48.3), (e)
cranial scoliosis with deviation of the vertex to the contralateral side
(Fig. 48.4), and (f) prominent and protruding parietal eminence of on
contralateral side (Fig. 48.5). Contrary with patients with positional
plagiocephaly, the forehead tends to be round and symmetrical. When
viewed from above, these patients have a “trapezoid” shape (Fig. 48.6)
in comparison to the parallelogram shape seen in positional
plagiocephaly.

Fig. 48.1 Six-month-old male presenting with left lambdoid synostosis. Significant occipital
indentation and plagiocephaly is seen in this view taken from above

Fig. 48.2 Eight-month-old female with left lambdoid synostosis demonstrates the classic
findings of the inferior displacement of the ipsilateral ear and mastoid process

Fig. 48.3 Three-month-old male with left lambdoid synostosis. A bony ridge is seen and can be
palpated on the left side along the stenosed lambdoid suture

Fig. 48.4 Cranial scoliosis is evident in this patient with right lambdoid synostosis. The yellow
line indicates patients midline through the neck and the foramen magnum. Red line indicates
midline axis of the cranial vault, which is significantly deviated to the contralateral side

Fig. 48.5 Another classical finding in lambdoid synostosis is the deviation of the vertex of the
side contralateral to the stenosis suture, as seen in this patient with right lambdoid stenosis

Fig. 48.6 When viewed from above, lambdoid craniosynostosis patients have a “trapezoid”
shape (as shown by the red lines) in contrast to the typical parallelogram shape seen in patients
with positional plagiocephaly

48 2 Diagnostic Radiology
Plain skull radiographs have high sensitivity and can easily provide the
diagnosis, but a Towne’s view is necessary. Evident is a sclerotic suture
where closure has taken place, as seen in this lateral radiograph (Fig.
48.7). Nevertheless, CT scans are the golden standard for definitive
diagnosis. However, 3D reconstructions will clearly show the stenosed
suture (Fig. 48.8), and the sagittal view will show if cerebellar tonsillar
ectopia is present. Premature suture closure can affect the entire suture
or portion of it. The scan will clearly show the location of the stenosis.

Fig. 48.7 Lateral skull radiograph clearly demonstrates a sclerotic area on the retromastoid
region consistent with the stenosed lambdoid suture

Fig. 48.8 The gold standard for definitive diagnosis is a head CT scan with 3D reconstruction.
This CT clearly shows a completely stenosed left lambdoid suture

48 3 Patient Positioning
The patient’s head is placed on a cerebellar horseshoe headrest. We
have tried placing the patient fully prone on the headrest as well as the
lateral decubitus position. The latter is our preferred position (Fig.
48.9). All of the standard precautions for placing a patient on the
horseshoe headrest are taken, particularly that the contralateral ear is
not under pressure.

Fig. 48.9 For surgery, the patient is positioned on the lateral decubitus position with the
affected suture placed superiorly. This patient, with the left lambdoid synostosis, is resting on a
cerebellar horseshoe headrest

48 4 Incisions
Proper placement of the incisions is extremely critical when operating
on lambdoid synostosis. If not properly placed, the procedure will be
very difficult to do. The use of X-rays is critical to localize the lambda
and the asterion on the affected side. The radiology technologist takes
both A-P, and lateral views (Figs. 48.10 and 48.11). In order to localize

lambda, metallic stick-on markers are placed on the estimated location
by the surgeon. Oftentimes, the markers need to be relocated and
several X-rays taken in order to localize the proper points (Fig. 48.12).
Once the proper location has been selected, a small strip of hair is
shaved/clipped for an incision of about 2–2.5 cm. One incision is
immediately on top of the lambda and the second immediately medial
to the asterion (Fig. 48.13).

Fig. 48.10 Intraoperative skull X-rays are obtained in order to properly localize lambda and
asterion. The tech is seen taking on A-P radiograph trying to localize lambdas

Fig. 48.11 Now the radiology technologist is taken a lateral X-ray for asterion identification

Fig. 48.12 The surgeon places stick-on metallic markers in the approximate location of the
lambda and asterion prior to taking intraoperative X-rays

Fig. 48.13 Once the proper location of lambda and asterion is made, a small strip of hair is
shaved over the proposed incision sites

48 5 Surgical Procedure
The dermis is open with the monopolar needle tip, and the cautery is
set on cut mode at 10 W. This setting causes minimal injury to the
dermis, and scars heal superbly and are hardly visible. Both incisions
can be opened simultaneously (Fig. 48.14). The next step is to develop
the subgaleal plane between the incisions. This can be done with direct
endoscopic visualization (Fig. 48.15) using a 0° endoscope.
Alternatively, a rhinoplasty lighted retractor and an insulated brain
ribbon can be used for the subgaleal dissection (Fig. 48.16). Once the
plane is fully developed, a brain ribbon is passed to document complete
plane dissection (Fig. 48.17). Identification of lambda is done at the
proximal incision using a 1 penfield dissector (Fig. 48.18).
Mobilization of the pericranium allows for the identification of the
sagittal suture and it’s junction with the contralateral opened lambdoid
suture. Burr holes are placed at each incision and enlarged (towards
each other) with a 4 or 5 Kerrison rongeurs. Elongation of the burr
hole allows for the insertion of a 30° rigid endoscope. With the scope
pointing towards the bone, it is advanced and the stenosed suture
visualized and followed distally. When coming close to the asterion, the
point where the closed suture joins the open asterion is clearly seen
(Fig. 48.19). The osteotomy is then created by removing bits of bone in
a piece meal fashion using bone cutting rongeurs (Fig. 48.20). The
osteotomy is continued until the open suture is found (Fig. 48.21). The
osteotomy is fully completed, bone hemostasis is obtained with the
Bovie suction coagulator set on coagulation mode at 60 W (Fig. 48.22).
Hemostasis is completely obtained with Surgiflo and the incisions
closed with absorbable 4-0 galeal suture (Monocryl or vicryl) Mastisol
and steri-strips are used to close the dermis.

Fig. 48.14 Both incisions are open simultaneously with needle tip Bovie set at 10 W on cut
mode

Fig. 48.15 Endoscopic view with a 0° scope, of the loose areolar tissue plane dissection from
Lambda to Asterion. (a) The stenosed lambdoid suture. (b) The loose areolar tissue between
the pericranium and galea. (c) The galea and the scalp being evaluated by the lighted retractor.
(d) The Bovie. (e) Used for dissecting the plane bloodlessly

Fig. 48.16 A rhinoplasty lighted retractor can also be used to develop the loose areolar tissue
plain under direct visualization

Fig. 48.17 A brain ribbon is placed under the galea between lambda and asterion incisions,
indicating complete release

Fig. 48.18 Two Ragnell retractors hold the incision apart. A 1 penfield is used to mobilize the
pericranium. The sagittal and open lambdoid sutures are identified

Fig. 48.19 A 30° endoscope is passed under the skull and advanced until the closed lambdoid
suture forms the open suture of the asterion

Fig. 48.20 Endoscopic view of the lambda and asterion osteotomies as they are about to unite
into a single osteotomy extending between both ends

Fig. 48.21 The lambdoid sutures opens as it joins the asterion, as seen in this endoscopic view

Fig. 48.22 A monopolar suction electrocautery is used to cauterize the osteotomy edges and
obtain complete bony hemostasis

48 6 Postoperative Management
After extubation, the patient is transferred to the PACU (recovery room)
and then moved to the floor for overnight observation. Pain
management includes alternating doses of ibuprofen and
acetaminophen every 3 h. Intravenous morphine is given as needed for
severe breakthrough pain. The patient is discharged the following
morning. The patient’s head is scanned (infrared) for a cranial orthosis
on the postoperative day (POD) 4, and the orthosis filled on (POD) 5.
Patient wears the cranial orthosis for 23-h a day for the ensuing 6–
10 months (Figs. 48.23, 48.24, 48.25, 48.26, 48.27, and 48.28).

Fig. 48.23 (a) Patient A is a 6-month-old female presenting with lambdoid synostosis. Top
view shows left-sided plagiocephaly. (b) Posterior-anterior (PA) view of same patient shows
downward displacement of ear and mastoid as well as contralateral bulging of the parietal
eminence

Fig. 48.24 (a) Patient A, 9 months after surgery shows improvement of the preoperative
findings on PA view. (b) Patient A shows complete correction of the left-sided plagiocephaly at
9 months

Fig. 48.25 (a) Patient A at 2.5 years postop. Notice almost complete correction of the skull
base asymmetry as seen by the alignment of the ears along the horizontal plane. (b) Patient
continues to demonstrate complete correction of plagiocephaly 2.5 years after surgery

Fig. 48.26 (a) Five-month-old male with classical findings on PA view. The right ear
significantly displaced inferiorly along with the mastoid suture. (b) Top view shows marked
indentation posteriorly along the stenosed lambdoid suture

Fig. 48.27 (a) Six years after endoscopic release, top view shows normalization of the head.
(b) Six years after surgery, P-A view shows complete correction of skull based deformity

Fig. 48.28 (a) Top view of the same patient 11 years after surgery. (b) PA view of some patient
shows persistent skull based abnormalities and asymmetry correction

48 7 Discussion
Lambdoid craniosynostosis is associated with significant skull-based
cranial and in some cases facial deformities. Traditional surgical
treatment involves a complete calvarial vault reconstruction of the
occipital parietal bones to round the back of the head. Many variations
on the theme have been proposed by multiple surgeons and
craniofacial centers. Given our immense success with treating the other
calvarial sutures using minimally invasive endoscopic techniques, we
decided to apply the same principles to the stenosed lambdoid. To our
surprise, the patients obtained major and significant correction of their
preoperative deformities. The correction is not immediate and requires
patience and time. This surgical approach is associated with minimal
blood loss. So far, not a single patient has been transfused intra- or
postoperatively, there’s minimal pain and swelling. Short anesthesia
times are one of the extreme benefits to the patient. We strongly believe
that the brain is fully responsible for the ultimate shape of the face and
entire cranial skeleton to include the skull base. As such, if a stenosed
suture is released and the brain allowed to assume its normal
morphology, the preoperative cranial and facial deformities will correct
as we have clearly shown with other suture synostosis to now include
the lambdoid. Endoscopic release is associated with excellent results
and is a surgical option that should be given to the parents of children
affected with this condition.

49 Lambdoid Suture Synostosis: Open
Vault Surgery, Key Points for the
Neurosurgeons
Martina Messing-Jünger1
(1) Pediatric Neurosurgery Department, Asklepios Children’s Hospital,
Sankt Augustin, Germany

Martina Messing-J nger
Email: m.messing@asklepios.com
Keywords Lambdoid suture synostosis – Open vault reconstruction
Lambdoid suture synostoses are rare. They are found in less than 5% of
all cases and diagnosis is often delayed, possibly due to the fact that
they are mistaken for positional plagiocephaly. Therefore, open vault
remodeling becomes necessary when the patient is older than
4 months of age. Evidence regarding the best surgical management in
lambdoid craniosynostosis is sparce, but occasional publications report
on similar cosmetic results in endoscopic strip craniectomy versus
open vault surgery [1]. Nevertheless, regardless of the applied surgical
technique, patients with lambdoid synostosis show persistent
asymmetry of the posterior cranial vault and the cranial base [1].
Additional cranial base fusion is not only found in syndromic
craniosynostoses, but also in nonsyndromic patients; however, in
lambdoid synostosis, no associated cranial base suture fusions could be
detected so far [2]. In order to address asymmetry adequately as well
as the underlying cause for further deformity progress, it is

recommended to perform surgery as soon as possible. Open vault
remodeling is best performed at 6 months of age [3, 4].
Growth restriction due to premature lambdoid suture closure can
lead to significant volume reduction of the posterior fossa, and it is
recommended to perform MRI prior to surgery to rule out secondary
Chiari malformation type 1 (Fig. 49.1). This condition can be even more
pronounced in bilateral lambdoid fusion (Fig. 49.2). In most cases, the
tonsillar displacement will disappear after appropriate cranioplasty,
but control MRI is recommended and additional bony foramen magnum
decompression should be discussed in persistent Chiari malformation
type 1.

Fig. 49.1 Secondary unilateral tonsillar herniation in left-sided lambdoid craniosynostosis: (a)
coronal and (b) sagittal T1 MRI

Fig. 49.2 Bilateral lambdoid synostosis with secondary Chiari malformation type 1: (a)
preoperative and (b) postoperative sagittal T2 MRI

Similar to the anterior plagiocephaly caused by coronal suture
fusion also, the posterior form leads to complex three-dimensional
skull deformity of varying extent. The ipsilateral forehead may be
retruded, whereas the contralateral parietal squama is bulging laterally
(Fig. 49.3). Both deforming aspects eventually have to be addressed by
the remodeling technique [3].

Fig. 49.3 Typical deformity in lambdoid suture synostosis. (a) Left-sided fusion with ipsilateral
mastoid and contralateral parietal bossing and downward displacement of ipsilateral ear
(coronal view). (b) Ipsilateral occipital and frontal retrusion with frontal ear displacement and
contralateral parietal bossing in right-sided suture fusion (axial view)

The essentials of open lambdoid suture synostosis correction are
the same as in other sutures: to open the fused suture, to expand the
restricted cranial volume, and to restore the entire head shape and
morphology [5]. It is advisable to communicate with the family prior to
the surgery that a complete cosmetic normalization will not be
achieved since the already existing displacement of the petrous bone
and the mastoid together with the ear position will persist to a certain
extend.
In our institution, all craniofacial procedures are managed
according to a specific standard operation procedure (SOP) protocol,
which includes preoperative hemoglobin elevation in anemic patients,
presurgical crystalloid hemodilution, tranexamic acid administration,
positioning on a warming mattress with extremity wrapping, central i.v.
line and invasive blood pressure monitoring, and an endotracheal
Woodbridge tube. Our technique involves prone positioning on a small
size face position cushion (Fig. 49.4) and a curved biparietal skin
incision. After preparation of the galeal layer a subperiostal excision of
the affected bone structures is performed. We do not follow a strict

excision pattern, but adjust the incision lines according to the
underlying skull deformity which needs to be corrected. Figure 49.5
demonstrates a left-sided lambdoid craniosynostosis with occipital and
additional parietal augmentation. In cases with ipsilateral forehead
retrusion, remodeling of the entire calvaria may become necessary. In
order to ensure appropriate surgical access, supine position in slight
head inclination is advisable in these cases (Fig. 49.6). Bone pieces
which are removed en bloc may be contoured ex vivo. Transposition of
the parieto-occipital bone flaps is also performed, if the shape allows a
good reconstruction. In any case, it is important to completely detach
and remove the affected suture from the original site in order to
prevent relapse of the deformity. Suture detachment from the
underlying dural structures can be difficult, and any injury of the
torcular and adjacent sinuses must be avoided. Additional in situ barrel
stave osteotomies are added as necessary to create a normal contour.
Since the weight of the head during lying position causes significant
pressure forces on the osteosynthesis sites, fixation must be as rigid as
possible. We therefore still recommend titanium implants, which have
to be removed after 3 months in order to prevent them from migration.
Alternatively, a postoperative helmet protection must be discussed. We
do not have sufficient experience with the use of distraction devices,
which are recommended by some authors [6]. Finally, the periosteum is
readapted following by a two-layer skin closure with intracutaneous
sutures covered by spray dressing and wound cover strips. We are not
using suction drains in our institution. Our technique is comparable to
the ones published by other groups [4, 5].

Fig. 49.5 Example of left-sided lambdoid craniosynostosis correction with additional
ipsilateral parietal augmentation

ipsilateral forehead retrusion (b). This case was operated on in supine position for better

50 Foramen Magnum Decompression
in Craniosynostosis
José Francisco M. Salom o1 and Tatiana Protzenko1
(1) Division of Pediatric Neurosurgery, Department of Pediatric
Surgery, Fernandes Figueira National Institute of Health for
Women, Children and Adolescents, Oswaldo Cruz Foundation (IFFFiocruz), Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

Keywords Foramen magnum – Syndromic craniosynostosis – Chiari I
malformation – Posterior vault expansion

50 1 Introduction
Foramen magnum decompression is performed in some selected cases
of craniosynostosis associated with Chiari Deformation Type I (CMI),
defined as a cerebellar tonsillar herniation greater than 5 mm below
the foramen magnum and also denominated tonsillar herniation (TH)
or tonsillar ectopia (TE). These malformations fit on what Raybaud
called secondary Chiari deformities on his classification of the Chiari I
malformations spectrum [1].
Until the introduction of MRI as a diagnostic method, CMI and
craniosynostosis were occasionally reported, usually, as late
complications related to hydrocephalus [2–6]. Francis et al. [2]
reported a series of patients with Crouzon syndrome in which CMI was
found in five out of ten cases. The role of multisutural and syndromic
synostosis as a cause of CMI was firstly stressed by the Parisian group
in 1995, that reported a high incidence of deformations in 95 patients
studied by MRI [7]. Three years later, the same group established the
basis of the treatment of this condition [8], and since then, many

controversies appeared regarding the best way to manage these
conditions. Mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptors
especially the FGFR1 and FGFR2 genes are identified in Pfeiffer and
Crouzon and these are identical [9, 10].

50 2 Incidence
CMI was diagnosed in 8% of the craniosynostosis patients treated by
Strahle et al. [11] and is rarely seen in a single monosutural
craniosynostosis, in which the incidence ranges from 1% to 5% of these
cases [12, 13], affecting especially the lambdoid suture [12, 14] and
occasionally others [13, 15, 16]. Cinalli et al. [7] stated that the
involvement of the lambdoid suture was predictive of tonsillar
herniation, both in isolated and multisutural forms. More recently,
some authors reported CMI in nearly half of all cases of lambdoid
synostosis [11, 17, 18]. It was established that CMI is much more likely
in patients with Crouzon–Pfeiffer syndrome than in those with Apert
syndrome because in the former the sagittal and lambdoid sutures
close significantly earlier and in the last one the posterior fossa attain a
normal volume [19].
In complex craniosynostosis, the incidence of CMI ranges from 40%
to 75%, being higher in oxycephaly [7, 17]. In syndromic cases, its
incidence may reach 82% in Pfeiffer’s, 70% in Crouzon’s, and 100% in
Kleeblattschädel’s deformities, being very low in Apert and SahtreSchotzen syndromes [7, 11, 13, 14, 20–24].

50 3 Pathophysiology
The pathophysiology of CMI in the sense of craniosynostosis involves
several factors such as the reduced posterior fossa volume, the block of
the venous outflow through the jugular foramen, and changes in and
around the foramen magnum leading to CSF disorders.
The Chiari 1 deformity and the posterior fossa volume: One of the
causes of CMI is the disproportionate growth between the hindbrain
and the abnormally small posterior fossa. The deformity is acquired
and may be progressive over time [25]. The size of the posterior

cranial fossa is related not only to the lambdoid suture but also to the
early closure of small sutures and synchondroses such as the parietosquamosal arches [7, 26, 27]. Thompson et al. [28] showed an inverse
relationship between the relative size of the posterior fossa and the
degree of tonsillar herniation. Consequently, a smaller skull and/or a
deformed posterior fossa may result in crowding of its components
and tonsillar descent in affected patients, mainly those with
lambdoid suture stenosis [8, 14, 19, 22].
It was demonstrated that although patients with craniosynostosis
are born with a significantly smaller intracranial volume, by the age
of 6 months, most achieve a normal cranial volume [23]. Rijken et al.
[29] showed that patients with CMI have similar cerebellar and
posterior fossa volume when compared to controls. According to the
authors, despite a significantly higher cerebellar volume/posterior
fossa ratio, it is not possible to predict which craniosynostosis
patients are more prone to developing CMI, and consequently, one
should focus on the skull vault and other contributing factors, since
the real relationship between them remains obscure.
The foramen magnum: Patients with different types of syndromic or
complex CS have a significantly smaller foramen magnum surface
area when compared with normal controls [30–32]. Studies have
shown that the inner-occipital synchondrosis (IOS) fuses
prematurely in patients with Apert, Crouzon, and Pfeiffer [29, 32]
and this may be already noted at birth, increasing over time [29]. It is
still unclear how much the premature closure of the IOS impairs the
development of the FM since it might be influenced by other factors
such as hypoplasia of the occipital bones [29]. Dissimilarity in the age
of fusion is seen in different series and different types of
craniofaciosynostosis, sometimes related to the difficulty to make a
clinical diagnosis without routine genetic testing [30].
Venous outflow: Venous outflow impairment is induced by stenosis
of the jugular foramen turning difficult CSF absorption and leading to
venous hypertension and increased ICP [33]. Abnormalities of
cerebral veins in the occipital region were identified in 28% of
Strahle’s series [11]. According to the literature, the most exuberant
collateral circulation in patients with syndromic craniosynostosis
occurs in the posterior fossa, being more frequent through the

mastoid and condylar emissary veins and seen especially in
Crouzon–Pfeiffer syndrome [33–35].
Hydrocephalus and ICP: Hydrocephalus is frequently associated with
craniofaciostenosis and is usually multifactorial, including increased
CSF pressure due to jugular foramina stenosis, hindbrain herniation,
reduced volume of the posterior cranial fossa, and abnormalities at
the level of the foramen magnum. The block of the subarachnoid
spaces at the FM area increases the pressure in the cranial
compartment and consequently dissociation of craniospinal pressure
[19, 28, 36]. These children are more prone to have tonsillar
herniation than those without hydrocephalus. As ventriculomegaly is
frequently observed during the investigation, serial images and
clinical follow-up may be necessary to establish or not the diagnosis
of active hydrocephalus and intracranial hypertension.
Syringomyelia: Syringomyelia is usually seen when there is tonsillar
herniation. In Strahle’s series, 10 out of 29 (34%) patients with
craniosynostosis also had syringomyelia and all had Crouzon
syndrome. Syringomyelia was present in 7 out of 34 patients of
Scott’s series and among these, 5 had postoperative images available
for review.

50 4 Signs and Symptoms
Chiari I malformation may be asymptomatic in syndromic
craniosynostosis, and in such cases, the diagnosis is usually established
by imaging and MRI is the gold standard. There is a wide range
regarding the number of patients that become symptomatic due to TH
[14, 19, 37, 38]. Doerga et al. [38] found neurological signs and
symptoms in 73% of all patients with syndromic CS, with or without
TH, a much higher prevalence than usually reported and that certainly
include also mental disabilities and structural brain malformations
often seen in patients with Apert syndrome. Phenotypically, syndromic
and complex craniosynostosis differ from each other but flattening of
the posterior cranium is an important predictor of MCI [7].
The symptoms of CMI are well known, and their detailed
description is beyond the scope of this chapter. These may include
suboccipital pain, painful torticollis, impaired cerebellar function,

motor deficit, coordination disturbances, cranial nerve dysfunction, and
other. It is important to emphasize that symptoms may develop rapidly,
especially in very young children who may present with breathing
problems such as central or obstructive apnea (OSA) or central sleep
apnea (CSA) that may lead rapidly to respiratory arrest [14, 20, 38–41].

50 5 Treatment
50 5 1 Hydrocephalus
Hydrocephalus may develop before or after treatment of
craniosynostosis. Whenever possible, vault expansion should be done
initially but, in some cases, especially those with marked intracranial
pressure, hydrocephalus should be treated first [37, 42]. There is no
consensus regarding the type of treatment with many authors
preferring shunting or third ventriculostomy as the first choice in
dealing with hydrocephalus [11, 43].

50 5 2 Surgical Treatment of CMI
Surgical treatment of tonsillar herniation in asymptomatic patients is
controversial [8, 44, 45] although the prophylactic decompression
premise lacks statistical data and long-term follow-up [14].
Cinalli [8] and the Dallas group [46, 47] proposed an occipital
decompression and an in-continuity enlargement of the posterior FM
region. This procedure is accepted with some variations by many
authors [11, 46, 48]. Figure 50.1 shows an example from the historical
series of the authors of a patient with Pfeiffer syndrome, presenting
closure of the coronal, sagittal, and lambdoid sutures, cooper beaten
sign and “coupe de serpe” sign, which characterizes the interruption of
the posterior curvature of the skull due to the hypoplastic posterior
fossa. The treatment proposed at the time, as there were no significant
associated venous anomalies, consisting of posterior vault remodeling
with wide foramen magnum opening and then fronto-orbital
advancement. In isolated NSCS, cranial vault remodeling [49] or
posterior vault distraction are options to address these conditions [21].
Figure 50.2 shows a case of CMI in a patient with scaphocephaly, where
only the remodeling of the skull was enough to correct the clinicalradiological issues of the CMI.

Fig. 50.1 Pfeiffer syndrome patient, presenting pansynostosis and Chiari I malformation.
Posterior vault remodeling and wide opening of the foramen magnum is shown

Fig. 50.2 Nonsyndromic scaphocephaly presenting Chiari I malformation treated with cranial
vault remodeling. Control MRI shows the resolution of the Chiari I malformation

However, even in syndromic forms, in most cases, the posterior
vault expansion is sufficient to increase the volume of the posterior
fossa. Figure 50.3 demonstrates posterior vault expansion in a patient
with Pfeiffer syndrome using springs, with significant improvement in
tonsil ectopia and posterior fossa volume. This technique, as well as
expansion with external distractors, is an option not only for the large
posterior volume acquired, but also to avoid access to the collateral
venous circulation commonly found in these patients and which can be
life-threatening.

Fig. 50.3 Pfeiffer syndrome patient presenting important venous collateral circulation.
Posterior vault expansion was performed with springs. Preop and postop CT scan shows the
difference in volume of the posterior fossa

Suboccipital and foramen magnum decompression should be
preferable in situations, such as syringomyelia [11], when the
correction of the supratentorial deformity and treatment of
hydrocephalus are ineffective or if there is a progression of the tonsillar
ectopia [11, 24]. Foramen magnum decompression alone has a limited
role in the treatment of CMI in the setting of craniosynostosis since the
options cited above are usually enough to resolve symptoms in most
patients [17].
Considering that a significant number of individuals with syndromic
craniosynostosis have intracranial-extracranial venous channels,
especially Crouzon-Pfeiffer and Apert, these patients should undergo
preoperative CT or MRI venography to identify venous anomalies and
avoid excessive bleeding with catastrophic results [33, 34, 38, 45] when
approaching the foramen magnum region.
The foramen magnum may be approached through a bicoronal
incision when planning the occipital expansion simultaneously or
through a midline incision when the isolated treatment is chosen. Some

authors recommend excising the posterior arch of C1 [11], but the
decompression of the foramen magnum and the adjacent bone of the
posterior fossa, as in cases of primary CMI seems to be enough.
Irrespective of the extension of the craniotomy, the dura mater is not
routinely opened due to the danger of uncontrollable hemorrhages
caused by collateral circulation around the foramen magnum. When the
signs and symptoms of CMI appear after correction of craniosynostosis,
the decompressive procedure is like that used in other forms of
deformity.

50 6 Complications
As stated by Renier [10], the main risk of posterior fossa
decompression in CMI/craniosynostosis is hemorrhage. Sandberg [50]
reported two cases in which occipital decompression was withheld due
to huge venous anomalies noted on imaging studies. Thompson [45]
presented the case of a patient with a cloverleaf skull syndrome in
whom division of occipital emissary veins during the elevation of the
skin flap led to an acute rise in ICP and death of the patient.

50 7 Outcome and Follow-Up
The association of CMI and craniosynostosis is rare, and it is difficult to
evaluate the results of FM decompression since the procedure is
seldom performed alone, and the treatment of craniosynostosis sensu
stricto involves decompression of the brain before or after addressing
the foramen magnum. Scott et al. [47] considered that the extent of
tonsillar descent and tightness of the foramen magnum are important
risk factors, and Addo et al. [20] reported that FM decompression
improved CSA in all five patients of their series. Regarding
syringomyelia, in all cases of Scott et al. [47], the syrinx was found to be
significantly smaller postoperatively. Patients with CMI should have a
regular follow-up and screening through MRI. There is no consensus on
how long this must be done.
