51 Evaluation Tools for
Craniosynostosis
Rebecca M. Burke1 and John R. W. Kestle1
(1) Department of Neurosurgery, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT,
USA

John R W Kestle
Email: neuropub@hsc.utah.edu
Keywords Craniosynostosis – Outcome measurement – Clinical
assessment

51 1 Introduction
Historically, the pre- and postoperative assessment of craniosynostosis
was largely subjective and employed the use of imaging modalities such
as computed tomography (CT) that resulted in radiation exposure to
the developing brain of pediatric patients [1–7]. Consequently, there
has been a movement to develop objective and reproducible evaluation
tools that do not rely on ionizing radiation to reliably characterize
preoperative cranial vault deformity and postoperative correction [8,
9]. Here, we describe the evolution of these assessment tools and their
clinical relevance with an emphasis on advancements in the realm of
scaphocephaly and trigonocephaly.

51 2 Early Attempts at Predicting the Need for
Revision Surgery: The Whittaker Classification

One of the earliest attempts to create an assessment tool for
postoperative outcomes in craniosynostosis surgery was in 1987 with
the development of the Whitaker classification, a 4-point scale that
stratifies the degree of revision surgery that would achieve cosmetic
normalcy [6, 7]. The classification scheme is as follows: (I) no
refinements or surgical revisions considered advisable or necessary by
the surgeon or the patient; (II) soft-tissue or lesser bone-contouring
revisions desirable, whether performed or not; (III) major alternative
osteotomies or bone-grafting procedures needed or performed; and
(IV) major procedure duplicating or exceeding in extent the original
surgery necessary (Table 51.1). Although this classification has been
widely used in the literature, it is limited by the subjective nature of the
reporting scheme, which has led to questions about its interrater
reliability demonstrating the need for more objective and reliable
assessment tools to properly evaluate the patient with craniosynostosis
[6, 10, 11]. In a retrospective analysis by Wes et al. [6], the Whitaker
classification demonstrated low interrater reliability and did not
successfully predict the need for future operative intervention. The
basic premise of this study highlighted the limitations of allowing
subjective aesthetic assessments to dictate operative decision-making.
Although the Whitaker classification laid the groundwork for a system
that could guide the need for further intervention, its significant
limitations were clear, leading to the development of alternative
assessment tools.
Table 51.1 Whitaker classification definitions
Classification Description
I

No refinements or surgical revisions considered advisable or necessary by the
surgeon or the patient.

II

Soft-tissue or lesser bone-contouring revisions desirable, whether performed
or not.

III

Major alternative osteotomies or bone-grafting procedures needed or
performed.

IV

Major procedure duplicating or exceeding in extent the original surgery
necessary.

Reproduced with permission from Wes AM, Naran S, Sun J, Mazzaferro
D, Xu W, Nguyen P, et al. The Whitaker classification of craniosynostosis

outcomes: an assessment of interrater reliability. Plast Reconstr Surg.
2017;140(4):579e–86e

51 3 Sagittal Synostosis
51 3 1 Anthropometric Analysis
Because sagittal synostosis represents the most common form of
single-suture synostosis, comprising 40–60% of isolated synostoses
cases, several parameters have been devised to facilitate its
preoperative evaluation and postoperative assessment [11–13].
Historically, the cranial index (CI) has been used as a two-dimensional
(2D), linear, quantitative measure of the severity of sagittal synostosis,
and its utility has also been observed in outcome assessment [4, 9]. The
CI is defined as the ratio of maximum cranial width, which is measured
from euryon to euryon, to the maximum cranial length, which is
measured from the glabella to the opisthocranion 100 [4, 14].
Patients with isolated sagittal synostosis (ISS) have an average CI of 60–
67%, in contrast to their unaffected counterparts with a CI of 76–78%.
Despite the wide utility of the CI in the assessment of ISS, it is not
without its limitations, and several studies have called into question its
reproducibility [3, 15, 16]. One criticism is the variability in technique
used to measure the maximal cranial width and maximal cranial length,
which can be further complicated by the variable degrees of frontal and
occipital bossing [9, 16]. In fact, the results of a study by Al-Shaqsi et al.
[17] indicated that the traditional method of measuring the CI
underestimates the severity of scaphocephaly. Instead, they proposed a
modified method of measuring the CI, calculated as the ratio of the
most anterior point on the cranium to the opisthocranion, to more
accurately reflect the severity of scaphocephaly by taking the degree of
frontal bossing into consideration (Fig. 51.1). Similarly, in isolation, the
CI does not provide information about regional severity [3]. The CI is
also generated from 2D measurements to describe a three-dimensional
(3D) object and is therefore a descriptive oversimplification [15].

Fig. 51.1 Lateral view of sagittal craniosynostosis with traditional cranial index (red line) and
modified cranial index (yellow line). (Reproduced with permission from Al-Shaqsi SZ, Rai A,
Forrest C, Phillips J. Standardization of cranial index measurement in sagittal craniosynostosis. J
Craniofac Surg. 2019;30:366–9)

In further recognition of a need for standardized assessment tools
in the evaluation of craniosynostosis, Fearon et al. [18] employed the
use of anthropometric measurements to evaluate long-term skull
growth and surgical outcomes in patients undergoing surgical
correction for ISS. Four measurements, including minimum frontal
breadth, head circumference, maximum cranial length measured from
the glabella to the opisthocranion, and maximal cranial breadth
measured from euryon to euryon, were obtained. The anthropometric
values obtained were compared with sex- and age-matched controls
and converted to standard ( ) scores for standardized comparison. The
authors demonstrated that the anthropometric measurements
normalized 6 weeks postoperatively. However, long-term follow-up
revealed a disproportionate restriction in growth in width when
compared with length, thus promoting a more scaphocephalic skull

morphology over time [18]. Although anthropometric measurements
have allowed for significant advances in our understanding of
craniosynostosis, they do not provide 3D information, and their use
also introduces significant inter- and intraobserver error [3, 9].
Furthermore, obtaining reliable and reproducible anthropometric data
from a young, uncooperative pediatric patient can be very challenging
[9].

51 3 2 Intracranial Volume Assessment
Early studies relied on the use of CT to evaluate intracranial volume as
a mechanism to follow preoperative and postoperative outcomes [19–
22]. One study employed thin-cut CT scans, fine-point calipers, a 0.5mm ruler, and a 1° protractor to evaluate 14 measurements based on
bony landmarks to evaluate the morphology of the midface and cranial
vault in ISS patients [19]. Another study evaluated scans on a slice-byslice basis with computerized counting of the number of voxels within
the intracranial cavity for the corresponding slice being evaluated [20].
This was repeated for each slice such that the intracranial volume could
be extrapolated. Using this methodology, the authors were able to
demonstrate that the preoperative intracranial volume and
postoperative cranial expansion in patients with ISS was approaching
or exceeding that of age-matched controls. David et al. [21] used a 3D
laser scan to measure the CI, morphology, and intracranial volume in
patients with scaphocephaly pre- and postoperatively (Fig. 51.2). A
ratio of anterior to total cranial volume was measured and
demonstrated a trend toward normalization after surgery. Although the
intracranial volume from a CT can be a useful and objective assessment
tool in the analysis of ISS, the radiation exposure required using this
modality is not ideal in the developing brain.

Fig. 51.2 (a) Portable laser Doppler scanning device. (b) Example of images obtained with
volume calculation using Delta Scan Comparison software. (Reproduced with permission from
David LR, Plikaitis CM, Couture D, Glazier SS, Argenta LC. Outcome analysis of our first 75
spring-assisted surgeries for scaphocephaly. J Craniofac Surg. 2010;21:3–9)

51 3 3 CT Vector Analysis
Midsagittal vector analysis has been used to assess pre- and
postoperative morphology after cranial vault remodeling [23]. This
method uses a radial vector analysis from a single point in the sagittal
plane at the level of the sella turcica to assess distances to the cranial
surface (Fig. 51.3). Vectors in the frontal, vertex, and occipital regions
were calculated pre- and postoperatively from CT scans. Postoperative
data demonstrated a reduction in the frontal and occipital prominence,
an increase in the height of the vertex, and correction in frontal and
occipital bossing [23]. Although this provided a more objective
assessment of pre- and postoperative morphology, this technique is
limited by its 2D assessment as well as the need for ionizing radiation
[9]. Similarly, the decrease in the biparietal diameter in scaphocephaly
would not be adequately evaluated using this purely sagittal plane
methodology [9].

Fig. 51.3 Set of radial vectors at 10° increments are created in radial pattern, emanating from
posterior ledge of sella. Measurements are taken to outer table. Analysis is performed pre- and
postoperatively to allow qualitative analysis and to provide data suitable for paired statistical
analysis. (Reproduced with permission from Marcus JR, Stokes TH, Mukundan S, Forrest CR.
Quantitative and qualitative assessment of morphology in sagittal synostosis: mid-sagittal
vector analysis. J Craniofac Surg. 2006;17(4):680–6)

Ruiz-Correa et al. [16] demonstrated the superiority of
scaphocephaly severity indices (SSIs) as compared with the CI in the
ability to predict ISS. SSIs were generated by tracing 2D planes defined
by several internal anatomical landmarks, including the top of the
lateral ventricles, the foramen of Monro, and the maximal dimension of
the fourth ventricle, and measuring the ratio of head width and length
in each of these planes (Fig. 51.4). It was determined that although CI
demonstrates a high level of sensitivity, it lacks specificity in contrast to
the SSI, which demonstrates high levels of both sensitivity and
specificity [16].

Fig. 51.4 SSI-A, SSI-F, and SSI-M were computed from CT bone slices defined by internal
anatomical landmarks based on cerebral ventricles just above the top of the lateral ventricles
(A-plane), the Foramina of Munro (F-plane), and at the level of the maximal dimension of the
fourth ventricle (M-plane). (Reproduced with permission from Ruiz-Correa S, Sze RW, Starr JR,
Lin HT, Speltz ML, Cunningham ML, et al. New scaphocephaly severity indices of sagittal
craniosynostosis: a comparative study with cranial index quantifications. Cleft Palate Craniofac
J. 2006;43(2):211–21)

Moreover, CT scan digital analysis has been employed in patients
with sagittal synostosis to address whether associated frontal bossing
requires direct surgical correction or if there is spontaneous resolution
of the frontal bossing over time after posterior cranial vault expansion
[24]. In this study, CT scans converted to 3D models were evaluated
immediately and 2 years after posterior-middle cranial vault expansion.
Quantitative angular and linear measures of frontal bossing were
obtained in a standardized fashion in the axial and midsagittal planes

and compared with healthy controls. Using CT scan digital analysis, the
authors demonstrated that patients with sagittal synostosis who
undergo surgery before 1 year of age spontaneously normalize the
frontal bossing within a 2-year postoperative window. Thus, using
standardized, objective assessment techniques, the authors were able
to illustrate that a single-stage operation, if offered within the first year
of life, helps avoid forehead contour deformities related to a more
extensive procedure as well as multistage procedures that are
associated with greater risk of morbidity [24]. Although this addressed
some of the limitations previously discussed, the use of CT scan digital
analysis still involved recurrent exposure to radiation.

51 3 4 Three-Dimensional Vector Analysis
3D vector analysis (3DVA) has been validated as a tool for craniofacial
morphologic assessment with the purposes of diagnosis, surgical
planning, and outcome assessment in the setting of the shortcomings of
cranial anthropometric and 2D techniques [3, 15]. However, 3DVA
software is used to generate a 3D matrix of the imported pre- and
postoperative CT scan DICOM data, which is presented as a concurrent
axial, coronal, and sagittal view. The user must then select the dorsum
sella, nasion, and vertex. Vectors are then generated from the dorsum
sella to the cranial surface such that a cranial point cloud
representation comprised of more than 37,000 points is created (Fig.
51.5, top) [3, 9, 15]. This results in a 3D representation in a graphical
form that is programmed to generate a set of clinically meaningful
anthropometric values, and a digital “craniofacial fingerprint” is created
(Fig. 51.5, bottom) [3]. This allowed for the generation of a color
histogram superimposed over the cranial point cloud that
demonstrates deviations from normal controls (Fig. 51.6) [3, 9]. The
same group went on to use 3DVA to generate a normative database that
was accurate and reproducible [3]. Strengths of 3DVA include its ability
to distinguish between varying pathologies and its ability to
differentiate subtle morphologic differences in patients with the same
disease process. Although 3DVA provides a 3D analysis of craniofacial
morphology and provides a quantitative and reproducible assessment,
long-term studies would necessitate repeat exposure to ionizing
radiation [9].

51 3 5 3D Digital Stereophotogrammetry
3D digital stereophotogrammetry has emerged as a useful tool to
obtain objective, reproducible, noninvasive information for the
assessment of craniosynostosis, with an additional advantage of not
requiring exposure to ionizing radiation [9, 25–29]. It has been used to
differentiate between patients with and without craniosynostosis,
predict what suture is fused, and objectively quantify postsurgical
aesthetic outcomes (Fig. 51.7) [26].

Fig. 51.7 Head shape metrics calculated for one example patient with sagittal craniosynostosis
from the preoperative computed tomographic image. (Top) Local malformations (mm) and
(bottom) curvature discrepancies (mm 1). Positive malformations represent overdevelopment,
and negative values represent underdevelopment. Positive curvature discrepancies represent
sharper areas than the normative model, whereas negative values represent flatter areas.
(Reproduced with permission from Porras AR, Tu L, Tsering D, Mantilla E, Oh A, Enquobahrie A,

et al. Quantification of head shape from three-dimensional photography for presurgical and
postsurgical evaluation of craniosynostosis. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2019;144(6):1051e–60e)

Weinberg et al. [29] evaluated 19 standardized, linear facial
measurements derived from 17 landmarks on the face favoring the
oral–nasal region with digital calipers as well as 3D photographs
captured with the Genex 3D system. The 3D imaging system allows
each point on the object’s surface to have a corresponding pixel in the x,
y, and z coordinates. They also assessed the precision and accuracy of
the measurements with and without landmarks. They demonstrated
that the precision of the 3D photographs was superior to that of the
digital calipers, and the highest precision was obtained from
measurements taken with 3D photogrammetry with landmarks labeled
before the images were captured [29].
Van Veelen et al. [28] used 3D photogrammetry to measure
intracranial volume in patients that underwent early extended strip
craniectomy or late total cranial remodeling, and volume
measurements were related to CI, head circumference, and signs of
elevated intracranial pressure. Additionally, the volume measurements
derived from the 3D photogrammetry were compared with those
obtained from 3D CT. The authors demonstrated that pre- and
postoperative volume was increased in all patients that underwent
surgery when compared with age-matched controls. Patients who
underwent late total cranial remodeling had a slightly larger
intracranial volume than patients that underwent early strip
craniectomy. Volume measurements obtained on 3D photogrammetry
demonstrated a high level of reproducibility and had a strong
correlation with measurements obtained on CT [28]. Mertens et al. [25]
used 3D photogrammetry to evaluate the effect of early extended strip
craniectomy for sagittal synostosis versus a late modified pi procedure
on intracranial volume and CI and showed that both techniques are
effective at normalizing these variables, but surgical duration and blood
loss were significantly lower in patients undergoing early strip
craniectomy.
In contrast, Seeberger et al. [27] used 3D photogrammetry to
compare the intracranial volume of children with sagittal synostosis to
age- and sex-matched controls and demonstrated that male patients
with sagittal synostosis had significantly smaller intracranial volumes
compared with their unaffected counterparts. Although these results

conflict with the previous studies, they illustrate the utility of 3D
photogrammetry in the evaluation of craniosynostosis and highlight the
benefit of reducing patient exposure to ionizing radiation. Other
strengths of this modality include its noninvasive nature, ease of
collection in potentially uncooperative pediatric patients, and the
ability to generate a 3D archive of a patient’s facial morphology [9].
Recent advances have coupled the use of 3D photogrammetry with
deep learning for craniosynostosis diagnosis [30]. Preoperative 3D
stereophotographs were obtained in patients with scaphocephaly,
trigonocephaly, and anterior plagiocephaly and in unaffected infants,
and a deep learning network was used to classify the shape as control
or one of the corresponding craniosynostosis subtypes. To validate the
deep learning network, a tenfold cross validation was used, and the 3D
stereophotographs were correctly classified in 195 of 196 subjects,
illustrating the ability of deep learning algorithms to accurately predict
subtypes of craniosynostosis as well as controls [30].

51 4 Metopic Synostosis
Similar challenges in the assessment of metopic synostosis such as a
lack of objective and reproducible measurements have been described
and further limited by exposure to ionizing radiation with serial
imaging assessments [31, 32]. In response to these challenges, several
techniques have been devised.

51 4 1 Quantitative Measurements Using CT
Patients with a diagnosis of isolated metopic synostosis were evaluated
pre- and postoperatively with high-resolution, thin-section CT scans
[33]. A total of 14 measurements were derived from the CT scans from
bony landmarks and quantified with a fine-point caliper, a 0.5-mm
ruler, and a 1° protractor. Preoperatively, patients had a narrowed
intercoronal distance at a value of 92% of the general population,
narrowed anteromedial wall interorbital distance at 79% of the general
population, narrowed lateral orbital wall distance at 94% of the general
population, and elevated medial orbital wall protrusion at 115% of the
general population. Operative intervention corrected these
abnormalities by 1-year postoperatively [33].

Trigonocephaly severity indices have been derived from CT scans of
patients diagnosed with metopic synostosis to stratify the severity of
the cranial dysmorphology [34]. CT scans underwent volumetric
reformatting to trace 2D planes defined by several landmarks, and
severity indices were generated. In concert, the metopic severity index
was also derived. The authors demonstrated that the severity indices,
which were outcome shape-based and therefore reflect outline
information that represents global information, achieved more
accuracy than the metopic severity index with is a linear distancedbased measurement [34].

51 4 2 The Metopic Angle
Data from a retrospective review of patients that underwent
endoscopic strip craniectomy for metopic synostosis were imported
into the STARscanner Laser Data Acquisition System to obtain cranial
vault contour data [31, 35]. In the system, reference is defined by the
tragus and root of the nose, and all measurements were fashioned with
respect to the reference plane. The metopic angle was derived from
images of the anterior–posterior diameter of the cranial contour. A line
perpendicular to this diameter is laterally extended until it meets the
contour of the frontal bone bilaterally. Tangential lines to the contour of
the frontal bones are then drawn, and the metopic angle is formed at
the tangential intersection (Fig. 51.8) [31, 35]. The authors
demonstrated that the metopic angle at 3 months and 1 year
postoperatively in patients that underwent endoscopic strip
craniectomy for metopic synostosis were comparable with those of agematched controls [31].

Fig. 51.8 Laser scans. The STARscanner Laser Data Acquisition System allows collection of
images of the vault circumference in different planes. Our reference plane is defined by tragion
(t) and sellion (Se), as surrogates for porion and nasion, respectively. All the measurements
were made in a plane parallel with the reference plane situated at 3/10th of the height of the
vault from the reference plane (a). To allow for direct comparisons, the cranial contour at each
point postoperatively (blue) was plotted on the same diagram with the preoperative vault
contour (red). The 1-year postoperative diagrams of 4 different patients are presented (b–e).
(f–i) The steps used to calculate the metopic angle. Initially, the anteroposterior diameter is
drawn and measured (f). A distance equal to 1/40th of this diameter is measured from the most
anterior point (g). A perpendicular line to the anteroposterior diameter is developed at this
level and extended laterally until it intersects the frontal bone contour bilaterally (h). At those
intersection points, tangential lines to the frontal bone contour are drawn bilaterally. The
metopic angle is formed at the intersection of these 2 tangents (i). (Reproduced with
permission from Gociman B, Agko M, Blagg R, Garlick J, Kestle JR, Siddiqi F. Endoscopic-assisted
correction of metopic synostosis. J Craniofac Surg. 2013;24(3):763–8)

51 4 3 Anterior-Posterior Volume Ratio
The STARscanner imaging acquisition system has been used to create a
novel assessment tool, the anterior–posterior volume ratio for the
evaluation of metopic synostosis patients that have undergone frontoorbital advancement [36]. This system uses multiple surface lasers to
create a 3D reconstruction of the patient’s head. A technician then
identifies several soft tissue landmarks on the 3D image including the
sellion, left tragus, and right tragus. Using this information, the system
creates several axial reference planes that are used to calculate multiple
linear measurements, which are ultimately used to create volumetric
data (Fig. 51.9) [36]. The volumetric data allow the cranial vault to be

divided into four quadrants that are further classified as anterior or
posterior. The anterior–posterior volume ratio is defined as the ratio of
the sum of the anterior cranial vault volumes to the sum of the
posterior vault volumes and was shown to increase postoperatively as
expected, although this study was limited by its small sample size [36].

Fig. 51.9 (Left) Schematic representation of the levels for which the STAR scanner produces
linear measurements and the landmarks that are used for acquisition. Level 3 was determined
to be the most useful plane for analysis. (Right) Line connecting the tragia delineates the
anterior and posterior segments and a line from the selion perpendicular to this line divides the
cranium into the left and right segments. (Reproduced with permission from Weathers WM,
Khechoyan D, Wolfswinkel EM, Mohan K, Nagy A, Bollo RJ, et al. A novel quantitative method for
evaluating surgical outcomes in craniosynostosis: pilot analysis for metopic synostosis.
Craniomaxillofac Trauma Reconstr. 2014;7(1):1–8)

51 4 4 The Metopic Index
The metopic index (MI) represents a simple anthropometric cranial
measurement that can be derived from CT scans as well as cranial
landmarks that can be palpated on physical examination [32]. In a
retrospective analysis of patients with metopic synostosis, CT scans
were converted to 3D reconstructions. The MI was calculated from the
midfrontozygomatic diameter (the minimum width between the
midfrontozygomatic points, or the midpoint along the recess above the
brow ridge between the anteroinferolateral frontal bone and frontal
bone zygomatic process) divided by the euryon–euryon distance

(maximal cranial width determined from the lateral extremes of the
skull) (Fig. 51.10). The authors showed that the mean preoperative MI
in patients with trigonocephaly was significantly lower than that of agematched controls but normalized after operative intervention [32].

Fig. 51.10 Superior projection of a 3D reconstruction of a CT scan obtained in a child without
craniosynostosis. Displayed are the midfrontozygomatic diameter (6.85 cm) and the eurioneurion diameter (11.67 cm). The metopic index is therefore 0.59, which is within the range of
normal based upon measurements obtained in control subjects. (Reproduced with permission
from Wang JY, Dorafshar AH, Liu A, Groves ML, Ahn ES. The metopic index: an anthropometric
index for the quantitative assessment of trigonocephaly from metopic synostosis. J Neurosurg
Pediatr. 2016;18(3):275–80)

51 4 5 3D Stereophotogrammetry
As previously discussed, the use of 3D stereophotogrammetry is
particularly advantageous because it provides objective, quantitative,
and reproducible data without subjecting the developing brain to
radiation exposure [25, 26, 28, 29, 37]. However, 3D photogrammetry
has been used to demonstrate that preoperative frontal and total
intracranial volumes are smaller in patients with metopic synostosis

but that fronto-orbital advancement normalized these values 10 days
postoperatively [38]. Similarly, Kuehle et al. [39] used 3D photography
to demonstrate that the preoperative intracranial volume in male
patients with trigonocephaly is lower than that of age-matched
controls, but fronto-orbital remodeling is corrective (Fig. 51.11).

Fig. 51.11 Volumetric heat maps of a patient with trigonocephaly showing changes after
fronto-orbital remodeling: (a) axial view; (b) frontal view. Pre- and postoperative 3D
photogrammetric data were merged, and areas of volume changes were indicated in colors: red
indicates an increase in intracranial volume in milliliters; blue indicates a decrease in
intracranial volume in milliliters. (Reproduced with permission from Kuehle R, Ewerbeck N,
Ruckschloss T, Ristow O, El Damaty A, Freudlsperger C, et al. Photogrammetric evaluation of
corrective surgery for trigonocephaly. Int J Oral Maxillofac Surg. 2022;51(1):70–7)

Meulstee et al. [37] analyzed 3D photographs of trigonocephalic
patients using principal component analysis to identify the mean
cranial shape in this population in comparison with the variation in
cranial shape that is observed in the general population. With the
principal component analysis, the authors distinguished metopic
synostosis patients from age-matched controls [37]. Linden et al. [40]
used 3D photogrammetry to evaluate forehead contours pre- and
postoperatively in patients that underwent corrective surgery for
metopic synostosis. Their results showed that forehead contours
differed significantly preoperatively and immediately postoperatively
but that the changes immediately postoperatively persisted at the 1year postoperative time point (Fig. 51.12). de Jong et al. [41] performed

a mean head shape and volume evaluation derived from 3D photos in
children with trigonocephaly who underwent endoscopic-assisted strip
craniectomy combined with helmet therapy. Using a mean shape
evolution analysis, they obtained the anterior fossa to total volume
ratio and showed that this value increased postoperatively. Thus, 3D
photogrammetry is a useful tool to evaluate pre- and postoperative
cranial morphology as well as long-term outcomes with the major
advantages of ease of use and lack of radiation exposure [9].

Fig. 51.12 Example of a color map overlaying a preoperative and over 1-year postoperative
images “best fit” in 3-D orientation. Color mapping was used to highlight changes in the upper
third of the face and further demonstrate the relative volume deficit at the midline, shown in
red, and the lateral expansion in blue after surgical correction. (Reproduced with permission
from Linden OE, Baratta VM, Gonzalez JA, Byrne ME, Klinge PM, Sullivan SR, et al. Surgical
correction of metopic craniosynostosis: a 3D photogrammetric analysis of cranial vault
outcomes. Cleft Palate Craniofac J. 2019;56(2):231–5)

51 5 Conclusions
Although predicting the need for operative intervention in
craniosynostosis surgery has its roots in subjective assessments such as
the Whitaker classification, major advances in the evaluation of cranial
morphology have been achieved. Driving these advancements is the
development of objective, reproducible, and quantifiable evaluation
tools that can be standardized across centers and surgeons. Although
the evolution of assessment has involved subjective measures, direct
anthropometric measurements from palpable patient landmarks,
quantitative analysis of 2D and 3D CT, and most recently 3D
photogrammetry coupled with deep learning, the primary goal of
improving patient care and patient outcomes has remained at the
forefront. Nevertheless, the future of evaluation tools in
craniosynostosis harbors much promise for further development.

52 Complications and Long-Term
Surgical Outcome in Craniosynostoses
Matthieu Vinchon1, 2 , Pierre-Aurélien Beuriat1 ,
Alexandru Szathmari1 and Federico Di Rocco1

Keywords Surgical complications – Prevention – Informed consent –

52 1 Introduction
The life of a child affected by craniosynostosis is impacted in many and
highly variable ways, on account both of his condition and of the
surgery it leads to. Craniosynostoses are serious malformations, with
often dire consequences, even more so when associated with
faciostenosis. On the other hand, despite constant effort to optimize
results and decrease morbidity, surgery is always an important

undertaking and is associated with a number of unwanted
consequences, during operation, in the immediate postoperative
course, or later in life. For these reasons, it is important to know the
complications of synostoses and of their treatment, in order to inform
the decision to operated, taken conjointly by the surgeon and the child’s
parents, as well as anticipate surgical difficulties. In the present chapter,
we shall review chronologically the different complications of
craniosynostoses before, during, and after surgery, their management
and prevention. We shall conclude on the issues of surgical decision and
informed consent and the need for consensual quantitative scales to
evaluate morphological results as well as surgical complications.

52 2 Preoperative Complications
52 2 1 Birth Difficulties
The calvarial sutures play an important role in the biomechanics of
birth, and their fusion can have dire consequences [1]. In an earlier,
unpublished study conducted in Lille during the years 2016–2021,
among 233 new cases of craniosynostoses, we found that the overall
prevalence of dystocia (difficult or instrumented birth) was 45.5%;
among these, 30.5% were delivered by C-section (compared with 20%
in the general population in France during that period), 24.4% of them
because of fetal distress. The prevalence of C-section was highest
among boys, and patients with metopic or multisutural synostosis (Fig.
52.1). Dystocia was the cause of birth trauma in four identified cases:
one with sagittal synostosis who developed a large subperiosteal
hematoma (Fig. 52.2a, b); one with metopic synostosis who had
petrous bone fracture and subdural bleeding associated with forceps
delivery (Fig. 52.2c, d); one with unilambdoid synostosis who
developed a subdural hemorrhage; and one with complex multisuture
synostosis who developed intracerebral hemorrhage (Fig. 52.2e).
Although the mechanical trauma was predominantly mild and had no
or few consequences, dystocia could also cause fetal distress during and
after birth, with potential impact on the patient’s later development.
Birth difficulties could thus be a confounding factor when studying the
developmental impact of brain compression by the synostosis.
Although the majority of children with craniosynostosis are delivered

by natural vaginal delivery, a prenatal diagnosis should reinforce the
vigilance regarding possible dystocia and lower the threshold for
cesarean section.

Fig. 52.1 Conditions of birth in 233 cases of craniosynostoses followed during the period
2016–2019 in Lille. Close to half of these children had delivery difficulties, 30.3% born by Csection, 24.4% by C-section for fetal distress. These birth difficulties can be anticipated in case
of prenatal diagnosis, and may be a confusion factor regarding the developmental outcome

Fig. 52.2 Birth trauma in children with craniosynostosis: (a, b) sagittal synostosis, with the
characteristic bilateral cephalhematoma, because no periosteal midline adherence limits its
spread; (c, d) metopic synostosis, with difficult forceps delivery, scalp laceration, fracture of the
petrous bone and subdural bleeding; (e) a newborn with complex multisuture synostosis who
developed intracerebral hemorrhage

52 2 2 Brain Compression

Brain decompression by calvarial expansion is the cornerstone of
surgery for craniosynostoses. However, the relation between reduced
intracranial volume and intracerebral pressure is complex, certainly
underpinned by poorly understood hydrodynamic mechanisms [2].
Multiple suture synostoses, mostly syndromic, are associated with
raised intracranial pressure (ICP), which increases with the number of
fused sutures [3]. Calvarial growth restriction is often the main
presenting symptom of multisuture craniosynostoses, sometimes
present at birth in case of cloverleaf malformation, or later during
progression toward oxycephaly, with progressive closure of the
different sutures [4].
By contrast, in unisutural synostoses, the initial presentation in
early childhood is mostly related to morphological concerns, and the
brain is generally not compressed initially. Typically, the closure of the
sagittal suture is compensated by the coronal and metopic sutures,
giving the child his typical dolichocephalic appearance with a bulging
forehead and an above-normal head circumference. However, in older
children, sagittal synostosis can mimic pseudotumor cerebri [5], and is
a not uncommon finding in clinically eloquent tonsillar herniation [6].
Similarly, ICP can rise late after correction of unisutural synostosis,
because of nonsynchronous multisuture synostosis [7].
Regarding metopic synostosis, the occurrence of brain compression
and the benefit of decompressive surgery are controversial. While some
authors have documented intracranial hypertension [8], others, using
sophisticated imaging techniques, found no evidence of brain
compression [9]. Better developmental outcomes have been reported in
all types of craniosynostoses when surgery was performed before the
age of 1 year [10]; however, in this retrospective study, the reason why
some children were operated early, and others later, was not analyzed.
A more recent study has found that late surgery was associated with
confounding factors susceptible to influence developmental outcome,
such as social context, prematurity, and comorbidities [11].

52 2 3 Psychosocial Impact of Morphological Disgrace
Difficulties can arise during childhood because of the morphological
disgrace, leading to problems of self-image, taunting, and even
harassment by schoolmates (and even occasionally by teachers!). The

psychological impact at school age should not be taken lightly.
Compounded with the parental stress, which children and infants feel
and absorb like sponges, this psychological burden may play a
significant role in the future life of these patients. Very rarely, the
demand for morphological correction is not expressed until adult age
[12]. Moreover, in familial cases, the demand for early morphological
correction for their child, coming from affected parents, is revealing.

52 3 Intraoperative Complications
52 3 1 Anesthesia and Installation
Complications of anesthesia and installation are the shared
responsibility of the surgeon and the anesthetist. Among these, the risk
of complications of venous and arterial catheters, and pression sores on
the scalp or eyeballs (Fig. 52.3) must be decreased by scrupulous
attention from both teams.

Fig. 52.3 Complications of arterial catheter (a), of peripheral venous catheters (b), of
positioning (c, d) are a shared responsibility of the surgeon and anesthetist

52 3 2 Bleeding
Intraoperative bleeding occurs whatever the technique chosen, is the
most threatening complications during surgery, with a potential for
fatal consequences, and requires blood transfusion in a number of
patients. The importance of bleeding relates to the body proportions in
infants, with a larger head and a limited blood volume (estimated
around 500 mL at 3 months and 750 mL at 3 months) compared to
adults. Diffuse bleeding comes from the scalp, the dura-mater (in
particular arachnoid villi, which appear around 9 months) and above all

from the bone, especially at the skull base. In craniosynostosis surgery,
bleeding is increased by enlarged trans-osseous veins and intracranial
hypertension. Clotting problems can result from profuse bleeding and
hypothermia, so a high degree of vigilance and close interactions
between surgeon and anesthetist are warranted, in order to avoid
entering a fatal spiral.
Rigorous anesthesia protocols are followed in order to monitor
hemodynamics; near-infrared spectroscopy can help to determine if
and when transfusion must be decided (Fig. 52.4). In case of profuse
bleeding, supplementation with platelets and clotting factors may also
be needed. Transfusion following all the security protocols incurs
extremely low additional risk, whereas reluctance or delay to transfuse
can have fatal consequences. Although all precautions to diminish the
risk of bleeding should be taken, we consider that transfusion should
not be regarded as a complication. In consequence, the acceptance from
parent that transfusion may be needed is a prerequisite for surgery.

Fig. 52.4 Near-infrared spectroscopy can be used when the forehead is not in the operative
field (sagittal synostosis and posterior pole surgeries), and helps to determine if and when
transfusion is needed

Intraoperative blood loss is anticipated preoperatively by iron
supplementation and/or erythropoietin, and mitigated during surgery

by hemodilution and volume expansion. Meticulous hemostasis at each
stage of the operation requires precise knowledge of where the
bleeding comes from, notably the location of trans-osseous veins (Figs.
52.5 and 52.6). Permanent communication between surgeon and
anesthetist before, during, and after surgery is vital for the successful
management of this potentially lethal complication.

Fig. 52.5 Location of trans-osseous veins in metopic synostosis, numbered according to the
timing of their occurrence during fronto-orbital remodeling

Fig. 52.6 Parietal emissary veins in sagittal synostosis: (a) 3D-CT scanner; (b) operative view
of the exposed sagittal sinus, patient in the prone position

52 3 3 Dural Tear
Even though most dural tears occur at a distance from the venous
sinuses, dural lesions, even when involving only the outer layer,
increase blood loss, and, if left unattended, can initiate a meningocele.
Bleeding can become catastrophic if a dural tear involves a venous
sinus (Fig. 52.7). The risk of dural tear is diversely evaluated, because
not all authors take note of minimal splits of the dural outer layer.
Endoscopic techniques may not lead to more dural tears [13], but make
these more difficult to cope with. The risk of dural tear is higher in
newborns, in children with longstanding intracranial hypertension, in
craniofacial advancement [14] and in redo surgery [15], especially after
previous dural repair. Dural adherences are intense along the sutures,
in particular underneath the fontanels and epactal bones, and on the
midline of the skull base. Opening of the sagittal sinus is thus at higher
risk when the metopic suture is still patent [1]. The adherence of patent
sutures to the dura is especially tricky in unilambdoid synostosis,
because the lateral sinus is often lacking on the synostotic side [16],

and the sinus on the nonsynostotic, adherent side is compensatorily
enlarged.

Fig. 52.7 Cloverleaf skull, operated on D5 of life because of life-threatening intracranial
hypertension with tonsillar herniation. (a) CT-scanner showing the lacunae and complex
sutural pattern around the lesser fontanelle. (b) Operative view showing limited dural tear
close to the posterior fontanel

Dural tear at the skull base is a not uncommon complication of the
different techniques of fronto-orbital advancement in
craniofaciosynostoses [14, 17], with a high risk of cerebrospinal fluid
leakage and meningeal infection. Although these leaks can often dry
spontaneously, intracranial dural repair is sometimes necessary (Fig.
52.8).

Fig. 52.8 Two-years female operated for Crouzon disease with Le Fort 3 osteotomy because of
severe sleep apneas. She developed rhinorrhea because of ethmoidal dural tear (empty arrow);
note intradural pneumocephalus (full arrow), which required craniotomy for duraplasty

Partial dural tears, limited to the outer dural layer, should be
reapproximated by a few stitches whenever possible, sometimes
completed with fibrin glue. Complete dural tears must be repaired with
a running suture as watertight as possible, which may require
harvesting an epidural graft.
The prevention of dural tears involves careful dissection of bone
from permeable fontanels, and of sutures from the underlying sinuses
before using the craniotome. Use of the burr over the pterional and
asterial fontanels should be especially cautious. Dissection of the dura
from the bone can be tedious, on account of adherences and uneven
inner surface of the calvaria, as well as frequent bleeding from the
middle meningeal artery or dural veins. In very small infants with
cloverleaf malformation, patient dissection of the lacunae and epactal
bones, followed by piecemeal removal of the bone septa, often
extending deep between the sulci, is the most delicate time of
suturectomy [18].

52 4 Early Postoperative Period
52 4 1 The Emotional Shock
In the immediate postoperative days, parental distress is almost
constant [19]. In addition to the child being in pain, or drowsy and
feeding poorly on account of opioid medications, he often presents with
facial edema, of variable severity but which can be major and
complicated by chemosis, and even subluxation of the tarsal cartilage.
The child’s ordeal appeals to his parent’s feelings of guilt over their
decision to have him operated, and echoes with the guilt which is very
widespread in parents of a child with inborn diseases, especially if
genetically determined. When the edema subsides, the change of facial
features, which was the purpose of the operation, can be difficult to
cope with. The rare complaint “it’s not my child anymore” is only the
most radical expression of a widespread parental unease. To make
things worse, parental stress is absorbed by the child, so that parental
and infantile stress amplify each other in a play of mirrors. This often
translates into sleepless nights back home, regressive reactions, with
often prolonged cosleeping. This postoperative stress should not be
overlooked and must be anticipated. Physical contact, cradling,
cuddling should be encouraged immediately after surgery. Before
surgery, parents should be informed of the oncoming physical changes
and convinced that the child’s appearance will be “more normal,” and
that he will have “the head he should have had.” Contacts with patients
associations can be a precious resource for these parents, who can thus
interact with others who “have been through that” before them.

52 4 2 Infection
Infection is a rare complication but can prolong hospital stay and have
dire consequences. A sepsis can result of operative site infection (OSI)
or venous or urinary catheter. However, aseptic fever is common, on
account of the large subcutaneous exposure, and should not lead to
untimely antibiotic treatments. By contrast, the reappearance of fever
and scalp edema after initial subsidence should raise alarm of OSI.
OSI occurs in up to 7% [20], and can be epidermal, dermal, or deep.
OSI is sometimes elicited by the child’s scratching his wound, or

initiated by inflammation caused by absorbable sutures, or skin
necrosis due to tension closure associated with ambitious calvarial
expansion. It can also be a consequence of incidental respiratory or
ocular infection present at the time of surgery; in these cases, it is wise
to postpone the scheduled operation, provided that the infection is
circumstantial and not chronic, in relation with faciostenosis, and also
that the child has no menacing intracranial hypertension. Other
potential factors associated with postoperative infection are the long
duration of surgery [21], the extended incision, opening of the facial
sinuses, the creation of an epidural dead space, skin breakdown, the
presence of implanted material, especially external distractors [22] or
springs, and prolonged use of venous or urinary catheter.
Whereas superficial scalp infection usually requires only local
measures (removal of scabs and remaining sutures plus local
antiseptics), superficial suppuration may be aggressive, the scab
protecting an ecosystem in which staphylococcus aureus thrives; in
addition to scab removal, oral antibiotics may be necessary. Deep
suppuration is rare but can be associated with septic signs, and require
debridement, drainage, and irrigation in addition to antibiotics [23].
The management of these postoperative empyemas should be as
conservative as possible, because wide opening and dismantling of the
construct would devascularize the bone flaps, and bone necrosis would
have catastrophic morphological consequences (Fig. 52.9).

Fig. 52.9 Crouzon syndrome, first operated for posterior pole expansion at 6 months,
reoperated at 5 years for fronto-orbital advancement. The child presented with fistulization of
an epidural empyema, which was treated with antibiotics, prolonged drainage-irrigation and
directed scarring

Prevention of local and deep infection implies rigorous asepsis,
before, during, and after surgery, and high-quality layered closure
without excessive tension. The child must be prevented from scratching
his wound, sometimes with the help of antihistamine medications.
Prophylactic antibiotics are administered routinely during surgery,
justified by the extent of surgery, its duration, and the potential gravity
of OSI; however, protocols vary and are mostly tradition-based [24].

52 4 3 Complications of Implants and Fixation Devices
Aseptic subcutaneous granulomas can develop on absorbable sutures
and plates, and take months to disappear, but require nothing more
than reassuring words. During surgery, simple precautions can
decrease these benign but vexing complications, like avoiding to place
knots over salient facial features, cutting threads short, and burying the
knots in bone perforations. Bone fixation with wires is generally well
tolerated but can lead to skin compromise or perforation [23], as well
as migrate inward into the dura as the calvaria grows by appositionresorption, and should be used sparingly (Fig. 52.10). The same
happens with much more serious consequences with non-absorbable
plates [25], springs, and prosthetic materials [26]. Absorbable plates
are generally well tolerated but can also cause aseptic granulomas, and
migrate, both inward and outward [27, 28].

Fig. 52.10 Complications of wires: outward migration of wires (a, b) can threaten or perforate
the scalp (b), while their inward migration (c, d), caused by resorptional calvarial growth,
brings these into contact or conflict with the dura (d)

52 4 4 Scalp and Calvarial Breakdown

Skin or bone disruption generally results of excessive tension of the
scalp, after generous volume expansion; it almost never happens after
external trauma.
Skin breakdown occurs mostly in children with multisuture
synostosis, especially in older children and after redo surgery. Even
when the underlying bone is exposed, it rarely causes serious infection,
but may require prolonged directed scarring, or sometimes
reoperation. Breakdown is prevented by progressive scalp traction,
which is one of the important advances brought about by distraction
techniques. Alternately, scalp expansion using a balloon expander can
be proposed, provided that the child’s calvaria is already rigid enough
not to cave in, and surgery can be programmed some time in advance.
Bone dislocation is a rare but worrisome complication.
Cranioplasties are at best semirigid constructs, especially in young
infants, and the mechanical compression by scalp traction can be
enough to cause breakdown of construct. The lordosis of the frontoorbital bandeau is caused by breakage of plates [29] or bone
dislocation at the pterion, especially if the coronal suture is
incompletely fused (Fig. 52.11). The fronto-malar synfibrosis is also a
weak point, where fixation of the lateral orbital pillar can give way.
Bone breakdown also occurs in redo surgery, because regenerative
bone becomes brittle. The occurrence of “gull-winging” (the uplifting of
the parietal bone by disjunction of sutures) happens after posterior
distraction [30], as the consequence of distracting a patent or
incompletely fused suture. Anterior distraction procedures can also
cause skull base dislocation, causing optic neuropathy after monobloc
osteotomy [31], or oculomotor paralysis on account of spheno-petrous
(“Le Fort 6”) dislocation (Fig. 52.12). All these complications impose
reoperations and/or reappraisal of the surgical strategy.

Fig. 52.11 Breakdown of construct caused by dislocation of the fronto-sphenoidal suture
under the tension of scalp, resulting in lordosis of the bandeau, lifted 12 mm, with eye exposure
and pulsating exophthalmos, and requiring reoperation for refixation of bandeau

Fig. 52.12 Fifteen-months child with Crouzon disease, operated for fronto-orbital
advancement with transfacial pin; axial CT scanner performed on D14 of craniofacial
distraction because of abducens palsy, showed spheno-temporal (“Le Fort 6”) dislocation
(arrows)

52 4 5 Growing Fracture

Postoperative leptomeningeal cysts or growing fractures develop as a
result of untended intraoperative dural tear or postoperative dural
necrosis, with the brain herniating through the rent and preventing it
from healing. It can develop after endoscopic surgery, because dural
tear can be unnoticed or because dural repair is most uneasy [32]. The
pressure gradient causes focal hydrodynamic disturbance, with
enlarged Virchow-Robin spaces [33].
Anatomical repair of the dura and calvaria is necessary (Fig. 52.13).
Whenever possible, autologous materials are highly preferable [33, 34].
The management of postoperative leptomeningeal cysts can be
challenging because of the tension of the brain (which may require
temporary lumbar drainage); of the proximity of the dural defect to the
sinuses; of the extent of bone defect requiring a large donor site; of the
young age of the child whose thin calvaria is difficult to split. However,
modern high-speed motors and piezoelectric saws allow the splitting of
calvaria in very young children [35].

Fig. 52.13 Figure growing fracture. (a) Seven-months male operated 2 months earlier for
sagittal synostosis (H-craniectomy with linear coagulation of the dura mater and no drainage,
causing dural necrosis). (b) Note the thickened bone margins (full arrows) due to uplifting of
the periosteal tissues. (b, c) The herniated brain tissue is highly edematous, due to expansion of
Virchow-Robin spaces. (e) The margins of the dural defect are much retracted (empty arrows),
requiring a large pericranial autograft (f). (g) The bone defect is bridged with split calvarial
autograft

52 5 Late Surgical Outcome
52 5 1 The Scar
Whatever the surgery, it leaves a scar. However much, as A. Raimondi
quipped, the infant’s scalp may be “forgiving,” the scar can be a problem
for the child’s self-image and a source of embarrassment. Its perception
is highly variable: while some children shun going to the swimming
pool for fear that their scar might show through wet hair, others glorify
it with creative hairstyle (Fig. 52.14). Like any bodily imperfection, the

scar can be a fixation point for teasing, taunting, and harassment at
school age, as well as self-depreciation at adolescence. In order to make
the scar as stealthy as possible, its curve should as much as possible
keep a 90° orientation relative to the direction of hair. When a father
has a receding hairline, his son’s incision may need to be more
posterior than usual. In complex synostoses, it should be kept in mind
that repeated surgeries may be needed in the future, and that the
bicoronal incision should be versatile enough to give access to both the
posterior and anterior poles. This may be problematic when the initial
surgery was endoscopic, with two scars, one very anterior, and the
other very posterior.

Fig. 52.14 (a) Discrete “lazy S” incision, curved in order to stay perpendicular to the natural
direction of hair, leaves the most discreet scar. (b) “Zig-zag” scar, intended to be easily hidden,
but glorified by creative haircut. (c) Early, wide and red scar, destined to whiten with time. (d)
Persistent cheloid scar of the scalp incision and of the drain

52 5 2 Redo Operations
Reoperations can be needed, sometimes many years after the initial
surgery. The larger or lesser importance of these reoperations led
Whitaker et al. to propose a grading of surgical results as: (1) not

requiring reoperation; (2) minor reoperation proposed; (3) reoperation
less than initial surgery necessary; and (4) reoperation as large or more
than initial surgery [36]. In addition to the operative complications
mentioned above, many of which can required additional surgery, other
operations may become necessary during follow-up.
Incomplete reossification of the calvaria leaves pulsating lacunae.
These occur in about 5% of operated cases, and appear to be more
frequent in fronto-orbital advancement [37], and occipital pole
remodeling [38]. Lacunae most often sit close to the midline, especially
at the vertex, and occur most often after extensive midline bone
resection [39], all the more in older children. On account of their
location, calvarial lacunae present no risk of traumatic brain injury, and
no limitations should be imposed on the child’s activities. Lacunae thus
present mostly an aesthetic problem, although some children also
experience the “syndrome of the trephined,” with headaches or
learning difficulties, and changes in the cerebral blood flow have been
documented in some cases [38]. The surgical management of persistent
lacunae can be proposed after the fifth or sixth birthday, and the most
desirable technique is autologous graft by split calvaria [35] (Fig.
52.15).

Fig. 52.15 Persisting lacuna at the vertex after craniectomy at 4 months for sagittal synostosis;
repair age 4 years, using split calvaria. (a) The craniotomy for the donor site is tailored on a
template outlined around the limits of the lacuna. (b) The flap is then split using the
piezoelectric saw. (c) Both bone tables are fixed rigidly in place is order to fill the lacuna and
the donor site

Temporal hollowing is specific problem with metopic synostosis,
and can result from atrophy of the temporal muscle compounded with
excessive restoration of frontal bosses. The progressive nature of this
imperfection, which becomes more apparent with time (Fig. 52.16),
suggests that bone growth is focally disturbed by surgery, possibly
because the greater wing of the sphenoid needs the strain of muscles to
sustain its growth. Temporal hollowing can be well accepted, or lead to
a demand for esthetic correction; this is easily performed by lipofilling,
which can be repeated as needed, but should preferably be delayed
until adolescence. Different technical refinements have been proposed
in order to reduce the prevalence of temporal hollowing, like large
temporal “elephant ears” [40], or tongue-and groove bandeau
advancement, with mixed results leaving room for improvement.

Fig. 52.16 Progressive temporal hollowing after surgery for metopic synostosis

52 5 3 Other Craniofacial Operations
Other major craniofacial operations are often needed in
craniofaciostenoses, in order to correct midface retrusion or
hypertelorism. Secondary multisuture synostosis should be expected in
syndromic craniofaciostenoses [4] as well as in lambdoid synostosis
[16], but are rare in sagittal synostosis, occurring in about 2% of cases
[39], and are almost never found in nonsyndromic metopic synostosis.
Secondary closure of new sutures attests of the progressive nature of
the disease, and these reoperations should not be regarded as
complications of surgery. However, this information regarding this

evolution should be given to parents as early as the first consultation, in
particular in case of prenatal diagnosis.
In addition, other relatively minor operations may be needed, such
as onlay grafts, rhinoplasty, removal of facial scars, correction of slant
eyes or of strabismus. Ideally, all these operations, which are mostly
destined to improve cosmesis, should be performed at the end of
growth and on demand from the patient himself.
The large array of different operations, implicating different surgical
specialists, at different ages, underlines the importance of prolonged
multidisciplinary follow-up.

52 5 4 Morphological Result
Although the Whitaker classification mentioned above [36] is
convenient and widely accepted [41], this classification is focused on
reinterventions, not on morphology, and does not quantify the
preoperative dysmorphism; for these reasons, it does not evaluate
accurately morphological results. Obviously, the objective
quantification of something as subjective as morphological disgrace has
proved difficult.
The evaluation of results by satisfaction questionnaires filled by the
parents may be fraught with complacency, or by the fear of another
operation. In one study, parents were generally as satisfied as surgeons
on all items, except for syndromic cases [42], where doctors appeared
ready to accept suboptimal results, possibly because no good surgical
solution exists. Similarly, another study found a better acceptance by
doctors, compared with parents, of what is inevitable (the scar,
alopecia) or for which they have no good surgical remedy (calvarial
asymmetry, bony bumps) [41]. This discrepancy shows a mismatch
between surgeons’ and parents’ expectations; whereas parents might
have inordinately high hopes of normalization, surgeons might be more
centered on what they can expect from their usual technique. Blinded
morphological evaluation by independent surgeons avoids the
complacency bias, but not the professional one [43]: the criteria by
which surgeons judge may be at odds from what the patients expect. In
a self-declarative evaluation by adult patients operated in infancy for
nonsyndromic craniosynostosis, values regarding self-esteem and
depression scores were in the normal range; these patients satisfied

themselves with all the imperfections of surgical techniques from a past
era, except asymmetry of facial features [44]. A blinded evaluation of
“attractiveness” by laypersons confirmed the negative impact of
craniofacial asymmetry [45]; the method in this study, enrolling as
evaluators independent female professionals of a daycare center, is
probably a step in the right direction. All these subjective evaluations
would also be more in line with the patients’ expectations, with the
input of patients associations.
Multiple efforts have been devoted recently to the creation of pre
and postoperative quantitative evaluation scales of the deformity,
much-needed tools if we want to scale postoperative results, and
compare one technique with another. The Rotterdam team has
proposed a score for scaphocephaly, summing semi-quantitative
subscores in the same spirit as the long-established Glasgow Coma
Scale [39, 46]. The evaluation by an independent panel is necessarily
based on documents, and 2D pictures are obviously misleading; for this
reason, 3D photogrammetry is a promising tool [47]. We hope that in a
near future, a consensus will emerge on quantitative morphological
scales adapted to each of the different craniosynostoses.

52 6 Clinical Outcome
52 6 1 Mortality
Overall mortality is very low in craniosynostoses, and it affects almost
exclusively syndromic cases [48]. Already from birth, some of these
patients are beyond surgical resources, and they die because of
breathing and feeding difficulties, and also possibly because of
associated tonsillar herniation. Intraoperative mortality is poorly
documented in literature, and mostly caused by uncontrolled bleeding;
this outcome, although hopefully exceptional, cannot be dismissed.

52 6 2 Development
What is the real influence of cerebral compression on development? As
mentioned above, the relation between intracranial volume and brain
compression is not linear. Furthermore, intracranial hypertension
occurs most regularly in multisuture synostoses, which have almost
always a genetic background, so that the two factors cannot be

separated. The correlation between developmental outcome and the
age at surgery might be an indication of the developmental impact of
brain compression [10, 49], but other factors, like a syndromic context,
or a lack of parental motivation for surgery are confusing factors [11].
The impact of focal cerebral compression on development is also
elusive. The Leeds group found a discrepancy between verbal and
performance IQ (VIQ PIQ) in unisutural craniosynostoses [50], which
they ascribed to parietal compression, and which could be reversed by
early surgery [49]. On the other hand, other researchers found no
correlation between the severity of deformity and cerebral
compression in metopic synostosis [8]. Shimoji found even paradoxical
results, development being more impaired in milder forms of metopic
synostosis [51]; this might suggest different referral patterns, and
confirms that the importance of trigonocephalic deformation plays a
secondary role, if any role at all in the patient’s development. Overall,
these studies suggest that the developmental impact of each type of
synostosis is a specific problem.

52 6 3 Influence of the Syndromic Context
In syndromic craniosynostoses, gene or chromosomal disorders as well
as environmental factors causing the synostosis can have a marked
impact on development. In a previous, unpublished series of 188 cases
of metopic synostosis operated over 20 years, the only significant and
independent variable impacting negatively the development was
syndromic context, which was identified in 31%. In FGFR3 mutation,
experimental models in mice have shown that a developmental impact
existed irrespective of the presence or absence of synostosis, and could
be salvaged by targeted therapy by high-affinity FGFR tyrosine kinase
inhibitor BGJ398 [52]. This suggests that the mutation affects brain
function directly, and opens exciting new treatment perspectives.
In addition, comorbidities and complications of many syndromic
craniosynostoses are susceptible to impact on psychomotor and
cognitive development [11]. Tonsillar herniation can cause sleep
apneas, predominantly central [53], which can combine with
obstructive apneas caused by midface retrusion, compromising wake
periods and hindering learning. Hand and foot malformations in Apert
syndrome require early management in order to allow psychomotor

development [54]. Optic nerve atrophy caused by raised ICP, found in
12.3% of syndromic craniosynostoses, affects predominantly FGFRrelated diseases [55], and deafness associated with Muenke syndrome,
or resulting from tubal dysfunction in faciostenoses [56], can also both
impair learning. In addition, careful brain imaging can disclose
alterations of the cerebellar vermis and corpus callosum, which can be
the consequence of deformation as well as associated malformations,
and can impact on the child’s development [57].

52 7 The Operative Decision and the Informed
Consent
The decision to operate is taken jointly by the surgeon and the child’s
parents, based on the expected positive and adverse effects of surgery.
The aims of surgery must therefore be clearly defined, and the potential
complications well known by the surgeon and exposed to the parents.
As mentioned above, much uncertainty surrounds the natural history of
unoperated craniosynostoses, while many unknowns lay in the future
after surgery, especially in syndromic cases. Unlike in multisuture
synostoses, for which consent for surgery is comparatively
straightforward, the aim of surgery for unisutural craniosynostosis is in
a large part morphological. In that regard, the treatment can be seen as
morphological surgery with a risk of severe morbidity and even
mortality; few other fields of cranial surgery have such potential
benefit-risk imbalance. The expected improvement of morphological
appearance and better conformity with the social norm, as well as the
potentially traumatic change of their child’s facial features contribute to
make the decision to operate an agonizing process for the parents.
Although emotions are the substance of which we are made, and
society is the medium in which we live, surgeons are often poorly
trained in psychology and sociology, often wrongly dismissed as “soft
sciences.” In addition, their position as professionals, which requires
objectivity, sometimes hinders a more heartfelt approach. In this regard
also, patients associations can be a precious resource for these parents,
helping them to cope with the mixed feeling and stress associated with
decision-making.

52 8 The Future
The invasiveness of classical craniofacial surgery and the potentially
high morbidity prompted the development of less invasive techniques
and the boom of endoscopic surgery for craniosynostoses. However, the
abundant literature published on these techniques appears to focus
almost exclusively on easily measured outcome variables, such as
transfusion rate and duration of hospital stay, with no indication on the
long-term morphological results.
This points to the need for a consensual quantitative morphological
rating based on objective criteria, which would allow to compare the
patients pre and postoperatively, and one technique with another. A
morphological scoring proposed for scaphocephaly allows the
comparison of techniques [39, 43], and other scales are in
development.
In order to weight the other pan of the scale, we also need a
quantitative grading of complications. A classification of complications,
sorted by their timing relative to operation, and their consequences for
the patient, was proposed by the team in Leeds [58], and should
certainly be a source of inspiration.
In order to be meaningful, the two quantitative scales, results and
complications, should not be simple lists of items, but require a
ponderation of variables. In that regard, direct interview or
collaboration of the patients themselves is invaluable to identify what
really matters to them [44]; and here again, the input of patients
associations would be a precious help.

53 Quality of Life Metrics in
Craniosynostosis: A Guide for Surgeons
and Healthcare Practitioners
Nebras M. Warsi1, 2 , Johanna N. Riesel3 and Abhaya V. Kulkarni1, 2
(1) Division of Neurosurgery, Hospital for Sick Children, Toronto, ON,
Canada
(2) Division of Neurosurgery, Department of Surgery, University of
Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada
(3) Division of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, Hospital for Sick
Children, Toronto, ON, Canada

Nebras M Warsi
Email: nebras.warsi@mail.utoronto.ca
Johanna N Riesel
Email: johanna.riesel@sickkids.ca
Abhaya V Kulkarni (Corresponding author)
Email: abhaya.kulkarni@sickkids.ca
Keywords Craniosynostosis – Craniofacial – Craniofacial surgery –
Quality of life – QoL

53 1 Introduction
A diagnosis of craniosynostosis can carry profound implications for
patients, caregivers, and their families [1]. Commonly, surgeons are not
only tasked with operative management, but also with providing

guidance throughout the challenging decision-making process
associated with these complex craniofacial disorders. Traditionally,
outcomes have been indexed by surgical variables such as cephalic
index, postoperative appearance, operative time, intraoperative blood
loss, and overall complication rates [2, 3]. However, a growing body of
evidence suggests that parents, caregivers, and—as they grow older—
patients themselves, have significant anxiety regarding and limitations
related to a broad range of health metrics including cosmesis, selfimage, societal integration, neurocognitive outcomes, and psychosocial
health [1, 4–6].
Quality of life (QoL), defined as the perception of the patient’s
position in life in the context of their goals and expectations, is an
overarching measure that may be used to index these key patient and
parental variables [5]. QoL analyses in this population are complex:
significant heterogeneity exists between outcomes for syndromic and
nonsyndromic diagnoses, and further prognostic challenges arise due
to the presence of comorbid deficits, baseline functional status of the
child, and operative approaches chosen. Specific to paediatric studies,
another question pertains to the relative emphasis of parental reports
versus those obtained from children themselves. Given that most
patients undergo surgery in infancy, if children are to be interviewed
for QoL outcomes, the optimal age(s) to do so are unclear. Across
paediatric QoL studies, parental- and child-reported measures have
been shown to differ, and children’s own reports and priorities may
shift as they enter schooling and adolescence [7, 8].
The present chapter serves as a guide for surgeons and other
healthcare practitioners to navigate a variety of QoL issues as they
relate to craniosynostosis. We begin with an overview of commonly
employed QoL metrics in craniosynostosis and then examine specific
issues pertaining to syndromic and nonsyndromic forms of this
disorder. Through this analysis, readers will be presented with a
detailed examination of patient and caregiver-level concerns that may
be employed to better counsel families and develop mutual surgical
goals and expected outcomes.

53 1 1 Pearls

In addition to commonly discussed surgical metrics, QoL outcomes
represent key components of preoperative counseling discussions.
Significant variation exists in expected QoL with and without
intervention across the spectrum of craniosynostosis pathology.
While novel surgical techniques are increasingly employed to treat
craniosynostosis, examination of associated QoL benefits has been
limited. As such, many open questions remain, and further research
is needed in this area.

53 2 Quality of Life Measures in
Craniosynostosis
A variety of qualitative, quantitative, and combined measures have
been employed to index QoL in craniosynostosis. Among these metrics,
the most general form of QoL analysis has been open-ended interview
of parents and older patients to discuss self-perceptions of function,
psychosocial wellbeing, developmental progress, and overall disease
impact [6, 9]. However, purely qualitative assessments provide limited
ability to directly compare responses between subjects and across
studies. Objective clinical scales utilized include the Short-Form Health
Survey 36-Item (SF-36) [10], Glasgow Children’s Benefit Inventory
(GCBI), World Health Organization Quality of Life Scale (WHOQoL) [11,
12], Who Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule
(WHODAS) [13], Health Utility Index Mark 3 (HUI-3) [14], Infant
Toddler Quality of life Questionnaire (ITQoL) [10], Child Health
Questionnaire Parental Form 50 and Child Form 87 (CHD-PF50/CF87)
[10], TNO-AZL Questionnaire for Children’s Quality of Life (TACQoL)
[15], and the Child Behaviour Checklist (CBCL) [15, 16]. Given the
prevalence of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in syndromic patients, the
OSA-18 is a targeted assessment of physical, cognitive, and sleep
disturbances related to sleep apnea [17]. More recently, the FACE-Q
craniofacial module has been developed to capture aesthetic and
functional outcomes, adverse events, and health-related QoL items
specific to paediatric craniofacial disorders including craniosynostosis
[18]. Notably, of all scales examined, the FACE-Q is unique in assessing

cosmetic outcomes explicitly. Table 53.1 provides an overview of the
different clinical factors encompassed by these QoL assessment tools.
