53 3 Nonsyndromic Craniosynostosis
Nonsyndromic synostosis commonly affects a single suture and is not
associated with significant medical comorbidities or extracranial
deformations. In rare instances, multisuture craniosynostosis can be
seen without identifiable affiliated syndrome, but for the purposes of
this chapter, “single suture craniosynostosis” will be synonymous with
“non-syndromic craniosynostosis.” In cases of nonsyndromic
craniosynostosis, the sagittal suture is most commonly affected [4]. In
the absence of elevated intracranial pressure, single suture
craniosynostosis has historically been considered purely cosmetic;
however, the recent literature suggests that subtle neurocognitive and
QoL impairments may also exist within these populations [15, 19, 20].
In comparison with syndromic craniosynostosis, QoL impairments in
nonsyndromic cases are more subtle, and there is substantially less
agreement between studies as to overall QoL across different metrics.
Subtle neurocognitive impairment has primarily been observed in
patients with isolated sagittal synostosis. This is likely due to the

relative prevalence of the condition as compared to synostosis of the
other cranial sutures. Boltshauser et al. reported on 30 patients with
untreated isolated sagittal synostosis at an average age of 9.25 years
[15]. Interestingly, the majority of patients and parents were pleased
with their current situation and rated the deformity as significantly less
evident than in infancy. TACQoL assessments were also within normal
range. However, patients reported a higher incidence of bullying and
their scores in attention and memory were significantly lower than in
healthy controls.
The data regarding the impact of surgical intervention are mixed. In
comparison to healthy controls, Cloonan et al. found that, at age 5,
parental reports of school functioning and social QoL were lower in
children treated for single and multisuture nonsyndromic
craniosynostosis as compared to healthy controls [16]. However, in
long-term follow-up of patients with a mean age of 23 years, Mazzafero
et al. found that treated patients report higher WHOQoL scores than
normative populations; however, a risk of bias does exist as this study
utilized mail-in questionnaires [11]. Forms were completed by 32/52
contacted patients, suggesting that perhaps those patients who were
more satisfied with their QoL and functioning better may have been
more likely to participate in the study. One additional study examined
patients treated for isolated sagittal synostosis and reported no
difference in education, employment, and psychosocial measures as
compared to healthy controls [21]. Sader et al. reported a North
American comparative study of operative versus conservative
management for single-suture disease [22]. When adjusting for disease
severity and patient age, no significant differences in the physical,
psychosocial, and total QoL domains were found between the treated
and untreated groups. While this study raises critical questions with
regard to the patient and caregiver-level benefits of craniofacial
intervention, the results must be interpreted with caution as the
treated group was comprised of much younger patients with a higher
severity of their deformity. Furthermore, head shape “severity” was
subjectively reported in a retrospective fashion, which makes this value
difficult to interpret. Additionally, there are currently no validated
methods for accurately rating head shape severity, and as such, there
are little data to correlate head shape severity with neurocognitive or

operative outcomes. Taken together, the existing literature suggests
that careful patient selection and identification of specific patient and
caregiver goals as related to QoL should form a core component of
presurgical consultation.
A single study examined the influence of surgical timing and
technique on outcomes in non-syndromic synostosis [23]. Shavlokhova
et al. reported that earlier surgical intervention is associated with
better familial function, higher self-esteem, and school performance.
The amount of intraoperative transfusion was also associated with
lower familial and school domain scores, perhaps associated with more
complex surgery and longer hospital stay, though these data were not
directly reported. No difference between the type of surgical technique
was reported in terms of QoL outcomes.
Regarding open versus endoscopic strip craniectomy (ESC) across
different forms of single suture synostosis, a pair of systematic reviews
have demonstrated lower intraoperative blood loss, operative time, and
surgical stay in association with endoscopic surgery [2, 3]. However, no
studies to date have examined QoL outcomes associated with this
technique. Based on Shavlokhova et al.’s results, it is possible that
reduced intraoperative transfusion rates and shorter hospital stays
associated with endoscopic surgery may correlate with improved QoL;
however, this will need to be formally examined and at present remains
an open question. Furthermore, the required orthotic helmeting
following the ESC may be a burden to families, but this has also not yet
been studied. Additional novel treatments, such as distraction and
spring-mediated distraction have not yet been assessed in the QoL
literature.

53 4 Syndromic Craniosynostosis
Syndromic forms of craniosynostosis generally represent complex
multisuture deformities often in combination with developmental,
behavioural, and systemic medical disorders [4]. Apert, Crouzon,
Pfeiffer, Muenke, and Saethre-Chotzen syndromes represent the most
common paediatric craniofacial syndromes associated with
craniosynostosis [24]. Worldwide, approximately 12–31% of total cases
of craniosynostosis are associated with a syndromic diagnosis [25–28].

Significant contributors to poor QoL in these populations include the
need for multistage craniofacial procedures, surgical and nonsurgical
management of comorbid conditions, associated physical deformities,
and comorbid neuropsychological impairments [4, 6]. It is important to
note that there is variability in the comorbidities seen in syndromic
cases of craniosynostosis. For example, patients with Crouzon
syndrome often have normal intelligence levels, and patients with
Pfeiffer syndrome have a broad range of associated comorbidities
ranging from mild to severely debilitating. The following QoL data
should be read with this variability in mind.
Psychosocial impairments in syndromic craniosynostosis are
commonly reported in the literature. Patients show lower self-esteem
and suffer from significantly higher rates of abuse, bullying, anxiety, and
depression as compared to normative populations [6]. Psychosocial
stressors such as these are also shown to worsen with adolescence as
patients gradually became more aware of their condition and
internalize negative body image perceptions [6, 10]. Overall social
integration, familial cohesion, and parental stress as indexed by the SF36, ITQoL, and CHD-CF87 rate significantly worse for syndromic
patients as compared to healthy controls [10, 29]. Subjective interviews
of adults living with Apert and Crouzon syndromes also demonstrate
higher proportions of patients continuing to live with parents and
requiring daily assistance than in the general population [13, 30].
Surgical management, at least for Apert syndrome, is associated with
partial improvement in the majority of psychosocial metrics [9].
Amongst these patients, significant impairments are also seen in the
domains of physical health and educational/professional attainment.
Anomalies most strongly implicated with functional limitations include
complex syndactyly, visual and/or speech impairment, cognitive
deficits, and behavioural issues [10]. Patients with Apert syndrome in
particular report increased incidence of daily pain limiting physical
function, mostly in the hands [10]. In comparison to these patients,
those with Crouzon syndrome demonstrate significantly higher
WHOQoL scores in measures of physical function, though still below
those of the general population [31]. In both Apert and Crouzon
patients, greater need for daily assistance and higher disability burden

were most often cited as reasons for poorer educational and
professional attainment [29, 30, 32].
OSA, thought to be secondary to midface hypoplasia and pharyngeal
collapse, has been observed in up to 75% of syndromic patients [33].
Midface hypoplasia is due to skull base fusion commonly seen in
patients with syndromic craniosynostosis. Bannink et al. found that the
presence and severity of OSA serve as independent predictors of QoL in
these populations [17]. Specifically, they found that OSA-18 scores for
sleep disturbance, physical suffering, and caregiver concerns were
significantly higher in craniosynostosis groups as compared to healthy
controls, and correlated with OSA severity [17]. Early intervention is
critical to mitigate the downstream sequelae that result from
unmanaged OSA. A variety of treatment modalities may be appropriate
based on the patient’s phenotypic expression of midface hypoplasia and
airway collapse, including, but not limited to adenoidectomy,
continuous positive airway pressure, nasopharyngeal tubes or airways
(NPT or NPA), and tracheostomy. One retrospective study by Randhawa
et al. found long-term nasopharyngeal airway (NPA) placement was
associated with clinically significant improvements in OSA-18 scores as
well as learning, vitality, and physicals measures across the GCBI [34].
This treatment was also subjectively preferred to tracheostomy based
on parental interviews; however, the NPA may not be sufficient in all
patient populations. Given that ongoing OSA is linked with hypoxiainduced cognitive and behavioural deficits, targeted treatments for
patients suffering from OSA is critical. Based on Randhawa et al. s
results [34], long-term NPA may serve as an effective treatment for
certain patients with this condition with demonstrated improvements
to QoL, though no direct comparisons between NPA and standard
tracheostomy have been performed to date.

53 5 Conclusions
Craniosynostosis is associated with diminished QoL as reported by
parents, caregivers, and patients. While QoL impairments in
nonsyndromic forms of craniosynostosis are less severe in comparison
to syndromic diagnoses, they remain common and relate
predominantly to self-esteem, perceived appearance by peers, and mild

neurocognitive deficits. In contrast, patients with syndromic synostosis
commonly present with associated deformities and comorbidities and
demonstrate significant impairment in psychosocial, physical,
educational, and professional domains of life, even after surgical
intervention (though the latter can improve certain domains of QoL).
Surgical treatment for both syndromic and nonsyndromic
malformations is associated with improved QoL, as is treatment of
comorbid OSA in syndromic synostoses. Surgeons and practitioners
should be aware of these salient QoL metrics such that they may guide
patients and families through informed decision-making and goal
setting regarding the treatment of children with craniosynostosis.

54 Long Follow-Up Results in
Craniosynostoses
Niina Salokorpi1, 2 and Willy Serlo3, 4
(1) Research Unit of Clinical Medicine, Oulu University Hospital and
University of Oulu, Oulu, Finland
(2) Medical Research Center Oulu (MRC Oulu), University of Oulu and

Niina Salokorpi
Email: niina.salokorpi@oulu.fi
Willy Serlo (Corresponding author)
Email: willy.serlo@oulu.fi
Keywords Craniosynostoses – Surgery – Outcome – Follow-up studies
The main goal of any health care intervention is to cure the patients,
relieve symptoms, prolong survival, and improve well-being along with
the quality of life (QoL) of the patient. Quality of life includes aspects
such as life satisfaction, wealth, levels of safety and freedom, health
perceptions and physical, psychological, social, and cognitive well-being
[1, 2].
These aspects should be held in mind when speaking about the
results of any treatment, not only the craniosynostosis surgery. As

described in previous chapters, the craniosynostosis include a wide
spectrum of pathologies, some of which have mainly aesthetical
influence while others additionally cause permanent problems in
physical health and cognitive performance levels.
Historically, the success of the craniosynostosis surgery has been
evaluated by measurable objective outcome parameters such as
anatomical measurements including cranial index (CI) and intracranial
volume (ICV). Additionally, evaluation of postoperative complications,
morbidity, mortality, and the necessity for reoperations were used [3–
8]. These, clinically very relevant measurements, reflect well the
surgeons’ opinions about the outcome. However, this does not reflect
what the patients themselves consider important as an assessment of
the outcome. This question becomes even more complicated when
taking into account that while craniosynostosis is treated in early
childhood, the patient’s own opinion about the outcome of the
treatment could be asked only many years later. The size and shape of
the skull and face develops until adulthood. Craniocerebral
disproportion and restrictions of the airways may cause delayed
morbidity. Thus, conclusions of the long-term outcome should not be
made before the growth of the patient is complete.
When evaluating the outcome at a certain age, one should keep in
mind that the patient has lived all their life so far with that residual
pathology. Nobody can say afterwards, if the patient’s life would have
been different if a different treatment decision would have been made
earlier since the particular patient has experience only of living with
this particular appearance. This aspect could be to some extent
surpassed by comparing some objective measurements and factors
between patients and controls. This could include, for example,
comparing self-esteem, depression score, QoL, satisfaction with own
appearance, and general physical health issues.
Depending on the type of craniosynostosis, the patients may have
only aesthetical problems, but also physical, mental, or developmental
disabilities due to the primary condition [9–11].
The primary goals of the surgery can differ and thus can change
what is accepted as a good outcome. In some cases, the primary goal is
normalization of the patient’s craniofacial appearance. Thus, when
evaluating the outcome, the main stress is on the aesthetics. In patients

who exhibit, for example, an increase in ICP, it could be considered that
a poorer aesthetic outcome is acceptable, since the main goal of the
treatment is to save the patient’s life and allow the brain to grow. In
such situations, one must pose the question: “I saved the patient but is
this enough?” Does the surgery prevent neurocognitive deficits and
improve QoL? What is the impact of the surgery itself on the patient’s
QoL and cognition?
Any craniosynostosis surgery aims to normalize patients’
appearance [12]. Despite the treatment, the facial appearance of
craniosynostosis patients can remain different from what we assume to
be “normal,” resembling what is expected, and preferably aesthetically
pleasing. This can negatively influence a person’s self-esteem, body
image, social relationships, and behavior later in life [6, 13–17]. Having
a residual dysmorphic face and head shape can attract unfavorable
attention and possibly even cause rejection from strangers and peers.
This may have a secondary psychosocial effect by negatively influencing
the patients’ social behavior and cause difficulties in educational
environments and even poor school performance [18]. Thus, patients
encounter psychological difficulties and must adapt to the demands of
their environment in many aspects including, behavior, psychological
well-being, social experiences, and satisfaction with appearance [15].
Thus, evaluation of long-term follow-up should be done from the
surgeons and patients’ points of view, preferably when patients have
reached adulthood. Such evaluation should be broad, covering the
earlier mentioned aspects.
Historically, several different simplified classifications for the
assessment of the results of craniosynostoses treatment have been
proposed. Whitaker in 1987 proposed a IV category scale for
assessment according to the need for additional surgery [19]. This
classification has been widely used in many studies [6, 8, 20, 21]. Sloan
et al. proposed classification of the surgical results into seven classes
[22], and Aryan et al. proposed in 2005 a simplified version of Sloan’s
classification [23]. The latter has four categories, where only one
category infers the need for operative corrections, while the other three
categories correspond to less severe degrees of deformity. These
classifications have their role, since they allow the evaluation of the

aesthetical outcome to some extent based on the surgeon’s opinion
retrospectively from usually rather reticent medical records [24, 25].
Whilst these evaluation scales are easy to use, they are very limited.
More sophisticated methods are required.
One of the first attempts to determine a correlation between
appearance and QoL after craniosynostosis surgery, thus evaluating the
results of the surgery from the patient’s point of view, was published by
Lloyd et al. in 2016 [21]. However, the facial aesthetics were evaluated
using the Whitaker classification, mentioned earlier. Another attempt
was made by Kluba and associates, who asked parents how satisfied
they were with the results of treatment using a 5-point rating scale.
They found that parents were mainly satisfied with the surgical results
and were stricter in their evaluation when compared to surgeons [26].
Joly and associates evaluated the results after suturectomy for metopic
and coronal synostosis by asking children and parents if the head shape
was normal in their opinion. They also used the Whitaker scale to
evaluate the results. In this study, the children’s mean age at the time of
evaluation was 14 years; thus, the follow-up was reasonably long, and
children were old enough to express their reliable opinion.
Interestingly, while surgeons were satisfied only with three patients’
appearances out of 17, the patients themselves found their head and
facial shape to be normal in 11 out of 17 cases [6]. In this study, there is
a discrepancy between the surgeons’ and patients’ opinions about
appearance, confirming the necessity for paying attention to what
matters to patients.
One option to standardize aesthetic evaluations is by using
independent third person panels. In orthodontics, there are numerous
studies on patients’ self-satisfaction with pre- and postoperative
aesthesis, as well as third person quantitative evaluation of aesthetic
outcome [27, 28]. When studying persons treated for severe
malocclusions, it was found that the QoL and self-perceived aesthetic
satisfaction improve extensively after treatment [27]. These variables
may be determinants of the outcomes among craniosynostoses
patients, as well.
The studies by Metzler and Bendon evaluated surgical results from
photographs; however, the grading was concentrated on deformity and
evaluation of the necessity for reoperations [29, 30].

During the last few years, a few studies were published evaluating
the impact of craniosynostosis on health-related quality of life (HRQoL)
[21, 31, 32]. The latest study on QoL in craniosynostosis patients was
published by Shavlokhova in 2021 and carried out on adolescents
operated on due to nonsyndromic craniosynostoses in infancy. They
found no QoL limitations in later life when compared to the average
population [33].
In previous studies, it was found that the overall quality of life is
lower than average in patients with syndromic and complex
craniosynostosis [31, 32].
In a study of 28 adults with Apert syndrome, it was found that the
patients managed relatively well in terms of education and
employment, although the highest level of education was lower than
with controls. The social relations (marriage, number of friends) of
these patients appeared to require improvement [11]. More optimistic
results were reported by Allam and associates who followed up eight
Apert syndrome patients for over 15 years and assessed their social
and educational progress. It was demonstrated that these patients can
function quite well in society, can achieve a high level of education, hold
full-time employment, and integrate well socially [10].
From a clinical viewpoint, surgically treated sagittal
craniosynostosis patients are expected to have a minimal risk of late
sequelae. Clinical follow-up is usually continued no later than school
age. There are several studies suggesting single suture
craniosynostoses are associated with mild to moderate developmental
and educational difficulties which become apparent at school age [34–
36]. However, patients with sagittal synostosis have the best
performance in neuropsychological tests [35].
The authors shed some light on this topic by carrying out a study
evaluating adult patients treated for sagittal synostosis with an average
follow-up time of 26.5 years (range 17–37) and comparison with age
and gender matched controls [37]. Patients filled in extensive
questionnaires and were asked to evaluate their own satisfaction on the
Visual Analogue Scale (VAS). Patients and controls standardized
photographs were evaluated by panels. The results were very
encouraging, since it appeared that patients managed as well in adult
life as controls.

The study revealed that the patients were equally satisfied with
their appearance as were controls. Lay and dentists panels found the
patients’ appearance to be slightly less attractive than controls, but the
difference was less than 10% on a 100 mm VAS. The socioeconomic
situation and general health of patients equaled that of controls. Being
operated on for sagittal craniosynostosis did not influence a patient’s
education level, employment status or finding a life partner [37].
Interestingly there was no significant difference between the
patients and controls complaints regarding their facial appearance. In
both groups, the most common subjects to complain about were teeth,
shape of head, or face. The majority of patients’ dissatisfaction with
their appearance was not related to the craniosynostosis itself [37, 38].
The authors attempted to find parameters from 3D images that
would correlate with subjective satisfaction with their own appearance
in adult metopic and sagittal craniosynostosis patients operated on in
early childhood. Though some difference was found between patients
and controls in 3D parameters, there was no significant correlation
between these findings and satisfaction with own appearance [39].
While exhibiting the correct direction, still neither of these studies
sufficiently reflects the results of the surgery from the patient-oriented
point of view. Different scales and questions are used in each study. The
heterogeneity of the deformities, the wide variety of operative
techniques and consequently a small number of patients in each series,
makes the comparison even more obscure.
To allow cross-study comparisons and to facilitate meta-analyses
the outcome measures must be validated and consistent. Core outcome
sets should include data meaningful to both patients and physicians
[40]. This creates a next challenge, since there is a necessity to ensure
accurate reporting of the patients’ subjective experience. Thus, there is
a requirement for structured validated patient-reported outcome
measurement instruments.
Several questions are important for the reliable comparison of
surgical results and should be considered.
First, the preoperative degree of pathology should be documented
properly including systemic findings. Second, surgical techniques have
changed over the decades and perioperative treatment improved
significantly. Thus, patients that have attained adulthood have been

often operated on with methods now abandoned [37, 38]. Additionally,
one should bear in mind that in the pediatric population, the health and
well-being of a child are inseparable from their parents’ well-being [40,
41]. Findings made by Feragen et al. suggest that many parents of
craniosynostosis children experience stressful and potentially
traumatic symptoms due to their child’s complex treatment, which may
in turn affect the family. These adverse experiences could have a
negative effect, and they could additionally serve as a trigger towards
personal growth and positive change [42]. This could include increased
compassion, valuing of close relations, and discovery of new strengths
within oneself or changing life’s perspective [43].
When evaluating long-term follow-up, social and cultural aspects
should be taken into account. Perception of beauty is influenced by the
individual’s geographic, ethnic, cultural, and demographic background.
However, objective measurements remain the foundation for aesthetic
evaluations. Differences in aesthetic preferences can lead to
dissatisfaction with the results. Increasing global environment, role of
social media, cultural differences, and international variability must be
considered when reporting outcomes [44].
When speaking of all these challenges, one should remember that
there is no means of 100% testing which treatment decision was better
after all, since there is no real basis for comparison. The surgery was
done in early childhood, and the patient outcome can be compared to
other patients or normal cohorts. Nobody really knows what a patients’
life would have been if different surgical decision would have been
made.
Since the studies on the previously discussed aspects of long-term
follow-up are so far scarce, with this chapter we pose more questions
than answers. The authors want to initiate discussion on this topic,
stimulating further and more profound research. The clinicians treating
patients daily should regularly have time for reflecting on their own
results and experience and share their thoughts with others.
